Circular Economy Index: Municipalities are becoming more efficient; the next stage of development is a change of the management model  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:48:31 UTC
01:48:31 KST

Municipalities with the highest circularity scores are able to turn individual initiatives into a unified system, but further growth will be determined not only by new solutions, but also by changes in the management model and everyday habits of the public, according to the results of the second Circular Economy Index.
On Wednesday, September 9, the key findings of the second Latvian Circular Economy Index were presented to the public, and the municipalities with the highest results in the index categories - smart resource management, business and economic transformation, skillful management and public involvement - were honored.
The Circular Economy Index, developed by Latvian scientists and measured every other year, was first published in 2024. One of the key findings at the time was that municipalities do not lack individual circular initiatives even without a strategic methodological framework. Realizing that municipalities use the Circular Economy Index as a guide for implementing circularity, the focus was refined in the 2026 measurement, giving greater weight to solutions with structural impact, which make the transition to circular management not only faster but also more purposeful.
“The first index showed where we are on the circular economy map in Latvia. The second already helps to understand which activities have the greatest impact on accelerating the introduction of circularity. Thus, local governments, analyzing these results, can plan where to invest time, funding and human resources for a more meaningful result. The goal is no longer just to count activities, but to understand which of them have a lasting and structural impact,” says Agita Baltbārde, the initiator of the Latvian Circular Economy Index, a Member of the AS CleanR Grupa Board, and the Ambassador of the European Climate Pact in Latvia.
Municipalities are strong in efficiency; next step – a change of the model
"The results of municipalities’ self-assessment show relatively high achievements in the areas of waste sorting infrastructure, digitalization and energy efficiency of buildings. Municipalities are investing in the use of renewable energy sources, building renovation, digital document circulation and solutions that reduce resource consumption," says Dr. oec. Dzintra Atstāja, a professor and leading researcher of the Circular Economy Index.
Circularity requirements are also increasingly used in public procurement, for example by focusing on the durability, repairability and reusability of products.
However, lower self-assessment scores are found in areas that require more significant changes in the business model. This is based on the choice of lease instead of purchase, the circulation of used goods, industrial symbiosis, as well as cooperation in research and innovation.
“The next stage of development is a shift from improving the efficiency of the current economic model to changing the model itself. This means making greater use of leasing, sharing, repair, and resource reuse, as well as systematically promoting innovation and industrial symbiosis. It is precisely in these areas that new business opportunities can also be created,” the researcher emphasizes.
Availability of opportunities does not mean change of habits
The Circular Economy Index consists of two complementary parts: a self-assessment by municipalities and a survey of residents, the integration of which into the Circular Economy Index was consulted by the University of Latvia. The survey of municipalities reflects the established processes, infrastructure, services and support instruments, while the survey of residents shows whether people see, use and consider these solutions necessary.
The results of the survey of residents show that the availability of services typical of the circular economy has remained or increased in many places, while changes in habits are slow. In addition, in some areas, the offer of municipalities and the priorities of residents do not yet match.
“Municipalities can invest in infrastructure, services and various support instruments, but the key question is whether people actually use them. If the offer does not match the needs and motivation of the population, even a good solution can go unused. Therefore, it is more important not only to create opportunities, but to understand how to make them a daily choice for people. At the same time, it is clear that civil society, or non-governmental organizations, can play an important role in developing new habits,” says Dr. sc. soc. Andris Saulītis, senior researcher at the Institute of Philosophy and Sociology at the University of Latvia.
For example, 58% of the surveyed residents believe that local governments should provide more financial support to organizations implementing circular economy initiatives - yet such support is provided in only 24% of cases. Meanwhile, 54% of those surveyed consider support for community cleanups and environmental improvement activities to be necessary, while local government activity in this area stands at 64%, exceeding public expectations.
Although environmental clean-ups are popular, in reality, the involvement of residents in clean-ups is passive - about 70% of respondents did not participate in them or did so very rarely
Methodology puts a greater emphasis on the systemic impact
To maintain data comparability, the 2026 index is based on the previous methodology, while specifying individual issues and their importance in the assessment. This year, more weight is given to systemic solutions with a higher impact on circularity, such as the targeted replacement of fossil energy sources with renewable sources, waste recycling and public involvement.
“Results of the first index revealed an asymmetry between the circular solutions implemented by municipalities and the habits of residents in using them, so this year significant attention was paid to public involvement. Informing is not enough – a change in habits can only be achieved when residents are practically involved and the opportunities created become part of people’s daily lives. That is why this year we also honored municipalities that have achieved the highest scores in individual categories of the index, because their examples show how a systemic approach works in practice,” explains Baltbārde.
Six municipalities in the group of leaders
The results of the Circular Economy Index are presented in two divisions – groups from the waiting to the leaders, as well as categories that reflect the success of municipalities in specific areas.
The groups are formed according to the total number of points: leaders – over 650 points; experts – 550–649 points; practitioners – 450–549 points; conscientious – 350–449 points; waiting – under 350 points
In contrast to 2024, when there were two municipalities in the group of leaders, this year six are ranked in the highest group: Daugavpils City (765), Valmiera Municipality (736), Cēsis Municipality (704), Dienvidkurzeme Municipality (665), Rīga City Municipality (657) and Liepāja City Municipality (654).
Ten municipalities made it to the group of Experts, followed by 16 municipalities ranked as the Practitioners, nine municipalities as the Conscientious, and one municipality was the Waiting.
“The examples of the leader group show that a successful initiative does not guarantee long-term change in itself. It begins at the moment when the solution becomes a permanent practice, is linked to other municipal instruments and can be developed further. Leaders are united not by everyone doing the same thing, but by the ability to make each municipality’s chosen solutions work as a system,” says Dr. oec. Dzintra Atstāja, the leading researcher of the Latvian Circular Economy Index.
Four categories, four leadership emphases
The leaders in the four circularity categories were also honored separately. In smart resource management, the highest score was earned by Liepāja City with 802 points, as it stood out with a wide and interconnected set of solutions that include the use of biomass for heating, solar panels and electric cars, as well as the use of secondary materials and long-lasting procurement.
The leader in business and economic transformation is the Valmiera Municipality with 780 points, as it provides an environment where entrepreneurs can practically implement circular principles: use shared and workshop infrastructure, receive knowledge and support, and build cooperation at the local and even international level.
Valmiera Municipality also earned the highest score (767) in the category of public involvement, putting the emphasis on practical public involvement: workshops, educational programs, a circularity center and other solutions that can be used in everyday life.
Riga City, with 774 points, earned the highest score in skillful management by embedding circular economy principles not only in individual projects but also in a comprehensive circular economy strategy, procurement requirements, sectoral regulations, funding, and other governance instruments.
From measurement to action
The aim of the index is to understand as precisely as possible in which direction it is possible to grow and how to achieve the best result and the most positive impact with the available resources. At the same time, it helps municipalities understand what investments can achieve the highest efficiency in circularity, as well as assess resident’s reaction to and involvement in municipal initiatives.
"The results of this year mark a five-step development path. First, identify existing activities and resource flows. Second, connect energy, mobility, waste, procurement and business solutions. Third, strengthen circularity principles in strategies, regulations and financing. Fourth, involve administration, capital companies, entrepreneurs, science, communities and residents. Fifth, turn successful pilot projects into permanent services and municipal practices. The next step is not more individual projects, but more connected solutions," says Atstāja.
The full results of the Circular Economy Index will soon be available on the website cleanrgrupa.lv.
About the Circular Economy Index
The Latvian Circular Economy Index is the first science-based tool in Latvia that allows to assess the circularity of municipalities and compare their performance. The first measurement was carried out in 2024. In 2026 it was compiled for the second time. The index combines two perspectives – self-assessment of municipalities and assessment of residents – analyzing 4 areas: smart resource management, transformation of business and economy, public involvement and skillful management. This year's index included all 42 Latvian municipalities, while 3,108 respondents participated in the representative survey of residents.
About CleanR Grupa:
JSC CleanR Grupa operates Latvia’s leading environmental services companies. The Group includes household waste management company CleanR, industrial and construction waste management company CleanR Verso, hazardous and medical waste management company Lautus, waste processing company CleanR Industry, producer responsibility system provider Zaļā josta, cleaning services provider Vizii, urban environment manager Vizii Urban, and regional environmental maintenance providers KOM-Auto and Tranzīts L.
CleanR Grupa provides services to more than 500,000 people in Latvia on a daily basis. The company is characterized by the highest level of digitization in the environmental services industry, high standards of customer service, as well as leadership in sustainability and circularity. JSC CleanR Grupa is a 100% Latvian-capital company, whose founder and chairman of the supervisory board is Guntars Kokorevičs.

MKM: Foreign demand is the main driver of tourism growth  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:48:30 UTC
01:48:30 KST

TALLINN - July's accommodation statistics confirm the trend of the first half of the year, with Estonia's tourism growth being driven primarily by foreign demand, according to Aleksandr Michelson, a tourism advisor at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM).
Estonia's accommodation market continued to grow in July. According to Statistics Estonia, guests spent 964,200 nights in accommodation establishments with at least five bed places, a 3.5 percent increase compared to the previous year. In total for the first seven months, just over 4 million overnight stays were recorded in Estonia, up nearly 5 percent from the same period last year, the ministry announced.
In July, the growth was driven almost entirely by foreign tourists. The number of their overnight stays increased by 5.9 percent year-on-year to 561,700, while the 402,400 overnight stays by Estonian residents remained essentially at the previous year's level with a 0.2 percent increase. Foreign tourists accounted for 58 percent of all accommodation nights in July.
"July is one of the most important months for Estonian tourism, and a nearly 6 percent increase in overnight stays by foreign tourists is a strong result. It is positive that in addition to Finland, demand grew from several other significant European markets, including Poland, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Italy, and the Netherlands. At the same time, we see that the growth is currently very heavily concentrated in Tallinn, and the regional picture is more uneven," Michelson said.
Tallinn was the clear driver of growth in July. The capital recorded 455,000 overnight stays, 12 percent more than a year ago, accounting for 47 percent of all accommodation nights in Estonia. There were 373,400 overnight stays by foreign tourists in Tallinn, a 13 percent increase from the previous year, and 81,700 stays by Estonian residents, up 6 percent. Two-thirds of all overnight stays by foreign visitors in Estonia during July were in Tallinn.
A comparison of absolute numbers also highlights Tallinn's significance. While Estonia as a whole added 32,200 accommodation nights year-on-year, Tallinn alone added 47,800. This implies that outside of Tallinn, the total number of overnight stays actually decreased by nearly 3 percent. The number of nights spent by foreign tourists outside the capital fell by 6 percent, and by domestic residents by 1 percent, compared to a year ago.
By region, the number of overnight stays saw the fastest growth in Valga County, with 37,000 stays in July, a 13 percent increase from the previous year. The number of stays grew by 11 percent in Harju County and 3.8 percent in Tartu County. In Harju County, excluding Tallinn, the growth was 3.6 percent, while in the city of Tartu, it was 5.2 percent.
However, in several key summer destinations, July's results were lower than the previous year. Parnu County recorded 122,900 overnight stays, a 10 percent decrease, with the city of Parnu itself seeing a 12 percent drop. Declines were also seen in Laane County (5.4 percent), Viljandi County (3 percent), and Saare County (1 percent). In Ida-Viru and Voru counties, the number of overnight stays remained essentially unchanged from the previous year.
Among foreign markets, Finland held a firm first place. In July, Finnish tourists spent 231,000 nights in Estonian accommodation establishments with at least five bed places, a 5 percent increase from the previous year. They accounted for 41 percent of all overnight stays by foreign visitors. The year-on-year increase from Finland was over 11,000 overnight stays, representing more than a third of the total growth in foreign demand.
Several other European markets demonstrated even faster growth. Overnight stays by Polish tourists increased by 28 percent, Norwegian tourists by 24 percent, British tourists by 23 percent, Dutch tourists by 20 percent, and both Italian and Swedish tourists by 17 percent.
However, growth was not consistent across all major foreign markets. Overnight stays by German tourists decreased by 2 percent and by Latvian tourists by 0.7 percent compared to the previous year. The number of stays by Lithuanian tourists fell by 12 percent, and by tourists from the United States by 16 percent. Consequently, the growth in foreign demand in July was primarily driven by Finland and several other fast-growing European markets.
The increased demand in July led to higher occupancy rates for accommodations. While Estonia had 1 percent more bed places and 0.6 percent more rooms available than the previous year, demand outpaced supply. The bed-place occupancy rate rose from 50 to 51 percent, and the room occupancy rate from 60 to 61 percent. The changes were more pronounced in Tallinn, where the number of bed places and rooms increased by 6.2 percent and 6.4 percent, respectively, while overnight stays jumped by 12 percent. Consequently, the bed-place occupancy rate in the capital climbed from 65 to 69 percent, and the room occupancy rate from 77 to 80 percent.
The average cost of an overnight stay per person in Estonia decreased from 56 to 53 euros, and in Tallinn from 65 to 56 euros. This price comparison is affected by the large number of major concerts last year, which drove up accommodation demand and prices in July 2025, especially in Tallinn. As a result, while occupancy rates were higher this year, the average price remained below the exceptionally high level of the previous year.

Morocco election campaign begins as 27 parties vie for power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:48:28 UTC
01:48:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco election campaign begins as 27 parties vie for power
Morocco's official election campaign kicked off on Thursday, with 27 political parties competing for 395 seats in the House of Representatives ahead of a nationwide vote later this month.
The campaign, which began on 10 September, will run until midnight on 22 September, with Moroccans heading to the polls the following day to elect members of the lower house of parliament.
The election comes five years after the 2021 vote dramatically reshaped Morocco's political landscape, propelling the National Rally of Independents (RNI) into first place and dealing a crushing defeat to the Justice and Development Party (PJD), which had led the government for a decade.
The RNI went on to form a governing coalition with the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and the Istiqlal Party.
Those three parties are once again among the major forces competing in the election, alongside the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP), the Popular Movement, the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), the Constitutional Union and the PJD.
The campaign is expected to focus heavily on domestic concerns, including employment, education, healthcare and purchasing power, as parties seek to win over voters amid economic and social pressures.
Authorities have introduced regulations governing campaigning, including rules on electoral spending, advertising, the use of public spaces and equal opportunities between candidates.
The 2026 election rules also address campaigning on social media and digital platforms, including the use of artificial intelligence and the dissemination of misleading or manipulated AI-generated content.
How does Morocco's election work?
Morocco has a bicameral parliament made up of the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors, but the September election concerns only the 395-seat House of Representatives.
Of those seats, 305 are contested through local electoral constituencies, while the remaining 90 are allocated through regional lists.
Under changes introduced for the 2026 election, the regional lists are exclusively made up of female candidates, strengthening women's representation in the lower house.
Moroccans do not directly elect their prime minister, officially known as the head of government.
Instead, voters elect members of parliament through a proportional representation system based on party lists.
A party would need 198 of the House's 395 seats to secure an outright majority, something that is difficult under Morocco's fragmented multi-party electoral system.
Under Article 47 of Morocco's constitution, King Mohammed VI appoints the head of government from the political party that finishes first in elections to the House of Representatives.
If the winning party falls short of the 198 seats needed for a majority, it must negotiate with other parties to form a governing coalition capable of securing parliamentary support.
The proposed government must then present its programme to parliament and win the confidence of an absolute majority of the House of Representatives, or at least 198 votes.
Following the 2021 election, the RNI emerged as the largest party with 102 seats and subsequently formed a coalition with PAM and Istiqlal.
Calls for election boycott
The election campaign has also been accompanied by calls for a boycott from Al-Adl wal-Ihsan, one of Morocco's largest Islamist movements.
The group has urged Moroccans not to participate in the election, arguing that the country's current electoral system does not provide the conditions necessary for genuine democracy, freedom and justice.
Al-Adl wal-Ihsan said elected institutions lack real political decision-making power and raised concerns about restrictions on political participation and what it views as an absence of genuinely free competition.
The movement stressed that its boycott did not amount to withdrawing from public life, but was instead a rejection of what it described as an ineffective political process.
It called for a new political horizon capable of bringing about meaningful democratic change in the country.

The Numbers People Quote for Back Injury Settlements Are Not Settlements  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:48:15 UTC
01:48:15 KST

Back injuries dominate the workplace injury statistics. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, back-related cases are at 38.5 percent of all work-related musculoskeletal disorders in its 2016 data, a figure the industry still quotes a decade later. What grew up around it is an entire category of average settlement content, most of which measures something other than a settlement.
The gap between those two things runs in the tens of thousands of dollars, in both directions, depending on which number gets quoted at whom.
What the Quoted Averages Actually Measure
The most repeated figure in this category comes from the National Council on Compensation Insurance and is published through the National Safety Council's Injury Facts. For accident years 2022 and 2023, the average lost-time workers' compensation claim ran $47,316. Head or central nervous system injuries topped the list by part of the body at $90,043, followed by multiple body parts at $77,614 and neck injuries at $70,575.
The figures above are claim costs. They combine medical spend and indemnity paid across the life of a file, which is a different quantity from the lump sum a worker signs at the end of it. Ask actual claimants what they received, and the numbers fall. The Martindale-Nolo claimant survey puts the median workers' compensation settlement at $21,800 and back injuries specifically between $20,000 and $25,000.
Neither figure is wrong, but quoting the first figure as a settlement can be misleading.
Practitioners who work on these files daily tend to say the truth plainly. Determining the average settlement for workplace back injury can be tricky since they are case-specific and depend on numerous factors.
The Figure Nobody Can Trace
One number circulates harder than the rest. The statistic that back injury claims cost an employer between $40,000 and $80,000 is always attributed to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Searching for the exact figure leads to nothing. Every source repeating it is a law firm page, an insurance blog, or a content site citing another law firm page. Some versions credit the identical range to the Bureau of Labor Statistics instead, which is the usual sign that nobody checked. OSHA publishes injury and illness rates and an estimator for the employer cost of individual incidents. It does not publish a per-claim average for back injuries.
A number that survives only through repetition is worse than no number at all. It may lead an injured worker to make plans based on information that is unreliable.
Where a Comp Claim Stops Covering the Problem
Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer for the injury itself in most states. It pays medical treatment and a fraction of wages, commonly around two-thirds, but it does not pay for pain and suffering. It also says nothing about what sometimes happens after the claim goes in.
Some workers find their hours cut, their duties reassigned, or their employment ended once they file. Employers sometimes reclassify an injured worker as an independent contractor after a claim is filed.
Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), employees have certain degrees of protection when there is an employment relationship between the worker and an employer, according to the Department of Labor. But this is not the same for independent contractors. As such, they are cut off from their eligibility for workers' compensation benefits.
Employment lawyers are usually the ones to handle these disputes and not compensation lawyers. Such distinctions become critical when an employment issue intersects with a workers' compensation claim. LA employment lawyer Emanuel Shirazi’s firm represents individuals whose legal rights have been violated in the workplace. The firm works exclusively on the employee side and has represented workers against businesses of all sizes.
What Actually Moves a Back Injury Number
Diagnosis sets the foundation for the settlement amount. A lumbar strain that resolves in six weeks and a herniated disc with radiculopathy do not have the same settlement numbers. A fracture or nerve compression is a separate case that can have an entirely different settlement amount.
The involvement of surgery definitely affects the number, but it is not guaranteed to increase the figure. A fusion permanently limits range of motion and tends to produce the largest numbers in the category. A discectomy that restores function can raise medical costs while lowering the permanent impairment rating, which in turn pulls the indemnity side in the opposite direction.
An impairment rating, which is assigned once a worker reaches maximum medical improvement, is what most state systems convert into the permanent disability portion. Pre-injury wages scale the whole calculation, since indemnity runs as a percentage of average weekly wage. According to Justia, a prior history of degenerative changes invites the carrier to argue that the incident aggravated a pre-existing condition rather than caused something new. Most states still compensate for these injuries on a standard that varies from one system to the next.
No average predicts an individual file, and the averages in circulation are not measuring settlements to begin with. The number depends on the diagnosis, impairment rating, injured worker’s wages, and whether the treating physician states in the medical record that the job caused the condition. Those four get assembled before negotiation, or they do not get assembled at all.

Latvijas Banka, in cooperation with critical service providers and merchants, has implemented offline card payments – a solution that enables the purchase of essential goods, such as food, fuel, and medicinal products, when conventional card payments are not possible due to disruptions to internet or mobile communications.
Not everyone carries cash in their wallet, as card payments have become the norm for everyday purchases. Offline card payments enable natural persons who are clients of critical financial service providers to purchase goods from certain food retailers, petrol stations, and pharmacies for a total value of up to EUR 200 per card when internet connectivity is unavailable. Residents should bear in mind that this solution can only be used by physically inserting the payment card into a card terminal and entering the card's PIN. The offline solution cannot currently be used for payments made with a smart device. It should also be noted that the solution does not work if the respective merchant has no access to electricity.
The solution is currently operational at 10 retail outlets:
- three food and essential goods retail chains – Rimi, Maxima, and Lidl;
- the petrol stations of four fuel retailers – VIADA, ASTARTE NAFTA, Virši, and Neste (which supports offline payments made with Neste client payment cards);
- three pharmacy chains – Euroaptieka, Mēness aptieka, and BENU.
Offline payments can only be made with cards issued by four banks – Swedbank AS, AS SEB banka, AS Citadele banka, and the Latvian branch of Luminor Bank AS.
Together with the ability for residents to withdraw cash, including through the critical ATM network, which will be replenished with cash as a priority, this solution enables residents to purchase the goods they need in a crisis situation.
The offline payment solution implemented in Latvia works in cases of communication disruptions. Since its introduction, the solution has already ensured the continuity of operations at retail outlets by enabling offline card payments using physical cards in the event of disruptions to internet or mobile communications.
The National Security Law establishes that the critical financial services that must be ensured in the event of a possible threat to national security are cash and non-cash payments provided by credit institutions, thereby ensuring the availability of financial resources to people in Latvia. Taking into account the National Security Law and the Regulation issued by Latvijas Banka, critical financial services in Latvia are provided by Swedbank AS, AS SEB banka, AS Citadele banka, and the Latvian branch of Luminor Bank AS.
To know how to act in a crisis situation, Latvijas Banka encourages all residents to familiarise themselves with the informational material "Learn about cash and other financial services in a situation of crisis".

People still living with false sense of security - CIREN  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:47:55 UTC
01:47:55 KST

RIGA - People in the Nordic and Baltic countries continue to live with a false sense of security, Janis Vanags, a board member of the Civilian Resilience Nordic (CIREN), said at the Nordic Resilience Summit, which is taking place in Riga on Thursday.
This conclusion is based on a survey conducted by the research agency Norstat in all three Baltic states, as well as in Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Poland.
The survey found that a majority of residents in almost all of these countries, with the exception of Lithuania, have never participated in civil defense or crisis management training. In Lithuania, 60 percent of residents have participated in such training at some point, while in the other countries these figures are lower: 40 percent in Latvia, 38 percent in Poland, 33 percent in Estonia, 30 percent in Sweden, 26 percent in Norway, and 24 percent in Finland.
Furthermore, in Lithuania, 39 percent of respondents have participated in such training over the past five years.
The survey also found that if such free one-day training sessions were offered near respondents’ homes, Swedish residents would be the most likely to take this opportunity. Sixty-four percent of respondents in Sweden said they would definitely or most likely participate. In Latvia, this figure is the lowest, with 44 percent of respondents saying they would definitely or most likely participate in such training.
At the same time, Vanags noted that the survey was conducted before the storm that struck at the end of August, and such events typically change people’s attitudes.
The survey also shows that Latvians would be the least likely to survive for three days with no or with only insignificant problems if they were left without water, electricity, communications, or the internet. Fourteen percent of the surveyed Latvians said there would be no problems, while 43 percent of respondents in Latvia acknowledged that they would face some difficulties. By comparison, 34 percent of respondents in Norway said this would not cause any problems, while 43 percent of residents said they would face minor problems.
Asked whether they have a bag at home containing the necessary items to leave the house in a hurry, or the so-called 72-hour bag, a relatively small proportion of respondents in all surveyed countries said they had the bag already in place.
A 72-hour bag containing all necessary items has been packed by 4 percent of people in Poland, 3 percent in Lithuania and Finland, 2 percent in Latvia, and just 1 percent of respondents in Sweden, Norway, and Estonia. Between 15 percent of respondents in Poland and Sweden to 24 percent of respondents in Lithuania stated that they have not packed a bag, but have the necessary items at home.
At the same time, a significant number of people do not plan to pack such a bag at all. The highest proportion of people giving this answer was in Sweden, where 47 percent of respondents do not plan such preparation. In Lithuania, by comparison, 29 percent of the surveyed people do not plan to pack a 72-hour bag. In Latvia, the figure is 38 percent.
Asked how likely it is that, within the next two years, they will be affected by an emergency that will seriously disrupt their daily lives, residents of Lithuania (35 percent), Latvia (50 percent), and Estonia (42 percent) were proportionally the most likely to respond that it is very likely or somewhat likely that this will happen.
The survey also found that Sweden is the only country where more than half of respondents reported that their workplace has a plan for an emergency. In Latvia, this figure is the second lowest, at 41 percent. Workplace readiness in Poland proved to be even lower, at 35 percent.
The survey was conducted in all seven countries in August of this year, with at least 500 residents aged 18 to 74 surveyed in each country.

Lithuanian GRAAS turns irrigation into a data-driven business  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:47:45 UTC
01:47:45 KST

A problem as ordinary as carrying watering cans around a greenhouse has developed into a Lithuanian technology business seeking to change how gardens, commercial landscapes and farms use one of their most valuable resources – water.
GRAAS AUTOMATION develops smart irrigation controllers that replace conventional timer-based watering with systems capable of responding to soil moisture, weather conditions and other real-time data. Designed and assembled in Lithuania, its technology now ranges from four-zone greenhouse controllers to professional agricultural systems capable of managing up to 100 irrigation zones and hundreds of sensors.
For CEO Mantas Lukosaitis, the starting point was not a grand technology strategy, but a familiar problem at home.
“Essentially, the idea of developing controllers arose from an existing problem. My mother has been a keen gardener for many years, and every evening she would carry watering cans around and water the plants in her greenhouse,” he told The Baltic Times Magazine.
That observation led Lukosaitis and a friend to investigate available irrigation technology. They concluded that the product they imagined – easy to install, compact and capable of watering according to actual conditions rather than simply following a timer – was missing from the market.
“We started testing and assembled our first proof-of-concept controller. We saw its potential and began improving the system,” the CEO said.
The resulting iRigator combines the controller and valve assembly in one unit and can manage four separate watering zones. GRAAS subsequently moved into lawn irrigation with LawnCare before targeting professional agriculture with AgroGator.
The shift matters because agriculture faces increasing pressure to use water more efficiently. For GRAAS, the underlying proposition is relatively straightforward: irrigation should be determined by what is happening in the soil rather than what time it is.
“The main difference is that our controllers make decisions based on actual soil conditions rather than the clock. Most solutions on the market are essentially timers: you set them to irrigate at 7 am on Tuesday, and they will do so regardless of whether the soil is already wet or completely dry,” Mantas Lukosaitis said.
From greenhouse to farm
The company's technology uses sensors, a controller and an app to create a feedback loop. Users can establish desired moisture ranges for individual zones. If moisture drops below the minimum level, irrigation begins automatically and continues until the upper threshold is reached.
GRAAS also uses digital RS485 ModBus communication, while its agricultural system can integrate measurements including soil moisture and temperature, pH, EC conductivity, water pressure, light, wind and precipitation.
AgroGator represents the company's biggest move into professional agriculture. Its base configuration manages 20 irrigation zones but can be expanded to 100. The system supports GSM connectivity and LoRaWAN wireless sensors, while its architecture allows integration with other equipment used on farms. GRAAS markets the product as an all-in-one combination of irrigation automation, analytics and remote control.
“Our latest solution is GRAAS AgroGator, designed for professional farms. It represents our biggest leap from the consumer to the professional segment: up to 100 zones, up to 700 sensors, LoRaWAN wireless connectivity with a range of up to 10 km, RS485 ModBus integration with systems already used on the farm, and the possibility of ordering customised solutions,” Mantas Lukosaitis said.
The ability to customise could prove important as GRAAS moves further into the business-to-business market. Lukosaitis says the company has already developed additional functionality ranging from generator activation to farm-gate control.
“Depending on the individual project, we can add functions designed to automate irrigation and other farm operations. We have even developed solutions for starting generators and controlling farm gates,” he says.
Saving water – and potentially improving yields
Water efficiency is central to the company's business case. GRAAS says its systems seek to maintain optimal soil moisture rather than irrigating unnecessarily. Its website markets AgroGator as capable of reducing water consumption by as much as 40%, although actual savings will inevitably depend on conditions and the system against which it is compared.
“Our tests have shown water savings of around 35%. Comparisons by customers who use flow sensors and accurately measure their water consumption indicate that water use has fallen by 30–40%,” Mantas Lukosaitis said.
Lukosaitis argues that maintaining more consistent moisture can also reduce plant stress, potentially improving crop quality and yields.
The company's ambitions increasingly extend beyond watering itself. By accumulating data across growing seasons, GRAAS wants its technology eventually to anticipate what plants need rather than merely react when soil becomes too dry.
“I believe Lithuania will follow the same direction as Southern Europe, only with a delay: from timers to sensors, and from sensors to data. The most interesting stage begins when the system accumulates several seasons of data about a particular plot of land. At that point, we can start talking not simply about reacting to declining moisture levels, but about predicting them,” Mantas Lukosaitis said.
That evolution could turn irrigation controllers into broader farm-management platforms – particularly as more sensors, analytics and automation are added.
GRAAS is already experimenting with controlled plant-growing conditions to refine its algorithms. Different combinations of moisture, lighting, pH and EC will be tested, with the resulting data used to improve software subsequently deployed to customers.
“We are currently improving our existing solutions, including autonomous irrigation algorithms and the configuration of our app. We are also preparing an automated testing and calibration station for our devices.”
The company says it has sold more than several hundred controllers, although Lukosaitis declines to disclose the exact figure for competitive reasons. Most operate in Lithuania, but GRAAS equipment has also reached Latvia, Estonia, Belgium, Italy, Denmark and the Netherlands.
For a business that began with one gardener carrying watering cans around a greenhouse, the longer-term opportunity is much bigger: turning irrigation from a repetitive physical task into an automated, measurable and increasingly predictive process.
“Climate change has transformed this issue in Lithuania from one of convenience into an economic consideration,” Mantas Lukosaitis concluded.

Beyza Binnur Donmez
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Finland's government has proposed tighter residence permit rules Thursday for international students, including a one-year waiting period before their family members can apply to join them and new language proficiency requirements, according to a media report.
The Yle public broadcaster reported that Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government submitted the proposed legislative changes to parliament, seeking to address financial difficulties faced by some foreign students.
Under the proposal, family members would be able to apply for residence permits only after the student has lived in Finland for at least one year. Currently, they can submit applications at the same time.
The government also wants to set specific financial requirements in euros for international students and review the required amount every three years to reflect inflation and living costs.
A new language proficiency requirement would allow authorities to reject residence permit applications from students who lack sufficient skills in the language of instruction.
Government reports have found that some students arrive without adequate language skills, while others use student permits primarily as a route into the Finnish or wider EU labor market, according to Yle.
“Students coming to Finland must have a genuine ability to pursue their studies, to get by with their own financial resources and to build their future here,” said Employment Minister Matias Marttinen.
The family reunification waiting period is scheduled to take effect April 5, 2027, with other changes from October 2027.

A Colombian judge has ordered the presidential administration to remove videos showing President Abelardo de la Espriella walking among bodies after military operations.
The order was issued by the 14th Labor Court of the Bogota Circuit after a constitutional protection lawsuit, known as a tutela, was filed by lawmaker Santiago Osorio.
The court ordered the presidency to remove two videos published Sept. 2 and 4 on its Instagram account.
The footage showed de la Espriella walking among bodies wrapped in white bags after military operations in the departments of Guaviare and La Guajira.
The first video was linked to Operation Azarias in Miraflores, Guaviare. The second showed the results of Operation Centinela de la Patria in La Guajira.
Among those killed was Nain Andres Perez Toncel, known as "Bendito Menor," who was identified as a leader of the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada armed group.
The judge's decision followed arguments that publication of the graphic material could affect children and adolescents.
The court cited Article 18 of Colombia's Childhood and Adolescence Code, which provides special protection for minors against content that could cause psychological harm or suffering.
The case also includes Meta Platforms, Colombia's communications regulator, the Ministry of Information Technologies and Communications, and the Colombian Family Welfare Institute.
Osorio welcomed the ruling, saying the state must be strong in confronting criminal groups but should not use images of dead people as political propaganda.
The videos had already triggered criticism on social media and from Colombian officials for the government's decision to publish graphic images from military operations.
The controversy comes as de la Espriella's government has made security and military operations against armed and criminal groups a central part of its agenda.
The administration has defended the operations as necessary to confront organized crime and strengthen security in Colombia.

Brent crude settled at $101.21 a barrel Wednesday, its highest close since May, as attacks involving Iran and the US disrupted shipping and raised concerns about oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
The European Commission's latest Weekly Oil Bulletin, published Thursday, provides the latest weekly comparison of petroleum prices in the EU, while national data show further increases at filling stations in several major European markets.
In Italy, petrol prices have reached about €2.05 ($2.39) per liter, while diesel is around €2.17, according to the data.
The Italian government had extended a temporary 17-cent reduction in diesel excise duties through Thursday to contain the effect of rising fuel costs.
The measure, which has been extended several times since March, is expected to give way to more targeted support for lower-income households and road transport operators.
France also recorded increases. The average price of diesel stood at about €2.30 per liter, while E10 petrol was around €2.13, according to data based on French government fuel-price reports.
Diesel prices rose by about 5.3 cents during the previous week, while E10 petrol increased by about 4.1 cents.
In Germany, the average price of E10 petrol was about €2.24, while Super petrol and diesel were around €2.30, according to an analysis by public broadcaster SWR, based on prices at 15,000 filling stations.
The Netherlands remains among Europe's most expensive fuel markets. Average E10 petrol was about €2.42, with diesel about €2.49, according to Dutch fuel-price data.
Belgium's average prices were lower, at about €1.99 for petrol. It was €2.29 for diesel.
In Czechia, petrol was averaging about €1.76 and diesel about €1.90, according to the latest European fuel-price data.
The UK has also seen a sharp weekly increase. Average petrol stood at about 167.9 pence ($2.27), up 4.6 pence in seven days. Diesel hit 189.4 pence, up 4.5 pence, according to data based on the government's Fuel Finder system.
Switzerland recorded average petrol prices of about CHF2.00 ($2.52) and diesel prices of CHF2.24, with prices continuing to rise from the previous week.
Fuel prices have also increased in the Baltic states. Lithuania's average petrol price was about €1.82, while diesel stood at around €2. Latvia recorded petrol prices of about €1.79 and diesel prices of €1.96.
Estonia's latest European Commission benchmark put petrol at about €1.81 per liter and diesel at €1.92.
Denmark remains one of the most expensive EU markets for petrol at about €2.37 per liter. Diesel was around €2.47.
Sweden remains among the cheapest EU markets. The latest European Commission benchmark put petrol at about €1.47 and diesel at €1.73.
Finland was also among the more expensive markets, with the European Commission's latest benchmark putting petrol at about €2.20. It is costing diesel at €2.33.
The latest price increases come as Brent crude has risen above $100 a barrel, with the conflict in the Middle East and disruptions to oil shipping raising concerns about inflation and household costs in Europe.
The European Central Bank raised its policy interest rate to 2.50% Wednesday, citing renewed inflationary pressure linked in part to the energy shock. The ECB raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 3%, underscoring the potential effect of higher energy costs on the euro area economy.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is considering withdrawing the country’s highly classified defense plan from Saxony-Anhalt if the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) forms a government there, German media reported Thursday.
The more than 1,000-page document, known as OPLAN Deutschland, sets out core measures for national and NATO defense in a crisis or war. Officials say the scenario they prepare for now is a confrontation with Russia. In that case, Germany would become a logistics hub for alliance troops moving toward NATO’s eastern flank.
RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) reported that Pistorius, a Social Democrat and a prominent opponent of the AfD, raised the idea on Tuesday in front of defense policymakers from the governing coalition parties. The discussion is driven by fears that Russia-friendly AfD politicians could pass the plan to Moscow, increasing Germany’s security risk.
Rainer Robra, a conservative CDU politician who still heads Saxony-Anhalt’s state chancellery, warned against any move to withhold security information. “I cannot imagine how the constitutionally required cooperation among the states is supposed to work if the state of Saxony-Anhalt is excluded from domestic or defense policy information,” he told RND.
The anti-immigration AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt’s Sept. 6 state election, taking 39 of 83 seats, short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority. Left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which officials also describe as close to Russia, announced that it has accepted AfD’s invitation for talks, to bring about a change in policies.
The conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party rejected any cooperation or coalition with the AfD, saying they would not work with a party that the state domestic intelligence service has classified as a “proven right-wing extremist” organization.
Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht has ruled out a formal coalition with the AfD but has not categorically excluded other forms of political support. She said the party wants a cross-party premier standing for a political new start who must also be acceptable to the AfD and its voters.
In a social media post, Wagenknecht said a majority in Saxony-Anhalt wants change and that the BSW would talk with the AfD about motions on shared priorities — affordable energy and a restart of Russian gas via the Nord Stream pipeline, reform of public broadcasting, and opposition to arms deliveries to Ukraine.

Gaza amputees tell TNA of life after devastating limb loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:44:41 UTC
01:44:41 KST

Breadcrumb
'Everything is difficult': Gaza amputees tell TNA of life without limbs and vital support
For Adli Obeid, even travelling a short distance through Gaza has become an exhausting ordeal.
The 40-year-old father of four from Shujaiya in eastern Gaza City lost his right leg during Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave and now relies on crutches to navigate streets filled with rubble and destruction.
He is among more than 5,000 Palestinians who have undergone amputations since the war began in October 2023, according to new figures from Gaza's health ministry. Obeid and other amputees told The New Arab that a severe shortage of prosthetic limbs, mobility aids and rehabilitation services has compounded the difficulties of living with their injuries.
"Everything has become difficult since I lost my leg. Before, I could walk wherever I wanted, take care of my children and go to work without thinking about whether the road was suitable for me. Now, even going a short distance can be exhausting because there are no proper roads and so much rubble and destruction everywhere," Obeid told The New Arab.
"The injury did not only take away my leg. It took away a part of my independence. I sometimes feel that I am a burden on my family because there are things I used to do myself that I now need help with. Mentally, it has been very hard. I have four children, and I want to be strong for them, but there are moments when I feel frustrated, angry, and helpless," he continued.
Obeid said he is constantly reminded of his disability, particularly because of a shortage of wheelchairs, crutches and medicine in Gaza amid Israeli restrictions on aid entering the Strip.
Gaza's health ministry said on Tuesday that it had documented at least 5,000 amputations since the start of the war, including around 980 children and 555 women.
The ministry's breakdown also included 595 men and more than 2,870 other cases.
Israel's war on Gaza has been determined to be a genocide by leading rights groups.
Another amputee, Mansour al-Qerem, a 42-year-old father of three from Gaza City, said one of the most difficult changes since losing his leg has been his inability to move freely and play with his children.
"You feel that your role as a father has changed because you cannot always do what you used to do. The psychological impact is very heavy. At first, I could not accept what had happened. You look at yourself and realize that your body has changed forever," he told The New Arab.
"There is no opportunity to recover mentally because the war is still affecting every part of our lives. You are not only dealing with the loss of your leg. You are also dealing with destruction, displacement, the loss of people you know and the fear of what comes next," he added.
Al-Qerem said that while a small number of organisations provide support for amputees in Gaza, the scale of need far exceeds the assistance and number of prosthetics available.
"An amputee needs more than a crutch. We need rehabilitation, prosthetic limbs, physiotherapy, medical treatment, and psychological support. I believe international disability organisations can do much more. The world has seen the number of people who have lost limbs in Gaza, but the needs of these people do not end when their wounds heal. An amputee may need years of rehabilitation and support to regain independence," he said.
Double amputations
The health ministry said the overall figure also includes people with double amputations and other complex injuries requiring urgent medical intervention to save remaining limbs.
Israel's offensive on Gaza, which is continuing despite an October ceasefire, has also left more than 10,000 people needing intensive and long-term rehabilitation programmes because of the nature of their injuries, the ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry described physical therapy and rehabilitation services in Gaza as a "crucial lifeline".
New data also shows that around 300 people have neurological and spinal cord injuries requiring specialised care and rehabilitation, while most medical centres and healthcare facilities have been targeted or severely damaged, according to the ministry.
Activists and human rights groups have warned that conditions in Gaza are putting sick and injured people at risk of serious health complications, particularly amid severe shortages of medical supplies, prosthetic devices and artificial limbs.
According to the World Health Organization, around 43,000 of 172,000 wounded people have suffered life-altering injuries.
Gaza's health ministry has called on international organisations and UN agencies to urgently facilitate the entry of vital rehabilitation supplies and equipment into the enclave.
It also reiterated calls for land crossings to be fully opened, particularly for critical cases requiring urgent treatment outside Gaza or care that is unavailable in the enclave.
Despite the shortage of medical equipment, doctors and specialists have continued working in difficult conditions, at times treating people in displacement tents because patients are unable to reach healthcare facilities.
UN agency UNRWA has said Gaza now has the largest group of child amputees in modern history.

US Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri
Rejection comes as Republican official in Missouri faces contempt charges for ignoring a lower court ruling.
The United States Supreme Court has again rejected a request from the administration of President Donald Trump to use electoral district maps that would favour his Republican party in the state of Missouri.
The court issued the latest order on Thursday, without noting any dissents to the decision, apparently clearing the way for Missouri to use the old map in mid-term elections this November that could determine which party controls the House of Representatives.

Earlier in the week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump -appointee, rejected another request from the administration to put the new Republican-backed map into effect, without referring the case to the full nine-member court, or offering an explanation for his decision. Kavanaugh handles emergency matters from Missouri.
Contempt charges for Republican official
Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.
The rejection on Thursday came hours after a federal judge allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing against Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins.
The state’s top court previously ordered Hoskins not to use a Trump-backed map in the general election and instead to use districts passed after the last census.
At the same time, US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump -appointee, on Tuesday barred Hoskins from using anything other than the new map Trump supports.
The state Supreme Court then ordered Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing on Thursday for not following its orders and instructing local election authorities to use the Trump-backed districts.
State attorneys representing Hoskins had asked Clark to halt the contempt hearing – but he declined.
Redistricting plans
Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw House districts to their advantage ahead of the midterm elections.
The revised Missouri districts target a Kansas City-based seat held by Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver by shedding parts into neighbouring districts and stretching the remainder into rural Republican areas. The goal is to help Republicans win seven of the state’s eight House seats in the midterm elections — a gain of one seat.
Redistricting opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking to force a statewide vote on the new districts. They submitted the signatures in December. But Hoskins waited until August — on the same day as Missouri’s primary — to reject the petition. Hoskins asserted that a referendum petition could not be used for congressional redistricting.
The delay allowed Missouri to use the new districts in its August primary. Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters’ federal rights to switch districts before the general election.
But the Missouri Supreme Court last week ordered Hoskins to put the redistricting referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled that the new districts never became law and instead were suspended retroactively to the December petition submission.
The state then appealed to the US Supreme Court to block the state court’s findings. Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected their request.
The court barred Hoskins from using the new map and said the old map — passed by Republican legislators in 2022 after the last census — must be used in the November election. The US Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal of that decision. But Clark issued his conflicting order moments later.

Trump’s Iran war now has a midterm election problem
Trump has tied the end of his war on Iran to the midterm elections. But with Iran holding firm, the political cost is mounting.
United States President Donald Trump has claimed that the seven-month-long war with Iran will end “immediately after” the US midterm elections in November, framing the ongoing conflict as an attempt by Tehran to influence the vote.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election,” he told reporters on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump vows to be at centre of US midterms: Republican convention takeaways
- list 2 of 4Benjamin Netanyahu has overseen a genocide: In his telling, he’s a victim
- list 3 of 4IAEA accuses Iran of ‘noncompliance’
- list 4 of 4Trump promises $5,000 payouts if GOP wins midterms: Can the US afford it?
Trump’s latest claims of Iranian capitulation are not new. Tehran has thus far withstood sustained strikes by the US and Israel intended to eradicate its military capacity, as well as a naval blockade of Iran’s ports intended to choke the country’s economy. In late August, the US ratcheted up the economic pressure even further, threatening secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners.
“It was a statement that was more likely meant for an internal [domestic] audience,” Ali Alavi, an Iran lecturer at SOAS University of London, said of Trump’s predictions of Iran’s post-election collapse. ”It was Trump’s method of communicating that the only reason it seemed as though he was failing in his Iran policy before the midterms is because Iran wanted it to be perceived that way.”
The cost of war
The cost of Iran’s failure to capitulate is being felt across the United States ahead of the midterms, which could see Trump’s Republican Party lose one or both houses of Congress.
Petrol prices – a key measure of the cost of living in the world’s largest economy – have climbed to a national average of $4.27 a gallon according to the American Automobile Association, up nearly 30 percent from a year ago.
Trump’s approval rating has also plunged from the high-40s when he returned to office in January 2025 to the low-to-mid 30s today.
The US electorate’s pain extends beyond the pump. A 2026 LendingTree survey found that 29 percent of buy-now-pay-later users had used the loans to buy groceries, while 47 percent said they had paid late on a buy-now-pay-later loan at least once in the past year.
Separately, economists at the University of Michigan have found that rising fuel costs and inflation linked to the war on Iran are weighing on consumer confidence and purchasing power.
“Iran has prepared for a long war,” Sanam Vakil, director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said. ”It may be that part of that was a secondary plan to hold out long enough to destabilise the US midterm elections once it realised that negotiations with the current administration were not going anywhere.”
Top Democrats, including the party’s Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, have been explicit in their calls for Trump to end the war on Iran.
Given Republican difficulties over the Iran war and other issues, Center for American Progress international policy analyst H.A. Hellyer described the situation ahead of the November 3 congressional midterms as one where the Democrats aren’t as much poised to win as the Republicans are positioned to lose.
“The question really is one of [voter] turnout,” he explained. “It’s not that many members of the Republican base will suddenly switch to supporting the Democrats, as much as they’ll stay home and not vote.”
Foreign policy, Hellyer said, rarely influenced voters, but “economics matter”.
“The price of things, like the petrol they get from the pump, matter – and it’s this that might swing [the election],” he added.
Irrespective of their claims of military success, both the US and Israel face a reckoning with an electorate that their leaders had promised easy victory: the US and Trump in November’s midterms and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu in a crucial general election in October. Iran, ruled by an unelected Supreme Leader and with no legislative elections scheduled until 2028, faces no such countdown.
“For Iran, victory is about surviving long enough to extract a serious diplomatic undertaking from its opponents that it won’t be attacked,” said Vakil of London-based Chatham House. “Victory is about demonstrating leverage, but negative leverage, in proving that it can still disrupt the world’s economy, no matter what the state of its military.”
“For some in the government, that includes retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “For others, that’s just a potential bargaining chip in negotiations, but for all: victory is survival and finding a way to convert it to stability. It’s a tall task.”

Israel ally Somaliland offers 2,000 troops for Gaza stabilisation force
Somaliland is willing to deploy 2,000 troops for a planned US-led force in Gaza, President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi on Wednesday, adding that he is waiting for Washington or Israel to formally request its participation.
Speaking on the sidelines of the MEAD conference in Washington, which focuses on developments in the Middle East, Abdullahi stressed that the breakaway region of Somalia was not volunteering for the mission.
“If they ask, we can provide,” he said, adding that, if requested, his forces are "ready", with an army of approximately 25,000 soldiers and a coast guard of around 1,500 personnel.
As part of the Gaza peace plan envisioned by US President Donald Trump's self-styled "Board of Peace", an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) would be deployed to Gaza to secure areas following the withdrawal of Israeli forces. The force would also train new Palestinian police forces and support the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Abdullahi's comments come after Uganda approved the deployment of army troops to the ISF last month, becoming the first African state to declare its participation in the stabilisation force.
However, the prospect of Ugandan troops joining the mission has prompted debate in the country.
Opposition lawmakers were probing further details about the nature of the deployment, while raising questions over Kampala's approval and whether it has wider African backing.
Politicians in the country were particularly skeptical regarding whether Uganda acted without consulting its partners in the African Union (AU), as the bloc has consistently expressed support for the Palestinian cause and backed the implementation of a two-state solution.
Meanwhile, Israel has spent decades developing relations with several African countries, signified recently in Tel Aviv's official recognition of Somaliland as an independent state -- a position rejected by Somalia and most countries.
Somaliland subsequently opened an embassy in Jerusalem in June during Abdullahi's first official visit to Israel.

Four night bus routes will be launched from the railway station in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
Starting September 10, buses will run through Kyiv during curfew hours—from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m. The service interval will be about an hour.
Four night bus routes are being launched in the capital from the Central Railway Station. They will operate during curfew hours, from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m. This was reported by Ukrzaliznytsia’s press service, according to UNN.
Sometimes, due to enemy shelling and the threat of air attacks, our trains arrive in Kyiv later than planned. For passengers, this means not only waiting but also a more difficult journey home—especially at night. Therefore, the city is launching four temporary night bus routes from the Central Railway Station. They will help passengers arriving in Kyiv at night continue their journey across the city
Starting September 10, the buses will operate during curfew hours, from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m.

We remind you

Finland plans tighter residence permit rules for international students
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:41:19 EEST
01:41:19 KST

Finland’s government has proposed making international students wait one year before their family members apply for residence permits, as part of changes to student immigration rules aimed at addressing financial problems among people studying in the country.
The government submitted the proposal to Parliament on 10 September. The package also sets out changes to financial requirements and introduces a language proficiency condition for residence permits issued for studies.
Under current rules, family members are able to apply for residence permits at the same time as the student. The proposed legislation would require the student to spend one year in Finland before the family submits an application for family reunification.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment said the waiting period would give students time to understand the amount of money required to support a family in Finland.
The government also wants to define the financial resources required from international students in legislation. The required amount in euros would be set by decree and reviewed every three years.
The ministry said authorities have identified cases in which international students struggled to support themselves after arriving in Finland, though government data shows most students progress with their studies and live in the country without significant financial problems.
Minister of Employment Matias Marttinen said students entering Finland should have the resources required to complete their education and support themselves.
“Students coming to Finland must have a genuine ability to pursue their studies, to get by with their own financial resources and to build their future here,” Marttinen said in the ministry’s statement.
The proposal follows a ministry report that examined financial difficulties among international students. According to the report, some foreign education agents have given students misleading information about employment prospects in Finland.
The ministry also found cases in which students accumulated debt after paying agency fees before moving to Finland.
Language skills to become part of student permit rules
Language proficiency forms another part of the proposed changes. Applicants for study residence permits would need to demonstrate sufficient ability in the language used for their studies.
Authorities would have grounds to refuse a permit when an applicant lacks the required language skills. The ministry said the system was designed to avoid additional requirements for applicants who have already demonstrated sufficient proficiency.
The government report identified cases in which students lacked the English or other language skills required for their courses, creating problems with completing their studies.
Authorities have also identified cases in which applicants primarily used study-based residence permits to enter the Finnish or wider EU labour market, according to the ministry.
The government also proposes extending refusal criteria under Finland’s Aliens Act to upper secondary students and their family members. The ministry said the change would give immigration authorities more grounds to address suspected circumvention of immigration rules during the residence permit process.
The family reunification waiting period is scheduled to take effect on 5 April 2027 if Parliament approves the legislation. Other changes in the package are scheduled to apply from October 2027.
Wider changes targeting international student rules
The government submitted separate legislation to Parliament on 30 April aimed at increasing oversight of foreign students who receive social assistance. Under those proposals, authorities would have greater scope to cancel a student’s residence permit when the person lacks sufficient resources and relies on social assistance in Finland.
Those changes are also scheduled to enter into force in autumn 2027.

Belgium should not hold everyone hostage over frozen Russian assets - MEP Auštrevičius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

Belgium should not hold everyone hostage over frozen Russian assets - MEP Auštrevičius
That’s according to the Lithuanian Member of the European Parliament, Petras Auštrevičius, who spoke in an exclusive comment for Ukrinform, following a new initiative by a group of MEPs to reopen the debate on Russian assets.
Commenting on the stance of Belgium, where the Euroclear depository holds the bulk of immobilized Russian assets, the politician called for preventing a single country from halting decisions that are crucial for the entire Europe: “One objection country as Belgium shouldn't keep everybody else as a hostage,” the MEP stated.
He pointed out that the scale of Ukraine's financial needs far exceeds current temporary instruments, making a comprehensive solution crucial.
“I think we have much more on the plate in order to discuss and find certain solutions. So that's why, even knowing how difficult it might be, it doesn’t stop us, and so we came with this letter in order to try to open the doors for discussions and finally, hopefully, find a certain way forward,” Auštrevičius added. “Ukraine will need much more than 90 billion loan money for its existential survival.”
In their joint letter to EU institutions, MEPs suggested establishing a technical vehicle or a new European instrument to manage the assets, which could decouple the process from national clearinghouses and mitigate legal pressure on Brussels.
“I guess that vehicle is something which might be useful, because not this kind of clearinghouse, but definitely a new institution might be in charge, and kind of a bit disconnected from Belgium,” Auštrevičius explained. “We have to be very practical, even suggesting some technical solutions.”
The Lithuanian politician noted that treating immobilized funds as untouchable is a fundamental mistake, as the aggressor must bear full financial accountability for destruction in Ukraine.
“We make a mistake, first of all, keeping those immobilized, frozen Russian assets as something holy, not touched by us,” the MEP declared. “It would be a very strong message to Russians that they are responsible and they have to pay, and we will use their money to the final penny.”
Addressing whether the EU political elite is ready to revisit the issue, the MEP admitted that while there may be hesitations, waiting is simply not an option.
“Well, I think the European Union is never ready for such a radical decision, but is there any better time? Do we have time just to sit back and do nothing?” Auštrevičius questioned.
He noted that despite the lack of immediate enthusiasm among some officials, the evolving circumstances are the reason while the issue must be pushed onto the agenda.
“The situation didn't improve, and we need more and more financial means and support for Ukraine. So that's why, even knowing that there will be no big political appetite to take this issue, we have to push it for an uneasy, but undeniably needed discussion once again to renew this debate about frozen assets,” he stressed.
Concluding his comment, Petras Auštrevičius rejected scenarios in which European taxpayers are forced to absorb the costs of rebuilding Ukraine while Russian funds remain intact.
“I don't see, even with the final peace solution on today's situation, that will we not use Russian money” Auštrevičius asked. “Who will pay for reconstruction of Ukraine? Not Russia? So then who, Belgium? I don't think so.”
As reported, the initiative by the group of MEPs aims to reactivate political consultations among the European Commission, the Council of the EU, and member states to establish a viable mechanism for utilizing Russian assets to secure long-term support for Ukraine.

Ukrainian intelligence agency shows how Russian drones are shot down using unmanned boats together with F-16 fighter jets – video
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has shown the joint operation of unmanned boats carrying interceptor drones and F-16 fighter jets as part of Ukraine's layered air defence. Footage of the operation was published on DIU's page.
Source: DIU
Details: Intelligence officers shared footage of an operation carried out by the Ferrata unit in September 2026 during a Russian attack drone strike on Kyiv. A special operations serviceman who goes by the alias "Deviatyi" (Ninth) said that the unmanned components were used in combination with Ukrainian aircraft.
"We are advocates of synchronising robotic equipment, technologies, other devices that can be used in combat operations, artificial intelligence and human determination," the serviceman said.
The operators of the Black Sea Legion naval division used Katran surface drones equipped with interceptor drones and radar reconnaissance equipment. The operation was conducted jointly with the Air Force and other defence forces' units.
"DIU unit operators worked out the interaction between the unmanned component and F-16 aircraft crews to protect the airspace and eliminate enemy targets from the air and water," the intelligence agency commented on the operation.
The stated operational range of the Katran family of maritime drones exceeds 1,500 km. Depending on their configuration, they can be equipped with MAC Thunder FPV attack drones, FPV drones and MAC Dead Fly interceptors.
Background:
- In May 2026, the Ukrainian maritime drone Katran X1.2 with 27 MAC Dead Fly interceptor drones was demonstrated during tests on the Dnipro. It can perform kamikaze functions, carry two R-73 short-range missiles and various types of aerial drones. The Katran X1.2 is nine metres long, has a 350-horsepower engine and a range of up to 1,600 km.
- Ukrainian companies MAC HUB and Sky Defenders signed a memorandum of cooperation that provides for the integration of Sky Defenders UAVs into the Katran family of uncrewed surface vessels (USVs).
