Building beyond Bilingual 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

Recent discussions about Bilingual 2030 have produced no shortage of disagreement. Educators do not always agree about education. More interesting is what happens when we look beyond those disagreements and consider what each perspective adds to the conversation.
Nigel Daly (“Taiwan wants bilingual, AI-ready graduates — but tests for yesteryear,” June 3, page 12) questioned whether assessment reflects the capabilities students increasingly need. Jye Smallwood (“Basic Misunderstanding of EMI,” Aug. 9, page 8) examined the pedagogical demands of English-medium instruction. Gerhard Erasmus (“Bilingual 2030: time’s up for opinions,” Sept. 5, page 8) emphasized rigorous research, stronger evidence and the need to adjust policy as that evidence emerges. My own contributions have focused on classroom experience and the connections between learning, assessment and teacher development.
Taken together, these perspectives begin to look less like competing diagnoses and more like different parts of the same education system.
Assessment matters, because what measure inevitably influences what students and teachers prioritize. As artificial intelligence (AI) changes the value of information retrieval and routine language production, greater attention to communication, judgement and the ability to use knowledge becomes increasingly important. Assessment can help signal those priorities while providing evidence of whether students are developing them.
The discussion around English as a medium of instruction (EMI) brings us closer to what happens when educational ambitions reach classrooms. Teaching academic content using English requires more than subject expertise or English-language proficiency. Teachers also need the pedagogical skills to make complex ideas accessible, check understanding and create opportunities for students to engage meaningfully with language and content.
If we expect classroom practice to evolve, teachers need opportunities to develop alongside the expectations placed upon them. Professional development can connect broader education goals with the daily decisions teachers make about tasks, interaction, feedback and learning.
Classroom experience and research provide evidence. Some of it can inform immediate adjustments; other patterns require systematic study over time. Evidence becomes most valuable when it can travel through the system and help inform what happens next.
These elements can reinforce one another. Stronger assessment can provide better information about learning. Teacher development can help educators respond to that information. Better-prepared teachers can create richer learning experiences. Classroom experience and research can then reveal where further development or adjustment might help.
An education system cannot communicate in only one direction. Policy travels from ministries toward schools, but classroom experience must also travel back through the system. Researchers, teachers, students, schools and policymakers each see something that others might not.
This raises a larger question about Bilingual 2030 itself. Governments need deadlines. Education needs direction.
The year 2030 is a useful milestone for setting goals, focusing investment and evaluating progress, but learning would continue long after it passes. A child entering elementary school today would still be in the education system after 2030. A teacher beginning a career now might still be teaching in the 2050s. AI, internationalization and changing workplaces would continue reshaping how English is learned and used.
Perhaps the most important legacy of Bilingual 2030 is not a final verdict on whether every ambition was achieved by a particular date. It is the education capacity Taiwan builds along the way.
The nation has already invested substantially in many of these areas. Bilingual 2030 has generated years of experimentation, professional development, classroom experience and public discussion from which to learn. Each contribution to that discussion helps illuminate another part of a complex picture.
None of these perspectives needs to contain the whole answer. Their value lies precisely in what becomes possible when we put them together.
The deadline 2030 would arrive soon enough. The larger opportunity is to ensure that everything Taiwan learns on the way helps its teachers, students and education system become even more capable in 2031, 2035 and beyond.
Daniel Eyrich is director of English studies at CenYing English in Keelung and has more than 15 years of experience in English-language teaching, assessment and teacher development in Taiwan.

A rodent’s interruption of a professional baseball game at Taipei Dome on Wednesday sparked renewed discussion of rat control efforts, weeks ahead of the city’s mayoral election.
Just before the eighth inning of Wednesday’s game between the Fubon Guardians and the Wei Chuan Dragons, a small rat was spotted running out onto the field at Taipei Dome between home plate and the first base dugout.
Stadium workers quickly surrounded the rodent, using a paper bag to pin it down and carry it off the field. Though quickly resolved, the incident nevertheless became fodder for political discussion the next day.
Photo: CNA
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said he had already asked Farglory Group, Taipei Dome’s owner and operator, to carry out disinfection procedures.
Taipei City’s sports, environmental and health departments also jointly inspected conditions at the dome, and tasked the sports department with monitoring the situation and imposing penalties if necessary, said Chiang, a member of the Kuomintang (KMT).
Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) nominee for Taipei mayor, was also asked about the incident during a campaign stop in the Dadaocheng neighborhood Thursday.
Shen said problems with rats have "always existed" in Taipei, but added that he had recently noticed more people complaining about rat sightings in their homes.
Based on feedback he has collected, Shen said, many Taipei residents also have strong feelings about the reduced number of public trash cans, which has caused inconvenience while also failing to reduce the number of rat sightings.
The discussion recalled a period of several-weeks in May, when talk of an alleged "rat problem" in Taipei spread from the internet into the media and city politics.
The issue receded from the public eye after the city government launched a multi-day cleaning drive and pledged more aggressive control measures.
Regarding the issue of public trash cans, Taipei Department of Environmental Protection Director Shyu Shyh-shiun (徐世?) confirmed last month that the city had been removing bins to stop people from illegally disposing of household garbage.
Excluding those in tourist areas and business districts, which are being kept in place, the city has decreased the number of public trash cans over several years from around 2,000 to 806, Shyu said.
Taiwan will hold its local elections on Nov. 28.

The death toll from a fire that erupted yesterday on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked in a Chinese port has risen to 25, including five people who had been listed as missing, state media said.
The bulk carrier, moored in the eastern shipping hub of Qingdao, had 42 people on board when the fire broke out, state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) reported.
Seventeen of those were evacuated, including five who were injured.
Photo: Qingdaowolin via AP
However, by yesterday evening “all 25 missing persons had been found, none showing signs of life,” CCTV said.
“The open flames were extinguished” by about 2:30pm, it said.
Xinhua news agency said earlier that the fire broke out at about 11:15am during the ship’s port call for maintenance, without specifying the cause of the fire.
A witness from a neighboring residential compound said he saw thick smoke coming from the ship, but did not hear an explosion.
“I saw the smoke from the ship by chance, but there was no visible fire,” he said. “I didn’t hear an explosion or smell anything.”
Xinhua shared a video of the scene showing a large ship called the Ocean Melody docked at Beihai Shipbuilding Co (中國船舶集團青島北海造船), with dozens of rescuers swarming its decks and entering the vessel.
Several fire trucks and ambulances were stationed on the dock in front of the ship.
Ocean Melody is a 190m-long bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to the vessel-tracking Web site MarineTraffic, which located the ship as moored in Qingdao.
The Beihai Shipbuilding yard operates as a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corp (中國船舶集團).

There have been several major industrial accidents in China over the past year, where safety regulations are often lax.
An explosion and ensuing fire at a shipyard in China’s Fujian Province last month killed one fire and rescue worker and injured 12 others, state media reported.
China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings in November last year after a huge blaze engulfed several residential tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.
A blast at a fireworks factory in central China killed 37 people in May, marking one of the nation’s deadliest industrial accidents in years.
A fire in a shoe factory in Fujian in July killed at least 28 people.

August hottest month ever recorded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:36 UTC
01:37:36 KST

The EU’s climate monitor yesterday said that last month was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN said that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940, but other evidence — such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons — allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.
Photo: AFP
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts strategic lead for climate Samantha Burgess said.
The center oversees Copernicus.
Global average air temperatures last month were 16.96°C, Copernicus said — surpassing by 0.01°C the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023.
Copernicus said it considered the two months joint-highest given the narrow difference.
Scientists say that human activity — primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas — has warmed the planet by about 1.4°C since preindustrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs last year.
“The evidence is irrefutable: This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling,” UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming, but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins such as the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength.
These events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the odds of wild weather thousands of miles away, from floods in Peru to droughts in Africa and wildfires in Australia.
The warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term background warming.
Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for next year — and maybe even this year — to become the hottest years ever observed.
“Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” Imperial College London climate scientist Friederike Otto said.
Last month also “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003, Copernicus said.
Elsewhere, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration on Wednesday said the contiguous US has endured its hottest summer on record.
Regions home to about 900 million people lived through the hottest July ever observed, an analysis of Copernicus data showed.
“We’ve had an exceptional summer — not only in Europe, but other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” Burgess said.
The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions,” she added.

Chen has confessed to that part of the charges, the office said.

EDITORIAL: PIF presence step in right direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:34 UTC
01:37:34 KST

The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) took place from Aug. 30 to Friday last week in Palau. Unlike last year, Taiwan this time had a strong presence at the event, in a diplomatic setback to China.
While Taiwan-China tensions featured prominently at the forum, Beijing’s disruption of the meeting with its “wolf warrior” diplomacy was the focus.
Ahead of the event, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked the PIF and Palau to adhere to the “one China” principle in handling Taiwan’s participation. Then, in retaliation against Ngerulmud’s decision to invite Taipei, the Chinese Ministry of Culture and Tourism warned its citizens to be wary of traveling to Palau.
Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) even said: “There will be consequences when China is unhappy.”
As Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr had insisted on the forum’s autonomous right to invite non-member partners, Taiwan sent a large delegation, led by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). They were warmly welcomed during “Taiwan night.” Lin was also invited to make a rare appearance at the opening ceremony of the PIF leaders’ summit.
Taiwan and its three diplomatic allies in the region — Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands — signed a joint statement pledging to work more closely. The US also announced that it is working with Taiwan and other partners to support the development of hospitals and drinking water sampling facilities in Palau.
In another diplomatic setback for China, the leaders’ summit released a joint communique expressing concerns over Beijing firing an intercontinental ballistic missile that fell into South Pacific waters without adequate notice, saying that such tests should “ensure transparency and eliminate doubts, including by providing at least 24 hours’ notice in accordance with international practice.”
Despite these setbacks, China’s growing influence in the region cannot be overlooked. Over the past few years, Beijing has caused divisions and geopolitical rivalry in the region, testing the solidarity of Pacific island nations.
For example, the PIF’s host country last year, the Solomon Islands, barred all non-member countries from the event after Beijing pressured it to block Taipei’s participation. That risked the loss of international support for the PIF and infringed on the sovereignty of countries in the region.
Additionally, Nauru opposed the joint communique criticizing China’s missile test, while Kiribati did not attend the negotiations, which showed that the two nations’ expanding ties with Beijing is undermining the unity of Pacific island countries in safeguarding regional security and stability.
China’s deepening cooperation with Pacific island nations in policing, security and infrastructure has also alerted Western democracies that the Pacific region — which is home to strategic facilities and resources such as ports, submarine cables, fisheries, maritime surveillance, seabed minerals and military corridors — has become the front line of strategic jockeying in the Indo-Pacific region.
During the PIF, the US in a statement pledged its commitment to the security and prosperity of Pacific island nations. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau also announced more than US$150 million in funding to support nations in the region.
Meanwhile, Australia pledged a A$600 million (US$432.54 million) package to help Pacific island nations combat transnational drug trafficking, and signed defense and cooperation agreements with countries in the region to limit China’s influence.
As for Taiwan, the PIF this year showed that Taipei’s status as “development partner” since 1993 remained unchanged, and it is set to be included in next year’s forum in New Zealand. China would likely ramp up efforts to pressure nations into obstructing Taiwan’s international participation.
As most nations grapple with more imminent threats such as rising sea levels, extreme weather, inadequate healthcare and fragile national finances, Taiwan should use its soft power and help Pacific island countries achieve sustainable development goals, and establish a replicable and scalable model of cooperation that could solidify more mutually beneficial relations in the region.
Taiwan cannot compete with China in terms of financial diplomacy or military coercion. Taipei should instead offer help that would not cause small countries to lose autonomy, make allies feel the value of cooperation and show the world that Taiwan could be a partner in Pacific governance.

Article 2(b) of the Treaty reads: “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.” So, tomorrow would be the Diamond Jubilee of Formosa’s freedom from Japanese sovereignty. AI and industrial sector gap widens: ratings firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

Taiwan’s artificial intelligence (AI) boom is widening the divide across its industrial economy, with technology companies benefiting from surging global investment while steel and petrochemical producers struggle with Chinese overcapacity, geopolitical risks and growing trade barriers, Taiwan Ratings Corp (中華信評) said on Wednesday.
AI has become the biggest source of revenue for Taiwan’s technology hardware companies, with continued capital spending by US cloud-service providers driving growth across the supply chain, the ratings agency said.
The gains are spreading beyond semiconductor and electronics manufacturers to power supplies, substrates and passive components, creating a broader technology investment cycle, it said.
Photo: Wu Hsin-tien, Taipei Times
“AI has become the most important revenue source for Taiwan’s technology hardware companies,” Taiwan Ratings chief analyst Raymond Hsu (許智清) told a news conference in Taipei.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) and Unimicron Technology Corp (欣興) have received ratings outlook upgrades on expectations of AI-related revenue growth, he said.
The boom is also benefiting Yageo Corp (國巨), the world’s third-largest multilayer ceramic capacitor supplier, Taiwan Ratings deputy chief analyst Anne Kuo (郭彥煒) said.
Yageo’s business has accelerated over the past two or three quarters as demand rises for high-end passive components used in AI applications, while supply constraints have also pushed up prices for lower-end products, Kuo said.
Strong AI demand has helped manufacturers absorb higher costs from building factories in the US and Southeast Asia, Kuo said.
At the same time, tight supply in the AI ecosystem has given companies pricing power to pass much of the increase on to customers, she added.
The technology sector could remain resilient even if AI investment slows, Taiwan Ratings said.
Under a stress scenario in which cloud AI revenue falls 50 percent, earnings margins decline 30 percent and cash-conversion cycles lengthen 10 percent, technology companies would still maintain relatively solid earnings, Hsu said.
The outlook is weaker for traditional industries, the agency said.
Taiwan’s steel and petrochemical producers are facing earnings below previous cyclical troughs as Chinese overcapacity weighs on prices and margins, it said.
Rising trade barriers aimed at containing Chinese exports are adding pressure to Taiwan’s export-dependent producers, while geopolitical tensions could raise energy costs and squeeze margins, Taiwan Ratings analyst Irene Lai (賴冠?) said.
Companies with greater exposure to specialty chemicals, vertical integration and diversified businesses are better positioned to weather the downturn, Lai said.
Steelmakers face similar challenges, she said. Although demand is growing in Southeast Asia, new capacity is coming online, limiting the prospect of meaningful improvement in global supply and demand, she added.

Army holds first voluntary marksmanship program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

The army’s first voluntary live-fire shooting program for reservists, with newly relaxed eligibility rules, took place in Taichung on Monday, allowing those who were discharged more than a decade ago to refresh their combat skills with T91 assault rifles.
The Taichung Reserve Command held the exercise amid Taiwan’s efforts to incorporate reserve infantry brigades in its war plans.
The drill was among the first to be held after the Ministry of National Defense lifted a restriction limiting participation in marksmanship refresher training to soldiers who left the service less than 12 years ago.
Photo: CNA
A reporter said 35 former service members took part in the target practice at Chenggong Ling (成功嶺) military training camp.
The participants included former draftees and retired professional soldiers, with many of the latter wearing their old helmets, uniforms, boots and other accoutrements.
Of the participants, 10 were former soldiers who had served more than 12 years ago, including one man whose service dated to two decades ago. Two were retired professional soldiers and some were former conscripts.
The reservists were required to hand over their mobile devices before donning current-issue helmets, body armor with ballistic plate inserts and T91 rifles.
The marksmanship exercise consisted of two parts — a virtual reality training component and a live-fire component — to ease them into weapons handling.
A command sergeant major of a Taichung-based reserve brigade walked the reservists through the design and handling of the unfamiliar rifles in the virtual reality training facility.
They simulated shooting in prone, half-kneel and standing positions for realistic training.
The senior non-commissioned officer supervised the live-fire component of the exercise, during which the reservists zeroed their rifles at 25m, then fired 30 rounds loaded in three magazines at a 175m silhouette target.
The reservists also fired three rounds each in the prone, half-kneel and standing positions behind a barricade at a 175m silhouette target.
Loading only a few rounds in each rifle magazine helped the trainee practice reloading magazines as they shoot, a military spokesperson said.
A new spotting scope enabled the instructor and trainee to observe hits and misses without inspecting the target up close, which would have taken more time than necessary, they said.
Casing catchers were installed on the rifles to protect instructors and trainees on the range, allowing them to focus on shooting instead of dodging hot empty shells, the spokesperson said.
A reservist in his late 40s said shooting a T91 “felt like entering in a new age,” as his issued weapons were the much older T57 and T65K.

Street acrobats entertain motorists stuck in the Kenyan capital’s notorious traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

As the light turns red at a busy intersection in the Kenyan capital, a young man costumed in leopard print emerges into the street to perform somersaults. He is joined by five others, dressed similarly, as they execute a combination of acrobatic stunts.
One of them, juggling woven hats, breaks away and approaches the drivers of vehicles that have come to a halt. He’s hoping for generous tips as he presents his hat to driver after driver while his mates continue their routine. The group breaks away as soon as the traffic lights turn green.
Nairobi’s street acrobats first began appearing in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and they have since become normalized at traffic stops in and around the city, with acrobats taking advantage of gridlocks to perform in exchange for cash tips. It is how they earn a living.
Photo: AP
Mohammed Nyale, 22, said he started doing acrobatics hoping for a life-changing occupation.
“I have always loved acrobatics since I started performing at 15 years old,” he said.
He and others left their homes on the Kenyan coast with dreams of on-stage careers and sold-out theaters, but they have so far settled for the streets, performing their stunts for motorists in Nairobi’s never-ending traffic.
Nyale’s group gathers in the early mornings in an abandoned field in Nairobi’s impoverished neighborhood of Kawangware to rehearse their routines. Next, they move into the streets as traffic starts to build up during the morning rush hour.
“We say a prayer before changing into our costumes,” Nyale said.
They usually perform until noon, taking turns to collect tips from motorists. The amounts given tend to be small, usually no more than 50 shillings (about 40 US cents). Because many Kenyans keep money in mobile wallets, the acrobats also hand out slips of paper with their phone numbers to which tips can be sent.
On a good day they might each earn roughly US$6, enough to look after their basic needs, though on some days they make more.
That is equal to the daily wage of most casual laborers in construction or agriculture in a country where unemployment is widespread. The youth unemployment rate stood between 4.9 percent and 9.9 percent in 2024, according to figures from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.
Earning money from street performances “is what enables us to live in Nairobi because we moved here from quite far and no one is helping us to pay rent,” Nyale said.
They have rivals. Acrobatic troupes have materialized in other parts of the city. Across town, a group including 28-year-old Jackson Okoth entertained motorists along Lang’ata Road.
“There are no opportunities for us that we can go to, so we like it when we are here because it keeps us busy and it keeps us fit also,” Okoth said. “Instead of staying at home and doing reckless things, we decided to come here and perform for motorists and pedestrians.”
Okoth dreams of playing in a professional circus and touring the world.
“I am still on my way, I am still trying, I am still working hard so that one day things might go well and I may find myself in Europe performing in a circus show,” he said.
Some motorists see the acrobats as a nuisance. Others welcome the distraction.
“They are a source of entertainment here on the road. They entertain us and we feel good,” said Geoffrey Kioi, a Nairobi entrepreneur who regularly gives tips to the acrobats. “They are young people. They need to hustle. They are like my sons.”

NTHU president apologizes for job hunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) president John Kao (高為元) yesterday apologized for applying to become chancellor of a US university just three days after being confirmed for a second term at the Taiwanese institution in May, vowing to donate his monthly salary every May for the remainder of his term to refurbish student dormitories and make amends.
Kao was not offered the position at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, despite being shortlisted with two other candidates.
He apologized over the incident in front of about 300 faculty members and students attending an explanatory session on campus, but it drew mixed reactions.
Photo: Hung Mei-hsiu, Taipei Times
Lin Burn-jeng (林本堅), dean of the Semiconductor Research College, and Huang Yi-long (黃一農), a professor of history, said that what Kao did was a matter of trust and honesty, which are now in question.
As the issue could affect NTHU’s operations, its administrators should reconsider Kao’s qualifications for the post so that the university can move forward from the incident, Lin and Huang said.
Former NTHU president Tai Nyan-hwa (戴念華) and other professors and alumni defended Kao and affirmed his contributions to the university during his first term, saying that his job search in the US was a private matter.
Whether Kao is honest and trustworthy should be judged by the way he handles NTHU affairs, rather than how he conducts personal matters, they said.
NTHU chief secretary Chan Hung-lin (詹鴻霖) and vice president Lu Ping-chiang (呂平江) said that the university would convene supervisory board and university council meetings to determine whether Kao should continue serving as president.
The next university council meeting is scheduled for Oct. 20.
Kao’s application for the position in the US sparked criticism following a report by the Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) in July.
Prior to yesterday’s session, Kao issued a letter last month, in which he said that he was deeply sorry for the inconvenience and unease caused by the news of his job hunting in the US and the public discussion of the matter.
“Recruitment and headhunting are common in higher education and in the business sector. However, it is rare for a university overseas to seek out a sitting university president in Taiwan. When such an opportunity arose, it did pique my curiosity. This reflected my insufficient understanding of the differences between workplace cultures in the East and the West,” he said in the letter.
In his speech yesterday, Kao again apologized, saying that he had experienced the most difficult time in his academic career in the past month.
He said that his failure to think matters through carefully has hurt those who believe in him and made the university the subject of gossip.
He let people in the NTHU community down by overlooking the distinctiveness of his duty as president and by beginning to seek other career possibilities during just the initial stage of the second term, he said.
His visit to the Manoa campus was to learn more about the US university’s expectations of him and vice versa, he said, adding that there was no further development afterward, nor did the UH Manoa hold a final vote on whether he should be recruited.
“NTHU did not know I would be given a job offer from another university when they voted to confirm my second term,” Kao said. “I cannot simply ask for your understanding and forgiveness with excuses of curiosity and cultural differences. My previous response to this incident was short and disappointing. This university is where people have dreams and aspirations, and one cannot simply come and go as they please.”
He would fully cooperate with the NTHU investigation, he added.

Spain approves citizenship for Sahrawis born under Spanish rule

01:37:31 KST

Spain approves citizenship for Sahrawis born under Spanish rule
MADRID, Sept 10 - Spain's lower house voted on Thursday to grant citizenship to Sahrawis born when Madrid administered the North African territory of Western Sahara as a colony, a move that could inflame delicate relations with Morocco.
The legislation, which a statement from parliament said was approved with 168 votes in favour, 31 against and 145 abstentions, would also allow descendants of those granted citizenship to acquire it.
Some 70,000 to 110,000 Sahrawis could be eligible for Spanish citizenship, according to local media.
Spain's ruling Socialist Party and its junior left-wing partner Sumar, which filed the initiative, were among those who supported the bill, while the opposition conservative People's Party abstained and far-right Vox voted against it.
"With the adoption of this legislation, we are restoring – and I emphasise, restoring – the Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held it and from whom this state took it away," said Tesh Sidi of the leftist Sumar coalition, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in parliament.
TENSIONS WITH MOROCCO
Tensions have grown between Spain and Morocco following the mass arrival of at least 70,000 migrants in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
Spain controlled Western Sahara under various administrative arrangements from 1884 until 1976. Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and began asserting control over the territory after Spanish rule ended.
The Algerian-backed Polisario Front independence movement seeks recognition of an independent state called the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.
Many Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, or elsewhere abroad, while others remain in Western Sahara.
Spain had supported a referendum in the territory — in line with United Nations resolutions — until Sanchez's government reversed course in 2022 and backed Morocco's position.
Tensions eased somewhat after that shift, with Madrid describing Rabat's autonomy proposal for Western Sahara as "serious, credible and realistic". REUTERS

Unknown

01:37:30 KST

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday pledged to send every US adult US$5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in the midterm elections, an extraordinary gambit to reverse his party’s sagging fortunes in November.
With approximately 270 million US adults, the idea would cost about US$1.35 trillion, require congressional approval and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly US$1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.
It was not immediately clear how the US$5,000 payments would work or whether they would be legal. The White House did not respond to a message seeking details.
Photo: Reuters
“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get US$5,000,” Trump said during the Republican’s midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”
He likened the payments to a corporation’s distributions to shareholders, citing “our tremendous strength and success economically.”
Within an hour, US Vice President J.D. Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy.
Vance suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues, although the sum of Trump’s promised payments would far exceed US tariff revenue even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The national debt last month topped US$40 trillion for the first time.
Trump has frequently lamented that, during the modern era, the president’s party almost always loses seats in the US Congress during the midterms, and he has looked for unorthodox ways to defy the trend, including this week’s convention.
“We’re going to change that,” Trump said. “There’s no reason for it.”
Marc Goldwein, the senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank in Washington, said Trump has no authority to send money to Americans without approval from Congress.
Companies pay dividends when there is a surplus, but the US is running US$2 trillion annual deficits and has US$40 trillion in debt, Goldwein added.
“The idea that we’ve had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable,” he said. “We don’t have surpluses to give away.”
The move was reminiscent of billionaire Elon Musk’s efforts to buy votes in last year’s Wisconsin state Supreme Court race, where he handed out million-dollar checks to voters to try to boost a candidate who ultimately lost.
Trump has discussed the possibility before, but has never tied it to his party’s electoral fortunes. Earlier this year, he proposed a US$2,000 dividend and said he did not think he needed approval from Congress.
Last year, Trump gave members of the military a US$1,776 check that he called a “warrior dividend.”
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” US Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote on X late on Wednesday. “Because Republicans (and America) will win!”

WHO's Southeast Asia regional chief Saima Wazed resigns amid fraud allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:30 UTC
01:37:30 KST

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization's Southeast Asia head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday, according to her resignation letter seen by Reuters, following fraud investigations by the UN agency and Bangladeshi authorities.
Wazed's case shows how the fallout from Hasina's ouster following a deadly uprising against her around mid-2024 has spread to her family members, beyond her political allies. Many of Hasina's allies face criminal charges, including for alleged corruption in Bangladesh, or live in self-imposed exile like Hasina.
In a statement to Reuters on Thursday, the WHO said a committee had recommended Wazed's dismissal the day before her resignation. The UN health agency had placed Wazed, who took office as its Southeast Asia regional director in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025 after Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission, under an interim government that replaced Hasina, filed charges against her in March that year alleging fraud and forgery.
The WHO accused Wazed of "committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China" and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026, seen by Reuters. Wazed has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country's independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, Hasina's father.
Wazed says she was prevented from carrying out duties
"I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done," Wazed said in her resignation letter to Tedros, sent late on Wednesday.
"Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO," she wrote. "Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside."
Wazed declined to comment further.
The WHO said its regional committee and executive board would now consider her resignation. A spokesperson said by email the matter had been handled "with due regard for fairness and due process, while safeguarding the interests of the Organization and its ability to fulfil its mandate."
Last month, it said Wazed was on leave but declined to comment further about her case to maintain confidentiality.
WHO to hold elections in January
Two sources said earlier the UN agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. On Thursday, the agency said Dr Nilesh Buddha would continue as officer-in-charge pending the appointment of a new regional head.
The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.
Regional directors are among the world's most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the Southeast Asia region.
In the July letter, Wazed, through her lawyers, denied any travel fraud, saying it was an administrative oversight by an assistant processing routine reimbursement requests and involved $901. On the credentials accusation, she said she holds an honorary doctorate for her work on autism in Bangladesh and had been clear with Tedros about this qualification.

Taiwan steps up chip R&D, homegrown design software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:30 UTC
01:37:30 KST

Taiwan is expanding semiconductor research infrastructure and developing homegrown chip-design software under a government initiative aimed at maintaining the country’s technological edge, the Cabinet said Thursday.
Cabinet spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said after a Cabinet meeting that the government plans to invest NT $300 billion (US$9.51 billion) through 2033 in areas including next-generation chip design and advanced semiconductor processes.
“Taiwan has a world-leading semiconductor ecosystem, but we still need to continue investing in advanced technology research and development and cultivating high- level talent to consolidate our advantages in the chip industry,” Lee quoted Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) as saying.
Photo: CNA
Peter Hong (洪樂文), head of the National Science and Technology Council’s Department of Engineering and Technologies, said two projects under the Taiwan Chip- based Industrial Innovation Program are being carried out from 2024 to 2028, focusing on research infrastructure and chip-design software.
Under the hardware project, seven university semiconductor institutes will receive subsidies for equipment that will be linked through a single service platform, Hong said.
Two research institutes under the National Institutes of Applied Research also plan to establish an atomic-scale process verification line for sub-1-nanometer processes, he said.
The most advanced semiconductor process currently in mass production is 2 nanometers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) began high-volume production using its 2-nanometer process in the fourth quarter of 2025.
The government-backed Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) will also build an advanced semiconductor pilot line for startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that need low-volume, high-mix trial production, Hong said.
On the software side, Hong said the government wants to strengthen Taiwan’s ability to independently develop electronic design automation (EDA) tools used in chip design, layout and verification.
Such software has traditionally been “in the hands of a few major international companies,” Hong said. However, EDA tools for emerging areas such as advanced packaging remain relatively underdeveloped, creating what he called “a very good opportunity” for Taiwan to enter the market.
Hong said universities will develop key EDA tools for advanced packaging, while ITRI will build an intelligent EDA cloud platform and integrate tools developed by industry and research institutions into a complete chip- design toolchain.
Support for SMEs
Separately, the Cabinet outlined an expanded support plan for SMEs and microenterprises, which together account for 98.9 percent of businesses in Taiwan and nearly 80 percent of employment.
GJ Lee (李冠志), head of the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ Small and Medium Enterprise and Startup Administration, said the government wants technological advances in Taiwan’s high-tech and manufacturing sectors to benefit smaller businesses across industries.
The government aims to help at least 1 million SMEs and microenterprises adopt digital technologies and artificial intelligence, with annual funding expected to reach nearly NT$25 billion from next year, Lee said.

How would Israeli Jews vote in a US election and how would US Jews vote in Israel? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:29 UTC
01:37:29 KST

My immediate curiosity was straightforward: How would Israeli Jews vote in a hypothetical 2026 US national election, and how would American Jews vote in Israel’s October 2026 Knesset election?
My principal conclusion is that Israeli Jews would vote considerably to the Right of Center in a US election, while American Jews would vote substantially to the Left of Center in an Israeli election.
Israeli Jews voting in America would likely produce a strongly Right/Center leaning office holder, from the most conservative to the most liberal on the Right side of the spectrum. American Jews voting in Israel would likely produce a broadly Zionist, centrist, and Center-Left coalition.
Both communities would be heavily influenced by their different sociological environments, political cultures, and geographic circumstances. I recognize that neither Israeli Jews nor American Jews are monolithic entities, but multiple distinct communities.
For the purpose of this exercise, I define the two populations principally by where they live, with the caveats noted below.
By and large, Israelis participate in a highly fluid political system. New parties emerge, disappear, and merge, and unforeseen events can substantially influence voter preferences.
The American political party system is more stable, perhaps even fossilized, dominated by personalities and coalitions within two large parties rather than by parties temporarily rising, falling, disappearing, or bursting onto the scene.
American Jews and Israeli Jews constantly have governmental institutions and political leaders pawing at each other for more power and control of budgetary allocations.
Voting Center and Center-Right in the US, Israeli views would be shaped by Israel’s political culture.
Possessing a collective political identity, they aspire to live in a democracy that is tied to compulsory civic duties, inhabiting a sovereign Jewish state, obliged (with some exceptions) to mandatory military service, pay heavy national taxation, run their lives on a Jewish calendar, have 24/7 security concerns, and experience fierce, unending, and unyielding political debates, remain starkly polarized between ultra-Orthodox and a majority secular population.
American Jews vigorously propound the separation of church and state and only voluntarily participate in politics. Both communities have common ancestral roots going back generations to European and Mediterranean regions.
When American Jews are placed in the Israeli political system, perhaps 65% to 70% of American Jewish voters would support parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, yet many of those votes would be centrist, security-minded, Zionist, and institutionally liberal rather than anti-Zionist.
Orthodox American Jews would strongly support Likud, the Religious Zionist Party, and Shas or United Torah Judaism, while Reform, Conservative, and unaffiliated Jews would heavily favor Yashar, the Democrats, and centrist opposition parties.
The resulting government, with American Jews voting in Israel, might therefore resemble a coalition of Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, the Democrats, and Avigdor Liberman, perhaps totaling 85 to 90 of the Knesset’s 120 seats. It would be a broad Zionist coalition excluding both Netanyahu’s harder Right and the anti-Zionist Left.
It is difficult to assume, however, that American Jews supporting a Center or Center-Left coalition in Israel could readily persuade a new Israeli government toward territorial compromise.
Geopolitical realities in both populations matter: security concerns for someone living in Kfar Saba, Nir Oz, or Hanita generated enormous concern for those who live in Dallas, Denver, or Delray Beach.
Methodology
This exercise is meant to be instructive, not authoritative. We did not conduct an independent survey or apply rigorous statistical methods to original polling. We used survey and polling data assembled by others in Israel and the United States from June through August 15, 2026, then applied several questions to those findings.
On August 18, using past Israeli polling data, we calculated the nine major issues motivating Israeli voters as they prepare for the October 27 Knesset election at our Center for Israel Education.
Naturally, no analysis conducted in August – or polling data collected before then – can incorporate subsequent events, statements, crises, or political developments that occur before October 27.
American and Israeli Jews share a religion and history, yet the two communities differ in significant ways thoroughly examined by many for decades, including Daniel Gordis in We Stand Divided: The Rift Between American Jews and Israel (Jewish Book Council, 2019); Dov Waxman in Trouble in the Tribe: The American Jewish Conflict Over Israel (Princeton, 2016); and Eric Alterman in We Are Not One: A History of America’s Fight Over Israel (Basic Books, 2022), and dozens of articles, surveys, and polls.
For purposes of this exercise, I divided Israeli and American Jews into five political categories: hard Right, Right, Center, Left, and hard Left/progressive.
I also divided each community into four broad categories of religious practice: haredi (ultra-Orthodox), Modern Orthodox, centrist/conservative practicing Jewish, and secular/not practicing.
These categories require considerable caution. Some are imposed on the project and do not correspond precisely with categories used in individual surveys or polls. Political and religious categories also do not align exactly between Israeli and American Jews.
Political self-placement: Israeli Jews and American Jews
The broad conclusions are clear. Israeli Jews are roughly two-thirds Right, one-seventh Center and one-fifth Left. American Jews are roughly one-sixth Right/conservative, one-third Center/moderate and one-half Left/liberal.
Religious practice and identity
These categories are even more approximate than the political categories. “Conservative” Jewish religious practice, for example, has a very different meaning in American Judaism compared with the way religious traditionalism is described in Israel.
Israeli Jews are, proportionately, more religiously practicing than American Jews. Both populations have become more internally polarized, while Israeli Jewish society is moving increasingly toward the religious end of the spectrum. Many Israelis on all sides of either the political or religious spectrum hold multiple outlooks and preferences simultaneously.
My best hypothetical estimate is that a hypothetical Knesset elected solely according to American Jewish political preferences would produce a government dominated by Center and Center-Left parties, with support from elements of the Israeli Right that oppose territorial concessions but are neither driven by haredi or other Orthodox priorities nor committed to Netanyahu.
American Jews would bring a basket-full of liberal political instincts into an Israeli party system that prioritizes security, religion-state relations and coalition politics.
Israel’s present contest includes Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar, the Bennett/Lapid-centered opposition constellation, the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu, the haredi parties, the parties to Likud’s nationalist Right, and potentially additional new parties.
If American Jews voted in Israeli elections and lived in Kfar Saba, Nir Oz, or Hanita, would their voting preferences change with their geographic setting, with news on the hour? What would it take for American and Israeli Jews to be less critical and more patient with the other?
There are 16 million Jews in the world, with seven-eighths of them living in the US and Israel. The last time there were 16 million Jews in the world was in 1939.
The writer is Emory emeritus university professor of Middle Eastern history, political science, and Israel studies, and heads the Center for Israel Education.

Taiwan, US develop non-red charger and battery supply chain
Unknown

2026-09-10

The military worked with the US to develop a non-China supply chain for batteries and chargers used by its Altius-600 drones, with the batteries to be manufactured in Taiwan, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) said yesterday.
Reports that the drones had been procured without chargers — as the original chargers were made in China — were only half correct, as they did not mention the solution being developed by Taiwan and the US, he said.
Reports had said that the chargers were not included in the US’ Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA), as they were made in China, and that as of April, no alternative supplier had been found, requiring US technical representatives to come to Taiwan to charge the drones.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
Wang said they were “suicide drones” that would provide significant firepower and deterrence against armored vehicles and amphibious landings.
Some components of the original charging system were made in China and could not be procured under a government policy restricting the use of any components made in that country, he said.
The military and the US have since completed work on alternatives for the batteries and charging systems, Wang said, adding that the batteries would be manufactured in Taiwan, with a major manufacturer already receiving technology transfers and beginning production.
The new supply chain would meet the military’s needs and could eventually allow Taiwan to become a supplier of batteries and charging systems to Anduril’s global customers, he said.
The Ministry of National Defense late last month announced a NT$26.9 billion (US$852.67 million) procurement of 1,554 Altius-700M anti-armor attack drones and 478 Altius-600 ISR drones.
The first batch of drones bolstered the army’s firepower and were delivered with fully charged batteries, Wang said.
The army said each Altius-600M is procured with one battery installed and one spare. The manufacturer has also developed a non-China supply chain for chargers, which is scheduled to be delivered according to the procurement timetable.
The military regards the Altius-600M as expendable ammunition, meaning the drones are treated as consumables during combat and live-fire training.

The manufacturing sector’s fixed-asset purchases, excluding land, increased for the second straight quarter, as firms in the advanced semiconductor processing, memory, packaging and testing, and artificial intelligence (AI) server segments continued to expand production, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said in a report yesterday.
Fixed assets include machinery, equipment, buildings and construction projects, as well as furniture, fixtures and vehicles.
Purchases rose 53.7 percent year-on-year to NT$956.3 billion (US$30.31 billion) in the second quarter, the ministry said in a report.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Last quarter’s figure was up 36.4 percent from the previous quarter, it said.
Meanwhile, total sales by the manufacturing sector, including overseas production, hit NT$1.1 trillion in the second quarter, increasing 24.2 percent annually and up 13.2 percent from a quarter earlier, the report said.
Last quarter, the electronic components industry posted the largest purchases in fixed assets, at NT$775.1 billion. The amount is a 71.5 percent increase from a year earlier and accounted for 81.1 percent of total purchases by local manufacturers in the quarter, it said.
The computer and optoelectronics industry ranked second in purchases, with firms spending NT$25.8 billion, up 29 percent year-on-year, it said.
The oil and coal, metal, power equipment and machinery equipment industries also reported their purchases increased 5.9, 5.3, 26.2 and 6.8 percent respectively, it said.
The chemical materials and fertilizer and the base metal industries decreased purchases by 12 and 34.3 percent respectively during the quarter, it added.
Overall, the manufacturing sector’s fixed-asset purchases in the first half of the year totaled NT$1.66 trillion, up 34.4 percent from the same period last year, the report said.
Total sales were NT$2.08 trillion, up 21.9 percent annually, it said.
For the second half of the year, driven by continued global AI infrastructure development and high capital expenditures by major cloud service providers, domestic semiconductor, server, related supply chain companies and some traditional industries should continue to expand production capacity, the ministry said.
Furthermore, the continued net zero transition and energy infrastructure investment trends are also expected to sustain investment momentum in the manufacturing sector, it said.
However, as geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties continue to affect global economic growth momentum, manufacturers should remain cautious in making investments and expanding production, the ministry added.

Travel: Traveling eastern Taiwan in style
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:26 UTC
01:37:26 KST

For most train journeys, where you are going is the main consideration. On the Shanlan train (山嵐號) in eastern Taiwan, however, it’s not the “where” but the “how” that matters.
On this pricey but meticulously crafted train journey running between Hualien and Taitung County’s Chihshang (池上), what you’re paying for isn’t to get from Point A to Point B, but rather a sensory, aesthetic and cultural experience.
On the platform, the train stands out vividly next to the other Taiwan Railway carriages. Its exterior is painted in a yellow-green gradient intended to blend harmoniously with the ripening rice paddies of the East Rift Valley floor and the mountains rising up on either side.
Photo: Tyler Cottenie
Stepping on board, I was met with the faint aroma of sandalwood and an interior with a gentle yellow-green color palette to match the exterior. Textured flooring and walls combined with indirect lighting give everything a soft appearance, while the swivel seats are upholstered in a soft green velvet. Large windows beside each seat give each passenger an excellent view of the passing scenery.
The first stop was at Shoufeng Station (壽豐), where we could get out for a few minutes, cross the road, and get a good look at the train on the elevated platform perfectly framed with the Central Mountains in the background, mirroring the plastic Shanlan train ticket.
After boarding the train again, we continued south toward Yuli (玉里), still an hour away. In the meantime, it was time for what could be called the main event of the journey: lunch.
THE DINING EXPERIENCE
The dining experience is undoubtedly one of the highlights of a trip on Shanlan. Though the lunch is served in a wooden box like the traditional Taiwan Railway lunchbox, the similarity ends there. Great effort has been made to make the experience feel like fine dining in a high-end restaurant, from the ambiance to the service to the quality of the ingredients.
Every passenger has a wide, sturdy tabletop on which to place their food. Meals are served from a meal cart by carefully trained wait staff and accompanied by a freshly poured hot beverage in a sturdy stoneware mug that blends harmoniously with the train’s interior. Wooden utensils are presented in a cloth pouch and can be taken home as a souvenir.
The presentation of the food in its wooden lunchbox is a work of art. The carefully selected culinary color palette, accented by delicate garnishes and aesthetic ceramic serving dishes, is sure to spur on your appetite.
About 10 minutes into the meal service, the train enters a series of tunnels and another design feature of the train comes to light, quite literally. Small holes spaced throughout the ceiling light up and transform the dark journey through the railway tunnel into a whimsical starry-night experience. It is this attention to detail in both the environment and the passenger experience that makes Shanlan such a unique ride.
And so, with views of the rice paddies and forested peaks of the East Rift Valley alternating with the artificial stars of the tunnel sections, the train rolls onward to Yuli as passengers enjoy their meals. Ingredients are locally sourced from Hualien and Taitung where possible: taro, seafood, tea, red quinoa and Chihshang rice are all featured on the current menu. Abai — leaf-wrapped millet dumplings common in southern Taiwanese indigenous cuisine — also make an appearance.
An experience on Shanlan is designed to immerse passengers in the natural and cultural world of eastern Taiwan. This extends beyond the colorful exterior of the train, the panoramic views and the local cuisine, to the cultural tour at the journey’s longest stop, in Yuli.
THE CULTURAL HEART OF THE TOUR
A local tour guide was waiting just outside Yuli Station to take Shanlan passengers on a walking tour of the town, explaining some of the history of local culture, industry, businesses and buildings along the way. Passengers are free to leave the tour and explore the town on their own if they wish, with strict instructions to return to the station before the departure time. The northbound Shanlan makes its long stop at Fuli (富里) instead of Yuli.
If you can understand Chinese, the Lion Travel local tours on the tourist trains are worth following, and they usually leave you a few minutes for exploring on your own at the end. If you cannot understand Chinese, however, you’re better off just walking around on your own for an hour.
I stayed with the tour long enough to learn about the former theater building that is now a Poya store, and then set out on my own to find Yuli’s most sought-after stinky tofu. Every time I had passed through Yuli before, the vendor wasn’t operating at that time of day, but this time it was open and I was feeling lucky. Unfortunately, it was a weekend and the queue was about 45 minutes long, so yet again my plan to try this food was foiled.
As a consolation, however, I was treated to other local delicacies from Yuli after getting back on the train. During this final 40-minute leg to Chishang, three gorgeous Japanese-style desserts on a deep-green stone platter were served to each passenger. They are creations of The Town Studio (九日良田) in Yuli, which sources ingredients from local producers.
A SWEET ENDING
There was a round namagashi adorned with tiny red candy flowers, two green crystal candies with a crunchy exterior and jelly interior, and two yokan (a gelatinous block made of red bean, agar and sugar and a frequent souvenir bought in Yuli). I missed the significance of the namagashi, but the leaf-shaped jelly candies clearly represented the forested hills on both sides of the East Rift Valley, while the yokan were shaped like a row of mountains, a miniature version of the Central Mountain Range passing by outside the windows on the west side of the train, and a reproduction of the shape of the Shanlan train ticket.
When I noticed the speck of gold leaf buried inside the transparent layer at the top, I immediately thought of the Dutch coming to eastern Taiwan looking for gold in the mountains in the 17th century, and the abandoned gold mining projects of the 20th century. Whether this was an intentional nod to the trace amounts of gold in Taiwan’s mountains or just a bit of decorative flair, I’m still not sure.
Admiring these creative desserts as the cloud-shrouded mountains and verdant rice paddies rolled by outside my window was as enjoyable as actually eating them, which I did only reluctantly, as it seemed a pity to destroy these works of art.
After dessert and another cup of local tea, the train pulled into Chihshang and we disembarked. The train would make the return journey to Hualien about an hour later with a new cohort of passengers. There was still quite a bit of time left in the day and I used it to rent a bicycle and follow the tourist route around a nearby lake and among the rice paddies. There is a lot to do with a half-day in Chihshang, making it a cleverly chosen end point for the Shanlan.

Rescuers save trafficked wildlife in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:26 UTC
01:37:26 KST

Nawee Changpirom has spent years working to rescue trafficked wildlife in Thailand, but even he can sometimes hardly believe the creatures he has found: leopards, hornbills and once an anteater.
“We even found living corals hidden in a ceiling,” he said.
Nawee heads a raid unit in the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation (DNP) that tries to stop the sale of everything from African elephant ivory to monkeys wanted as pets or for laboratory testing.
Photo: AFP
Alongside weapons, drugs and human trafficking, the illegal wildlife trade is among the most widespread and profitable forms of organized crime globally, run by cross-border cartels.
Thailand occupies a rare position because of its abundant local wildlife, the availability of rare species in nearby countries and its accessibility by sea, air and land.
The DNP set up a dedicated Wildlife Crime Intelligence Unit (WCU) in 2023 with three permanent staff charged with tracking and intercepting illegal purchases.
They spend much of their time trawling social media, which is “the key channel” for buying and selling illegal animals, WCU Director Polawee Buchakiet said.
Wildlife traders often describe animals as needing to be “rehomed,” rather than explicitly offering them for sale, and post tightly cropped images of their wares to avoid revealing their locations.
However, the WCU has undercover officers who can track them down.
One undercover officer — known by the pseudonym “Tee” — has shinned up electricity poles disguised as a repairman to peer into courtyards and take photos, and posed as a land surveyor to look into windows on neighboring plots.
The WCU needs such evidence to obtain court warrants to go in and seize the animals.
He is still haunted by cases where sellers could not be located, or the team arrived too late, finding the creatures either dead or so sickly they died soon after rescue.
Trafficked animals are often weakened by the process of smuggling, stressed by the loss of their habitat and family group and vulnerable to unfamiliar diseases.
“I wonder to myself if we could have done something to get there sooner,” Tee, 43, said. “Whether they are big or small, all animals’ lives are precious.”
At just six months old, the leaf monkey curled up inside DNP vet Thanawadee Phaichana’s rubber-gloved hand is small indeed.
He was intercepted in a luggage at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport, bound for India, where demand for exotic animals as pets has been growing.
A second monkey found in the same bag died after being rescued.
“Most of these smuggled animals will be in a weak condition ... some are given sedatives or even mild anesthetic to keep them from moving or making noise,” Thanawadee said.
Animals rescued in and around Bangkok often come to the DNP’s small facility for initial treatment before being transferred to a sanctuary.
Older, healthier animals might eventually return to the wild, but younger ones struggle to learn the skills needed to survive.
“I feel sorry for them,” Thanawadee said.
Wildlife traffickers can face up to 10 years in prison for crimes involving protected species, or 15 years for endangered species.
There has been a string of recent high-profile arrests, including a July raid that rescued a leaf monkey, a gibbon and hundreds of turtles, as well as multiple interceptions at airports.
There have also been setbacks.
In 2019, a Thai court dismissed the case against suspected wildlife trafficking kingpin Boonchai Bach. While the Thai Supreme Court later sentenced him to prison, he remains at large.
The team also struggles with stonewalling from social media sites and chronic shortages of staff and funds.
Officers posing as undercover buyers sometimes have to use their own money, Nawee said.
What would make a real difference? An end to the exotic pet trade, he said.
“These are wild animals, they don’t belong in a cage,” he added.

Shelton’s four-hour and 28-minute quarter-final defeat of Alcaraz wrapped up at 3:34am on Wednesday — the latest finish in the 145-year history of the US Open.
While late-night finishes are nothing new — in 2022 Alcaraz himself battled Jannik Sinner until 2:50am in the previous latest finish — this year’s tournament has reached new levels.
Photo: Getty images via AFP
So far there have been four finishes which stretched past 2:00am, while other sessions have seen players on court past 1:00am.
Shelton and Alcaraz’s late-night thriller did not get under way until after 11pm on Tuesday, while Venus Williams’ first-round loss to Sofia Kenin did not start until after midnight, eventually wrapping at just after 2:00am.
Writing on X on Tuesday, US tennis great Martina Navratilova suggested the scheduling had reached a tipping point.
“Something has got to give,” Navratilova wrote. “This is not ok and it is not normal,” she said.
Talking about the scheduling earlier in the tournament, Navratilova suggested the US Open should limit the evening session to either one men’s or women’s singles match, in addition to a doubles tie.
At the moment, the US Open typically places a men’s and women’s singles clash on Ashe during its primetime night session.
That though is fraught with risk if either of the two matches goes the distance.
“I think they need to fix the night session. It’s too late,” Navratilova said.
“You’re never on the court at midnight and you never start a match at midnight, so it’s counterproductive for everybody, spectators and the players,” she said.
Former British tennis star Tim Henman, working at the US Open as an analyst for Sky Sports, believes while the raucous night sessions in New York are an integral part of the tournament, a provision could be introduced to move matches to another court if they have not started by a certain time.
“It’s hard. It is not ideal as a professional athlete when you’re playing at that time, but if you look at it from a tournament’s point of view, it’s a massive part of their business model to have those two sessions, to sell, you know, tickets here on Ashe,” Henman said.
“So, for me, we need night sessions, they’re iconic for this event. But also, I think there should be sort of almost protected start times,” he said.
Some commentators though have floated an even more dramatic solution: Reduce the length of tennis matches by slashing the number of sets.

The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:25 UTC
01:37:25 KST

If you wandered down Las Ramblas or lazed on a beach in the Balearics this summer, you probably paid a tourist tax for the privilege. In fact, if you enjoyed any of Europe’s beauty spots in recent years, it is likely that an overnight levy was added to your bill.
Britons have become used to paying these fees abroad but ministers have shied away from introducing them in the UK. The furious response from UK hospitality bosses helps to explain why.
The trade body UKHospitality estimates that a 5% tax on overnight stays in England would result in 12m fewer visits and 33,000 job losses, piling further pressure on an industry battling an increase in taxes and employment costs, as well as the effects of war, Covid and Brexit.
In places like the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales, which rely heavily on tourism, businesses are concerned that visitors will instead go to other parts of the country that choose not to impose such a levy.
Large parts of England’s east coast, for example – from the seaside resort of Skegness to the town of Hartlepool – are expected to remain levy-free after their mayors, from Reform UK and the Conservative party, opposed the proposals on Thursday.
But are overnight levies a success? The evidence suggests that it depends what mayors want to achieve, but they could be very lucrative.
They were introduced in cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona and Venice as a way to prevent over-tourism. But there is little evidence they kept visitors at bay: trips to all three destinations have risen consistently over the past decade (despite Amsterdam charging an additional 12.5% for an overnight stay, believed to be the most expensive tourist tax in Europe).
In April 2023, Manchester became the first place in the UK to introduce an overnight visitor levy, charging £1 per room per night in the city centre. A study published in the journal Tourism Management in 2025 found that the tax had had “no significant impact” on the occupancy of hotels in the city.
In sharp contrast to the vocal opposition of national trade bodies, in Manchester it was hospitality businesses that introduced the levy through a business improvement district.
Local leaders say the £1-a-night levy has raised £10.5m in its first three years of operation, with the revenue ringfenced for cultural projects such as the Brit awards and Mobo awards, both hosted in Manchester this year.
When Labour MPs visit Liverpool for their party conference later this month, they too will be paying a tourist tax: a £2-a-night charge was introduced by its hospitality firms last June, raising more than £2m for projects in sports, culture and conferencing.
Councils in Scotland already have the power to introduce local overnight levies, with Wales following suit next April.
Only Edinburgh has taken the plunge so far, introducing a 5% tourist tax on 24 July, although Cardiff, Glasgow and three other regions of Scotland are expected to follow next year.
Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said on Thursday that Edinburgh’s new charge was “already having damaging effects” on the city.
However, Edinburgh Tourism Action Group, which represents the city’s tourism industry, told the Guardian it was “too early to draw any meaningful conclusions” on its impact. It said many of the cities that had adopted the scheme, including Manchester, had “not experienced a decline in visitor numbers” as a result.
While there is little detailed international research on the economic impact of tourist taxes, a study by Bangor University in Wales in 2024 found no evidence to suggest they deter visitors.
Researchers found they had been introduced in 125 destinations and 26 countries across Europe by 2019, with exceptions mainly in the Nordics and Baltic region. The modest nightly charges were being used to fund hundreds of millions of pounds worth of public projects, they found.
In the Balaeric Islands, for example, the tourism tax had funded €263m (£226m) worth of projects since 2016, including social housing and scientific research.
Zoë Billingham, the chief executive of IPPR North, a thinktank which has campaigned for a tourist tax, said it was wrong to assume that the entire hospitality industry was against the move, pointing to Manchester and Liverpool, where local businesses led the charge.
She added: “With climate change and other uncertainties in the world, I would expect visitor numbers in the UK to increase – that’s not just domestic holidays, but also people from other countries coming here. This is a real way to share in the benefits of tourism growth in this country.”
Henri Murison, chief executive of the business lobby group Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said there was little evidence tourists would be put off by an extra few pounds on their hotel bill.
“The current system, where all the tax paid by businesses goes to central government and none of it benefits the destination, is wrong. It’s just wrong,” he said.
