Yemen’s Houthis seize strategic Red Sea city of Mocha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:16:42 UTC
23:16:42 KST

Yemen’s Houthis seize strategic Red Sea city of Mocha
Houthis deliver ‘significant blow’ to the Yemeni government, expand control over Bab al-Mandeb, analysts say.
Yemen’s Houthis have seized the crucial Red Sea city of Mocha, expanding control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important trade routes.
The Iran-backed group took over Mocha on Thursday while internationally recognised government forces withdrew, sources told Al Jazeera’s Yemen correspondent, Yousef Mawry. Three Yemeni government sources also told the Reuters news agency that the city had been taken.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Back to work, not school: Yemen’s crisis forces children to drop out
- list 2 of 3Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could activate defence pact, Pakistan says
- list 3 of 3Yemen envoy warns of wider war as Houthis threaten Bab al-Mandeb Strait
“The Yemeni government tried to put up a fight; they called reinforcements … but the overwhelming military pressure of the Ansar Allah Houthis eventually [led to them taking] over the port and the city itself,” Mawry said. The Houthis are now moving south towards Dhubab, according to Al Jazeera correspondent Yasser Hassan, reporting from Taiz.
Following the Houthi advance on Thursday, the deputy head of Yemen’s internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council directed government forces on the western coast to regroup. Council member Tariq Saleh described the move as a “tactical withdrawal” to reorganise forces.
Council head Rashad al-Alimi said that developments around Mocha port and Bab al-Mandeb “are not a purely Yemeni affair”, but a regional and international matter tied to global trade. He called on the international community to intervene “to end what the Houthis have done” at both the strait and the port.
Al-Alimi said Bab al-Mandeb “cannot become another Strait of Hormuz” and that “Yemen cannot become another Iran”, calling for decisive international action.
Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba separately sent a message to the United Nations Security Council calling for a firm international stance on the situation on Yemen’s western coast.
‘Not overly surprising’
Wolfgang Pusztai, a defence analyst, said seizing Mocha was a major development as it puts the Houthis in a position to cut off the road leading to Taiz, in a “very significant blow against the government”.
It also enables them to “control pretty much all of Yemen’s coast on the Red Sea” and Bab al-Mandeb, Pusztai told Al Jazeera.
The Strait of Hormuz is about 34 kilometres (21 miles) wide at its narrowest point, compared with about 29km (18 miles) for Bab al-Mandeb.
“This means they could control it just with artillery; they wouldn’t need to even use missiles or drones to attack ships. This would certainly be a major blow to Saudi Arabian shipping and international shipping,” the analyst said.
From Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Hassan said government forces have pledged not to let the Houthis advance further, with field commanders in Taiz and on the western coast saying there are active attempts under way to return to Mocha and retake it.
Saudi foreign policy analyst Abdulaziz Alghashian described the rapid Houthi advance in southern Yemen as “concerning; it’s disappointing, but maybe not overly surprising”.
Taking control of Mocha was not necessarily enabled by “the strength of the Houthis, but probably a discombobulation of the anti-Houthi forces”, he told Al Jazeera.
He added that Saudi Arabia would likely go for a tit-for-tat response as it does not want to enter into “a long-winded campaign”.
‘Safe and uninterrupted’ shipping
Yemen’s ambassador to Qatar, Rajeh Badi, accused Iran of reigniting the war after a lull of about five years and using the Houthis to tighten its grip on Red Sea shipping routes.
Badi said the relationship between Iran and the Houthis was “no longer a secret”, describing the group as one of Iran’s key regional arms alongside Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) in Iraq.
Pusztai said that while Iran has “a huge influence on the Houthis”, “the Houthis are not only proxies of Iran. They are fighting also their own war”.
As part of the Houthis’ offensive against Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, the group has staged attacks on oil facilities and civilian infrastructure deep inside Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi-affiliated Saba news agency on Thursday said Saudi forces launched an additional 40 air strikes on the governorates of Taiz, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.
Yemen’s Supreme Political Council, the de facto Houthi-led governing authority in Sanaa, said on Thursday that clashes on the western coast had been halted following what it described as the expulsion of government-aligned reinforcements.
The council reaffirmed its commitment to international obligations regarding Red Sea navigation and called on parties concerned with maritime security to press Saudi Arabia not to send further reinforcements to Mocha.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam described the coastal offensive as a “national operation” aimed at asserting Yemeni sovereignty. He said the group had no further territorial ambitions and that a “just and honourable peace” remains its strategic choice.
Salam also said that navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait “remain safe and uninterrupted”. However, the group said its ban on Saudi ships remains in place, reported Saba news agency.
Pakistan has warned Iran to restrain the group and said its defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could become operational if Houthi attacks on Saudi territory persist.
The three nations last month finalised a new mutual defence pact, named the Mecca Defence Alliance, after a meeting of senior officials.

Britain has named Israel’s crime. It must act accordingly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:15:42 UTC
23:15:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Britain has named Israel’s crime. It must act accordingly
Britain’s acknowledgement that Israel is carrying out ethnic cleansing in parts of the occupied West Bank should be a watershed moment.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s statement that the forced displacement of Palestinians is being perpetrated by “terrorist settlers”, while members of the Israeli government have supported it through their words and actions, goes significantly further than the language successive British governments have traditionally been willing to use.
This matters. For decades, Britain has condemned Israeli settlements as illegal under international law while maintaining political, economic and military relations with the state responsible for building and expanding them.
But if the British government now accepts that what is taking place is not simply “settlement expansion”, settler violence or another deterioration in an endlessly managed conflict, but ethnic cleansing, then its response must match the gravity of its own words.
So far, it does not.
The government has announced plans to restrict imports from illegal Israeli settlements, take action against companies involved in settlement activity and extend restrictions on arms sales connected to Israel’s occupation of the West Bank.
These measures are welcome. They are also long overdue.
But a glaring contradiction exists between recognising an ongoing crime of such magnitude and proposing measures that may take another six to nine months to implement.
Palestinians being driven from their land cannot wait months for Whitehall to decide which settlement products should be barred from British shelves.
Nor should Britain’s response be confined to the settlements themselves.
Israeli state policy
Israeli settlements are not autonomous entities operating independently of the state. They have been created, protected, financed and expanded through Israeli state policy. Settlers operate under the protection of the Israeli military, while senior ministers openly champion annexation and Palestinian displacement.
The distinction between violent settlers and the state enabling them has therefore become increasingly impossible to sustain.
The scale of the enterprise makes that clear. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers now live in settlements across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, amid roughly 3.3 million Palestinians whose movement, access to land and basic rights are constrained by an occupation Britain itself considers illegal.
The latest expansion of settlement activity, including plans for around 1,200 homes in the strategically crucial E1 area east of Jerusalem, further threatens the territorial continuity of a future Palestinian state.
Britain cannot continue treating each new settlement announcement as an isolated provocation while maintaining largely normal relations with the government implementing the wider project.
Political pressure works
Another reason this announcement matters is that it shows political pressure works.
For years, Palestinian organisations, solidarity movements, human rights groups, MPs and ordinary members of the British public have demanded consequences for Israel’s violations of international law. They have often been dismissed, vilified or accused of pursuing unrealistic demands.
Yet the political ground has shifted.
Polling commissioned by the Council for Arab-British Understanding has found around half of the British public supporting a comprehensive ban on trade with Israeli settlements, with only a small minority opposed. Hundreds of MPs have publicly backed stronger action, while parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee has also called for a settlement trade ban.
The Palestine Solidarity Campaign is therefore justified in arguing that sustained public mobilisation helped produce this change. Millions of people have marched, organised and lobbied during Israel’s war on Gaza, demanding sanctions and an arms embargo.
Government policy does not change in a vacuum.
But campaigners are equally right to insist that the latest measures cannot be the endpoint.
For Palestinians, there is little consolation in Britain finally adopting tougher language after years in which Gaza has been devastated, tens of thousands have been killed, and displacement and settlement expansion have accelerated across the occupied territories.
Britain also cannot credibly invoke international law selectively.
The International Court of Justice’s July 2024 advisory opinion found Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and said states must neither recognise the situation created by that unlawful presence nor render aid or assistance in maintaining it.
That principle should provide the starting point for British policy.
If London believes Israel is engaged in ethnic cleansing, it must examine the entirety of Britain’s relationship with Israel through that lens: arms transfers, trade, financial relationships, companies profiting from occupation, diplomatic protection and any other form of support that could help sustain an unlawful occupation.
Britain must act now
A comprehensive ban on settlement goods should be implemented urgently, not after another six to nine months of deliberation. Companies materially involved in settlements and occupation should face meaningful consequences. Arms restrictions should become a comprehensive embargo wherever there is a risk that British equipment will facilitate violations of international law.
And Britain must be willing to impose costs on the Israeli government itself when its policies facilitate displacement, annexation and settler violence.
This is not about imposing sanctions for their own sake. Sanctions are a way to give international law consequences.
For too long, Western policy towards Israel has operated according to the opposite principle: condemn the settlements, warn against annexation, express concern about civilian deaths, and then preserve the political and economic relationship that allows those policies to continue without meaningful cost.
That approach has failed.
Britain’s new language suggests its government increasingly recognises the scale of that failure. But describing ethnic cleansing while responding with a limited trade measure would merely replace one contradiction with another.
Moreover, Britain bears a particular historic responsibility. From the Balfour Declaration onwards, it played a foundational role in enabling the Zionist project in Palestine and has continued to provide political and material support to Israel.
That history makes Britain’s responsibility to confront the consequences of its policies, rather than merely condemn them, all the more pressing.
If the British government has finally found the courage to name the crime, it must now find the political courage to act accordingly.

Kyiv shopping malls are changing their operating rules during alerts: who will operate when there is a drone threat
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:14:10 EEST
23:14:10 KST

Kyiv shopping malls are changing their operating rules during alerts: who will operate when there is a drone threat
Kyiv • UNN
DREAM, Retroville, and River Mall may operate under the “yellow” level, while TSUM and Ocean Plaza will close during an alert. Individual tenants determine their own operating mode.
Some Kyiv shopping malls will operate during the “yellow” level of air danger starting September 10. UNN reports this, citing information from retailers’ official websites.
Details
According to information circulating about the new operating regime for the capital’s shopping centers, DREAM, Retroville, River Mall, and Kyiv’s Victoria Gardens, among others, may operate during the “yellow” level. However, it should be noted that the operation of the shopping center itself does not mean that all stores, restaurants, cafés, and other establishments inside it will necessarily be open. Tenants may independently determine their operating hours in accordance with their own safety protocols and business conditions.
At the same time, some shopping centers in the capital are still maintaining their previous approach to operating during an air raid alert. In particular, according to the available information, TSUM and Ocean Plaza continue to close when an air raid alert is announced, regardless of the threat level.
What visitors should take into account
Before traveling to a shopping center during the “yellow” level, it is worth checking its current operating hours. Even if the shopping center administration has decided not to suspend operations, individual stores or establishments may temporarily stop serving visitors.
In addition, visitors should pay attention to the current threat level. If the nature of the danger changes, the alert system automatically switches to the corresponding level. For example, after a drone threat alert, a missile threat alert may be announced. In such a case, a separate “all clear” signal between different types of threats is not issued.
What has changed for Kyiv residents and visitors to the capital during an air raid alert in September 2026
The Kyiv Defense Council adopted the decision on the new rules for the operation of the city’s economy on September 7. They came into force at 00:00 on September 10. One of the key changes was the introduction of differentiated alerts for air threats in the capital.
From now on, the alert in Kyiv may have different levels depending on the nature of the danger. The “yellow” level means a drone threat. The “red” level is announced in the event of a massive drone, missile, or missile-and-drone threat. This system has been in effect in the capital since September 6.
The Kyiv city authorities separately reported that the operating schedule of catering establishments, entertainment venues, and shopping centers would not change from September 10. At the same time, business entities of various ownership types may operate in accordance with the government’s decision. This means that during the “yellow” level, a shopping center may continue operating if this complies with the established safety requirements. At the same time, the city’s decision itself does not require every shopping center to automatically remain open during every drone threat.
The situation is different during the “red” level. It applies in the event of a massive drone, missile, or missile-and-drone threat. Thus, a signal at this level indicates a significantly broader range of dangers than the “yellow” level. In such a case, decisions to suspend businesses’ operations and restrict visitor access may be stricter. Therefore, the mere fact that a shopping center is operating during the “yellow” level does not mean that it will remain open after the threat escalates to the “red” level.
Context
It should be noted that recently, the operation of a shopping center after a drone threat was announced became the cause of the deaths of 16 people, while 130 visitors and employees were injured at the time. This refers to the attack by the russian federation’s strike drones on the “Soniachna Halereia” shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, Dnipropetrovsk region, which occurred on August 21.
As local media write, citing testimony from the establishment’s employees, most stores have recently stopped closing, and their salespeople have stopped moving to shelters. The reason was the administration’s requirements. The administration also insisted that one of the food court employees remain on duty near the escalator during the alert, because security personnel went down to the shelter at that time.
Overall, according to estimates by the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers, since the beginning of 2026, the Russians have destroyed three shopping centers and damaged another 9 in Ukraine during missile and drone attacks. Most of the attacks on shopping centers in 2026 occurred in August. Within just a few weeks, the "Olympia" shopping and entertainment center in Pavlohrad, the "Soniachna Halereia" shopping and entertainment center in Kryvyi Rih, "Oscar" in Kherson, and "Karavan" in Dnipro were affected.
The industry's direct losses from this year's attacks reached UAH 3.226 billion ($72.5 million at the NBU exchange rate as of August 31).
"According to our estimates, the direct losses to commercial real estate from Russian attacks in 2026 have already exceeded UAH 3.2 billion. And this is only the cost of restoring destroyed and damaged facilities. This figure does not include lost profits, forced downtime, the costs of restoring operations, business relocations, or other indirect consequences. In fact, the real cost to the industry is significantly higher," said Maksym Havriushyn, head of the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers.
We remind you
On September 9, the Russian army deliberately attacked the grounds of a shopping and entertainment center in Sumy. There are dead and injured.

Trump promises $5,000 payouts if GOP wins midterms: Can the US afford it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:13:03 UTC
23:13:03 KST

Trump promises $5,000 payouts if GOP wins midterms: Can the US afford it?
United States President Donald Trump has promised a $5,000 payout for every adult US citizen if the Republican Party holds onto its narrow control of both houses of Congress at the upcoming midterm elections in November.
Trump headlined a large Republican convention in Dallas, Texas, this week, in a bid to energise Republican supporters amid poor polling that indicates there could be a surge of support for the Democratic Party across the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Republicans divided over Trump’s economy as RNC begins
- list 2 of 3Trump vows to be at centre of US midterms: Republican convention takeaways
- list 3 of 3Trump: Every American gets $5,000 if Republicans win House & Senate
But at a time of rising energy prices, inflation, an ongoing and deeply unpopular war with Iran and rising national debt, the move has prompted questions about whether the world’s biggest economy can actually afford to pay what has been dubbed the “Trump dividend” to 270 million adult Americans – and whether it would even be legal to do so.
What has Trump promised?
“Because we’ve done so well and because our country is making so much money, that only I can make you this promise,” Trump told Republican supporters at Wednesday’s convention.
To loud applause and chants of “USA, USA”, he said: “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” as long as the Republican Party keeps its majorities in both the House of Representatives and the US Senate.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us,” he declared.
Trump did not elaborate on how or when the payments would be made – or how they would be funded – stipulating only that people would be required to spend it in the US. “We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money.”
How much would this proposal cost?
There are up to 270 million adult US citizens, meaning the dividend could cost $1.3 trillion before the administrative costs for the implementation and processing of the payments are taken into account.
Vice President JD Vance suggested the money would come from revenues raised by Trump’s trade tariffs.
He told Fox News: “What the president is talking about is fundamentally a dividend for American workers. We’re taking in an extraordinary amount of revenue because the president of the United States is actually standing up to both foreign companies, but also foreign countries who’ve been taking advantage of America’s workers. I don’t think it’s a controversial idea.”
But the US-based Tax Policy Center projects that tariffs will raise about $1.7 trillion “in fiscal years 2026 through 2036, with $177bn raised in 2026”.
A “Trump dividend” of $5,000 for every US adult, therefore, amounts to about three-quarters of the total revenue projected across 11 years.
Most of that money has not yet been collected, as it is an economic forecast only. Additionally, it does not take into consideration the burden of countertariffs imposed by other countries on US exports.
So how would the US pay for this?
Ultimately, it would have to be funded by national debt, analysts say.
This means the money Trump is promising to the American people would add to the massive mountain of debt the state has borrowed from domestic and foreign investors alike. That extra borrowing drives up the total interest payments the government has to make. That bill will ultimately have to be paid back by the American people.
Currently, the US is paying about $1.1 trillion annually to service its debt, slightly more than it spends on defence.
US national debt hit $40 trillion in August, the highest it’s ever been. The Congressional Budget Office initially projected it would not reach this level for another two years.
Total US debt has been climbing by $1 trillion every five months since 2020 and has doubled since 2017, according to the Peter G Peterson Foundation, a US-based nonpartisan organisation focused on fiscal policy and the national debt. The COVID-19 pandemic – and now the war on Iran – accelerated the debt.
Public debt borrowed from domestic and foreign investors makes up 80 percent – roughly $32 trillion – of the gross debt, according to data from the Department of the Treasury.
About $21 trillion of this public debt is owed domestically, to a variety of creditors including the Federal Reserve ($4.528 trillion), which buys and sells Treasury securities to influence federal interest rates and manage the money supply, according to analysis by the Peter G Peterson Foundation.
Other creditors are mutual funds ($5.195 trillion), pension funds ($1.135 trillion), state and local governments ($1.636 trillion), commercial banks and depository institutions ($2.083 trillion) and other corporate and individual lenders ($6.660 trillion).
Is Trump’s dividend promise legal?
Federal laws in the US prohibit any payments which are designed to influence the way someone votes.
Criminal defence lawyer John W Day told The Associated Press news agency that Trump’s campaign promise does appear to be legal, however: “It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way,” he said. The distinction lies in not handing someone money first and then asking them to vote in a specific way, he added.
Day also notes the fact that the payout would be for everyone, no matter which individuals may have voted. The difficulty might be less about the legal aspect of it and more about whether Congress is likely to approve the payout. A one-off payment to American citizens would have to be approved by Congress. “It doesn’t just exist out there in a slush fund for the president to hand out. So Congress would have a say in whether or not it gets authorised,” Day said.
Has Trump proposed such things before?
Trump has previously promised cash payments. After the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) was set up under Elon Musk at the start of Trump’s second term, Americans were told they would receive part of the money saved by slashing red tape, government workforce reductions and the termination of government contracts.
When DOGE was established, Musk said he expected to cut “at least $2 trillion” from government spending, without identifying a timeframe for doing it. He later lowered that to $1 trillion.
In June 2025, DOGE claimed to have cut $180bn in government costs, although this figure has been disputed. No payments have reportedly been transferred to citizens.
Another dividend payment was promised to citizens in November 2025, when Trump wrote on social media that trillions had been collected in tariff revenues: “A dividend of at least $2,000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.”
There have been no reports of such payouts following this promise, however.

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will visit India on a working trip from September 11-13, where he will take part in the BRICS summit, Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov said at a briefing.
Putin will hold meetings with several international leaders there.
TASS has compiled the Russian presidential aide’s key statements.
Putin’s schedule in India
Russian President Vladimir Putin will visit India on a working trip from September 11 to 13, where he will take part in the BRICS summit.
The Russian president will fly to India this evening.
On September 11, Putin will address the BRICS Business Forum in India: "Our president will participate and deliver a speech outlining initiatives for trade, economic, investment and transport cooperation among the group’s member countries."
Putin will hold a series of international bilateral talks: "As is customary, such multilateral events provide an opportunity for bilateral meetings. This time, too, we have scheduled several bilateral meetings."
Putin will begin his marathon of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the BRICS summit with a meeting with the event’s host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The leaders will also inspect the industrial achievements of Russia and India at the INNOPROM exhibition: "This is a truly important joint event that will undoubtedly provide fresh impetus to trade and economic cooperation between the two countries."
Informal communication between Putin and Modi is invaluable: "We highly value the kind of relationship that has developed between the two leaders."
Modi may visit Russia in 2027 if his schedule does not allow him to make the trip before the end of this year: "Our doors are open and should any opportunity emerge that we can literally jump at then the prime minister will probably come to see us [this year]. Putin also plans to meet with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on September 11: "Contacts between the two countries’ leaders have become regular."
On the same day, Putin will meet with Dilma Rousseff, head of the BRICS New Development Bank: "Our President meets with her frequently, and naturally, priority issues of Russia’s cooperation with the bank will be addressed. These include the financing of projects in Russia’s interests, as well as the modalities of the bank’s participation in implementing promising BRICS financial and economic initiatives -- including those proposed during the Russian chairmanship back in 2024, such as the new investment platform initiative."
On September 11, Putin will hold a bilateral meeting with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa: "We believe that this meeting will allow for a substantive discussion on many aspects of bilateral cooperation and the global agenda."
Putin may meet with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi on September 11 on the sidelines of the BRICS summit: "After [South African President Cyril] Ramaphosa, we are now working out the possibility of a meeting with the President of Egypt. A signal has reached us from the Egyptian side."
Putin will meet with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on September 12, on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India: "It will be an interesting meeting, which undoubtedly is important for both sides in terms of reviewing both bilateral and international issues, including the situation in the Middle East and the ongoing developments around Iran."
Putin will hold a meeting with Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan: "The program of bilateral meetings will conclude with a conversation with the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan. He is the son of the UAE President and will lead his country’s delegation at the BRICS summit."
The Middle East situation will be the main topic of discussion: "The topic is clear -- primarily the situation in the Middle East, Iran, and so on."
No separate full-format meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has been scheduled on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, though they are almost certain to converse during "a so-called pull-aside meeting."
Putin does not plan to hold a news conference for the Kremlin pool on the outcomes of the upcoming BRICS summit in New Delhi.
BRICS summit
The key agreements of the upcoming BRICS summit in New Delhi are expected to be enshrined in the final declaration: "It will reflect the consolidated approaches of the member states to international and regional issues, as well as to developing cooperation within the association."
Three key tracks of joint work will be addressed: politics, security and the economy, including finance and humanitarian and cultural ties.
The main program will begin on Saturday, September 12: "Modi himself will welcome the guests at the exhibition and convention center. Then all the leaders will take part in a meeting of the heads of state of the association."
The meeting is expected to address pressing issues on the global and regional agenda, the results of 20 years of interaction within the strategic partnership in the political, economic and humanitarian spheres, as well as prospects for strengthening coordination among the association’s members.
Particular attention will be paid to reforming the global governance system and strengthening multilateralism in international relations.
Following the meeting, the leaders are scheduled to jointly visit the "Innovations of India" exhibition and a photo exhibition dedicated to the 20th anniversary of BRICS.
In the evening, Indian Prime Minister Modi will traditionally host a gala reception.
On September 13, an expanded session in the "outreach" / "BRICS Plus" format is expected.
Putin and Xi Jinping reach agreement
Putin and Xi Jinping have agreed to hold full-scale bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, scheduled to take place in China’s Shenzhen in November: "This agreement has been reached, and, most notably, it has been explicitly agreed that these will be substantive discussions, as I have already said, and they will require a certain amount of time."
Results of Putin’s talks with Vietnamese president
Talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Vietnamese counterpart To Lam on September 9 were very useful, eventful and comprehensive: "Our leaders had a lot of conversations during this long day and they held meetings both during the official negotiations and while sitting together at lunch. They also enjoyed a lot of positive discussions on the sidelines."
The leaders have agreed to continue communication; specifically, a meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in November has not been ruled out.
Vietnamese President To Lam has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to pay a state visit to Vietnam in 2027.

Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:10:12 UTC
23:10:12 KST

Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran war
Houthis try to take control of more of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government, giving Iran and its allies control over a key shipping lane
Violence has erupted again in Yemen, killing and wounding around 1,000 people and displacing tens of thousands. It is the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have targeted each other with air, missile and drone strikes, threatening to open another front in the US-Iran war. At stake is the balance of power in Yemen, as well as another waterway critical to global shipping.
Though the immediate catalyst for the fighting has been the US-Iran war, it stems from years of conflict in Yemen itself.
Who are the warring parties in Yemen’s civil war and who are their backers?
The two main parties fighting in Yemen’s civil war are the Yemeni government forces alongside their allies, and the Houthi movement. Yemen’s government controls the north-east of the country, and its southern port. The government is the internationally-recognised authority in the country, but is chiefly backed by Saudi Arabia and a coalition of Arab countries which intervened on behalf of the government during Yemen’s civil war.
The Saudi-led coalition, in addition to supporting the Yemeni government forces, directly intervenes militarily in the country, mainly through airstrikes.
The government’s control of the country is contested by the Houthis, who hold the western part of the country, including its capital, Sana’a. The Shia group is broadly aligned with Iran and comprises part of the “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Iran-aligned armed groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah. But while the group is aligned ideologically with Iran, which supplies some arms shipments, the Houthis are considered an independent group with their own policies.
A variety of smaller armed groups are also active in the country.
How did the war in Yemen begin?
The civil war began in 2014 when fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Yemeni army after Houthi supporters were shot at during mass protests against fuel subsidy cuts in the capital, Sana’a. The Houthis promptly seized the capital, and by 2015 had toppled the government.
A coalition of mostly Arab countries, led by Saudi Arabia, then intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was widely criticised for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen.
The Yemeni government declared the southern port city of Aden to be its temporary capital, while the Houthis continued to maintain their control over Sana’a and much of the rest of north-west Yemen.
The government-aligned side was made up of several groups that fractured over the course of the war, primarily along the lines of their two chief backers: Saudi Arabia, which backed the Yemeni government itself, and the United Arab Emirates, which mainly supported the Southern Transitional Council (STC) and the Joint Forces.
The country also fractured, with al-Qaida seizing territory in east Yemen, and separatist groups, such as the STC, pushing for division of the country. The Saudi-led coalition also brought foreign mercenaries into the conflict.
Frontlines hardened and the war entered a deadlock. The Saudi-led coalition’s intervention was becoming increasingly unpopular internationally and had not led to the defeat of the Houthis. Weary of fighting, warring parties agreed to a temporary UN-mediated truce in 2022. The truce was extended twice, and calm largely held across the country until this September.
Why has the UN-brokered peace plan broken down?
The peace plan has been strained since the war in Gaza started on 7 October 2023. Israel launched the war in response to a Hamas-led attack in Israel that killed around 1,200 people. Israel’s war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians and earned widespread condemnation for what a UN committee said was genocide, drew the axis of resistance into the fray.
The Houthis, in what it said was a move of solidarity with the people of Gaza, began targeting ships in the Red Sea that it said were heading for Israel. The western coast of Yemen occupies a strategic position for global shipping because it overlooks Bab al-Mandab, a strait that links the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
The Houthi campaign brought about a US military intervention and strained the truce in Yemen. At the same time, its intervention brought the Houthis support regionally and within the territory they hold.
With the Houthis’ position strengthened, the group stopped seriously engaging in negotiations, frustrating Saudi Arabia.
In July, an Iranian plane landed in Sana’a airport, despite the protests of the Yemeni government, leading Saudi Arabia to strike the airport. The Houthis then declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, a key route for Saudi oil since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz in March.
Why did fighting start again last week?
Last week the Houthis launched a wide-ranging offensive to take parts of the western coast of Yemen and gain a more strategic position over Bab al-Mandab. Fighting then broke out across multiple fronts in Yemen as the Saudi-backed government forces tried to reconsolidate their position, with clashes starting in al-Jawf, al-Baydaa, Taiz and Hodeida.
The Yemeni government forces then released a statement saying they were launching their own campaign to try to retake Sana’a from the Houthis.
It was the most significant fighting in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
What has been the humanitarian impact of the war?
The war in Yemen, and the Saudi-led coalition aerial campaign in particular, has devastated the country’s population. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014 by fighting alone, while hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes, such as hunger and disease. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.
The renewed fighting has further exacerbated humanitarian conditions. The World Health Organization said the latest clashes have killed or wounded more than 1,000 people and displaced tens of thousands.
Why is Bab al-Mandab emerging as a new flashpoint in the region?
Bab al-Mandab is a critical waterway for shipping, with about 10% of global maritime trade passing through the strait. It has become more important since the US started its war against Iran and the latter closed the strait of Hormuz.
The Red Sea, via Bab al-Mandab, has become a vital lifeline for Saudi Arabia to export its oil. If the Houthis gained control over the strait, the group would be able to virtually close shipping through the waterway, or charge tolls. It would give Iran and its allies control over two key shipping lanes in the region.

Israeli legislative election and Netanyahu's politics of enmity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:09:15 UTC
23:09:15 KST

Tugce Ersoy Ceylan is a professor of International Relations at Izmir Katip Celebi University in Türkiye.
Israel is heading to a legislative election on Oct. 27. This election marks the first time since 1988 that a Knesset has completed its full four-year term. It is worth noting that the survival of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition -- comprising far-right, ultra-Orthodox, and religious Zionist parties -- was driven less by popular domestic policies and more by the regional war that erupted in Gaza following Oct. 7, 2023.
As soon as the election date was finalized, Netanyahu wasted no time launching his campaign. It was no secret that a core pillar of his strategy would involve dodging responsibility for the events of Oct. 7. However, it was equally clear that he would struggle to convince the Israeli public of this. Consequently, Netanyahu has built the second pillar of his campaign using a new narrative of hostility, fueled by AI-generated videos.
In a recent AI-generated video posted on Netanyahu’s official X account, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Iranian leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are depicted preparing to celebrate Netanyahu's electoral defeat. The celebration is cut short when it becomes apparent that Netanyahu is going to win. The underlying message here is unmistakably clear: "My defeat is a victory for these actors."
But why is Netanyahu grouping such vastly different figures together on a shared stage of "enemies," and how does this rhetoric serve him in the upcoming election?
Rather than inventing a new enemy, Netanyahu is drawing false equivalencies between his existing and potential adversaries. By lumping together figures ranging from the Iranian leader and President Erdogan to Mamdani and Abbas, he conflates tensions of these actors with Israel and political and legal criticisms directed at him personally, framing them all as a single security issue. Consequently, an attempt is being made to portray the election not as a democratic assessment of the government's track record, but rather as a referendum on "defending Netanyahu against Israel's enemies."
It is worth noting that this video is the second phase of a Likud billboard campaign launched in August. This proves the video isn't just a throwaway social media stunt, but a carefully calculated campaign narrative. The original August billboard featured the Iranian leader, Erdogan, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem, and Mamdani alongside the slogan: "They want Netanyahu to lose; don't let them win." In the latest video, Mahmoud Abbas replaces the Hezbollah leader.
Taken together, the two campaigns place an armed non-state actor, the president of a NATO member state, the President of Palestine, and a democratically elected American mayor at the exact same threat level. This reveals that the campaign defines threats not by their actual capabilities, but solely by their opposition to Netanyahu.
The reality is that President Erdogan is hardly a new bogeyman in Israeli right-wing rhetoric. Tensions between Türkiye and Israel were already deeply personalized, fueled by Israeli genocide in Gaza, geopolitical rivalry over Syria, and competition for regional dominance. Türkiye's push for Netanyahu to face accountability -- coupled with its vocal backing of the ICC arrest warrants against him -- has only poured fuel on the fire.
Mamdani's inclusion is equally telling. In the campaign video, his political critiques -- specifically his remarks on the ICC warrants -- are treated as indistinguishable from the kinetic security threats posed by Iran and Hezbollah. This framing tries to strip President Erdogan and Mamdani of their actual status as critical foreign politicians, and goes on to try to typecast them instead as the regional and American proxies of an anti-Israel enemy front.
Ultimately, the "enemy" label has been hollowed out, losing any connection to actual intent or military capability. In this narrative, wanting Netanyahu out of office is made perfectly synonymous with wanting the destruction of Israel itself. The true target of this fear-driven messaging is not the foreign leaders shown on screen. While not a single Israeli opposition figure appears in the video, they are undeniably its real intended audience.
The underlying logic is straightforward: Khamenei, Erdogan, Abbas, and Mamdani want Netanyahu to lose; so does the Israeli opposition. Therefore, putting the opposition in power would be handing a victory to Israel's adversaries. Rather than labeling his domestic rivals as outright traitors, Netanyahu frames them as the vehicles that will deliver the enemy's desired outcome. This deliberately blurs the line between legitimate political dissent and national betrayal.
Thus, the campaign peddles the idea that Netanyahu's political survival is a matter of state security. His traditional claim of "Only I can keep Israel safe" has mutated into a more straightforward warning: "If I fall, the enemy wins." This conflation of personal and national security is a classic, highly effective page out of the Netanyahu playbook.
It would be misleading to suggest that this campaign has won over the entire Israeli public. Moreover, attributing the backlash entirely to the political left ignores the deep complexities of Israeli society. Tellingly, condemnation of the AI-generated video didn't just come from the left-leaning Haaretz. Even an op-ed in the right-leaning Israel Hayom described the August billboard campaign as Likud's desperate "search for an enemy to survive at the ballot box." Meanwhile, opposition lawmaker Naama Lazimi released a parody of the campaign, replacing the original targets with figures from Netanyahu's own inner circle who have come under fire for their ties to Qatar.
Still, it would be naive to assume that Netanyahu's rhetoric doesn't have any electoral base. Although polling varies by firm, Netanyahu hasn't completely lost his "Mr. Security" persona, even amidst widespread domestic discontent. However, a Sept. 7 poll orchestrated by Channel 12 showed Gadi Eisenkot edging out Netanyahu 42% to 35% as the preferred choice for prime minister.
Currently, the pro-Netanyahu bloc lacks a clear path to a majority, even though the margins between the opposing camps fluctuate wildly. Ultimately, this aggressive campaign strategy is not the product of a confident incumbent, but rather a symptom of a polarized and volatile electoral landscape.
The objective of these provocative visuals is to feed on the security anxieties of right-wing voters, driving turnout at the ballot box and enforcing strict bloc loyalty. Far from a simple stunt, Netanyahu's AI-generated video executes four political maneuvers. Firstly, it actively pivots the electoral debate away from the government’s culpability for Oct. 7, the staggering toll of the war, the hostage crisis, and Israel’s deepening diplomatic isolation. Secondly, it rebrands vulnerability as strength by framing the sheer volume of Netanyahu's detractors not as a diplomatic collapse, but as proof of his defiant strongman leadership. Thirdly, it is purposefully designed to consolidate a fractured right-wing base -- which risks bleeding votes to marginal parties hovering near the electoral threshold -- by weaponizing the fear that a split vote only serves the enemy. Lastly, the campaign methodically hollows out the legitimacy of domestic democratic dissent by treating opposition to Netanyahu as perfectly synonymous with hostility toward Israel itself.
Netanyahu may be deploying the technology of tomorrow, but the playbook he is running is as old as statecraft itself. It relies on tethering the survival of the leader to the survival of the nation, turning foreign adversaries into the ultimate referees of domestic politics, and casting an electoral loss as a national capitulation.
The true artificiality in this video, then, is not in the pixels; it is in the premise. The real fabrication is the claim that these vastly disparate actors constitute a single, monolithic threat. Rather than discovering new adversaries, Netanyahu is simply constructing a catch-all "enemy" category broad enough to swallow anyone who opposes him. In the process, the distinctions between a kinetic military threat, a diplomatic rival, a legal critic, and a democratic opponent are consciously and deliberately erased.

Regions Calling: Russia’s Indigenous Activists Assemble in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:08:48 UTC
23:08:48 KST

Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
MT’s special correspondent Leyla Latypova traveled to Berlin last week for the Indigenous Vision forum, which brought together some of the leading Indigenous voices from Russia and allies from the U.S., Europe, Central Asia and Oceania.
For this week’s edition, Latypova spoke with conference organizers and attendees to understand where Russia’s Indigenous rights movement sits on the global political stage.
The Spotlight
BERLIN — Dozens of Indigenous activists from Russia and allies from around the world gathered in Germany’s capital last week for the second annual Indigenous Vision Forum.
Organized by a consortium of NGOs led by exiled and diaspora activists from Russia’s ethnic republics and Indigenous communities, the first forum was held in July 2025 under an umbrella theme of “centering Indigenous voices, resilience and knowledge.”
This year’s topic, “navigating the future,” reflects the transformation that Russia’s Indigenous opposition has undergone since 2022. What began as a grassroots movement united by anti-war sentiment at the start of the invasion of Ukraine has since evolved into a political force aiming to shape global discourse and policies on Russia.
“This was a natural transformation,” said Sargylana Kondakova of the Free Yakutia Foundation, an exiled anti-war group from the republic of Sakha that co-organized the event.
“We understand that if we won’t speak on the international stage, if we won’t enlist the support of our allies, then everything could end very tragically for our peoples,” she added.
Kondakova, who rose to prominence in 2022 with a video condemning the invasion of Ukraine that she filmed on the streets of Melbourne, is reluctant to call herself a politician. Yet she said she realizes that everything Indigenous campaigners from Russia do is political.
“Our future also depends on who we are negotiating with, where we speak, what we say and how we say it,” she said.
Since last year’s forum, Indigenous activists from Russia have appeared at the UN, the OSCE and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), where they gained five out of 15 seats in the body’s Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces.
In a likely nod to these achievements, the forum’s inaugural panel tried to locate where the West stands on the discourse surrounding the decolonization of Russia.
Mariia Mezentseva-Fedorenko, a Ukrainian MP and chairwoman of Kyiv’s delegation to PACE, kicked off the event with a speech highlighting Ukraine’s efforts to codify the notions of “decolonization” and “oppressed nations” of Russia in international law.
Mezentseva-Fedorenko — who spoke via videoconference from Kharkiv, where air raid sirens wailed as she spoke — is among a growing number of Ukrainian foreign policy figures who believe Russia’s Indigenous communities could hold the key to ensuring Europe’s long-term political security.
“I'm here out of solidarity, both personal and Ukrainian,” said Tetiana Katrych from the Ukrainian NGO Decolonization. “The same empire colonized us…We are just at different stages of leaving it.”
Katrych believes that a Ukrainian victory in the war can’t guarantee that Russia won’t attack its neighbor again, meaning “stable peace for both Ukraine and Europe can be achieved only when the empire ceases to exist in its current form.”
“We want to cooperate with the republics and Indigenous peoples to ensure stable peace,” said Katrych.
Events in Germany, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party won a historic victory in Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt state election, hung over nearly every discussion at the forum.
Activists warned that the global rise of the far-right risks pushing the fight for Indigenous rights to the margins of international policymaking and further threatens vulnerable groups who fled Russia for the West but remained outspoken about their causes in exile.
Indigenous activists said they are also forced to face off with mainstream Russian opposition movements and politicians, who they accuse of trying to “co-opt and hijack the decolonial agenda.”
“Seeking policy change and publicity for Indigenous people [of Russia] on international platforms is about Indigenous people currently inside the country. This is a foundation for the future, although the results of these efforts will not be immediately noticeable,” said Seseg Jigjitova of Nomads Indigenous Collective, a German NGO that co-organized the forum.
Jigjitova said every discussion at the forum — whether about Indigenous political prisoners in Russia or the revitalization of the Indigenous Māori language in New Zealand — “appealed to all Indigenous peoples, including those inside Russia.”
As Russia is home to more than 180 ethnic groups, the country’s Indigenous rights movement likewise boasts a rich ethnic and political diversity.
While some prominent figures belong to nations numbering fewer than 2,000 people, others number in the millions and have ethnic homelands in Russia’s republics that were once nearly equal players in the federation or attempted to secede from it altogether.
As well as its diversity, the Indigenous rights movement’s growing visibility since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has also exposed its divisions.
The sources of these divisions range from left-right political lines to differing understandings of who should be considered Indigenous in Russia to varying degrees of support for economic and political independence of the republics to backing cooperation with mainstream opposition groups.
The Berlin forum further shed light on these cracks, with a handful of high-profile Indigenous figures notably absent. Kondakova said this was because organizers were limited to about 100 attendees.
“We couldn’t even invite some of our allies,” said Kondakova.
“There are [Indigenous] organizations whose political views we don’t share and have debates or even conflicts with them, but that’s normal. We still have contact, we talk, we don’t label anyone as enemies and don’t ban them from our platforms],” Kondakova told The Moscow Times. “That’s already a good thing, since we are striving to build democracy [in Russia].”
Forum co-organizer Batlay Matenov, a member of the PACE Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces, saw it somewhat differently.
He said he “actually did send out invitations” to his fellow PACE Platform members, none of whom were present at the event.
“Some people didn't reply, and there were others I decided not to invite,” he said.
Matenov, the only Indigenous activist at the event who currently holds public office, described his time on the PACE Platform as “tough” and “difficult.”
“If a politician promises you something, you 100% won’t see it followed through, or maybe you will, but in three years or something like that,” he said. “I actually became a little disillusioned with politics.”

The Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine is working on a return ambassador initiative involving volunteers who will help Ukrainians abroad get more information about life and opportunities in specific communities in Ukraine, the ministry said on its website on Thursday.
The initiative is primarily focused on Ukrainians who do not have the opportunity to return to their previous place of residence.
The ambassador operating model was developed on September 7-10 in Vinnytsia during a workshop titled "Return Ambassadors in Communities: From Idea to Implementation."
In particular, representatives of non-governmental organizations and 20 communities from various regions of Ukraine participated in the workshop.
"Our task is to ensure that Ukrainians abroad have as much information as possible to make their personal decision to return to Ukraine: what support programs are available in the state, which community to choose for life, what documents to process, and so on," Deputy Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity for European Integration Ilona Havronska said.
According to her, it is also important that Ukrainians abroad can feel that they are expected not only at the state level, but also at the level of people. The return ambassador initiative should facilitate the introduction of potential returnees to a specific community and help them establish local contacts.
At the same time, the ambassadors will not replace professional return consultants. The ambassadors will help people learn more about life in a specific community from a resident's perspective and establish local contacts, while consultants will provide professional information about available state and local programs, services, and tools.
Such consultants will work in Unity Centers and partner organizations of the Unity Network.

Shadow network of brokers and fixers exploits Syrians at Lebanon border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:08:33 UTC
23:08:33 KST

A market of fixers, travel agencies and border brokers charges Syrians between $180 for a 48-hour stay and $4,700 for annual residency, far above Lebanon's official fees, as procedures have tightened sharply since al-Assad's fall.
Syrian travellers crossing into Lebanon pay up to 60 times the official entry fee to brokers, fixers and travel agencies behind a profitable parallel market around Lebanese border procedures that have tightened sharply since Bashar al-Assad's fall in December 2024.
A driver working the Damascus-Beirut route, speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity for security reasons, described a system in which travel agencies in the Syrian capital, paperwork fixers at the crossing and partners in Beirut sell packaged entry solutions to Syrians who cannot navigate the official process alone.
Lebanon's General Security Directorate charges up to $75 in official fees. The actual cost borne by travellers, according to Euronews' sources, is nowhere near that figure.
A 48-hour stay arranged through the network costs $180, a week costs around $260 and a month runs to $400. A six-month option — currently suspended — was priced at $1,500, while arranging an annual residence costs approximately $4,700.
The difference between the official fee and what travellers actually pay goes to the fixers as "bribes" or "kickbacks" to facilitate paperwork and bypass requirements such as proving cash reserves, presenting a hotel booking, or producing an onward airline ticket.
The process runs on enforced discretion. Travellers must not reveal to Lebanese General Security personnel that a driver or agency arranged their paperwork.
"Revealing this relationship could lead to the driver's arrest and a ban on his entering Lebanese territory," the source said.
Under what he described as the "tourist group" arrangement, travellers must also surrender their passport or identity card to a guarantor or company representative for the duration of the stay, to be returned on departure. Those granted a "free document" arrangement can keep their papers.
Lebanon's punishing penalties
Even categories of travellers who should theoretically benefit from smoother procedures are charged.
Holders of professional union cards, first-category commercial registrations or electronic visas for third countries are asked to pay a $60 "service fee" at the border on top of other costs, with waiting times that remain long and permitted stays that are kept short — 15 days for traders and union members, 24 hours for transit travellers.
The penalties for overstaying are punishing. Exceeding a one-month permit by a single day results in a $60 fine and a one-year ban from Lebanon. Violating a six-month residence limit costs $270 in fines, rising the longer the overstay continues.
Lebanon hosts an estimated 1.5 million Syrian refugees, the highest per capita refugee population in the world relative to the host country's size.
Lebanese authorities have cited pressure on public services, the labour market and the broader refugee dossier as justification for restricting Syrian entry.
The procedures have tightened over several years and have intensified since the fall of al-Assad's regime, which has drawn significant numbers of Syrians back toward the border.
The Syrian side of the crossing has become easier since December 2024. Checkpoints run by the Fourth Division and other Assad-era security units — notorious for extortion and harassment — have gone. The complications are now mostly on the Lebanese side.
Infrastructure issues not helping
Physical damage to infrastructure has added to the journey's cost. Israeli air strikes before al-Assad's fall destroyed the Daboussieh and Arida crossings, which remain closed.
Vehicles from Syria's coastal cities must now travel a significantly longer inland route through Homs, Qusayr, Hermel and Baalbek before entering Lebanon.
The Jisr Qamar-Bekaa crossing is open only to pedestrians after sustaining damage. A car from Damascus to Beirut — 114 kilometres — costs around $100 one way.
The same journey from Latakia, forced along the detour, costs roughly $250, or $500 return, over what becomes up to 800 kilometres of travel.
The source said he and colleagues now frequently cross with only one or two passengers, whereas previously they would have filled a vehicle.
Before 2014, he recalled, a Syrian could present an identity card at the border and receive six months' entry.
He said he hoped movement between the two countries would ease again, restoring business to drivers and opening up travel and tourism that the current system has effectively priced out of reach for many Syrians.
Euronews could not independently verify all figures provided by the source. Lebanese authorities had not responded to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Photos: Spanish Air Force F‑18s join NATO air defense mission in Estonia

Photos: Spanish Air Force F‑18s join NATO air defense mission in Estonia
Estonia's air defense capability has been significantly beefed up by the recent arrival of a contingent of Spanish Air Force F/A‑18 Hornets.

A ceremony at Ämari Air Base on Tuesday marked the start of the deployment, which will last a month.
"Our priority is to be ready to take over operational duties at the earliest opportunity and make the most effective possible contribution to Baltic air defense," said Maj. Antonio Mancebo Marín, commander of the Spanish Air and Space Force's Ámbar unit. "Cooperation with our Estonian hosts and Turkish allies allows us to quickly align procedures and operate safely and effectively from the very first mission," he went on, via a press release.
"We welcome the Spanish Air Force contingent to Ämari Air Base, where it will support the Turkish‑led NATO air defence mission over the Baltic states," said outgoing Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk. "With its F‑18 fighter jets, the Spanish unit strengthens one of the most visible expressions of NATO collective defense – a continuous presence that ensures the protection of our shared airspace every day," Kuusk added.
The Spanish Ámbar tactical air unit arrived in Estonia from Zaragoza in its home country, starting operations in late August.
Spanish F-18 fighter jets have joined the -led NATO air defence mission at Ämari Air Base, strengthening Allied air power in Estonia and on NATO's eastern flank.
The Spanish detachment will operate from Estonia for around a month. 
 Sgt. Siim Verner Teder#kaitsevägi… pic.twitter.com/pmpAxmpTX3
The unit also trained with their Estonian Air Force (Õhuvägi) and Turkish allies, with the F‑18s joining the Turkish F‑16 Fighting Falcons already at Ämari. Aircrews rehearsed working together and familiarized themselves with the specifics of flight operations in the region.
Training did not only take place in the air: The rescue team at Ämari Air Base together with Spanish medical personnel jointly practised rescue and emergency response procedures.
This is the fourth time since 2015 Spanish personnel have contributed to the air defense mission at Ämari.
The Turkish deployment at Ämari is for four months and involves five F‑16s and close to 80 personnel. It is part of an expanded air defense mission which came into being on August 1 following the NATO summit in Ankara and superseding the Baltic air policing mission, which had been in existence for nearly 20 years.

In Tuscany, more than 63,000 lightning strikes were recorded over 12 hours, while 115 millimetres of rain fell in the Grosseto area.
More than 200 operations were carried out by the regional Civil Protection system and firefighters, including rescues from flooded underpasses.
In Lombardy, 45 people were evacuated after a major landslide in Val Masino, in the province of Sondrio, while flooding also affected parts of the Spedali Civili hospital in Brescia.

In Milan, the Lambro River overflowed its banks overnight, temporarily flooding streets in the city.
Several cars were also trapped in an underpass in nearby Vimodrone, with firefighters responding to assist those inside.
Flooding and heavy rain also disrupted rail services in Friuli Venezia Giulia, where underpasses in Latisana, San Giorgio di Nogaro and Torviscosa were submerged.
Delays of up to an hour were reported, while replacement buses were deployed on some routes.
In Liguria, the Lavagna River overflowed in several places in Calvari, near Genoa, while flooding and fallen trees were reported in parts of Tuscany, Marche and Piedmont.
An orange weather alert is in effect in four regions, Veneto, Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany and Marche, as an Atlantic low-pressure system brings further heavy rain and thunderstorms across central and northern Italy.
Authorities have warned of further flooding, landslides and rapid rises in smaller waterways in areas affected by the rainfall.

German foreign minister urges voters to back Ukraine, NATO as far right surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:03:24 UTC
23:03:24 KST

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul addresses a press conference at the Franz Liszt University of Music Weimar in Weimar on Sept. 3, 2026. | Jens Schlüter/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — German officials must do more to convince voters of continued support for Ukraine and the country’s commitments to NATO, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday.
NATO is undergoing a “political stress test” both from the external threat posed by Russia and from skepticism at home that had become “visible and tangible” in recent state elections, he said at the conference of German ambassadors in Berlin.
He made a similar appeal over Ukraine, saying Germany would continue to stand by Kyiv and arguing that its support was not only for Ukraine but “for the benefit of our security in Europe.”
Advertisement
The call comes after the AfD won 43.8% in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result and leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats a distant second at 17.2 %.
Wadephul argued Thursday that the way forward was not to retreat from Germany’s commitments, but to do a better job of explaining why they matter.
He cast the challenge in stark historical terms, invoking the collapse of Germany’s democracy between the two World Wars. “Germany knows from the Weimar Republic what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system,” he said. “We have to show that we have learned our lesson.”
The Weimar Republic, Germany’s first parliamentary democracy, was progressively hollowed out amid economic crisis, political paralysis and growing support for anti-democratic forces before Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in 1933.
As for the results of Sunday's vote, they were not only the AfD’s strongest-ever showing, but the highest vote share won by any party in the state since German reunification.
During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund repeatedly presented spending abroad as money missing at home. He told regional broadcaster MDR that Germany was “giving away money all over the world” and pointed specifically to support for Kyiv: “Every minute, €20,000 goes to Ukraine. That is all money we are missing.”
Advertisement
That message is feeding into an increasingly uncomfortable guns-versus-butter debate in Berlin, just as Merz’s coalition negotiates the 2027 budget. Germany is set to spend roughly €140 billion on defense next year while facing mounting pressure over pensions, health care and other public services.
The scale of the shift is stark: Defense spending next year will almost match the roughly €145 billion federal contribution to the pension system, according to Kiel Institute calculations. In 2022, Germany spent about €50 billion on defense compared with €115 billion on pensions.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte backed Wadephul’s broader message, telling the ambassadors that Germany’s choices had consequences far beyond its borders.
“I count on every one of you in this room to carry that message with you: that a stronger Germany makes Europe stronger, that a stronger Europe makes NATO stronger,” he said, speaking at the same conference.
Rutte also played down the risk that electoral gains by far-right parties could weaken the alliance. NATO would work with “whoever is elected,” he said, adding that he had “no doubt that the alliance will stay very strong.”

Shyness makes facial expressions seem more intense, but only in certain cultures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

People with higher levels of shyness tend to perceive other people’s facial expressions as more intense, but this effect appears to depend heavily on their cultural background. A recent study found that shyness heightens the perceived intensity of emotions among young adults in Mainland China, but the same pattern does not appear in Canadian populations. The research, published in Psychological Reports, suggests that cultural rules about how we display our feelings play a major role in how personality shapes our perception of others.
Emotions are a universal human experience, but the way we display and interpret them depends on where we grow up. In Western societies, expressing emotions openly and directly is generally encouraged. In contrast, many East Asian societies place a higher value on social harmony, which often translates to more subdued emotional displays. This idea is supported by a variety of prior studies. For example, a 2016 review noted that people in Western cultures tend to experience and value high-energy emotions, while people in Eastern cultures tend to prefer and experience calmer, lower-energy emotional states.
Because emotional displays are more restrained in collectivist cultures, individuals in these environments might learn to pay closer attention to subtle changes in facial expressions. This cultural tuning can even be seen at the neural level. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that simply hearing an emotion word changed how the brains of Chinese immigrants processed facial expressions, while having no such effect on the brains of White American participants.
Beyond cultural background, individual personality traits also influence how we read faces. Shyness is a personality trait characterized by feeling nervous, timid, or self-conscious in social situations. People with high levels of shyness often experience a strong fear of being judged by others, which can cause them to become highly vigilant when navigating social interactions. Prior research hints that shy individuals might overestimate the intensity of negative emotions, seeing them as more threatening than they actually are.
Until now, it was unknown how a person’s shyness and their broader cultural environment might combine to shape how they judge emotional intensity. Emotional intensity refers to the physical strength or energy of a feeling displayed on someone’s face. A slight smile represents a low-intensity emotion, while a wide grin represents a high-intensity emotion. To address this gap, researchers led by Xiaoxue (Sonia) Kong, an assistant professor at the University of Northern British Columbia, and Gabriel (Naiqi) Xiao, an associate professor at McMaster University, set out to see if the link between shyness and emotion perception changes across different cultural contexts.
“Previous research has shown that both cultural background and individual personality traits can influence how people perceive facial emotions, but very few studies have examined these two factors together,” Kong and Xiao told PsyPost.
“We were particularly interested in shyness because shy individuals may be more sensitive to social and emotional cues and shyness is also a personality trait whose expression and implications can be shaped by culture. So we wanted to bring these two areas together.”
The researchers recruited 160 young adults for their experiment. This included 47 participants living in Mainland China, alongside 59 White participants and 54 East Asian participants living in Canada. The East Asian Canadian group primarily consisted of individuals originally from regions like Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan who had been living in Canada for four to ten years.
To measure shyness, the participants completed a widely used questionnaire that asked them to rate how strongly they agreed with statements about feeling nervous or tense in social settings. Next, the participants completed a computer-based emotion perception task.
During this task, participants looked at photographs of faces expressing happiness, sadness, anger, fear, or a neutral state. To prevent the participants from struggling to read the faces of people from unfamiliar backgrounds, the researchers only showed faces that matched the participant’s own racial group. The researchers used specialized software to blend emotional faces with neutral faces, creating five specific levels of emotional intensity: zero percent, 25 percent, 50 percent, 75 percent, and 100 percent. Each face appeared on the screen for a brief moment, and the participants then used a sliding scale from zero to 100 to rate how intense the emotion looked.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that participants across all three groups were generally accurate at tracking emotional intensity. As the physical intensity of the facial expression increased in the photographs, the participants’ intensity ratings reliably increased as well.
However, the participants’ level of shyness had a distinct impact on these ratings depending on their cultural group. Among the participants living in Mainland China, shyness acted as a strong amplifier. The higher a Chinese participant scored on the shyness scale, the more intense they perceived all the facial expressions to be. This heightened sensitivity applied across the board, whether the face was showing a positive emotion like happiness or a negative one like fear.
“One finding that surprised us was that the effect of shyness was not limited to negative emotions,” the researchers explained.
“Previous research has often linked shyness to heightened sensitivity to socially threatening or negative emotional cues, but in our study, shyness was associated with greater perceived emotional intensity more broadly among the Mainland Chinese participants.”
This amplifying effect of shyness was completely absent in both the White Canadian and East Asian Canadian groups. For the participants living in Canada, being highly shy did not change how intensely they rated the facial expressions.
“We included both White Canadian and East Asian Canadian participants, in addition to participants living in Mainland China,” the researchers noted. “The fact that the two Canadian groups showed similar patterns, while the Mainland Chinese group differed, suggests that where people live and the cultural environment they experience may be important alongside ethnic background when we think about personality and emotion perception.”
“The way personality influences our perception of other people’s emotions may depend on the cultural context in which we live,” they added. “This suggests that shyness does not necessarily operate in the same way across cultures.”
The researchers suggest that in Chinese culture, where emotional restraint is the norm, shy individuals might develop an intense sensitivity to subtle facial changes to avoid social missteps. Because they are less exposed to loud or exaggerated emotional displays, they might react more strongly when reading expressions. Their heightened vigilance makes any emotional display register as stronger. In contrast, Western cultures encourage more direct emotional communication, which might reduce the need for shy individuals to be on such high alert. The social costs of misreading a facial expression might simply be lower in a Western environment.
The fact that East Asian Canadians did not show the same pattern as Mainland Chinese participants suggests that they may have adapted to Western communication styles. It is also possible that the varied backgrounds within this immigrant group diluted the cultural effect observed in the Mainland Chinese sample.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, the study relied on static photographs of facial expressions. In real-world social interactions, people express emotions dynamically through moving facial muscles, body language, and tone of voice. A photograph might not fully capture how a shy person reads a shifting emotional situation in everyday life.
The study also focused on three specific groups, which means the results cannot automatically be applied to people from other ethnic or cultural backgrounds. Different societies have their own unique rules about emotional expression, and incorporating a wider variety of global populations could provide a more complete picture of how personality and culture interact.
Additionally, while the study included East Asian Canadians, the researchers did not measure exactly how much these individuals had adopted Canadian cultural norms. Tracking how immigrant populations adapt their social perception over time could offer deeper insights into the way cultural shifts alter emotional processing.
“Our findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that all shy Chinese individuals perceive emotions in a particular way, or that culture alone causes these differences,” the researchers clarified. “Our sample consisted of young adults from three specific groups, and we used static facial expressions in a laboratory setting.”
“Future research with more culturally diverse samples and more naturalistic emotional interactions will be important for determining how broadly these findings generalize,” they concluded.
The study, “Shyness and Facial Emotion Perception: A Cross-Cultural Study,” was authored by Xiaoxue Kong, Wei Fang, Skade Fernando, Naiqi G. Xiao, and Louis A. Schmidt.
