Hiroshima survivor, baseball legend Harimoto dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:52:19 UTC
22:52:19 KST

Dilara Hamit
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Korean-Japanese baseball legend Isao Harimoto, the all-time hits leader in Japan’s top professional league and a survivor of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, has died at the age of 86.
The Japanese Professional Baseball Meikyukai, an association of elite former players also known as the Golden Players Club, announced Thursday that Harimoto died Wednesday afternoon.
The organization expressed its “deep respect and gratitude” for Harimoto’s achievements and contributions to baseball and offered condolences following his death. No cause was immediately announced.
Known as the “Hit Machine,” Harimoto accumulated 3,085 hits during a 23-season career from 1959 to 1981. He remains the only player to record 3,000 hits entirely in Nippon Professional Baseball.
He finished his career with a .319 batting average, 504 home runs, 1,676 runs batted in and 319 stolen bases across 2,752 games.
Harimoto is the only Nippon Professional Baseball player to combine at least 500 home runs with 300 stolen bases. Only Barry Bonds, Willie Mays and Alex Rodriguez have achieved the same power-and-speed combination in Major League Baseball.
He began his professional career with the Toei Flyers in 1959, earning Pacific League Rookie of the Year honors during his debut season.
Harimoto won seven batting titles, including four consecutively from 1967 to 1970, and was named the Pacific League’s Most Valuable Player in 1962, when he helped the Flyers capture their first Japan Series championship.
He later played for the Yomiuri Giants and Lotte Orions before retiring in 1981.
Harimoto was inducted into the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame in 1990. 
- Overcoming injury, discrimination and atomic bombing
Harimoto was born Jang Hun in Hiroshima on June 19, 1940, to Korean parents who had moved to Japan while the Korean Peninsula was under Japanese colonial rule.
At the age of four, he suffered severe burns to his right hand in an accident. The injuries left several fingers permanently damaged and forced the naturally right-handed Harimoto to learn to throw and bat left-handed.
He later used a specially designed glove that fit over his injured right hand, allowing him to field the ball despite his limited movement.
A year later, Harimoto was in Hiroshima when the US dropped an atomic bomb on the city on Aug. 6, 1945.
His family home was about two kilometers (1.2 miles) from the hypocenter and stood behind a small hill. Harimoto and one of his sisters survived after their mother shielded them, although she was wounded by flying glass.
Harimoto eventually spoke publicly about his experience as a hibakusha, or atomic bomb survivor, and advocated against war and nuclear weapons.
Harimoto retained his South Korean citizenship for most of his life despite being born and raised in Japan. He revealed in a 2024 interview that he had obtained Japanese citizenship several years earlier.
After retiring as a player, Harimoto became a prominent baseball commentator and television analyst.

Russian Orthodox Church Sends Bones of Medieval Warrior Prince to Ukraine Front to Boost Troop Morale

Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church's latest show of support for the war.
The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow's Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.
Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince's well-preserved remains in August, hailing them as "an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery" that reinforced the foundations of Russian history.
The Russian Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy's right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Russia claims to have annexed in 2022.
Referring to Donskoy as "the holy commander," the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russian Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russian troops.
"A fragment of the Grand Prince's right hand — the very same right hand with which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field — has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers' spirits," it said in a statement.
The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russian combat units along the front line, it said.
Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War II, was declared a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988.

Netherlands, Sweden sign deal on GlobalEye early warning aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:51:06 UTC
22:51:06 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The Netherlands has signed a letter of intent with Sweden to acquire a Saab GlobalEye airborne early warning aircraft, the Dutch Defense Ministry said Thursday.
The aircraft can monitor activity in the air, at sea and on land over long distances while flying at high altitude, the ministry added.
Equipped with advanced radar systems, sensors and communications equipment, the GlobalEye can simultaneously monitor large areas and detect difficult-to-spot threats, including drones and cruise missiles. It can also identify radar installations, gather intelligence and operate as an airborne command center.
Information collected by the aircraft can be processed immediately and shared with aircraft, ships and ground units to help provide an up-to-date operational picture.
The Dutch aircraft is expected to be delivered in 2031 and will join a shared pool with three Swedish GlobalEye planes. Dutch and Swedish crews will have access to all aircraft in the pool.
The Netherlands is expected to gain access to Sweden’s aircraft in 2028, allowing Dutch personnel to begin training and potentially deploy the system before the delivery of their own plane.
The two NATO allies will also cooperate on further developing the system, strengthening bilateral ties and European defense cooperation, the ministry added.
“GlobalEye will enable the Netherlands to detect threats earlier, respond faster and strengthen both national and collective defense,” Saab President and CEO Micael Johansson said in a separate statement.
Johansson also said GlobalEye will strengthen NATO's ability to “operate in an increasingly complex security environment.”

Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:51:00 UTC
22:51:00 KST

Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
September 10, 2026
Uganda's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor.
Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence.
Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. His ascension celebrations were attended by longtime Ugandan strongman President Yoweri Museveni.
His reign was overseen by a series of relatives acting as regents until he turned 18 in 2010.
He died on August 27 at the age of 34 while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.
Who are the main players in the succession fight?
On Wednesday, the royal clan's succession committee named the late king's cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the next monarch.
Kijanangoma is a television anchor at public broadcaster UBC.
However, Oyo's mother and sister announced on Thursday that they rejected this proposal, indicating that the king had left a will declaring his son his successor.
His mother Queen Kemigisa called the committee a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had named a new king despite knowing the contents of Oyo's will.
She also accused the Ugandan military of placing her family under house arrest.
The identity of Oyo's son and the son's mother remains a mystery. A campaigner for HIV/AIDS prevention and environmental causes, he had not publicly acknowledged a son until Toroo's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced the boy's existence after Oyo's death.
The controversy grew after Andrew Mwenda, a well-known journalist and relative of Oyo's, wrote on social media site X that a son could only succeed a father in Toroo if he was born to a queen, and said that the family had not produced so much as a picture of the boy.
Prime Minister Armstrong called for both sides to remain calm on Thursday, saying the process "should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial."
Oyo's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Ukraine’s Bulava drone can now hunt in the dark—one camera handles day and night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:49:50 UTC
22:49:50 KST

Ukraine's Bulava strike drone can now hunt around the clock, its crews no longer switching optics between day and night. Its maker, DeViRo, showed the upgraded drone at a defense exhibition in Poland, the Military news outlet Militarnyi reported. The overhaul brings a new camera and lengthens the drone's flight time, and the developers say they substantially improved its flight characteristics. The company said every future production batch will carry the new optics.
Ukraine's war effort increasingly runs on small private firms that keep sharpening cheap drones in months, reworking weapons already in the fight rather than waiting years for a new model. A drone that sees in the dark can work the same targets after sunset that it hunts by day.
One camera for day and night
The updated loitering munition carries a multispectral optical station that lets it operate at any hour, a company representative told Militarnyi at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland. The station packs a daytime channel and a thermal-imaging channel into one body, so crews no longer swap in different camera modules depending on the time of day. Operators flip between the two modes in the control station's software while the drone is already in the air.
Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO
Longer in the air, 120 to 130 km out
Bulava now stays aloft for up to 110 minutes, and its guaranteed working range runs from 120 to 130 km, with room to grow depending on conditions and crew training.
DeViRo tied the drone to a summer campaign against Russian logistics, in which it says Bulava crews cleared the way for deeper strikes.
"We knocked out enemy radars and air defenses so that deep strikes could fly as deep as possible," the company representative said.
The company says its crews took a very active part in that campaign, which hit Russian supply routes across the south.
An interceptor in the same family
DeViRo builds more than strike drones. In March, it introduced the Sokyra interceptor, a prototype built to shoot down Russian attack drones. The prototype was listed at 240 km/h, a 45 km range, 30 minutes aloft, and a 750-gram warhead at the alpha-testing stage.

The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) will organise a Latvian business trade mission to the United States from 20 to 28 September, with the main business events taking place during President Edgars Rinkēvičs’ working visit from 24 to 27 September. The programme will cover New York, Los Angeles and San Diego, focusing primarily on defence and dual-use technologies, biomedicine, pharmaceuticals, start-ups and the film industry.
The trade mission aims to help Latvian companies establish new contacts with potential customers, partners and investors, promote high-value-added exports and technological cooperation, and strengthen their positions in one of the world’s largest and most competitive markets.
“Latvia’s exports of goods and services to the United States exceeded €1 billion in 2025, demonstrating that our companies can compete in one of the world’s most demanding markets. We must now raise our ambitions and expand Latvia’s presence in sectors where we possess competitive expertise, technologies and products. The United States is a strategically important economic partner for Latvia, and the President’s visit adds further weight to Latvia’s economic interests in this market. A stronger presence in the United States means more high-value-added exports and a more resilient Latvian economy,” emphasised Economics Minister Viktors Valainis.
United States: An Export Market Worth More Than €1 Billion
The United States is one of Latvia’s most important economic partners outside the European Union. Trade in goods and services between Latvia and the United States reached €1.63 billion in 2025, increasing by 13% year on year and making the United States Latvia’s ninth-largest foreign trade partner. Latvia’s exports to the United States rose by 2% to €1.01 billion, while the positive trade balance amounted to €395.9 million. The United States was Latvia’s eighth-largest export market.
Exports of services are particularly significant. They increased by 10% in 2025 to €510 million, making the United States Latvia’s fifth-largest services export market. Information and communication technology services accounted for €206 million, or 40.4% of Latvia’s services exports to the United States.
The latest figures show that services export growth continued in 2026. In the first quarter, Latvia’s services exports to the United States reached €110 million, an increase of 9% year on year, while the services trade surplus amounted to €54 million. This underlines the importance of the US market for Latvia’s knowledge-intensive services exports.
At the end of the first quarter of 2026, accumulated US direct investment in Latvia amounted to €443 million, while Latvia’s accumulated direct investment in the United States stood at €77 million.
“A good product alone is not enough in the US market—you need to reach the decision-makers and build trust over time. Our task is to bring Latvian companies together with potential customers, partners and investors to discuss concrete opportunities for cooperation. The programme has been tailored to the companies’ interests, so every meeting has a clear objective. The real measure of this mission’s success will be export deals, joint technology projects and investment,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Programme Includes Meetings with Companies, Investors and Research Centres
During the US trade mission, representatives of Latvian companies in defence and dual-use technologies, biomedicine, pharmaceuticals and the film industry, as well as members of the start-up ecosystem, are scheduled to meet internationally significant US companies and organisations in their respective fields. The film industry programme includes meetings with Paramount and Disney; defence and dual-use technology companies will meet Anduril, Shield AI and Qualcomm; and technology and biomedical companies will meet Illumina, Element Biosciences and Thermo Fisher Scientific.
Discussions involving defence and dual-use technology companies will focus on incorporating Latvian technologies into joint solutions, developing new products and enabling Latvian companies to join US supply chains.
Visits are also planned to the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), and the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). The Latvian delegation is scheduled to meet representatives of UCLA’s Technology Development Group, the University of California San Diego’s Office of Innovation and Commercialisation, and San Diego State University’s Technology Transfer Office to discuss the commercialisation of research results, technology transfer and cooperation between universities and companies. Meetings with investors are also planned.
The programme includes sector-specific roundtable discussions, visits to companies and research institutions, start-up presentations and individual business meetings. A networking event between representatives of Latvia’s start-up ecosystem and US investors is planned in New York. Companies will be able to present their solutions and receive feedback on their development prospects in the US market. A meeting with representatives of the Latvian diaspora is scheduled for 26 September.
“SAF Tehnika regularly participates in LIAA-organised trade missions to the United States because they allow us to meet senior executives from partner and customer organisations and strengthen our company’s reputation. During this September’s mission to California, for example, we will meet the senior management of a major US semiconductor manufacturer together with Riga Technical University. Opportunities provided by LIAA produce results only when a company has done its homework and can state precisely whom it wants to meet and what it wants to achieve. If you do not know where you are going, any road will take you there,” said Jānis Bergs, Member of the Management Board and Vice-President of Sales and Marketing at SAF Tehnika, commenting on the importance of trade missions.
LIAA organises participation in overseas trade missions under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises. The programme is supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state. Companies may participate in a trade mission either for a fee or with support covering eligible expenses.

Anthropic reveals fourth AI hacking incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:49:06 UTC
22:49:06 KST

Beril Canakci
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Anthropic said Wednesday it had identified a fourth incident in which one of its artificial intelligence models gained unauthorized access to a real third-party system during a cybersecurity test.
The incident occurred in January and involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, the company said in an assessment.
Anthropic said it discovered the case last month after an initial review had missed a group of relevant test transcripts.
As with the three incidents the company disclosed in July, the model was supposed to operate in a simulated environment without internet access. A configuration error instead connected the testing environment to the open internet.
Anthropic said the model subsequently accessed a third-party computer and obtained personal information belonging to an individual associated with the system. The company has notified affected parties.
The company initially reviewed about 141,000 transcripts to identify the three earlier incidents. After finding the fourth, it expanded the search to about 481 million transcripts, including records from cybersecurity evaluations and other testing environments.
The disclosure came amid the resignation on Tuesday of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, whose post on X accusing AI companies of “gambling with our lives” went viral, reaching more than 140 million people. Coxon also warned that AI systems would soon be able to “hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” while saying some people developing the technology believe it could kill humanity by the end of the decade.

Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:45:08 UTC
22:45:08 KST

Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The roof of the Torentje, or Little Tower, at the Binnenhof in The Hague was built in 1547 as a construction kit and has been largely untouched since, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.
The research on the eight-metre-high spire above the office of the prime minister was carried out by the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, the government’s property agency, during the ongoing renovation of the complex.
The ceiling was opened last year to check the area for asbestos, which was found, revealing the oak roof structure behind it.
The wooden construction has needed practically no repair work in 478 years.
 An inspection revealed that the beams were sawn by hand, typical in the days before the widespread use of sawmills. The wood came from an oak tree felled in southern Sweden around 1546.
Roman numerals are also chiselled into the beams, indicating that the roof was built in a workshop, taken apart and transported to the building site. The numerals show which parts belong together, like the instructions for a piece of Ikea furniture.
The tower itself is older: the earliest records date from 1497, and Emperor Charles V had it completely rebuilt in 1547, when the spire was added.
The renovation of the Binnenhof began in 2021. The work was initially expected to take five years and cost €475 million, but the bill has since risen to at least €2.7 billion and completion has been postponed until 2031.
Earlier this year, archaeologists found an early 14th-century city gate at the site.

IAEA detects new activity at Iran’s fortified Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:44:35 UTC
22:44:35 KST

The UN nuclear watchdog has detected signs of renewed activity around Iran’s heavily fortified Pickaxe Mountain complex, a secretive underground site that inspectors have never entered, Bloomberg reported Thursday.
International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi told Bloomberg Television that satellite and other remote imagery showed movement around the facility, but stressed that the agency has no evidence establishing what is taking place inside.
“There are some indications that there is movement around this construction site,” Grossi said. “We don’t have any concrete information as to activities that may be taking place there.”
The site has come under renewed scrutiny as tensions over Iran’s nuclear program intensify. U.S. President Donald Trump has publicly referred to Pickaxe Mountain at least twice over the past week, signaling that Washington is closely watching developments there.
“We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe,” Trump said Wednesday at a Republican rally. “I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.”
According to Bloomberg, the IAEA’s latest observations come as its board of governors has referred Iran’s nuclear file to the UN Security Council over Tehran’s failure to comply with requirements surrounding its nuclear activities.
The agency is also still unable to account for Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to near-weapons-grade levels. Inspectors have not verified its condition or location since June 2025, when Israel and the United States attacked major Iranian nuclear facilities.
Pickaxe Mountain, located in the Zagros Mountains roughly 220 kilometers south of Tehran, began drawing particular attention after an Iranian centrifuge workshop was sabotaged six years ago. Iran subsequently said it intended to move sensitive nuclear-related infrastructure underground to protect it from attack.
“They said at the time, ‘we are going to put everything in tunnels, inside a mountain,’” Grossi told Bloomberg. “This was going to be impermeable and protected from attacks.”
The United States and Israel have demanded that Iran dismantle its centrifuge program and end uranium enrichment. Centrifuges are used to separate uranium isotopes, a process required to produce fuel for civilian reactors but also essential to producing material for nuclear weapons at much higher enrichment levels.
The latest censure of Iran at the IAEA adds another layer of pressure to an already volatile confrontation. Bloomberg noted that the resolution could increase the possibility of renewed military action against Iranian nuclear facilities, particularly after Trump repeatedly framed preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon as a central reason for confronting Iran.
Tehran, meanwhile, has accused Western governments of using the IAEA to prepare the ground for military action.
In a diplomatic note circulated this week and cited by Bloomberg, Iran pointed to June 2025, when Israel launched attacks on the Islamic Republic one day after the IAEA found Tehran in non-compliance with its nuclear obligations.
“The aggressions of the Israeli regime and America against Iran just a few hours after its adoption, are solid proofs of the sponsors’ hidden agenda,” Iran’s representative to the agency wrote, urging diplomats to “condemn the unlawful attacks.”
Grossi said the dispute with Iran is unfolding against a broader and increasingly dangerous global nuclear backdrop, as more governments reconsider the role nuclear weapons could play in their security strategies.
“It has to do with a world where there is more conflict, where there are more wars,” Grossi said.
He warned that wider nuclear proliferation would dramatically increase the chances that such weapons would eventually be used.
“There would be nuclear weapon use for sure, 100% guaranteed,” Grossi said.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's NEV sales share hits record high as auto industry shifts to high-quality growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:42:44 CST
22:42:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The dominant position of new energy vehicles (NEVs) in China's auto market was further consolidated in August, with NEV sales accounting for a record 60.6 percent of the monthly new car sales, industry data showed on Thursday.
In August, NEV output and sales reached over 1.65 million and 1.64 million units, respectively, both up nearly 20 percent year on year, according to data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM).
Overall auto output and sales in August stood at 2.68 million and 2.71 million units, respectively. CAAM Deputy Secretary-General Chen Shihua attributed the month-on-month growth in auto production and sales mainly to the sustained auto consumption subsidies.
A fresh round of upgraded auto consumption subsidy measures has been rolled out across multiple cities, with a focus on streamlining application procedures, increasing subsidy amounts, and expanding the range of eligible vehicles.
Analysts noted that the upgraded subsidy policies, supported by tangible financial backing, have lowered the threshold for current car owners to trade in and upgrade their vehicles. These measures have boosted consumer confidence and converted hesitant demand into actual orders, invigorating the auto market.
China's vehicle exports continued to grow rapidly, with monthly export volume exceeding 1 million units for three consecutive months.
In August, vehicle exports reached 1.01 million units, up 65.3 percent year on year. Notably, NEV exports of the month rose 1.3-fold to 526,000 units.
In the first eight months, auto exports totaled 7.15 million units, up 66.7 percent year on year, including 3.44 million NEVs, a 1.2-fold increase.
NEVs have accounted for more than 50 percent of China's total auto exports for three consecutive months, which means one out of every two exported vehicles is an NEV.
This fundamental change in export structure shows that China's auto exports are shifting toward an NEV-led model and opening up global markets through the electrification technology route, Chen said.
Behind the strong sales and export figures, China's auto industry is undergoing a deeper transformation driven by a series of policy measures aimed at steering the sector toward high-quality development.
In early September, China issued a notice on regulating supplier payment and optimizing account period management for auto enterprises, aiming to further regulate the competition in the NEV industry and foster a fair, just, honest and mutually beneficial cooperative relationship between vehicle manufacturers and parts suppliers.
The notice encourages automakers to complete payments to small and medium-sized supplier enterprises within 30 days of goods acceptance, with a maximum of 60 days, and encourages cash payments.
Separately, China issued a guideline to regulate automakers' overseas competitive practices and strengthen compliance, so as to promote the sound and orderly global expansion of the country's auto industry.
The guideline focuses on overseas marketing and covers compliance in production safety, quality management, labor protection and data security, encourages cost-based pricing in accordance with international market supply and demand and urges automakers not to disrupt competition for unfair advantages.
A Ministry of Commerce official said the guideline emphasizes legal compliance, fair competition and win-win cooperation, helping Chinese automakers fulfill social responsibilities overseas and integrate into host countries.
China's auto exports are entering a phase where quality, rather than sheer volume, should be the priority, Chen noted.
The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) has called for accelerating the development of strategic emerging industries such as intelligent connected NEVs. The country also aims to increase the share of NEVs in the total vehicle fleet to 30 percent by 2030, according to an action plan for carbon peaking during the period. ■

Lives ‘at serious risk’ as Gaza’s hospitals, homes battle fuel shortages
Doctors say hospitals have resorted to rotating power cuts between buildings, putting patients in ‘severe danger’
As power cuts cascade through one of Gaza’s largest functioning hospitals and patients wait for treatment in sweltering wards, doctors warn that shortages of engine oil and spare parts are causing generators to seize up, putting lives at risk.
The crisis is spreading beyond hospitals, where soaring costs for oil and diesel are making electricity from neighbourhood generators increasingly unaffordable for families that depend on it.
Gaza has been without grid electricity since the start of Israel’s military offensive in the territory, launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Israel halted electricity supply and restricted the import of fuel as well as engine oil, describing them as measures to punish Hamas.
Those restrictions have continued despite an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire that brought an end to full-scale fighting but has failed to halt Israeli attacks, secure Hamas’ disarmament or relieve Gaza’s humanitarian and energy crises.
Ahmed Al-Nabris, an internal medicine specialist at Nasser Hospital, said shortages of fuel, engine oil and spare parts had forced the hospital into an austerity plan that includes rotating power cuts between buildings.

ECB hikes interest rates by 25 basis points
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:42:26 CST
22:42:26 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday that it will raise the key interest rates by 25 basis points, marking its second rate hike this year amid rising inflationary pressures.
The latest rate hike will push the interest rate on the deposit facility through which the ECB steers its monetary policy up to 2.5 percent. The interest rates on the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will be increased to 2.65 percent and 2.9 percent respectively.
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," said the ECB in a statement.
In the latest staff projections unveiled on Thursday, the ECB now expects headline inflation to average 3 percent in 2026, 2.5 percent in 2027 and 2.1 percent in 2028. The inflation projection for 2026 remains unchanged while that for 2027 and 2028 have been revised up compared with June.
Meanwhile, the baseline projections for economic growth in 2026 and 2027 have been lifted to 0.9 percent and 1.4 percent respectively.
"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth."
The euro area inflation edged up to 3.3 percent in August from 2.9 percent in July, according to the statistical office of the European Union.
The inflation surge was attributed largely to energy prices, which soared by 14.3 percent in August on an annual basis and 2.9 percent compared with July.
The euro area economy grew by 0.4 percent in the second quarter compared with the first quarter, beating estimates.
The latest upward revision of the economic growth projections by the ECB reflected "the greater-than-expected resilience of the euro area economy," said the ECB statement.
Commenting on the ECB rate hike, economists with ING bank wrote in a note on Thursday that "the hawkish bar is set high for the ECB."
Describing the hike as "an insurance move", the economists warn that "further hikes would push policy further into restrictive territory." ■

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change announced Thursday that it has banned the harvesting of cedar nuts through the end of the year.
The move followed multiple reports of brown bears entering residential areas after a poor crop left them short of food. At least 17 bear sightings have been reported in residential areas of eastern Mongolia's Khentii province since the beginning of August.
"Cedar nuts are not only a valuable forest resource but also an important source of food for wildlife, including bears and squirrels," the ministry said in a statement, noting that the decision has been made "in light of food shortages among wild animals and the findings of a study on the 2026 cedar nut crop."
Under Mongolian law, illegally harvesting cedar nuts is punishable by a fine ranging from 5.4 million to 27 million Mongolian tugriks (about 1,500 to 7,504 U.S. dollars), or imprisonment for one to five years.
Experts said encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have increased in recent years, citing factors including climate change, food shortages in bears' natural habitats, overexploitation of natural resources, and forest fires. ■

The figures were released at a subforum on immigration management cooperation during the 2026 Conference of the Global Public Security Cooperation Forum in Lianyungang, east China's Jiangsu Province.
VISA-FREE & EASIER ACCESS
Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added to the program last month, bringing the number of eligible countries to 57.
Video clips and other online content about traveling in China and experiencing the Chinese lifestyle have also gained traction worldwide, with hashtags such as "China Travel" and "Chinamaxxing" going viral.
Improved travel infrastructure and more convenient visitor services in China have made it easier for overseas travelers to "return and explore the country's cities, heritage sites and natural attractions," according to an article published this month by Travel and Tour World, a multilingual travel media platform.
The article cited China's 40,000-kilometer high-speed rail network, which links major tourist destinations and simplifies multi-city trips, as well as improvements in digital payments and multilingual services for international visitors.
FROM MEGACITIES TO COZY VILLAGES
As travel to China becomes more accessible, foreign visitors are venturing beyond traditional gateway cities to explore smaller inland destinations, including towns and even villages.
Data from travel platform Qunar showed foreign passport holders had booked inbound flights to 160 Chinese cities through the platform in the first half of 2026. Homestay platform Tujia said foreign travelers experienced homestays in 330 cities across 31 provincial-level regions during the period.
First-tier and new first-tier cities remain the main entry points for foreign visitors, but other destinations are gaining traction. According to Tujia, provincial-level regions such as Gansu, Xinjiang, Ningxia, Qinghai and Shanxi saw the fastest growth in foreign tourist homestay bookings in the first half of the year.
Foreign visitors are also staying longer. Their average homestay visit reached 2.8 days in the first half, up about 10 percent from a year earlier, according to Tujia.
"Longer stays allow foreign tourists to see a more authentic, diverse and vibrant side of China," said Hu Yang, senior vice president of Tujia.
DIVERSIFIED EXPERIENCES
Beyond sightseeing, foreign visitors are exploring a wider range of professional, efficient and personalized services in China, from hairstyling and dental care to traditional Chinese medicine and custom tailoring.
"They are increasingly incorporating everyday services into their trips, marking a shift from product-focused to service-driven inbound consumption," said Cao Yixia, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences.
Chinese authorities released a package of measures in March to improve tourism services, including optimizing departure tax refund services, encouraging everyday service apps to offer multilingual versions and further improving visa procedures.
In 2025, the country recorded more than 150 million inbound tourist visits, up more than 17 percent from a year earlier. Spending by inbound travelers surpassed 130 billion U.S. dollars, up nearly 40 percent from the previous year.
In July, China announced ambitious inbound tourism goals. The country's 2026-2030 tourism development plan proposes attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars.
As Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, observed, tourism offers an immersive showcase of China's progress in manufacturing and services.
"Easier access to China for foreign visitors is not enough. We should provide better services to help them travel to more places, stay longer and have a good experience," Dai said. ■

2,800-yr-old agora unearthed at ancient Troy in NW Türkiye
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:41:52 CST
22:41:52 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists excavating the ancient city of Troy in northwestern Türkiye's Canakkale province have uncovered the remains of an agora -- a public marketplace and gathering place -- believed to date back about 2,800 years.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Reyhan Korpe, deputy head of the excavations, said the discovery proves Troy wasn't permanently abandoned after the Bronze Age, solving a long-standing puzzle about how the legendary city became the later Greek city of Ilion.
Korpe said the discovery is part of a dedicated research initiative launched in 2014 to map the connection between Bronze Age Troy and the subsequent city of Ilion.
Archaeological findings show that after the civilization collapsed, the site was left empty for only 80-90 years before new settlers arrived. Rather than starting over, they built their homes atop the ancient stone walls and continued using the old public square as an agora.
Traditionally associated with the legendary city described in Homer's Iliad, Troy has been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998. ■

“When do you put your foot down?” Why this de-mining group is rejecting US funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:40:08 UTC
22:40:08 KST

Share & more
Norwegian People’s Aid will turn down millions in US government funding due to wide-reaching restrictions on reproductive health and equity, the mine action group announced, in a rare example of a humanitarian organisation publicly rejecting US cash.
The decision could affect 40% of NPA’s de-mining budget and 1,700 jobs, and will have “major consequences” for the organisation, NPA said.
Few humanitarian groups have spoken publicly about the so-called “global gag rules” since the Trump administration expanded the discriminatory restrictions this year. The regulations, known as the Mexico City policy, handcuff organisations receiving US cash even if potentially banned work is paid for in separate budgets by other donors.
Over decades, the US has repeatedly rescinded then reinstated the global gag rule as the government lurches between Democrat and Republican-led administrations.
“I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.”
Previous versions have tried to block organisations that receive US health funding from providing or promoting abortion care as part of family planning – even if the money came from other sources. This year, the Trump administration has expanded the rules to cover almost all foreign aid including humanitarian funding, and to target gender identity and diversity, equity, and inclusion.
“We see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally,” Gry Ballestad, NPA’s director of policy and communications, said in an interview. “And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.”
The restrictions affecting NPA cover funding from the US State Department’s Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement.
Critics say the global gag rules are an attempt to co-opt international aid along US ideological lines. The US made drastic cuts to humanitarian budgets when it dismantled its aid programme last year, which could lead to millions of deaths, a study published in The Lancet estimated. But other governments are also cutting back – leaving the US as a top humanitarian donor that can shape how and where the system works by sheer volume.
For example, the US has earmarked some $3.75 billion to UN-run pooled funds – roughly 83% of total funds so far, and $3.6 billion more than the next largest donor. It has also promised hundreds of millions more directly to UN agencies like the World Food Programme and UNICEF, or non-governmental organisations like World Vision. The initial $2 billion to UN pooled funds was signed just before the global gag rule’s new restrictions came into effect.
Ballestad spoke to The New Humanitarian about NPA’s decision, its consequences, and what this moment means for the wider humanitarian and development sectors.
This interview was edited for length and clarity.
The New Humanitarian: Can you describe the decision-making process: What were the considerations?
Gry Ballestad: It’s been a difficult decision given the implications, the programmes it affects around the world, the size of the funding, all the people that will be losing their jobs, and the impact on the ground. It’s been a very difficult decision to take.
In [2026], the big change for us was that now the requirements are not just for the American funding – not just the mine action programmes funded by the State Department, but it would affect also all our other activities and programmes… This would put limitations on everything we do – not just the American funding.
When we started working with the Americans, these were not the requirements we signed on to – actually, quite the opposite. For a long time, it’s been a requirement that we do take into consideration equal opportunities and all these things that are now a problem.
We see that now, with the change in the requirements, and looking at our core values and principles, that it’s such a big change that we cannot accept it. Because there’s a change in the regulation, we would basically have to change our core values, our activities – really, who we are.
NPA is not just working on mine action. We are the humanitarian solidarity organisation of the labour movement. That’s our origin. Our core values are very much linked to the labour movement. They’re very close to us still. Basically, we would have to change who we are. We would have to change our core values.
We have a big programme in Norway that’s working on search-and-rescue activities, but also integration activities. For example, today we had the launch of our new anti-racism guidelines for our members, and other organisations, on how to work on anti-racism. We have local chapters all over the country, and they are very much involved in integration and anti-racism activities. We couldn’t do that. It would affect what we do also in Norway together with our partners around the world. And it’s not something we can accept. It’s beyond the American funding.
It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements.
The New Humanitarian: I think what people might not understand is how far the global gag rule reaches.
Ballestad: It’s very broad. For us, it’s very much about who we are. What are the core values of an organisation like NPA?
The first paragraph of our principles… says “Norwegian People’s Aid’s values are based on equal rights for all regardless of gender, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, functional ability, and social status. Norwegian People's Aid is an anti-racist organisation.” That’s the first paragraph. So already there, we’re in trouble.
What’s the game-changer this time: The [US] requirements that came out in [2025] were similar, but they were only for American-funded activities. This time, it would cover all of what we do. You can’t compensate for what you can’t do with American funding with other funding.
It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. It’s basically about our political freedom.
The New Humanitarian: Many mine action programmes have focused on recruiting women as de-miners. Is something like that – the US would consider that to be non-compliant?
Ballestad: Yes. When we advertise, for example, sometimes we encourage women to apply so that we can have more of a gender balance in, for example, our management positions. This, we wouldn’t be allowed to do. And we do that for everything. That’s part of our HR policies.
There’s a lot of levels that we would have to change. We can’t accept it. Of course, Americans set their requirements for their funding. But we have to assess if this is something we can accept to remain true to our foundational values.
The New Humanitarian: Looking at the entire aid sector, why do you think it’s important that NPA made this decision? What’s the significance of it?
Ballestad: In the bigger picture, we see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally. And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years. It costs, if you stand up for rights. And I think it’s the time to do so.
It’s a slippery slope… Currently, these are the rights we’re discussing. You don’t know what’s next. When do you put your foot down?

====================================================================================================

Will AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt win push Germany into political crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:40:08 UTC
22:40:08 KST

Since WWII, Germany adopted a migrant-friendly policy, supported European unification under NATO, and grew into Europe’s largest car manufacturer with a vibrant economy.
Reunified after the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germany has driven EU enlargement into Eastern Europe and supported the Western alliance through close US ties.
But recently, Germany’s fortunes and the EU's have declined as rising European populist movements oppose migration and EU expansion at the expense of sovereignty. Meanwhile, globalisation favours Chinese EVs over German cars.
In addition, the Trump administration pressured European countries, especially Germany, over NATO’s defence contributions, citing insufficient spending.
Germany, which severed energy ties with Russia after Ukraine, faces energy pressures and a more assertive Russia.
These problems — migration, security concerns, prolonged economic stagnation and energy pressures — have contributed to the rise of the country’s pro-Trump far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which advocates expelling migrants, opposes what it sees as EU measures that undermine national sovereignty and economic globalisation, and urges Berlin to re-establish ties with Russia.
Despite its illusory nature, AfD’s promises attract many Germans worried about rising migration and Chinese vehicles impacting Europe, threatening Berlin’s car industry and increasing unemployment, says Raoul Motika, a professor at Hamburg University.
“People do not trust politicians anymore,” Motika tells TRT World, saying many believe politicians cannot address these problems and therefore want to vote for a party that promises to make “radical changes”.
Is the Merz government in danger?
On Sunday, the AfD claimed a significant victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a state in the former communist East Germany.
Although the state election did not give the far-right party a majority, analysts say the AfD aims to use its strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt to expand its influence nationwide and deepen opposition to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government.
While Motika does not want to exaggerate the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt, a state with one of Germany’s oldest populations and a relatively small population for its size, he concedes that the far-right party is also gaining ground in western states such as Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria.
“In any case, it's a real sign of mistrust against the Merz government. That's obvious. The overwhelming majority of the population is not content with the work of the current government,” Motika tells TRT World.
But he also notes that an AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt would have “no influence to change anything on the federal level”.
Motika says the overall pressure on the government is “very high” because opposition to and disappointment with Merz are growing within his own Christian Democratic Union (CDU), partly due to U-turns on promises he made during the federal election campaign.
Merz had previously promised to limit state debt, but after becoming chancellor, he backed loosening Germany’s debt rules.
Germany’s social welfare system, among the largest in Europe, is another subject of debate in the country.
“German life expectancy is not better than in Italy or even worse than in Italy and in other European countries, and this means the system overall is ineffective,” Motika says.
Despite growing problems and what Motika sees as shortcomings in Merz’s leadership, opposition to the chancellor has not reached the point where his government is in immediate danger, the professor says.
But he warns that adopting parts of the far-right agenda might not help Merz politically.
“All kinds of populist propaganda he made before the elections turned out against him afterwards because now the AfD is using the term that he's a liar, that he betrayed the population, that he made wrong promises.”
Other experts also believe that adopting the AfD’s populist positions might not help the Merz government.
“While a strengthened AfD is seen as the genuine defender of populist ideas, Merz looks like a copycat,” says Bulent Guven, a Hamburg-based political scientist.
Can the AfD take over Germany?
The AfD’s victory at the state level marks a historic breakthrough for a country that has long grappled with its Nazi legacy since WWII.
Despite periodic bans on neo-Nazi groups, Germany’s far right has steadily gained ground over the past two decades, paving the way for the AfD’s rise in the early 2010s.
Today, the AfD holds around a quarter of the seats in the German parliament and has steadily increased its representation in the European Parliament.
Co-chaired by economist Alice Weidel, the party draws support not only from ordinary voters but also from parts of Germany’s intellectual circles.
“Emerging signs show that they will eventually come to power” at the federal level, says Guven.
According to polls, the far-right party can claim nearly 30 percent of votes in upcoming federal elections.
“Not good days are ahead for us,” says Guven, a German citizen with Turkish ancestry, fearing that people like him with migrant backgrounds will be targeted under a potential AfD rule in a country, one-quarter of whose population from 21 to 25 million has non-German or immigrant roots.
“If we exclude voters with migrant backgrounds, we can say that the AfD has the potential to win the vote of nearly one in every two ethnic Germans on the street,” says the political analyst.
‘More radical than others’
Guven draws attention to the AfD’s increasingly “radicalised rhetoric”, contrasting it with other far-right parties, such as Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally, which have considerably moderated their anti-EU and anti-migrant positions as they have gained political ground.
“We won’t bend and we will not water down our fundamental positions,” said Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s potential premier of Saxony-Anhalt, declaring its policy proposals from security to migration and energy policy as “nonnegotiable”.
The AfD has a broad agenda, ranging from cracking down on migration and changing the education system to strengthening local policing through a proposed volunteer militia, which the party says would help secure neighbourhoods.
Germany’s school curricula include extensive teaching about atrocities committed during the Nazi era.
The AfD wants to change how some of that history is addressed and cut funding for projects it considers to have “anti-German goals”.
“The AfD is not softening,” says Motika, who describes the party’s political evolution as “not comparable” with nationalist parties in Italy and France.
While the AfD does not have a long history, its trajectory shows that “they became more radical and more open to fascist groups,” he says.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by the state’s domestic intelligence agency, Motika adds.
“Some of the candidates who are now new members of parliament in Saxony-Anhalt are real neo-Nazis. This really means a complete shift for Germany.”
But Motika does not believe Saxony-Anhalt can serve as a laboratory for the AfD’s future plans for Germany, particularly because the party did not secure a majority in the eastern state.
Saxony-Anhalt, a state with a relatively small budget and high debt, cannot provide the AfD with the kind of testing ground some envisage, he says.
Guven, however, sees the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt as a sign of a dangerous path for Germany’s future.
“They see Saxony-Anhalt as a pilot project for their governance experience, designating critical posts in the state as their targets to implement their intended policies,” he tells TRT World.

How Different Are Philosophers? (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:39:43 UTC
22:39:43 KST

How Different Are Philosophers? (guest post)
“Do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?”
That’s the question taken up by a team of researchers in a recent study published in Philosophical Psychology. Focusing on differences between philosophers and non-philosophers in regard to neurodivergent traits and responses to thought experiments, the researchers found some support, in the aggregate, for a “yes” answer to that question.
The following guest post is by Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), and is based on the article, “Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population,” co-authored with Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), and Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston).
How Different Are Philosophers?
by Thomas Nadelhoffer
“The history of philosophy is to a great extent that of a certain clash of human temperaments [. . .] Yet, his temperament really gives him a stronger bias than any of his more strictly objective premises. It loads the evidence for him one way or the other” — William James
Neurodiversity and Philosophical Intuitions
In addition to being abstract thinkers, philosophers are stereotyped as being argumentative, overly self-absorbed in their own thoughts, and enjoy creating increasingly fine distinctions regarding everyday terms while imagining novel hypothetical situations and debating the conclusions they draw. It’s possible that many philosophers have quite distinctive personalities.
More than two millennia before the modern notion of stereotypes existed, Plato used humor to poke fun at philosophers in the Theaetetus by telling a story of Thales contemplating the stars, so engrossed that he forgot where he was walking and fell down a well. However, do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?
This was one of the questions behind the paper we recently published in Philosophical Psychology. We surveyed 1,254 individuals, 632 with formal training in philosophy and 622 members of the general public, and explored whether philosophers exhibit significant cognitive differences from non-philosophers using multiple measures of neurodiverse traits. To get enough responses from philosophers, we recruited participants here at Daily Nous and on Leiter Reports. We recruited the general population participants from Prolific. We preregistered our experimental design, research questions, and hypotheses.
Philosophical Temperament?
Recently, experimental philosophers and psychologists began investigating philosophical temperament, that is, the study of relationships between psychological traits and philosophically relevant judgment. Several studies have linked various personality traits to judgments concerning issues like free will, moral responsibility, intentional action, and metaethics. Research has also demonstrated that although trained to reason about certain things rationally, philosophers are susceptible to psychological factors influencing their philosophical intuitions. Our aim was to investigate this area further.
Rather than continuing to focus on personality characteristics that researchers typically measure using personality surveys (e.g., The “Big Five”), we decided to examine characteristics that relate to the following neurodiverse traits:[1] autism; ADHD; aphantasia (low visual imagery); anendophasia (i.e. low levels of “inner speech”); and representational manipulation (the ability to mentally manipulate and modify representations).[2]
Of the four significant differences found amongst participants from the general population and those with some degree of formal training in philosophy:
- Philosophers exhibited higher levels of ADHD-related traits (moderate effect size, d = .5).
- Philosophers exhibited lower levels of visual imagery (substantial effect size, d = -.6).
- Philosophers exhibited higher levels of internal speech (smaller effect size, d = .34).
- Philosophers demonstrated higher levels of representational manipulation (substantial effect size, d = .76).
All four differences found were very stable, even after we limited the criterion for “philosopher” as only participants with PhD degrees or postdoctoral appointments in philosophy.
Therefore, our findings suggest that, as a group, philosophers have a distinct cognitive profile (relative to the general population). This profile consists of higher levels of internal verbalization, enhanced capacities for mentally manipulating internal representations, lower levels of visual imagery and higher levels of ADHD traits.
Philosophers and Thought Experiments
 All participants completed two classical versions of this type of experiment: the “bystander at the switch” version of the trolley problem and the “rollback universe” deterministic universe.
We also assessed how often each group misinterpreted determinism, through either bypassing (treating an agent’s beliefs, desires, and deliberation as having no causal relevance to their actions) or indeterminate intrusion (allowing multiple possible outcomes while maintaining identical initial conditions and laws).
As before, there were significant differences between philosophers and non-philosophers.
In the trolley case, philosophers were significantly more likely to believe it is acceptable to sacrifice the one person but not obligatory and less likely to believe that it is unacceptable.
In short, there was a small yet statistically reliable correlation between being a philosopher and intuitions about the bystander at the switch scenario.
However, there were larger differences in the responses to the determinism case. Approximately 50% of philosophers believed that agents in the deterministic universe have free will. In comparison, approximately 37% of members of the general public reported the same intuition. For moral responsibility, approximately 69% of philosophers and 54% of the general population judged that agents in the rollback universe are responsible. Moreover, philosophers made the bypassing error much less frequently than did members of the general public. While 17% of philosophers made this error, 63% of those in the general public made it. Similarly, while approximately 25% of philosophers made the intrusion error, approximately 33% of members of the general public made it.
Our next goal was to assess if there existed a connection between the cognitive characteristics of our subjects and their responses to philosophical thought experiments. We found that psychological traits are correlated with responses to thought experiments independently of the subject’s exposure to philosophy. Visual imagery provides a good illustration. Those who reported lower levels of visualization were more likely to make utilitarian judgments in response to the bystander at the switch scenario. Conversely, those who reported more vivid visual imagery were less likely to indicate that flipping the switch was permissible but not obligatory.
Furthermore, visual imagery influenced judgments regarding determinism. Those who indicated higher levels of visual imagery were less likely to assign free will and moral responsibility to agents in the rollback universe. Additionally, individuals with lower visualization scores were more susceptible to both bypassing and intrusion errors.[3]
Machine Learning and Sorting Philosophers and Non-Philosophers
The final analysis that we ran involved using various machine learning algorithms to see whether we could predict whether we could accurately distinguish between philosopher and non-philosophers using neurodiverse traits, responses to thought experiments, and both taken together. So, we trained various machine learning models to determine if they could categorize participants into either philosophers or non-philosophers.
For the first round of analysis, we provided the models with only participants’ answers to philosophical thought experiments. This resulted in reasonable success. The top performing model achieved approximately 78% accuracy. The strongest predictor variable was whether participants committed the bypassing error when reasoning about determinism.
Next, we provided the models with only participants’ cognitive-trait profile. We found that neurodiverse traits were more predictive than responses to thought experiments when it came to whether a participant was a philosopher or non-philosopher. The strongest predictor traits were representational manipulation, visual imagery, and ADHD symptoms. Using just these three traits, the classification accuracy was 81%. In short, if we choose someone at random from our study and we want to determine whether that person has studied philosophy, we could just use responses to the scales for measuring visualization, representational manipulation, and AHD to make reliable predictions that are quite significantly above chance.
Lastly, we asked the models to use both types of information (that is, responses to thought experiments and neurodiverse traits. By combing the two, the classification-accuracy of the models went up to 86%. The three best predictors for this mixed model were scores on bypassing, representational-manipulation, and visual imagery.
In closing, I just want to point out that our study had several limitations (e.g., it relied on self-report) and it also left several unanswered questions (e.g., we can’t speak to whether philosophy attracts people with certain cognitive styles or whether philosophical training influences cognitive style). You can find our discussion of these limitations (and more detailed discussions of our findings) in our full article. But because Justin was kind enough to post our call for participants on Daily Nous and many readers took the time to complete the survey, I thought I would share the results.
[1] It’s worth emphasizing that we were examining traits (measured via scales), not attempting to diagnose participants with autism spectrum disorders, ADHD, aphantasia (“mind blindness”), anendophasia (no internal dialogue), etc.
[2] This trait is not normally considered to be a neurodiverse trait; however, scores on the scale measuring this construct are significantly correlated with several of the neurodiverse traits listed above.
[3] We also found that other cognitive characteristics similarly correlated with philosophical judgments. However, due to space constraints, I will refrain from detailing them here (those interested can check out the paper).

ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
September 10, 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Rising oil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%.
"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin.
The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.
Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches.
Economic outlook remains uncertain
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB.
For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services.
Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said.
