UK studies options for retiring Army Wildcat fleet
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:00 BST
22:00:00 KST

The Ministry of Defence is examining possible uses for the Army Air Corps’ Wildcat AH1 helicopters after their planned withdrawal from service from 2027, but has declined to say whether aircraft could be retained for new operational roles, transferred elsewhere or used as a source of spares.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard set out the position in two written parliamentary answers to Liberal Democrat MP Gideon Amos, following the decision announced in the Defence Investment Plan on 30 June to begin withdrawing the Army’s Wildcat AH1 fleet from 2027.
Amos asked whether Defence had assessed alternative uses for the aircraft, including employment as airborne command-and-control platforms for uncrewed systems, transfer to support Royal Marines littoral operations, and further work involving crewed-uncrewed teaming and counter-drone capabilities.
Pollard replied: “Further to the Defence Investment Plan announcement of 30 June 2026, Defence continues to examine options associated with the planned withdrawal of the Wildcat AH1 fleet from service from 2027. Work is being undertaken to understand potential opportunities, and it would be inappropriate to comment further while this work remains ongoing.”
The same response was given to a separate question asking what would happen to the airframes following withdrawal and, specifically, whether any could be retained to provide certified spare parts for the Royal Navy’s Wildcat HMA2 fleet. The answer confirms that disposal arrangements have not yet been publicly settled and that Defence is still looking at opportunities connected with the aircraft, although the MOD did not confirm that any of the individual options raised by Amos are themselves being pursued.
Among the possibilities put to ministers was retaining Wildcat AH1 in an alternative operational role as an airborne command-and-control platform coordinating uncrewed systems. Amos also pointed to work conducted by Leonardo, the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory and the Royal Navy involving crewed-uncrewed teaming and counter-drone capabilities on the Wildcat platform.
A second proposal raised in the question was the possible transfer of airframes to support Royal Marines littoral operations, rather than removing the aircraft entirely from military use once the Army fleet is withdrawn.
The future of the helicopters could also have implications for the Royal Navy’s Wildcat HMA2 force. Amos asked whether withdrawn Army aircraft might be retained as a source of certified components for the naval fleet, but Pollard did not disclose whether this is among the options being considered.
The AH1 and HMA2 are variants of the same Wildcat family, with the Army aircraft operated in the battlefield reconnaissance and utility role while the Royal Navy version is configured for maritime operations.

Senior White House advisers have privately warned U.S. President Donald Trump that the conflict with Iran could continue for years, potentially lasting through the remainder of his term, according to a report on Sept. 9 by The Wall Street Journal.
Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and other senior officials have discussed with Trump the possibility that Tehran could continue resisting U.S. pressure despite a naval blockade, sanctions and military operations, the report said.
The private assessments contrast sharply with Trump’s public assurances that the conflict will end soon.
On Sept. 9, he told reporters that the war would end “immediately” after the November midterm elections, claiming that “they can’t hold out any longer.”
The war, now in its seventh month, has killed 18 U.S. servicemembers and raised concerns over military resources and disruptions to global energy markets.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for a quick resolution while supporting a broader economic campaign against Tehran.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has described the strategy, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” as an alternative to major combat operations.
White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales defended the administration’s approach, saying: “President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions,” she added.

A new exhibition by Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan has opened at Berlin's Neue Nationalgalerie, bringing together works that question power, violence and belief.
Among them is 'Him', a 2001 sculpture of a kneeling child with Adolf Hitler's face. The curator says the work remains relevant because it presents an image of evil while leaving its meaning uncertain. Other works include 'Charlie Don't Surf', showing a child fixed to a school desk.
The exhibition, titled 'Night', explores authority, dictatorship, death and doubt. The title also suggests a period of reflection before morning comes.

Russia has reportedly amassed 120 assault groups, with around 150,000 troops, towards the city of Orikhiv in southern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
Orikhiv is a city close to the contact line with the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia region, which analysts previously described as a stronghold threatened by Russian advances, alongside the regional capital of Zaporizhzhia, after advances towards another regional stronghold of Hulyaipole.

Serhiy Skibchik, the press officer of Ukraine’s 65th separate mechanized brigade “Velyky Lug,” noted the formations on television, calling the situation difficult but under control, according to state media Ukrinform on Thursday.
“The only thing that has changed is the hypertrophied kill zone, it has grown significantly, and it affects our logistics,” he said.
Skibchik said Russia would have to amass major forces to take the city before noting the newly spotted formations nearby.
According to Ukrinform, Skibchik said 120 assault groups are in neighboring areas, including Russia’s 58th Combined Arms Army, particularly the 19th and 42nd motorized rifle divisions.
He said nearby Russian troops total around 150,000 – which is on par with the entirety of Russia’s initial invasion force across Ukraine in 2022.
But Skibchik said he’s confident that the formations are “not enough to claim success.”
“It must be said that these groups consist of assault troops trained from the 98th Airborne Division and the 7th, 11th, and 104th Airborne Assault Brigades,” he continued.
Ukraine’s ‘Sudden’ Victory in Lyman-Kharkiv: 5 Things to Know
Orikhiv under threat?
Analysts previously warned that Orikhiv could be targeted next after the potential fall of Hulyaipole, which happened in early 2026.
Orikhiv is located about 38 kilometers (23.6 miles) southwest of Hulyaipole.
In late December 2025, Russian troops began marching toward the city of Hulyaipole, during which military analyst Denys Popovych warned Kyiv24 that if Hulyaipole fell, Zaporizhzhia itself and Orikhiv would be next.
Since then, Russian troops have taken over Hulyaipole and pushed toward Orikhiv, with both sides trading territory on the southern front, according to data from the open-source battlefield map DeepState UA.
The data shows that Russian troops have pushed westward and northward after the occupation of Hulyaipole, while Ukrainian troops have had some successes pushing back Russian advances south and east of Orikhiv.
As of late 2025, Russia claimed to control around 70% of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, while Kyiv Post’s August tallies put 73% of the region under occupation.
The region is one of five that Russia claimed through illegal referendums, alongside Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kherson regions, as well as the Crimea peninsula. However, Kyiv and the West have firmly rejected the legitimacy of Moscow’s supposed referendums.

Realising the potential of the EU’s outermost regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:56:29 UTC
21:56:29 KST

Home to 5 million people, the EU's outermost regions - French Guiana, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Mayotte, Réunion, Saint-Martin (France), the Azores, Madeira (Portugal), and the Canary Islands (Spain) – are its most remote territories. They extend the EU’s presence across the globe and play a key geostrategic role. The Commission has put forward a new strategy that will ensure these remote regions can fully realise their potential, with stronger support, greater resilience and fairer opportunities for their people.
The Commission has also proposed targeted adaptations to EU laws to better reflect the outermost regions' unique realities and constraints. Tailored to the needs of the regions concerned, the proposals cover areas such as agriculture, forestry, fisheries, migration, and taxation.
The strategy is built around four objectives:
- Harness geostrategic potential and strengthen regional integration: better align EU internal and external policies to deepen cooperation with neighbouring countries.
- Increase competitiveness and access to the single market: support smart specialisation in local competitive areas, such as the blue economy, renewable energy, biotechnology, research and space.
- Improve resilience and preparedness: improve climate adaptation and tackle environmental challenges while better protecting biodiversity. Strengthen disaster response, support energy autonomy, protect critical infrastructure like ports and submarine cables, and reinforce food security and self-sufficiency.
- Promote social fairness and support people: help create jobs, improve access to education, affordable housing, clean water and healthcare, reduce poverty, while supporting people's right to stay in the place they call home – particularly for young people.
At a broader level, the EU is also ensuring its support to the outermost regions is more coherent overall. For instance, the Commission's proposal to review the EU Emissions Trading System includes several important provisions for these regions. As does the proposed Public Procurement Act that allows for the tailoring of certain procurement rules to the outermost regions' specificities.
In future, the Commission will take the specific situation of the outermost regions into account when preparing future initiatives. It aims to foster a robust partnership between these regions, EU countries and the Commission, including through a yearly structured dialogue and a dedicated portal.

Giorgos Mazonakis: Interrogation over Greek star's death in a private clinic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

The case dominating debate in Greece and Cyprus involves one of the country's biggest music stars, also popular in the Balkans. He suffered a cardiac arrest at an Athens medical practice. Investigators are examining two plasma-exchange machines and the timeline of events.
The investigation into the sudden death of Giorgos Mazonakis, one of the most popular Greek singers of the past three decades, is at the centre of public debate in Greece and Cyprus.
In a significant development on Thursday evening, Greek authorities arrested the two doctors linked to the private medical practice in central Athens where Mazonakis had gone for scheduled plasmapheresis before suffering cardiac arrest.
A case file has been opened against them for the Greek criminal offence of exposure resulting in death. The case is now expected to proceed through the prosecutorial process.
The death of the 54-year-old artist remains the leading story in the news in both countries, where Mazonakis enjoyed huge popularity, while media outlets across the Balkans are also following the case.
Attention has now shifted to the circumstances that preceded his death. Giorgos Mazonakis had gone to a private medical practice in central Athens for a scheduled plasmapheresis, a specialised therapeutic procedure to remove blood plasma, before suddenly collapsing.
The authorities must now answer a series of critical questions: what exactly had been planned, whether the procedure had in fact begun, who was in charge of it, what medical assessment had preceded it, and whether the premises had the required licence, the appropriate equipment and specialised staff.
At the same time, the forensic examination is expected to determine the cause of death and help clarify whether there is any link to what happened at the practice.
Three decades on the Greek music scene
Giorgos Mazonakis was born in Nikaia, Piraeus, in 1972 and stood at the forefront of Greek music for more than 30 years.
He began singing professionally at a young age. In 1992, while performing at a night-time venue in Patras, he was spotted by the record company PolyGram and the following year released his first album.
In the years that followed, he became one of the most recognisable figures in contemporary Greek laïko music, a pop-folk Greek music style from the 50s and 60s, delivering a string of commercial hits and maintaining a constant presence on the country's nightlife and live music circuit.
Beyond Greece, Mazonakis had a strong fanbase in Cyprus and among Greek diaspora communities, with performances in Germany, Australia and the United States.
In recent years, he has also been a judge on the popular programme The Voice of Greece.
His appeal extended beyond Greek-speaking audiences, particularly in the Balkans. He had appeared in Sofia as early as 2012 and returned for a concert in 2023, while in December 2024, he performed in Tirana.
News of his death was reported immediately by media outlets in Bulgaria and Albania.
What police are examining
One of the main issues authorities are seeking to clarify is what exactly happened before the cardiac arrest and whether the scheduled treatment had begun.
According to reports in Greek media, the doctor said to have been responsible for Mazonakis's treatment testified that the plasmapheresis had not yet begun and that his condition deteriorated abruptly while preparations for the procedure were under way.
The same reports, citing her testimony, say that Mazonakis had visited the practice the previous day as well. The doctor is said to have described his condition as already compromised and to have referred to difficulties with his speech.
Authorities are therefore expected to examine which symptoms had been recorded, what tests had been carried out, what medical history had been taken and on what basis it was considered that the planned procedure could go ahead.
The doctor's husband, who is also a doctor and in whose name the medical practice is registered, is reported to have told investigators that he had not personally treated Mazonakis and that his wife had undertaken the singer's treatment.
New findings from the police investigation have raised further questions about what happened inside the practice.
On Thursday, police carried out a lengthy search of the premises and seized digital devices, files, medical products and other material. A subsequent search was also carried out at the doctors' home.
According to Greek National Television, ERTnews, paramedics told investigators that the plasmapheresis machine was operating when they arrived at the practice. An initial technical examination is also reported to have shown that, during its most recent operation, the machine had remained switched on for 45 minutes. A more detailed examination is expected to establish when exactly it had been in use.
Police are also examining a discrepancy in the timeline. The doctor is reported to have said that Mazonakis arrived at around 16:30, while the emergency services had already been called shortly beforehand. Investigators believe the singer had been at the practice for at least three hours.
Following the examination of the new evidence, the two doctors were arrested and a case file was opened against them for exposure resulting in death.
Greek health minister: 'A very arduous procedure'
A separate inspection is underway into the licensing and operating conditions of the premises.
Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said that the facility was registered as a simple internal medicine practice and not as a clinic.
In his initial comments, he stated that, in such a practice, performing plasmapheresis is not permitted, according to him, and he ordered an immediate inspection by the Athens Medical Association.
On Thursday, he returned to the issue, describing plasmapheresis as a "very heavy" procedure which, he said, is carried out "only in a hospital setting".
The minister has stressed from the outset that the precise causes of death and whether there is any liability will have to emerge from the forensic and wider investigation.
'Specialised medical procedure'
During Thursday's inspection of the practice by police and representatives of the Athens Medical Association, two plasmapheresis machines were found. According to Greek Media, the machines had not been identified during Association inspections in 2024 and 2025, while questions remain over whether the relevant authorisation was in place
Athens Medical Association president Giorgos Patoulis had earlier said that the premises were licensed as an internal medicine practice and that the Association had no record of such equipment.
He also stressed that plasmapheresis is "a specialised medical procedure" which requires not only appropriate machinery but also specialised staff and specific standards.
The doctors' lawyer, however, has maintained that the machines had been duly declared to the Medical Association and that the practice was operating lawfully.
Greek media reports are also raising questions about the regulatory framework governing specialised medical procedures in private practices. The Central Health Council is expected to examine the issue and the conditions under which such therapeutic interventions may be carried out.
What is plasmapheresis?
Therapeutic plasmapheresis (therapeutic plasma exchange) is a procedure in which blood passes through a special device that separates and removes the plasma, while the red and white blood cells and platelets are returned to the body. The plasma that is removed is replaced by a special solution.
According to doctors Konstantinos Giannakas and Thanos Dimopoulos of the Therapeutic Clinic of the University of Athens, who spoke to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency, the method has specific therapeutic indications, including for certain serious haematological, neurological, and immunological diseases.
It requires an assessment of the patient's condition beforehand and continuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation. It is generally considered safe when carried out under the prescribed conditions, but it can cause adverse effects, ranging from a drop in blood pressure and hypocalcaemia to, more rarely, allergic reactions, bleeding or arrhythmias.

Switzerland sees hottest summer since records began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:55:20 UTC
21:55:20 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Switzerland experienced its hottest summer since measurements began, with the national average temperature reaching 17.2C (63F), the country's meteorological authority said Thursday.
The average temperature between June and August was 0.4C (0.7F) higher than the previous record set in 2003, according to the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, known as MeteoSwiss.
It was also 3.4C (6.1F) above the average for the 1991-2020 reference period.
Northwestern Switzerland was particularly affected, with temperatures averaging 4C (7.2F) above the reference period.
The temperature at the Basel-Binningen monitoring station reached 39.7C (103.5F) on July 30, equaling the record for the highest temperature measured north of the Alps. The previous record was registered at Geneva-Cointrin on July 7, 2015.
Thirty MeteoSwiss stations recorded new summer heat records, nearly half of which were set as early as June.
The number of hot days and tropical nights also rose sharply during the summer.
Several monitoring stations recorded nearly two additional weeks of hot days compared with their previous records. Neuchatel and Glarus each registered 18 more such days.
Switzerland recorded 50 tropical nights, when temperatures did not fall below 20C (68F), during the summer, eight more than in 2003, according to MeteoSwiss.

13:55:18 BST

Armed police, military personnel and a military helicopter will take part in a planned multi-agency exercise in Cambuslang on Friday, with blank ammunition expected to be heard during the afternoon, Police Scotland has said.
The activity will take place at the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service Headquarters as part of Exercise Tartan Kukri, involving Police Scotland, the military and other emergency services. Police said local residents may see armed officers and military personnel arriving at the site, alongside a military helicopter.
The force said: “On Friday 11 September, we will be using facilities at the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service Headquarters in Cambuslang.”
It added: “This means you may see armed police officers and military personnel, as well as a military helicopter, arriving at SFRS HQ in Cambuslang.”
Blank ammunition will also be used during the exercise, with Police Scotland warning that it may sound like live gunfire to people nearby.
The force said: “You may hear blank ammunition, which sounds like gun shots, being used from around 12pm – 2.30pm.”
There will be no public access to the exercise area and Police Scotland said activity will not be visible once those taking part are inside the grounds of the fire service headquarters.
Exercise Tartan Kukri forms part of a larger RAF-led training activity known as Exercise Kukri Dawn, which is running from 2 to 18 September.
Police Scotland said: “Exercise Tartan Kukri is a multi-agency training exercise nested within the wider Exercise Kukri Dawn, a routine RAF-led exercise running from 2 to 18 September 2026, which is designed to train new Chinook aircrew by replicating operational scenarios.”
The wider exercise is therefore focused on training new Chinook crews in scenarios intended to reproduce aspects of operational flying, while the Cambuslang element brings in police and emergency service personnel.
Chinook helicopters are used by the RAF for heavy-lift and troop transport tasks and regularly support training involving rapid movement of personnel and equipment.
The use of armed police and blank ammunition in Cambuslang is part of the planned scenario rather than a response to a live incident.
Police Scotland said exercises of this kind are intended to improve coordination between organisations that may need to work together during major incidents or operational deployments.
The force said: “Exercises are a crucial way for different organisations to work together, share knowledge and strengthen our response.”
The Cambuslang activity is scheduled for Friday 11 September, with the period of greatest audible activity expected between noon and 2.30pm.

Kabir Adeniyi
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The death toll from the diphtheria outbreak in Nigeria’s central Plateau state has risen to 27, while the number of suspected cases has more than doubled to 303, health authorities said on Wednesday.
The state epidemiologist, Maren Damulak, disclosed the figures while briefing journalists, saying the number of suspected cases had increased from 149 to 303, while fatalities rose from 23 to 27.
About “99% of the cases are in Jos North,” Damulak said, according to a statement shared with Anadolu.
He said most of those affected had not received diphtheria vaccination, while children accounted for a significant proportion of the suspected cases.
Rikkos community in Jos North Local Government Area was identified as one of the worst-affected areas.
The state government has intensified surveillance, contact tracing, community sensitisation and vaccination campaigns in affected communities as authorities seek to contain the spread.
The government had earlier ordered the temporary closure of all public and private primary and secondary schools across the state from Sept. 7 after suspected cases were reported in Jos North, Jos South, Bassa and Wase local government areas.
The closure is intended to reduce transmission among pupils, students and school staff while health authorities step up surveillance and response activities.
Some patients are receiving treatment in isolation at the Jos University Teaching Hospital and Plateau Specialist Hospital.
The latest figures represent a sharp increase from the 23 deaths and 143 suspected cases reported by the Plateau health commissioner earlier this month. At the time, officials cited late presentation of patients and shortages of diphtheria antitoxin as major challenges to the response.
Diphtheria is a highly contagious bacterial disease that can spread through respiratory droplets and close contact. It is vaccine-preventable, and health authorities have urged residents to seek early medical attention and ensure children receive recommended vaccinations.
Nigeria's disease control authorities have identified Plateau among eight states accounting for 98% of the country's confirmed diphtheria cases.

The firm's expansion into the Middle East is being led by Abaza, with recruitment already under way to build a team of estate agents who could potentially appear in a Dubai-based reality series.
The Dubai office will join the agency's existing locations in Newport Beach and San Diego in California, alongside its Cabo San Lucas office in Mexico.
The 6,500-square-foot Dubai office is expected to launch in December, according to The National.
The UAE operation will initially comprise 20 brokers and feature a growing portfolio of luxury residential properties across Dubai, backed by the firm's international client network.
The brokerage plans to grow its Dubai team over the coming months, while its agents are also expected to pursue opportunities in Abu Dhabi's property market.
In a separate interview with People, Oppenheim confirmed that the company aims to increase its UAE workforce to as many as 40 agents, saying he wants “to keep the family atmosphere, and we want agents that are experienced and successful”.
Oppenheim, who is currently filming the 10th season of Selling Sunset, also hinted that viewers could eventually see the franchise expand into the Middle East.
“Let’s put it this way, the show covers the brokerage and the brokerage is moving to Dubai. So it could be that people will see it be discussed when season 10 comes out," Oppenheim told People. "Obviously, they won’t see the finished office,” he noted, as the season is already in production.
Selling Sunset centres on luxury property agents operating in Los Angeles, Orange County and Tampa.
The series is also known for its distinctive deal-closing bell, which agents ring after completing a sale.

Hong Kong’s policy address next week will continue with measures to help local news outlets expand overseas and build global networks, the South China Morning Post has learned.

China, U.S. make fresh headway in counternarcotics cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:32 CST
21:52:32 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and U.S. law enforcement agencies have made fresh headway in counternarcotics cooperation, jointly cracking a transnational case involving precursors used to manufacture synthetic cannabinoids, China's Ministry of Public Security said Thursday.
The case was jointly handled by the ministry and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), according to the ministry.
In early May, the U.S. side provided information on two Chinese nationals suspected of involvement in drug-related activities. Chinese police later determined that the leads were connected to an ongoing case in China, leading authorities to consolidate the investigations.
Following further investigation, Chinese police in mid-August carried out coordinated operations in north China's Hebei Province and elsewhere, arresting 21 suspects and seizing a batch of non-scheduled precursor chemicals commonly used in drug production, the ministry said.
Previously, the U.S. authorities had arrested two U.S. nationals suspected of drug-related crimes. The two allegedly purchased non-scheduled precursor chemicals to produce drugs in the United States, which were then distributed to inmates at multiple federal and state prisons across the country, according to the ministry.
The successful solving of the case, the ministry said, underscores the effectiveness of the China-U.S. counternarcotics law enforcement cooperation mechanism and offers another concrete example of the two sides' efforts to deepen practical cooperation in combating transnational drug-related crimes.
Counternarcotics has long been an important area of China-U.S. law enforcement cooperation. The two countries have worked together on cases involving drug smuggling and trafficking, as well as the cross-border trafficking of new psychoactive substances.
In August, a Chinese court convicted two men of trafficking precursor chemicals abroad. The case was cracked with information provided by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration in 2023.
The China-U.S. counternarcotics intelligence exchange mechanism, established in 2002, convened its 11th meeting in February 2026, with discussions focusing on drug trends, joint investigations, precursor chemical controls and other areas of cooperation.
China has strengthened regulatory controls over non-scheduled precursor chemicals. In November 2025, it added 13 types of precursors for fentanyl-related substances to its export control list and included the United States, Mexico and Canada in the Catalogue of Specific Countries (Regions). In May 2026, three more types of fentanyl-related precursors were added to the list applicable to the three countries.
Zhang Li, deputy director of the Center for Drug Control Theory and Policy Research under the People's Public Security University of China, said the growing counternarcotics cooperation demonstrated China's commitment to helping the United States address the fentanyl crisis. ■

Economic Watch: China's green industries bring solutions, cooperation opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:31 CST
21:52:31 KST

XIAMEN, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- When 121 electric buses rolled into Copiapó, Chile, last year, they helped turn the city into the first in Latin America to operate a fully electric public bus system.
Made by Chinese bus manufacturer King Long and shipped thousands of miles from Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province, the buses are a great example of how Chinese companies offer the world green solutions and help other countries shift to cleaner energy.
"Equipped with high-power motors, these buses can cope with steep slopes across Chile," said Yu Danyao, chief brand officer of Xiamen King Long United Automotive Industry Co., Ltd.
King Long entered the Chilean market in 2007 and has since sold more than 1,500 buses in the country, Yu said. The company develops pure-electric, hybrid and hydrogen-fueled vehicles and adapts them to local conditions.
In Saudi Arabia, it has developed a battery thermal-management system designed to withstand high temperatures and dusty conditions. In Europe, it has introduced buses designed to reduce energy consumption and meet stringent environmental standards.
King Long's green vehicles have been sold to more than 150 countries and regions, with cumulative sales exceeding 160,000 units, according to the company.
Apart from King Long buses, exhibitors at the 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade in Xiamen are also showcasing a range of green technologies, including smart energy-storage systems, water reclamation technology, and new power systems.
Tackling the climate crisis calls for joint global efforts and China boasts highly advanced green solutions, making bilateral cooperation in this field essential, said Janna Laine, counselor for public diplomacy and communication at the Embassy of Finland in Beijing. Finland is a guest country of honor at the fair this year.
The Finnish trade and economic delegation, comprising over 40 enterprises and institutions, pays particular attention to sectors including the circular economy, resource recycling, advanced manufacturing, industrial digitalization and healthcare, according to Sakari Puisto, minister of economic affairs of Finland.
"We look forward to concluding multiple business cooperation deals during this visit," said Puisto.
The fair, which runs from Tuesday to Friday, attracted delegations from 129 countries and regions, with 60 setting up exhibition areas. Its exhibition space expanded to 200,000 square meters from 120,000 square meters last year, according to the Xiamen Municipal Bureau of Commerce. The figures offer tangible signs of growing international interest in China as a partner in trade, investment and supply chain cooperation.
The energy storage sector is no exception. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centers is generating huge demand for electricity and energy storage systems.
"For 24-hour high-load scenarios such as data centers, short-duration energy storage solutions cannot meet requirements. Long-duration energy storage has become standard for new-energy infrastructure," said Ding Changfu, senior product strategy manager with Xiamen Hithium Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.
The company is investing 400 million euros in a battery and energy-storage production base in Spain, which is scheduled to begin operations next year.
By 2025, Hithium had sold its products in more than 40 countries and regions, while its order book extends into 2027, said Wang Pengcheng, the company's co-founder and president.
"Green and sustainable development represents an unprecedented global consensus and a profound industrial revolution," Wang said.
"As Chinese enterprises speed up global expansion, green investment has become a new highlight of external investment," said Zhou Xiaoyan, executive vice president and secretary-general of the China Council for International Investment Promotion.
From photovoltaic and wind-power equipment to lithium-ion batteries and new-energy vehicles, China is bringing its green development solutions to the world, Zhou said. ■

AU marks 24th anniversary amid call for continental unity, global influence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:18 CST
21:52:18 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Marking the African Union (AU) Day, Chairperson of the African Union Commission (AUC) Mahmoud Ali Youssouf has called for a renewed commitment to the ideals of Pan-Africanism, solidarity, and continental unity.
Celebrated every year on Sept. 9, this year's 24th anniversary commemorated the historic Sirte Declaration of 1999, in Libya, in which African leaders took the decision to establish the African Union to accelerate integration and strengthen Africa's voice globally.
The annual African Union Day serves as an avenue to celebrate some landmark achievements of the union, and an opportunity to reflect on the major challenges faced by the continent and the successes of the continental bloc.
In a press statement issued late Wednesday, the AUC chief emphasized that the priorities of the AU are heavily centered around accelerating economic integration, advancing peace and security, and reinforcing Africa's global voice.
Youssouf also highlighted that this year's commemoration arrives shortly after the United Nations General Assembly endorsed a significant African-led initiative, adopting a non-binding resolution that encourages the use of the Equal Earth cartographic projection in maps worldwide to replace the Mercator projection.
"A map may change how the world sees Africa, but Africa's destiny will ultimately be shaped by how Africans see themselves. The time has come to see Africa in its true size, its true strength and its true potential," he said. "Africa is not seeking a larger place in the world; Africa is reclaiming its rightful place in the world. Our task is to translate this renewed confidence into unity, prosperity, peace and influence."
The chairperson underscored that Africa's remarkable progress must also be measured by the tangible quality of life enjoyed by its people, pointing directly to the AU's 2026 focus on sustainable water availability and safe sanitation for citizens.
He called upon member states, regional economic communities, private sector actors, civil society organizations, women, and the youth to persistently collaborate toward building an integrated, self-confident African continent fully capable of independently shaping its own future destiny.
Though the historic declaration was formally signed in 1999, the Pan-African bloc was officially launched during the Durban Summit in 2002 in South Africa. It succeeded the Organization of African Unity (OAU) to boost economic cooperation, continental unity, and peace across the entire African region. ■

NAIROBI, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Kenyan researchers are set to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) in tracking and surveilling mosquito populations, marking a major technological advancement in the fight against malaria.
Eric Ochomo, a lead entomologist at the Kenya Medical Research Institute's Center for Global Health Research, stated on Wednesday that the AI-powered technology, known as VectorCam, is being integrated into ongoing malaria vector research to augment conventional surveillance techniques.
The VectorCam system combines standard smartphones with specialized light boxes and artificial intelligence algorithms to quickly identify mosquito species and analyze population characteristics, enabling researchers to collect high-precision field data more efficiently.
"The technology is helping to tell the mosquito species, feeding status and the sex. The mosquito collected is then placed on the AI device to allow collection of the data," Ochomo said in comments published by a local daily newspaper.
Ochomo noted that malaria remains a major public health challenge across Sub-Saharan Africa, and in Kenya specifically, continuing to drive high rates of morbidity and mortality despite decades of intensive control interventions.
Sunny Patel, co-founder of VectorCam, who was also quoted by the newspaper, explained that field operations will leverage local networks, with Community Health Promoters utilizing smartphone-based tools during routine community engagements.
He added that artificial intelligence holds transformative potential for national malaria control programs by strengthening vector surveillance, forecasting localized outbreaks, refining diagnostics, optimizing treatment strategies, and guiding targeted resource allocation.
The two researchers noted that AI-powered mosquito surveillance will be carried out in part by Community Health Promoters across malaria-endemic regions.
This technological integration complements core vector control interventions, including Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets, Indoor Residual Spraying, and larval source management, which have been instrumental in reducing malaria transmission across Kenya. ■

====================================================================================================

Whispers of Chinese characters on ceramic glaze: A ceramic micro-calligraphy inheritor's story
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:01 CST
21:52:01 KST

Liu Dachuan creates a ceramic micro-calligraphy artwork at his studio in Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, Aug. 14, 2026.
There goes an old Chinese saying that "the scenery changes with each step." This saying can be true when you look at a ceramic micro-calligraphy artwork, on which Chinese characters are written in tiny little sizes so that you can not even notice them from a distance.
Micro-calligraphy, or weishu, is an age-old Chinese art that wields the traditional Chinese writing brush to produce Chinese characters of astonishing minuteness with naked vision. This art form has deep roots in antiquity, with its earliest traces found in the oracle bone inscriptions from the Western Zhou Dynasty (1046 BC-771 BC).
Ceramic micro-calligraphy, which combines the delicate art with polychrome ceramic, demands high in its making as the ceramic needs to go through high-temperature firing in kiln after the writing. To create a piece, the craftsman, relying solely on his naked eyes, uses a custom fashioned brush, with ultra-fine hairs and high-temperature-resistant pigments, to paint delicate motifs directly onto the ceramic's surface, no errors or corrections allowed. When the ceramic goes through repeated firings in the kiln, even the slightest deviation in temperature control can make all previous labors in vain. Upon completion, the artwork is seen with tiny little Chinese characters interlaced with paintings, complementing each other beautifully.
The art has become a treasure of traditional Chinese crafts with irreplaceable artistic values, and was inscribed as one of China's national-level intangible cultural heritages in 2014.
Liu Dachuan, a 47-year-old senior craftsman from south China's Guangdong Province, has dedicated himself to the art of ceramic micro-calligraphy for decades. He can inscribe up to 163 Chinese characters on a single square centimeter of porcelain, all perfectly distinguishable under a magnifying glass. Liu has formed a modern artistic style while carrying on the traditions, and his works have won multiple widely recognized awards.
"Writing micro-calligraphy with the naked eye tests not only your eyesight, but also your very soul," Liu said, adding that a machine might replicate the shapes of characters, but it could never depict the flowing spirit unique to the tip of a brush.
To bring ceramic micro-calligraphy to a wider audience, Liu held solo thematic exhibitions, and further established a studio in Jingdezhen, where he formally accepts apprentices and guides them step by step in the art. He also hosts public welfare open classes and intangible cultural heritage experiencing salons, where he offers lectures on the history of micro-calligraphy to local ceramics artisans and tourists on study tours.
Regarded as premium collectible art pieces, ceramic micro-calligraphy artworks have won great favor from cultural institutions and museums, collectors and art lovers across the country. Meanwhile, as craftworks embodying the charm of oriental beauty, they have also appeared in exhibitions of many foreign countries, often being selected as gifts for culture exchanges, and being collected by overseas museums. In a way, they have become artistic carriers to promote the traditional Chinese culture and the exchanges between China and the world. (Xinhua)

====================================================================================================

Former high-ranking EDF officers: Who is running the government in Estonia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Former high-ranking EDF officers: Who is running the government in Estonia?
Strengthening Estonia's defense capabilities is commendable, but we must now turn our attention to the powers the prime minister is prepared to grant the next defense minister to achieve that goal, write Meelis Kiili, Vello Loemaa, Riho Ühtegi, Margus Koplimägi, Leo Kunnas and Neeme Väli.
Under the Government of the Republic Act, the prime minister must submit a proposal to the president to change the composition of the government. Although two ministers have currently resigned, attention is focused on the nomination of a candidate for defense minister. The next defense minister must have access to state secrets and classified foreign information, follow the governing coalition's program and work to resolve acute problems within the Ministry of Defense's area of responsibility.
The Reform Party is nominating (reserve general) Martin Herem as its candidate for defense minister, but the biggest problem with the Cabinet reshuffle is the prime minister's approach and the reasons behind his choices.
Herem has outlined his conditions to journalists as follows: the authority to make personnel decisions, a political mandate to act across ministries and government agencies and the ability to quickly change laws, rules and procedures. This is being justified by the need to rapidly strengthen Estonia's defense capabilities.
The candidate for defense minister does not intend to join the Reform Party and has remained tight-lipped about whether he will run in the spring elections. Herem reportedly has a plan to rapidly resolve problems within the Ministry of Defense's area of administration. One justification offered has been the assessment that the war in Ukraine could end within the next six months, after which the direct military threat to Estonia would rise sharply. Personnel changes began even before the next minister was appointed, when Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk was dismissed at Herem's request.
Strengthening Estonia's defense capabilities is certainly a commendable goal, but we must now turn our attention to the model of governance and the powers the prime minister is prepared to grant a single minister to achieve that goal.
One fundamental distinction must be made. Neither a minister nor the prime minister changes laws. Laws are passed and amended by the Riigikogu. The government can initiate legislation and request that it be fast-tracked, but legislative power does not belong to the executive branch. If one of the preconditions for the ministerial candidate's mandate is the ability to quickly change laws that impede his actions, what is actually being promised through such a political mandate?
The prime minister is the head of government and his job is to ensure that the government functions as a whole, that ministers' areas of authority are clear and that power, oversight and responsibility lie within the same chain of decision-making. In this system, the prime minister should be the guardian of institutional balance, not the broker of special powers for a single minister.
What happens if one minister's mandate comes to include the authority to intervene across ministries and government agencies, replace personnel and seek the rapid removal of laws and procedures that he believes impede action? In effect, we would be creating a chief executive with special powers. Why did the prime minister agree to such a model of governance?
It may be somewhat reassuring that the coalition's order of succession for replacing the prime minister puts the minister of education and research first and the finance minister second, although it has been fairly common practice for the foreign minister and defense minister to serve as substitutes.
If the chief executive's mandate extends into the areas of responsibility of other ministers, then who ultimately leads whom? The prime minister is supposed to lead the Cabinet, but a chief executive could emerge alongside him whose actual decision-making authority extends beyond the Cabinet's customary division of responsibilities.
From a national defense perspective, there is another fundamental contradiction. Estonia's national defense is based on a broad approach, meaning that defending the country is not solely the responsibility of the Ministry of Defense and the Estonian Defense Forces. Defense capability depends on the economy, energy, internal security, infrastructure, healthcare, education, communications, local governments and many other areas. The more complex the security environment becomes, the more closely these areas must work together.
The natural leader of such a system cannot be the minister responsible for a single area, no matter how strong his mandate. The leader of that system must be the prime minister.
This creates a strange paradox. The broader modern national defense becomes, the stronger the prime minister's leadership role should be. The proposed model of governance appears to be moving in the opposite direction: The more important national defense becomes, the more its leadership is to be concentrated in the hands of a single minister with special powers. But that could begin to fragment the broad-based national defense model.
If the defense minister receives a mandate to act across other ministries and government agencies, what role remains for the other ministers and, ultimately, for the prime minister himself? Who weighs the needs of defense against economic, fiscal, internal security or social policy needs? Who resolves problems and conflicts spanning multiple ministries? Who is responsible for the whole? These are all the prime minister's responsibilities.
A state is not a company and the Cabinet is not a corporate board where the prime minister hires a powerful chief executive, gives him a goal and resources and then steps aside. Governance in a democratic state is based on the division of powers, checks and balances and political accountability. The debate over the potential powers of the candidate for defense minister therefore reveals how the prime minister himself understands his role.
If the prime minister believes that resolving Estonia's security problems requires a chief executive alongside him with a mandate extending across the government, why does the prime minister not perform this coordinating role himself?
The analysis in the national defense report highlighted another important problem: The prime minister has not wanted to be the substantive leader of national defense, but rather its supervisor — someone who assigns tasks, coordinates others and waits for results.
Those two roles are not the same. It is worth taking a close look at the Crisis Preparedness and National Defense Act, which is itself the product of the current coalition's work. It establishes many rights and obligations for the government, but the government is still led by the prime minister.
A supervisor can delegate a task and demand that it be completed. A leader must understand the system as a whole, set the objective, make choices between competing needs and take responsibility for the consequences of those choices. In the case of broad national defense, this distinction is particularly important because no one else in the government has a mandate to simultaneously lead defense, internal security, the economy, energy, infrastructure, healthcare and the other areas necessary for the country's continuity.
The current debate over a defense minister with special powers makes the problem identified in the national defense report even more pressing. If the prime minister does not himself assume the role of substantive leader of the entire national defense system, a need inevitably arises to find someone to whom that role can be delegated. But that does not solve the leadership problem. Leadership is simply shifted to a place where political responsibility for the whole does not belong. Interestingly, the defense minister candidate's answers so far suggest a conviction that he will be given authority to act outside government policy.
From this perspective, the emergence of a "chief executive" with special powers is not accidental. It may be a symptom of a much deeper problem: that the prime minister wants to preside over the government, but not necessarily lead it.
There is another issue the prime minister cannot ignore in making such a personnel choice: the so-called revolving door between the state and the defense industry.
The Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) has highlighted in its annual review the risks associated with people moving between national defense decision-making positions and the defense industry. That does not in itself mean that a person should not be allowed to move from one sector to another. The development of the defense industry requires people who understand both the state's needs and the business environment. The problem arises when there is no sufficiently clear boundary between roles and a decision-maker may have direct or indirect interests stemming from previous activities in the sector that he or she is about to oversee politically.
It is therefore strange that, at a time when the state's own security service is drawing attention to this risk, the prime minister appears prepared to move in precisely the direction about which the ISS is urging caution.
This does not concern Martin Herem alone. If other people who have, or recently had, direct business interests in the defense industry are also being considered for a potential defense minister's team, the issue becomes systemic. Who assesses conflicts of interest in such a situation? What restrictions apply? When must someone recuse themselves from a decision? How much time should have to pass between leaving business and entering political decision-making? And who assures the public and competing companies that decisions are made solely in the interests of national defense?
These questions do not imply that anyone is planning to abuse their official position. The principle of good governance is precisely the opposite: The system must be designed so that the state does not depend solely on the goodwill of decision-makers. In addition to actual conflicts of interest, any reasonable appearance of such a conflict must also be avoided.
Paradoxically, a poorly managed revolving-door problem can also harm the company from which people enter public service. If its former key personnel begin taking part in shaping defense policy, capability development or procurement, it becomes more difficult for the company itself to demonstrate in the Estonian market that its success is based solely on product quality, price and fair competition. Even a tender won entirely fairly could be subject to legitimate criticism.
Clear conflict-of-interest rules therefore protect not only the state. They also protect companies and the credibility of the market. And that brings us back to the prime minister.
The prime minister's job is to find someone who promises to deliver results quickly, but it is also his job to assess what institutional risks a personnel choice creates for the state.
If the ISS has already publicly identified one such risk, it is important to know how the prime minister intends to mitigate it. If the government itself does not consider it necessary to take seriously a systemic risk identified by the country's security service when making personnel choices, what practical significance are such ISS warnings supposed to have at all? When granting special powers, it is also necessary to assess how a person has previously used extensive decision-making authority entrusted to him in a crisis.
One such example comes from the COVID-19 crisis. As commander of the Estonian Defense Forces, Martin Herem implemented a vaccination requirement that resulted in dozens of people being dismissed from service. Courts later found some of those dismissals unlawful. Hostilities were already underway on Ukrainian soil at the time and Estonia's threat assessments were by no means less serious.
The issue is not whether one is for or against vaccination, but rather the practice of leadership. How does a leader in a crisis weigh the objective, the speed of decision-making, the proportionality of measures, an organization's human resources and legal constraints?
One previous decision does not prove that the same leader would make the wrong decision in the future. It is, however, relevant information for a prime minister considering granting him even greater decision-making authority than usual. The greater the power being granted, the more important it is to assess how that power has previously been exercised when checks and constraints were in place.
We have a very recent example from the defense sector of what can happen when speed becomes a substitute for the quality of decision-making. Gen. Colin Powell articulated a simple principle of leadership: "The key is not to make quick decisions, but to make timely decisions." The distinction is fundamental. Hopefully, the rush was not driven by the idea of outperforming our ally, the Czech Republic, which took responsibility for a major program to procure artillery shells for Ukraine. Instead, the alliance relationship should have been used to learn from its experience.
In the shell deal, urgency was the central argument. Shells were needed quickly, and decisions therefore had to be made quickly. We have now arrived at the paradoxical outcome that we have neither the shells nor the money, but the damage does not end there. Another resource critical to national defense has also been lost: trust.
Cases like this damage public confidence that money allocated to defense is being used thoughtfully and responsibly. They also damage Estonia's credibility in the eyes of our partners. In national defense, trust is a strategic resource on which both society's willingness to support defense spending and our partners' willingness to cooperate with us depend.
The true cost of rushing is therefore greater than the monetary value of a failed deal. We do not have the shells, we do not have the money spent on them and we have damaged trust both within our society and among our partners. One consequence is a visit by European Commission inspectors, who are coming to examine how the Estonian state fulfilled its due diligence obligations.
One of the advantages of a small country like Estonia should be its ability to make decisions faster than larger systems, but speed is an advantage only when the decision is sound. A bad decision does not become better because it was made quickly.
That is precisely why it is strange to respond to problems that have emerged in the defense sector's chain of decision-making, oversight and accountability by proposing that the next minister be given even greater personal decision-making authority and the ability to more quickly change or eliminate procedures that stand in his way.
If the problem was excessively slow bureaucracy, such a solution may be justified. But if the problem was the quality of decisions, inadequate risk assessment or weak oversight, the same solution could instead exacerbate the problem. Making that distinction is the prime minister's responsibility.
Traditionally, important ministerial posts go to people who have received a mandate from voters — that is, members of parliament. Ministers appointed from outside parliament are also politically accountable under the governing coalition's program and mandate, something that cannot be overridden by any action plan they draw up themselves. This brings us to another fundamental issue: the balance between power and responsibility.
In a democratic state, power cannot be treated as a stand-alone resource given to a leader so that he can "get things done." Power, oversight, accountability and responsibility must form a coherent whole. The greater the power, the clearer the mechanisms of oversight and responsibility for its use must be. This is precisely where the model of a chief executive with special powers becomes problematic.
If the defense minister is given greater-than-usual authority to make personnel decisions, act across ministries and government agencies and seek rapid changes to rules and procedures that constrain his actions, it must be equally clear to whom he is accountable for the exercise of that power.
Under the conventional model of government, the chain of accountability is at least clear in principle. A minister is responsible for his or her area of government, the government acts collectively, the prime minister leads the government and the Riigikogu exercises oversight over the executive branch. But if one minister's actual mandate begins to extend into the areas of responsibility of other ministers, the boundaries of accountability also become blurred.
If a minister with special powers makes a decision whose consequences are felt within another ministry's area of responsibility, who is accountable? The minister whose area was intervened in? The minister with special powers who pushed the decision through? Or the prime minister who granted such a mandate? After all, the boundaries between ministries' areas of responsibility are determined by the government, not the prime minister.
These questions concern one of the central principles of democratic governance: Power cannot be granted where accountability cannot follow.
The situation becomes even more problematic when reducing oversight and procedures is presented as justification for greater freedom to make decisions. Oversight mechanisms can indeed be cumbersome, duplicative or outdated and they must be changed when necessary because well-designed oversight is part of good governance.
The experience of the shell deal should make this especially clear to us. If, after an incident that has left us without either the shells or the money spent on them and has damaged trust both within society and among our partners, the conclusion is that the next leader should be given even greater decision-making freedom and face fewer constraints, then the diagnosis may be more dangerous than the problem itself.
Strong leadership is, of course, necessary in national defense. But does a strong leader mean someone with as much power as possible or someone capable of achieving results within a system where that power is matched by oversight, accountability and responsibility? These are two very different understandings of leadership. Ultimately, the choice between them is not the defense minister's to make, but the prime minister's.
If the prime minister gives one minister greater power than usual, it is the prime minister who must be able to explain to the public and the Riigikogu what oversight corresponds to that power and who bears responsibility if decisions prove wrong. Otherwise, we end up with a model in which power is personalized but responsibility is collectivized. When things go well, the leader gets the credit; when they go wrong, responsibility dissipates throughout the system. Such a model of governance follows the logic that if mistakes are repeated often enough and long enough, they become procedure.
If Estonia's problem is excessively slow bureaucracy, the bureaucracy must be improved. If the problem is flawed defense policy, better defense policy must be developed. If the problem is weak cooperation between government agencies, the prime minister must lead that cooperation. If the problem is the quality of decisions and the diffusion of responsibility, concentrating even more power in the hands of one person cannot be the solution.
One of the fundamental rules of leadership is that the problem must be correctly diagnosed before a solution is chosen. Otherwise, the solution may end up treating the symptom while making the underlying illness worse. That is precisely why it is strange that, after problems have emerged in defense-sector leadership, oversight, procurement and accountability, the answer appears to be an even more personalized model of governance.
Moreover, this model could begin to change the established logic of how Estonia's national defense is governed. The purpose of broad national defense is to integrate defense with the functioning of the rest of the state. The proposed model could move in the opposite direction, creating a vertical chain of command for the defense sector that enjoys a special status relative to the rest of the government. That is a strategic choice for which the candidate for defense minister is not responsible. The prime minister is.
A state is not a company and the prime minister is not an owner who hires a chief executive and says, "Here is the goal and the money. Get it done." Still less can he give that chief executive a mandate to override other ministers' areas of authority when necessary, restructure personnel, eliminate procedures and expect the legislature to adapt the legal framework to suit his operational needs.
In a democratic state, power must always be accompanied by authority, oversight, accountability and responsibility. The greater the power, the clearer the responsibility must be.
If Estonia's national defense is based on a broad approach, then national defense encompassing the entire government must be led by the prime minister. If that requires a chief executive with special powers alongside him, it inevitably raises questions about the prime minister's own role — in other words, about who is actually leading the government in this system.
Meelis Kiili is a reserve major general and member of the Riigikogu; Vello Loemaa is a retired major general and former commander of the Estonian Air Force; Riho Ühtegi is a reserve major general; Margus Koplimägi is a former commander of the Estonian contingent in Afghanistan; Leo Kunnas is a reserve lieutenant colonel and member of the Riigikogu; and Neeme Väli is a reserve major general and member of Isamaa.

BRICS 2026: Who’s coming and what’s on the agenda?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:50:17 UTC

BRICS 2026: Who’s coming and what’s on the agenda?
The BRICS summit comes to New Delhi this weekend, bringing leaders from the expanded group of major emerging economies together for two days of talks. 
India will host the September 12-13 meeting at Bharat Mandapam, the convention center that hosted the Group of 20 (G20) summit in 2023. Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to arrive in India this weekend for the summit, along with other heads of state and government of the group of emerging economies. 
The agenda is broad but straightforward: trade and development, technology, energy and food security, reform of global institutions, and closer cooperation among BRICS members. The leaders will also exchange views on major global and regional issues. 
India has framed its 2026 chairmanship around ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’, under a broader ‘Humanity First’ approach. 
This is India’s fourth time chairing BRICS, after 2012, 2016, and 2021. It also comes as the group marks 20 years since its establishment. 
Which countries are in BRICS now? 
The BRICS grouping has grown considerably from its original five members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It now also includes Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Indonesia. BRICS has emerged as a major grouping because of its economic weight and population size.
 Together, they now account for nearly half of the world’s population, around 40% of global GDP, and 26% of international trade, according to Indian government data.
The group’s growth comes at a time when the ability of groupings such as the G7 and G20 to influence the world economy is waning amid narrow geopolitical agendas and attempts at economic coercion.
Who is attending the BRICS summit in India? 
The gathering is expected to bring together leaders of the Global South who also have the ability to set the direction of the global economy – individually and collectively.
Host country India has recorded strong economic growth this year, the fastest among major economies, reflecting well on Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is attending, the Kremlin has confirmed. Modi and Putin are also slated to hold talks in New Delhi on the sidelines of the summit, with bilateral ties and international issues expected to feature prominently in the discussions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is attending, the Chinese Foreign Ministry confirmed on Thursday. The ministry said it “sets great store by BRICS cooperation” and supports India in hosting a successful summit. Some reports suggest that Xi will arrive with a 400-member delegation.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has confirmed that he will attend. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the other leaders expected in New Delhi, with Modi and Pezeshkian also scheduled to meet.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will not travel to New Delhi and is expected to be represented by a senior government official. Bangladesh, which was invited by New Delhi, has said it will not send a representative.
Leaders and representatives from other BRICS members, partner countries, and outreach invitees will also take part.
What will BRICS leaders discuss in New Delhi? 
India has divided its presidential agenda into four broad areas.
‘Resilience’ covers issues that directly affect economies and households – health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster preparedness, and supply chains.
‘Innovation’ covers startups, small businesses, science and technology, digital public infrastructure, and AI. ‘Cooperation’ includes development and reform of global governance institutions.
‘Sustainability’ covers renewable energy, climate action, and adaptation.
Trade, investment, and financial cooperation will also feature, along with efforts to give developing and emerging economies a greater voice in international institutions. 
Current global developments will form part of the discussions as well. The Indian Foreign Ministry said the leaders will share perspectives on “global and regional matters of mutual importance.” 
A packed schedule focused on inclusive global growth
Saturday is primarily for the group’s full members. Leaders will first meet behind closed doors for a session on ‘Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism’. 
They will later visit the ‘Bharat Innovates’ exhibition, followed by a group photo, tree-planting ceremony, and a dinner hosted by Modi. The table gets wider on Sunday, when leaders from BRICS partner countries and outreach invitees join the summit. 
The main session will focus on ‘Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth’. The summit is expected to conclude with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration, setting out the positions and priorities agreed on by the group.

Damaged equipment at Ryazan oil refinery will take weeks to repair – Reuters
The Ryazan oil refinery belonging to Rosneft, a major Russian state-controlled oil and gas company, stopped operating after a drone attack on 6 September, and repairs to the damaged units may take several weeks.
Source: Reuters, citing two industry sources

Germany misappropriates over a third of additional defense debt in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:47:42 UTC
21:47:42 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The German government misappropriated more than a third of the new debt intended for defense spending in 2025 to finance other areas of the federal budget, an economic report revealed on Thursday.  
The ifo Institute's report detailed how Germany utilized its 2025 defense debt exemption; Emilie Hoeslinger, the author of the study, stated that the state took on €28.6 billion ($33.2 billion) in additional debt under the exemption.
Hoeslinger found that €11 billion of these funds failed to generate additional defense spending, resulting in a 38.5% diversion rate.
The researcher explained that this mechanism created financial leeway in the tax-financed core budget for other nonmilitary purposes.
The institute revealed that the government allocated €900 million from this defense exemption to the federal highway company Autobahn GmbH.
The report noted that the largest legitimate defense spending increase went toward ammunition procurement, with a surge of €2.32 billion.
Hoeslinger highlighted that spending on military research and development remained low at €883.8 million, making up only 1.2% of the total exemption expenses.
The author warned that this concentration on conventional equipment ignored future-oriented capabilities like unmanned systems and cyber defense.

Hundreds of thousands lack adequate shelter at Sudan’s Tawila camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:47:35 UTC
21:47:35 KST

Over 665,000 displaced people face shelter crisis in Sudan’s Tawila
Insufficient aid and shelter increase hardship for displaced in Tawila, as malnutrition and disease spread rapidly.
Blue tents stand in tight rows at the Daba Naira camp in Tawila, 68 kilometres west of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur in Sudan, racked by war.
The tents were set up by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), with support from the Turkish Disaster and Emergency Management Authority.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mass grave with 25 bodies found in Sudan’s Kurmuk after army retakes town
- list 2 of 3Is Sudan’s battlefield shaping the terms of its next political phase?
- list 3 of 3Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
Relief teams have erected 3,000 new tents in recent months, but the number is negligible compared with the needs of more than 665,000 displaced people, the IOM said in a statement.
The most pressing question remains: how can this number of tents possibly be enough for hundreds of thousands of displaced people, especially when rainfall threatens to turn the low‑lying ground into swamps?
Promises of aid
Abdelbagi Mohamed Hamid, the minister of social welfare and humanitarian affairs coordinator in the Darfur region, told Al Jazeera Arabic that the regional government appealed to donors, including the Turkish ambassador, to provide tents for the displaced.
As a result, Turkiye allocated 30,000 tents to be distributed in Darfur and Kordofan through the IOM. Abdelbagi said 3,000 of 6,000 expected tents were erected in the Daba Naira camp in Tawila. Another 2,450 were delivered to the Salam, al‑Wihda and al‑Nakheel camps in Shaeria locality in South and East Darfur.
The minister said the Malha locality had the greatest need for humanitarian assistance in Darfur, followed by Tina, Karnoy and Um Baru areas. The Tina border crossing should be opened to allow the delivery of aid to these isolated areas, which suffer from acute shortages of food, medicine and fuel, while the war has deepened their isolation and worsened their humanitarian situation, he said.
Abdelbagi warned that providing shelter alone is not enough to confront the crisis, given the looming danger of famine, which could prove deadlier than the war itself, as humanitarian organisations struggle to reach many affected regions.
Worn‑out tents
The arrival of the new tents coincided with the beginning of the rainy season and an outbreak of fires sweeping through displacement camps, increasing the suffering of displaced people living under tattered canopies without protection from wind and rain, amid acute shortages of food, clean water and healthcare.
The IOM warned of persistent and worsening humanitarian needs in Tawila, as services deteriorate and diseases like cholera spread amid a lack of clean drinking water, resulting in watery diarrhoea and skin infections. The camps are overcrowded and lack basic sanitation.
The organisation, while continuing to expand the number of shelters in the Daba Naira camp, cannot keep up with the rapid pace of displacement.
‘Dropping like flies’
Ahmed Mousa, a displaced man from el-Fasher who is staying in the Daba Naira camp, told Al Jazeera that the new tents do not cover even a tenth of the camp’s needs, with people sleeping in the rain in the open and children falling ill without adequate care.
Fatima Ibrahim, a displaced woman in the same camp, said people fled el-Fasher in search of safety – only to find themselves exposed to the elements, hunger and disease.
“We see the new tents from afar, but they are not enough. We are dropping like flies from hunger and disease. Our children fall ill before our eyes, and we don’t even have medicine,” she said, adding that many families slept on bare ground without protection from the cold of night and the heat of day.
Famine ‘may be more dangerous than war’
The Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Darfur region, Al‑Sadiq Barango, told Al Jazeera in a statement that the famine may be more dangerous than the war, amid declining seasonal rains and the drying of agricultural lands and livestock pastures.
He says the war has driven farmers to abandon their land, while cultivated areas, particularly fruit farms and cash‑crop plantations, have been attacked and destroyed by armed groups.
Barango described the situation as “ominous signs of a looming catastrophe,” and called for urgent humanitarian intervention, as starvation threatens thousands of people across Sudan, with Darfur the most affected due to years of conflict and the collapse of agricultural infrastructure.
‘Tawila is not just numbers’
Tawila hosts about 665,000 displaced people, most of whom fled el-Fasher and its surroundings, according to the IOM’s statement. Their number had more than doubled between March and September 2025, from 238,000 to more than 652,000.
More than 70 percent of households in Tawila lack healthcare, while half of families have been unable to obtain treatment, according to the organisation’s estimates. Children under the age of five and pregnant women are the most affected, with rising rates of malnutrition and infectious diseases.
Adam Rijal, spokesperson for the Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees, told Al Jazeera that “Tawila is not just numbers,” noting that needs exceed capacities dozens of times over, and warning of more deaths, especially among children and the elderly, due to hunger, disease and the absence of basic services.
Relief challenges
Humanitarian organisations face major difficulties reaching displaced people because of rough terrain and the spread of checkpoints belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which is at war with the Sudanese government and controls vital routes in the area.
Local activists say that aid trucks are sometimes subjected to looting and extortion, which raises the cost of relief and delays its arrival to those who need it. Many displaced people – according to field reports – have been forced to walk long distances to obtain limited food rations, while others go weeks without assistance.
In Tawila, where hundreds of thousands live in worn‑out tents amid disease outbreaks and the hazards of the rainy season, the need for shelter, food and care is growing, while 3,000 tents are nowhere near enough to confront a humanitarian catastrophe that is worsening by the day.

The International Skating Union (ISU) has rejected appeals from Russian figure skaters Kamila Valieva and Mark Kondratiuk, who had challenged the revocation of their neutral athlete status — a status that would have allowed them to compete internationally.
“Following individual eligibility assessments, the ISU has determined that Mark Kondratiuk and Kamila Valieva no longer satisfy the requirements to participate as Individual Neutral Athletes,” the press release said.

The ISU granted Valieva and Kondratiuk individual neutral athlete status in August 2026 but reversed the decision by early September, without officially disclosing its reasons. Under ISU rules, an athlete cannot receive neutral athlete status if they serve in the armed forces or national security agencies, are participating in the war with Ukraine on Russia’s side, or are actively and publicly supporting it.

Poland says it has lost about €113.5bn due to war in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:45:00 EEST
