Mao Zedong, Israel and the road not taken - 50 years after leader’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:26:52 UTC
21:26:52 KST

Wednesday, September 9, marked 50 years since the death of Mao Zedong, the Chinese revolutionary leader whose long shadow is still cast over Asian and world geopolitics.
For almost three decades after proclaiming the establishment of the People’s Republic of China in Beijing in October 1949, Mao stood at the center of a political transformation that altered China entirely and reshaped the balance of the Cold War.
Under his leadership, the world’s most populous country emerged from decades of civil war, foreign occupation and internal collapse as a Communist power determined to chart its own course, eventually challenging both the United States and, after the Sino-Soviet split, the Soviet Union for influence across Asia, Africa and the developing world.
His domestic rule brought immense upheaval and suffering, from the Great Leap Forward to the violence and political convulsions of the Cultural Revolution, which together inflicted enormous loss of life and upheaval on China. But abroad, Mao became something larger than the leader of China alone. To revolutionary movements from Vietnam to Africa and the Middle East, Maoism offered an ideology built around guerrilla warfare, peasant revolution and resistance to imperialism, while Beijing sought to present itself as the natural patron of peoples struggling against colonial or Western-backed powers.
Israel occupied a curious place within that worldview, because Mao’s China had not begun as its enemy.
A relationship with an extraordinary trajectory
In fact, the relationship followed an extraordinary trajectory. Israel was the first country in the Middle East to recognize the new Communist government, and the two countries briefly appeared to be moving toward full diplomatic relations, as Chinese officials spoke warmly of friendship with Israel and the Jewish people. Within little more than a decade, however, Mao was receiving the leaders of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) in Beijing, supplying Palestinian terrorists and describing Israel alongside Taiwan as one of the West’s “bases of imperialism in Asia.”
A little over a month before Mao died in Beijing, then-Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin attempted a relatively uncomplicated gesture of international sympathy.
On July 28, 1976, an enormous earthquake had devastated the Chinese city of Tangshan, killing hundreds of thousands of people in one of the deadliest natural disasters of the 20th century. Rabin sent Chinese premier Hua Guofeng a cable expressing Israel’s sorrow over the loss of life and offering medical and other assistance to the Chinese people. Beijing sent it back.
Attached to the returned message was an explanation that, since the People’s Republic of China did not have diplomatic relations with Israel, the Chinese government could not accept the cable.
For a brief moment in the 1950's, full diplomatic relations appeared within reach
It was a final footnote to the relationship that a quarter of a century earlier had appeared capable of ending very differently. Israel had been the first country in the Middle East to recognize the People’s Republic, Israeli officials traveled through Maoist China as guests of the government, and senior Chinese officials had spoken openly of their friendship with Israel and the Jewish people. For a brief period during the 1950s, full diplomatic relations appeared within reach.
Mao, born in Hunan province in 1893, had risen from the son of a prosperous peasant farmer to become one of the founders of the Chinese Communist Party and, eventually, the dominant figure of the Chinese revolution. After decades of civil war, Japanese occupation, the Long March, and the final defeat of Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalists, Mao stood in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square on October 1, 1949, and proclaimed the establishment of the People’s Republic of China.
On January 9, 1950, less than four months after Mao declared the People’s Republic, Israel formally recognized his government as the legitimate government of China. At the time, there was some Chinese sympathy for Zionism, which could be viewed through the lens of revolution and a national liberation movement that had fought British imperial rule.
The Korean War, which broke out later that year and eventually saw Chinese troops fighting American-led UN forces, complicated Israel’s efforts to develop the relationship. Israel was increasingly conscious of its close relationship with the United States, which continued to recognize Chiang Kai-shek’s government on Taiwan as the legitimate government of China and viewed diplomatic engagement with Communist Beijing with deep suspicion.
Even so, the possibility never entirely disappeared, and several years later an unlikely Israeli diplomat in Burma began trying to reopen the door.
David Hacohen, Israel’s man in Rangoon, had become convinced that the young Jewish state could not afford to neglect Asia. Beginning in late 1953, he held discussions with China’s ambassador to Burma, Yao Zhongming, and later met premier and foreign minister Zhou Enlai as the Chinese leader passed through Rangoon following the 1954 Geneva Conference.
The talks quickly became serious enough for trade to be discussed, and produced one of the stranger episodes in the story. According to Hacohen’s account, the Soviet ambassador in Burma joined the conversations and, confronted by the possibility that Washington might object to direct trade between Israel and Communist China, suggested simply sending the goods on a triangular route through Odesa and Siberia.
Beijing subsequently invited an Israeli commercial delegation to China, and in early 1955 Hacohen led a group that spent several weeks touring the country, visiting cities, factories, industrial plants and villages before holding talks in Beijing.
The reception appears to have been extraordinarily warm. A Chinese undersecretary of trade told the delegation that “the Chinese people and their government are great friends of Israel and the Jewish people,” while Hacohen returned convinced that China wanted commercial ties and would respond positively if Israel moved toward diplomatic relations.
There were discussions behind the scenes about what formal relations might look like, yet Israel hesitated. Hacohen later complained of what he called “friendly American pressure,” while Israeli diplomats in Washington worried that moving too quickly toward Mao could damage the country’s increasingly important relationship with the United States.
By the time of the Bandung Conference in April, 1955, China was moving in another direction.
Bringing together 29 Asian and African states in Indonesia, Bandung became a defining moment in the emergence of what would later be called the Third World. Israel was kept away following opposition from Arab participants, while Zhou used the gathering to cultivate governments emerging from colonial rule and to align China increasingly with their causes.
Another blow to Sino-Israeli relations was Israel's participation alongside Britain and France in the 1956 Suez Crisis against Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, which proved particularly damaging in Beijing, where Mao’s China was attempting to present itself as one of the foremost opponents of Western imperialism. Whatever the Chinese had once made of Israel’s own struggle against British rule, the image was now of Israeli forces fighting beside two former European imperial powers against perhaps the most celebrated Arab nationalist leader of his generation.
During the following decade, that perception only hardened.
PLO greeted warmly by China's leadership
The transformation was unmistakable in March 1965 when Ahmad Shukeiri, then chairman of the recently established PLO, arrived in Beijing at the head of a Palestinian delegation. He was given the sort of welcome usually reserved for the representatives of a state, greeted amid flags, drums and crowds before meetings with China’s most senior leadership, including Mao himself.
During his conversation with Shukeiri, Mao offered perhaps the clearest explanation of where Israel had come to sit in his conception of the world.
“Israel and Formosa (Taiwan) are bases of imperialism in Asia,” Mao said. By then, he had come to see Israel and Taiwan in much the same light: as Western-backed footholds in Asia, Israel positioned against the Arab world and Taiwan against Communist China.
Taiwan was among the defining obsessions of Mao’s foreign policy. Chiang Kai-shek and the remnants of the Nationalist government had fled there following their defeat in 1949, surviving under American protection as Mao remained determined that the island would eventually come under Beijing’s control.
China provided PLO with arms, money, military training
China’s support for the Palestinians soon extended well beyond rhetoric. The Chinese provided money, small arms, expertise and military training to Palestinian organizations, although the scale was considerably smaller than was sometimes claimed at the time. Small groups of Palestinian terrorists traveled to China during the late 1960s, where their instruction included guerrilla warfare alongside immersion in Maoist political doctrine and visits to factories, agricultural communes and revolutionary sites.
Some returned to the Middle East as instructors themselves, carrying with them an ideology then reaching the height of its global influence. Even Mao’s Little Red Book found its way onto the battlefield; following an Israeli operation against Palestinian guerrillas in Lebanon in 1972, Israeli troops were reported to have found an Arabic edition of Mao’s sayings among captured propaganda material.
Even during the years of Maoist hostility, however, Israel maintained the position it had taken in 1950 - that Beijing, rather than Taipei, was the government of China.
In October 1971, despite China’s support for Palestinian terror groups and years of bitter rhetoric against Zionism, Israel voted in favor of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, which transferred China’s seat at the United Nations to the People’s Republic and expelled the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek. Israel was among the 76 countries voting in favor.
Five years later came the Tangshan earthquake and Rabin’s returned message.
Mao died several weeks afterward, on September 9, 1976. In the years that followed, China gradually moved away from the revolutionary foreign policy of the Mao era, as Deng Xiaoping placed more emphasis on economic modernization and pragmatic relations abroad. Quiet contacts with Israel developed behind the scenes, and on January 24, 1992, the two countries finally established full diplomatic relations.

Charismatic churches have expanded influence to 3 million Ukrainians during war – interchurch council head
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:26:09 EEST
21:26:09 KST

Ukraine has 1,300 evangelical charismatic churches that have stepped up their activity since Russia's full-scale invasion and now engage with roughly 3 million citizens, said Andriy Tyshchenko, head of the Ukrainian Interchurch Council (UMR) and senior bishop of the Charismatic Evangelical Church of Ukraine.
"Right now we have 1,300 churches with 100,000 members, and during the war they now reach probably around 3 million people, because we distribute a lot of food and carry out evangelization. Our church alone has led 300,000 people to repentance during the full-scale war," Tyshchenko said at a press conference titled "The Role of Evangelical Churches in Strengthening Ukraine's Resilience" at Interfax-Ukraine on Thursday.
He stressed that the UMR is counting on productive dialogue and cooperation with all religious denominations and with the authorities, "because we are not only Christians but also citizens of our country, who take a very active part in all aspects of public life."
UMR deputy head Ruslan Kukharchuk, head of the "All Together!" Christian civic movement, said Ukraine has three major interdenominational associations: besides the UMR, which unites newer evangelical Protestant churches, there is also the All-Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organizations (VRTsiRO) and the Council of Evangelical Protestant Churches of Ukraine (REPTsU), which includes traditional Protestant churches. He said the UMR maintains close and friendly relations with all Christian denominations and churches belonging to REPTsU and VRTsiRO, and expressed hope that the UMR would join VRTsiRO.
"The largest churches in Kyiv are UMR churches — in terms of the number of people who come to a single Sunday service in one hall, in one location, that's 500, a thousand, 1,500, 2,000 people every Sunday.... So it would undoubtedly be natural and logical for the UMR to also become part of VRTsiRO. That's exactly what would allow interdenominational Christian representation to be presented more fairly and objectively at such a high level, including in interaction with state authorities," Kukharchuk said.
He also noted the high level of religious freedom in Ukraine and stressed that this is not typical for all countries and is a major asset for Ukraine that should be highlighted internationally.
Liudmyla Fylypovych, doctor of philosophy and president of the Ukrainian Association of Religious Scholars, said that when charismatic churches began operating in Ukraine, they faced a degree of rejection from traditional churches, but since the war began they have shown themselves to be very active.
"These churches became a kind of hub where people would come, having been displaced, and where they were fed. This isn't unique to the charismatics — you understand that all Protestants have shown themselves to be fairly active in this respect. But charismatic Christianity stands out from classical Protestantism in the speed of its response.... That's because these churches operate not on a vertical chain of command but on horizontal relationships. If, say, some charismatic church suddenly runs short of bread, medicine, clothing or something else, they quickly arrange things among themselves and those needs are covered right away," she said.
Fylypovych said today's believer wants a quick response and answers to their questions, "and believers in charismatic churches get those answers in a timely way."
Viacheslav Horshkov, head of the religious affairs department at Ukraine's State Service for Ethnopolitics and Freedom of Conscience (DESS), said the scale of religious organizations' interaction with state bodies has grown substantially since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. "In 2021, on the eve of the full-scale invasion, our DESS received nearly 4,000 incoming letters, of which about 1,500 concerned religious matters and were communications from religious organizations. In 2025, the total number of incoming documents grew to 14,239, more than 3.6 times higher. And the number of documents on religious topics reached 10,500, an increase of more than sevenfold. That shows the intensity of religious communities' communication with the central state body — and we're not the only body religious organizations communicate with, so this points to an intensification of this interaction overall," he said.
According to the DESS representative, these documents cover issues including regulating chaplaincy service, the ability to travel abroad to advocate for Ukraine internationally, assistance to refugees, the import and provision of humanitarian aid, alternative service, and electricity and gas prices for religious organizations running charitable projects.
"It's naturally much easier for the state when religious organizations unite, when they create a single center, because then communication becomes simpler and its effectiveness grows. The state deals with one entity representing others who have pooled their positions, and the effectiveness of such cooperation increases significantly," Horshkov said.

France pushes back against English-first EU trade deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:26:08 UTC
21:26:08 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrive for their meeting at the Hyderabad House in New Delhi on Feb. 28, 2025. | Money Sharma/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — France is pushing back against the European Commission’s bid to fast-track trade deals with Indonesia and India by using English-language texts before they are fully translated, four people familiar with the matter told POLITICO.
Brussels floated a new plan in February with EU capitals to prioritize an “English-first” approach, allowing member countries and the European Parliament to approve the English-language version of trade agreements rather than waiting months for translations into all the other 23 official EU languages.
The language row risks delaying the drive by Brussels to diversify the EU’s trading relationships — away from U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade protectionism and China’s growing export dominance — through a string of trade deals with Asia, Latin America and the Middle East.
Advertisement
“We want to ensure equal treatment of all the European Union’s official languages, including French, of course, in the context of the agreements with Indonesia and India,” said a French official, granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door discussions.
The European Commission estimates that prioritizing the English version would cut almost a year off the time it takes to get those trade deals over the line.
The dispute is particularly sensitive for Paris, where defending the French language — once the principal language of international diplomacy — has been a core tenet of its foreign policy. France is meanwhile headed into a presidential election cycle where Euroskeptic and protectionist voices are increasingly shaping the political debate, making concessions on trade or national prestige especially explosive.
“However procedural it may appear, this measure touches on highly sensitive issues surrounding trade, language and French national prestige — handing powerful political ammunition to populist parties that polls repeatedly show are already standing at the gates of power,” said François Chimits, head of the Europe Program at the Paris-based Institut Montaigne.
Italy initially joined France in expressing concern, with Rome and Paris warning that the fast-track procedure would set a democratic and legal precedent. But it dropped its opposition on Thursday according to one of the people familiar.
“France isn’t dragging its feet; France cannot commit to an international document — such as a trade agreement — that is drafted in a language other than French,” a second French official said, citing constitutional obligations. “Voting on an English-only version would be a violation of the EU’s principle of multilingualism.”
Advertisement
Indonesia is the more pressing case. The text of the agreement has been on the table since late June but has yet to be put to a vote among EU ambassadors — one of the final hurdles before Commission President Ursula von der Leyen can sign it and it can enter into force.
Indonesia will cease at the start of next year to be a beneficiary of the EU’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences — which grants lower tariffs to developing countries — making an agreement important if it wants to preserve preferential access.
Brussels is meanwhile slated to present the trade deal with India to EU capitals in the coming days. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected in Brussels in mid-December as a guest at the European Council, with a signature ceremony expected on the sidelines.
Despite the time pressure, two of the people played down the prospect of a serious roadblock. The objections are still being handled at the technical level and are not expected to derail either deal.
Koen Verhelst contributed reporting. This article has been updated.

Algeria says cutting diplomatic ties with UAE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:26:06 UTC
21:26:06 KST

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE
Relations have been strained for years, as the two countries took differing positions on several regional issues.
Algeria says it has decided to cut diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates after what it described as a series of “provocative or hostile” actions by Abu Dhabi despite “repeated warnings”.
Algeria’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that the UAE’s actions had reached a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable and that it had “exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations”.
It said the Emirati ambassador had been summoned to the ministry, informed of the decision and given 48 hours to comply.
Later in the day, Algeria said it will close its airspace to all UAE-registered civilian and military aircraft from Friday, Ennahar TV reported, citing the defence ministry. UAE commercial flights to and from Algiers will be exempt from the ban until the end of 2026, when the current contract expires, the ministry added.
The UAE hoped Algeria’s decision to cut diplomatic ties would be “temporary”, its foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirms the UAE’s appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors,” the ministry added.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, wrote on X that diplomatic relations should be based on “rationality, communication and clarity of interests” rather than “riddles and signals that require decoding”.
Gargash did not explicitly mention Algeria or directly link his comments to Algiers’ announcement.
Strained relations
Relations between the two countries have come under growing strain in recent years, as Algiers and Abu Dhabi have taken differing positions on several regional issues.
Algeria opposes normalisation with Israel, while the UAE and Algeria’s regional rival Morocco established diplomatic ties with Israel under the United States-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
The two countries are also on opposing sides of the decades-old Western Sahara dispute. The UAE supports Morocco’s claim to sovereignty over the territory where it has a consulate, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks an independent Western Sahara.
The two countries’ interests have increasingly crossed in the Sahel, where the UAE has expanded ties with several governments in recent years, while Algeria’s relations with some of its southern neighbours have become strained following a series of military coups.
Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune has often referred to the UAE in speeches as a “micro-state” or “statelet” seeking to destabilise several countries in the region.
“Wherever they set foot, blood flows,” he said in a televised interview in July, adding that the UAE has had a “very negative impact”.
“We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country,” he added.
At the time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break “would have happened long ago” had Algeria not sought to avoid “deepening divisions” in the Arab world.

How the war in Gaza is changing pregnancy and parenthood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:25:38 UTC
21:25:38 KST

Breadcrumb
'Is it safe to have a child?': How Israel's war is reshaping fertility, pregnancy and parenthood in Gaza
Before Israel's war, for many women in Gaza, the decision to become pregnant began with a simple desire: another child, another room, another name to add to the family. Today, the question has become far more painful: is this the right time to bring a child into the world?
Through my work and conversations with women from Gaza, I began to notice that the ongoing genocide has affected more than women’s ability to become pregnant or access infertility treatment. It has reached a stage that comes even before pregnancy itself: the decision to have a child.
Some women are postponing pregnancy because they do not know where they will be living a month from now. Others fear pregnancy because of shortages of food and medication, or because they no longer trust that they will find a functioning hospital when labour begins.
Couples who married during the war have decided to delay starting a family after diapers, infant formula, medicine, and even basic food became difficult to secure. Others became pregnant during the war, only to have their experiences of pregnancy and childbirth leave them traumatised and unwilling to consider another pregnancy.
In this sense, war does not affect only the children who are born during it. It reshapes the decisions of women and men who are still asking themselves, "Should we have children? When? And how many children can we bring into this world?"
Postponing the idea of family amid war
Amal, 26, has been married for two years and has not yet had a child. Before October 2023, she was preparing for her first pregnancy.
She and her husband, Mahmoud, had begun undergoing the necessary medical tests, and she saw pregnancy as the natural next step in their married life.
Then the war overturned those plans.
Amal now lives in a displacement tent in the al-Mawasi area of southern Gaza. She says she no longer thinks about pregnancy in the same way she did before the war.
"Mahmoud and I were preparing for our first baby. We had started the tests before October, but when we were displaced to a tent in Khan Younis, everything disappeared. How am I supposed to get pregnant when I can’t even find an aspirin or clean food? Pregnancy during war isn’t just a risk; it’s like putting your life in danger."
She pauses before continuing.
"Every day I see women in the tents bleeding and unable to find a hospital. I told my husband to forget about having children altogether until the war ends — if I’m even alive by then."
For Amal, postponing pregnancy is no longer a decision about comfort or financial planning. It has become an attempt to protect herself and a child who has not yet been born.
She once dreamed of having four children. Today, she says that if the situation stabilises, she may have only one.
This change in her idea of family size may seem deeply personal, but it raises a larger question: what happens when war becomes part of the calculations behind fertility decisions that were once based mainly on desire, financial circumstances, and social expectations?
Amal is not the only woman who has spoken to me about delaying pregnancy.
Ibrahim, 28, and Reem, 22, married in the middle of the war, after their second displacement. Before getting married, they had planned to start a family immediately.
But their marriage itself took place under circumstances that bore little resemblance to a normal beginning to married life.
They now live in a remaining room of a damaged house in Deir al-Balah.
"Our wedding was held under a tarpaulin, with a displacement meal of canned beans. I can’t carry the guilt of bringing a child into a tent, where they might have to drink salty water," Ibrahim tells The New Arab.
"The price of a pack of diapers alone now requires months of budgeting. It’s absolutely not the time to have children. We’re barely surviving one day at a time."
Reem says, "My heart breaks every time I see displaced children. I wanted to become a mother as soon as I got married, but fear is stronger than emotion. Postponing pregnancy hurts us, but right now it is the only form of mercy available to us."
For the couple, the desire to have children has not disappeared. What has changed is the timing.
When access to a hospital becomes part of the decision to become pregnant
Under normal circumstances, pregnancy requires regular antenatal care, medical tests, medication, skilled birth care, and rapid access to a hospital if complications arise.
In Gaza, however, access to these services can no longer be taken for granted.
The destruction of health facilities and shortages of medicines and equipment have made reproductive care increasingly difficult, while international organisations have been working in 2026 to restore some essential services.
In July 2026, UNFPA reported that 94 percent of hospitals in Gaza were either destroyed or only partially functioning, while fewer than half of health facilities were able to operate at any level.
During the first half of 2025, around 17,000 births were recorded in the Gaza Strip, compared with approximately 29,000 during the same period in 2022 — a decline of more than 41 percent.
During the same period, health authorities recorded more than 2,600 miscarriages and 220 maternal deaths before childbirth, according to data cited by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
UNFPA also reported that around 33 percent of babies born during the first six months of 2025 — approximately 5,560 infants — were premature, had low birth weight, or required admission to neonatal intensive care units.
The decline in the number of births alone cannot be interpreted as evidence that women’s desire to have children has declined. It may also be linked to delayed marriage, poor nutrition, deteriorating general health and fertility, and reduced access to reproductive healthcare.
But the figures reveal something more immediate: a woman deciding to become pregnant today is doing so in an environment radically different from the one that existed before the war.
One of the women I spoke with, a 31-year-old, was 33 weeks pregnant when her story took its most devastating turn.
She was living in a displacement site in northern Gaza when the nearby area came under attack, and she went into premature labour.
She was taken to a temporary medical point, but the care she and her baby needed was unavailable.
"I gave birth to the sound of bombardment, without even a single drop of anaesthesia. I was screaming from the pain and the fear at the same time."
Her baby was born prematurely and needed oxygen and neonatal care, but the available resources were insufficient.
"I gave birth to my baby, and he was struggling in front of me, needing oxygen, and no one could do anything. He died in my arms a few hours later because the hospital went out of service."
She describes what the experience left behind: "Loss during war is not like any other loss. I feel as if the grief has suffocated me. I am not ready to go through that terror again or become pregnant with another child who could be lost in the same way."
Before that experience, she had not been afraid of pregnancy. Now, pregnancy itself has become a source of terror.
'Women have started asking about contraception'
To understand this shift more closely, I also spoke with Dr Hiyam Jaber, an obstetrician and gynaecologist who has worked at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital and in field displacement clinics.
Dr Hiyam says that what she witnessed during the war was not simply an increase in pregnancy and childbirth complications, but a change in the questions women were asking.
"We began receiving daily inquiries about safe, long-acting contraceptive methods, such as intrauterine devices and injections, particularly because birth-control pills are not consistently available," Dr Hiyam tells The New Arab.
She describes women’s fears as being directly connected to their everyday experiences.
"The greatest fears are giving birth without anaesthesia, giving birth in unsterile conditions, being unable to provide infant formula if the mother is suffering from malnutrition, and the fear of postpartum haemorrhage in a situation where blood supplies are limited," she adds.
She says the cases she sees include an increase in preterm births and miscarriages, as well as emergency cesarean deliveries associated with deterioration in maternal health and delays in reaching hospitals.
These observations do not exist in isolation. UNFPA has warned that one in three pregnancies in Gaza is now considered high-risk, while the food crisis and collapse of the health system have increased risks for mothers and newborns.
In its report for the first quarter of 2026, UNFPA said it continued supporting sexual and reproductive health services in Gaza, including six mobile maternity units providing emergency obstetric and newborn care, as well as medicines, contraceptives, and medical equipment.
But the very need for these mobile units reflects the scale of the crisis: safe childbirth is no longer a guaranteed service available everywhere. It has become a humanitarian issue, and health organisations are trying to rebuild amid the destruction.
From four children to one
According to Dr Hiyam, the shift she has observed is not limited to the question, "When should I become pregnant?" It also extends to another question: "How many children do I want?"
In her experience, many women are now inclined to postpone childbearing or have fewer children until the war ends and living conditions stabilise.
This shift matters socially. Family size is not simply a number in demographic statistics. It reflects how people imagine their future.
When a family is confident that there will be a home, a school, a hospital, food, and job opportunities, having another child can feel like a natural part of the future.
But when the future itself is uncertain, the decision about how many children to have changes.
Amal, who once dreamed of four children, now thinks about having only one.
Ibrahim and Reem, who had planned to have children immediately after marriage, have decided to wait.
And the woman who lost her baby says she cannot even contemplate another pregnancy.
Three different decisions, shaped by the same fear.
What will happen to the image of the Palestinian family?
It is too early to say whether the war has created a permanent demographic shift in Palestinian family size.
The data currently available describe an ongoing crisis and are not sufficient to answer the long-term question of fertility intentions after the war.
But what can be said is that the war has intervened in nearly every factor shaping reproductive decisions: marriage, housing, food, healthcare, fertility, contraception, antenatal care, and the ability to protect a child after birth.
In 2026, UNFPA estimated that around 55,000 pregnant women in Gaza were facing severe conditions, including displacement, hunger, and limited access to healthcare, while 120,600 pregnant women across the occupied Palestinian territory required pregnancy-related health services.
These figures mean that the question of the future of the Palestinian family cannot be separated from the future of Gaza’s healthcare system and living conditions.
When I asked Amal what she feared most, she did not talk about pain. She talked about giving birth to a child in a place where she could not protect them.
When Ibrahim spoke about postponing parenthood, he did not say that he did not want to become a father.
He said he did not want to feel guilty about bringing a child into these circumstances.
And Reem summed up the entire struggle in one sentence: “Postponing pregnancy hurts us, but right now it is the only form of mercy available to us.”
Perhaps this is the larger story.
War does not only determine who will be born and who will survive. It can reach the moment before conception — the conversation between a couple in the darkness, the woman calculating the risks of childbirth before buying a pregnancy test, and the mother who has lost a child and decides that her heart cannot endure the experience again.
In Gaza, the decision to have a child now carries questions that were not part of parents’ calculations before the war:
Where will we live?
What will our child eat?
Will there be a hospital when I need one?
Will I be able to secure treatment for my child?
And will I be able to protect them?
War does not only affect the children who are born.
It also enters the lives of those who are still considering whether to have a child.
"What hurts me most is that I have started hearing women ask a question I never heard before the war: ‘Is it safe to have a child?’ As a doctor, I used to help women welcome their babies. Today, I sometimes find myself trying to tell them that they have the right to be afraid," Dr Hiyam Jaber says.
Perhaps the cruellest legacy of the war is not only the children who have lost their lives, but the mothers who have lost the ability to imagine a safe future for children who have not yet been born.
In Gaza, where a child was once a symbol of life continuing, the decision to bring one into the world has, for many women, become suspended on a single question:
Will this fear end before my child comes into the world?
Dr Haya Hijazi is a gynaecologist and obstetrician from Gaza

The French Football Federation (FFF) has withdrawn its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino's bid for another term, French broadcaster Franceinfo reported Thursday.
The decision was announced following an FFF executive committee meeting on Thursday.
Infantino is currently the only declared candidate for the FIFA presidency ahead of the election scheduled for March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.
Potential challengers have until Nov. 18 to enter the race.
France's decision follows similar moves by several other national football federations, including those of Sweden, Scotland, Italy and Belgium, which have also withdrawn their support for Infantino.
Infantino has faced growing criticism since the 2026 World Cup, with disputes over his leadership contributing to divisions within world football.
One of the most controversial issues was a FIFA proposal to create a commercial company that would allow private investors to acquire a 20% stake in the management of World Cup commercial rights.
The proposal was developed without consultation with FIFA's member associations and drew strong opposition before Infantino abandoned it several days later.
Despite the withdrawals, Infantino remains the only declared candidate for the March election.

ECB hikes rates to 2.5% as energy shock pushes eurozone inflation higher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:24:37 UTC
21:24:37 KST

The European Central Bank has raised interest rates by a quarter point, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, as the energy shock driven by the Iran war pushes eurozone inflation higher and forces a second hike in three months.
Frankfurt has tightened again.
The European Central Bank's governing council lifted the deposit facility rate from 2.25% to 2.5% on Thursday. It is the second hike since 11 June, when the ECB moved for the first time in three years.
The ECB sets monetary policy for the eurozone through three key interest rates, with the deposit facility rate serving as its main policy benchmark.
The main refinancing rate was lifted to 2.65% and the marginal lending facility to 2.9%.
In its statement, the central bank noted that "the conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," while ensuring that "with today’s decision, the Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the uncertainty caused by the conflict."
The ECB staff projections continue to estimate that headline inflation will average 3% this year. However, it has revised up the expectations for 2027 and 2028 to 2.5% and 2.1% respectively, compared with June.
An energy problem, not a demand problem
The decision follows an August inflation reading of 3.3%, up from 2.9% in July and the highest since September 2023.
Energy costs did nearly all the work, with energy inflation jumping to 14.3% from 10.3%, as fighting around the Strait of Hormuz kept crude supply constrained. The problem persists as Brent crude crossed $100 a barrel again on Wednesday due to renewed exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.
Underneath, the picture is calmer.
Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, actually fell to 2.4% from 2.5% in August, while services inflation, the component most sensitive to wages, dropped to 3% from 3.3%. There is still little sign that expensive energy is spreading into the rest of the economy.
That distinction has been central to the ECB's own thinking.
In a paper published earlier this month, its economists found that adverse energy supply factors accounted for around 90% of the rise in energy inflation between January and May of this year.
"This time the energy supply shock dominates, while demand and public policy stimulus have minor roles," the economists wrote, contrasting it with the 2021-22 surge that prompted a far more aggressive response.
A single rate for very different economies
The eurozone inflation average conceals a wide spread.
August inflation ran at 4.5% in Spain, 2.9% in Germany and 2.7% in France, three economies facing the same energy shock with markedly different outcomes.
Growth complicates matters further.
The bloc has held up better than expected, but resilience is not overheating, and even at 2.5% the deposit rate remains within the range the ECB considers neutral. Going further would mean deciding that policy must actively restrain the economy.
Christine Lagarde had signalled this move in July, when the council held rates but instructed staff to model oil and gas scenarios ahead of September.
"The burden of proof is on data," Lagarde said then, adding that "the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out."
Thursday's decision comes alongside fresh staff projections, though their cut-off date falls roughly two weeks before the meeting, meaning neither the latest leg higher in oil nor the surge in European government bond yields to 15-year highs will be reflected.
Attention now turns to Frankfurt's peers.
The Federal Reserve will announce on 16 September and the Bank of Japan on the 18, with both expected to consider hikes of their own.
Meanwhile, the Bank of England will decide on 17 September and is expected to hold rates as it currently maintains a much higher benchmark than the rest at 3.75%.

OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:23:21 UTC
21:23:21 KST

OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity.
Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”
He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”
Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation.
He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.
This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face.
Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy, claimed on Tuesday there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.
Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields.
Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic researcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction.
“The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”.
But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.”
Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.”
Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week.
Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, from Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”.
Meanwhile, Anthropic has admitted a new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR.
Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”.
Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database.
The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach to pacing frontier AI development.”

Hostage-takers hold Tartu family at gunpoint for a million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:23:00 UTC
21:23:00 KST

Hostage-takers hold Tartu family at gunpoint for a million euros
According to the charges, the crime was committed by a group of people who travelled to Estonia from Bulgaria for precisely that purpose, Eesti Ekspress writes.
Two Romanian men have appeared in Tartu County Court accused of taking hostages and demanding €1 million from a person working in IT and cryptocurrency.
Constantin Ligi and Ionut-Dorin Soimosan deny the charges, which prosecutors say relate to a four-member group that travelled to Estonia specifically to carry out the crime.
According to the Prosecutor's Office, three masked men entered a Tartu apartment on the evening of March 10 last year, tied up four people and threatened them with a firearm and what they claimed was a bomb.
The hostages were relatives of the intended extortion target, whom the attackers contacted by video call to demand payment.
The men eventually left the apartment, warning the victims not to leave or contact police, before fleeing Estonia and using false information and vehicle changes to conceal their movements.
Prosecutor Lauriine Tšitškan described the case as an example of "crime-as-a-service," in which international organized crime networks carry out offences for clients.
Four suspects were arrested in different countries this year, with Ligi and Soimosan the first to be extradited to Estonia.
At the preliminary hearing, both sought release from custody: Ligi cited his role as his family's sole breadwinner in Germany, while Soimosan said he needed to manage his business in Malta.
The prosecutor opposed their release, citing nine previous convictions for Ligi and five for Soimosan and questioned how Soimosan could attend future hearings if, as he indicated, authorities in Malta would confiscate his passport upon his return.
Judge Heli Sillaots is expected to rule on their continued detention later on Thursday.

Partisans Cut Russian Drone Communications Deep Inside Oryol Region
Agents of the pro-Ukrainian ATESH partisan movement destroyed a communications tower used to support Russian drone operations in the Oryol region, disrupting control links and forcing UAV crews to adjust their positions, the group reported on September 10.
The tower was located near the settlement of Zhudersky and was used by Russian forces to host radio repeaters that extended and stabilized communications with drones operating in the area, according to ATESH.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
By disabling the equipment, the partisans said they reduced the effective range of Russian drone operations and disrupted the stability of UAV communication and control channels.
Russian operators were consequently forced to search for alternative locations and reconfigure radio frequencies, creating delays in ongoing missions, the group said.

Atesh said repeated sabotage against such support networks can interfere with the coordination of Russian unmanned systems while forcing military units to divert personnel and resources toward repairs, troubleshooting, and rebuilding communications coverage.
Previously, the ATESH said its agents targeted three communications towers used by Russian forces on the Kursk axis, disrupting military command and communications in the area.

Russian mercenary operations in Mali—now functioning as the Kremlin-aligned “Africa Corps"—have subjected local populations to widespread abuse. Russian fighters have routinely abducted civilians, holding them in secret detention centers across the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Human rights monitors document that detainees face severe torture, starvation, and summary executions—a calculated strategy of terror that researchers warned only deepens regional instability and drives local communities toward insurgent groups.
The attack occurred near the village of Kaka in Mali’s Mopti region. Following the ambush, JNIM claimed to have captured 14 motorcycles, two PKM machine guns, six Kalashnikov assault rifles, six grenades, ammunition, and a DJI drone.

The incident follows a previous major insurgent attack against a military convoy in northern Mali. That convoy was transporting more than 200 Russian mercenaries and over 100 Malian soldiers. Preliminary estimates indicated that around 60 Malian troops were killed and at least 30 were captured, with dozens more wounded.
JNIM, the official al-Qaeda branch in the Sahel, was formed in March 2017 through the merger of several jihadist factions, including Ansar Dine, Al-Mourabitoun, and the Macina Liberation Front, Militarnyi wrote.
While its primary stronghold remains in Mali, the group has steadily expanded its operations into Burkina Faso and Niger and has recently increased its presence toward Benin and Togo, gradually widening its zone of activity from the central Sahel to coastal West African states.
This ambush follows a similar attack, when Russian Africa Corps mercenaries previously abandoned their Malian allies during a rebel ambush in the Gao region. Russian personnel retreated from a joint convoy without deploying available ground or air support, leaving at least 60 Malian soldiers dead and 30 captured.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence noted the episode demonstrates that Moscow treats Malian junta forces as expendable “cannon fodder” in its pursuit of the country’s gold and uranium deposits.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) on Thursday rejected suggestions that Taiwan lacks the will to resist a potential takeover by China.
Wu’s remarks came after the US magazine The Atlantic published an article titled “Will Taiwan Just Give Up?” It questions the country’s resolve to face down Chinese political and military threats.
The article has also drawn criticism online, including claims of inaccuracies and unfamiliarity with Taiwan and China.
Wu called the article's premise flawed. “It’s a mistake to assume that Taiwan doesn’t have the will to defend itself. With more investment, better equipment, tougher training & realistic exercises, the will has never been stronger,” Wu responded in English on X.
At the Taipei Security Dialogue dinner the previous night, he emphasized that Taiwan “will never abandon ourselves” and “surrender has never been an option,” per CTS News.
National security officials cited by CTS pointed to a long-running poll by the Institute for National Defense and Security Research. It commissioned the Election Study Center at National Chengchi University to track public attitudes beginning in September 2021.
In a March 2025 survey cited by the officials, 41% of respondents said they were “very willing” to fight to defend Taiwan, and 25% said they were “somewhat willing,” for a combined 66%. CTS reported that according to seven surveys since 2021, the share of people “willing” to defend the country has hovered around 70%, despite escalating Chinese military threats and shifts in US politics.
Wu’s comments came after Taiwan hosted the Taipei Security Dialogue on Wednesday. The annual gathering of defense and security experts focused this year on regional security, deterrence, emerging technology, and resilience against gray-zone threats.
At the event, Wu warned that Chinese pressure has spread across the entire First Island Chain, with Taiwan at the center. However, he insisted that Taipei is strengthening both defense capabilities and societal resilience while deepening cooperation with like-minded democracies.
The Atlantic article by Simon Shuster, published earlier this week, is subtitled, “The Taiwanese don’t trust Trump, and they don’t believe America will come to their defense. A deal with China is starting to look inevitable.” The article features KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) and describes her April trip to China, where she met CCP leader Xi Jinping.
Shuster suggested that Cheng and the CCP are aligned on Taiwan’s future: “Cheng told me that she did not ask Xi to ease up on the military threats. Their talks focused instead on a plan for Taiwan to drop its claim to independence, stop preparing for war, and move toward reconciliation with the mainland.”

Ukraine Knocks Out 17 Russian Air Defense Systems, Six Bridges and 20+ Depots in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:22:12 UTC
21:22:12 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Knocks Out 17 Russian Air Defense Systems, Six Bridges and 20+ Depots in August
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck 17 Russian air defense systems, six bridges, more than 20 storage facilities, and over 30 command posts in August as part of a sustained campaign targeting Russia’s operational rear and military-economic capabilities, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on September 10.
According to the ministry, the strikes were carried out using middle-strike capabilities as Ukraine continues to expand attacks against Russian military targets at operational depth.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A major focus of the August operations was Russian air defense infrastructure. Ukrainian forces struck positions of S-400 Triumf systems in Gelendzhik and Russia’s Bryansk region, as well as Pantsir systems in Yeysk and Tor systems in the Rostov region. Buk-M3 and Strela-10 air defense systems were also targeted in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine’s Luhansk region, including near Kreminna.
Ukrainian forces also destroyed several Russian radar stations, according to the ministry. Among them were a long-range Nebo-U radar in temporarily occupied Sevastopol, as well as Nebo-SV, Kasta, and Podlet radar systems. Electronic warfare equipment was also targeted, including a Peresvet-M system in temporarily occupied Luhansk.
The ministry said degrading Russian radar, air defense, and electronic warfare capabilities is intended to create opportunities for Ukrainian weapons to penetrate deeper into Russia’s rear.
Alongside air defense systems, Ukrainian forces continued targeting Russian military logistics. Strikes hit railway bridges near Chonhar, Vladyslavivka, and Svitlodolynske, as well as road bridges across the Seym River in Russia’s Kursk region and the Molochna River in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. A crossing over the Mokri Yaly River in the Donetsk region was also targeted.
More than 20 ammunition and logistics depots, as well as repair facilities, were struck in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and Russian regions bordering Ukraine, according to the ministry. Such attacks are intended to disrupt supply routes and reduce the combat effectiveness of Russian units.
Ukraine also continued targeting infrastructure used for Russian unmanned systems and uncrewed maritime vessels. A base for uncrewed surface vessels in Russian-occupied Chornomorske, Crimea, was among the facilities struck during August.
More than 30 strikes were carried out against command posts, storage sites, and launch positions associated with Russian attack drones in the Bryansk and Donetsk regions and Russian-occupied Crimea. Ukrainian forces also disabled several ground-based relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera attack drones, according to the ministry.
Middle-strike weapons were additionally used against Russian command facilities, including primary and reserve command posts in Russian-occupied Donetsk, an FSB unit in Shchaslyvtseve, and a drone training center in Russian-occupied Luhansk.
The middle-strike operations form part of Ukraine’s broader campaign to push attacks deeper into Russia’s rear. In August, Ukrainian long-range strikes reached targets more than 1,500 kilometers from the state border, hitting critical components of Russia’s military-industrial and energy infrastructure.

NCSIST is contributing its defense research and technical expertise to the partnership, while Thunder Tiger is responsible for drone platform design, system integration, manufacturing, and mass production.
Blue UAS certification helps clear unmanned systems for US defense procurement and use, though the Defense Department can also acquire systems through other approved pathways. Green UAS certification provides similar cybersecurity and supply-chain assessments for commercial and non-Defense Department government users.

Cho doubles down on refusal to countersign passed bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:21:21 UTC
21:21:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Wednesday that it was impossible for him to countersign eight bills passed by the legislature, suggesting that the deadline for doing so had already expired.
Cho has continued to clash with opposition lawmakers over his refusal to countersign legislation, including amendments to the Radio and Television Act, which he says violate the Constitution. During an interview Wednesday, Cho said the bills had already passed the 10-day period stipulated by the Constitution for the premier to countersign them, leaving him unable to complete the process, per ETtoday.
Cho also responded to criticism from University of Warwick School of Law Reader Kuo Ming-sung (郭銘松), who said the premier had transformed a legacy mechanism from a time when Taiwan's government more closely resembled a parliamentary system into an "ultra-executive veto.” Cho argued that Kuo's assessment reflected a lack of understanding of Taiwan's Constitution, saying the president could simply replace the premier if the premier refused to countersign legislation, per CNA.
Cho emphasized that while the president has neither veto power nor the authority to dissolve the legislature at will, the premier can support the president by refusing to countersign legislation that threatens to violate the Constitution, national security, or the commander in chief's authority. Kuo noted in his analysis that the 1997 constitutional reforms significantly weakened the role of countersigning by giving the president sole authority to appoint and dismiss the premier.
Stanford University's Hoover Institution Research Fellow Kharis Templeman said Cho's actions were politically understandable given that the Constitutional Court had been paralyzed by opposition lawmakers, per UDN. Although new quorum rules and repeated rejections of Constitutional Court justice nominees had temporarily paralyzed the court, a controversial ruling subsequently allowed it to resume operations.
Templeman said he understood the Cabinet's political reasoning and that the court could potentially rule that the opposition-backed bills were unconstitutional once it resumed normal operations. However, he argued that Cho had "created whole cloth a veto power for himself," calling the move "blatantly unconstitutional.”
Templeman also said the current design of Taiwan's Constitutional Court was flawed and prevented it from effectively serving as an arbitrator when the executive and legislature clash. He noted that the process for nominating justices undermined opposition parties' trust in the court.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) rejected Cho's characterization of the countersignature mechanism, suggesting that Cho was confusing its constitutional function with the political consequences of the president exercising appointment authority, per FTNN. He argued that if the Cabinet could opt not to countersign bills passed by the legislature, the executive branch could effectively ignore decisions made by lawmakers.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended Cho's decision, arguing that the premier should not serve as a rubber stamp for the legislature, per Liberty Times. He said that if not for the controversies surrounding the opposition-backed bills, Cho would have countersigned them and allowed President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) to promulgate them within 10 days.
Chuang added that because the Constitutional Court remained paralyzed by the opposition, lawmakers could initiate a no-confidence vote to remove Cho.

SC directs protection for minor CJP protester, warns against ‘browbeating’ victim
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday took serious note of allegations that a 14-year-old girl associated with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests was harassed and that her residence was subjected to stone pelting, directing authorities to act on her FIR and provide protection to her and her family.A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure action on the girl's FIR and sought status reports from the Delhi and Uttar Pradesh governments on the allegations, security arrangements and action taken against those allegedly involved.The court stressed that nobody could be allowed to intimidate a victim or her family to prevent them from pursuing criminal proceedings."Such matters cannot be taken lightly. Nobody should be protected if violence against a child is involved... if persons accused of such acts were roaming free and attempting to browbeat the child or her family so that they do not pursue criminal proceedings, it would be a serious matter."There cannot be any second opinion about it. Such matters cannot be taken lightly. Nobody should be protected. If violence against a child is involved and persons are roaming free and trying to browbeat the child or the family so that they do not pursue the criminal proceedings, that may be a serious matter," the bench observed.
The counsel appearing for the minor told the court that she had been harassed and her house vandalised after she registered an FIR against a person who allegedly claimed in a video that he had attacked her father during the CJP's protest.The lawyer alleged that instead of prosecuting people who accompanied the accused and were allegedly captured on camera, an FIR had been registered against the child. The counsel also submitted that this was contrary to an earlier Supreme Court order and that video evidence showing stone pelting at the girl's residence could be placed before the court."The high-powered committee will take time, but if something happens to the child in the meantime, that cannot subsequently be reversed or repaired through the committee," the counsel submitted.Responding to the submission, CJI Surya Kant said, "If there are anti-social elements who indulged in violence against child, and they are roaming free, and are trying to browbeat the child, that may be a serious thing."The Chief Justice further told the Solicitor General, "Child is a child. Some measures to protect the child can be taken. This incident can be taken as a standalone [case] by local police."Justice Joymalya Bagchi also directed that immediate action be taken on the FIR and that the minor and her family be provided police protection."We would like immediate action on that FIR and police protection to victim and family by UP police. Investigation be conducted by Parliament Street PS".The counsel also alleged that videos showed four policemen accompanying the persons who attacked the protesters and claimed that no action had been taken against them.Delhi Police action against accused
The Supreme Court proceedings came days after Delhi Police on September 5 added provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and criminal intimidation to an FIR against Hindutva influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj over the alleged assault on the minor activist's father during the CJP-led protests.Bhardwaj was detained in Bulandshahr after the CJP staged a protest outside Parliament Street police station demanding his arrest over the alleged assault.The police action followed an interview in which Bhardwaj allegedly claimed that he had "cracked the skull" of the minor activist's father during the July 20 protest and escaped arrest because of his political connections.During Thursday's hearing, Senior Advocate PV Dinesh also mentioned a plea filed by second-year law student Akshat Tripathi challenging a notice issued to him by the Executive Magistrate, Greater Noida. The notice was subsequently withdrawn.Dinesh urged the court to hear the plea, arguing that a strong message needed to be sent to IAS officers.

British rabbis back UK sanctions on Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:20:40 UTC
21:20:40 KST

Breadcrumb
British rabbis back UK sanctions on Israeli settlements, denounce BDS
Several leading British rabbis have backed the UK's new sanctions on Israeli settlements, amid protests from prominent Jewish groups and leaders against the measures.
A day after the sanctions were announced by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, senior Masorti rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg took to X to express his support for the sanctions.
"What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” Wittenberg wrote on X.
The rabbi highlighted that he had been in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair when Miliband's announcement was made, where he witnessed the horrors of settler violence with his "own eyes".
“We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away."
Wittenberg expressed his opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, while also describing Israel as his "family".
Elsewhere, Rabbi Alexandra Wright of the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London said that the "occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis".
"The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’," Wright said.
The rabbi also urged the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Other rabbis who came out in support of the measures include Jeremy Gordon of the New London Synagogue, and Lev Taylor of Kingston Liberal Synagogue.
Their statements came as prominent Jewish leaders and groups attacked the sanctions against illegal settlements.
UK Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis said on Tuesday, the day that the sanctions were announced, that it was a "dark day for British Jews".
"The measures announced amount to little more than political flag-bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric and those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish State. These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah and at a time when our community is more vulnerable than ever to the wave of extremism that has been building over recent years, these sanctions do nothing to advance the cause of peace," Mirvis said.
"Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews," he added.
Mirvis, who has at least one child who took part in the Israeli war on Gaza, has frequently expressed support for Israel, including calling the country's genocide-accused army "our heroic soldiers".
The announcement was also slammed by the Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies for British Jews, which said it viewed the measures with "deep regret".
While British Jewish groups have come out with contrasting statements on the sanctions, there is currently no definitive polling on the broader community's attitudes towards Miliband's announcement.
A survey conducted by YouGov on Tuesday found that 52% of a sample of over 4,000 members of the public expressed support for the sanctions. Of that figure, 33% said they "completely approve" of the measures.
Seventeen percent said they disapproved of the sanctions, while 33% said they "don't know".
The measures announced by Miliband on Tuesday will see the UK ban all goods from illegal Israeli settlements -- a move which supporters say underscores the UK's commitment to upholding international law.
Pro-Palestine critics of the sanctions, however, have said the move does not go far enough, particularly as Britain continues to supply military hardware to Israel.

Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:17:52 UTC
21:17:52 KST

Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder.
Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.
“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.
The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority.
Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.”
Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial.
The Council of Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.
During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary.
“If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?”
Malta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in.
Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder.
“The targeted assassination of a journalist in the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out.
“I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.”
The public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity.
It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented.
Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year.
Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.”
She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.
