BRICS 2026: Putin and Modi have high expectations going into key summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:17:08 UTC
21:17:08 KST

BRICS 2026: Putin and Modi have high expectations going into key summit
Russian President Vladimir Putin is due to arrive in India for the BRICS summit in New Delhi, where he is meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday.
The meeting is expected to build on the warm spirit and progress made in bilateral relations based around the personal relations between the two leaders.
India and Russia also have kept up high-level diplomatic and economic contacts, amid geopolitical turbulence. Putin and Modi most recently met last week in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
Three Russian IL-76 planes, carrying advance teams and military officials, reportedly landed in the Indian city of Greater Noida on Thursday morning. The teams are reviewing preparations and security arrangements as Delhi gears up to host world leaders for the BRICS summit on September 12-13.
Energy the bedrock of the relationship
India has become the second biggest importer of Russian oil as New Delhi seeks to secure the energy needs of its 1.4 billion population. Russia sold around 2.1 million barrels per day of oil to India, or 45% of the country’s total imports, in August – even as New Delhi has widened its crude basket.
But it is not a simple buyer-seller relationship, with both sides invested in each other’s energy ecosystem. India’s state-run ONGC Videsh holds a 20% stake in Russia’s Sakhalin-1 oil field project. A consortium of state-run Indian oil majors have sizable stakes in Russian oil company Rosneft’s subsidiaries, Vankorneft and Taas-Yuryakh Neftegazodobycha.
Rosneft holds nearly half of India’s Nayara Energy, which owns a refinery in Gujarat and a wide downstream network.
The implications of India’s Russian oil purchases are global. Indian refiners play a major role in preventing crude prices from surging out of control as the Middle East conflict chokes off a large chunk of global supply. More specifically, Europe buys about 60% of its diesel and 15% of its jet fuel from Indian refiners, which it has – counterintuitively – tried to sanction over Russian oil.
Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready to supply “as much oil as India needs,” despite the threat of Western sanctions on New Delhi.
Nuclear energy is another key dimension of the relationship, with India setting itself an ambitious nuclear power target to generate 100 gigawatts by 2047. Two of the six units of the Koodankulam nuclear power plant, built in collaboration with Russia’s Rosatom in south India, are generating electricity, and four more are under construction.
Putin and Modi agreed in December to further discuss a second nuclear power plant and finalize the site for it – reportedly in Tirunelveli district in Tamil Nadu.
India also is eyeing Russia’s small modular reactors, or SMRs, to achieve its energy targets.
Expanding economic ties is imperative
Bilateral trade has jumped in volume since Putin’s last visit to India, when a $100 billion target was set to be achieved by 2030. However, India has run up a massive trade deficit against Russia through its oil purchases. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Russian businesses are looking to buy more Indian goods and establish joint projects to address the trade gap.
The same geopolitical tensions that have pushed India to buy more Russian oil are also opening up avenues to expand bilateral economic ties to new areas.
Russian aviation companies could lead the charge. The CEO of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation, Vadim Badekha, said a licensing agreement with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for producing the SJ-100 regional jet is being finalized and the contract could be signed soon.
The first localized version of the Superjet could be made in India in three years, with the company looking at selling 100-200 planes. Indian airlines have also expressed interest in buying up to 100 Il 114-300 planes from Russia.
The Northern Sea Route, or the Arctic Route that skirts thousands of miles of Russia's coastline is high on the agenda this year. India plans to send its first ship along the route next year to take advantage of the time and cost efficiencies.
In addition, India is looking to Russia for its requirements of rare-earth minerals, which go into key components such as magnets needed for green energy transition. New Delhi is also exploring options to buy coking coal assets and import more nickel from Russia to boost steel production.
The two countries signed a labor mobility and migration agreement in December. First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in February that Russia can accept an “unlimited” number of Indian workers. Tourism is another area that saw progress during Putin’s December visit, with both countries agreeing to provide 30-day e-tourist visas to travelers.
Both countries now settle the bulk of their transactions in local currencies, smoothing out frustrations over payment bottlenecks. It is a topic other BRICS leaders will also be interested in.
Defense and space ties bind India to Russia
India remains the top customer of Russian military hardware, inking deals to buy and manufacture many top-end Russian systems.
Joint production of the Russian fifth-generation Su-57 fighter aircraft is expected to feature prominently in the Putin-Modi talks. A Russian offer for full licensed production of the Su-57 in India, along with unrestricted transfer of technology, is already on the table, and talks are reportedly ongoing.
“We are ready to supply India with this aircraft, to keep developing it. We don’t have any issues or limitations,” Putin said in June.
Other weapons such as the S-500 missile system could also be discussed.
New Delhi and Moscow have partnered in the space sector since the early 1960s. Russia is collaborating on India’s manned spaceflight program, Gaganyaan, by providing crew training and supplying spacesuits. The collaboration will include engine building, rocket fuel, and the development of national orbital stations, Russian space agency Roscosmos has said.
Why India’s farmers need Putin’s helping hand
The Middle East conflict has disrupted fertilizer supplies from the Gulf countries, with implications for food production and food security in the world’s most populous nation – pushing the item to the top of the agenda for Modi and Putin.
Russia increased fertilizer exports to India by 20% in the first half of this year, and is ready to continue deliveries, First Deputy Prime Minister Manturov said in a recent interview.
Putin also reiterated this to Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar in Moscow last month, saying “we’re doing everything to close this issue for Indian farmers, for agriculture.”
Why the Modi-Putin personal chemistry matters
Putin’s visit comes as the threat of steep US tariffs looms over India for buying Russian oil. The challenge before the two leaders is to deepen the relationship while keeping their respective national interests front and center amid Western coercion.
Kremlin spokesman Peskov said on Tuesday that both leaders are in close personal contact and able to discuss sensitive matters in open and constructive ways.
It’s a moment in history when the rapport Putin and Modi share will matter more than ever.

Israel will never stop me speaking up for Palestine

Israel will never stop me speaking up for Palestine
Israel’s decision to bar British MPs exposes how far it will go to avoid scrutiny over its treatment of Palestinians.
Over my lifetime, it’s been my privilege to visit Palestine on several different occasions. I’ve witnessed what Palestinians endure on a daily basis. Endless checkpoints. Manned watchtowers. Arbitrary arrests. Violent settlers. This is the daily reality of apartheid, which dictates who can and cannot move freely. This is how Israel’s occupation operates, denying any vestige of autonomy to the occupied. This is the daily rhythm of Palestinian life.
In Gaza, the Israeli occupation controls most of what goes in and out. Its illegal blockade has resulted in the mass starvation and displacement of Palestinians. As more and more people have woken up to the genocide in Gaza, Israel has also denied entry to UN investigators and international journalists – a transparent attempt to stop the world from finding out the full extent of the war crimes it has committed. Do not forget the thousands of Palestinian refugees, as well, who are still denied the right to return.
This is the real scandal. The Israeli government’s decision to ban me – and 10 other British MPs – from entry offered but a tiny glimpse into the authoritarianism that Palestinians are subject to every single day.
I won’t lose any sleep over being condemned by Israel. What I deplore is its despicable treatment of the Palestinian people. What I deplore is Israel’s denial of freedom of movement to thousands of Palestinians on a daily basis. What I deplore is Israel’s denial of entry to UN investigators and journalists, shielding itself from accountability for the crimes of apartheid, occupation and genocide.
What this ban is really about is preventing British MPs from visiting Gaza and the West Bank and stopping the world from seeing what is happening. The Israeli government’s decision tells us all we need to know. It tells us that Israel does not want the world to know the truth. It tells us that Israel resorts to increasingly absurd and desperate measures as it loses support across the globe. Above all, it tells us that we should not give up in our pursuit of truth, accountability and justice.
Israel made the decision to ban us in response to the government’s welcome decision to impose sanctions on illegal settlement goods. International law is clear. In July 2024, the ICJ ruled that Israel’s presence in the Palestinian territories was unlawful and imposed obligations on the UK not to aid or assist the illegal obligation. This ban on settlement goods is long overdue. It reflects growing opposition to state-backed settler violence against Palestinians in the West. The hysteria from those who oppose it proves just how much impunity Israel has enjoyed so far.
Ultimately, this decision is a first step toward the government finally fulfilling its legal obligations. These obligations, however, go beyond refraining from assistance to illegal settlements. Any meaningful package of sanctions would recognise how “settlement goods” are subsumed into Israel’s wider economy. That means ending all trade and all forms of support that sustain Israel’s unlawful presence as a whole.
I also re-iterate my demand for this government to recognise the genocide in Gaza, end all military coperation (including the sale of F-35 components and the performance of surveillance flights over Gaza) and heed my repeated calls for a public inquiry into British complicity.
I have lost count of the number of demonstrations I have been on in solidarity with Palestine. At each one, I carry the memories of Palestine with me. I endeavour to quote at least one Palestinian in any speech I give. In my mind, it’s important to amplify the lived experiences of those enduring occupation, apartheid and genocide. It is their freedom which is egregiously curtailed – and it is their freedoms that we must defend. The Israeli government can ban me, but they can’t stop me from exposing the truth: they have been committing genocide and I will never stop campaigning until there is justice for the Palestinian people.
In our discussions of Palestine, we always emphasise the horror stories. But in my visits to Palestine, I have experienced the humanity, the music, the art, the poetry, the joy and the resilience of the Palestinian people. I have no interest in being given a tour of apartheid by the Israeli government. I am, however, unwavering in my determination to campaign for the only path to peace: the end of the occupation. It has been many years since I have visited Palestine. No matter what Israel does to intimidate us into silence and despair, I have not given up hope that one day, I may return to visit the children I once met – in a free and independent Palestine.

Brussels prepares post-2030 renewable overhaul as grids struggle to keep up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:16:33 UTC
21:16:33 KST

The European Commission’s renewable push comes as the EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the Council, are working to tackle one of the biggest bottlenecks to new clean-power projects — the electrical grids.
The European Commission is preparing to reshape the European Union's renewable-energy rulebook after 2030, signaling a major shift from less regulation to greater focus on investment, grids and storage, according to a draft impact assessment seen by Euronews.
The internal document states that the existing renewable energy law is no longer enough to deliver the EU’s 2040 climate ambition to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% compared to 1990 levels, which EU lawmakers agreed last November.
A new EU proposal to revamp the bloc's renewable energy framework is due by the end of the year to ensure the post-2030 climate framework aligns with all sectors that must contribute to the common goal of reaching climate neutrality by 2050.
In 2025, clean power accounted for 26.2% of EU final energy consumption, while current national plans put the bloc on track for only about 41% by 2030, below the 42.5% binding EU target, the draft document warns.
However, the Commission is skeptical that its 27-nation bloc will achieve even the 41% target.
"While the situation varies from one member state to another, the current trajectory for renewable energy deployment suggests that even the projected 41% share may be difficult to achieve with current progress at member state level," reads the draft document.
At the same time, the Commission appears reluctant to address the EU's renewable deployment gap by simply piling on new mandatory targets.
Brussels seems to reject additional mandatory measures on self-consumption and renewable-energy communities, mandatory regional cooperation and joint projects as well as further permitting legislation, arguing that recent reforms still need implementation.
“The stakeholder feedback received at stakeholder workshops emphasised the importance of regulatory stability in this area and pointed at insufficient implementation of the current framework as the key issue to tackle," reads the draft document.
Grid congestion — a major barrier
While the bloc needs to increase clean power production to meet the targets, it also needs to ensure its electrical systems can receive and transport it. The EU excels at producing clean power, but it struggles to dispatch it where it is needed, which is a major barrier to the bloc's overall climate and energy transition.
Renewable electricity reached almost 50% of EU generation in 2025, but the power system is increasingly struggling to use all that cheap electricity, the draft document acknowledges. Grid congestion, insufficient storage and inflexible demand are producing more negative prices and renewable curtailment, often to the detriment of clean power producers.
In 2024, more than 10TWh of renewable electricity — enough to power around 2.85 million European homes for an entire year — could not be used because of grid congestion and insufficient cross-border capacity.
A recent audit from the European Court of Auditors stated that renewable energy capacity gains linked to the bloc's REPowerEU, the 2022 plan to ditch Russian energy and become energy sovereign, are "negligible" compared with the Commission's 103GW goal. They also pointed out that grid infrastructure — particularly cross-border electricity connections — is the plan's most striking weakness.
Redispatch — effectively switching on more expensive generation because cheap renewable power cannot reach consumers — cost around €4.3 billion in 2024. Without action, annual redispatch costs could reach €26 billion by 2030, the Commission estimates.
Brussels knows it needs dramatically more clean energy to hit the 2040 climate target, but the draft acknowledges that simply adding wind and solar without grids, storage, flexible demand and electrification can create its own costs.
To address the remaining challenges, the EU executive proposes better monitoring of curtailment, clearer rules for hybrid renewable-and-storage projects, stronger investment signals for flexibility and greater use of electric vehicles and smart charging as sources of system flexibility.
Veerle Dossche, renewable energy programme manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said the Commission's impact assessment makes a "compelling case" for an ambitious and binding post-2030 renewable energy target. However, it notes that delivery must go beyond ambition.
"This requires robust national contributions, clear trajectories and effective compliance mechanisms, backed by measurable KPIs, so that early warnings trigger corrective action when member states fall off track,” said Dossche.
Power struggle over the power grid
Meanwhile, the legislative train has departed.
MEPs in the Parliament's industry committee backed a draft report on the future governance of the EU's power grid on Thursday, paving the way for adoption in plenary next week in Strasbourg, followed by the inter-institutional talks among the EU co-legislators, the Parliament and the Council.
EU lawmaker Tsvetelina Penkova (S&D/Bulgaria), leading negotiator on the legislative file, said the new rules should also help reduce electricity price disparities among EU countries and regions
"The Commission will now have a stronger role in defining the strategic framework, while ACER (the EU's energy regulators) will provide greater independent scrutiny. This is an important step towards making our infrastructure planning more democratic, transparent and accountable," said Penkova on Thursday.
EU lawmaker Virgil-Daniel Popescu (EPP/Romania) said Thursday's vote — backed by MEPs from the centre-right, liberals, Socialists and Greens — offers a “balanced and pragmatic” approach to turning Europe’s energy goals into the infrastructure needed to strengthen energy security and bring down energy costs.
“We have strengthened the Commission proposal by introducing a more strategic approach to infrastructure planning. Europe should have a clear picture of where the major bottlenecks are, which strategic corridors and network reinforcements are needed, when they should be developed towards 2040 and 2050, and what level of investment will be required," Popescu told Euronews.
Parliament backed plans to centralise Europe’s energy infrastructure planning, giving the Commission a leading role in drawing up an overview of the bloc’s future energy system as the first step towards a more coordinated process for identifying new grid needs.
However, this position risks clashing with the Council, with several EU countries rejecting a centralised takeover from the Commission, fearing loss of national sovereignty.
Another legislative file on permitting rules linked to the "Grids Package" is already underway, with official talks expected in October.

Spain's spy agency warned of Ceuta border breach plans before crisis, declassified files show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:15:16 UTC
21:15:16 KST

Spain's spy agency warned of Ceuta border breach before crisis, declassified files show
Madrid — Spain's national intelligence agency issued multiple warnings before the Ceuta border crisis about a potential mass crossing of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave in late July, according to declassified documents released by the government on Wednesday.
The trove of 40 documents, which includes alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies, appears to undermine what Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said about the level of warning the government had before the sudden influx took place.
There have been major protests in Spain in response to the migrant arrivals, with critics blaming the Sánchez government for its handling of the crisis, and his political opponents accusing him of pandering to Morocco.
On July 29, a day before more than 72,000 people began pouring into the Spanish city neighboring Morocco, Spain's spy agency, the National Intelligence Center (CNI), sent an alert via WhatsApp to the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta about calls on social media "for an assault on the fence and by sea tomorrow at 8 p.m."
"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified WhatsApp message from the intelligence agency said, "just to give you an idea of its scale."
A report from Spain's spy agency sent that day to Moroccan intelligence services warned of plans on social media for migrants to enter Ceuta on July 30 by climbing a border fence separating the exclave from Morocco, or by swimming around it, the documents show. It mentioned that migrants might take advantage of Morocco's national Throne Day, celebrated on July 30.
That same day, Spain's national intelligence agency issued similar warnings about "several groups on Facebook and WhatsApp encouraging these attempts" in messages to Spain's Civil Guard police force.
Once thousands of people were streaming across the border on July 30, a Defense Ministry intelligence report issued that day stated that Moroccan forces were passive and acted negligently to stop migrants.
"It cannot be ruled out that Morocco may attempt to exploit the situation that has arisen in Ceuta to further its strategic interests," the report went on.
Morocco's foreign ministry didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press about the documents.
On Wednesday, Sánchez rejected the idea that the declassified documents revealed that there was prior warning about a border crisis of the scale that took place between July 30 and 31.
"The existence of this campaign was known ... and was being monitored, but in no way did it constitute or could it be interpreted as an indicator of the scale, nature, or probability of what happened afterward," Sánchez wrote on X, referencing the spy agency's July 29 warning about what was brewing on social media.
Sánchez has defended his government's handling of the crisis and said last week there was no evidence that Morocco's government orchestrated the incident. That sparked further criticism, particularly after a leaked police report alleged the involvement of Moroccan police in the episode.
Several weeks after the initial border rush, Ceuta is dealing with a prolonged humanitarian crisis because of some 5,000 migrants who remain in the small city, according to the national government. Local officials cite a higher figure of up to 10,000 people.
They include unaccompanied minors, the Reuters news agency notes, adding migrants are living in makeshift camps or on Ceuta's streets and beaches, according to local authorities.
The Spanish leader pledged last week to release documents related to Spain's deadliest mass crossing, in which NGOs reported that more than 140 migrants died.
In the days immediately before the mass crossing, hundreds of migrants had swum from Morocco to reach Ceuta, which Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska acknowledged at the time.
He said authorities were facing "an extraordinary, exceptional situation," and that the Spanish government was "dealing with it with the means that we already have deployed there permanently."
Wednesday's document trove includes reports from multiple agencies that detailed the increasing number of arrivals, a surge that overwhelmed authorities beginning July 30.

Why star TV presenter Sarah Khalifa faces the death penalty in Egypt and what comes next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:14:24 UTC
21:14:24 KST

Egyptian law allows capital punishment for some serious drug offences, while a 2024 reform gives felony defendants a full appeal before the Court of Cassation. Euronews examines how the process works before a death sentence becomes final in Egypt.
Popular Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa will sign appeal papers against her death sentence on Tuesday, her lawyer Mohamed El-Gendy said.
Khalifa was convicted last week alongside 11 others in a synthetic drug manufacturing and trafficking case.
She has consistently denied any involvement, saying she had never even smoked a cigarette in her life.
Euronews looked into what Egyptian law says about capital punishment in drug cases and what the appeals process could mean for Khalifa and her co-defendants.
Why can a drugs case carry the death penalty?
Egyptian drug law allows the death penalty for some of the most serious narcotics offences, while simple possession for personal use does not carry the same charges.
Under Article 33, capital punishment can apply to offences including importing narcotics without authorisation, manufacturing them for trafficking, and forming, managing or joining a drug trafficking gang.
Prosecutors accused the 28 defendants in Khalifa's case of taking part in an organised network that brought in materials used to manufacture drugs and divided responsibilities between sourcing, production, storage and distribution.
The Cairo-born Khalifa, known for hosting the crime show "Mission Impossible," was accused of providing money used to buy materials for the operation, travelling abroad to meet senior members of the network and helping coordinate its activities.
Her brother Mohamed, who was also sentenced to death, was accused of manufacturing the drugs and helping test batches after they were produced.
Forensic experts identified MDMB-4en-PINACA among the seized substances. It is a laboratory-made synthetic cannabinoid that can produce effects similar to cannabis but can be much stronger and more unpredictable.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime says the substance has been associated with severe adverse effects, including fatal intoxications.
Its legal status also became an issue at trial. A court-appointed committee said MDMB-4en-PINACA was not specifically named on Egypt's controlled narcotics list, but concluded that it was still covered by the law because its chemical structure and effects were similar to substances already listed.
The defence challenged that interpretation, but the court accepted the committee's findings.
What happens next for Khalifa?
Egypt changed its criminal procedure in 2024 by introducing a full appeal stage for felony cases.
Previously, felony judgments did not have the same two-level trial structure. Under the new system, a person convicted of a felony can appeal to a higher criminal court called the Felony Appeals Court.
Egypt's Court of Cassation says the change allows the appeals court to reconsider the case. In practical terms, judges can review the evidence, the prosecution's case, and the role attributed to each defendant.
The court can uphold the judgment, change the sentence or overturn the conviction.
Only after that stage can a further challenge go to Egypt's Court of Cassation.
The Court of Cassation has a different role. It does not rehear the whole case, but looks mainly at whether the law was applied correctly and whether there were serious procedural problems.
Before the Cairo court formally sentenced Khalifa to death, it referred her case and those of 12 other defendants to Egypt's Grand Mufti.
Under Egyptian procedure, judges who intend to impose the death penalty must agree unanimously and seek the Mufti's opinion before formally delivering the sentence.
The Mufti's opinion is advisory and does not bind the court.
After receiving the opinion, the court sentenced Khalifa and 11 others to death. Their right to appeal remained.
Can a death sentence really change on appeal?
Recent cases show that Egypt's Felony Appeals Courts can significantly change earlier judgments.
In August, a Felony Appeals Court in Mansoura overturned a death sentence in an unrelated murder case and instead sentenced the defendant to 15 years in prison. The court heard witnesses and reviewed the case papers before changing the sentence.
Appeals courts have also significantly reduced sentences in drug cases. In March, a Cairo Felony Appeals Court reduced a life sentence to seven years for a defendant convicted of trafficking the drug commonly known as "ice".
The defence had challenged issues including the arrest and search procedures and an alleged confession.
In the high-profile case of Karim Salim, known in Egyptian media as the "Fifth Settlement Serial Killer", the Felony Appeals Court upheld his death sentence, and the Court of Cassation later rejected his challenge, making the sentence final.
The cases do not indicate how Khalifa's appeal will be decided, but show that the first appeal can significantly change a judgment.
If the Court of Cassation ultimately upholds a death sentence or rejects the final challenge against it, the sentence becomes final.
Separate procedures then take place before it can be carried out, including sending the case through the justice minister to the president, who can pardon the defendant or reduce the sentence.
What has changed since the verdict?
Khalifa has made no new public statements since the verdict. During the court proceedings, however, she repeatedly denied involvement in drugs and insisted she was innocent.
Another lawyer on her defence team, Mohamed Hamouda, has called for the appeal proceedings to receive wider media coverage, including the defence arguments and witness questioning.
Separate court documents released this week have provided new details about an assault case in which Khalifa was sentenced to three years in prison.
The case also involved Fathi el-Abyad, another defendant in the same drugs case, who prosecutors described as one of the alleged founders of the network. He was also among those sentenced to death alongside Khalifa.
According to the judgment, the driver had told his own brother, who worked for Egypt's Interior Ministry, where el-Abyad could be found.
The court said Khalifa learned of this and then lured the driver to her apartment in Cairo's Agouza district. Two other defendants later arrived and assaulted him, stripped him and filmed him while el-Abyad remained in contact by phone.
The footage was discovered when investigators examined Khalifa's phone during the drugs investigation.

Inflation in Ukraine accelerated to 8.1% in August. The NBU named the reasons
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:13:50 EEST
21:13:50 KST

Inflation in Ukraine accelerated to 8.1% in August. The NBU named the reasons
Kyiv • UNN
In August, annual inflation in Ukraine rose to 8.1%, while prices increased by 0.1% over the month. Fuel prices saw the sharpest increase.
In August 2026, inflation accelerated to 8.1% year-on-year. On a month-on-month basis, prices increased by 0.1%. This is evidenced by data published by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, reports UNN.
Details
According to the National Bank, headline inflation slightly exceeded the projected path, primarily due to a more pronounced-than-expected rise in fuel prices, as well as higher administratively regulated inflation amid increases in water supply and wastewater tariffs. At the same time, core inflation was slightly lower than forecast due to slower-than-expected increases in service prices.
Fuel inflation accelerated significantly to 38.7% year-on-year
This dynamic was caused by a sharp rise in petrol and diesel prices at the end of July amid a surge in global oil prices. In August, petrol prices continued to rise both month-on-month and year-on-year, while diesel prices increased in the first half of the month due to a shortage, then declined and stabilized in the second half thanks to increased import volumes. Gas prices also stabilized in early August owing to the arrival of cheaper imports.
The increase in prices for raw food products slowed slightly (to 1.0% year-on-year)
According to the NBU, this dynamic was primarily driven by a slowdown in the rise in prices for borscht vegetables thanks to the new harvest. Meat became cheaper due to lower demand and sufficient supply on the market. In particular, increased investment in poultry farming contributed to a larger supply of chicken. Tomato prices declined due to ample supply amid the active arrival of the new harvest. At the same time, sugar prices fell more slowly than in July as a result of an expected reduction in supply due to a decrease in the area sown with sugar beet this year.
Core inflation remained at the level of the previous two months – 8.1% year-on-year
The pace of increase in prices for processed food products remained unchanged in August. On the one hand, dairy products, particularly cheeses and fermented milk products, became more expensive rapidly due to higher procurement prices for milk and increased producer costs resulting from war-related and logistical risks. At the same time, the decline in butter prices accelerated thanks to substantial stocks, promotional offers and high volumes of predominantly inexpensive imports. Non-alcoholic beverages became cheaper amid ample supply and significant competition in the market.
The increase in prices for non-food goods accelerated somewhat (to 1.1% year-on-year). Clothing and footwear became cheaper more slowly than in the previous summer months.
At the same time, the increase in service prices slowed (to 13.4% year-on-year). In particular, the rise in mobile communications prices slowed due to the base effect, as did increases in health insurance and financial service prices. At the same time, taxi and goods transportation services became more expensive faster amid high fuel prices. The cost of housing rentals, café, hotel and boarding-house services, dental and veterinary services, footwear repair and dry cleaning also increased more rapidly.
The increase in administratively regulated prices accelerated to 13.0% year-on-year
The National Bank notes that this dynamic was driven by higher public transport fares and water supply and wastewater tariffs in many Ukrainian cities. In addition, alcohol prices rose faster amid higher costs for certain raw materials and increased logistics costs due to Russian attacks on warehouse infrastructure and the loss of commodity stocks.
Price pressures remain elevated due to the consequences of Russia’s military aggression and the war in the Middle East
The intensification of Russian attacks on logistics, production and energy infrastructure facilities increases business costs and limits the domestic supply of goods and services. Air terror also puts additional pressure on the expectations of households and businesses, the National Bank concluded.

Details: In the statement, the leaders condemned Russia's war in Ukraine and paid tribute to the courage of the Ukrainian people and their defenders.

China says yuan’s global rise is ‘irreversible’ – and has a strategy to back it up

China says yuan’s global rise is ‘irreversible’ – and has a strategy to back it up
From bilateral swaps to keeping premier tech firms on mainland exchanges, Beijing details the blueprint to build a financial powerhouse
Chinese financial authorities have pledged further steps to expand the yuan’s global use amid a broader de-dollarisation trend, while vowing to make listing on mainland stock exchanges the “primary” choice for top-tier domestic companies.
“The internationalisation of the yuan is a continuous and steady process, and an irreversible trend,” said Lu Lei, deputy governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), at a press conference on Thursday.
To meet growing demand from market participants seeking more diverse currency options, the PBOC had steadily strengthened the yuan’s global monetary functions and international standing, Lu said.
The central bank would also expand cross-border use cases for the digital yuan and QR-code payments, Lu added, while it planned to optimise market access schemes – including Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Swap Connect – to further open up China’s onshore financial markets.
Authorities also pledged to reinforce Hong Kong’s role as the premier offshore yuan hub, while supporting tailored, differentiated market development in London, Singapore and Dubai.
Shanghai’s growth as a global hub for yuan asset allocation and risk management would be further enhanced, Lu added.

Ryanair has said it will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while in flight.
US investigators are examining the incident which left Ljubisa Karović, 61, severely injured when the window beside him shattered on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany in July.
Karović’s lawyer said the Serbian businessman was hauled back in after his head and right arm were sucked through the window of the Boeing 737 owing to the sudden depressurisation.
However, Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said the airline would be “disputing” that account, telling reporters after the airline’s annual general meeting (AGM) in Dublin on Thursday that Karović was “certainly sucked towards the window, but he didn’t get out the window”.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the US is leading the accident investigation, alongside Boeing, engine manufacturer GE, and Ryanair.
O’Leary said: “He wasn’t partially out the window. Part of his face didn’t get out the window. We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window.”
He said the passenger had been “belted into the seat”, adding: “We will be certainly at the end of the process disputing that he or any part of his anatomy will bend out the window.”
O’Leary said he was “not trying to downplay it” and the airline would “have to await the outcome of the NTSB report”.
In an interview with the Guardian, Karović said he believed his seatbelt had kept him in the plane as he blacked out, while his wife, Svetlana, said one passenger played a crucial part in his rescue, as she watched her husband “half in and out of the plane”.
She said the unknown male passenger, believed to be Albanian, “did all he could to bring him in and then tried to block the window, first with a bag that was immediately sucked out and then with a suitcase, which worked”.
Meanwhile, about a third of shareholders at the AGM voted against O’Leary’s latest pay deal, worth €150m (£129m). The package, agreed over the summer, would give him options on 10m shares if he hits profit and share price targets, and stays at the helm of the Irish carrier until 2032.
Ryanair said it would later publish the results of the votes, which approved the deal by about 2-1.
O’Leary also continued to dispute the account of the British air traffic control provider National Air Traffic Services (Nats) over the reasons for the latest failure on Tuesday, which disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers flying in and out of the UK and cancelled more than 2,100 flights.
Martin Rolfe, the Nats boss, told the BBC on Tuesday: “This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation.”
Continuing his long vendetta against Rolfe, O’Leary accused him of “telling lies to save his own skin”.
A Ryanair spokesperson said Nats told a call with its teams on Tuesday that the reason was a “spurious flight plan”. A separate flight plan problem caused an outage in 2023.
Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.
Speaking in the Commons on Thursday, the aviation minister, Keir Mather, said Nats had “experienced an issue with its flight processing system at its Swanwick centre affecting the data that was available to controllers”.
He said the fix “took time as the systems needed to be tested to ensure that they had fully recovered and operations could safely return to normal”. Nats, he added, had “confirmed that it was a technical issue and it does not believe it to be cyber-related”.
Nats is due to submit a report next week while ministers have instructed the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review.
O’Leary stoked further outrage by comparing his competitors to “rapists”, a term he has used for some rivals since the 2000s but less often publicly in recent times.
He told reporters people were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe”. After repeating the “high-fare rapists” comments, and when challenged whether this was appropriate language, O’Leary told reporters: “Absolutely.”

Satellite images confirm Ukraine’s strike on Russian warship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:10:37 UTC
21:10:37 KST

- Ukraine's Defense Forces struck Russia's Novorossiysk naval base overnight on September 8-9, hitting the frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its superstructure.
- Ukraine's General Staff also reported hits on the frigate Admiral Makarov, the small missile ship Buyan-M and the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck Russia’s naval base at Novorossiysk overnight on September 8-9, hitting the Kalibr-missile frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its deck superstructure, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence agency, known as HUR.
HUR said operators from its Active Operations Department carried out the strike as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, targeting both port infrastructure and the Project 11356 frigate. Ukraine’s General Staff separately said the attack also hit a second Kalibr-capable frigate, the Admiral Makarov, the Project 21631 small missile ship Buyan-M, and the Project 22160 patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Robert Brovdi said the operation additionally destroyed several Russian missile boats in the port, a Su-33 fighter jet and a Mi-8 helicopter near Anapa, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) northwest of Novorossiysk, along with two air-defense radar systems near Gelendzhik. Ukraine has not disclosed how many drones or missiles took part in the operation.
Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian OSINT monitoring group Exilenova+ shows fires and apparent damage at the port consistent with the reported strikes on the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov and the Buyan-M. The same channel said the attack combined drones with at least one Ukrainian Neptune cruise missile, a detail that has not appeared in HUR’s or the General Staff’s own statements on the operation.
Both the Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov have been hit before. Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck both frigates in August 2026, along with the Vasily Bykov, in an earlier raid on the same base. Novorossiysk has served as the Black Sea Fleet’s main operating base since repeated Ukrainian strikes pushed Russian warships out of Sevastopol in occupied Crimea.
Russian officials in Novorossiysk said debris from intercepted drones struck a church, industrial sites and residential buildings, killing four people and injuring about 30. Moscow has not issued its own account of damage to the naval vessels named by Ukraine.
The extent of damage to the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov, the Buyan-M and the Vasily Bykov has not been independently confirmed, and Ukraine’s General Staff said assessments of some of the reported strikes were still being finalized.

Estonia's government dismisses Ministry of Defense permanent secretary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

Estonia's government dismisses Ministry of Defense permanent secretary
At its Thursday session, the government dismissed Ministry of Defense permanent secretary Kaimo Kuusk from his position.
The corresponding proposal was submitted by Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur.
Kuusk's departure from office was prompted by the imminent change of minister. Namely, Martin Herem — who has been put forward as the candidate for defense minister — set as one of his conditions for taking the post that the current permanent secretary of the Ministry of Defense, Kaimo Kuusk, would leave, so that the new minister would have freer hands in personnel decisions.
A ministry secretary general (permanent secretary) can be dismissed from service if, in the minister's assessment, cooperation between the minister and the secretary general does not function. The Public Service Act states that a secretary general may not be dismissed from service before six months have passed since the beginning of the minister's and secretary general's cooperation.
Kuusk himself stated in a letter to Ministry of Defense employees on Tuesday that he would not submit a resignation request and that the government must dismiss him from office.
Hanno Pevkur, who is also stepping down, but for now still serving as defense minister, said on the proposal to dismiss Kuusk that the leadership of national defense cannot be in a situation where there is no basic trust and ability to cooperate between the minister and the ministry's highest official.
"Defense minister candidate Martin Herem has unequivocally ruled out cooperation with Kaimo Kuusk. In a situation where the prime minister wants to see Herem as the next defense minister, this decision must also be looked at substantively — national defense development cannot remain hostage to mutual distrust between the minister and the permanent secretary," Pevkur said.
According to Pevkur, in the current security situation it is not justified to knowingly leave a conflict in the leadership of the Ministry of Defense that would begin to affect the ministry's and the entire national defense leadership.
"Estonia does not currently have the luxury of spending the next six months on internal power struggles. If the next defense minister's position is that cooperation with the current permanent secretary is not possible, then a decision must be made that allows national defense leadership to move forward," Pevkur noted.
At the same time, Pevkur emphasized that the decision does not diminish the importance of Kaimo Kuusk's work to date or his contribution to Estonia's national defense.
Kuusk's last working day as permanent secretary of the Ministry of Defense is 15 September. Kuusk has served as permanent secretary of the Ministry of Defense since 1 September 2024.
SDE leader turns to justice chancellor
Social Democratic Party (SDE) Chair Lauri Läänemets sent a written request to the chancellor of justice on Thursday, asking for a review of the legality of Kaimo Kuusk's dismissal.
Läänemets asked the chancellor of justice to assess whether the actions of the government and the defense minister comply with the Government of the Republic Act, the Civil Service Act, the principle of good administration and the principle of a professional and politically independent civil service.
"In my view, the issue concerns more than simply the termination of one permanent secretary's employment. At a fundamental level, the situation raises the question of whether protections granted to the civil service by law can effectively be circumvented following a change in political power through a decision that appears formally correct and whether the power to dismiss a civil servant may be used to implement agreements made in the interests of a political party," Läänemets explained.

Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:09:00 UTC
21:09:00 KST

Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
September 10, 2026
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.
There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.
As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.
"Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.
"Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital.
Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low
Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.
Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.
Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.
That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.
Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.
"The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.
Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar
Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.
Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings.
Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.
Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.
Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed.
Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University.
Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.
With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.
Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston.
Japan willing to restore normal ties?
Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.
Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar.
"I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said.
Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.
Will the West reengage with Myanmar?
As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.
Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.
Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.
"But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said.
Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.
On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.
"I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now."

Gaza's hospitals and homes struggle to keep generators running as oil shortages bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:07:30 UTC
21:07:30 KST

Gaza's hospitals and homes struggle to keep generators running as oil shortages bite
CAIRO/GAZA, Sept 10 - As power cuts cascade through one of Gaza's largest functioning hospitals and patients wait for treatment in sweltering wards, medics warn that shortages of engine oil and spare parts are causing generators to seize up, putting lives at risk.
The crisis is spreading beyond hospitals, where soaring costs for oil and diesel are making electricity from neighbourhood generators increasingly unaffordable for families that depend on it.
Gaza has been without grid electricity since the start of Israel's military offensive in the territory, launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Israel halted electricity supply and restricted the import of fuel as well as engine oil, describing them as measures to punish Hamas.
Those restrictions have continued despite an October 2025 U.S.-brokered ceasefire that brought an end to full-scale fighting but has failed to halt Israeli attacks, secure Hamas' disarmament or relieve Gaza's humanitarian and energy crises.
Ahmed Al-Nabris, an internal medicine specialist at Nasser Hospital, said shortages of fuel, engine oil and spare parts had forced the hospital into an austerity plan that includes rotating power cuts between buildings.
"Patients are in severe danger, because any power cut puts their lives at serious risk," said Nabris.
One of the hospital's four generators is now out of service, and the largest two of the remaining three are under strain, he said. Normally, engine oil in generators should be changed every 250 operating hours, but shortages have forced technicians to extend that interval to around 1,000 hours.
Al-Nabris said the hospital's electrical system had suffered repeated damage since an Israeli military raid in early 2024. A solar energy system was destroyed and never replaced, while both a main and backup generator were lost. Israel has accused Palestinian militants of using Gaza hospitals as bases.
DWINDLING SUPPLIES
Fatima Abu Taima, a patient at Nasser Hospital who suffers from pulmonary fibrosis, says those needing to be hooked to a ventilator or nebulizer have to wait as electricity is rotated among departments.
"We keep waiting, counting down the seconds and minutes," she said. "You have to wait for the electricity to come back."
The mother of four said her condition had worsened since the outbreak of war in 2023, forcing her to move into the hospital.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement in August that thousands face greater risks of illness and death because restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts are undermining hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps and water trucks.
Dwindling supplies had forced humanitarian groups to turn to the local market, it said, where locals say prices have surged to $1,300 per litre from about $3 before the war.
Israel's COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, said in a statement that a mechanism coordinated with the international community facilitates the entry of engine oil, generator spare parts, ambulances and other hospital equipment into Gaza under monitoring and oversight.
COGAT said that mechanism is "aimed at preventing advanced equipment from falling into the hands of Hamas and ensuring that such equipment reaches the population directly".
COST OF HOME ELECTRICITY HAS SOARED, RESIDENTS SAY
Beyond hospitals, the shortage has hit Gaza's network of private and neighbourhood generators that provide homes with a few hours of electricity a day.
Palestinian and U.N. records showed earlier this year that at least two-thirds of Gaza's population of about 2 million were still living in more than 1,000 displacement sites across the territory, with severe shortages of water and electricity. Residents say only a tiny portion can afford to pay for private generators.
Yasser Ashour, who sells electricity from generators he owns, said that despite the pressing need for steady power supplies — especially for those with medical conditions or serious injuries — staying in business has become increasingly difficult as prices for engine oil, diesel and spare parts have soared.
The shortages have driven up the cost of electricity supplies to homes around 20-fold in the past months, residents said. Still, many have little choice but to pay.
Alaa Al-Hourani, 65, who suffers from liver fibrosis and low oxygen levels, said his struggles to secure costly food and water sometimes left him unable to afford electricity.
"It is suffocating and agonizing, but there is nothing we can do. We have nothing but cardboard to fan ourselves," he said. REUTERS

UMCC plans to draw about $70 mln from NEQSOL Holding over two years if regulatory environment improves
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:05:26 EEST
21:05:26 KST

Operating and capital investment at United Mining and Chemical Company (UMCC, UMCC Titanium) has exceeded UAH 2 billion since its privatization in October 2024, and a two-year investment plan agreed with the supervisory board envisages drawing about $70 million more from owner NEQSOL Holding B.V.
Implementation of this investment plan, which would allow UMCC to reach breakeven by 2028, depends on decisions to lift export controls on rutile and zirconium concentrates, company management told journalists.
Rishad Aliyev, NEQSOL Holding B.V.'s head of investor relations and UMCC's first deputy general director, said the company increased production this year after privatization and operational stabilization last year: output in the first half of 2026 exceeded 84% of the company's entire 2025 output, and it managed to win back customers in the U.S., Mexico and EU countries.
However, the company faces a number of challenges affecting its operations, particularly export restrictions: it currently cannot fully sell its main products, which account for about 50% of gross value, on external markets, referring to restrictions on rutile and zircon exports introduced after privatization.
UMCC lost out on about $35 million in foreign currency revenue since privatization was completed due to its inability to sell its products, according to Aliyev.
"The company could have earned this money and invested it both in modernizing production and increasing output volumes," he said.
Lifting restrictions on the sale of rutile and zircon concentrate would also positively affect NEQSOL Holding's ability to participate in the auction for the sale of the Demurinsky mining and processing plant (Dnipropetrovsk region), scheduled by the State Property Fund for Oct 20, since there is currently no final decision on the matter, Aliyev said.
State Property Fund head Dmytro Nataluha, for his part, said the introduction of new forms of control over the company's products after privatization negatively affects its investment appeal, since the investor purchased it under different conditions.
The fund said it is ready to work together with business and relevant state bodies to find balanced solutions to the issue.
UMCC also faces logistics difficulties exporting products from its Vilnohirsk mining and metallurgical plant (VMMP) to the U.S. Due to shelling and problems with the Odesa route, the company is considering alternative shipping routes by rail to Romania or Poland, with subsequent loading onto vessels. The company spends millions of dollars a year on such shipments, according to UMCC operations director Valeriy Zakharenko.
"So this is a big problem for us. Doubling the cost of transporting one tonne of product, for example, reduces our margin to zero," Zakharenko said.
Other factors affecting the company's operations cited included a shortage of workers, proximity to the front line, and electricity costs.
UMCC CEO Dimitri Kalandadze said the company currently needs to stabilize production and reach planned capacity, carry out modernization, and subsequently move from exporting raw materials to deeper processing and producing higher value-added products in Ukraine.
The company plans to soon begin extracting raw materials at the "Phase II" section of the Yurske deposit in Zhytomyr region, while three quarries are currently operating at "Phase I," according to the operations director. The company is also considering the Bukynske site as another prospective extraction area.
As previously reported, UMCC's net loss grew 2.5-fold year-on-year in January-June this year, to UAH 745.4 million, while revenue for the period rose 34.8% to UAH 1.1171 billion.
UMCC posted a net loss of UAH 2.1182 billion in 2025, compared with a net profit of UAH 17.1 million a year earlier, while its revenue fell 47% to UAH 1.5108 billion.
"The 2025 financial results were negative, a loss, but this was largely due to the company's transition to international financial accounting standards, and to writing off liabilities that were on the company's books," Aliyev explained.
In October 2024, Tsemin Ukraine LLC, part of the NEQSOL Holding group, acquired UMCC at a privatization auction for nearly UAH 4 billion. After completing the necessary regulatory procedures, the company officially passed into the new investor's ownership in June 2025. UMCC has since operated as part of the international NEQSOL Holding group, which has businesses in several countries and industries.
UMCC has two branches — the Vilnohirsk mining and metallurgical plant (VMMP, Dnipropetrovsk region) and the Irshansk mining and processing plant (IMPP, Zhytomyr region). UMCC's core business is open-pit titanium ore mining, along with the production and wholesale trade of titanium ore concentrates (zircon, ilmenite, rutile, kyanite-sillimanite, staurolite and quartz sand).

Yellow level of drone threat — can children remain in classrooms and what should teachers do
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:05:19 EEST
21:05:19 KST

Yellow level of drone threat — can children remain in classrooms and what should teachers do
Kyiv • UNN
During a yellow threat level, students must move to a shelter, and classes in classrooms are suspended. If there is insufficient space, blended or shift-based learning is recommended.
In the event of a yellow level of drone threat being declared, educational institutions without equipped civil protection shelters are required to suspend the educational process. Students and staff must be evacuated to shelters, where education may be resumed if the relevant conditions are available. This was reported by Education Ombudswoman Nadiia Leshchyk, UNN writes.
Details
Resolution No. 1092 "Certain Issues Concerning the Optimization of Population Protection and Response to Threats from Air Attack Weapons" defines two threat levels:
-  red level - a missile or missile-and-drone threat, as well as a massive drone threat; 
-  yellow level - a drone threat. 
Under subparagraph 3 of paragraph 1 of the resolution, when a yellow threat level is established, the educational process in educational institutions, except those with equipped civil protection shelters, is suspended.
Can lessons continue in classrooms during the yellow danger level?
Leshchyk emphasizes that establishing a yellow threat level does not mean that children may remain in classrooms and continue studying.
In such a situation, the educational process is interrupted, and all participants in the educational process must move to a shelter.
If the shelter is adapted for conducting classes, the educational process may be resumed there.
Thus, the procedure for educational institutions during the yellow and red threat levels is effectively the same: the educational process is suspended, participants move to a shelter, and, where possible, education continues there.
What to do if there is insufficient space in the shelter
A separate problem arises in schools where the shelter's capacity does not allow all students and staff to be accommodated at the same time.
The authorized official recommends organizing the educational process so that the number of participants in the educational process simultaneously present in the building corresponds to the shelter's capacity.
Possible options include:
-  blended learning - on designated days, some students study in person while others study remotely, after which they switch; 
-  shift-based learning; 
-  organizing in-person education for certain categories of students, such as children in primary and fifth grades, while the other students study remotely. 
The specific format, the Education Ombudswoman notes, should be chosen by the school principal together with the teachers, depending on the capabilities of the particular educational institution.
Should teachers go to school during the yellow danger level?
The Education Ombudswoman separately drew attention to situations in which employees of educational institutions are required to be at their workplaces during a threat.
Employees of educational institutions must not be forced to leave a safe place and go to school, the authorized official emphasizes. According to her, such actions are unacceptable, since an employer cannot require an employee to leave a safe place where they are supposed to remain during an air raid alert.
This is especially important given that the yellow threat level may escalate to red.
The authorized official reported that she had received complaints about cases in which employees of education departments checked whether teachers were present at their workplaces during an air raid alert.
Regarding children, parents should take into account the security situation on a particular day: whether the teachers have reached the educational institution and whether the school will be able to accommodate the child in the shelter.
According to the Education Ombudswoman, under conditions of constant changes in the security situation, these issues effectively have to be resolved every day.
The route to school must also be safe
The authorized official draws particular attention to the route to the educational institution. Due to constant air raid alerts in some regions, the journey to school may be dangerous, as an alert signal may catch students and teachers while they are on the way.
Transporting children by school buses is particularly risky.
The ombudswoman suggests that communities where the level of security risks has increased take into account the experience of cities located close to the combat zone. In particular, during business trips to Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia, she saw mobile shelters installed at stops and in places where people gather.
In her opinion, other communities where security risks are increasing should consider developing a safe route to school and the possibility of installing such mobile shelters.
They plan to install 840 mobile shelters on roads leading to schools
The Office of the President of Ukraine has initiated the “Safe Route for Schoolchildren” project. As part of it, 840 mobile shelters are planned to be installed on roads leading to schools in frontline regions.
At the same time, the Commissioner notes that the use of such structures has certain problematic aspects. In particular, mobile shelters are expensive, and in some cities they were used for purposes other than intended, as a result of which some of them had to be closed.
Leshchyk also emphasizes that such mobile shelters should not be placed on the balance sheet of an educational institution. They should be on the balance sheet of the community, which should be responsible for their maintenance and proper use.
The Commissioner is currently awaiting relevant clarifications from the Ministry of Education and Science.

Gallery: Mythbústers' comics exhibition opens at Estonian Academy of Arts

Kruusmägi added that she does relatively little with comics herself. "I've contributed to that comics magazine a few times and published a little on my own. I would also like to publish a graphic novel myself, but for me it is difficult because it also requires good writing skills," she added.
The exhibition is open in the foyer at EKA at Põhja pst 7 until the end of the month.
