Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:12:29 UTC
20:12:29 KST

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE
Sept 10 - Algeria abruptly severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, citing what it described as a series of "provocative or hostile" actions by Abu Dhabi but giving no specific reason for the move.
The UAE hoped Algeria's decision to cut diplomatic ties would be temporary, its foreign ministry said in a statement later in the day, adding that Abu Dhabi remained committed to preserving ties between the two countries' peoples and shared interests.
Relations between the two countries have come under growing strain in recent years, with Algerian media outlets sharply criticising the UAE and accusing it of seeking to sow regional discord.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirms the UAE’s appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors," the ministry said.
The Algerian foreign ministry said the UAE's actions had reached a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable and that it had "exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations."
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, said on X that diplomatic relations should be based on "rationality, communication and clarity of interests", rather than "riddles and signals that require decoding".
Gargash, who did not explicitly mention Algeria or link his comments to its decision, said successful diplomacy depended on clear positions and the effective management of interests and disagreements.
Following its decision to cut diplomatic ties with the UAE, Algeria will close its airspace to all UAE-registered civilian and military aircraft from Friday, Ennahar TV reported, citing the Algerian defence ministry.
UAE commercial flights to and from Algiers will be exempt from the ban until the end of 2026, when the current contract expires, the ministry added.
DIFFERING POSITIONS ON REGIONAL ISSUES
The UAE ambassador was summoned to Algeria's foreign ministry, informed of the decision and given 48 hours to comply, the ministry said.
Algeria and the UAE have taken differing positions on several regional issues. Algeria opposes normalisation with Israel, while the UAE and Algeria's regional rival Morocco established diplomatic ties with Israel under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
The two countries are also on opposing sides of the decades-old Western Sahara dispute. The UAE supports Morocco's claim to sovereignty over the territory where it has a consulate, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks an independent Western Sahara.
The two countries' interests have increasingly intersected in the Sahel, where the UAE has expanded ties with several governments in recent years, while Algeria's relations with some of its southern neighbours have become strained following a series of military coups.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune said last year his country's relations with all Gulf states were warm except for one — a thinly veiled reference to the UAE.
He described ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as "brotherly", while accusing the unnamed country of meddling in Algeria's internal affairs and seeking to destabilise it.
In February, Algeria began the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE that was signed in Abu Dhabi in May 2013. REUTERS

ISLAMABAD, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Pakistan said on Thursday that no military action was currently under discussion under its Makkah Joint Defense Agreement with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan made the remarks at a weekly media briefing when asked how Pakistan planned to fulfill its obligations under the trilateral defense pact.
"There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When the time comes, we will act under the agreement," Khan said.
The agreement, signed last month, stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be considered an attack on all of them.
He also strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed Pakistan's solidarity with the kingdom. ■

Market for Russian helicopters in India could reach 5,000 aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:10:23 UTC
20:10:23 KST

NEW DELHI, September 10. /TASS/. India's potential demand for Russian helicopters could amount to around 5,000 aircraft, Tatarstan Industry and Trade Minister Oleg Korobchenko told TASS.
He previously said that Tatarstan was exploring the possibility of localizing production of Russian helicopters in India. These include the Mi-38, Mi-8, Mi-34, and Ansat helicopters.
"We have more than 1,000 helicopters in Russia and a population of 150 mln, while they have a population of 1.5 bln. So if we were to compare the figures even at 30%, and they had the same proportion as we do in Russia, they would accordingly need at least 5,000 helicopters to transport people. Five thousand helicopters would be a huge market for us," he said on the sidelines of the Innoprom India international industrial exhibition.
According to the minister, Tatarstan intends to work with the Indian side on options for localizing Russian helicopter production, maintenance services and technology transfers. The potential volume of investment has yet to be determined. "Our task now is to explore as many possibilities as possible so that India's civil aviation market is receptive to resolving this issue with our Russian helicopters. If that happens, we can then reach agreements on both the market and investment," Korobchenko said.
He added that developing local production and service infrastructure would help expand the presence of Russian helicopters in the Indian market and strengthen cooperation between the two countries.
The Innoprom India international exhibition is being held in New Delhi from September 9 to 11. TASS is the event's general information agency.

The perfect storm: Why this Rosh Hashanah may start Israel's most challenging year yet - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:10:17 UTC
20:10:17 KST

It would be more fun to write a feel-good column on the promise of a much better year. But reality points the other way. A convergence of trends and events – some global, some local – threatens to turn 5787 into a “perfect storm”: several forces coming together, each likely to confront us with challenges even greater than those we have already endured.
At home: political instability, intensifying internal conflict, accelerating net emigration, and continuing security threats. Abroad: artificial intelligence; a climate spinning out of control; instability in the international system and intensifying great-power competition; and, as a result of all these, the continued rise of antisemitism, which, true to form, blames Jews for every ill.
I hope I turn out to be wrong. But I may not.
The problems facing Israel in the new year
Let’s start in Israel. Elections will be held shortly after the holidays. Months of polling, including surveys conducted in recent days, point to a political deadlock. Like two wrestlers in the ring, the political “blocs” have each other by the throat, with neither able to prevail. If that holds, we can expect a replay of the election years of 2020–2023 and prolonged instability. This time, however, the social reality is more extreme – most Israelis identify the social rift as the greatest risk facing Israel –despite the immense challenges of the security environment. As conditions deteriorate, more Israelis are leaving the country, including many who are part of the backbone of the economy.
The security and foreign-policy fronts are also unstable – and in some respects, worsening. Israel has failed to achieve a decisive victory on any front. The IDF is stretched to the limit in Lebanon, Gaza, and the West Bank, while another “round” with Iran looms as a very real possibility. The security burden on military personnel and the Israeli economy is enormous – almost unprecedented.
The international outlook is no brighter. On the eve of the new year, Britain – once a close Israeli ally – imposed unprecedented sanctions on Israel. Eleven other European countries have followed suit, including major EU members. Israel’s standing in the United States is deteriorating as well. On both sides of the political divide, rhetoric toward Israel and Jews is becoming more extreme. Israel has already become a major issue in the midterm elections – not to its advantage – and as the 2028 presidential race heats up, the situation is likely to worsen. Public support for Israel is at a historic low. Then there is antisemitism. In Europe, this is old news – and the situation is bad. But over the past year, antisemitism in the United States, together with denial of Israel’s right to exist, has also surged and gained legitimacy, with such views now openly voiced by influencers and politicians. Antisemitism and rejection of Israel have become intertwined, threatening Jewish life in the Diaspora and becoming a national-security challenge for Israel itself.
Added to these are global challenges that will significantly affect Israel. The first is artificial intelligence. Many experts now expect AI to advance faster than previously thought – and to reshape our lives sooner than expected. There will be benefits, but the labor market and global economy also face the real prospect of a severe crisis – one that could last until economies and governments adapt to this new environment. Israel, whose economy is driven by its technology sector, is especially exposed.
Over all of this hangs the climate crisis. On its own, it might not drastically alter the international system. Combined with other pressures, however, it could become a major factor. Together, these trends intensify instability in the international system and sharpen great-power competition – both with consequences for Israel.
Some of these trends are beyond our control, and Israel has little influence over them. That does not exempt Israel from confronting them and preparing for their effects. Others – those directly involving Israel – are much more within our power to shape. Some result from government policy; others from external forces. But in both cases, we can do more to address them. The challenges awaiting us in 5787 could coalesce into a perfect storm. But this outcome is not inevitable; the choices we make can soften the blow. Despite it all – happy new year!
Dr. Shuki Friedman is director-general of JPPI – the Jewish People Policy Institute – and a senior lecturer in law at the Peres Academic Center.

The satellites of the Yaogan-53 and Yaogan-56 groups were launched at 5:00 p.m. (Beijing Time) aboard a Long March-4B carrier rocket, and they entered the preset orbits successfully.

Yemen's Houthis seize control of Red Sea city of Mocha

ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in southwestern Taiz province on Thursday amid a rapid advance toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical route for international shipping, a military official told Xinhua.
Houthi forces entered Mocha after hours of intense fighting, forcing government troops to withdraw southward toward Dhubab, a coastal area between Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the official said on the condition of anonymity.
The fighting in and around Mocha and other areas along the western coast has displaced thousands of families, according to the local official.
Meanwhile, the state-run Saba news agency said Saudi warplanes had carried out about 40 airstrikes in recent hours across Taiz, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib provinces. There was no immediate Saudi comment on the report.
The capture of Mocha and its port marks a major battlefield shift along Yemen's western coast, bringing Houthi forces closer to Bab al-Mandab, the narrow maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Mocha lies about 70 km north of the narrowest point of the strait.
Fighting has intensified across western and northern Yemen in recent days, in one of the sharpest escalations since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

Authorities in Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region have unveiled major plans to extend the Russian capital’s metro network deep into its outer suburbs over the next decade.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announced Wednesday that around 30 new metro stations will open in the next five years, followed by an additional 35 stations by 2035 — twelve of which will be built in the Moscow region.
“The quality of life will improve for 2 million Moscow residents and 3.7 million residents of the Moscow region,” Sobyanin said, noting that the Moscow metropolitan area is home to roughly 20 million people.
On Telegram, Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov published a video showing the scale of the planned expansion into the suburban districts of Krasnogorsk, Khimki, Mytishchi, Balashikha, Odintsovo and Leninsky.
Those metro stations will serve approximately 600,000 daily commuters, Vorobyov said, cutting travel times into central Moscow by up to an hour. The governor said construction of the new lines is expected to begin after 2028.
The transit expansion marks the latest phase in the rapid development of Moscow’s metro system under Sobyanin, who has served as mayor for nearly 16 years.

====================================================================================================

World Insights: From fragile calm to widening war, can Yemen's escalation be contained?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:09:58 CST
20:09:58 KST

by Murad Abdo
ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- After more than four years of fragile calm along Yemen's major front lines, fierce fighting between government forces and the Houthis has spread across the country's western and northern regions, while the Houthis have resumed large-scale attacks inside Saudi Arabia.
Analysts say the latest escalation is putting mounting strain on the informal Saudi-Houthi understandings forged in the wake of the UN-brokered truce in 2022, and should the latest exchange of attacks and retaliatory strikes evolve into a sustained cycle, the risk of a broader escalation would increase substantially.
CURRENT SITUATION
The latest escalation first gathered momentum in western Yemen, where intense fighting erupted in southwestern Taiz province and neighboring Red Sea province of Hodeidah. Houthi forces sought to cut key roads linking Taiz with the government-held Red Sea port of Mocha and advance toward territory near Bab al-Mandab.
"The battle for Bab al-Mandab is not simply about gaining territory inside Yemen," Aden-based political analyst Muqbil Naji told Xinhua. "Whoever can threaten this waterway acquires leverage that extends well beyond Yemen's borders."
The fighting did not remain confined to western Yemen. Government forces subsequently launched a major offensive in Al-Jawf, a northern province bordering Saudi Arabia and located east of the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Fighting has also intensified on other fronts.
The widening battlefield has changed the military dynamics. The Houthis initially pressed their offensive in western Yemen toward areas near Bab al-Mandab, but additional fronts subsequently opened elsewhere, forcing them to redistribute forces.
"Opening multiple fronts by Yemen's government will weaken the Houthis," said Abdul-Salam Mohamad, chairman of the Abaad Studies and Research Center.
As military pressure expanded inside Yemen, the Houthis widened the confrontation beyond the country's borders. The group said Tuesday it fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military and energy facilities across southern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities said attacks on civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran wounded 73 people and caused fires at several energy facilities.
"The attacks on Saudi Arabia should not be viewed separately from what is happening on the ground in Yemen," Naji said, adding that by increasing the costs for Riyadh, the Houthis could be seeking to create a new equation in which Saudi Arabia has greater incentive to restrain military pressure from Yemeni government forces.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg on Monday described the renewed escalation as "extremely alarming," warning that increasingly intense clashes threatened to expand the conflict and further complicate prospects for a political settlement.
BEHIND THE ESCALATION
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government.
The UN-mediated truce that began in April 2022 formally expired six months later, but relative calm largely persisted for years afterward. The period of direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation gradually gave way to an undeclared arrangement under which cross-border attacks and Saudi air operations sharply declined even though no comprehensive peace agreement was reached.
That informal arrangement now lies at the center of the current crisis. Salah Ali Salah, a researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described what remains of that relationship as a "gray area."
Salah said years of conflict management without resolving the war's fundamental political, security and economic disputes helped produce today's vulnerability. Temporary de-escalation can give the parties time to "catch their breath and reposition their military and political strategies," he said.
According to Salah, recent attacks do not necessarily mean the undeclared understandings have collapsed, but they are becoming more fragile and less capable of containing escalation. "Both Riyadh and the Houthis understood the enormous costs of returning to sustained direct warfare," he said, adding that the greater danger lies in "repeated exchanges becoming a sustained cycle of retaliation."
If that happens, Salah said, both sides could begin reassessing the informal "rules of engagement" that have helped contain direct confrontation in recent years, increasing the risk that "a calibrated escalation becomes harder to control."
For now, however, Naji believes Saudi Arabia has not yet decided to return to the open-ended military intervention seen during earlier stages of Yemen's war. "Saudi Arabia still appears to be calibrating its response," he said. "The objective at this stage seems to be deterrence and gradual pressure rather than immediately entering a decisive war."
WHERE DOES ESCALATION LEAD?
The Yemeni analysts agree that a return to the calm of recent years is becoming more difficult, but they differ on what may come next.
Mohamad outlined three possible scenarios. His most likely scenario is continued fighting followed by another temporary truce after significant changes on the battlefield. "The war might halt, or a temporary truce might be reached," he said.
In his assessment, however, such as pause would come after changes in the military balance rather than through an immediate restoration of the pre-escalation status quo.
A second possibility is a much wider war. Continued Houthi attacks inside Saudi Arabia could alter Riyadh's calculations, Mohamad said, potentially leading to stronger Saudi backing for a broad government offensive.
His third scenario -- an early Houthi move toward de-escalation and a restoration of the previous status quo -- is less likely because the military and economic conditions underlying the current confrontation have already changed. "The situation is poised to explode," Mohamad said.
Salah described "a full-scale Saudi-Houthi confrontation as the most dangerous potential outcome, though not the most likely for now." That calculation could change, he said, "if cross-border attacks persist, ground operations widen or a high-impact strike inflicts enough casualties to force either side to fundamentally reassess its response."
The risk, Salah said, is that a confrontation could develop beyond the calculations that initially produced it. A confrontation can begin with controlled attacks designed to signal resolve, he said, but retaliation and counter-retaliation could create a chain reaction that becomes increasingly difficult to stop.
According to Salah, the more likely scenario is "a prolonged period of limited, intermittent escalation." Under this scenario, the parties would continue using military pressure to gain territory and strengthen their bargaining position while keeping some channels of communication open and seeking to avoid an all-out war. ■

University professor brings "Journey to the West" to young readers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:09:47 CST
20:09:47 KST

Zhao Yulong (R) speaks with an online platform editor via video link on the performance of his online video lessons at Chongshan campus of Liaoning University in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Sept. 9, 2026. Zhao Yulong, born in 1984, is a professor and doctoral supervisor of Liaoning University, whose academic focus lies in fiction and traditional Chinese operas in Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911). His recent work has centered on the research on the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West," and how its stories shifted and spread across different ethnic groups, regions and media forms.
Alongside research and teaching, Zhao has also actively engaged in the promotion of this centuries-old classic to the public. He has given talks and public lectures on the tale, and posted educational audio and video lessons on Chinese social platforms, encouraging young people to read the original book and explore the old classic in a new light. He often shares with his students that an open and relaxed attitude is the best way to enter the world of the book. (Xinhua/Li Gang)

IAEA board refers Iran to UN Security Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:09:09 UTC
20:09:09 KST

Breadcrumb
IAEA board refers Iran to UN Security Council
The IAEA board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance" in a diplomatic move to pile pressure on the Islamic Republic.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged to be given access.
The resolution, seen by AFP, was adopted by 23 votes in favour, three votes against and eight abstentions, two diplomats told AFP. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
It "requests the (IAEA) director general to report" Iran to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move is seen as largely symbolic as Iran allies China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against Tehran.
'Counterproductive'
Iran condemned the resolution, saying it would "not bring any results".
"This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis," Iran's representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Reza Najafi, told state television.
He also told AFP that the resolution was "completely counterproductive".
The text notes "with grave concern... Iran's continued non-compliance with its obligations" and "reiterates its call upon Iran to urgently remedy its non-compliance".
It also calls on Tehran "to engage seriously and without preconditions in talks aimed at building international confidence in the exclusively peaceful nature of Iran's nuclear programme".
The IAEA has repeatedly said that its lack of information and access poses a "proliferation concern" and has called on Iran to address this with "utmost urgency".
IAEA head Rafael Grossi on Monday said giving the Vienna-based UN nuclear agency access to key nuclear facilities in Iran would have "positive repercussions" for the Islamic Republic.
'Exercise in futility'
Before the June 2025 strikes, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%, which is close to the 90% needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67% limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
Israel and the United States have long accused Iran of wanting to build a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied having any military nuclear ambitions, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group, told AFP that "some see it (the resolution) as an opportunity to add legal pressure to economic strangulation and naval blockade to turn the screws on Iran".
"Ultimately, though, it is an exercise in futility," he added, with Russia and China "likely to ensure that Western pressure hits a wall at the Security Council".

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:08:20 EEST
20:08:20 KST

Scheduled annual maintenance at Finland's largest nuclear reactor, Olkiluoto 3, began on Thursday.
The reactor will be offline for a period of around 50 days and should be wrapped up at the end of October, according to operator Teollisuuden Voima (TVO).
The company noted that scheduled maintenance of the Olkiluoto reactors often tends to raise end-user electricity prices.
According to TVO, the autumn timing of the maintenance was a result of extending its operating cycle to 18 months. OL3 was last serviced in spring 2025, with the next maintenance scheduled for March 2028.
The maintenance includes uranium fuel replacement, necessary repairs and possible modification work. Annual maintenance of Olkiluoto 1 and 2 was already carried out earlier this year.
TVO reported on Thursday that a few hours before the unit's planned disconnection, Olkiluoto 3 was automatically disconnected from electricity production due to a technical fault. The unit was already operating at low power level ahead of the planned shutdown, and the incident posed no danger.

Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:07:29 UTC
20:07:29 KST

Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
MOSCOW – Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church’s latest show of support for President Vladimir Putin’s war.
The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.
Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince’s well-preserved remains in August, hailing them as “an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery” that reinforced the foundations of Russian history.
The Russian Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy’s right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Putin said he had incorporated into Russia in 2022, a move Kyiv rejected as an illegal land grab.
Referring to Donskoy as “the holy commander”, the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russian Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russian troops.
“A fragment of the Grand Prince’s right hand – the very same right hand with which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field – has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers’ spirits,” it said in a statement.
The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russian combat units along the more than 1,000km front line, it said.
Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War II, was declared a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988.
Patriotic push
The carefully choreographed effort to use his remains in a public relations exercise to boost patriotism and morale comes ahead of a parliamentary election later in September.
Russian military and church officials have presented the discovery as a fortuitous find that could help Russian forces prevail in Ukraine, now in the fifth year of a grinding war.
The tour also comes as Russian forces seek full control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and as diplomatic efforts to end the war have yet to yield a breakthrough.
Donskoy’s relics were carried through the streets of Moscow at the weekend in a huge Orthodox procession.
At a ceremony at a World War II memorial in Donetsk on Sept 8, Sergei Kiriyenko, Putin’s first deputy Kremlin chief of staff, joined military commanders and the Russian-installed regional head in kissing the relic and making the sign of the cross as a priest read a prayer.
“Both our military personnel and the people who live in Donbas need strengthening from above, need God’s help and the blessing of our saints,” said Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol, a senior Moscow-appointed cleric. Donbas is a broader area incorporating Donetsk and neighbouring Luhansk which Russia controls almost in its entirety.
Elsewhere, commanders have presented Donskoy’s remains as evidence that God is on Russia’s side.
The Defence Ministry on Sept 9 released footage of troops in the Sverdlovsk region attending a church service carrying icons and Orthodox flags, alongside an interview with a commander who said the relics would support Russia’s victory.
Critics, however, have accused the Church of breaking with religious protocol to please the Kremlin. They have also questioned why Donskoy’s remains, whose location was broadly known for decades, were recovered and venerated only now, 38 years after he was declared a saint.
“By the fifth year of war, the Church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’,” Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, wrote in a note for the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, whose director Russia has designated a “foreign agent”.
“It had already sent priests to the front lines, instituted mandatory prayers for Russian victory in every church, and flown icons over cities. A state embroiled in war will try to compel all institutions, including religious ones, to participate in it.” REUTERS

Germany says NATO must ramp up defense output for ‘credible deterrence’ against Russia

Ayhan Şimşek
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
NATO allies must accelerate defense manufacturing if the West is to keep a “credible deterrence’ against Russia, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Thursday.
Speaking to reporters alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, Wadephul said an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month had shown how serious the threat from Moscow has become. German investigators have pointed to Russian intelligence services, and Berlin has announced extensive sanctions in response.
“It is part of a pattern of increasing Russian aggression against Europe and NATO, be it drone incidents or airspace violations affecting a number of allies on the Eastern Flank,” Wadephul said. “We are also seeing an increasing number of hybrid attacks, cyberattacks, hostile activities, sabotage, disinformation campaigns, and attacks on critical infrastructure.”
He said some of those campaigns were meant to spread fear and shape public opinion ahead of recent regional elections in Germany. Wadephul thanked Rutte and other allies for standing with Berlin after Germany made its findings on the Leipzig incident public.
Allies, he said, must stay politically united and do more to build up military strength. “That means investing more, producing faster, and procuring more quickly. Ultimately, it is about credible deterrence—and that only works if we actually possess the necessary capabilities.”
Wadephul repeated that Germany, together with other European allies, will keep raising defense spending, strengthen its armed forces and take on a larger share of responsibility for security inside the alliance.
He said Berlin will continue to give Ukraine strong military support, above all air defense. That includes extra interceptor missiles before winter to protect cities and energy infrastructure, he added.

Swiss Senate pushes back on VAT increase for funding army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:05:45 UTC
20:05:45 KST

Swiss Senate pushes back on VAT increase for funding army
The Swiss government is facing opposition to its plans to increase Value Added Tax (VAT) to fund the armed forces. Two Senate committees have called for a smaller VAT increase than that proposed by the government, as well as an alternative funding model.
The government wishes to increase the standard rate of VAT by 0.5 percentage points for a period of twelve years to finance defence projects. The Senate’s Security Policy Committee (SIK-S) rejected this proposal by 8 votes to 3, with 1 abstention, as the Parliamentary Services announced on Thursday.
There was no dispute within the SIK-S that, given the deteriorating security situation, a fund with borrowing powers is necessary to finance defence equipment for the armed forces. However, it wishes to finance it through a different approach.
+ Why Switzerland is struggling with its national defence
Like the Finance Committee of the Senate (FK-S) before it, the SIK-S also came out in favour of increasing the standard VAT rate by just 0.2 percentage points. The SIK-S also intends to follow the FK-S’s lead regarding the overall funding concept for the fund. It had previously discussed several different concepts.
In addition to VAT, the committees wish the fund to be financed from ordinary budget surpluses. The SIK-S is also proposing additional contributions to the fund from the general federal budget, divided into earmarked and non-earmarked contributions.
Both committees wish to decouple the creation of the legal framework for the fund from the referendum on the VAT increase.
The Senate will decide on the matter this autumn.

The DVZ is unable to process the files in time, which means the students cannot leave for Belgium – even though their paperwork is completely in order.’
Administrative processing can drag on
The DVZ confirms that applications are numerous and that deadlines are not always met. “Embassies and consulates grant approval when there is a very strong case. The other cases are sent to the DVZ in Brussels for assessment, often all at the same time,” says spokesperson Paulien Blondeel.
Hoste says the delays are outrageous. “Students and researchers spend months getting everything in order. They have to have 12,000 euros in a blocked account and also pay for the increasingly expensive applications. And then things go wrong in the administration. We’re missing out on top talent as a result.”
“In the meantime, the conditions on being able to stay here during their academic careers have also become stricter. Governments don’t seem to grasp that these top talents represent enormous added value. They aren’t just anyone, but people who truly excel in their disciplines.” Hoste estimates that there are nearly 10,000 foreign students and researchers working across Flanders.
‘Our knowledge-based economy needs highly skilled professionals’
Industry federations Agoria and VOKA have not commented on specific issues but support the general call for action. “Our technology companies, knowledge institutions and research centres need these high-calibre professionals to remain innovative and competitive. We cannot afford to lose them. Especially now that the recent PISA results show that the number of high-calibre professionals in our own country is declining,” says Jan Gatz of Agoria.
“In Ghent, there is a thriving (bio)tech scene where international talent is in huge demand. There is clearly competition to attract people, including from other countries. So, the red tape must be kept to a minimum,” adds Arne Oosthuyse of VOKA.
“These people are developing new techniques, procedures and materials here. We benefit from these innovations, and they also pay off. Without these students, we will quickly fall behind internationally. Our governments are making things difficult for these people, whilst other countries – such as Canada – are specifically targeting these top-tier profiles. There, they are actually allocating more money for this in the budget,” says Hoste.
Hoste disagrees with the assessment recently made by Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt (Flemish nationalist N-VA). In a report on the 13 students from Gaza who wanted to come here, she stated that she feared a domino effect.
“There is absolutely no evidence to support this. The minister is making an unfounded statement about people who are ambitious and want to contribute to our society.”
Last year, the faculty was expecting three people from Gaza. They never arrived.

Russia’s recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in its war against Ukraine amounts to “human trafficking,” according to a report published Thursday by Amnesty International.
The human rights organization says Moscow has used “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices” to recruit citizens from low-income countries such as Sri Lanka, Sierra Leone or Somalia. The tactics include “hollow promises of civilian or non-combat roles,” Amnesty’s Secretary-General Agnès Callamard said.
Amnesty’s report draws from testimonies and interviews of foreign citizens detained in Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps. Some of them told the NGO that Russian authorities coerced them into joining the force when their residence permit in Russia was about to expire.
Advertisement
A Sri Lankan national named as Dinesh said he was approached about joining the army after his Russian work visa had expired. After the two weeks of training, Dinesh was sent to the front line, where he was captured by the Ukrainian army two months later, the report reads.
Others say they were lured into joining the army from abroad under the pretext of doing a different kind of job. A Brazilian man referred to as Pedro in the report told Amnesty he thought he was signing a contract for a well-paid IT job in Russia, and was in fact taken to a military training center and later sent to the front line.
The Kremlin’s tactics to recruit foreign nationals have been the subject of multiple reports and have triggered diplomatic disputes. Countries such as Kenya and Ghana have demanded that Russia stop recruiting their citizens to fight in the war.
Ukrainian authorities estimated in March that at least 27,000 foreign nationals from 135 countries had been recruited by Russia since 2022. The main groups come from Tajikistan, Belarus and Kazakhstan — countries from which there has traditionally been a large flow of migrants to Russia.
A Kremlin spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

====================================================================================================

Family environments shape authoritarian traits differently than dominance preferences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:39 UTC
20:00:39 KST

Genetic predispositions and family environments both shape extreme political views, but they do so in entirely different ways depending on the specific type of attitude. A new study reveals that a desire for social conformity is heavily influenced by household upbringing, while a preference for group dominance stems more from outside personal experiences. The research was published in Behavior Genetics.
Political scientists and psychologists often examine two distinct personality traits to understand polarized socio-political attitudes. The first is Right-Wing Authoritarianism. This concept describes a person’s preference for strict adherence to social conventions, collective security, and obedience to authority.
The second concept is Social Dominance Orientation. This captures a person’s desire for group-based hierarchies and the belief that their own social group is inherently superior to others. Both traits reliably predict prejudice, support for extreme political movements, and a tolerance for discrimination.
Researchers want to know why people develop these distinct views in the first place. Past research has shown that both biological genetics and life experiences play a role in shaping them. It has remained largely unknown whether the specific environmental and genetic sources differ between the two traits.
Psychologists Christian Kandler and Jana Instinske of Bielefeld University in Germany, along with sociologist Edward Bell of the University of Western Ontario, wanted to map exactly how these influences combine. They also aimed to see if the roots of these political attitudes shift as people grow from adolescence into young adulthood.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study of 1,440 German families. This group included identical and fraternal twins, their parents, and their non-twin siblings, encompassing more than 5,000 individuals. The twins belonged to three distinct age cohorts averaging 15, 21, and 27 years old.
Participants answered survey questions designed to measure their levels of both authoritarianism and social dominance. By comparing the attitude similarities between identical twins, who share all their genes, and fraternal twins, who share about half, the team could estimate the mathematical contribution of genetics.
Adding parents and non-twin siblings to the analysis allowed the researchers to account for the specific environments families create. It also let them measure assortative mating. This is the well-documented tendency of people to marry partners who share similar political and social views.
The results showed that genetics shape about the same total amount of variance for both personality traits. The genetic components themselves differed slightly in their structure. Authoritarianism was influenced by both additive genetics, which are straightforward traits passed directly from parents, and nonadditive genetics, which involve complex interactions between different genes.
Social dominance was driven entirely by additive genetic factors. Beyond that basic genetic contribution, the two political orientations diverged completely in their environmental origins. Authoritarianism showed a strong connection to family inheritance and upbringing.
The data indicated that parents who favor social conformity tend to choose partners who feel the same way. These parents then pass down both genetic predispositions and a home environment that reinforces those exact traditionalist views. Researchers refer to this combined biological and environmental inheritance as a passive genotype-environment correlation.
In this scenario, children receive genes that might make them lean toward conformity, and they are simultaneously raised in a household that actively promotes obedience and tradition. Social dominance showed almost no link to this kind of passive family inheritance.
The tendency for parents to match with partners based on dominance preferences was lower, and the home environment played a negligible role in shaping the trait in their children. Instead, a person’s preference for group hierarchy was heavily shaped by their own unique, individual experiences outside the family home.
The researchers suggest this divergence makes sense based on what the traits represent. Authoritarianism involves moral regulation and conformity, which are central to keeping a family unit cohesive. Because these values dictate household rules and religious traditions, they heavily influence mate selection and parenting.
By contrast, a preference for social dominance usually applies to intergroup competition in the broader outside world. A belief in societal hierarchy is less relevant to daily household dynamics, making it less likely to be directly programmed by the family environment.
The team also looked at how these influences changed as the twins aged. They initially suspected that the impact of the family environment would fade as adolescents grew into adults and selected their own surroundings. They hypothesized that genetics would play a larger role as adults sought out social circles and news sources that matched their natural predispositions.
Instead, the data pointed in the opposite direction. For both traits, the total genetic influence remained relatively stable across the age groups. The influence of environments shared specifically by the twins actually increased from adolescence to adulthood.
This twin-specific shared environment was essentially nonexistent for 15-year-olds but became highly relevant for 21-year-olds and 27-year-olds. The researchers suspect that as young adults become eligible to vote, they might engage in more political discussions with their peers and twin siblings. This co-development process could amplify shared social influences during the exact years when political identities solidify.
A few limitations shape how these findings should be interpreted. The study compared different age groups at a single point in time, rather than tracking the same individuals across their entire lives. This makes it difficult to separate genuine developmental changes from generational effects related to the specific time period in which a given cohort was born.
The statistical tests did not yield statistically significant differences between the age cohorts for many of the mathematical model parameters. The researchers note that an even larger sample might be needed to confirm other age-related trends. The study also relied on relatively short survey measures, which can sometimes limit the precision of personality evaluations.
Additionally, the mathematical models required the researchers to assume that genetic and environmental variances remain identical across different generations, which may not perfectly reflect reality given shifting cultural norms. Understanding these origins provides a foundation for making sense of political polarization.
The study, “Sources of Differences in Right-Wing Authoritarianism and Social Dominance Orientation from Adolescence to Adulthood: A Multi-Cohort Twin Family Study,” was authored by Christian Kandler, Jana Instinske, and Edward Bell.

====================================================================================================

We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down | Garrison Lovely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

On Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, warning that “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”
As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.
Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.
The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quickly find serious holes in even the most secured systems on the planet, including the NSA’s software.
OpenAI quickly followed with an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, which broke out of their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.
And a separate rogue agent swarm gained administrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.
Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systems surpass us at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.
There are growing calls to change that, by creating mandatory incident reporting and third-party auditing, liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?
Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casar announced a bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.
This is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.
This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has written, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in its charter as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?
Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.
At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. The OpenAI executive Dean Ball explains:
“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”
Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”
We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.
After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agents broke their way out of their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader and successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.
Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.
This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reuters reported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”
The site’s logs indicate OpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers that uncovered this swarm said that there had been more discoveries since.
And last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest ever leaps in benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantly harder to monitor because it can do more reasoning without verbalizing it.
The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institute found would also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is also better at figuring out when it is being tested, which researchers have long warned breaks the main way safety is evaluated.
Sam Altman soberly warns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.
Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing to render us obsolete.
That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientists synthesized the first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institute found that AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.
On Tuesday, amid a dispute over credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAI announced “an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russia reportedly used a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.
What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?
The bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts will tell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.
And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.
The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored using verification techniques that don’t assume any good will.
One quick and dirty idea would be to embed auditors within frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.
This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said of advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.
And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.
- 
  Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September)

Teachers at schools can now arrange a deferment in "Reserve+"
Kyiv • UNN
Teachers can arrange a deferment in "Reserve+" without certificates or visiting an Administrative Services Center. The system automatically verifies employment and workload data.
Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions can now apply for a deferment in the Reserve+ app. The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
There is no need to collect certificates or contact a CNAP. The system automatically verifies the data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine
The following conditions must be met to apply for a deferment:
-   the educational institution is the primary place of employment; 
-   teaching workload – at least 0.75 of a full-time position; 
-   the position belongs to the teaching staff of a general secondary education institution; 
-   the employer data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine match. 
It is noted that to apply for a deferment, users need to open the "Services" section in the "Reserve+" app, select "Deferment request," and then — "Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions."
After the automatic data verification, the result will appear directly in the app. If it was not possible to apply for a deferment, the Ministry of Defence advises checking whether the information about the place of employment, position, and teaching workload in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine is up to date.

Japan’s AI satellites and other space ambitions ‘a serious threat’, China warns

The Japanese Nikkei newspaper reported last week that the planned AI-equipped satellites would be capable of analysing surveillance intelligence in space. The aim is to speed up targeting decisions and strengthen the country’s “counterstrike capability”, such as missile guidance.
According to the report, the defence ministry will develop a prototype satellite with domestic companies and conduct ground tests in the coming years, with space launches expected from the 2030 financial year.
Funding for the project has been included in Japan’s draft defence budget request for the 2027 financial year, although the exact amount has not been disclosed.
While traditional reconnaissance spacecraft send raw images to the ground for processing, these devices will collect data from other satellites and process the information in orbit.
By only sending the AI-generated analysis results, the Japanese project aims to significantly reduce the time for space-to-ground communication, according to the Nikkei report.

9/11 and the Substitute Mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

In 2001, I lost the world I knew. Twenty-five years later, I’m accidentally rebuilding it.
“I think people think you’re my mother,” my six-year-old niece whispered to me as we walked through the parking lot toward CVS.
“I think you’re right,” I said, smiling back at her impish grin that suggested we were pulling one over on the world. I had picked her up from school and was indulging her request to buy fake nails for our sleepover. She gripped my hand tightly, as a daughter would. We proudly walked through the automatic sliding doors, as one.
I don’t have children of my own, which means my niece is the beneficiary of my pent-up maternal love and obsession. She was born in 2020, and four months later, I left my job as the executive producer of a morning news show in New York and moved to Los Angeles. It was the first time I’d disrupted my ambitious climb up the media ladder, and when my feet landed in the California sand, my role as an aunt became the foundation of my daily life.
Birthdays, ballet recitals, and school performances anchored my calendar. Playing hide-and-seek before dinner, getting ice cream on a Tuesday, and letting her empty my closet for dress-up replaced late-night calls, breaking news, and media dinners. Recently, when my sister traveled abroad for work, my niece wanted assurance that her “substitute mother” would be around. The phrase made me laugh, but also squeezed my heart like a vise. Because I know what it’s like to have a substitute mother.
Daphne Pouletsos worked for the insurance company AON, her office was located in the south tower of the World Trade Center, and she was among the 2,977 victims killed in the 9/11 attacks.
Saza, as we called her, was my mother’s younger sister. Her nickname was a name given by my oldest cousin, Dayna, whose toddler tongue couldn’t say “Aunt Daphne.”
Although Saza lived in New Jersey and I grew up in Virginia, she was a constant light in my life. We drove up north for summers and holidays, and Saza would visit us throughout the year. Once, she hid in the back of our Chrysler minivan when my mom picked my siblings and me up from school, and she revealed herself by suddenly piping into the conversation. We squealed with excitement.
Saza knew how to make a mundane moment sparkle. Her sense of humor was the first thing to enter the room, and sleepovers at her house meant staying up late to watch Saturday Night Live. In my young mind, “The Church Lady” and “Coffee Talk” were extensions of my aunt (it helped that she also had a New Jersey accent). Shimmying our shoulders like “Sprockets” was like a special inside joke. Her laugh could sweeten the sourest mood.
But the best moments with her were always Christmas morning. Saza would come to my grandparents’ house first thing in the morning, the jingle bell on the back door announcing her arrival. She’d sit in the big, blue upholstered wingback chair, her feet tucked under her like a teenager, eyes shining behind her ‘90s rimless glasses. I can’t separate the thrill I got from opening a new baby doll from the joy I got from showing it to her. She would coo with enthusiasm, amplifying my delight. One time, she gave all of her nieces and nephews thick black plastic glasses with rubber banana noses attached. It was the silliest gift I’ve ever received, and one of the best. We took a picture, all piled on top of each other: laughing, goofy, family. Her presence carried a promise that everything was okay. As a kid, I assumed it always would be.
I was studying abroad in the fall of 2001. Classes at University College London hadn’t started yet, so I was traipsing around Europe with a sorority sister. We were at a restaurant in Barcelona when a waiter expressed dismay about “what happened at the World Trade Center.”
“My aunt works there,” I told my friend. But I was sure she was fine. How could she not be?
Still, I found a payphone and called home. My father tried to convey a stoic message: “We don’t know anything yet, we’re calling all the hospitals.”
Then I saw the footage on the TV in our hostel. I couldn’t believe that she could be one of the victims. Not Saza.
As a journalist, I know the questions that are typical in the wake of a tragedy. How old were they? Did she or he have kids? It’s natural. We’re inclined to measure loss by what, or rather, who, is left behind. But the true impact of a person’s life is not reflected in titles or preconceived roles. Every one of the 2,977 victims on 9/11 had a world that was wide and meaningful. You may not know the details of that world, but someone does. And they mourn not just the loss of that person, but the moments they made possible. For me, saying “I lost my aunt on September 11th” doesn’t begin to tell the story. My loss isn’t constricted by norms. Her legacy doesn’t fit neatly into a headline.
How old was she? Forty-seven. No, she didn’t have kids, but she had us. Twenty-five years later, I am 45, and I have my niece. Saza was the person who gave me the gift of knowing what an aunt can be.
While I could never fill her slippers, I feel Saza with me every day. She’s there when my niece and I are feeding the stray cat in my backyard. She’s there when we’re laughing at the Sunday comics. She’s there as we get dolled up in fancy dresses to go to the neighborhood pizza place. I am alive in these moments because she lived.
I wonder what else her life would have included if she had kept living it. What it would be like to have her visit me in Los Angeles. How she, my sister, and I would stay up late watching SNL together. How much love she would pour into life’s middle moments.
And most of all, what joy she would take in getting to know my niece, her namesake: Daphne.

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron

Unknown Publisher

20:00:00 KST

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
September 10, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China.
"Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris.
European-crewed spaceflight
"We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts."
Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station."
He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board."
Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport.
The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance.
'Passengers or pilots?'
Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space.
After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?"
The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration.
"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said.
Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion).
"Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically."
