Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.
Best Bluetooth Speaker Overall
Specs
Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.
Best Smart Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
If your house is already full of Sonos speakers, the Sonos Play is an easy addition to justify, with ample smarts and connectivity built-in. It sounds significantly better than the smaller Sonos Roam 2, with an audio performance closer to the brand’s excellent Sonos Era 100, despite being battery powered.
Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.
At 2.9 pounds, it’s just about portable enough for travel, although I was very aware I was carrying it in my backpack. You can also charge your phone from it or add an analog source using Sonos’ optional line-in adapter. If you’re already invested in Sonos’ ecosystem, and don’t mind a regularly-changing Sonos app, it’s hard to think of a more smart speaker.
Best Budget Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Great looks, cute size, and instantly stolen by my tweenage daughter, the Go 5 is my ideal tiny speaker. It weighs next to nothing and fits in the palm of my hand, but the 4.8 watt output sounds considerably less weedy than it has any right to.
The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. Its tough little enclosure is drop-proof and IP68 dust and waterproof. Connectivity is also impressive with Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, 7-band app EQ, and clever pairing (where you bump two Go 5s together to create a stereo pair).
It’s speakers like this that remind me just how we’ve come since the days of sticking my phone in a mug to amplify the tiny built-in speaker. If only I knew where my daughter had put it.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Battery Life
Specs
I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.
Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.
In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. It’s loud enough for small- to medium-sized rooms, and cut through when used outdoors, with weighty bass, decent balance, and no obvious distortion when pushed. The 360-degree presentation spreads music evenly too, so it feels less directional than many rivals.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Sound Quality
Specs
Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.
The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.
Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

AMD unveils ‘personal super computer’ for new era of computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:59:40 UTC
19:59:40 KST

The American chipmaker launched what they have described as a ‘personal supercomputer’ in Berlin on Friday, designed and made for a “completely new era of computing” driven by AI.
The supercomputer, called the Threadripper Halo Station, was unveiled at the German tech event Internationale Funkausstellung by AMD Senior Vice President Jack Huynh.
The Threadripper Halo is an ultra-high-performance workstation equipped with up to two terabytes of system memory, up to 576 gigabytes of high bandwidth memory (HBM3E), along with 96 cores of Threadripper Pro, two MI350P data centre accelerators, all supported by liquid cooling.
Huynh said the new supercomputer is the “most powerful workstation in the world”, capable of running AI models with more than a trillion parameters.
The AMD executive gave a brief demonstration of its potential at the event by generating an entire 3D world and flight simulator from a single prompt.
The company’s pitch is to bring data-centre level AI performance and capacity to a desktop format, as demand for AI rapidly grows around the world.
The supercomputer is slated for release early next year, however AMD are yet to reveal how much it will cost. It is expected that it could exceed €100,000, geared towards corporate and institutional budgets rather than as personal computers as originally pitched.
Yet it will give its consumers a platform to deploy large-language models and agentic AI systems themselves rather than rely on increasingly expensive cloud computing.
The Threadripper Halo Station’s direct competitor is the NvidiaDGX Station, with both able to run large AI models in a desktop form, however they differ in how they approach this challenge.
AMD’s supercomputer dominates on memory capacity and bandwidth, offering more than three times as much memory than Nvidia’s, allowing it to run on trillion parameter AI models locally.
However, Nvidia’s offering more seamless integration when moving code from a local workstation to the cloud and, crucially, it is already available, retailing at around €100,000.
Industry analysts see AMD's announcement as a potential catalyst for reshaping the competitive landscape of the local AI computing market.
With cloud AI subscription costs adding up for many institutions and businesses, demand for computers such as the Threadripper Halo Station to run large models on their own infrastructure will continue.
Therefore, AMD's approach of delivering data-centre-class performance using standardised components to lower the barrier to entry could be a major turning point in the expansion of the AI and personal computing sectors.

IAEA accuses Iran of ‘noncompliance’
Nuclear watchdog has gone more than a year without inspecting key sites; however Iran says US attacks have made access unsafe.
The Board of Governors of the United Nations nuclear watchdog has passed a resolution accusing Iran of failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation commitments and referring the matter to the UN Security Council (UNSC).
The diplomatic move – backed by the United States and its key European allies – comes more than six months into the US-Israeli war against Iran, and as tensions flare in the Strait of Hormuz, where the US and Iran have traded attacks on vessels in recent days.

Here’s what’s to know about the resolution by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and its implications during the ongoing conflict:
What has the IAEA accused Iran of?
The IAEA resolution expressed “grave concern” over Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), to which it is a signatory.
Under the NPT, Iran is forbidden from producing nuclear weapons and is required to meet IAEA safeguards to verify that any nuclear material it has is for peaceful purposes.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against Iran in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
In its latest resolution, the IAEA board said its “lack of information about previously declared nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it” is a “proliferation concern” that needs to be urgently addressed.
It called on Tehran “to engage seriously and without preconditions in talks aimed at building international confidence in the exclusively peaceful nature of Iran’s nuclear programme”.
It is the first time in 20 years that the IAEA board has passed such a resolution.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has condemned the resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
“This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis,” said Iran’s representative to the UN in Vienna, Reza Najafi.
Najafi said Iran has been unable to provide inspectors safe access to its nuclear sites due to the ongoing conflict. However, he said Iran has “neither stopped nor suspended its safeguards obligations,” adding that “performance is currently impossible under continuing military operations and persistent threats”.
Tehran “will cooperate only to the extent that circumstances and safety permit”, he added.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi appeared to accuse the US, which sponsored the IAEA board resolution along with the United Kingdom, France and Germany, of political posturing.
“They attack Iran’s safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the IAEA Board of Governors,” said Gharibabadi in a post on X.
Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons but insisted it has the right to pursue civilian nuclear technology.
US President Donald Trump has demanded that Tehran completely dismantle its nuclear enrichment programme. The US launched the current war, saying Iran was on the verge of making a nuclear bomb – an assertion not backed by the IAEA as well as the US’s own intelligence agency.
Iran has a legal right to run a civilian nuclear programme under the NPT.
What is the UNSC expected to do?
It is unlikely to take any further action, as Iran’s allies Russia and China are veto-holding members.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group, told the AFP news agency that the IAEA resolution is ultimately “an exercise in futility”, with Russia and China “likely to ensure that Western pressure hits a wall at the Security Council”.
Darya Dolzikova, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Service Institute’s proliferation and nuclear policy programme, said she also does not expect the UNSC to adopt a resolution condemning Iran for non-compliance.
“Nevertheless, referral to the UNSC is intended to send a strong message that the US and the E3 [France, Germany and the UK] are unwilling to accept the status quo and to let Iran get away with continuing to refuse the IAEA access to its nuclear facilities,” Dolzikova told Al Jazeera.
What impact could this have on the US war against Iran?
The US, which has made Iran’s nuclear programme a central point in the ongoing conflict, could cite the IAEA referral as evidence of a potential Iranian nuclear threat.
On the same day as the IAEA report, US President Donald Trump renewed threats to target Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, which has two underground complexes near Iran’s damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
Trump said the US had observed “a little activity” there and would “advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard”.
The US president also reiterated his claim that Iran is seeking a nuclear weapon, adding that the world would be “in deep trouble” if they secured one.
Trump’s repeated warnings about an Iranian nuclear risk and his threats to strike Iran’s nuclear sites come despite his claim last summer that US strikes had “totally obliterated” Iran’s key enrichment facilities.
Bahram Ghiassee, a nuclear analyst and associate fellow at the UK-based Henry Jackson Society think tank, said the IAEA’s decision to refer Iran to the UNSC could serve as an opportunity for Washington to delay major military action until the US mid-term elections in November.
“Post-November elections, Washington’s political and military calculus may prove to be different, and a far less diplomatic approach may be adopted,” Ghiassee told Al Jazeera.
What is the IAEA’s history with Iran?
The IAEA was highly critical of Iran in the early 2000s, accusing it of failing to declare nuclear material and activities. In 2006, the UNSC imposed sanctions on Iran after it failed to comply with a resolution demanding it end its uranium enrichment programme.
But after Iran agreed to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) with six major global powers, including the US, it agreed to curtail its nuclear programme and open up nuclear sites to extensive, unprecedented IAEA inspection.
Iran remained in compliance for years, but the agreement went south after Trump withdrew the US from the deal in 2018 and reimposed US sanctions on Iran. Tehran retaliated by intensifying its nuclear programme, abandoning the restrictions imposed by the deal.
In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was not complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks against it just days later.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, however, did not back the US claims that Iran was capable of making an atomic bomb. “We did not have any proof of a systematic effort to move into a nuclear weapon,” he told CNN.
The IAEA suspects that Iran has about 400kg (882lbs) of highly enriched uranium, with which 10 nuclear weapons could potentially be manufactured if enriched further.

US urges NATO allies to leave ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:57:16 UTC
19:57:16 KST

The US, further complicating already tense international relations, is pushing for a “systematic dismantling” of the International Criminal Court, urging NATO members to abandon the Rome Statute, writes Politico.
According to three anonymous NATO diplomats, at a closed meeting of ambassadors from 32 NATO member states in Brussels in July, US envoy Matthew Whitaker asked for the alliance’s help in dismantling the ICC and called for abandoning the Rome Statute. Whitaker reportedly concluded his speech by saying that Americans would be careful who supported them.
The pressure to leave the ICC is part of a broader campaign by US President Donald Trump’s administration against international institutions and rules that it sees as restricting US freedom of action. The campaign is driven by US concerns that its officials could be tried for war crimes. The White House is also moving to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, and has pressured companies to withdraw from the Space Summit in Paris. The White House has also launched a series of trade spats.
In addition to Whitaker’s comments, the US mission to NATO issued a statement saying the US would systematically dismantle the ICC’s capabilities and called for steps to withdraw from the Rome Statute. It also called on allies to assess the risks posed by the ICC to their countries, publicly condemn the court’s abuse of power and end support for the ICC. The document says the ICC’s charade must be ended immediately and permanently. Although NATO is not a signatory to the Rome Statute, all alliance members except Turkey and the US have ratified it.
Opposition to the ICC was launched this summer by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio,
who accused the court of undermining US sovereignty. He said on the 13th of July that the ICC and its friends were waging war on the US, not with bullets or missiles, but with the force of statutes and so-called international law. Rubio added that if the court believes it can take away US sovereignty, Americans will show the extent of their resolve.
The ICC was established in 2002 to try individuals accused of the most serious international crimes, including genocide and war crimes. The last investigation against US officials was launched in 2020, when the ICC opened a case into alleged war crimes committed by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The case lost priority a year later. The ICC is now facing calls to investigate US attacks on boats in the Caribbean, which the Americans say are part of a fight against drug trafficking.
The US campaign marks a sensitive moment for NATO. The alliance has been strained by the refusal of many European countries to join Trump’s war on Iran, drawing Trump’s ire. Washington also rattled the alliance when Trump threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland. The alliance managed to bridge the gap at an annual summit in Ankara, but just days later, the US demand to dissolve the ICC renewed tensions. One NATO diplomat said Whitaker’s comments were “quite shocking,” while another added that they were “disappointing.”
Diplomats said that in response to Whitaker’s remarks,
France and the Netherlands defended the ICC and made it clear that they opposed the court’s dissolution.
The US delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment. The French delegation declined to comment on the situation, but stressed its support for the ICC. The Dutch delegation referred to the country’s Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen as saying that the Netherlands fully supports the ICC.
American envoys also spoke of the dual position of European countries. The US State Department said it was determined to closely monitor countries that refuse to “reject the ICC’s false authority” while relying on US assistance. In August, Washington imposed sanctions on top officials of the ICC.
An ICC spokesman said the court remains focused on the independent and unbiased exercise of its mandate, as set out in the Rome Statute, to protect victims and ensure justice.
The campaign against the ICC comes against the backdrop of other US efforts. Washington is trying to get Canada and Europe to take greater responsibility for their own defense. A survey sent to NATO countries in August, asking for their opinions on US foreign policy, including in the Middle East, is being seen as an effort to force them to align with US views in exchange for defense assistance.

One local resident recounted what happened: “My wife was at the concert. During the evacuation, people were falling, running in panic. Explosions could be heard all around. “Everyone started running once the explosions were already very close. At first everyone just watched, because that’s normal for Sochi. But something exploded just 300 meters (984 feet) from us, and then everyone ran. It was incredible chaos. Everyone is screaming, children are crying. Here's what Gemini says about the current automated transcription process:
Q: How does Google now create Youtube transcripts ?
A: Google creates YouTube transcripts by using advanced automated speech recognition (ASR) technology and AI models to process video audio.
How the Process Works
Audio Extraction: YouTube pulls the audio track from newly uploaded or existing videos.
Speech Recognition: Google uses specialized speech-to-text AI models (evolving from older models like Chirp to advanced tools like Gemini 3.5 Transcribe) to listen to the spoken words.
Timestamp Generation: The system matches the recognized words with specific points in the video's timeline to create clickable timestamps.
Automatic Publishing: YouTube makes the auto-generated transcript available in a side panel for viewers to read, search, or copy. Creators can also edit or upload custom transcript files.

This problem spans several levels. At one level we want a system that can turn a raw sound wave into phonemes. At another level we want a system that can turn /oʊpən/ into "open" and /eɪaɪ/ into "AI". We may or may not want a system that can turn /oʊpəneɪaɪ/ into "OpenAI"; the name feels like more of a word-by-coincidence. There will never be a system that can accurately transcribe arbitrary brand names it doesn't have preexisting knowledge of.
When the sound -> phonemes level gives us /oʊʔmeɪaɪ/, we don't want a system that will turn that into "OpenAI", or into "open AI". We might want a third level above the other two that can resolve processes like "well, 'OpenAI' would make sense in context here, and this string of sounds with no valid interpretation isn't thaaat far off"; this is basically my understanding of how a human would handle the task.

Disengagement 710: Extremist Israeli minister Ben-Gvir's new ethnic cleansing scheme for Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:54:23 UTC
19:54:23 KST

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir presented a plan last week to ethnically cleanse almost the entire population of Gaza from Palestine over the next seven years, an initiative he has named ‘Disengagement 710’ and made a central plank of his election campaign.
The forcible displacement of civilians from occupied territory is classified as a war crime under the Geneva Conventions, and rights groups, UN experts and governments have already described the plan in those terms.
The scale of the proposal leaves little ambiguity about what it would mean in practice.
It targets 250,000 Palestinians for forced removal from Gaza in its first year, rising to 1.11 million within three years and roughly 1.86 million within seven, a figure that covers nearly the entire population of the Palestinian enclave.
The proposal is built around the premise that Palestinians in Gaza can simply be relocated elsewhere. Each person leaving would reportedly be assigned a destination country, along with funding, legal status, housing and a support package.
But Palestinians in Gaza have made clear that they do not want to leave their homes or be removed from their homeland. For them, the question is why they should be expected to surrender their homes and land in the first place.
This is certainly not voluntary migration, according to Dr Munir Nuseibah, human rights lawyer and professor of law at Al-Quds University.
"Ben-Gvir is using this term (disengagement) because he knows that forced displacement is illegal under international law. It is a war crime according to the Fourth Geneva Convention and a crime against humanity,” Nuseibah tells TRT World.
"This is something Israel has been doing since the Nakba of 1948, displacing Palestinians from their homes to create Jewish-majority areas in regions it has been colonising ever since.”
“Now the Zionist ambition is to colonise Gaza, and the objective is to displace Palestinians, evict them from Gaza, ethnically cleanse them, and then make Gaza ready for Israeli colonisation," Nuseibah adds.
Ben Gvir has also put a price tag on the project. The plan calls for an initial Israeli outlay of 10 billion shekels (approximately US$ 3.3 billion), with a financing framework of up to 50 billion shekels contingent on countries abroad agreeing to take people in.
Yet no amount of funding answers the basic question at the heart of the proposal; why should Palestinians be expected to leave their homes and land in the first place?
When ‘voluntary’ stops being voluntary
Ben Gvir's answer is that they would be choosing to leave. But that choice would happen under conditions that make genuine consent impossible.
Much of Gaza's housing has been destroyed, reconstruction materials remain restricted, and movement in and out of the enclave is heavily constrained.
A person who has lost a home and cannot rebuild it, cannot safely return to it and has limited ability to leave or move freely is making a decision under circumstances fundamentally different from ordinary migration.
Nuseibah describes conditions in Gaza that leave people with little real choice but to leave.
"The Palestinian population in Gaza, which before the genocidal campaign was living in one of the densest areas in the world, is now living on only a third of the territory, in tents, seeking the very essentials of life on a daily basis.”
“They wake up every morning seeking water, food and mere survival. There is no development, no jobs, no education. Everything has been destroyed,” Nuseibah explains.
“Their lives have been set back to the Stone Age, and Israel is blocking every attempt to allow Gaza to be rebuilt,” he adds.
UN human rights experts have warned that removing Palestinians from Gaza under current conditions would amount to forced transfer, regardless of whether the policy is presented as voluntary.
Eight Arab and Muslim states, including Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Qatar, have likewise rejected any displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, calling it a flagrant breach of international law and warning against any attempt to impose a new demographic reality on the occupied Palestinian territory.
The objection is therefore also to creating the conditions and incentives under which leaving becomes the practical alternative to remaining.
That distinction is central to the legal argument.
What Israel is doing is building a coercive environment, using difficult living conditions to push people out of a territory, which is a crime against humanity of forcible deportation and transfer, according to Nuseibah.
"Under such circumstances, we cannot talk about a choice for people to leave.”
“Any Palestinian currently leaving Gaza is not leaving by choice, they are leaving because they are looking for survival, because they are looking for a way to educate their children and simply to live,” he adds.
Gaza as an election issue
Ben-Gvir is not leaving ‘Disengagement 710’ as a campaign slogan. His Otzma Yehudit party wants a dedicated Emigration Ministry, with its own minister and budget, and has made its creation a condition for joining Israel's next coalition.
That would give the plan a direct place in coalition negotiations after October's elections, while allowing Ben-Gvir to position himself further to Netanyahu's right as Israel's far-right competes over what Gaza should look like after the genocide.
Controversial former general Ofer Winter has also included a similar idea in his platform.
Netanyahu has so far kept some distance from the proposal, reportedly voicing reservations in Cabinet even as he has previously used the idea of Palestinian emigration to keep Ben-Gvir inside the government.
Defence Minister Israel Katz has said Israel is waiting for US approval to move forward.
The idea, however, did not begin with Ben Gvir's election campaign. The US proposed in February 2025 that Palestinians leave Gaza, before the White House backed off and said in its subsequent 20-point Gaza plan that the population would remain in the besieged enclave.
For Nuseibah, that history is important because reducing the proposal to an election tactic risks missing the broader policy behind it.
"Ben-Gvir is likely trying to use this ethnic cleansing plan as an element of his upcoming election campaign. But we cannot look at it only as election propaganda.”
“Israel has been trying to displace millions of Palestinians out of Gaza for quite some time. It has tried to pressure Egypt and Jordan, through the US and Germany, to take in Gaza's Palestinian population."
"It has been looking for places to send Palestinians to, and it has facilitated flights to different countries around the world to absorb more of them."
But Nuseibah also sees a clear electoral calculation in the proposal, particularly among the constituency Ben-Gvir is trying to mobilise.
"But of course Ben-Gvir wants to use it in the elections too, because his political base is a group who wants to ethnically cleanse the land and colonise it, driven by a messianic religious framework of thought and ideology," he adds.

Morocco's campaign for parliamentary elections kicked off Thursday, with 27 political parties vying for 395 seats in the House of Representatives ahead of a Sept. 23 vote.
More than 15.8 million voters are registered for the elections, which will determine the makeup of the lower chamber of Parliament.
Campaigning will continue until midnight Tuesday, Sept. 22, with voters heading to the polls the following day.
According to official data, 15,801,162 voters were registered on electoral rolls as of July.
The elections will test the standing of the parties that have governed Morocco since the last parliamentary vote in 2021, when Aziz Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI) emerged as the largest party with 102 seats.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) came second with 86 seats, followed by the Istiqlal Party with 81.
The three parties went on to form a coalition government headed by Akhannouch.
Ahead of this year's vote, Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit pledged in November 2025 to ensure transparency in the elections.
He said the main “major challenges” facing the upcoming elections involve establishing rules that would ensure transparency in political and electoral life in the kingdom.
Members of the 395-seat House of Representatives are elected by direct universal suffrage using party lists.

The Trump dividend: What $5,000 would cost and what it could cover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:53:04 UTC
19:53:04 KST

What would Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend buy — and could the US afford its estimated $1.2 trillion cost?
The US president has promised to give every adult citizen a $5,000 (€4,290) payment if Republicans retain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
The proposal could cost almost $1.2 trillion (€1.03 trillion), exceeding the Pentagon’s full 2026 budget request.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend,” Trump told the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, as the party struggles in the polls against the Democrats.
He compared the payments with the dividends distributed by companies to their shareholders, citing “our tremendous strength and success economically”.
Within an hour, Vice President JD Vance appeared to scale back Trump’s proposal, at least in part, by suggesting that wealthy Americans would not receive the payments.
The US had around 240 million adult citizens at the time of the 2024 presidential election, including 174 million registered voters, according to the latest comprehensive US Census Bureau figures. Only about 70% of the voting-age population was registered to vote.
Giving every adult citizen $5,000 would therefore cost almost $1.2 trillion. That is around $220 billion (€189bn) more than the Pentagon’s entire $961 billion (€825bn) budget request for 2026, according to figures by the Congressional Budget Office. Limiting the payment to registered voters would cost around $870 billion.
A $5,000 cheque would give each adult more than they received through the two rounds of direct federal payments approved during Trump’s first term.
What could it cover?
Average US household spending was $78,535 (€67,400) in 2024, or $6,545 (€5,620) a month, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
If two adults sharing a home each received $5,000 (€4,290), their combined payment of $10,000 (€8,580) would cover around 11 months of an average household’s total food spending, or about 18 months of grocery spending. These calculations use 2024 expenditure figures adjusted for the 6.45% increase in consumer prices by July 2026.
Housing was the largest expense, accounting for 33.4% of the average household budget. Households spent $26,266 (€22,540) on housing in 2024, equivalent to around $27,960 (€24,000) in July 2026 prices. Two $5,000 payments would therefore cover just over four months of average housing costs.
The combined payment could also cover around eight-and-a-half months of average transport costs or 18 months of healthcare spending. At almost six times the average household’s annual education spending, it could theoretically cover nearly six years of those costs.
However, the education figure is an average across all households, including those with little or no education spending.
What would it cost?
Trump’s proposal comes shortly after the country’s national debt passed $40 trillion (€34.3 trillion) for the first time. The US is also running an annual budget deficit of nearly $1.8 trillion (€1.54 trillion), while inflation remains a concern.
“The idea that we’ve had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable,” said Marc Goldwein, senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a Washington-based think tank. “We don’t have surpluses to give away.”
Concerns about the country’s debt are being compounded by high government borrowing costs.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note rose above 4.85% on Wednesday, its highest level in nearly three years, before easing slightly, while the 30-year yield climbed to 5.29%, close to the 18-year high of 5.33% reached in August.
Treasury yields help determine borrowing costs across the US economy, so sustained increases can make mortgages and business loans more expensive, slow economic growth and weigh on share prices.
With the government already running a large deficit, it remains unclear how the proposed payments would be financed.
Vance suggested that they could be funded using US tariff revenue.
The government expects to collect about $406 billion (€348 billion) in customs duties during the 2026 fiscal year, according to the US Treasury Department. This includes all customs duties, not only tariffs introduced by Trump.
That would cover only around a third of the estimated $1.18 trillion (€1.01 trillion) cost of paying every adult citizen $5,000 (€4,290). Even limiting the payments to the country’s 174 million registered voters would cost around $870 billion (€747 billion) — more than twice the projected annual customs revenue.
When Trump discussed a similar payment earlier this year, he proposed a $2,000 (€1,720) dividend and said he did not believe he needed congressional approval.
Last year, Trump gave members of the military a $1,776 (€1,520) cheque that he called a “warrior dividend”.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote on X late Wednesday. “Because Republicans (and America) will win!”
However, Congress would need to approve the proposed payments.
Trump’s proposal would be legal because the payment would be available regardless of how someone voted — or whether they voted at all — according to New Mexico-based lawyer John Day.
“This is a campaign promise,” Day said. “It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way.”
Republicans are on the defensive as they seek to protect their narrow House majority against strong political headwinds. Trump is unpopular and polls indicate that most Americans oppose the war in Iran. Even the Senate, which Republicans once appeared well placed to retain, is now considered competitive.

Erik Gamzejev: Both locals and outsiders deliver big at Station Narva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Erik Gamzejev: Both locals and outsiders deliver big at Station Narva
The atmosphere at this year's Station Narva festival was a stark contrast to the repulsive power struggles and throne games over positions that have gone on for years in the same municipality, notes Erik Gamzejev.
The Station Narva festival held last week has, both during and after the event, received abundant praise for its atmosphere, artists, and diverse program, which includes not only music but also art, discussions, excursions, and culinary experiences. Equally important is that this festival has, over nine years, matured in increasingly close cooperation with the capital and local people.
The organizing team led by Helen Sildna, in which the share of Ida‑Viru County residents themselves is steadily growing, has succeeded in making people believe that this festival is done precisely for Narva and Ida‑Virumaa, and not at their expense. That it is not a traveling circus that sets up its tent on site, collects money from locals for the tricks shown, and moves on to the next city. Rather, it is entirely a local thing.
Some distrust between those who live and operate daily in Ida‑Virumaa and those who come from the capital has existed throughout the ages. It intensifies and sharpens when something bigger is undertaken and the parties look only to their own interests.
Hendrik Agur, who moved to Ida‑Virumaa seven years ago and first led Kohtla‑Järve High School and then the Ida‑Viru Vocational Education Center Cosmos, wrote this spring in Põhjarannik newspaper that the development of Ida‑Virumaa is hindered by fragmentation, behind which are specific human patterns: ego, the need for recognition, and the habit of being the only "right voice," and intolerance of another's success.
To those who come from elsewhere, it may seem that some locals are indeed in a defensive circle and do not particularly want to let anyone beside them, because there is a risk that their job, money, and position will be taken away. What has happened in the leadership of some Ida‑Viru towns in recent years also gives reason to feel this. But it is not only an Ida‑Virumaa syndrome, where extreme provincial patriotism and the arrogant attitude of the capital intersect and ruin even initially good intentions. A reasonable and fruitful middle ground often remains unfound.
In Ida‑Viru Russian‑language social media groups, the attitude is constantly reinforced that people have come here from elsewhere in Estonia who are incompetent in their field, but whose only trump card or magic wand is their knowledge of Estonian. One group that has to operate amid such accusations includes, among others, the hundreds of teachers who have come in recent years to help Ida‑Virumaa schools by teaching in Estonian. Let us acknowledge their patience and steady nerves.
Some newcomers, however, create distrust toward themselves when they take the attitude that before them nothing was done here. Or if it was, then completely wrong.
The pot of money in Ida‑Virumaa in recent years called the Just Transition Fund has attracted people who sincerely want to accomplish something transformative for Ida‑Virumaa by investing their time and money.
But certainly there are also those who have little warmth or coldness toward Ida‑Viru, yet still see an earning opportunity through certain projects or programs whose usefulness or positive impact on the region is, to put it mildly, questionable. When support measures open, the winners are primarily the acrobats of project linguistics, of whom there are inevitably more in capital‑city agencies than on site. Thus part of the money intended to improve life in Ida‑Viru tends to accumulate in companies or institutions in the capital.
The best success story is born when local people and capital‑city experts who truly care about Ida‑Virumaa's well‑being manage to create a balanced team. A good result comes from combining the know‑how of experienced actors with the experience and initiative of local people, where both sides feel dignified and equal.
The Station Narva organizers have succeeded in this remarkably well, and that is the key to the festival's success. And this is also what Hendrik Agur strives for at Cosmos, although in that large educational institution it is a much more complicated task.
The atmosphere at this year's Station Narva was a stark contrast to the repulsive power struggles and throne games over positions that have gone on for years in the same municipality.
Among the festival visitors, about half were people from Ida‑Virumaa and the rest were guests from farther away. This is a mutually beneficial ratio. For many open‑minded local people, this is the most anticipated event of the year, by which they set their calendar. Guests, in turn, get a direct personal experience of Ida‑Virumaa and become friends of this region. It is important that a festival visitor brings Ida‑Virumaa emotionally closer to the rest of Estonia. In terms of kilometers, it is close anyway, just a two‑hour drive.
In addition, only at this festival can one experience unique surreal feelings. You stand between the walls of a 700‑year‑old castle. On one side, a couple hundred meters away, is Narva City Hall; on the other side, across the river, equally close, is hostile Russia. Between them are people with gloomy faces waiting at the border point to be let into that country. The castle courtyard is full of joyful and exuberant people. On stage is Propeller, and Peeter Volkonski, gripping the microphone tightly with both hands, sings passionately: "Eila veel muretu ja meeldiv maailm näis…". ("Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away…" – an Estonian-language punk song inspired by The Beatles – ed.)
--

Switzerland experienced hottest summer ever in 2026

Switzerland experienced hottest summer ever in 2026
The summer of 2026 was the hottest in Switzerland since records began. The average temperature for the period from June to August was 17.2°C, 0.4 degrees higher than that of summer of 2003, MétéoSuisse announced on Thursday.
The national average temperature was also 3.4°C higher than that of the 1991–2020 reference period. The heatwave hit the north-west of the country particularly hard, with a difference of 4.0 degrees compared with the reference period.
The temperature also rose to 39.7°C on July 30 at the Basel-Binningen station, equalling the record high temperature recorded north of the Alps (in Geneva/Cointrin on July 7, 2015), as noted by the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology in its Summer 2026 Climatological Bulletin.
More
Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Many locations reached unprecedented levels: in total, 30 MeteoSwiss stations recorded a new heat record during the summer of 2026. And nearly half of them set this record as early as June.
In Graubünden, Scuol also recorded an “impressive” record: on June 27, 2026, a temperature of 35.1 °C was measured there at an altitude of 1,304 metres.
The number of hot days and tropical nights also soared this summer. Several stations recorded nearly two extra weeks of tropical days compared with the previous record, notably in Neuchâtel and Glarus (+18). The number of tropical nights, meanwhile, reached 50 this summer – eight more than in 2003, according to MeteoSwiss.

Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:50:58 UTC
19:50:58 KST

Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
Russia exploits and deceives foreign nationals to enlist them in its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, and in many cases these practices amount to human trafficking, the human rights organization Amnesty International said in a report published Sept. 10.
Russia primarily targets people from low-income countries in the Global South, the report said. Russian recruiters lure people from abroad under false pretenses and exploit the precarious situation of migrants in Russia by weaponizing overstayed work visas or supposed criminal offenses and offering military service as an alternative to detention or deportation, it added.
"Once victims sign the paperwork, often in a language they do not understand, military commanders restrict their movements, deploy them to the front lines with minimal preparation, and threaten those who seek a way out," the report stated.
The Russian army misrepresents the nature of the work and the risks involved to these foreign nationals as a key tactic to recruit them, according to Amnesty International. Russian recruiters also offer lucrative payments and pathways to Russian citizenship as incentives that rarely are fulfilled, the report said.
Many foreign recruits lack any kind of military training and get deployed to active combat zones after just two weeks of training, in what Amnesty International called "an apparent disregard for human life."
Two Sri Lankan nationals interviewed in the report said they were led to believe they would be working as cooks but were sent to fight on the front lines and captured within weeks by Ukrainian forces. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one said.
"I would never go back there."
Once in the military, Russia often takes away the passports of foreign nationals and severely restricts their movement, the report said.
Pedro, a Brazilian IT professional recruited after signing what he thought was a contract for a well-paid tech job in Russia, said he asked his commander to leave but was told, "If you try to escape, you will either go to jail or we will kill you."
Amnesty International called on Russia to "immediately end all abusive practices involving the military recruitment of foreign nationals" in its report.
"The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol," said Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International.
On March 30, Ukraine had identified 27,407 foreign nationals fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine, up from more than 18,000 in November, with Moscow recruiting them from at least 135 countries, according to the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War.
The headquarters said much of the data on foreign nationals serving in the Russian army is compiled when those fighters are taken prisoner, including through Ukraine's "I Want to Live" project, which encourages those fighting on Russia's side to surrender to Ukrainian forces.
"In total, hundreds of foreigners are currently held in Ukrainian captivity, and their number continues to grow. Each week, Ukraine’s Defense Forces take captive one to three citizens of third countries, whom the Kremlin regime is effectively sending to certain death," the headquarters said.

National Ethnographic Museum celebrates its 120-year history

The National Ethnographic Museum, which is part of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, offers a true journey through time to mark the 120th anniversary of its founding in 1906. The celebrations are held under the motto "120 Years – 120 Minutes at the NEM," providing visitors with even more opportunities to explore the traditions, customs and way of life of Bulgarians across different eras and regions. To mark the anniversary, the museum is offering free admission every weekend from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at its premises located at 1 Knyaz Alexander I Street.

museum’s entire 120-year history has been quite eventful. Its

on Sofia.

majority of the collection was destroyed or suffered water damage,
but
part of it
was saved. In 1953, the museum moved into its current premises—the
former Royal Palace.

have been here ever since—that makes 70 years in the Palace,"
says Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva, current Director of the Institute
of Ethnology and Folklore Studies with Ethnographic Museum at the
Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS), in a special interview for Radio
Bulgaria.
Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva
PHOTO BGNES
In addition to offering a chance to explore diverse collections, the National Ethnographic Museum (NEM) invites friends and enthusiasts to a series of special events, exhibitions and initiatives dedicated to Bulgaria’s rich cultural and historical heritage. Program highlights include the temporary exhibition "Moving to the Countryside" and the exhibition "The Starry Sky: Mythology and Science”. A bilingual album accompanying the latter is also available.
PHOTO BGNES
The
exhibition "The Starry Sky – Mythology and Science"

the
choices made by those who decide to leave the city for small

habits.
PHOTO BGNES
The idea behind the commemoration of the 120th anniversary of the National Ethnographic Museum is to present the entire cultural heritage to the general public in an accessible, engaging and interactive way. "When we speak about culture and ethnographic museums, we often primarily think of jewellery, ceramics, and architecture, yet ethnography is actually much more than this. It is linked to people, communities and culture. It is precisely culture that embodies the link between our nation's past and present," Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva says.
PHOTO BGNES
Since its creation, one of the country's oldest museums has been dedicated to the traditional culture of Bulgarians and the communities living in Bulgaria. "It is interesting to see how the museum has shifted its focus over the years. Thanks to the long-standing efforts of various researchers, artists, and museum staff, we have amassed the richest collection in Bulgaria," Mila Maeva says.
PHOTO National Ethnographic Museum - BAS
"We plan to significantly enrich our anniversary program over the coming months. We aim at attracting a diverse audience, including children, students, young people, as well as people who have never visited our museum before. We want to make it better known and more visible. Our goal is not merely to showcase our rich collection or host various events but we aim to go further by opening our halls as a space for interaction and engagement with our cultural heritage, which is vast," the director of NEM said in conclusion.

Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role

Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role
Court also acquits Dow Jones on the charge of dismissal over Selina Cheng’s leadership role with the Hong Kong Journalists Association.
A Hong Kong court has convicted Dow Jones for trying to deter a journalist from taking a union role, but also acquitted the publisher on the charge of dismissal over the role, in a case that raised concerns about media freedom in the city.
Selina Cheng, who was fired by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) in July 2024, had accused the newspaper’s publisher Dow Jones of unlawfully terminating her employment over her role chairing the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) and of trying to prevent her from standing for a union position.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Hong Kong appeals court overturns Jimmy Lai’s fraud conviction
- list 2 of 3Jimmy Lai sentenced: What happened to other HK pro-democracy protesters?
- list 3 of 3Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai sentenced to 20 years in prison
The court found the company guilty on Thursday of trying to prevent Cheng’s right to run for the union chairmanship.
However, the judge sided with Dow Jones’ argument that she was made redundant because of corporate restructuring, and not due to her role as HKJA chair.
The right to take part in a trade union is protected by Hong Kong’s labour laws. An employer found guilty on “prevent or deter” charges could be fined up to 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,755).
“If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters,” Cheng told reporters outside the court after the ruling.
The judge said the company’s requirement that Cheng seek prior permission to take a union role was an “unjustified deterrent” of her rights.
Dow Jones said it disagreed with the ruling and was evaluating next steps.
“The Wall Street Journal has a long and proud history as an employer in Hong Kong. Throughout that time, we have remained deeply respectful of its labour laws and supportive of our employees’ rights, while publishing excellent, impartial journalism about the region,” a spokesperson said.
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.
Cheng launched a private prosecution last year for illegal termination, after filing a complaint with the Labour Department that did not result in a prosecution.
Founded in 1968, the HKJA is Hong Kong’s longest-established journalists’ organisation and one of the last remaining groups advocating for media rights in the city.
Although Hong Kong was once known for its independent news outlets, media freedom has come under strain and many outlets have disbanded since Beijing imposed a 2020 national security law following sometimes violent pro-democracy protests, according to international rankings and HKJA surveys.

A historical view of the defenders through the prism of the continuity of the Ukrainian military tradition, a master class on Cossack songs, as well as the development of lessons for high school. After the webinar, teachers will have ready-made materials, two songs for working with children, and new ideas on how to talk about the Pokrova through the prism of traditional culture," – said Gnat Korobko.
Participation in the webinar is free, but you must register in advance at the link: https://forms.gle/tNcZr1Y81qMSHTW16.
"Know Your Ukraine" is an online course about Ukrainian traditional culture that introduces children and adults to the main holidays of the annual calendar cycle. This is a joint project of the Kolo Charitable Foundation, the National Center of Folk Culture "Ivan Honchar Museum", patron Gnat Korobko, and the EdEra educational platform.

Zelenskyy In Canada Seeking Support Amid Destructive Russian Attacks

PAVLOHRAD, Ukraine -- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ottawa will provide Ukraine with air defense support as he visited Canada in an attempt to shore up support from the country's allies amid deadly Russian drone and missile attacks.
"This is a very important package of air defense," he told reporters on September 10, adding that Canada will also provide aid to Ukraine's energy industry. He provided no further details.
The Ukrainian president arrived in Canada's western city of Calgary a night earlier after a visit to Norway for the funeral of King Harald V and talks on air defense support.
His plane was delayed on its way to Oslo after an alert in Moldova that a Russian drone had entered the nearby airspace.
"Canada remains one of our closest partners," Zelenskyy wrote on X after his arrival in Canada. "We value the support of the Canadian people and the decisions that help Ukraine to withstand the war and to protect our people."
Zelenskyy's visit came as Russia continued to launch intense air attacks on Ukraine, with fresh strikes reported on September 10 in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Mykolayiv regions.
At least 10 people were killed in Russian strikes across these regions, while more than 100 others were injured, including children.
In Dnipro, the capital of the east-central Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian forces struck a food-industry facility that had already been damaged in an earlier attack the same day, while in neighboring Pavlohrad, a shopping area and cars caught fire after an evening strike.
"There was a hit in central Pavlohrad by a Shahed drone," RFE/RL Ukrainian Service correspondent Roman Pahulych reported from the aftermath site, adding that another strike followed less than a minute later.
"There are shopping premises here. There was heavy traffic here -- a bus stop is located here," he added, as he filmed devastating images showing ruined buildings and burnt-out cars.
Farther east, in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region, regional authorities said Russian forces had struck four times, with impacts reported near educational facilities and a multistory residential building.
Russian air strikes also hit the southern port city of Mykolayiv, as well as civilian and industrial infrastructure in the surrounding region.
Moscow has stepped up its air war in recent months, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have taken advantage of Ukraine's dwindling air defenses. Among other targets, the attacks have hit Ukraine's power grid ahead of the upcoming fifth wartime winter.
Since the beginning of its invasion, Russia has sought to paralyze Ukraine's energy system, leaving thousands of people across the country with no heating and electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued its own long-range strikes inside Russia.
Overnight on September 9-10, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala in Daghestan. Elsewhere, Russian authorities reported one person died and two were injured in another attack in the Voronezh region. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.
The intensifying exchange of strikes has put air defense and the protection of Ukraine's energy infrastructure at the center of Zelenskyy's trip.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on September 9 that Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."
"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," the statement said, adding that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."
Renewed Diplomatic Efforts
As fighting remains intense, Zelenskyy's latest international trip comes amid renewed US-mediated efforts to find a path toward ending the war.
After months of stalled talks aimed at ending the conflict, US special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv and Moscow over the past weekend in what appeared to be the latest attempt to narrow the gap between the two sides' negotiating terms.
Days later, Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump, a conversation the Kremlin described as "constructive and quite frank."
"We had a great conversation. He [Putin] is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters on September 9, adding, "These are two people that are tired of fighting."
Putin has given no sign he is ready for a cease-fire unless Kyiv makes major concessions it has rejected, including ceding territory in the eastern Donbas region that Russian troops have been unable to take by force.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov suggested Putin told Trump that an immediate cease-fire could be secured if the United States would end all support for Kyiv.
On September 9, the Financial Times reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a bigger role in US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, citing unnamed sources the paper said indicated the roles of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner might be scaled back to make room for Ratcliffe.
In a post on X, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called the FT story "incorrect and ridiculous." CIA spokeswoman Liz Lyons, also on X, wrote: "This reporting is false."
Witkoff and Kushner have led the talks with Moscow and Kyiv for the last year and a half.
According to the FT, officials close to Ratcliffe have told their European peers that in addition to maintaining contact with intelligence agencies in both Russia and Ukraine, the CIA director would now play a more active role in shuttle diplomacy.

AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton says 10% risk of human extinction from AI 'not unreasonable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:42 UTC
19:45:42 KST

Büşra Nur Çakmak
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Nobel laureate and artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton said estimating a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction within the next decade is "not unreasonable," adding to a growing chorus of warnings from researchers working at the forefront of the technology.
Hinton, often described as the "Godfather of AI," told BBC's Newsnight on Wednesday that humanity has never before created entities that could potentially become more intelligent than humans, making the risks difficult to predict.
"We've never created beings that may soon be smarter than us. We don't know what's going to happen," Hinton said.
Asked whether there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans, potentially within a decade, Hinton said it would be "very foolish" to assume the risk was as low as 1%.
"A 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate to me. But nobody really knows how to give a sensible estimate," he said.
Hinton warned that advanced AI would not necessarily need to control physical systems to pose a severe threat.
"The first thing to realize is it doesn't even have to be able to act in the real world to cause devastation," he said, adding that AI could create "complete chaos just by talking to people."
He said highly capable systems could also be used to design dangerous biological or computer viruses and conduct devastating cyberattacks.
Hinton's warning comes amid similar concerns raised by researchers working at leading AI companies.
Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who has previously worked on foundational AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday, accusing both companies of racing toward self-improving superintelligence despite the potential risks.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon said.
He also warned that people developing advanced AI systems privately harbor fears that the technology could pose an existential threat by the end of the decade.
Evan Hubinger, who leads Alignment Science at Anthropic, publicly backed Coxon's concerns, saying Tuesday that he personally believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Hubinger stressed that current AI systems pose little immediate danger, saying his main concern is the potential emergence of superintelligence through recursive self-improvement, where AI systems could autonomously create increasingly powerful successors.
Hinton stressed that researchers need to determine how to build advanced AI systems that do not develop goals harmful to humanity.
"We have to figure out how to design it so that it won't want to," he added.

Ukrainian sea drones injure dozens in Russian resort city – officials
Nearly 30 people, including two minors, were injured overnight after Ukraine launched naval kamikaze drones at the Russian Black Sea resort city of Sochi, according to local officials.
The Russian Investigative Committee said the strikes deliberately targeted civilian infrastructure and were part of a pattern of Ukrainian terrorist attacks. The city authorities subsequently closed several beaches that were damaged in the raid.

Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin visited the victims on Thursday morning and said their condition was stable, with doctors giving positive assessments of their recovery prospects.

The drone alert in Sochi lasted roughly 12 hours. An aerial attack conducted alongside the naval raid also disrupted air traffic across Krasnodar Region, delaying almost 60 flights.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously threatened airlines operating in Russian airspace, suggesting their aircraft would not be safe because of Ukrainian drone attacks. Moscow said the remarks amounted to confirmation that Kiev was deliberately employing terrorist tactics.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces intercepted 448 Ukrainian long-range aerial drones overnight but did not comment on the naval drone attack.
Kiev has regularly targeted the southern Russian region. Drone attacks on the port city of Novorossiysk the previous night killed four people, including a minor, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
