‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.
It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.
“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.
Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.
The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.
“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.
“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.
Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.
In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.
Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”
Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.
The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.
“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.
Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.
The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.
Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”

RNLI steps up security after abuse by far-right agitators over small boat rescues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:44:13 UTC
19:44:13 KST

The RNLI is increasing security after a backlash from far-right agitators over the lifeboat charity’s involvement in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing them to UK shores.
Volunteers have been told by the charity’s bosses that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they feel this might put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.
There has been a heavy security presence around RNLI bases on the south coast of England over the last few days, with police and private guards monitoring some areas.
At the charity’s headquarters in Poole, barriers have placed around a memorial sculpture to RNLI volunteers who lost their lives and around a rose bed to mark the 200th anniversary of the charity. A viewing platform into the headquarters has been closed off.
The RNLI has said it will continue to rescue asylum seekers in the Channel despite the intimidation from far-right activists after its involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth.
But after Sunday’s protest, the RNLI’s chief executive emailed volunteers to say security processes were being reviewed.
Volunteers were asked to challenge people near lifeboat stations if they did not have ID, but advised not to engage with members of the public if they felt uncomfortable.
Staff at the Portsmouth lifeboat station close to where the asylum seekers landed on Sunday have been approached by members of the public and asked to explain the RNLI’s actions.
The RNLI has said workers have been subjected to “online and physical abuse” and there have been “baseless” rumours circulating that the charity had housed asylum seekers or moved them to secret locations after helping them to shore.
Three police forces have been involved in protecting RNLI volunteers, staff and buildings. Dorset police have been helping keep the headquarters secure while Hampshire officers have patrolled RNLI stations in Portsmouth.
Sussex police were investigating “offensive and threatening commentary towards RNLI volunteers”. Images of some RNLI crew members who were apparently involved in the operation on Sunday were published on social media with the accusation that they were complicit in an “invasion” of the UK.
About 50 protesters, including members of the Poole Patriots and Hampshire Resistance attended a demonstration outside the RNLI’s headquarters in Poole on Wednesday.
Protest leaders handed out rape alarms to women, claiming they were at risk from men brought into the UK by the RNLI, and called for people to stop donating to the charity.
An RNLI spokesperson said: “Given the unacceptable abuse our people have faced, and with protest activity taking place at RNLI locations, we have taken action to help ensure the safety and wellbeing of our volunteers and staff.
“As well as enhancing security at RNLI locations, we issued guidance to our people earlier this week on how to keep themselves safe. This guidance included how to manage potentially challenging interactions with members of the public, and where appropriate, choosing not to wear RNLI-branded clothing.
“Our people have been reminded that their safety comes first, and they are encouraged to report relevant incidents internally and, where appropriate, to the police.”

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ comes to auction at Sotheby’s, may fetch up to $377,000

- The black silk gown, designed by Christina Stambolian, was worn the same night Prince Charles admitted infidelity, symbolising Diana's confident public statement.
- The dress will be exhibited in London, Hong Kong, and Geneva before the auction, marking its first public display in nearly 30 years.
AI generated
The “revenge dress” worn by the late Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1994 is up for auction at Sotheby’s for the first time in nearly three decades.
The black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian is estimated to fetch as much as £220,000 (S$377,050) when it goes on sale on Dec 9 during Sotheby’s Luxury Week in New York, the auction house said on Sept 10.
Diana wore the dress in June 1994 as she arrived at the Serpentine Gallery in London for a fund-raising dinner. It gained notoriety because the then Prince Charles (now King Charles III) – from whom she had been separated for nearly two years but not yet divorced – was widely expected to say in a national television interview broadcast that same evening that he had been unfaithful to her.
According to a later documentary, her decision to wear the dress was a last-minute one after initially setting aside a more traditional Valentino outfit. “She wanted to look a million dollars,” her former stylist Anna Harvey said on the programme, according to Vogue. “And she did.”
Stambolian’s off-the-shoulder dress features an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train. It will make its first public appearance at Sotheby’s in London during Fashion Week from Sept 17 to 21, followed by further exhibitions in Hong Kong and Geneva, before it goes to New York for the auction.
The dress was previously sold at auction in 1997, according to Sotheby’s, without giving details.
In 2023, a black, ballerina-length velvet gown owned by Diana was sold at Julien’s Auctions in Hollywood for US$1,148,080 (S$1.45 million), 11 times its estimated price.
Charles and Diana were divorced in 1996 and she died in a car crash in Paris the following year at age 36. BLOOMBERG

The Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement has dismissed as “empty talk” an apology posted by Adidas over an ad campaign featuring an amputee Israeli soldier.
Speaking to Anadolu, BDS co-founder Omar Barghouti said: "The fact that Palestine is home to the highest number of child amputees in the world makes this marketing choice even more obscene; it celebrates the very instrument of that suffering."
The German sportswear brand has faced growing criticism and calls for a boycott after choosing retired Israeli soldier Shalev Biton as the face of its “single shoe service” campaign.
Critics have called the campaign tone-deaf, saying it ignores the large number of Palestinians who have lost limbs as a result of Israeli attacks on the Gaza Strip.
"It's no wonder that an immediate and organic global boycott took off," said Barghouti, a Palestinian human rights activist and recipient of the 2017 Gandhi Peace Award.
"This isn't Adidas just being tone-deaf or insensitive; it is an absolute affront to the Palestinians whose loved ones have been killed by Israel, and who have lost limbs to Israeli attacks," he said.
Commenting on Adidas' apology, which was posted on a regional account rather than through a broader corporate statement, Barghouti said: "Now Adidas is in damage control mode. Their so-called apology is empty talk.
“Those affected by this image are millions of Palestinians living under Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza, its illegal military occupation of Palestinian territory, and its decades-long settler-colonial apartheid regime."
Barghouti said the company's decision to feature the soldier “normalizes the violence of an occupying army and profits from the normalization of apartheid.”
Barghouti called on Adidas to remove the Israeli soldier from all promotional materials and channels immediately and establish a company-wide ethical policy governing partnerships, spokespersons, ambassadors and testimonials.
"Until then, we reiterate our full support for holding Adidas accountable via global boycotts," he said.  
How BDS works
Barghouti said the BDS movement advocates boycotting companies, services and institutions it considers complicit in Israel's actions against Palestinians, based on clear criteria.
"BDS targets complicity, not identity. It targets institutions, not individuals," he said.
He said boycotts seek to exert financial pressure on corporations.
"Boycotts apply pressure on corporations, for instance, by speaking their language: profit.
“If a corporation faces financial, legal, or reputational risks due to its complicity in Israel's crimes, it is more likely to end its involvement, as our long experience proves."
Barghouti stressed, however, that boycotts are only one part of the movement's strategy.
"BDS also calls for divestment and other forms of nonviolent pressure as well as lawful, targeted sanctions," he said.
He said the three strategies -- boycotts, divestment and sanctions -- are designed to reinforce one another by applying pressure on institutions, corporations and governments.
"With these three tactics we can, and will, achieve our goal of freedom, justice and equality for Palestinians everywhere," he said.

Swiss firms ‘in line for $2bn US tariff refunds’
Swiss companies could receive as much as $2 billion in United States tariff reimbursements, according to economists at UBS bank.
The biggest potential refunds for goods exported between April 2025 and February 2026 relate due on precision and medical instruments as well as watches, UBS said on Thursday. The remainder is primarily for coffee, machinery and electrical equipment.
The reimbursements are due after the tariff regime initially imposed by President Donald Trump was struck down by the Supreme Court. UBS cautioned that exporters may not receive the full benefit because refunds formally accrue to importers.
+ US tax yo-yo blurs situation for Swiss companies
Looking ahead, the bank expects that headline US tariffs on Switzerland will eventually rise to 15% from the current 12.5%, in line with the framework trade deal both countries agreed in November.
Economist Meret Muegeli highlighted that effective levies are well below that level – currently around 6% – because pharmaceuticals, Switzerland’s biggest export, are largely exempt.
UBS analysts also said Switzerland’s outsized 1.5% growth in the second quarter probably overstates the economy’s underlying strength, though it still points to an improvement.
+ ‘We’ll have to live with US tariffs,’ warns SECO head
“That seems somewhat exaggerated and not fully reflecting reality,” said Alessandro Bee. “But we are seeing signs of a recovery.”
For 2027, UBS expects unemployment to decline and inflation to remain below 1%.
He sees the Swiss National Bank deliver its first interest-rate increase around the middle of the year, though there’s a risk that policymakers start raising borrowing costs earlier. Officials meet for their third rate decision of the year later this month.

It also said the nature, timing and course of the investigation in the case were not inspired by political vendetta, reported PTI.

The charges include corruption, criminal conspiracy and cheating against Lalu Prasad, while Rabri Devi and Tejashwi face conspiracy and cheating charges.The case stems from alleged irregularities in the award of contracts to operate two IRCTC hotels. The CBI has alleged that the tender process was manipulated and conditions were tweaked to favour Sujata Hotels during Lalu Prasad's tenure as railway minister. The ED has alleged that the transactions were part of a larger money-laundering conspiracy.The accused have pleaded not guilty and the case will now proceed to trial. The framing of charges and the court's observations at this stage do not amount to a finding of guilt.

It follows a winding legal saga that has seen the exact boundaries of Missouri’s congressional districts for the 2026 election kept in protracted limbo, with election day less than two months out.

Last week, the Missouri supreme court ruled that the new maps weren’t valid until they were put to a public referendum. That meant the state’s congressional districts would revert to their 2022 borders ahead of the midterms. Zaluzhny: lack of technology, funding prevents Ukraine from seizing initiative from Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:40:51 EEST
19:40:51 KST

Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience, but state funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited, which is why private investment can and must become a mutually beneficial solution for both sides, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny notes.
"Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience. No other country can offer more relevant experience for developing new arms, modernization, and tactics for their application. However, the lack of technology and funding prevents seizing the initiative from Russia and its partners," Zaluzhnyi said during a speech at the Defence & Resilience Tech Scale Up Showcase in London, the text of which was published in his column on the Interfax-Ukraine agency's website on Thursday.
He called on Ukraine's partners to increase financial and technological investments in arms production in Ukraine, not only to reduce Russia's military potential, but also to strengthen their own defense capabilities.
"State funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited. Therefore, private investments can and must become a beneficial solution for both sides. Creating clear mechanisms for cooperation with Great Britain at the institutional level will help attract private capital, technologies, and ultimately create new markets and develop long-term cooperation between the defense industries of Ukraine and its partners," the diplomat said.
Zaluzhnyi stated that Ukraine has gained significant experience in drone production, but the component base, and especially its production, currently remains outside Ukraine, which precludes possibilities for scaling and modernization in the long term, "where marketing gives way to strategy and the outline of victory finally becomes visible." "Even now, these investments are vital in countering urgent threats such as ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
He noted that achieving victory or a dignified peace requires systemic impact on Russia's ability to continue the war, rather than isolated technological solutions.
"Systemic impact means implementing strategies to achieve the main goal: victory over the enemy. Naturally, building such a systemic impact is possible only with appropriate strategies. These strategies must be based on implementing financial and technological policies that enable producing today what is needed tomorrow, or better yet, the day after tomorrow. And what is needed today should be taken from storage facilities as something produced yesterday. Defense production must be part of a war strategy, not the other way around, where war is made to justify someone's promises and profits. Only in this way is it possible to seize the initiative, impose one's will on the enemy, and demand terms from them," Zaluzhny concluded.

OpenAI urges mandatory US safety rules as AI systems grow more autonomous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:39:24 UTC
19:39:24 KST

Dilara Hamit
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
OpenAI urged the US Congress on Wednesday to establish mandatory national safety requirements for the most advanced artificial intelligence systems, warning that voluntary commitments were no longer sufficient as AI capabilities rapidly advance.
"We want to work with Congress on mandatory, capability-based national AI safety regulation," Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane wrote in a company blog post.  
“The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments," he added.  
OpenAI called for capability-based regulation that could evolve with the technology, including common testing standards, independent safety assessments, stronger cybersecurity protections and mandatory reporting of serious incidents.
The requirements should apply to the small number of well-resourced laboratories developing frontier systems rather than to startups, smaller developers or researchers working with less capable models, the company said.
OpenAI also called for mechanisms to monitor progress toward recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems would independently help create increasingly capable generations of artificial intelligence.
The company said fully autonomous recursive self-improvement was not taking place and should not be pursued unless it could be done safely.
AI was already accelerating parts of the research used to develop and align new models, however, with some agents completing tasks that would take skilled researchers several days, it added.
OpenAI said governments should establish shared safety thresholds for determining when AI development should be slowed or stopped, while preserving meaningful human oversight.
The company said it would halt the development or deployment of systems that presented unacceptable risks and could not be sufficiently safeguarded.
It also advocated for compatible international standards for measuring AI capabilities, managing risks and determining when development should be restricted, arguing that failures involving frontier systems could have consequences beyond the countries where they were created. 
OpenAI backs California legislation
OpenAI also announced its support for four AI-related bills in California, saying it would continue backing state-level safeguards until Congress adopted a national framework.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed two of the measures, SB 813 and AB 1405, into law on Wednesday.
SB 813 requires the California Government Operations Agency to establish a process for designating qualified independent organizations capable of assessing AI risks. AB 1405 requires the agency to establish a registry for AI auditors and introduces independence, transparency and accountability standards for their work.
The two other bills endorsed by OpenAI have passed the state legislature and await action by the governor.
SB 1119 would introduce child-safety requirements for companion chatbots, including age assurance, risk assessments, independent audits, parental controls and safeguards against harmful content.
AB 1864 would require gene-synthesis providers and manufacturers of benchtop synthesis equipment to comply with federal screening standards intended to reduce biological risks.
OpenAI acknowledged that it had not previously supported some of the bills but said it reconsidered its position following recent advances in AI capabilities. 
Agents accessed external systems during tests
The policy call follows a series of incidents in which advanced AI agents gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
OpenAI disclosed in July that models being tested with reduced cybersecurity restrictions exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to escape an isolated evaluation environment and obtain access to the open internet.
The agents subsequently accessed production infrastructure belonging to AI platform Hugging Face in an attempt to obtain answers for a cybersecurity benchmark.
OpenAI’s investigation found that agents had established unauthorized communication channels, including a persistent message board, allowing otherwise separate agents to exchange information, coordinate their efforts and divide tasks.
The company said the incident did not affect OpenAI customer data, product functionality or availability.
AI developer Anthropic separately disclosed Wednesday that it had identified a fourth incident involving one of its Claude models gaining unauthorized access to a real third-party system during testing.
Anthropic said all four incidents occurred during cybersecurity evaluations conducted in a third-party environment. The company said a configuration problem had left the systems connected to the internet and that the models were running without the safeguards normally used in publicly available versions.

How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:38:53 UTC
19:38:53 KST

How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach
Long-range Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s key gas plants, raising questions about the conflict’s next phase.
Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border, on Wednesday, signalling that Ukraine has further developed its military capabilities as the Russia-Ukraine war continues through its fifth year.
Unconfirmed videos circulating on social media show large clouds of thick, dark smoke and fire at the Novy Urengoy plant in western Siberia, recorded from a distance. Dmitry Artyukhov, the governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region, wrote on Telegram that the drone attacks had been intercepted and “debris from the drone caused a fire upon impact”. There have been no reports of deaths or injuries.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Zelenskyy’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone on way to Oslo, Norwegian PM says
- list 2 of 3Trump says Putin wants to make a deal to end Ukraine war
- list 3 of 3Russian strikes kill 11 in Ukraine as Kyiv targets gas plants in Arctic
Since the start of the war, Ukraine has dramatically increased its capacity for the mass production of low-cost drones and has more recently been specifically targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure and logistical hubs.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the latest long-range attack “completely justified” on social media. It came just days after special United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv with new proposals to end the war, although no specific details were shared on the new proposals.
While attacks on Russia’s and Ukraine’s capitals were halted during the three-day visit earlier this week, they immediately resumed following their departure.
But what does this new, long-range capability on Ukraine’s side mean for the next phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war?
What do we know about the Ukrainian drones used in the strike?
The Ukrainian Armed Forces says it hit two critical Russian gas processing plants, in Novy Urengoy and Purovsky district, with FP-1 drones produced by Fire Point, a Ukrainian company specialising in the production of long-range drones.
The pink FP-1 drone – Fire Point FP-1 UAV – is about 6 metres (20ft) wide and can travel at 140-180km (87-112 miles) per hour. It costs less than $60,000 to produce each drone, an amount that is considered low.
The furthest an FP-1 drone had travelled before the Novy Urengoy attack was in July, when it hit an oil refinery in the city of Omsk in southwestern Siberia, about 2,500km (1,550 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
How significant are these attacks?
The Kremlin’s envoy to the Urals, Artem Zhoga, said Wednesday’s attack by Ukraine was the first to reach the Arctic.
The targets were two Russian gas processing plants in the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky districts of Yamalo-Nenets.
The Yamalo-Nenets region hosts about 80 percent of Russia’s natural gas production and two-thirds of its gas reserves, as well as 13 percent of the country’s oil reserves. Gas reserves in this region stand at 26.5 trillion cubic metres; global gas needs stand at about 4.2 trillion cubic metres per year.
Novy Urengoy is known as the gas capital of Russia due to its vital production for the Russian gas and oil industry.
The ability of Ukraine to reach targets here means it could unleash much more damage on Russia’s economy, which depends heavily on energy exports for income – especially as Russia has been under international economic and trade sanctions since it first invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Videos of Russian citizens queueing for petrol were shared widely on social media earlier this year, despite Russia holding one of the world’s largest reserves of gas and oil.
How will this affect Europe?
The attack on Russian gas infrastructure could have serious consequences for the European Union as member states heavily depend on supplies of Russian gas.
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the EU implemented sanctions on Russian oil and gas and began to invest in efforts to become less reliant on Russian energy.
But the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which previously moved about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, means that Europe is once again struggling for gas imports.
Gas prices in Europe rose above 80 euros ($93) per megawatt-hour this week, the highest price since 2023, according to the Dutch TTF, a wholesale market that sets the price benchmark for European gas.
Current gas reserves in Europe stand at about 65 percent, compared with 80 percent last year, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Dwindling reserves are currently a particular worry for the continent as it heads into winter.
EU member states were urged to start storing gas in March, shortly after the US and Israel started the war on Iran. But the European Court of Auditors released a report on Wednesday stating that member states have not invested enough in other energy sources to be able to phase out Russian gas, and that the bloc’s “crisis‑response objectives often cannot be demonstrated”.

Ukraine’s GrimTech Develops LA-80 Counterpart to Russia’s Molniya Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:38:22 UTC
19:38:22 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine’s GrimTech Develops LA-80 Counterpart to Russia’s Molniya Drone
Ukrainian defense company GrimTech is finalizing the development of the Grim LA-80, a fixed-wing strike drone designed to carry payloads of up to 5 kilograms and operate at ranges of up to 80 kilometers, Militarnyi reported on September 10.
According to the outlet, the company representative presented details of the new system during the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland. The drone is structurally similar to Russia’s Molniya-type UAVs, while its developers are focusing on combining extended range and payload capacity with a relatively low production cost.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Grim LA-80 is primarily intended to strike stationary targets behind Russian lines, including fortifications, dugouts, protective shelters, and military equipment that remains in fixed positions for extended periods.
According to Militarnyi, the drone’s range varies depending on the payload. With a payload of around 2 kilograms, the LA-80 could theoretically fly up to 100 kilometers, although the reliability of the communications link remains the main limiting factor at longer distances.
The company is considering several options for controlling the drone, including a conventional radio link, digital video transmission, and Starlink satellite communications. GrimTech views satellite connectivity as the preferred option for maintaining more stable control over longer distances.
For serial production, the LA-80’s fuselage is expected to be manufactured using vacuum forming, a process intended to reduce weight, increase durability, and facilitate faster production. The wings will be made from foam, while aluminum tubes and plywood will also be incorporated into the airframe.
GrimTech does not manufacture warheads for the LA-80, with munitions instead expected to be installed by Ukrainian military personnel. The drone’s payload compartment is being designed to accommodate different types of munitions, including those with relatively large diameters. The configuration will also allow the position of the payload to be adjusted to maintain the aircraft’s balance.
“We are finalizing and refining the product to ensure its quality, and we are working to produce a test batch that can be sent to the front for testing and field trials,” GrimTech representatives told Militarnyi.
About Molniya
Russia’s Molniya drone first appeared in November 2024 as a low-cost, mass-producible strike UAV designed primarily for frontline operations.
Built like a small aircraft, the Molniya uses inexpensive materials such as plywood, plastic, and cardboard. Its simple construction contributes to a relatively low radar signature, making conventional detection more difficult.
Powered by an electric motor, the drone can carry a payload of around 3–5 kilograms, fly up to 30–40 kilometers, and reach speeds of up to 90 km/h. Twin-motor variants have also been developed.
With an estimated cost of just $300–$400 per unit, Russian forces can deploy Molniya drones in large numbers, relying on their low price to make mass attacks economically viable.
The Grim LA-80 is one of several new Ukrainian defense systems presented at the MSPO exhibition. Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom also unveiled a new surface-to-air missile intended for modernized Strela-10 systems and the newly developed Desna air defense system.
The RK-2PZ missile is based on the Barrier anti-tank guided missile, which was developed from the R-2 missile family.

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Hit 2,379 Russian Targets in One Day, Including Aircraft and Drone Launch Sites

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Hit 2,379 Russian Targets in One Day, Including Aircraft and Drone Launch Sites
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) struck or destroyed 2,379 Russian targets over the past 24 hours, including personnel, drone launch sites, electronic warfare systems, and aircraft, the force reported.
According to the USF, its units struck 437 Russian personnel during the reporting period, with 193 reported killed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes also targeted 51 drone launch sites and 26 radar, electronic intelligence, electronic warfare, and communications systems. Ukrainian drone units also hit 191 vehicles and 13 artillery systems.
A significant share of the targets were Russian unmanned aerial vehicles. The USF reported striking or destroying 379 drones, including copter- and fixed-wing-type UAVs, as well as Shahed and Gerbera drones.
Two Russian aircraft or helicopters were also among the targets hit during the day, according to the statement. The USF did not specify the types of aircraft involved or the extent of the damage.
The latest figures add to a broader campaign by Ukraine’s drone forces targeting Russian personnel and military equipment. Between September 1 and 9, USF units reported striking a total of 18,580 Russian targets, including 3,726 personnel.
The campaign comes amid continued Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian civilians, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning that Moscow must face consequences for its strikes.
Kyiv came under a Russian drone attack on September 9, when a drone struck a residential high-rise, injuring six people, including a pregnant woman.
Fragments of Shahed drones and shattered glass were scattered around the residential buildings following the attack. A response headquarters was subsequently established at the site to assist residents.
“Moscow must not enter the winter believing that its missile and drone terror will simply go unpunished. Aggression must be stopped here and now so that it does not spread further. It is important that sanctions and support for Ukraine work effectively toward precisely this goal,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine has also increasingly used long-range drones to target high-value Russian military assets far from the frontline. In separate operations over a six-week period, Ukrainian forces damaged two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers at the Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region, targeting aircraft that Russia is no longer able to produce.
The Telegraph reported on September 9 that both operations were carried out by a specialized long-range unit of Ukraine’s Security Service. Satellite imagery shows that one Tu-95 lost its tail section in a July 19 strike, while another sustained significant damage to its right wing in a second attack on August 28.

Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike

- Category

Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
Ukrainian drones struck the Makhachkala International Commercial Seaport on Russia’s Caspian coast overnight on September 10, hitting a strategically important transport hub linked to maritime traffic with Iran roughly 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
The Ukrainian OSINT community Exilenova+ published footage of the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Makhachkala reported explosions around the port during the overnight raid, marking the first known Ukrainian strike on port infrastructure in the city.
The target is particularly significant because Makhachkala serves as one of Russia’s principal maritime gateways on the Caspian Sea and maintains extensive shipping links with Iran.
The port has been used by vessels traveling between Russia and Iranian ports, including routes associated with the movement of military cargo and components for Iranian-designed drones supplied to Moscow.
Cargo arriving through Makhachkala can then move farther into Russia by road, rail and air, making the port part of a broader logistics network connecting Iranian suppliers with Russian military infrastructure.
Makhachkala is also Russia’s only ice-free deepwater commercial port on the Caspian Sea, allowing it to operate year-round.
The facility handles both liquid and dry cargo, with oil and petroleum products playing an increasingly important role in its operations.
Cargo volumes have surged during Russia’s war against Ukraine. During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, an increase of 42.5% compared with the same period last year.
Oil accounted for more than 2.08 million tons of that total, rising nearly 50% year over year.
The acceleration was already evident earlier in 2026. Cargo turnover reached 1.4 million metric tons during the first four months of the year and climbed to 2.11 million tons by the end of June, roughly 50% above the same period in 2025.
Liquid cargo drove most of that expansion. During the first half of the year alone, the port handled nearly 1.57 million metric tons of oil and other liquid cargo.
Previously, Ukraine’s Security Service used long-range drones to strike multiple military and logistical targets across Russia overnight on July 25, including maritime targets in the Caspian Sea.
Ukrainian drones struck several targets in the Caspian Sea, including the Filanovsky offshore oil platform, the sanctioned cargo vessel Port Olya 2, the dry cargo ship Begey, and a Russian Project 12418 Molniya missile boat.
Ukrainian military intelligence further reported that Begey had been used to transport ammunition, artillery shells, body armor, and helmets from Iran across the Caspian Sea. During voyages between Iranian and Russian ports, the vessel’s crew allegedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to Ukrainian authorities.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine carried out a drone attack against a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Mediterranean Sea, striking the vessel 12 times as it allegedly transported Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia.

Of the five tankers targeted by the U.S. military, three are linked to Russia’s shadow fleet, V lasiuk says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:35:55 EEST
19:35:55 KST

Of the five tankers targeted by the U.S. military, three are linked to Russia’s shadow fleet, V lasiuk says
Kyiv • UNN
The Kaviz, Charminar and Riesco tankers transported Russian oil and operated in circumvention of sanctions. All three vessels are under sanctions imposed by Ukraine and the U.S.
Three of the five tankers struck by the U.S. military on September 8 have direct ties to Russia’s shadow fleet. Specifically, these are the tankers Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco. They transported Russian oil, called at Russian ports, and were used to operate under sanctions. This was stated by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the President of Ukraine’s Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, for example, Kaviz called at Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk, transported Russian oil, and had a practice of switching off its AIS tracking system. The vessel was linked to Fractal Marine DMCC, a company described as one of the key operators of Russia’s shadow fleet in the first years after the introduction of oil sanctions.
Also, according to him, the vessel Charminar called at Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk, and St. Petersburg. After the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on Fractal Marine, vessels linked to it began to be transferred to other managers, but operations involving Russian oil continued. At the same time, Charminar is linked to a shipping empire controlled by Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani — Hossein Shamkhani (an Iranian oil magnate) — which works simultaneously with Iranian and Russian oil.
Vlasiuk emphasizes that the vessel Riesco clearly demonstrates how this system operates: the tanker transported both Russian and Iranian oil, including through ship-to-ship transfers with other sanctioned tankers.
All three vessels are under sanctions imposed by Ukraine and the United States. Kaviz is also under sanctions imposed by the EU, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Switzerland. The Russian and Iranian shadow fleets intersect through vessels, managers, intermediaries, and oil routes. That is why the response to such vessels must be tough, regardless of whose flag they sail under and whose interests they formally serve. If the shadow fleet helps sanctioned states sell oil and generate revenue, it becomes part of the sanctions-evasion infrastructure. The shadow fleet is increasingly perceived as a real threat rather than as a formal sanctions-compliance issue. For Ukraine, this approach is fundamentally important: sanctions must work not just on paper but physically deprive sanctioned states of the ability to profit from oil and finance the war
We remind you
On Tuesday, the U.S. military destroyed five Iranian tankers carrying crude oil. The U.S. Central Command stated that the strikes were in response to attempts by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to attack a U.S. warship with ballistic missiles.
Over the course of a day, Ukrainian forces struck eight infrastructure facilities in the Russian Federation. In particular, they hit an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Dagestan.

In Ukraine, testing of 5G connectivity is being expanded in Odesa following the launch of pilots in Lviv, Borodianka, Kharkiv and Kyiv, the Ministry of Digital Transformation said Thursday.
According to a statement by the ministry on Telegram, the average 5G speed is 600-700 Mbps, while peak speeds exceed 1 Gbps.
"The technology takes on part of the traffic and unloads LTE networks, so even in places with large crowds of people, connectivity remains stable," the Ministry of Digital Transformation explained.
Deputy Minister of Digital Transformation Stanislav Prybytko said on Facebook that the ministry had received the first results of the nationwide pilot project: in particular, 340 5G base stations are currently operating, and 3.85 million unique users have already used the technology.

Prybytko said that going forward, the ministry will continue preparing Ukraine for further scaling of the technology after martial law is lifted.
Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest telecom operator, added in a press release that 5G coverage in Odesa will include the historic center, Primorsky Boulevard, the Potemkin Stairs and adjacent areas.
According to the operator, during testing, the maximum data transmission speed on the 5G network exceeded 2.4 Gbps.
In turn, LLC lifecell, the third-largest mobile operator, said in a press release that the share of users of 5G devices on its network is growing and currently stands at 35%, while in Odesa it is 41%.
The company specified that average daily traffic consumption by lifecell 5G subscribers is 10 TB, while the maximum data transmission speed reaches 1.5 Gbps.
At the same time, Ukraine's second-largest mobile operator, VF Ukraine (Vodafone Ukraine, VFU), said in a press release that its coverage in Odesa will be available on Primorsky Boulevard, Kobleva Street, Soborna Square, Deribasivska Street, Hretska Square, Starosinna Street, Pryvokzalna Square and Kulikove Pole.
As reported, 5G technology in Ukraine will operate in two frequency bands – 3,500 MHz (to provide high data transmission speeds) and 700 MHz (to expand coverage).
Testing will continue, according to preliminary data, until the end of 2026, Vodafone Ukraine said.

"It is important that the Pantsir systems can be equipped with various types of anti-aircraft missiles, including short-range interceptor missiles. Each vehicle can carry up to 48 short-range interceptor missiles, which allows them to effectively counter an attack by an entire swarm of drones," the holding company noted.
At the ultra-close range, High Precision Systems added, facilities are protected by the TKB-1167 air defense system. It is capable of autonomously detecting and tracking targets, which reduces the operator’s workload and shortens the response time to individual UAVs.
"Thus, the combination of solutions from Rostec’s High Precision Systems Holding makes it possible to form a unified reconnaissance and information network and several firing lines with different ranges and types of weapons," the holding company concluded.

FACTBOX – How El Nino could reach your shopping basket: 5 global commodities at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:07 UTC
19:32:07 KST

- -Drought, heat and shifting rainfall patterns threaten key producing regions
- Rice, sugar, palm oil, cocoa and coffee face supply risks as El Nino strengthens
A powerful El Nino is strengthening in the Pacific Ocean, and the United Nations says its effects are already visible around the world.
El Nino is a natural climate cycle that begins when surface waters in the tropical Pacific warm well above normal. That shift reroutes the atmosphere's jet streams, drying out some farming regions while flooding others.
The UN weather agency, World Meteorological Organization (WMO), said on Sept. 3 that the phenomenon is firmly established and has a nearly 100% chance of continuing through February 2027.
Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador are already suffering erratic weather and drought linked to El Nino, driving severe crop losses across Central America's "Dry Corridor." Indonesia has been battling wildfires that sent haze drifting into Malaysia and the Philippines.
Because so many food crops are grown in a handful of climate-sensitive regions, the ripple effects can show up months later in supermarket prices worldwide.
El Nino does not, however, automatically mean every commodity will become more expensive. The World Bank notes that its effects vary by crop and region, while the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) says global cereal supplies and stocks remain relatively strong despite weather risks.
At the same time, the combination of a strengthening El Nino, extreme weather and existing geopolitical and trade disruptions is already putting pressure on food markets. FAO said its global Food Price Index rose to 133.3 in August, the highest since November 2022.
Here are five commodities analysts and industry groups say are most exposed. 
Rice
Rice is one of the crops most consistently identified as vulnerable to El Nino because much of its production is concentrated in South and Southeast Asia, where the weather pattern can reduce rainfall.
India alone handles about 40% of global rice exports. During the 2023 El Nino, New Delhi banned most non-basmati rice exports as domestic prices climbed, a move exporters said had a bigger impact on world markets than Russia-Ukraine war had on wheat.
This year, the US Department of Agriculture has already flagged a below-average Indian monsoon as a risk to rice, cotton and other crops.
In September, Indian rice export prices reached their highest level in a year amid concerns over below-normal rainfall, while prices in Thailand and Vietnam also rose.
The World Bank estimates that severe El Nino cycles can slash regional rice output by 20% to 50%.
For consumers, lower harvests or tighter exports can raise the cost of rice in importing countries, particularly in Asia and Africa, where the grain is a staple food. 
Sugar
Sugarcane is highly dependent on adequate rainfall, making major producing regions in Asia and South America vulnerable to prolonged heat and dry conditions.
The FAO said its sugar price index jumped 11.9% in August, with weather-related production concerns in Brazil, Europe and Asia contributing to the increase. The agency also cited anticipated El Nino risks to sugar production in Asia.
India, the world's second-largest sugar producer, has already faced pressure on supplies and has restricted exports, while its government has allowed some duty-free imports to help replenish domestic supplies.
A tighter global sugar market can raise costs for products ranging from soft drinks and chocolate to processed foods. 
Palm oil
Indonesia and Malaysia together produce roughly 85% of the world's palm oil, an ingredient found in everything from packaged snacks and instant noodles to soap and cosmetics.
Extended rainfall deficits and high temperatures linked to El Nino reduce fresh fruit bunch yields on oil palm plantations.
Indonesia is already battling wildfires that have sent haze drifting into Malaysia and the Philippines. The country's meteorological agency has separately warned that some provinces, including Kalimantan, Papua and Java, face a real chance of a drier September-to-November period than even the severe 1997 El Nino brought.
Because palm oil is cheaper than other vegetable oils and widely used as a substitute, a supply squeeze tends to push up costs across the broader edible-oils market, not just for palm oil itself. 
Cocoa
Cocoa production is heavily concentrated in West Africa, particularly Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana, leaving the market sensitive to changes in rainfall and temperature.
Cote d'Ivoire, the world's largest cocoa producer, slowed forward sales for its 2026/27 crop in June because of concerns that El Nino could bring drought and reduce yields.
The International Cocoa Organization said in its latest quarterly bulletin that cocoa prices remained highly sensitive to weather and production risks and specifically noted growing concerns about the potential impact of El Nino.
Analysts note the crop is especially vulnerable this cycle because much of West Africa's cocoa acreage is now more than 25 years old, past its most productive age, leaving trees less able to withstand heat and drought stress. 
Coffee
Coffee is vulnerable because major growing areas in Southeast Asia and Latin America can experience heat, drought or excessive rainfall during El Nino events.
Vietnam, the world's second-largest coffee producer and a leading supplier of robusta beans, is particularly important.
USDA says the country accounts for about 17% of global coffee production and warns that El Nino's warmer and drier conditions could reduce coffee productivity and production.

Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:01 UTC
19:32:01 KST

Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
A massive attack by Yemeni’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia has become the first serious test for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement – a defense pact between Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad established just a month ago. We’re no longer talking about a future security architecture in abstract terms. Rather, a very concrete question is being posed: What actions should Saudi Arabia’s allies undertake following a strike on its territory?
According to the Saudi-led coalition, Houthi missiles and drones struck civilian and economic targets in four southern cities. At least 73 people were injured, including women and children. Fires broke out at energy facilities and damaged utility infrastructure; operations at some enterprises were temporarily suspended. The Houthis claimed to have attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Abha, Jizan, and Najran, as well as the King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.
The city of Jizan is of particular significance. Its oil refinery has a capacity of around 400,000 barrels per day and is one of Saudi Arabia’s largest refineries; it primarily supplies the domestic market. Through this attack, the Houthis demonstrated their ability to achieve three goals: threaten the population, disrupt energy infrastructure, and cast doubt on Saudi Arabia’s reliability as a key oil supplier.
The geography of the attack is notable. Khamis Mushait is a vital military hub for Saudi Arabia, Jizan is an oil refining center and port, Najran lies near the Yemeni border, and Abha serves as the administrative center of the Asir province. It was a distributed operation targeting various sites and one of the largest operations launched against Saudi Arabia since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28, 2026.
The Houthis claim that the operation is a response to Saudi strikes on Yemen; they claim that 121 airstrikes were carried out over the preceding three days. Riyadh speaks of a dangerous escalation and a violation of sovereignty. The previous model of limited deterrence, established after the 2022 truce, has effectively ceased to function, and hostilities have once again spilled beyond Yemen’s borders.
This brings up the delicate issue of the Mecca Agreement. The document was signed on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan; its publicly stated formula clearly implies that an armed attack on any one of the three states is considered an attack on all. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even likened this arrangement to Article 5 of NATO. However, an impressive-sounding collective defense formula does not automatically imply a functioning military mechanism.
The full text of the agreement has not been disclosed publicly. It is thus unclear who determines whether a specific incident constitutes an attack that triggers mutual obligations, whether the assistance is automatic, and who would command the designated forces. The first meeting of the joint political-defense committee took place on August 31. The parties agreed to establish a secretariat in Riyadh and began discussing joint exercises, military interoperability, and defense production. While the political commitment has been proclaimed, the framework for its implementation is still taking shape.
Even NATO’s Article 5 does not require all allies to automatically enter into war; each state takes whatever measures it deems necessary. In the case of the Mecca Agreement, the scope for interpretation is likely even broader. Assistance could entail intelligence sharing, the strengthening of air defense systems, arms supplies, and the deployment of specialists – but not necessarily joint strikes on Yemen.
The reaction of the allies confirms this interpretation. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described the Houthi attack as “cowardly,” condemned it “in the strongest terms,” and declared unwavering solidarity with the leadership and people of Saudi Arabia. The Turkish Foreign Ministry also issued a strong condemnation, affirmed its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and demanded that the Houthis immediately cease their attacks. However, neither country has publicly announced the convening of an emergency committee, heightened military readiness, or the provision of military aid to Riyadh in response to the new strike.
This does not mean that the agreement has failed. Collective defense is not limited to an immediate retaliatory strike, especially if the affected state has refrained from requesting specific assistance. Riyadh may currently be more interested in discreet cooperation regarding intelligence, missile launch detection, and counter-drone measures than a conspicuous entry of its allies into the war.
However, relying solely on rhetoric will not be sustainable in the long run. If the attacks persist, members of the alliance will need to define the threshold at which the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’ takes on practical meaning. Otherwise, the Houthis and other regional forces will receive a signal that the pact does not alter the cost of exerting military pressure on Saudi Arabia. For any defense alliance, this poses a greater risk than limited military damage: Deterrence only holds as long as a potential adversary believes that the commitments will be backed by action.
Ankara and Islamabad have reasons to avoid direct involvement in the Yemen campaign. Despite close military ties with Riyadh, Pakistan seeks to maintain a working relationship with Iran; its parliament refused to send troops to Yemen in 2015. Türkiye is also reluctant to transform the agreement into an anti-Iran bloc or risk being dragged into a protracted conflict.
A phased response is therefore the most likely scenario. It will likely start with consultations, followed by the strengthening of Saudi air defense capabilities, intelligence sharing, and the supply of anti-drone systems. Pakistan may provide specialists and additional personnel, while Türkiye can offer drone technology, electronic warfare capabilities, and munitions. Joint strikes would only be considered in the event of continued attacks, heavy casualties, or major disruptions to oil exports, and would require a separate political decision.
Following the strikes, the price of Brent crude approached $99 per barrel, although the initial surge remained within the 2% range. While the market does not yet view the damage as critical, it is reacting to multiple sources of risk. On September 4, Iran and the US targeted each other’s oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Houthis are intensifying pressure on shipping around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Before the war, around one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. A simultaneous threat to two key shipping routes could rapidly alter the relatively calm outlook of traders.
For the signatories of the Mecca Agreement, the attack does not serve as a trigger to automatically enter the war; rather, it is a test of their ability to devise a unified course of action. Condemnation by Sharif and the Turkish Foreign Ministry represents only the initial level of the response. It now remains to be seen whether the joint committee will be convened, whether Riyadh requests assistance, and what would happen in the event of a follow-up strike.
If political statements are followed by consultations, the strengthening of air defense capabilities, intelligence sharing, and the coordination of joint actions, the Mecca Agreement will acquire real, practical meaning. However, if the practical response is limited to rhetoric about a ‘cowardly attack’, the reputational gains derived from the August summit will quickly evaporate. The Houthis struck more than just Saudi targets; they effectively tested whether the alliance exists beyond the text of the joint communiqué. Currently, there is no definitive answer to this question – and there is a feeling that none may come.

Macron, von der Leyen call for stronger European space sector amid rising security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed their commitment to space at a major summit co-hosted by France and Germany in Paris.
French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to strengthen its space industry on Thursday, the second day of the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.
Speaking at the summit, Macron described Europe’s space sector as “fragile” and emphasised the need to bolster its capabilities, calling for “shared governance” of the industry.
“Outer space remains the only major global commons that is not subject to regulations that match the stakes,” he said. “Shared governance is necessary to address these challenges.”
Macron reiterated that more than 51 deals are set to be signed over the course of the summit, with some €20 billion of investments, listing a series of future milestones for Europe.
"In two years' time, I want to see the first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station; in five years' time, the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, the first European manned capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board," he added, referring to Europe's spaceport in French Guiana.
Meanwhile, von der Leyen stressed the importance of Europe stepping up, as she emphasised the crucial role space plays both in terms of both scientific exploration, but also defence — pointing to Russia's war in Ukraine.
"The ability to access and act in space not only underpins our prosperity, it increasingly determines our security and independence. Nowhere is this clearer than in Ukraine."
"Satellite communications keep soldiers connected, while satellite imagery reveal movements hundreds of kilometres away"."
Europe's Space push comes amid aim to cut dependence on US
Europe's push to build up its military space assets has been driven by Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as its decision to distance itself from its longstanding dependence on the US in the space domain.
"Security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space", said von der Leyen, as she went on to underline the significance of IRIS², the European Union's upcoming flagship satellite constellation programme.
"Last month, we decided to accelerate the system, by expanding it to more than 350 satellites."
Von der Leyen also underlined the need for the Commission, the European Space Agency and national governments to "pool" their strengths, while also calling for investment "at scale."
Ahead of the summit, several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."
A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”
Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US. But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.
Macron and Joseph Aschbacher, Director of the European Space Agency (ESA) — who also addressed the summit — were joined for a live call with astronaut Sophie Adenot, who is currently on a nine-month mission aboard the the International Space Station (ISS) named the εpsilon mission.

Heat not seen ‘for the last 100,000 years’ – climate monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:30:42 UTC
19:30:42 KST

Heat not seen ‘for the last 100,000 years’ – climate monitor
Global heat hit an all-time high in August, with temperatures averaging 16.96C worldwide, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Western Europe suffered its hottest summer on record, as heatwaves, drought, and wildfires battered the region.
August 2026 was 1.65C hotter than the 1850-1900 average, a period commonly used as the benchmark for temperatures before large-scale industrial warming, Copernicus said on Thursday. It was the hottest August in records dating back to 1940 and effectively matched July 2023, the previous all-time monthly high, with less than 0.01C separating them.
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess of the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP. Copernicus records extend back to 1940. Scientists use evidence including ice cores, tree rings, and corals to reconstruct temperatures further in the past.
The record followed an exceptionally hot summer across Western Europe. France, the UK, and Belgium all recorded their hottest summers; France endured 53 heatwave days and received almost 40% less rainfall than normal, making it the country’s second-driest summer since 1959.
The extreme heat also triggered a sharp rise in mortality. France registered an estimated 5,764 excess deaths from all causes during the June 17-July 2 heatwave – 36% above the expected level in affected areas, according to Sante publique France. Another 1,243 excess deaths were recorded during heatwave periods from July 3-22.
The combination of scorching temperatures and scarce rainfall hit crops and transportation. Germany’s grain harvest fell an estimated 7.3% year-on-year, with the authorities blaming heat and drought, while falling water levels on major rivers including the Rhine disrupted shipping.
France announced more than €1 billion ($1.16 billion) in emergency aid for farmers as tens of thousands of farms faced financial difficulties.
Dry vegetation fueled wildfires across the continent. More than 647,000 hectares had burned across the EU by early September, nearly twice the 20-year average for that point in the season, according to the European Commission’s Joint Research Center.
Oceans outside the polar regions reached their joint-highest monthly sea-surface temperature, extending a three-month run of record warmth. Scientists attribute the long-term warming trend primarily to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, while natural phenomena such as El Niño can further boost temperatures in the short term.
UN climate chief Simon Stiell called the latest records “the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction,” warning that extreme heat will continue while coal, oil, and gas are burned. Long-term global warming is currently around 1.4C above pre-industrial levels.

Own a piece of aviation history: Icelandair’s iconic Northern Lights plane turned into keychains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:30:20 UTC
19:30:20 KST

Icelandair’s Hekla Aurora, a Boeing 757-200, was retired in October last year having delighted plane spotters with its stunning livery since 2014.
From EVA Air’s Hello Kitty plane to JetBlue’s Super Mario-themed jet, AV geeks (and, if we’re being honest, everyone else) love a special aircraft livery.
Over the years, one of the best known was Icelandair’s Hekla Aurora, a Boeing 757-200 given a Northern Lights-themed makeover in 2014.
Artists used elaborate airbrushing techniques to recreate the Aurora Borealis, and the plane remained in service until 12 October last year.
Now, Icelandair has teamed up with Aviationtag to take the aircraft skin and transform it into a limited edition series of keychains.
Writing about the move on social media, Icelandair said: “Last year we farewelled a beloved member of our fleet: Hekla Aurora, the Boeing 757 painted in the colors of the northern lights.
“Saying goodbye to such a beauty wasn’t easy, so we collaborated with Aviationtag to preserve the aircraft’s livery.”
How to get your hands on one
Prices for the keychains start at €39.95. The team at Aviationtag have said that thanks to the design, which features a mix of blues, greens and blacks, “no two pieces look exactly alike”.
For serious collectors, there are sets of nine or 14 available, priced at €409.35 and €634.30 respectively.
Icelandair also has 10 tags to give away – fans of the livery are being asked to comment on the flag carrier’s social media pages with memories of flying on Hekla Aurora, or of viewing the Northern Lights in the country.
Other aviation accessories
Icelandair isn’t the first, and certainly won’t be the last, to upcycle plane parts into merchandise.
Air France sells key chains made out of leather headrests and wallets made out of lifejackets, and you can even buy engine blades that have been turned into works of art.
Lufthansa Group airlines – including Lufthansa, Austrian, Brussels and SWISS – all sell products made from recycled parts on Worldshop, with everything from coasters and cufflinks to lamps and tables on offer.
Our pick would have to be either the bar made with a window panel from an Airbus A320-211, or the armchair made from an Airbus A321 aircraft nose. Or maybe the sideboard made from an overhead locker.

Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait

Breadcrumb
Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, government sources said on Thursday, marking a major development in the renewed fighting as tens of thousands have been displaced across the country.
Three Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had entered Mocha and taken control of the coastal city, while local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing towards the southern city of Aden.
The takeover comes after weeks of escalating Houthi attacks on Mocha and its port and amid a broader offensive by the Iran-backed group across western Yemen.
Mocha is strategically important because of its location on Yemen's western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The city's capture could therefore have wider implications for security around the strait and commercial shipping through the Red Sea, as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast.
The Houthis launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces last week aimed at advancing towards Bab al-Mandab, prompting government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country.
Mocha had already come under repeated Houthi missile, drone and explosive-laden boat attacks in recent weeks.
The city's port suspended all commercial and maritime operations in mid-August after it was struck by more than 25 Houthi missiles, according to information provided by sources.
The attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged facilities and property, with material losses estimated at around $16 million.
The takeover coincides with an escalation in fighting along Yemen's western coast, particularly in southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, where government and allied forces have been carrying out military movements and withdrawing from several positions.
Yemeni government forces withdrew overnight from Hays district in southern Hodeidah as military units operating around Hays and western Taiz began a process of reorganisation and redeployment, military and local sources said.
It remains unclear how many troops withdrew from Hays and Al-Wazi'iyah or where they have been redeployed. Military sources said the movements were part of preparations for a coordinated field operation.
Tareq Saleh orders western coast forces to regroup
Tareq Saleh, deputy chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said on Thursday that government forces on the western coast had suffered heavy losses in recent days while confronting the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said forces had been ordered to regroup and establish an alternative command centre in a secure location in consultation with the Saudi-led coalition and the Presidential Leadership Council.
Military media affiliated with Saleh's National Resistance said the joint forces had established a command centre south of Mocha following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts under heavy fire.
The forces involved in the western coast fighting include the National Resistance, the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield forces, alongside units from the Taiz military axis.
Saleh accused Iran of planning, supporting and participating in the Houthi offensive through what he described as its "various tools", without providing further details about Tehran's alleged involvement.
Iran has rejected accusations that it is interfering in Yemen, saying this week that it supports the country's unity and territorial integrity and a Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.
Meanwhile, military media sources reported air strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah province.
The National Resistance's military media also said the Houthis had targeted Zuqar Island with two ballistic missiles.
The latest developments come amid the most significant escalation on several Yemeni fronts following years of relative calm. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but clashes resumed in July and have since widened.
Fighting has also spilled across the border into Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh accusing the Houthis of targeting Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities said this week that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.
