Two Palestinian amputee athletes from the Gaza Strip condemned the global sports equipment company Adidas for using an Israeli soldier as an advertising figure for its products, describing the move as “a blatant bias toward the Israeli killers and a whitewashing of the crimes of genocide.”
The two athletes, speaking to Anadolu, said they had decided on a “comprehensive boycott and abandonment of the company’s products” and called on the Arab and Muslim sporting community and free people around the world to support them and stop buying its products.
Former Israeli soldier Shalev Biton, who participated in the Israeli aggression against the Gaza Strip in 2021, appeared in a local campaign promoting the Single Shoe service launched by Adidas.
The service allows amputees, or those who need only one shoe, to purchase it for 50% of the price of a full pair.
The campaign sparked widespread international, Arab and Palestinian discontent, amid the suffering of thousands of amputees in the Gaza Strip due to a shortage of prosthetic limbs and the raw materials needed to manufacture them. 
‘Whitewashing the image of the killers’
Ahmed Abu Nar, an amputee football player in Gaza, said that Adidas, a company of its size, using an Israeli sniper who participated in the war on the Strip was “a provocative act and a deliberate attempt to whitewash the image of those committing war crimes against civilians.”
Abu Nar, who lost his left leg as a result of direct fire from an Israeli sniper, expressed his astonishment at “using an Israeli soldier to advertise and market this shoe, at a time when it could have used many other people.”
He added: “The company has expertise and specialized teams to study every step, and what happened was not a mere coincidence, but a calculated decision to ignore the victims and celebrate the killer.”
Abu Nar criticized the company’s handling of the controversy and its decision to limit the apology and removal of the advertisement to pages directed only at the Middle East, noting that “the company’s global page did not address the matter.”
Under pressure and amid calls to boycott it, the German sportswear company Adidas apologized Monday through its Arabic-language Instagram account for launching an advertising campaign featuring an Israeli soldier.
The Adidas Arabia account has relatively limited reach, with only 1.4 million followers, a figure that is dwarfed by the more than 29.6 million followers of its global account.
Abu Nar confirmed that he had made a firm decision to boycott Adidas and dispose of all its sports equipment, saying: “This decision is irreversible for us as athletes in Gaza.”
He added: “The company applies double standards, between us being victims and being exposed to death, bombing and destruction at every moment, while on the other hand they said the war had stopped, and to this day it has not stopped. On our way to the field, we are at any moment afraid that a bombing may occur.”
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has been committing genocide in Gaza, leaving more than 73,000 Palestinians dead, more than 174,000 wounded, and destruction affecting 90% of the infrastructure. 
Bias toward the occupation
For his part, Hassan Abu Karim, 43, a board member of the Palestine Amputee Football Association, denounced what he described as “racial discrimination and double standards” practiced by global companies in their handling of the Palestinian issue.
Abu Karim, who lost his foot to an Israeli shell in 2006 during an incursion into the Maghazi area, said: “At a time when our association has struggled since its establishment in 2018 to provide the most basic necessities, including shoes and crutches for amputee athletes, we find the global company opening its doors and providing its capabilities and sponsorship to a soldier who participated in massacres against our people.”
“This greatly affects the sporting situation in Palestine, particularly people with amputations who had been waiting for international institutions and companies to sponsor them or stand by their side,” he added.
Abu Karim, a former player for Maghazi Services Club who participated in international sporting initiatives for amputees, explained that it would be more appropriate for global companies to show solidarity with victims living under siege and bombardment and to safeguard the rights of people with disabilities.
He continued: “As an athlete, when I saw this advertisement, it became clear to me that they had ignored the suffering of people with disabilities or amputees in Gaza.”
He considered the use of the Israeli soldier as an advertising figure to be “abhorrent racial discrimination,” calling on Adidas “not to be racist and not to side with the occupation and killing.”
Abu Karim called on Arab and Muslim athletes and sporting institutions around the world to stand alongside Palestinian athletes and confront what he described as “racist policies” through a broad boycott of the company’s products until it “complies with humanitarian values and justice.”
Days after the advertisement was published, criticism escalated across social media platforms as accounts supportive of the Palestinian cause republished images of the campaign, pointing out that Biton had lost his leg while participating in the Israeli aggression against the Gaza Strip in 2021.
Israel’s Channel 15 said posts that recirculated the advertisement received millions of views, while a hashtag calling for a boycott of Adidas spread, accompanied by thousands of calls to boycott the company.
Users compared the Israeli soldier with the thousands of Palestinians whose limbs had been amputated during the genocide, accusing Adidas of ignoring their suffering. 
More than 5,000 amputation cases
The figures concerning amputees in the Gaza Strip reveal the extent of the contrast highlighted by Adidas’ critics.
According to World Health Organization estimates issued in May 2026, the Strip recorded between 5,161 and 6,710 limb amputations since October 2023.
The organization indicated that around 43,000 people in Gaza sustained injuries likely to permanently change their lives, including approximately 10,000 children.
It noted that the number of serious limb injuries had reached around 22,000 cases by May, while the total number of injuries at that time had reached approximately 172,000 since Oct. 8, 2023.
In a related context, figures reported by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) on Aug. 14, 2026, confirmed that children account for around 18% of amputation cases in Gaza, while specialized rehabilitation services for children are unavailable in the Strip.
The suffering of amputees does not end with the loss of their limbs, as it is followed by a long process of surgical operations, physical therapy, rehabilitation and the search for a suitable prosthetic limb.

Timeline: How a Russian drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane in Moldova
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:04:31 UTC
19:04:31 KST

Russia’s latest drone incursion into Moldova and NATO airspace comes as Moscow increasingly deploys jet-powered attack drones, blurring the line between traditional UAVs and low-cost cruise missiles and making them much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was preparing to leave Chișinău for Oslo on Tuesday afternoon when Moldova’s military detected an unmanned aerial vehicle in the country’s airspace.
What initially appeared to be another Russian drone incursion took on greater significance the following day, when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre revealed that Zelenskyy’s plane had almost been hit by a drone.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
The timeline shows how the events unfolded.
Moldovan military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle at 4:20 pm EEST (3:20 CEST).
Moldovan officials confirmed to Euronews that the country’s airspace was closed shortly after 4:30 pm.
“The airspace was closed to protect the aircraft flying over Moldova at the time - three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result.”
By 4:37 pm, Romania’s Defence Ministry said the drone crossed into Romanian — and therefore NATO — airspace.
Two minutes later two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it.
The jets did not intercept the drone. Romanian radar continued to track it until 5:02 pm, when contact was lost.
Five minutes later at 5:07 pm the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it later crashed about 25 km east of the Romanian border.
According to Moldovan officials, the flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 pm, when authorities confirmed the drone had come down and exploded near Mihăilenii Vechi, in the Râșcani district, about 160 km from Chișinău International Airport.
“For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took off from Chișinău International Airport later than scheduled," officials said.
According to monitoring channels, Zelenskyy’s plane took off from Chișinău around 5:57 pm.
For much of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine that began in early 2022, Zelenskyy has travelled abroad primarily through Poland, with Rzeszów serving as a regular departure point.
In recent months, however, his presidential aircraft has also begun using Chișinău more frequently for foreign trips.
What type of drone was it?
The exact model of the drone involved in Moldova and Romania has not been officially established.
Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia’s newer jet-powered attack drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 are among the newest additions to Russia’s expanding Geran family, although they differ significantly in design and capabilities.
The Geran-4 has a wingspan of about three metres and is roughly 3.5 metres long. Its maximum take-off weight is around 450 kilograms.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-4 can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h and carry a warhead weighing between 50 and 90 kilograms.
Russia has recently stepped up its use of jet-powered drones, including in complex barrages alongside ballistic and cruise missiles designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
Their speed makes them much harder to intercept than conventional Shahed-type drones, particularly for the mobile fire groups and other relatively inexpensive systems Ukraine has relied on to counter slower-moving UAVs.
Ukraine is instead forced to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against the faster threats, putting additional pressure on already limited interceptor stocks.
Several Ukrainian companies have reportedly begun testing missiles specifically designed to shoot down the new jet-powered Geran models.

====================================================================================================

Russia is going all in on a baby boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:04:13 UTC
19:04:13 KST

Russia is going all in on a baby boom
Russian President Vladimir Putin poses with children of Russian officers involved in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and with participants of youth and student organizations at Red Square in Moscow, Russia, on Nov. 4, 2024. (Contributor / Getty Images)
Liubov Tsybulska
Director of Join Ukraine
The Kremlin promises money to people who have children, expands benefits for large families, and publicly "cares" about pregnant students and schoolgirls.
The sums involved are enormous: by 2030, the national "Family" project is expected to receive funding equivalent to about two of Ukraine's annual state budgets in terms of expenditures.
The money will go toward measures intended, in one way or another, to boost the birth rate — from subsidized mortgages for young families to promoting large families.
But there is a problem. Our monitoring of two of Russia's most popular social networks, Telegram and VKontakte, conducted in early 2026, shows that absurd legislative initiatives and relentless demographic propaganda are openly irritating the Russian public. A policy that Russian authorities call "family support" is becoming yet another source of conflict between the state and society.
To wage aggressive wars in the future, Russia needs people above all else. That makes it critically important to understand how successful the Kremlin's demographic programs are.
More than two-thirds of humanity lives in countries where birth rates are insufficient to replace the population. The problem of population decline has plagued Ukraine since its independence, but it became catastrophic after the full-scale war began and triggered mass migration. Ukraine's total fertility rate has now fallen below one.
Russia is in a better position, but the picture is far from straightforward. In 2024, 1.22 million children were born in Russia, one of the worst figures in its modern history. The total fertility rate stood at 1.4 children per woman at the end of 2025.
To simply replace the population, the rate needs to be 2.1.
After the invasion of Ukraine, the issue took on strategic importance for the Kremlin. Enormous battlefield losses and the exodus of young people have turned the Soviet slogan "the women will give birth to more" into a new political priority.
Just recently, Putin once again said that "the long-term task is to preserve and increase the population of Russia." Regional birth rates have also been included in assessments of governors' performance.
The carrots and sticks of "family values"
Russia has enough resources to actively shape its demographic policy. The Kremlin has a broad set of tools at its disposal to increase the birth rate — from financial incentives to outright bans.
There are plenty of "carrots": maternity capital, family mortgages, tax breaks, support for large families, and more.
The Kremlin is not sparing money on the "production" of new soldiers. The national "Family" project is expected to receive 17.9 trillion rubles (more than $200 billion) between 2025 and 2030, including 3.2 trillion rubles ($36 billion) in 2026 alone.
Most of the program consists of various financial incentives and benefits for families, such as reduced-rate mortgages and maternity capital. Yet Russian authorities understand that this is not enough. The program's goal is to raise the total fertility rate to 1.593 — still far below the target of 2.1.
For those who are not tempted by financial incentives, the Russian authorities have a "stick" in the form of pro-natalist propaganda and various restrictions.
These include Putin's law banning the "promotion of refusing to have children," penalties for "coercing" women into having abortions, a ban on private clinics performing abortions, and, more recently, discussions in the State Duma and the Russian Orthodox Church about requiring a husband's consent for an abortion.
The state's "concern" for citizens' sexual health sometimes reaches absurd levels.
Among the latest government initiatives are referring women who do not plan to have children to psychologists, while men who enjoy going to saunas are sent for sperm tests.
And however comical these measures may look from the outside, the Kremlin is using them to relentlessly pursue its goal of overcoming the demographic crisis.
At the same time, the public views these initiatives quite critically, and sometimes even with hostility, creating yet another deep conflict within Russian society.
"Like it or not, give birth, my beauty"
At Join Ukraine, we analyzed discussions about childbearing in more than 700 communities on Telegram and VKontakte across virtually all regions of Russia. The scale of the sample allows us to see both individual bursts of discontent and a clear broader social trend.
The biggest wave of outrage among Russians was triggered by announcements of payments for pregnant students and schoolgirls: 72% of reactions on Telegram were negative, while only 3% were positive.
This “support” was seen not as assistance to young women, but as an incentive for early pregnancy at the expense of education and professional development.
Disgruntled social media users asked, "And when are they supposed to study?" Others went even further, wondering: "Are women being pushed to have children instead of pursuing careers? What happens if the marriage doesn't work out? Will the state take care of the children? Of course not."
The second most negatively received issue was abortion restrictions. Users were particularly concerned by the government's proposal to allow a married woman to terminate a pregnancy only with her husband's consent.
For example, under one post in a Rostov-based public channel, the proposal received 1,473 negative reactions. Another post on a similar topic, this time in a Voronezh-based community, received 2,023. In the comments, users pointed to overcrowded orphanages and argued that banning abortions does nothing to eliminate the reasons why women seek them.
Russians were also deeply unhappy with the Health Ministry's idea of encouraging women to become pregnant through consultations with psychologists.
Posts about introducing mandatory consultations for women who say they do not plan to have children, announced in March 2026, generated tens of thousands of reposts and received overwhelmingly negative reactions.
Purely economic programs failed to generate much enthusiasm either. Posts about family mortgages were largely met with negativity. The main reason is that the program is becoming increasingly inaccessible to Russians as its terms are repeatedly changed and housing prices continue to rise.
Russians reacted relatively calmly to posts about maternity capital, although government attempts to restrict how the funds can be used also faced sharp criticism from commenters.
"Have children yourselves!": Why Russians reject the government's demographic initiatives
The core of social media users' criticism of the Kremlin's demographic initiatives was distrust of the authorities and a belief that they are hypocritical, reflected in the sarcastic call: "Have children yourselves!"
This argument accounted for roughly a quarter of substantive comments on Telegram and VKontakte.
Next came more mundane arguments: poverty, high prices, and unaffordable housing. Commenters also condemned the cynicism of calls to have more children amid the systematic closure of schools, maternity wards, and clinics, as well as inadequate infrastructure.
A xenophobic line of argument was also prominent — a predictable consequence of years of state propaganda that has taught Russians to look for someone to blame among migrants and other "outsiders."
Nearly one in seven substantive comments on Telegram and VKontakte concerned the claim that child-related benefits were supposedly going to "the wrong people."
Direct state interference in private life was mentioned less frequently, but consistently.
People were even more cautious when discussing the war: only 5.8% of comments on Telegram and 7.5% on VKontakte explicitly linked calls to have more children with the need to replenish the army and compensate for human losses in the so-called "special military operation."
Still, given the censorship and repression prevalent in Russia, even these figures are significant.
Women's rights were mentioned the least. One could joke that women's rights in Russia are so reliably protected by the state that women themselves are simply never given them.
Seriously, however, the reason is the scale of "traditional values" propaganda and religious pressure, as well as the dominance of patriarchal notions of the family, particularly outside Russia's largest cities.
Whether all of these measures are successful matters not just to Putin but also beyond Russia's borders.
A shrinking population does not automatically make Russia less dangerous. On the contrary, the Kremlin's efforts to reverse demographic decline are closely tied to its long-term economic, military, and geopolitical ambitions.
If Moscow sees people primarily as a resource for the state — including a pool of future soldiers — its demographic policy is a variable worth monitoring, as well as public discussion around it.

Hezbollah’s use of cluster munitions against Israel may be war crime, HRW says in rare condemnation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:02:25 UTC
19:02:25 KST

Hezbollah’s use of cluster munitions in attacks against northern Israel on March 4 and March 15 may have constituted a war crime, Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday in a rare condemnation of the terrorist group.
Hezbollah launched cluster munitions at civilian towns in the North in response to the assassination of Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, drawing Lebanon into renewed conflict. The terrorist group had already reinitiated hostilities on October 8, 2023, with intermittent ceasefires in support of Hamas following the October 7 massacre.
A cluster munition is an explosive weapon that releases dozens or hundreds of smaller submunitions over a wide area. It was used repeatedly by Iran against Israel during the war in March.
Although Hezbollah’s cluster munitions did not result in civilian casualties, Human Rights Watch said cluster munitions can kill and maim for decades after they are used, as many submunitions fail to explode on impact and can act as land mines.
“Cluster munitions should not be used under any circumstances, and their use may amount to a war crime,” said Patrick Thompson, a crisis, conflict, and arms researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Not only are they inherently indiscriminate, but unexploded submunitions can kill and injure civilians long after hostilities conclude.”
The 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions, which includes 112 state parties and 12 more states that have signed, prohibits the use of these weapons. Lebanon is a state party held to the treaty, although Hezbollah is not formally bound by it as a non-state armed group.
Hezbollah's use of cluster munitions against northern Israel is a war crime, HRW says
“The use of cluster munitions in civilian areas is a flagrant violation of international law,” Thompson said. “Hezbollah and all parties to the conflict should abide by the laws of war.”
Researchers from the NGO visited Metula in May and confirmed Hezbollah’s use of the banned weapon after analyzing impact sites and interviewing four witnesses.
Although Hezbollah publicly claimed responsibility for the attacks against Metula in March, Hezbollah denied to Human Rights Watch that it had cluster munitions in its possession or used them.
The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, HRW said, has also confirmed that Hezbollah fired unguided rockets into populated civilian areas. These weapons indiscriminately kill and cannot distinguish between military or civilian targets, making their use a violation of the laws of war.
Multiple civilians were killed or wounded by Hezbollah’s attacks between March and June.
Cluster munitions in civilian areas 'a flagrant violation of international law'
Hagai, 57, witnessed Hezbollah’s March 4 attack. He told the NGO he remembered running to the shelter with his wife and two children at around 4 p.m. before hearing multiple explosions.
On March 4, an attack struck a residential street on the southern side of Metula near the cemetery. Hagai, whose full name is not used for his safety and who lives in the town with his wife and two children, said he and his family ran to their shelter outside their house after hearing sirens around 4 p.m. They were instructed by authorities to remain inside for a full day as the IDF cleared his neighborhood of submunitions that fell during the attack.
The submunitions damaged his family’s two cars beyond repair, damaged 12 of his windows, and cut two water pipes in half. The authorities found a submunition on his roof.
Hagai told Human Rights Watch he continues to worry for his children’s safety.
“My son plays basketball here,” he said. “If the ball goes down the hill into the grass, I tell him to leave it. They checked the whole area for unexploded bombs, but who knows? I don’t know how thoroughly they can check the bushes.”
Hagai said the military counted about 50 impact craters. Although the road had been repaved by the time Human Rights Watch researchers arrived, they still identified seven impact craters consistent with submunition impacts.
Having analyzed photos taken by journalists before the road was paved outside Hagai’s home, HRW also concluded that additional craters had been created by the attack.
A house 50 meters from Hagai’s was also severely damaged, with the windows broken from the impact. The anonymous homeowner said multiple unexploded submunitions had been collected from outside her home.
HRW also found a photo released by the Israel Police that showed an unexploded BRB1-type submunition from a 122-mm. rocket, which held between 45-56 BRB1-type submunitions. The NGO said it was credible even if it could not independently authenticate the image.
Although HRW could not independently confirm the photograph’s location, researchers found no version of it uploaded online before March 4, and witness reports of about 50 submunition impacts in Metula on March 4 are consistent with the numbers reportedly contained in the BRB1 delivery system, as are the craters HRW analyzed.
A witness to the March 15 attack also told HRW she had heard multiple simultaneous explosions and was instructed by the military to remain at home for 24 hours as the streets were being cleared of cluster munitions.
By the time researchers arrived, the road had been paved over, but they were able to identify one crater consistent with a submunition.
A geolocated video uploaded to Telegram on March 15 also showed about 30 small explosions around the entry gate consistent with a cluster munition attack. Researchers were able to identify the area where witnesses reported seeing the cluster munition strike.

UAV certification in Ukraine: how a drone goes from development to operation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:02:05 EEST
19:02:05 KST

UAV certification in Ukraine: how a drone goes from development to operation
Kyiv • UNN
The company “MS AVIA-GRADE” explained which documents and tests are required for a drone to be approved.
Amid the full-scale war in Ukraine, drone production is developing rapidly. The front's need for drones is constantly growing, and manufacturers are forced to quickly create new aircraft. However, developing a drone and putting it into serial production are not the same thing. For UAVs to be fully used and supplied to the front, they must undergo the necessary verification, testing, and certification procedures. UNN spoke with Dmytro Parkhisenko, director of the aviation company "MS AVIA-GRADE," about how exactly the drone certification process takes place and what difficulties manufacturers face.
Details
For a drone to carry out combat missions at the front, it is not enough simply to fly well and maintain communications. To become a fully-fledged aviation product and enter service, its characteristics must be confirmed with documentation.
According to the director of "MS AVIA-GRADE," the certification and codification of unmanned systems in Ukraine involve officially verifying and confirming that the aircraft complies with technical regulations, safety standards, and the requirements of government customers.
Such verification is necessary for the legal supply of equipment to the Defense Forces, participation in open tenders, as well as ensuring reliability and safety during operation
In practice, the certification process covers several important stages. First, the manufacturer submits an application with a detailed technical description, the design and operating documentation undergoes expert review, and practical flight tests are conducted. The stability of the design, the reliability of communications and navigation channels, resistance to interference, and the software's compliance with safety standards are then assessed.
This procedure is quite resource-intensive and technically detailed, and its duration depends on the aircraft's class and purpose. In recent years, the state's approaches have evolved substantially: on the one hand, efforts were made to accelerate the procedures for authorization to operate as much as possible due to the needs of the times; on the other hand, requirements for standardization, the quality of components, and the implementation of military standards have increased (in particular, requirements related to NATO models)
For manufacturers, this means the need to work in two areas at once: on the one hand, to rapidly develop their technologies, and on the other, to meet the requirements and standards.
According to the director of "MS AVIA-GRADE," the most common barriers to UAV certification include bureaucratic delays during approval stages, difficulties adapting internal documentation to strict military standards, a shortage of safe locations for conducting flight tests, as well as intellectual property protection issues during state examinations.
At the same time, for companies with experience in aviation, a significant portion of these requirements is nothing new.
"MS AVIA-GRADE" has been working with aviation equipment for more than 15 years and has a team of engineers and aviation specialists with experience in regulatory and certification processes. Among other things, the company specializes in the repair, maintenance, and modernization of airplanes and helicopters, has its own design bureau, and operates in the international market.
MS AVIA-GRADE's many years of experience in the repair, maintenance, and modification of piloted airplanes and helicopters provides a fundamental engineering foundation. Working under strict aviation regulations fosters uncompromising quality control, which is critically important for unmanned aviation as well
At the same time, the company is developing its unmanned systems division. Its structure includes a separate UAV unit that works on its own unmanned products and those developed jointly with partners, prepares technical documentation, handles standardization and certification, and supports the commissioning process for drone developers.
The company’s activities in the field of unmanned systems are based on deep scientific and technical expertise, engineering development, and the conduct of specialized tests. Key competencies in this area include an understanding of aerodynamics, the design of aviation systems, the ability to integrate complex technical solutions, and the preparation of design documentation in accordance with international and domestic requirements
For security reasons, MS AVIA-GRADE does not disclose the specific projects its specialists are currently working on. However, the company’s approach to working with unmanned aerial vehicles continues, in many respects, its “aviation school.”
The unmanned aviation sector is demonstrating rapid growth, as the technologies require continuous improvement and scaling. MS AVIA-GRADE has a strong position thanks to the synergy of its classical aviation school, its own design and production base, and its ability to adapt advanced engineering practices to modern challenges
Through many years of experience working with aviation equipment, MS AVIA-GRADE has developed competencies encompassing the repair, modernization, and certification support of aviation systems. Today, the company also applies these competencies in the field of unmanned aviation, in particular by working on the development of technical documentation and the commissioning of UAVs.

The Ministry of Defence has said work is continuing on a more integrated approach to domestic and international military rail movements, but no completion date has yet been set.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided the update in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked when the department expected to establish the integrated approach referred to in an earlier answer in July.
Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence recognises the important role rail can play in strengthening military mobility and is progressing work to develop a more integrated approach to domestic and international rail movements.”
The work forms part of wider efforts to improve the resilience of Defence’s strategic logistics network, including the ability to move personnel, vehicles, equipment and supplies within the UK and across international borders. Military rail transport can provide an important means of moving heavy equipment over long distances without relying solely on road transport, particularly when large formations or armoured vehicles need to be moved rapidly between bases, ports, training areas or allied territory.
The MOD said it is working across government and with industry and international partners as it develops future rail arrangements.
Pollard said: “Defence is engaging across Government, with industry and with international partners to ensure that future rail capability development supports operational requirements at home and overseas.”
The issue has taken on greater importance as NATO focuses on military mobility across Europe, where the ability to move forces and equipment quickly between countries is a central part of reinforcement planning and collective defence. However, the MOD has not yet established a deadline for completing the work.
Pollard said: “Whilst no specific completion date has been established, this remains an important area of ongoing capability development.”

====================================================================================================

New psychology research reveals why people tend to hide their successes and share their failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

People often adjust what they share about their own achievements or setbacks based on what their conversation partner has just revealed. New research suggests that these communication choices are driven less by a desire to manage one’s own image and more by an intention to protect the other person’s feelings. This tendency leads people to share mutual failures far more often than mutual successes, published in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes.
When people spontaneously share their successes or failures, they often do so to shape how others perceive them, such as appearing competent or seeking sympathy. But conversations are usually interactive. Responsive outcome disclosure occurs when an individual learns about a counterpart’s personal outcome and then must decide whether to share their own experience.
“A lot of existing research on disclosure has focused on why people initially choose to share good news or hide bad news, largely through the lens of self-presentation,” Irene Scopelliti, a professor of marketing and behavioral science at Bayes Business School, told PsyPost. “But conversations do not always work that way, because often we are responding after someone else has already told us their news.”
Traditional theories of communication suggest that people tend to match the tone of their conversation partners. According to this idea of reciprocity, a person should be equally likely to reply to a success with their own success as they are to reply to a failure with their own failure. But sharing personal outcomes is a highly emotional process. For instance, a 2019 study found that sharing one’s failures can reduce feelings of malicious envy in observers.
In addition, people often try to protect the feelings of those around them. Research covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicated that people frequently conceal personal information to avoid causing distress to a close conversation partner. Building on this idea, the current research proposes an other-focused framework for responsive disclosure. If a person cares about the feelings of their counterpart, they might actively shape their own disclosures to provide comfort or avoid causing harm.
To investigate this, the research team, led by Emily Prinsloo of Rice University and Scopelliti, tested this concept through nine separate studies. “So we wanted to understand how people navigate these interactions and what we are more likely to disclose when responding to others’ disclosures,” Scopelliti said.
Across the nine experiments, the researchers evaluated the responses of 8,229 participants in various scenarios and live interactions. They tracked whether people chose to reveal their own successes and failures after a counterpart shared theirs.
“These are not tiny statistical effects,” Scopelliti explained. “Across nine studies and more than 8,000 participants, in contexts ranging from job interviews to health outcomes to financial setbacks, we saw large, consistent shifts in disclosure behavior.”
In the first study, 900 online participants imagined receiving the results of a biological age test. Half were told their biological age was seven years younger than their actual age, indicating a positive health outcome, while the other half were told it was seven years older, indicating a negative outcome. They then read a scenario in which a colleague disclosed either a positive health result, a negative health result, or no result. The participants then allocated points to indicate how likely they were to reply by sharing their own outcome.
The results showed a general preference for matching. Participants were generally more likely to share a success if the colleague also had a success, and a failure if the colleague had a failure. But two interesting asymmetries emerged. First, participants were much more likely to disclose matching failures (87 percent) than matching successes (70 percent). Second, when outcomes did not match, participants were more willing to reveal a failure to a successful colleague (54 percent) than a success to a failing colleague (16 percent).
“For example, participants disclosed a failure of their own much more often after hearing about someone else’s failure compared to someone else’s success,” Scopelliti noted. “Across our studies, this was one of the largest and most consistent effects we observed.”
In fact, she pointed out, “In one study, people who had failed were more than twice as inclined to share their failure when the other person had disclosed a failure compared to when the other person had disclosed a success, and even in our most conservative, real-conversation studies, disclosure rates still rose by a third or more.”
To understand the motives behind these choices, the researchers conducted a second study with 812 participants who imagined receiving either a job offer or a rejection. The participants interacted with an acquaintance who also shared a job outcome. The researchers manipulated how much the participant liked the acquaintance.
When participants liked the acquaintance, the asymmetrical disclosure patterns were especially strong. Open-ended responses showed that participants who shared matching failures often did so to help the other person feel better. Those who withheld their successes from a rejected acquaintance often explicitly stated a desire to avoid causing harm. When participants were told they disliked the acquaintance, they cared less about protecting the other person’s feelings, and the asymmetries were noticeably reduced.
A third study involving 801 participants tested whether the topic of the disclosure mattered. Participants were placed in situations where their outcome either matched the topic of their colleague’s disclosure or involved a completely different topic. The tendency to share mutual failures was highest when the topics were exactly the same. When the topics differed, participants were less likely to share a failure in response to a failure. This indicates that people recognize that a completely unrelated negative outcome might feel dismissive or unhelpful to a struggling friend.
“When a friend shares a failure, many of us choose to mention a related failure of our own, not to compete but to offer solidarity,” Scopelliti said.
The researchers also investigated how people adjust the wording of their messages. In two studies, participants wrote open-ended replies after learning about a friend’s successful or unsuccessful financial investments and job applications.
When participants had a success to share but the friend had failed, they wrote longer messages and frequently used apologies to soften the blow. Sometimes they delayed sharing their own positive news until later in the conversation, or they offered words of consolation and help before mentioning their own outcome. A small percentage of participants even engaged in deception, misrepresenting their own success to protect the friend’s feelings.
“When we have succeeded when someone else has not, many of us hold back or soften the news, weighing how it will land rather than worrying about self-interest,” Scopelliti explained. “When we decide what to share about our own lives in these moments, we are often responding more to the other person’s emotional needs than to our own image.”
To test these patterns in real time, the final study paired 946 participants in live, online chat rooms. Participants completed a puzzle task that was secretly manipulated to be either very easy or very difficult, resulting in genuine feelings of success or failure. They were then paired up, and one participant was given a small financial bonus to spontaneously share their outcome in the chat.
The live interactions closely mirrored the hypothetical scenarios. When both individuals failed, 96 percent of the participants chose to share their failure. When both succeeded, only 73 percent shared their success. In mismatched pairs, participants shared failures in response to successes 81 percent of the time, but they only shared successes in response to failures 40 percent of the time. The chat logs also showed frequent use of compensatory apologies and delayed disclosures when participants were better off than their partners.
“Our data suggests that people calibrate what they share to protect the other person’s feelings,” Scopelliti summarized. “So this effect consistently shows up whether people are choosing between pre-written responses, writing their own replies, or having real, live conversations.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study mostly involved participants from Western countries, and cultural backgrounds could influence how people handle personal news. In cultures that heavily emphasize social hierarchies or individualism, people might be more willing to share successes or less focused on protecting others from upward comparisons.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the types of outcomes evaluated. The scenarios focused on definitive successes and failures, but everyday life often involves events with varying degrees of intensity. A massive career breakthrough might prompt different disclosure behaviors than a minor daily win.
Additionally, the researchers did not measure whether these well-intentioned communication strategies actually succeed in making the other person feel better. Withholding a success to protect a friend might backfire if the friend later discovers the truth and feels patronized.
“One thing we are eager to look at next is whether these disclosure strategies actually work the way responders intend them to,” Scopelliti told PsyPost. “Our studies show what people choose to share and why, but not how those choices land on the other end.”
Future research could explore how different types of relationships, such as romantic partnerships or rivalries, alter these communication habits. Evaluating how the original discloser reacts to these intentionally crafted responses could also shed light on the long-term relational impacts of hiding positive news. “So the next step is studying both sides of the conversation at once, to examine whether and when these well-intentioned strategies actually achieve their goal, and why,” Scopelliti added.
The study, “Responses to Outcome Disclosure: People Asymmetrically Disclose or Hide Their Outcomes to Protect Others’ Emotions”, was authored by Emily Prinsloo, Irene Scopelliti, George Loewenstein, and Joachim Vosgerau.

The UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginning | Em Hilton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:23 UTC
19:00:23 KST

The announcement on Tuesday by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, of an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, as well as a comprehensive sanctions regime, is a hard-won victory for the Palestine solidarity movement.
This is not simply a change of heart by the government: it is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement, who have consistently held the government’s feet to the fire over its complicity in the atrocities being committed in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband’s announcement shows us what organised and persistent campaigning can achieve, and inspires confidence that movements can force political change.
Over the past three years, Palestine has become a political and electoral challenge for the Labour party, as well as a fundamental issue of public conscience. This move signals a political reset in the UK government’s foreign policy approach to Israel. But as the UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese has said, a ban on goods from settlements must be part of a “true paradigm shift”; the government can, and must, go further.
There has already been sustained backlash at the move, with the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, accusing Miliband of “Jew hate” on the Today programme. As a Jewish campaigner, let me be clear: holding Israel to account for its human rights violations in the West Bank is not antisemitic. To conflate the actions of violent settlers and the Israeli government with Jewish people everywhere makes us accountable for the actions of those who do not represent us.
There is also warranted scepticism about the Labour government’s commitment to holding Israel accountable. But an “all or nothing” approach would be a mistake, when there is so much that can be built on here. We can certainly retain our anger at the government’s complicity. No sanction can offset the foreign policy decisions made by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and former foreign secretary David Lammy, the repression of domestic pro-Palestine advocacy, or the sheer loss of life. But we must balance this with cautious optimism that the political tide is turning.
Political victories are mobilising – they fuel the belief that collective action can work. So now is the time to push at the open door. But what comes next? How do we ensure that accountability for Israel’s oppression of Palestinians is not limited to the settlements, but builds momentum for further meaningful action in support of Palestinian human rights?
First, we should demand that these trade sanctions are enforced and expanded. Eleven nations, including Canada and France, have joined the UK in these measures; we must call for further coordination and alignment with other western governments.
The necessary next step is a full arms embargo and an end to cooperation with Israeli security forces – to truly have teeth, these sanctions must not take with one hand and then give with another. Miliband has said that “we’ve already suspended over 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza. That suspension remains fully in place”, and that the government will “now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation”. But components of F-35 jets continue to be exported to Israel and used for operations in Gaza, as are surveillance technologies such as drones and radar made in the UK by Elbit Systems. This is a total dereliction of duty by the British government.
Miliband’s announcements were a necessary reminder that a just political future is possible and, within it, a reckoning with past crimes. As a campaigner, I have borne witness to Israel’s most egregious human rights violations: I have documented Israeli settlers committing pogroms against the community of Al-Mufaqara, sat in Palestinian villages threatened with home demolitions and army raids, and witnessed the ongoing daily misery of Israel’s apartheid policies. This has all strengthened my motivation to see the end of the Israeli occupation.
This announcement is the beginning, not the end, of the road. It is a hopeful indication of what happens when collective power is translated into political change. We must sit with the idea that Palestinians will see some justice and reprieve from relentless destruction and displacement. I hope I’m not wrong.
- 
  Em Hilton is a Jewish writer and organiser. She is the co-founder of Na’amod: UK Jews Against Israeli Occupation, and the policy director at Diaspora Alliance

Twenty-five years after 9/11, the daughter of a hero remembers the mother she lost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

Anna Sweeney Rossman was only five years old when her mother, flight attendant Madeline Amy Sweeney, died aboard an airliner that terrorists hijacked and deliberately flew into the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. And for years, she said in an interview on Wednesday, Rossman’s grief primarily centered on her mother’s absence from certain milestones in her life.
She recalled how planning her 2023 wedding – particularly shopping for a dress – hit her especially hard without her mom there. And Rossman said it was as much a blow to not have her mom there for the birth of her daughters, each younger than 2, as the US prepared to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks on Friday.
Rossman furthermore admitted that it is “really scary” to think about how she was approaching the age her mother was when she was killed: 35.
Nonetheless, in remarks arriving as hundreds of millions across the US sought ways to pay tribute to those taken by the deadliest terrorist attack in the country, Rossman said she has drawn strength to confront her circumstances from the valor her mom showed in her final moments on American Airlines flight 11.
Officials credit Rossman’s mother, who also went by just Amy Sweeney, with helping authorities on the ground identify the flight’s hijackers by telephoning details about them to her supervisor. She did shortly before becoming one of nearly 3,000 people killed that day as terrorists crashed planes into New York City’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon in Washington DC and a field in Pennsylvania.
“Thinking about it now, the gravity of that, is truly remarkable,” Rossman said. “I don’t know how many people would be able to do that. And … as I’ve grown, matured, and learned more about the details of the day, it’s just really, really incredible.”
Lawmakers in her and Amy Sweeney’s home state of Massachusetts agree. In 2002, they created an award named after Rossman’s mom, which is given to civilians who demonstrate “exceptional bravery, without regard for their own personal safety”.
Among those to receive the award posthumously was a boy who battled to rescue a kayaker stricken with a medical emergency from waters off Salem, Massachusetts – less than a year before the child, aged 10, was fatally struck by a train. Another such recipient was a man who was fatally stabbed while successfully protecting a pregnant food server from a knife-wielding assailant.
Rossman said she planned to spend part of Friday at the Massachusetts state house for the latest Madeline Amy Sweeney award for Civilian Bravery ceremony. She called it “an honor” to have a role in presenting the annual award, adding: “It’s always been a nice focus for my family to be able to meet anyone else who truly put their life in harm’s way – with no regard for their safety – to save someone else.”
Otherwise, beforehand and afterward, Rossman said she would dedicate herself to raising her daughters in the same Acton, Massachusetts, neighborhood where she and her younger brother grew up, in an area where their father, Michael, still lives.
She shared how she frequently takes her daughters to the same playground where she remembers her mother bringing her and gently pushing her on a swing – before they were torn apart from each other during Rossman’s first week of kindergarten.
“It will be special to say to them, ‘I used to do this with my mom, and now I get to do this with you,’” Rossman said.
She said she would also continue pursuing her professional career investigating money laundering, the culmination of a criminal justice education – including a master’s degree in anti-terrorism – that she embarked on because of the brutal fate that met her mother.
Perhaps as a result of the line of work she chose, Rossman said she has followed the legal processes for four men who have spent years incarcerated at the US’s Guantánamo Bay detention camp in connection with 9/11.
She recounted even traveling to Guantánamo Bay at one point for some of the defendants’ myriad pre-trial hearings, which have largely dealt with disputes over what evidence can be used to try the men.
Yet Rossman said she has had to take some distance from the proceedings, the more prolonged they have become, with the trial not set to happen until at least June 2028.
“Having this drag out doesn’t help any of the families” affected by the September 11 attacks, Rossman said. “Twenty-five years and still awaiting trial – that’s a lot to put the families through.”
Rossman, when asked, said she had little to say about the defendants, one of whom is the accused 9/11 mastermind, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.
“I haven’t moved on – I definitely haven’t forgiven them,” she remarked. But she said she “genuinely” believed there were no words from her to them that could make a difference.
She had much more to say when asked what her message to the US was as the quarter-century mark of the post-9/11 era loomed.
“I still remember those who showed up for us back then – and have kept showing up,” Rossman said.
“So I say, ‘Be kind to your neighbors’ – our communities and having them to lean on are what got us through all of this.”

Driverless cars are taking us on a road to nowhere | Adrian Chiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

I’ve found a hill to die on. Driverless cars. Why? Really, why? If driverless cars are the answer, then what is the question? Who asked for them? Oh yes, they’re fine for the novelty value, for the lols, for the clicks. We probably know someone who’s been to California or China and sent home a video of their driverless journey. Fine fun for feeble minds, if you ask me. And feeble-minded is how we’re all going to end up if this madness takes hold.
It’s been a slippery slope since the invention of automatic transmission, rendering our left legs and arms redundant and sparing us the trouble of feeling our way up and down through the gears. Then there was the coming of satnav, before which time we needed a sense of where we were in the world and which direction we were facing. Now that’s gone, we can find our way anywhere without really knowing where it is. Not good.
But OK; I drive an automatic and I use satnav, so I’ll concede on those, as well as on some of the safety features, cruise control, speed limiter and so on. But the line has got to be drawn somewhere – and it’s time to get the pen out.
There are inventions that fall the right side of that line – washing machines and dishwashers spring to mind. But there’s a difference between labour-saving and lobotomising. I do a lot of driving and, while I often despair at the recklessness and stupidity of some drivers, mostly I marvel at the miracle of skill and cooperation that is the craft of driving. Each of us at the wheel takes responsibility for powerful, heavy machines, working with hundreds, thousands, millions of others to keep things moving. Yes, things can go calamitously wrong, but overwhelmingly things don’t. It’s astonishing, when you think about it.
Will driverless cars do any better? I doubt it. And where will that leave us, the ex-drivers, slack-jawed, de-skilled, slouched without purpose in the back seat? With nothing to do except stare out of the window and dream up more clever-dick tech we could do without.
And here’s the real tragedy – how much the tech-bro willy-wavers could achieve if they put their undoubtedly brilliant minds to better use. How about a gamechanging alternative to fossil fuels, for example, or road surfaces that don’t develop potholes. Feel free to add to this wishlist. If driverless cars are anywhere near your Top 10, then I’m afraid we can’t be friends.
Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

Last week, Donald Trump suggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize the Falkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations.
The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast.
Trump characteristically turned the conversation toward a grievance, and his disappointment with the UK’s initial reluctance to provide support for the Iran war launched on 28 February by Israel and the United States.
That reluctance was fairly easy to understand at the time, given that the White House refused to consult Nato allies as it planned its sneak attack, and the goals of the war were (and remain) imprecise and inconsistent.
It should be added that Nato is a defensive alliance, designed to resist a Russian invasion from the east, not support a US invasion from the west, to seize Greenland from a Nato ally. Further, Nato has no business in the Middle East. The words “North Atlantic” inside “North Atlantic Treaty Organization” make it clear that Nato is all about Europe, bringing North American troops (including both Canadians and Americans) into an interlocking defense structure with European partners.
That includes roughly 80,000 US troops stationed in Europe, a strategic fact of the highest order, one that would suggest careful vetting of remarks about a Nato ally like the United Kingdom. Roughly 10,000 of those troops are based in the UK, in fact.
Emboldened by Trump’s careless remarks, the president of Argentina, Javier Milei (a fan of Margaret Thatcher), delivered a windy speech about “the winds of change”, designed to shore up his sinking popularity, approximately 37% in July. He hinted that the US would back Argentina if it were to renew its territorial ambitions, and called the UK a nation “in decline”.
Those tremors deepened early this week, as the UK’s announcement of sanctions on Israeli settlers released a predictable explosion from the Trump administration, and Israeli threats to recognize Argentinean sovereignty in the Falklands.
The UK will survive Milei’s speech, which stemmed from Trump’s unfocused complaints, and the surreal fabrications that get so much attention yet contribute so little knowledge. The diplomatic flare-up will fade, but memories will linger of Trump’s poorly chosen words, and the ease with which he chose to abandon Britain – on British television, no less.
It’s also another stark reminder of how foreign the themes of democratic aspiration are to the 47th president. Were Argentina to seize the Falklands, it would overturn the result of a very democratic election, the 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islanders chose to remain connected to the UK. More than 90% voted; of 1,517 votes cast, a whopping 1,513 were for remain. That’s the voice of the people speaking.
Democratic presidents have never had a problem talking about democracy. Similarly, most Republican presidents have understood this language. Nixon was not gifted in this way, and George W Bush got many things wrong – Iraq above all – but he seemed to mean it when he spoke of the yearnings of peoples to be free.
Ronald Reagan could achieve poetry at times, as he spoke of those suffering behind the Iron Curtain, and in other autocracies, and meditated on how the US had historically given hope to the world’s disenfranchised. In his 1989 farewell address, he argued: “She’s still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home.”
It’s impossible to imagine these words being spoken from today’s Oval Office, just as it would be difficult to find a president more alienated from the goals of genuine self-determination.
In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter – a statement about their commitment to democracy, free trade and peace.
A year later, they issued an anniversary statement about their shared goals and values. It offers wistful reading at a time when the language of great ideals appears to be woefully dated:
“When victory comes, we shall stand shoulder-to-shoulder in seeking to nourish the great ideals for which we fight. It is a worthwhile battle. It will be so recognised through all the ages, even amid the unfortunate peoples who follow false gods today. We reaffirm our principles. They will bring us to a happier world.”
- 
  Ted Widmer is a former White House speechwriter, and the author of an anthology, American Speeches. His most recent book is The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text (Library of America)

HOW KOREAN DESIGNERS ARE RESHAPING 1,000-YEAR-OLD HANJI PAPER
For Paris Design Week 2026, running from September 10 to 14, 2026, the Korea Craft & Design Foundation (KCDF) brings the tactile qualities of traditional Korean craftsmanship to Maison&Objet with ‘Hanji House’. Crafted from paper mulberry bark fibers, Hanji is a thousand-year-old handmade substrate reimagined as a high-performance biomaterial for contemporary furniture, lighting, and spatial architecture. Inside the exhibition, a dynamic interior skin diffuses light demonstrating how this renewable plant-based medium offers solutions for modern built environments.
Korea Craft & Design Foundation presents ‘Hanji House’ at Maison&Objet 2026 | all images courtesy of KCDF
KOREAN CRAFT SHAPED INTO A BIOMATERIAL FOR CONTEMPORARY SPACES
Promoted jointly by the Republic of Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism (MCST) and KCDF, the showcase brings Hanji into international design dialogues. Traditionally applied across writing, windows, and flooring, the material now spans cultural heritage conservation, art restoration, furniture, and lifestyle elements. This international showcase arrives at a pivotal moment, anticipating UNESCO’s decision later in 2026 on whether to inscribe ‘Traditional knowledge and skills associated with the production of Hanji and related cultural practices in the Republic of Korea’ on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
‘Hanji embodies centuries of craftsmanship and traditional papermaking knowledge while offering the sustainability and versatility sought by today’s design industry. In this meaningful year marking the 140th anniversary of Korea-France diplomatic relations and with UNESCO’s decision approaching, we hope to share the beauty and contemporary potential of Hanji with the world and create greater opportunities for businesses rooted in Korean traditional culture to expand internationally,’ says Kyungbae Kim, President of KCDF.
marquage g’s signature ‘Hanji Shakerbox’ leverages the paper’s physical resilience to form continuous curves
WEAVING ORGANIC FIBERS INTO DESIGN AT MAISON&OBJET 2O26

In the center, industrial design studio SWNA presents an experimental furniture collection showing how Hanji blends with rigid elements like metal and stone to form floating curved lights, cabinets, and luminous partitions.
Across the pavilion, seven Korean makers show how this durable, plant-based medium transitions into functional design objects. Participating studios, including HANJI PARK Materials Lab, FIDES INTERNATIONAL Co., toolpress, SOMIDANG, marquage g, CURATED COLUMNS, and PULBAT, bring together handmade heritage sheets, art restoration supplies, stationery, fragrance pieces, and interior fixtures. Uniting traditional handcraft with modern production, the exhibition provides architects and designers with a practical, sustainable material for contemporary spaces.

Trump’s Attacks on the Environment Are Out of Touch With America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

The most pro-American stance a leader can take is to defend our best ideas. America's national parks and our nation’s beautiful environment are part of our heritage, identity, and are ultimately our greatest strength.
From President Theodore Roosevelt dramatically expanding public lands protections to President Richard Nixon signing the Clean Air Act, our best days have come when protecting the environment was led by leaders on both sides of the aisle.
The current administration is not honoring that shared American value. Nearly two years into President Donald Trump’s second term, his administration is failing the American people on the environment, on our national parks, and on the public lands that are supposed to unite us.
Plenty of people in the environmental movement would’ve opposed anything pro-environment this president did on mere partisan principle. I’m not one of them. Early last year I worked closely with the president’s team and several cabinet officials to help shape a well-intentioned and potentially powerful executive order: “Make America Beautiful Again.” This initiative called on his cabinet to secure a historic investment in our public lands, our forests, our water, and outdoor recreation. I firmly believed in the concept, and I still believe in its potential, but we’ve gotten the opposite of what was promised.
This president labels his policies “America first,” but on public lands and national parks he’s simply put America last. As someone who was in those rooms making the case, I could not be more disappointed. And it doesn’t need to be this way.
Their record is dark. Thus far, the Trump Administration has gutted national park staff, opposed by around 86% of Americans. They’ve proposed sell-offs of public land, which is opposed by nearly 90% of voters in Western states, where these spaces are concentrated. They’ve prioritized rollbacks to policies like the Endangered Species Act, which is opposed by 85% of Americans. They’ve stripped protections for clean water, clean air, national forests, and more, also opposed by the vast majority of Americans.
On issue after issue, this administration has landed on the wrong side of the American people on the environment. Public blowback has stopped a few of these decisions, but a new threat to the great American outdoors seems to surface almost every week. These are quite possibly the two worst years for our environment under a president in my lifetime.
I’ve sat across from dozens of White House officials, and I can tell you there are people who care deeply about conservation. My sense is that their voices are being drowned out by those who primarily act in opposition to the Democratic Party, many of whom have never spent real time in America’s grandeur and do not understand what it means to the rest of us. They are doing the president a disservice. His single most popular act in his first term was arguably signing the immensely bipartisan Great American Outdoors Act, the largest investment in our national parks in history. Now, on an issue that could unify the country and win him support from every walk of life, he and his team are deliberately walking the other way.
The President and his team could defend any one of these choices on its own, justified by claiming they’re making the government more efficient, that local management of our land is better, or that they are unleashing economic growth. Yet, taken together, their actions add up to a plain refusal to treat our environment and our public lands as a priority in any real sense. More than that, I am concerned by their lack of proactive, positive environmental policies. It’s backwards, and it cuts against the American voter and against our national character.
Two things can exist simultaneously. The economy is, understandably, the country’s top concern right now. But it does not have to come at the cost of shrinking or dismantling the country’s natural resources and beauty. Smart, limited government does not require slashing America's grandest idea. It does not mean choosing polluters over citizens. It does not mean railroading projects through communities that never asked for them. It does not mean overriding the will of the people.
Nearly a third of all land in the United States is publicly owned and managed by the federal government. The current approach compounds decades of these lands being mismanaged and desperately underfunded.
Our air quality and water quality are worsening, invasive species are spreading at alarming rates, soil health is degrading, and much more. How we care for these resources should not be a partisan policy fight. It should be a productive dialogue that shapes the American landscape itself and improves the lives of families in every corner of the country.
Our national parks aren’t political; they’re American.
I am often told by friends on the political left that Trump will never make conservation a priority, that Republicans simply hate the environment. I understand the cynicism.
But it is neither productive nor true to who Americans actually are. The vast majority of the American voters want the same things when it comes to our National Parks and environment. Our leaders, specifically around this Administration, just aren’t reflecting that right now. Outside of Washington, Americans would love to see this president, and every president, protect these places.
My prediction: The Republican Party will continue to lose voters if they fail to protect our environment, and it should. Americans believe our nation’s beauty is worth defending. We ought to follow the public, not an endless political game of ping-pong.
Americans don’t wear a party patch on their sleeve when it comes to the health of our environment. They wear pride in this nation's beauty. Today, a record-low share of Americans believe our environment is healthy. If there was ever a wrong moment to make cuts, this is it. Not when energy demand, AI, data centers, and screen addiction are straining this country like never before. Not when visits to National Parks and public lands are near an all-time high — and those lands need more care, not less. Not when Americans expect their tax dollars to build historic investment in our environment, not strip it away.
America has always found a way, albeit imperfectly, to balance protecting our environment with growing our economy. We do not have to ruin our public lands to save our economy. Investing in the places that keep us whole benefits our mental health, our physical health, and our economic health.
History will never look kindly on a leader who lets America’s most beloved places decline. President Trump has two years left to prove he’s better than that. He can work across partisan boundaries and accomplish popular, common-sense environmental wins, or he can be remembered as the worst president for America’s environment in modern history.
The choice is his. And it shouldn’t be a hard one.

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Europe eyes a role in Ukraine settlement talks; the US is unlikely to reduce its Middle East military presence after the Iran war; and Vietnam sees relations with Russia as a key strategic choice. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Europe eyes role in Ukraine settlement talks
European Union institutions are discussing ways to join talks on Ukraine, a European Parliament member told Izvestia. However, experts believe that Europe shares a consensus on the need to continue military operations, which is why meaningful dialogue with Russia has not yet been launched.
