August 2026 ties for hottest month ever recorded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:51:11 UTC
18:51:11 KST

August 2026 has tied for the hottest month ever, sharing the record with July 2023, according to new data from the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.
The global surface air temperature for August was 16.96 degrees Celsius, or 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit. It’s the warmest August ever recorded and some 1.65 degrees C above the preindustrial average. That exceeds the 1.5- degree-C increase that the Paris Agreement once identified as the tipping point for irreversible damage from global warming. The United Nations admitted last week that consistently surpassing that threshold is now “unavoidable.”
That temperature statistically matches the previous record, which was set in July 2023 at 16.95 degrees C, or 62.51 degrees F.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
World ocean temperatures this August also tied with March 2024 for the highest on record across all months. Western Europe and the U.S. had their hottest summers overall, according to Copernicus and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.
The record may come as no surprise after a summer marked by extreme weather, from wildfires to floods, and on the cusp of what scientists believe will be a historic El Niño. This cyclic climate phenomenon drives up temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, altering the world’s climate and weather patterns for months. Together, these factors all likely contributed to August’s record-breaking heat—but human-driven climate change is the main cause of extreme temperatures and is only set to accelerate.
Marc Alessi, a climate scientist at the Union of Concerned Scientists, noted in a statement to Scientific American that “this El Niño is occurring on top of a changed climate from the burning of fossil fuels.” Indeed, scientists believe that, regardless of whether 2026 breaks the record for hottest year ever, 2027 almost certainly will do so because of the El Niño conditions.
“We now live in a completely different climate than the one that existed 50 years ago,” he said.

UK Light Guns can only parachute from allied aircraft
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:50:27 BST
18:50:27 KST

British L118 105mm Light Guns can still be deployed by parachute, but only from suitably cleared allied aircraft, while 16 Air Assault Brigade retains the option of flying the weapons into a Tactical Landing Zone using RAF A400M Atlas aircraft, the Ministry of Defence has said.
The position was set out by Defence Minister Luke Pollard in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what impact the current restriction on parachute deployment of the Light Gun was having on 16 Air Assault Brigade’s operational airborne capability.
Pollard said: “16 Air Assault Brigade remains able to deploy Light Guns by air, including through Rapid Air Landing using A400M ATLAS aircraft once a Tactical Landing Zone has been established. The Light Guns may also be deployed by parachute from suitably cleared allied aircraft when operating as part of a coalition. The Department keeps all operational capabilities under regular review.”
The answer confirms that the brigade retains an airborne route for moving its artillery, but distinguishes between rapid air landing from British A400M aircraft and parachute delivery from allied aircraft that have been cleared for the task.
The L118 Light Gun is the British Army’s lightweight 105mm artillery system and is closely associated with rapidly deployable formations because it can be moved by air and operated in areas where heavier artillery would be more difficult to deploy. For 16 Air Assault Brigade, the ability to move artillery quickly is particularly important because the formation is designed around high-readiness forces capable of deploying at short notice by air.
The answer is pretty clear that one option remains to transport Light Guns aboard A400M Atlas aircraft and land them once a Tactical Landing Zone has been established. That method differs from dropping the gun directly by parachute and therefore depends on access to a suitable landing area. Where the brigade is operating as part of a coalition, however, Pollard confirmed that the gun can still be parachuted from allied aircraft that have the appropriate clearance.
Pollard added that Defence keeps operational capabilities under regular review, leaving open the possibility of further changes to the arrangements governing airborne deployment of the L118.

Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:48:13 UTC
18:48:13 KST

Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has failed to persuade the European Commission to help crack down on people renting out their own homes to tourists.
Halsema travelled to Brussels in the spring with the mayors of other big European cities that struggle with mass tourism – like Barcelona and Paris – to lobby for tougher powers to regulate holiday rentals through sites like Airbnb.
But the EU Affordable Housing Act, presented on Wednesday, would not ban or limit holiday lets but instead establishes a standard for when an area is under “housing stress” – defined as one where house prices are at least eight times per capita disposable income and have risen over the past decade.
It then gives local authorities a legal basis to restrict commercial short-term rentals and second-home purchases in those areas.
Combating local damage
 Amsterdam had asked the commission for two things, according to the Telegraaf: more powers to act against people letting out the home they live in, and for the right to intervene once an area’s liveability has been damaged by tourist rentals.
The commission seemingly dismissed both requests. The text of the act explicitly excludes a host’s primary residence from any restriction, on the grounds that renting out your own home does not take housing off the market. It also only covers measures justified by affordability and availability, not neighbourhood nuisance.
“It is questionable whether this proposal is going to help us,” Amsterdam housing alderman Zita Pels told the paper. Dirk Gotink, an MEP for the centre-right NSC, also told the Telegraaf: “we don’t need a European law to solve local problems.”
Amsterdam already restricts renting your own home through sites like Airbnb to 30 nights per year but has tried to go further in the past. In July 2020 the council banned holiday rentals outright in the red light district and part of the canal ring.
The Amsterdam district court overturned that ban in 2021, and the Council of State, the highest administrative court, upheld the ruling in 2023, saying a total ban was disproportionate and the city should first have tested less drastic measures, such as a lower night limit.
For people in the Netherlands with a second home in Spain, Portugal or France, nothing will change for now. The law would allow local authorities in stressed areas to restrict purchases of homes not used as a primary residence, but only for property bought after the measure takes effect.
The proposal must first be negotiated by the European Parliament and member states, a process likely to take a year or more.

Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank are choking the Palestinian economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank are choking the Palestinian economy
An escalating matrix of military closures and roadblocks is devastating local businesses and fragmenting Palestinian land.
In the village of Rujeib, southeast of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian-owned dairy farm suffered a severe blow when a routine shipment of raw milk was delayed at an Israeli military checkpoint.
Al-Kamel Dairy Factory, established in 2022, has two distribution trucks permanently parked in its yard due to a sharp decline in market demand and mobility issues.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Which countries banned goods from settlements but trade with Israel?
- list 2 of 4Israel tells UK to close East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days
- list 3 of 4‘Overdue first step’: UK reacts to gov’t ban on Israeli settlement trade
- list 4 of 4The limits of the UK’s ban on Israeli settlement goods
The reason for this is the proliferation of military roadblocks across the occupied West Bank since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
These checkpoints were established to maintain Israel’s ongoing occupation of the West Bank and to guard Israeli settlements, considered illegal under international law. This has coincided with a wave of pogroms by Israeli settlers on Palestinian towns and villages.
There are about 925 checkpoints and military gates across the occupied West Bank, 147 located in the Nablus governorate, which is Al-Kamel’s primary market, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC).
There has been a drop of more than 50 percent in transport movement in the occupied West Bank since the onset of the genocidal war on Gaza.
The disruptions caused by travel obstructions in the occupied Palestinian territory have severely inflated production and transport costs for Palestinian companies. Al-Kamel has seen sales decline by 30 to 40 percent, forcing the company to lay off at least 12 workers.
“Since the beginning of the company’s establishment, there were several challenges, and among the most prominent of these challenges were the checkpoints and gates spread across the West Bank, and especially the city of Nablus,” Dweikat told Al Jazeera.
“There is a severe siege on the city of Nablus, as you can barely find an entrance to the city of Nablus without a permanent or semi-permanent checkpoint. These checkpoints have led to obstructing movement and increasing transport costs, which necessarily reflects on the product’s price and production costs.”
High unemployment rates, particularly after the suspension of work permits for Palestinian workers in Israel during the genocidal war on Gaza, and a decrease in salaries, have all affected economic activity in the occupied West Bank.
“Unfortunately, in light of the bad economic situation we suffer from due to recession and economic contraction, factories sometimes cannot reflect this increase in cost onto the citizen, because the economic situation is originally deteriorating,” Dweikat said.
Al-Kamel milk trucks now wait for two to three hours to exit Nablus and for longer at surrounding checkpoints. For a commodity as vulnerable to spoilage as milk, these delays are hugely costly for the company.
“We work in the dairy products sector, which is a very sensitive sector that requires refrigerated trucks, and therefore the volume of challenges is very large for us,” said Dweikat. “Frankly, we were forced to sacrifice many of our customers located outside the city of Nablus as a result of these obstacles.”
At the Awarta checkpoint outside Nablus, approximately 2km from the factory, milk trucks can wait for up to four hours to pass through. Delays at checkpoints have seen 10 tonnes of Al-Kamel’s milk go to waste.
“In the end, when it is midday, we tell the driver: ‘That’s it, there is no longer room to exit … and this represents a real danger to the safety of our employees in light of the deteriorating security situation,'” Dweikat said.
Empty markets
A March 2025 study published by the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute (MAS) provides an alarming analysis of the situation.
After monitoring 14 military checkpoints, MAS found that wait times range from 15 to 50 minutes, with the average delay for trips outside the Nablus governorate reaching 42 minutes – a 77.9 percent increase in original travel time.
It is estimated that 191,146 working hours are lost daily due to these delays, costing the Palestinian economy approximately 2.8 million shekels ($764,600) per day, or 62.2 million shekels ($16.8m) a month.
Drivers are forced to cover extra distances to bypass closed checkpoints, costing an estimated 71,000 shekels ($19,203) in additional fuel daily.
This is affecting the local economy in Nablus badly, with Mansour Aliwi, a local spice merchant, describing the city as a ghost town.
“Frankly, the crisis is deepening month after month due to Israel’s closure of crossings and checkpoints, and the prevention of the entry of Arab Israelis into the West Bank,” Aliwi told Al Jazeera. “We rely heavily on shoppers from the rural areas and villages, but the checkpoints have prevented people from arriving”.
The Israeli separation barrier, which cuts into the West Bank, is another major obstacle to mobility.
“The annexation and expansion wall built by the occupation state in 2002 still isolates more than 295sq km [114sq miles] of citizens’ lands,” the CRRC said.
“If the occupation state completes building the planned parts, it will completely isolate 560sq km [216sq miles], approaching 9 percent of the total land in the West Bank.”
Palestinian business journalist Jafar Sadaqa told Al Jazeera that the repercussions of the checkpoints and restrictions on movement prevent workers from reaching their jobs and affect business operations.
“The intensification of these checkpoints over the past three years has led to far-reaching consequences, such as the bankruptcy of companies and their cessation of operations, and subsequently the loss of jobs for thousands of workers and employees, pushing unemployment to unprecedented rates,” Sadaqa said.
“An economy with severed ties cannot be built. There is a complete separation between the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, and a siege and isolation for each of them, not only from each other, but also from the outside world.”
He believes the true cost goes beyond direct financial losses for businesses and workers in the West Bank, but it means that economic growth here is almost impossible.
“It is difficult to calculate the total size of the loss in the Palestinian economy due to these measures,” Sadaqa said.
“They are not limited only to direct financial losses resulting from preventing the movement of individuals and goods, and the destruction of agricultural lands and facilities, but also include the lost opportunities for the Palestinian economy to exploit natural and commercial resources, and the prevention of any possibility to develop regional and global economic relations.”

Russia Spends Record $125 Billion on Military in First Half of 2026, Nearly 44% of Federal Budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:46:41 UTC
18:46:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Spends Record $125 Billion on Military in First Half of 2026, Nearly 44% of Federal Budget
Russia allocated a record 44% of its federal budget to military needs during the first half of 2026.
According to calculations by Janis Kluge, a senior associate at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs based on Russian Ministry of Finance figures, direct defense spending reached 10.7 trillion rubles ($125 billion), as reported by Defence Blog.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This marks a 30% surge compared to the same period in 2025. These expenditures accounted for 10.5% of Russia’s first-half GDP and equaled 57.3% of total federal government revenue, indicating that over half of every ruble collected in taxes went toward funding military operations.
The rise is primarily driven by classified budget items that Kremlin officials do not publicly detail. While Russia’s 2026 budget set a full-year limit of 11.6 trillion rubles ($135.5 billion) for classified spending, the government spent over 8.4 trillion rubles ($98 billion) in these categories in just six months. Historical budget data analyzed by Kluge suggests that approximately 85% of these hidden expenditures fund military requirements.
The proportion of federal resources consumed by the military has grown consistently since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In the first half of 2018, defense spending made up 24.5% of the federal budget, dropping to around 20% in 2020 and 2021.
It rose sharply to 29.6% in the first half of 2023, reached 36.6% in 2024, and climbed to 39.3% in 2025 before hitting 43.8% in 2026. Publicly detailed defense line items remained stable between 11% and 15% annually, meaning virtually all financial growth occurred within secret budget classifications.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, total direct military allocations from the federal budget reached 57.1 trillion rubles ($666 billion).
This figure excludes regional government spending, such as enlistment bonuses and family compensation payments. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, military spending reached 5.9 trillion rubles ($69 billion), driven by a 43% increase in classified spending compared to the prior year.
Kluge noted that part of this spike might reflect delayed 2025 expenses rolled over into 2026 to artificially meet past deficit targets.
The funding expansion coincides with declining oil and gas revenues, which fell 45% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2026 due to Western sanctions and currency fluctuations. Non-energy revenues rose 7%, failing to cover the gap.
Consequently, military costs consumed nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue in the year's opening months. Reports indicate Russian financial officials privately warned Vladimir Putin that current defense spending trends are becoming unsustainable.
Spending intensity typically slows in the second and third quarters, which could lower the full-year military share relative to total economic output.
According to a recent analysis, Russia had directed nearly every second ruble from its federal budget toward military-related spending during the first quarter of 2026.
This record surge pushed defense expenditures to 5.9 trillion rubles ($75 billion)—consuming nearly two-thirds of all government revenue during those three months—and ultimately drove the country’s cumulative federal budget deficit to approximately 6 trillion rubles ($76.4 billion) by the end of May.

Russia’s Prison Service Expands Recruitment to Teenagers Amid 70,000-Staff Shortage

Russia’s Prison Service Expands Recruitment to Teenagers Amid 70,000-Staff Shortage
Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) plans to involve cadets from its educational institutions in working at correctional facilities amid a shortage of over 70,000 employees, according to The Moscow Times.
This initiative is detailed in a draft order published by the FSIN on September 8, which updates 2022 regulations governing higher education standards. Under the new rules, vocational education programs at departmental schools will be tailored to meet the requirements of future prison staff.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Cadets will undergo practical training in correctional facilities and institutions, including colonies, prisons, and pre-trial detention centers.
Their pre-graduation training will take place directly at the institutions where they have signed service contracts. In late August, the agency issued a separate order establishing a new admission process for its vocational secondary schools, allowing applicants to enroll after completing basic general education (at age 15) or secondary general education (at age 17).
In March, FSIN Director Arkady Gostev stated that the personnel shortage reached more than 30.5% in 2025. Given the service's official staff capacity of 234,100 positions, the current deficit exceeds 71,000 employees, up from 54,000 at the end of 2024.
Meanwhile, as inmates were sent to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the country's prison population dropped to an all-time low of under 300,000 people in colonies and detention centers, compared to roughly 466,000 prior to the full-scale invasion.
Expanding the system to include teenagers aged 15 and 16 could negatively impact educational standards, according to Anna Karetnikova, a former analyst at the Moscow FSIN department and former member of the Public Monitoring Commission.
"Now there is a risk that a very poor education will start not at the university level, but already after the 9th grade," she noted, adding that departmental institutions previously produced graduates with weak professional preparation.
These initiatives coincide with broader efforts by state authorities to address staffing shortages across law enforcement agencies, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Emergency Situations, alongside public statements regarding an oversupply of university applicants.
Meanwhile, Russian citizens have repeatedly reported that school administrators refuse to admit children into the 10th grade under the pretext of poor academic performance and low diploma scores.
Earlier, Russia’s central bank gold reserves fell to their lowest level in more than six years as Moscow increasingly relied on liquid reserve assets to meet rising budget demands.

Army vehicle policy breaches more than double in two years
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:46:24 BST
18:46:24 KST

The number of Army vehicles identified in cases involving the incorrect movement or authorisation of non-taskworthy vehicles more than doubled between 2023 and 2025, according to figures released by the Ministry of Defence.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the figures in response to a written parliamentary question from Liberal Democrat MP Alex Brewer, who asked what assessment had been made of cases involving Army vehicles with reported defects being used by personnel and what action had been taken.
Pollard said the Army routinely monitors the condition and safety of its vehicle fleet through engineering management processes, with inspections, supervisory checks and assurance activity recorded through the Joint Asset Management and Engineering Solutions system, known as JAMES.
He said: “The Army routinely assesses the serviceability and safety of its vehicle fleet through established engineering management processes. These include maintenance inspections, supervisory checks and assurance activity recorded and managed on the Joint Asset Management and Engineering Solutions (JAMES) Management Information System.”
According to the figures, Land Equipment Assurance Team inspections identified eight vehicles in 2023 in cases involving the incorrect movement or authorisation of a non-taskworthy vehicle. That rose to 10 in 2024 and 18 in 2025. The 2025 figure represents an increase of 80 per cent compared with the previous year and more than double the number recorded in 2023.
Pollard said: “The Land Equipment Assurance Team inspections capture findings specifically related to the incorrect movement or authorisation of non-taskworthy (NT) vehicles. The findings recorded over the last three full years are as follows; 2023, 8; 2024, 10; 2025, 18.”
The MOD stressed that the figures should not be interpreted as showing that soldiers were unknowingly operating vehicles that were unsafe.
Pollard said: “This data should not be read as evidence that unsafe vehicles were unknowingly used but instead it records a policy breach associated with the journey or authorisation of a NT vehicle on JAMES.”
In practice, the figures therefore relate to breaches of Army engineering and vehicle-authorisation procedures involving vehicles recorded as non-taskworthy on the management system, rather than a count of accidents or confirmed cases in which personnel were unknowingly placed in unsafe vehicles.
Pollard said units are required to act when breaches are discovered, dealing with the immediate issue while reinforcing the relevant engineering procedures.
He said: “Where non-compliance is identified, units are instructed to take corrective action by addressing the immediate issue, reinforcing engineering policy and capturing lessons to prevent recurrence.”

MEPs push to use frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:45:33 UTC
18:45:33 KST

A letter signed by 122 EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum calls for the controversial debate over immobilised assets to be reopened, as Ukraine faces a budget crunch.
More than 100 MEPs have called on European Union leaders to reopen talks on using Russia’s frozen assets to support Ukraine, as Kyiv flags a €23 billion shortfall in defence funding and EU countries remain reluctant to commit more money from their national budgets.
A letter sent on Wednesday and seen by Euronews argues that Moscow should pay for the damage caused by its war, backing a renewed push started by four EU countries at the end of August to unlock the immobilised assets.
The EU holds more than €200 billion in Russian assets, most of it in Belgium. The European Commission put forward a plan last December to convert them into a zero-interest loan to finance Ukraine’s defence against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
But EU countries failed to agree to unlock the funds amid fears over the legal risks, and the plan fell apart at a leaders’ summit in Brussels.
Earlier this year, the bloc gave the final green light to a €90 billion support loan for Ukraine. Still, MEPs warn that it will not be enough, with the estimated cost of Russian destruction already exceeding €600 billion.
Lawmakers from the European People's Party, Renew Europe, the Socialists and Democrats, the Greens/EFA, the European Conservatives and Reformists and The Left signed the letter, which was launched by liberal MEPs Karin Karlsbro, Nathalie Loiseau and Petras Auštrevičius.
It is addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis, European Council President António Costa and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin, who holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
The signatories are urging the European Commission to come forward with a new proposal to overcome the objections raised by some member states, in particular Belgium, which opposed the plan from the outset.
The Belgian government led by Prime Minister Bart De Wever feared being left exposed to Russian litigation since Belgium is the host of Euroclear, the assets’ main custodian. Other countries, including Italy, Bulgaria and Malta, also expressed concerns.
The MEPs’ letter suggests transferring the assets into a new EU instrument that would assume the legal obligations towards Russia’s central bank. This would provide financial support to Ukraine while maintaining economic pressure on Moscow.
“Russia should bear the financial consequences of its war of aggression,” reads the letter, in a blunt political message shared by most of the Parliament’s political groups.

A Teen Girl’s Death Is Prompting Calls to Ban Choking in Porn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

An Australian teenage girl’s death, suspected to be preceded by consensual “choking” during sex, has renewed calls to ban showing the act in porn.
This latest tragedy, reportedly believed to involve sexual strangulation, comes just months after the UK banned porn showing the practice. But despite all the noise, most people still aren’t aware of just how dangerous the trend is.
Sexual strangulation or “choking” during sex, as it’s referred to colloquially, has become wildly popular—especially among adults aged 18 to 35, despite the risk of severe injury, brain damage, and even death. Some researchers argue that porn is to blame for that normalization, but members of the adult industry say that banning depictions of choking won’t stop this kind of content from flourishing or serve as the kind of sex education and media literacy the public sorely needs.
“With the misinformation that’s out there, especially online, many people do think that maybe at lighter pressures they might be ‘safe,’ and that’s not the case,” says Debby Herbenick, a professor at the Indiana University School of Public Health and one of the leading researchers on sexual strangulation. Herbenick cautions that applying sustained pressure to the front and sides of the throat—via your hands, an object, or otherwise—can lead to blood clots and stroke, tears in the carotid arteries, vision impairment, and cumulative brain injuries.
“It’s these things that we wouldn’t even notice,” she says. “Those tiny, incremental changes in your vision, or your brain, or so on.”
Or, in the most extreme cases, death. Pressing on the front of the throat can lead to airway collapse, Herbenick says. Two weeks ago, a 16-year-old girl in Sydney passed out after authorities believe she was strangled by her equally young partner during sex. She died after being taken to a local hospital in critical condition, and the investigation is ongoing. It’s unknown what her exact injuries were.
The Australian Social Services Minister has since said the government is “very seriously” looking at efforts to ban pornographic depictions of choking in sex, in line with the country’s recently passed age-verification laws that ban social media for children under the age of 16. But critics of these social media bans say they don’t actually work and make it harder for teens to access news and information they need, including sex education around the dangers of choking and strangulation.
The data regarding rates of young people choking and being choked during sex can appear staggering. In Herbenick’s 2021 survey of nearly 5,000 college students in the US, 58 percent of women had been choked during sex and a quarter had been first choked by age 17. Researchers in Australia similarly found rates of around half of people aged 18 to 35 engaging in the practice. Herbenick found that women are usually the ones being choked by men during heterosexual sex and that sexual and gender minorities are also more likely to be choked during sex.
“There are other people who say ‘I asked them to choke me or I said it was OK, but then they really pushed past my limits or it was a lot harder than I expected, or I asked them to stop and they didn’t,’” Herbenick says. She also says that while some young men enjoy the act, others “tell us that they don’t want to be choking their partners, but they think they’re supposed to, or they get asked all the time.”
Most of the self-reported occurrences of sexual strangulation among US college students Herbenick surveyed were described as consensual, but when choking is nonconsensual, it can be even more dangerous. In fact, strangulation is one of the strongest predictors for murder in an abusive relationship.
It’s important to distinguish between the different types of intimate partner strangulation: as a form of abuse, nonconsensual introduction of strangulation into what may have started as a consensual hookup, fully consensual choking, and fictional depictions of choking, like what is usually happening in legal pornography and television. But with the exception of staged or implied choking (like placing a hand over a partner’s neck without actually applying pressure), all of these kinds of strangulation carry major and even deadly health risks for the person on the receiving end.
Clare McGlynn, a law professor at Durham University whose work has contributed to pornography regulation in the UK for 20 years, says the amount of porn involving strangulation has risen over the past few decades and corresponds with an increase in children viewing strangulation content.
“If you ask young people, ‘Where do you get your ideas for sex or sexual activity?’ they say ‘porn.’ And you think, ‘Well, yeah, of course you do,’” McGlynn says. “I think its ubiquity in porn does mean that’s why we see large numbers of young people engaging in this practice consensually, because they think through scripts they’ve seen in mainstream porn that it’s normal, it’s expected.”
The UK’s recent ban on porn showing strangulation or suffocation falls under the country’s Online Safety Act, which requires social media platforms, search engines, and other web services to proactively remove illegal material and employ controversial age-verification measures. According to McGlynn, the strangulation ban was adopted in April but hasn’t been implemented or enforced yet, meaning the government has yet to take action against any companies or individuals.
“The platforms aren’t going to act in and of themselves,” she says. “They’re only going to act if they think the regulator is going to take action against them.”
McGlynn believes that within a few years of the ban on strangulation in porn actually being enforced, a new generation of young people may grow up without seeing choking as a standard part of sex. It’s an optimistic view—one that isn’t shared by everyone.
Cherie DeVille, a well-known pornographic actress, points to the fallout from age-verification laws—requiring proof of age to access adult content—as an example of the futility of banning porn. Consumers can simply use VPNs to get around local laws and turn to the unregulated world of sexually explicit content, often hosted by foreign platforms that don’t comply with any of the laws that major companies are forced to obey.
DeVille, who was a physical therapist prior to entering the adult film industry, describes how talent liaisons assist in the negotiation of what is allowed in specific scenes before filming, including choking, which she says never involves putting actual pressure on the trachea.
Pornhub echoed its consent policy for performers in an email statement to WIRED, writing, “We can be confident that the acts that appear in our content are completely consensual, unlike other platforms that don't have the same consent requirements.” Meanwhile, adult creators on OnlyFans are wary of posting anything involving choking after the service was forced to clamp down on most hardcore content in 2021 to avoid banks freezing payments. (OnlyFans didn’t respond to a request for comment about whether choking and sexual strangulation are technically banned on the platform.)
While Herbenick says that young men are more likely to learn about sexual strangulation from porn, young women are more likely to learn about it from memes, mainstream entertainment, or even erotic fanfiction about One Direction. HBO director Sam Levinson featured it in early episodes of Euphoria and The Idol. It was the opener to a chart-topping Jack Harlow song, where he crooned about choking a woman but not being a “killer.”
“Porn is an appealing boogeyman to say we can stop this by regulating this very specific type of speech, despite the fact that this is ubiquitous throughout culture,” says Mike Stabile, the director of public policy for the Free Speech Coalition, which is the nonprofit trade association for the US adult industry. “The solution is education. The solution is to talk about consent rather than try and find a singular cause that, if you were able to censor it, will solve the problem.”
Herbenick agrees about education. She says one of the biggest cultural changes we need to make is for parents to talk to their kids and teenagers about the dangers of strangulation and the type of messaging they’re consuming about choking during sex—whether it’s in porn or the Billboard Hot 100.

OpenAI and Anthropic incidents fuel pressure for AI regulation
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:44:31 EEST
18:44:31 KST

Pressure for stronger artificial intelligence rules is growing across the United States, European Union and United Nations after new security incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic added to warnings from researchers about the risks posed by advanced AI systems.
The debate intensified after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned this week and said leading AI companies were moving too quickly towards systems that exceed human capabilities.
“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote on social media.
Coxon, who previously worked at OpenAI, said researchers inside the industry believe advanced AI poses a risk of human extinction before the end of the decade. Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger also said he placed the risk above 10 per cent within the next decade.
The warnings drew responses from US lawmakers across party lines.
Republican Senator Ted Cruz described AI as a “catastrophic risk”, while independent Senator Bernie Sanders called for a pause in the development of artificial superintelligence until clear safety standards are established.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also warned this week that advanced AI systems pose an “existential risk to humanity” and called for agreed international limits, independent verification and stronger cooperation between governments and developers.
“The need for AI governance is widely acknowledged, but where is the action?” Türk told the UN Human Rights Council.
He pointed to incidents involving AI systems that left controlled environments or acted to avoid restrictions imposed by developers.
Europe has already adopted a different regulatory approach from the United States through the EU AI Act, the bloc’s risk-based framework for artificial intelligence.
The law bans uses considered an unacceptable threat to safety or fundamental rights and imposes obligations on high-risk systems. Rules for general-purpose AI models include requirements covering transparency and, for models judged to pose systemic risks, risk assessment and mitigation.
Transparency requirements under the Act took effect in August 2026, while stricter requirements for some high-risk systems will follow.
The European Commission has also sent information requests to more than 30 AI companies as part of checks on compliance with the law, with a focus including safety and copyright.
European Commission Vice-President Henna Virkkunen said the aim was to ensure that AI developed and used in Europe meets safety and transparency requirements.
The EU approach contrasts with the position taken by the US administration, which has argued against broad AI-specific regulation and favours rules that do not target individual technologies.
The regulatory debate has gained urgency after a series of incidents involving autonomous agents.
Reuters reported that OpenAI agents used more than 10 previously undisclosed websites to communicate with one another despite instructions preventing them from posting online. Six sets of independent investigators examined traces of the activity.
Some researchers identified activity across 18 or more sites, while another group reported evidence involving 23 previously undisclosed sites. Reuters said it was unable to verify every claim but confirmed that investigators agreed the number exceeded 10.
OpenAI said it was reviewing the activity and had not identified other cases matching the severity or scale of an earlier breach involving AI platform Hugging Face.
Anthropic separately disclosed a fourth incident involving one of its models. The company said an early version of Claude Opus 4.6 gained unauthorised access to a third-party system during testing in January.
Anthropic said the incident was not detected until August despite an earlier internal review. The company identified recurring problems involving faulty reasoning about whether models were operating on the live internet and a willingness to take harmful actions while pursuing tasks.
Anthropic has asked independent research organisation METR to examine the incidents.
AI companies themselves have also called for some form of regulation. OpenAI has backed national safety requirements tied to model capabilities, while Anthropic has supported stronger safeguards as systems become more capable.
Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis has called for international oversight of AI safety, while OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has argued that governments should make international coordination on advanced AI a priority.

Tice also said the sanctions damage the security relationship between the UK and the United States and the passing of intelligence between all three nations [US, UK and Israel].
“These tit-for-tat sanctions set everything in the wrong direction; and it achieves nothing,” Tice told the Post.
He also echoed the concerns of many British Jews that Labour’s sanctions stem mainly from a domestic political bid.
“I’m afraid it’s just an excuse by this hard socialist government to kowtow to their Islamist voters, some of whom are still in the Labour Party and some of whom drifted off to the Green Party. I mean, that’s the bottom line,” Tice said.

Leipzig drone could be controlled from anywhere in world — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:43:37 UTC
18:43:37 KST

BRUSSELS, September 10. /TASS/. Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office believes that the technical equipment of the drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport allowed it to be controlled from anywhere in the world, Bild reported.
According to the results of the newspaper’s investigation, the UAV intercepted in Leipzig is a racing drone that was modified using commercially available parts and 3D-printed components. Its battery allowed it to remain airborne for 10-15 minutes.
The device was not equipped with a GPS module, meaning it was actively controlled remotely via a joystick. This control was carried out via a standard mobile network through a built-in 4G module. The Federal Criminal Police Office believes this allowed the operator to "be located anywhere with internet access of sufficient quality."
According to the newspaper, the Federal Criminal Police Office’s assessment sounds like a damning verdict on Germany’s drone defense system. Bild explained that since the drone was controlled via mobile internet, a signal not monitored by the military, it would have been impossible to detect it via radio signals, and electronic countermeasures would have been useless without jamming mobile communications. Radar, cameras, and microphones remain the only available means of detecting such drones, but these methods may become obsolete as drone technology changes rapidly, the newspaper emphasized.
On September 1, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced countermeasures. Specifically, the Russian Consulate General in Bonn will close on September 18. Other measures include terminating the agreement governing the activities of the Russian House in Berlin and tightening entry controls for Russian citizens. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev rejected all accusations made by Germany, calling them unsubstantiated and absurd.
Russian President Vladimir Putin noted that Germany's recent anti-Russian decisions, made under the pretext of the Leipzig Airport drone incident, are another grave mistake by the German authorities that goes against the interests of their people. According to him, these decisions are linked to Germany's domestic political situation and, in particular, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's difficult position.
On the evening of August 4, a drone carrying a homemade explosive device was found on the tarmac at Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Thankfully, the detonator failed to go off. That same night, a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane. Ten days later, investigators found a third drone, as well as traces of a powerful explosive, presumably containing about 50 grams of hexogen. The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office is handling the investigation.

World Suicide Prevention Day: what do latest EU and Spain data show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:43:24 UTC
18:43:24 KST

Suicide deaths in the EU fell slightly in 2023 and are below levels a decade ago. Three in four victims are men. In Spain, figures show a fall, as the WHO calls to end stigma.
48,370 people died by suicide in the European Union in 2023, but the mortality rate continues to fall and is now below the level recorded a decade ago.
This is the picture painted by the latest Eurostat data (source in Spanish), published to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, marked every 10 September to raise awareness of this public-health issue, tackle stigma and promote prevention. Suicide accounted for 1% of all deaths recorded in the EU that year. The standardised rate was 10.4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, compared with 10.6 in 2022 and 12.2 in 2013.
Differences between countries remain large. Lithuania recorded the highest rate in the EU, with 18.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, followed by Slovenia (16.4) and Hungary (16.1). The lowest rates were in Cyprus (3.5), Greece (4.3) and Malta (5.5).
Men accounted for 76.4% of all suicide deaths in the EU. The crude rate was 16.9 per 100,000 men, compared with 5 among women. Mortality also increases with age, reaching 17.3 per 100,000 among people aged 65 and over.
Suicides fall for the third year in a row in Spain
The most recent national figures point in the same direction. In 2025, 3,808 people died by suicide in Spain, 3.7% fewer than in 2024, when 3,953 deaths were recorded, according to provisional data from the National Statistics Institute (INE). (source in Spanish)
This is the third consecutive year of decline since the 4,227 deaths recorded in 2022. In 2025, suicide was the third external cause of death in Spain. Among men, however, it was the leading one, with 2,784 deaths.
Spain has an Action Plan for Suicide Prevention 2025–2027, which tackles the issue from a public-health perspective. Its priorities include improving the information available, addressing stigma and the myths surrounding suicide, strengthening early detection and healthcare provision and improving coordination between the different sectors involved.
The plan (source in Spanish) also focuses on awareness-raising and responsible communication, making it easier to access support services and preventing suicide among people and groups in situations of particular vulnerability.
Breaking the stigma, talking and seeking help
The World Health Organization (WHO) is dedicating its World Suicide Prevention Day campaign (source in Spanish) to the slogan "Changing the Narrative on Suicide" ('cambiar la narrativa sobre el suicidio'). In 2026 its call to action is "Start the Conversation" ('iniciar la conversación'), which aims to challenge myths and stigma and encourage people to talk about what is happening to them and seek help.
For the WHO, changing the narrative also means driving changes in public policy, improving access to quality care and implementing evidence-based prevention strategies. The organisation estimates that more than 720,000 people die by suicide every year worldwide. Seventy-three per cent of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, and suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 globally.
The WHO stresses that asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase the risk and can help them feel understood.

Burnham’s ‘reset’ of foreign policy on Israel and Palestine is promising, but still falls short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:41:47 UTC
18:41:47 KST

When Andy Burnham took the reins from Sir Keir Starmer at the end of July 2026, becoming Britain’s seventh Prime Minister in the last decade, pro-Palestine Britons watched with bated breath.
The last two years under Starmer’s Labour government have all but diminished any hope left on both the home and foreign policy fronts.
They undelivered when it came to fixing the national healthcare system, the NHS, failed to tackle a historic rise in racism, anti-Muslim hate crime and far-right sentiment. And economic growth slowed to a trickle.
When it came to Palestine, a key area of British foreign policy, Starmer’s government refused to recognise Israel’s merciless onslaught on Gaza as a genocide and the forced displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as ethnic cleansing.
Some Britons felt a sense of promise that Burnham would fix the mess that is British domestic policy. But given his strong ties to the Labour Friends of Israel, most were not too optimistic that things would change on the government’s stance on Palestine.
So, it came as a complete surprise when Burnham admitted that Labour “didn’t get it right” when it came to Gaza and, at the start of September, hinted he would take a tougher stance on Israel.
Seven weeks into his new role, Burnham’s government has charged ahead by imposing trade sanctions on Israel for its continued expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, among a series of “new powers to respond to moral emergency in Palestine.”
Products made by Israeli traders on illegally occupied Palestinian land will no longer be imported, such as the Medjool dates that are sold on British supermarket shelves.
In a statement published on social media platform X, Burnham said that the “suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world” and declared that the British government would be doing a 180-degree turn by confirming that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian land is unlawful.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has called it a “reset” of UK policy on Israel.
Is this for real?
It’s a seismic shift in the country’s Palestine policy, which under the last two governments had rested on unequivocal support for Israel.
The recognition of Israeli settlement expansion via the forced displacement of Palestinians as ethnic cleansing has been welcomed by many, but it falls short on several fronts.
Burnham has still not called the slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide, despite the United Nations concluding so.
But given the UK government’s track record of being the last one to hop on the bandwagon – it only took them a year and a half into the genocide to call for an “end to the war” – it is no surprise that Britain has taken eight decades to call a spade a spade: that the construction of Israeli settlements on Palestinian land is illegal and the forced displacement of and violence against Palestinians are forms of ethnic cleansing.
Given its track record, it can very well be said that only when the rest of the world has recognised the Israeli government’s mass slaughter of Palestinians as genocide, will Burnham’s government do the same.
In fact, Miliband said that the British government would not call it a genocide until the International Court of Justice reaches the same conclusion.
Some other measures prove the half-hearted nature of this policy shift.
Britain’s new set of measures includes a ban on arms sales and “other exports that materially contribute to the occupation”.
However, what was not announced in its new policy was whether or not the UK will ban or impose restrictions on Elbit Systems, the Israeli arms manufacturing giant which continues to operate across 16 factory sites in the UK and has had two military export licenses.
For the arms ban to be taken seriously, words and actions must match.
Weapons aside, if we are just talking about the illegal occupation and annexation of the West Bank, which Burnham and Miliband say Britain will not support,
Elbit Systems has also played a part in the occupation and illegal annexation of the West Bank through the production and supply of technologies that the Israeli military uses to build “smart” electronic barriers in Jerusalem, cutting Palestinian residents off from other parts of the occupied territories.
This shift in foreign policy also clashes with prevailing domestic policy.
For Burnham and his government to have truly rectified its stance on Palestine, it must review legislation that enables the restriction of and crackdown on peaceful pro-Palestine protests under the expanded powers granted to police last September by Shabana Mahmood, who retained her position as Home Secretary in Burnham’s new cabinet.
Why it does not add up
While it is still against the law to express support for Palestine Action, which remains a proscribed terrorist group, protests that have had no relation to the group have also experienced crackdowns.
Last year, Palestine Solidarity Campaign reported that the police have imposed conditions on protests, including the banning of banging of pots and pans in solidarity with the famine in Gaza, as well as the use of drums and megaphones.
In December, leading Palestine activists Ben Jamal, who is Palestine Solidarity Campaign’s director, and vice-chair of Stop the War Coalition Chris Nineham, will appear in court to appeal suspended prison sentences after they were found guilty in April of breaching police-imposed conditions on a protest in January 2025.
There has been no indication since Burnham assumed control whether this hardline approach towards pro-Palestine protests will be reviewed.
The Crime and Policing Act, which came into effect earlier this year, has given police further powers to restrict protests, including limiting repeat protests.
This is a blow to the national marches for Palestine, which have been taking place every Saturday in multiple cities since the end of 2023, whose very nature is repeat protests.
On these marches, protestors call for an arms ban, the imposition of sanctions and the recognition of the State of Palestine, the same three actions that Burnham and Miliband stress they are implementing.
In the House of Commons, Miliband admitted that pro-Palestine campaigners, including those who have marched for Palestine, have played an important role.
Hence, right now, domestic policy and foreign policy aren’t tallying up.
The implementation of sanctions on Israel is the first concrete step Britain has taken in decades, but we must not applaud the government for doing the bare minimum.
For Burnham’s government to truly rectify years of appeasing the Israeli government, it must stand strong in the face of the latter’s threats of retaliation, and not give in to pressure from the US.
Perhaps Burnham can take inspiration from the fictional UK Prime Minister in the 2003 film Love Actually: “A friend who bullies us is no longer a friend. And since bullies only respond to strength, from now onward, I will be prepared to be much stronger.”

====================================================================================================

Al-Qaida: 25 Years After 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:41:00 UTC
18:41:00 KST

Twenty-five years after the fateful terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, the fraternity of terrorism scholars and practitioners is divided over al-Qaida’s status. Some believe that al-Qaida still poses a potent threat to global peace and security, albeit of a different nature, while others think it has lost its mojo.
Indeed, al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate it promised its followers. In fact, the global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State (IS), which weakened the former. IS has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor. The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and IS have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world to cut them to size.
The strategic defeat that al-Qaida desperately wanted to inflict upon the United States has not materialized. Indubitably, the U.S. is struggling to retain its global hegemony in the face of China’s meteoric rise, but it is for a different set of reasons. Attributing power challenges to the U.S.-led unipolar system to al-Qaida would be a gross exaggeration and distortion of facts.
In terrorism, violence is the central benchmark of evaluating the success or failure of a terrorist group. Al-Qaida Core, operating out of Afghanistan, has not carried out an international terrorist attack in more than a decade.
The majority of al-Qaida’s top leaders, barring the current de facto chief Saif al-Adel and his deputy Abd al-Rahman al-Maghrebi, have been eliminated by the U.S. in drone strikes and targeted assassinations. Saif al-Adel likely lives in a safe house in Iran and is dependent on Iranian intelligence for his own security. This has undermined his credibility and capacity to command loyalty and obedience from various al-Qaida affiliates.
Of al-Qaida’s various affiliates, Somalian al-Shabab, al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen, and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Mali are the strongest, while al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS), notwithstanding its proximity to the core group, is the weakest.
AQIS has been trying to grow its network in India, especially in Indian-administered Kashmir, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. Barring some nominal successes, it has miserably failed to make an impression since its emergence in September 2014. Nevertheless, it regularly issues a flagship propaganda magazine, “Nawai Ghazwa-e-Hind,” which articulates al-Qaida’s official stance on critical developments. AQIS has been embedding its fighters with various Pakistani jihadist groups to obfuscate its involvement in terrorist attacks, which is consistent with al-Qaida Core’s strategy of focusing on the near-enemy, as discussed below.
Al-Qaida is currently facing a serious leadership crisis, and it will not be surprising if various affiliates still loyal to the mother group adopt the pathway of IS and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). The former’s defection made it the most feared jihadist group and leader of the global jihadist movement, while the latter’s rebellion eased its path to victory in Syria and helped it gain international recognition.
Al-Qaida’s Malian affiliate, JNIM, which has made great territorial strides in Mali, is contemplating following HTS’ footsteps and disassociating from al-Qaida to avoid isolation and reprisals ahead of its complete victory.
At its peak, al-Qaida funded and strategically guided different jihadist groups around the world, including the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Ironically, it is now dependent on the Taliban both for its finances and security. Al-Qaida Core has been reduced to a former shadow of itself; it inspires no confidence in the younger generation of jihadists who self-radicalize online and engage in lone-actor terrorism.
Those who believe al-Qaida continues to be a threat to international peace and security argue that after two decades of the war on terror, the U.S. left Afghanistan by handing back power to the Taliban. Al-Qaida successfully weathered the U.S. strategic pressure and retained its presence in Afghanistan, which constitutes a victory even if it is a pyrrhic one, they claim.
In five years of Taliban rule, al-Qaida has reconstituted itself by embedding with local jihadist movements in Pakistan. It is actively supporting an umbrella militant alliance, Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP). The resurgence of militant violence in Pakistan since August 2021 has increased al-Qaida’s footprint, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Likewise, al-Qaida affiliates in Yemen, Somalia, and Mali have made substantive territorial, financial, and organizational gains.
The threat al-Qaida poses today is qualitatively different from the security challenges it posed to international peace in 2001. The absence of an international mass casualty attack does not make al-Qaida less relevant. Rather, there is a need to take a more nuanced view of the threat it poses.
The terror group has not changed its goal of creating a global Sunni Caliphate or carrying out attacks in the West. However, as the international security environment has evolved, al-Qaida has also changed its trajectory and modus operandi. Now, it is focusing on the near-enemy, i.e., Muslim democratic states that it deems apostate, instead of the “far-enemy,” meaning the United States.
Al-Qaida is no longer investing its time and focus in high-profile attacks like 9/11; rather, it is creating space for itself by aligning with local jihadist movements and obscuring its presence to avoid counterterrorism pressure. It is adopting emerging technologies like drones and 3D-printed technology to build weapons, investing in maritime capabilities, and striving to achieve financial self-sufficiency. All these elements make al-Qaida a potent threat in the long run.
Over a period of 25 years, al-Qaida has shown resilience. It has survived by adapting, decentralizing operations to regional franchises, and moving ideological indoctrination to encrypted social and digital media platforms.
The current threat from al-Qaida is diffused. It relies on homegrown, lone-actor terrorists to carry out low-end attacks, such as stabbing, vehicle ramming, and shootings in the West. This threat, due to its low intensity, is more manageable but less detectable and preventable because people are self-radicalizing online. Furthermore, al-Qaida is engaging in hybrid warfare tactics where violence is one of several elements it is using to achieve its objectives.
So, the singular fixation with al-Qaida’s violent credentials is flawed. Al-Qaida engages in information, ideological, and cognitive warfare alongside violent extremism. It has advised its affiliates to focus on governance by moderating their aggressive jihadist postures.
On balance, al-Qaida has survived the war on terror, and it is far from a spent force; however, the threat it poses is now manageable. At the same time, it is facing credibility and leadership crises that are not likely to subside anytime soon.
On the one hand, for the Taliban regime, al-Qaida is a liability. It can neither own the group nor disown it. The former will result in international diplomatic and security pressure, and the latter will dent the Taliban’s ideological legitimacy in the jihadist world. Likewise, for flourishing regional affiliates like Al-Shabab, JNIM, and Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), al-Qaida Core is more of a nuisance than an ideological mothership.
Al-Qaida remains relevant, but it has evolved and the threat it poses has also evolved. Putting this fact in perspective will help both practitioners and scholars to develop a better understanding of the terror group.

Clyde infrastructure programme expands industry capacity
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:39:57 BST
18:39:57 KST

The Clyde Infrastructure Programme is expanding its industry framework arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity and capability are available to sustain delivery over the life of the programme, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided the update in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made on recruiting staff and securing the level of industry support required for the programme. Pollard said the programme already has established commercial frameworks in place with industry and that its supply chain is working to an agreed delivery plan.
He said: “The Clyde Infrastructure Programme has existing frameworks in place with industry to sustain delivery, with supply chain following an agreed delivery plan.”
The Defence Infrastructure Organisation is now increasing the capacity available within those arrangements to support continued delivery.
Pollard said: “The Defence Infrastructure Organisation (DIO) is extending and uplifting headroom within these frameworks to support delivery and has commenced work to establish successor framework arrangements, ensuring sufficient enduring capacity and capability are available to meet the demand for the life of the programme.”
The reference to additional “headroom” means the DIO is increasing the amount of work that can be placed through the existing frameworks, while the successor arrangements are intended to provide longer-term access to contractors and specialist capability.
The Clyde Infrastructure Programme supports the development of the naval base and associated facilities required for the Royal Navy’s submarine enterprise at HM Naval Base Clyde. Long-term infrastructure work at the site is intended to provide the facilities needed to support current and future submarine operations, maintenance and associated activity as the Clyde continues to develop as a central part of the UK’s naval nuclear infrastructure.

The new segmented approach to procurement is designed to enable programmes to get to contract faster by tailoring of acquisition processes to the type of capability and risk involved.”

Pollard said guidance had now been issued across all three segments.
He said: “The Procurement Segmentation programme has published acquisition guides for all three segments to enable MOD practitioners to apply best practice to drive pace in our acquisitions. These are supported by ‘test and learn’ demonstrators on a variety of Defence programmes.”
The use of demonstrator programmes is intended to test the new arrangements before they are applied more widely across the equipment programme. However, the minister made clear that the reforms remain at an early stage, meaning Defence is not yet presenting a measured result against the two-year contracting ambition cited in Anderson’s question.
Pollard said: “The segmented approach is at an early stage, and benefits will be tracked as its use is expanded across a wider range of procurement programmes.”

Benjamin Netanyahu has overseen a genocide: In his telling, he’s a victim
Ahead of Israel’s national elections, Netanyahu reaches for an old playbook: grievance, blame-shifting and victimhood.
Benjamin Netanyahu is Israel’s most electorally successful — and longest-serving — prime minister. He has overseen Israel’s greatest internal security failure and a genocide in Gaza, yet clung on to power.
Now, as he heads to his 13th parliamentary election, Netanyahu is relying on an old strategy that he has deployed for years, critics say — responding to accusations that might normally end a political career with deflections, subterfuge and claims of victimhood.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What’s behind Netanyahu’s condemnation of this weekend’s settler pogroms?
- list 2 of 4Israeli PM Netanyahu in Gaza, ‘we are not withdrawing’
- list 3 of 4Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands
- list 4 of 4ICC leaders condemn efforts to erode international legal order
In the last few days, a story carried by the Israeli daily Haaretz, claiming that the United Arab Emirates had given Netanyahu advance warning of the Hamas-led attack of 2023, has been met not with reflection, but with legal action, counter-accusations and claims of “foreign interference” in Israel’s elections.
A week earlier, Netanyahu oversaw the launch of a political advertisement likening himself to a bullied child.
In the video, a child is portrayed who – it is revealed – is being picked on by anti-Netanyahu classmates, with signs of “anyone but Bibi”, referring to Israel’s prime minister and leader of the right-wing Likud party.
Netanyahu has been prime minister for 18 years across three separate periods and has been widely acknowledged as a key player in shifting Israeli politics to the right.
But despite this, he has still been eager to use populist discourses to portray himself as fighting the establishment as a perpetual victim of the system.
Israeli political psychologist Neta Oren from George Mason University told Al Jazeera that self-victimisation is an important part of Netanyahu’s playbook, and this is continuing into his next election campaign.
“For years, he has presented himself as the representative of ‘the people’ against the elite. Populism works especially well from the opposition, but what happens when you are the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history?” she said.
“Netanyahu’s solution has been to blame his failures on other forces — particularly the ‘deep state’ — and to portray himself as their victim, just as he portrays his supporters as victims of the old elite.
“This can make him appear weak or ineffective as a leader, but the sense of victimhood among his base, and their animosity toward the old elite, is so strong that this framing can still be an effective political tool for maintaining their support.”
Recently, Netanyahu has appeared to compete with the country’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for the legacy of the far-right Zionist militia Irgun, which was contained once the first Israeli government, led by David Ben-Gurion, came to power in 1949.
Rival news conferences have been held by the two Israeli party leaders to commemorate the “oppression” of the militia, which was responsible for the deaths of hundreds of Palestinian civilians and British soldiers during the Palestinian Mandate period.
These tactics appear drawn from the same political playbook as those used by populist politicians across the world: to ally themselves with those who feel opposed to the state and distance themselves from their previous scandals.
Earlier this month, Netanyahu attempted to deflect blame for his alleged failures ahead of and during the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, claiming that “defence officials” had deliberately chosen not to wake him during the first hours of an attack that he would otherwise have contained.
His wife Sara Netanyahu appeared to go further, suggesting to the pro-government Channel 14 last month that opposition leader and former General Yair Golan’s reaction to the assault — when he woke up and drove directly to the site of the attack — suggested that he must have known of Hamas’s plans in advance.
Global trends, Israeli audiences
Such methods have been used by other politicians, such as United States President Donald Trump, Hungary’s Viktor Orban and India’s Narendra Modi. But Netanyahu’s use of victimisation by the “establishment” goes back further to around when former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995, claiming that Israel’s left had forgotten what it meant to be Jewish.
Analysts describe Netanyahu’s particular brand of populism as intended for a specifically Israeli audience and a shared sense of Zionist and Jewish identity among his party’s Likud base.
Similarly, many of Likud’s supporters are Mizrahi, drawn from migrants from across the Middle East and North Africa and typically come from lower-income backgrounds. They are attuned through experience as seeing themselves opposed to the Ashkenazi European establishment in Israel, something Netanyahu has been eager to feed on.
Dani Filc, a professor at Ben Gurion University and author of the book Hegemony and Populism in Israel, said that Netanyahu’s claim to victimhood is a common feature in populist narratives.
“Populism builds on a victimised people … His acting out of victimhood echoes with the fact that many Likud supporters have a collective memory of being excluded and sometimes oppressed by the mainly Ashkenazi establishment, and also plays with Jewish collective memory as victims,” he told Al Jazeera.
This discourse has dominated Netanyahu’s repeated confrontations with the judiciary and media since 2023.
Both Netanyahu’s 2020 corruption trial and his judicial overhaul have been cast by the Israeli right-wing not as legal or constitutional processes, but as a battle against a so-called unelected “deep state”, with its members, they claim, including the media and judiciary.
Daniel Bar-Tal, professor of psychology at Tel Aviv University, said this narrative has allowed him to distance himself from government failures.
“Netanyahu desires the status of victim,” Bar-Tal told Al Jazeera.
“He blames the deep state that he built, the officers that he nominated … just to be clean and not responsible. To be a victim has many advantages. You can be a perpetrator, you can disengage from ethical norms, and so on.”

Companies hand over more than 255 tonnes of used tyres for recycling during summer campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:38:00 UTC
18:38:00 KST

During the four-week “Give Tyres a Second Life” environmental campaign organised by AJ Power Recycling and 3R, more than 210 companies handed over 255.30 tonnes, or more than 25,500 used tyres, for recycling. The campaign organisers will continue accepting used tyres in September.
From 14 to 25 September, legal entities will be able to dispose of used passenger vehicle tyres free of charge at the 3R waste management facility at 4 Atlasa Street in Riga. To use this opportunity, companies must complete an online application form in advance and reserve a tyre drop-off time at www.3r.lv/akcija. Tyres will only be accepted at the pre-booked time. They will not be accepted without prior registration and electronic confirmation.
Only passenger vehicle tyres may be handed over during the campaign. Each legal entity may dispose of up to 500 tyres. Tyres from trucks, tractors and industrial machinery will not be accepted free of charge. The tyres must be clean and without rims; they must not contain leaves, mud, soil or plastic waste. Before handing over their tyres, companies are encouraged to review the campaign rules, which will be sent to the email address provided in the application form once the registration has been confirmed.
Passenger vehicle tyres will also be accepted free of charge from private individuals. During the campaign, up to four passenger vehicle tyres without rims may be handed over per car. Tyres from trucks, tractors and industrial machinery will not be accepted. Private individuals may bring their used tyres without prior booking on any working day until 25 September, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., at the 3R waste management facility at 4 Atlasa Street in Riga.
Large quantities of accumulated used tyres pose environmental and safety risks. Sending tyres for responsible recycling helps reduce their adverse environmental impact and allows their constituent materials to be reused. After collection, the tyres undergo pre-treatment, sorting and preparation for further recycling. Specialised recycling plants process the tyres into rubber granules used in the production of sports surfaces, mats and other products, as well as in construction, including road building.
Outside the campaign period, passenger vehicle tyres may be handed over for a fee at sorted-waste collection sites and other tyre collection points. These collection sites also accept lead-acid and other types of batteries, oil filters and lubricating oils. A list of the collection sites is available at https://ajpower.lv/laukumi.
