Formula 1 sends Madrid holiday rents soaring: up to €20,000 near circuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:37:53 UTC
18:37:53 KST

The Spanish Grand Prix is driving luxury short-term rents in Madrid up by as much as 1,000%, and in Valdebebas some flats are being listed at up to 20,000 euros for the race.
Madrid is bracing for Formula 1's arrival in the city with a parallel contest to the sporting one: that of soaring accommodation prices. The Spanish Grand Prix, to be held from 11 to 13 September at the Madring circuit, has sent the cost of short-term rentals in areas close to the track, as well as in some of the most exclusive neighbourhoods in the city centre, soaring.
In recent weeks, it was still possible to find homes to rent in Valdebebas, where the circuit is located, next to Ifema, for prices reaching as high as €20,000 for stays of barely a few days. In some cases, owners explicitly restricted availability to the period of the race.
"A 1-minute walk from the Madring circuit: experience the Formula 1 GP of Spain 2026 from the best-located luxury chalet in Madrid," read one of the listings that could still be found on the Airbnb platform last Tuesday, which was asking €11,400 for four days in "a house designed for VIP groups."
The increase is particularly striking when compared with usual prices in the area. Some of these properties are priced at several multiples of the cost of a standard monthly rent, which in this neighbourhood is usually around €2,500 a month, taking advantage of the intense demand concentrated into a single weekend.
"There are homeowners, some of whom are even living in their properties, who are putting them up for rent," said Mario Serrano, founder and director of Inmobiliaria Valdebebas, in comments to 'Antena 3'. "Thanks to Formula 1, the spotlight has been put on the Valdebebas neighbourhood."
Up to €500 for a parking space
The pressure on accommodation is spilling over even into parking spaces. In Valdebebas, offers of up to €500 for a garage space for this coming weekend have been recorded.
The strong demand also reflects attendance forecasts. More than 120,000 tickets have already been sold and, according to organisers' estimates, more than 80,000 spectators will travel from outside the Madrid region, including some 45,000 from other countries.
The expected economic impact helps to explain the corporate interest the event has generated. A report by audit agency PwC, cited by the Grand Prix organisers themselves, puts the economic impact of the race on the region at €467 million and forecasts the creation of around 8,850 jobs.
Accommodation for teams, sponsors and VIP clients
Proximity to the circuit has become one of the clear selling points of the properties on offer. Many listings highlight the advantage of walking to the circuit, having views over the track or being able to avoid the expected transport problems that will arise during the Grand Prix.
According to estate agents consulted by local media, a large part of this demand comes from the teams and sponsors, as well as organisational staff and VIP clients, all of them profiles with far greater spending power than most of the spectators.
The phenomenon is not limited to private homes. Hotels have also raised their rates ahead of the arrival of the thousands of visitors expected to travel to Madrid for the race. An analysis by Simon-Kucher, cited by the 'Antena3' channel, puts the average price offered over the Grand Prix weekend at €1,071 per night, 147% more than the previous week.
The city centre, a meeting point for 'prime' visitors
Although the circuit is located around Ifema, on the outskirts of the city centre, the luxury rental market is experiencing particularly strong pressure in the historic centre of the capital. Barnes, an estate agency specialising in high-end homes, estimates that 'prime' rentals have seen increases of up to 1,000% compared with a normal week, local media reports.
The districts of Salamanca, Chamberí, Chamartín, and Los Jerónimos are among the areas where this effect is most evident. According to the agency, visitors with high spending power do not necessarily prioritise staying next to the circuit, but rather look for central locations and neighbourhoods regarded as upmarket.
"This unique place has its own style. Enjoy the Madrid Grand Prix from a privileged location and with maximum comfort," reads an advert posted on Airbnb, offering an "entire accommodation" with five bedrooms, in the Chamartín district, for €17,100, from Friday to Monday.
Slightly cheaper is the flat that, for those same dates, is being rented in the Salamanca district for €14,600, which is advertised as "ideal for enjoying the Grand Prix with a high-level experience."
So the arrival of Formula 1 in Madrid has not only launched a new sporting competition in the Spanish capital, but also, at least for the coming days, has turned proximity to the circuit, the availability of a parking space or having large rooms in the historic centre into key elements in the other big race taking place in the city: that of those looking to squeeze the maximum return from their homes thanks to the Grand Prix.

Chemical disposal feared in Gülistan Doku case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:36:43 UTC
18:36:43 KST

Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek (AA Photo)
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek stated on Sept. 9 that the body of Gülistan Doku, a university student who disappeared in eastern Türkiye in 2020, may have been destroyed using chemicals, as investigators continue work on the long-running missing-person case.
Speaking to court reporters in Istanbul, Gürlek said prosecutors were working with particular sensitivity on locating Doku’s remains. He also said some statements contained in the case file indicated that Doku’s body may have been moved several times, and at some point may have been dissolved using a chemical substance.
Doku, a 21-year-old university student, disappeared in the eastern province of Tunceli on Jan. 5, 2020. Her disappearance has remained unresolved. The investigation was significantly expanded in 2024 and has since focused on possible homicide and an alleged cover-up, with dozens of suspects detained or jailed and investigators examining possible evidence tampering, deleted digital records and DNA traces from vehicles linked to former officials.
Gürlek also provided updates on several other high-profile investigations. Regarding the 2011 death in prison of former intelligence officer Kaşif Kozinoğlu, he said the grave would be opened to obtain DNA samples and determine whether there were signs of poisoning or other findings that could shed light on his death.
On the investigation into the religious organization associated with Alihan Kuriş, Gürlek said the focus was on financial links and that Turkish authorities were cooperating with German judicial authorities.
Gürlek stressed that the investigation was not directed at any religious community but at alleged fraud and illicit financial structures.
He also discussed the investigation into the death of Rojin Kabaiş, whose body was found on the shores of Lake Van. He said DNA examinations had been conducted but that questions surrounding her mobile phone remained unresolved and that investigators had yet to reach a definitive conclusion.
Gürlek further addressed investigations involving musician Haluk Levent and the Ahbap charity, saying authorities were examining financial transactions, promissory notes and property transfers amid allegations that donations were misused. He said the investigation remained ongoing.
Finally, regarding the Istanbul Municipality corruption case, Gürlek said prosecutors were examining new reports and evidence that could potentially lead to an additional indictment.

One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:34:33 UTC
18:34:33 KST

Moldova closed its airspace on the afternoon of 8 September and delayed the plane carrying Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Norway after a Russian drone crossed into the country, its government said in a statement to Reuters. The aircraft was cleared for takeoff once officials established that it had come down on Moldovan territory. Norway's prime minister described the episode as a near-miss, and neither government has said how close the drone came.
Russia runs three things at once along the EU's eastern frontier—mass drone attacks on Ukraine, drones crossing into Moldovan and Romanian airspace almost weekly, and strikes on the border checkpoints tying the three countries together—and states without interceptors can answer only by closing their skies.
What happened, and when
Moldova's National Army detected a Shahed-type drone entering from Ukraine at 16:20, the country's Defense Ministry reported. It flew toward Bender, a city in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria, then turned toward the capital, Chișinău, by 16:32. At 16:37, it left the country over western Moldova and headed into eastern Romania, across the Prut river border.
Controllers restricted the airspace over central Moldova at 16:30. The same drone came back from the Romanian side, crossed the north of the country, and came down outside a village in the northwest, near the Romanian border, setting dry vegetation alight, according to the log. Nobody was hurt, and the airspace reopened at 17:39, more than an hour after it closed. The BBC's Ukrainian service placed the crash near a different northern village, without naming a source, so the exact spot is unsettled.
The violation fell in the window when Zelenskyy's aircraft was preparing to take off, Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The civilian airport he was leaving from suspended operations and the border service closed the nearby crossings, the outlet added. Three departures and four arrivals were delayed in all, Reuters said.
A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy’s plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king’s funeral, Norway’s PM says
How the plane and the drone crossed paths
Zelenskyy flies an Airbus A319 corporate jet, and the threat to it probably came from a jet-powered Geran drone that crossed Romanian and then Moldovan airspace at around 17:00 that day, Militarnyi wrote, publishing the drone's track from the monitoring channel Oko Hora. That fits the return leg in the army's log, though no authority has tied a specific aircraft to the delay.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the broadcaster NRK the plane was almost hit as it prepared to leave, without naming his source. His office later described a danger recorded in Moldovan airspace that forced the delay. Norway's Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said Zelenskyy recounted the details himself at a closed meeting in Oslo.
Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska attended the farewell ceremony for King Harald V, who died on 28 August. Around it, the president worked on air defense, meeting Støre and then executives of defense companies from partner countries about the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, which Norway's government casts as a cheaper alternative to the Patriot.
Trending Now
The next night, the border crossing
Overnight on 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing on Ukraine's border with Moldova, killing two people and injuring three. The dead were Ukrainians, and a Moldovan citizen was among the injured, Moldova's Foreign Ministry told the broadcaster TV8. Border guards reopened the crossing that afternoon.
Russia claimed it had struck the crossing because it was used for military logistics. Moldova's Foreign Ministry rejected that outright, saying no weapons move through its territory, and that the people crossing there are families, children with their mothers, and the elderly. It is one of the working crossings on the Odesa Oblast stretch of the Ukrainian-Moldovan border, where the heaviest traffic runs through Palanca and Giurgiulești.
Moldova's President Maia Sandu condemned both the strike and the Geran-type drone that had forced her country to close its airspace the day before, and said the events show Ukraine needs more air defense.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
The pattern, and Moldova's empty sky
Russia has hit at least five checkpoints on Ukraine's western borders since late August, four of them facing Moldova and one facing Romania, and the drone that struck the Kotlovyna crossing on 20 August flew in through Moldovan airspace. Euromaidan Press has covered part of that campaign, including burned food cargo near the Giurgiulești crossing in August. The State Border Guard Service has called such strikes an act of terrorism, because people are present at the crossings when they are hit.
In the air, Moldova can do little. It is still buying its first serious air defenses, so it restricts airspace and waits while Romania scrambles jets against the drones that reach its side. It logged three airspace breaches in nine days in August, and more than 100 drones were detected near Romania in four days that month.

Ricardo Reis warned that tariffs could drive up prices in the United States and potentially trigger a new wave of inflation.
Portuguese economist Ricardo Reis is reported to have been removed from the race for the post of chief economist at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) after criticising Donald Trump’s tariffs.
According to the Financial Times, which cites three anonymous sources, Ricardo Reis had been lined up for the role, but the IMF is said to have backed away after learning of the economist’s views on US trade policy.

Ricardo Reis declined to comment on the story or make any statements to the Financial Times.
The case comes against a backdrop of pressure from the Trump administration on economists who are critical of US tariffs.
The IMF refused to comment on the selection process, citing confidentiality, and insisted that the choice had been "rigorous and competitive".

Interministerial meeting on measures benefitting Polish community and Poles abroad
09.09.2026
Joint measures of the Polish government and the Senate benefitting the Polish community and Poles abroad in 2026 and plans for 2027 prevailed on the agenda of a meeting of the Interministerial Team for the Polish Diaspora and Poles Abroad. The session was chaired by MFA Secretary of State Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski.
Held on 8 September, the meeting brought together representatives of government ministries, the Office for War Veterans and Victims of Oppression, Statistics Poland, and the Senate of the Republic of Poland: Senator Bogdan Borusewicz, Chair of the Senate’s Emigration Affairs and Contacts with Poles Abroad Committee, and Minister Ewa Polkowska, Head of the Senate Chancellery.

The participants emphasised the need for further cooperation and coordination of measures with individual beneficiaries of programmes and calls for proposals for Poles living abroad. They also brought up the significance of the system of subsidising calls for proposals.
The meeting saw a presentation of 2027 budget plans of institutions engaged in cooperation with the Polish community and Poles abroad and an agreement on the direction of further work under the Government Strategy for Cooperation with the Polish Community and Poles Abroad for 2025–2030. A key task for the coming months will be to prepare an analysis and evaluation of the state of play in terms of the priorities and strategic objectives envisaged in the Strategy for 2025–2027. The evaluation will mark an important stage in the implementation of the Strategy and offer a summary of the first three years since its launch. The gathering discussed the guidelines for an interim report.

====================================================================================================

‘Clean energy is the surest path’: Europe should be leading the energy transition, says UN executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:31:04 UTC
18:31:04 KST

“If humanity doesn't cut the fossil fuel pollution baking our planet, this summer's brutal heat, fires and droughts will seem mild compared to the permanent climate nightmare that will follow,” said Simon Stiell, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary.
“Europe’s summer has been hot as hell. This is the price of global fossil fuel addiction hitting home,” warns Simon Stiell, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Executive Secretary.
Speaking to the European Parliament Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety in Brussels, Stiell appealed to lawmakers to “double down” on “Europe’s longstanding climate leadership” and speed up the transition to clean energy.
“It’s entirely in Europe’s interests to stand firm behind climate action – and to boost it: to build resilience to climate impacts – protecting global supply chains, on which all economies depend. And to slash global emissions.”
Climate action is Europe’s cheapest insurance policy
Europe’s summer of extreme heat was the hottest on record for the UK and Italy, with more countries likely to announce the same. Stiell listed just some of the costs: “We’ve seen mass evacuations. Power stations closed. And trade routes choked. Crops lost. Yields down. And food prices up – and set to rise further.”
There were also tens of thousands of excess deaths across Europe, with 14,000 in Germany and 5,232 in Spain, its highest figure since 2015.
“Disasters are pushing up insurance premiums. Leaving some entirely uninsurable,” said Stiell. The cost of insuring a home in an area hit by extreme weather or climate-related disasters has been going up for years, with some insurers refusing to cover homes in areas hit by the 2025 wildfires in Los Angeles.
A 2024 report by Insure Our Future found that climate change was behind more than a third of all weather-related insurance losses in the previous 20 years. But it is not private insurers that absorb climate damage – it is the public budgets, which EU politicians are responsible for, that take the hit.
A study earlier this year found that between 1980 and 2021, extreme weather and climate events caused economic losses of over €560 billion in the EU’s 27 member states, of which only 25–33 per cent was insured. The Vienna University study was commissioned by MEP Lena Schilling (Greens/Austria).
“Investing just 1–2 per cent of global economic output can avert losses of 11–27 per cent of GDP, with every dollar spent delivering savings of five to 14 dollars,” says the study’s author Professor Sigrid Stagl. She explicitly describes climate action as “life insurance for the planet”, a systemic risk-management strategy in which the costs of mitigation and adaptation are small relative to the scale of potential losses.
Climate action boosts – or stalls – economies
No doubt aware of the importance of economic growth to the lawmakers he was speaking to, Stiell laid out the costs of extreme heat: “One study calculates this summer’s extremes will cost Europe €180 billion – in lost labour productivity, and disruption to food, energy and transport. That’s equivalent to carving a full percentage point from European GDP – the same amount the EU economy is forecast to grow.”
Stiell linked climate action with the economic markers politicians are often judged on when elections loom: “To be soft on climate action is to be soft on inflation and the cost of living, soft on sovereignty and security, and soft on economic growth and jobs.”
“Climate cuts across the core concerns of voters, whatever their politics: family health, community safety and economic stability. Affordable food and available water. Jobs, business costs, and household bills.”
So what is Stiell suggesting EU policymakers should do?
To achieve affordability, economic stability, energy security, and policy-making autonomy, Stiell asserts: “Clean energy is the surest path to deliver, cheaply and safely.“
While China leads the way on energy generated from clean sources, Stiell asserted that EU countries are doing well. “Thanks to growing investment, renewables now provide around half of Europe’s power. In the first six months of this Middle East conflict, solar alone saved Europe more than €30 billion in avoided gas imports.”
Stiell drove home the many economic opportunities in clean energy, saying Europe is already leading the way on clean tech.
What does the UN want Europe to focus on at COP31?
Stiell used his speech to emphasise the importance of “throw[ing] itself behind helping COP31 in Türkiye deliver further progress.”
This year’s UN-led climate talks – COP31 – will be held in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026.
The talks bring together governments and industry from all over the world, making them the catalyst for climate-related policy – the Paris Agreement was born at COP21 in 2015. Based around days of negotiation to reach the final deal, lawmakers’ commitment to attend and push for strong climate action during COPs is vital.
Stiell explained how each set of recent talks has built on the last: “No single COP can solve the climate crisis overnight, but each moves global efforts forward – building on the last, and looking to the next: From a global agreement in Dubai to transition away from all fossil fuels. To a new climate finance goal in Baku. And steps forward on a just transition in Belem, which ushered in the era of implementation.”
Stiell asked politicians to arrive at the talks prepared with what they want the final deal to include, and prepared to make compromises.
One of the COP Presidency’s priorities is for 35 per cent of final global energy demand to be met by electricity by 2035. Stiell emphasised the EU’s strength here: “Around one in four new cars sold in Europe is now electric. And battery deployment is accelerating.”
He also pointed to methane, food waste and security, and making cities more resilient to climate extremes as “areas where the impact and urgency are greatest”.

‘Clean energy is the surest path’: Europe should be leading the energy transition, says UN executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:31:04 UTC
18:31:04 KST

“If humanity doesn't cut the fossil fuel pollution baking our planet, this summer's brutal heat, fires and droughts will seem mild compared to the permanent climate nightmare that will follow,” said Simon Stiell, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary.
“Europe’s summer has been hot as hell. This is the price of global fossil fuel addiction hitting home,” warns Simon Stiell, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Executive Secretary.
Speaking to the European Parliament Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety in Brussels, Stiell appealed to lawmakers to “double down” on “Europe’s longstanding climate leadership” and speed up the transition to clean energy.
“It’s entirely in Europe’s interests to stand firm behind climate action – and to boost it: to build resilience to climate impacts – protecting global supply chains, on which all economies depend. And to slash global emissions.”
Climate action is Europe’s cheapest insurance policy
Europe’s summer of extreme heat was the hottest on record for the UK and Italy, with more countries likely to announce the same. Stiell listed just some of the costs: “We’ve seen mass evacuations. Power stations closed. And trade routes choked. Crops lost. Yields down. And food prices up – and set to rise further.”
There were also tens of thousands of excess deaths across Europe, with 14,000 in Germany and 5,232 in Spain, its highest figure since 2015.
“Disasters are pushing up insurance premiums. Leaving some entirely uninsurable,” said Stiell. The cost of insuring a home in an area hit by extreme weather or climate-related disasters has been going up for years, with some insurers refusing to cover homes in areas hit by the 2025 wildfires in Los Angeles.
A 2024 report by Insure Our Future found that climate change was behind more than a third of all weather-related insurance losses in the previous 20 years. But it is not private insurers that absorb climate damage – it is the public budgets, which EU politicians are responsible for, that take the hit.
A study earlier this year found that between 1980 and 2021, extreme weather and climate events caused economic losses of over €560 billion in the EU’s 27 member states, of which only 25–33 per cent was insured. The Vienna University study was commissioned by MEP Lena Schilling (Greens/Austria).
“Investing just 1–2 per cent of global economic output can avert losses of 11–27 per cent of GDP, with every dollar spent delivering savings of five to 14 dollars,” says the study’s author Professor Sigrid Stagl. She explicitly describes climate action as “life insurance for the planet”, a systemic risk-management strategy in which the costs of mitigation and adaptation are small relative to the scale of potential losses.
Climate action boosts – or stalls – economies
No doubt aware of the importance of economic growth to the lawmakers he was speaking to, Stiell laid out the costs of extreme heat: “One study calculates this summer’s extremes will cost Europe €180 billion – in lost labour productivity, and disruption to food, energy and transport. That’s equivalent to carving a full percentage point from European GDP – the same amount the EU economy is forecast to grow.”
Stiell linked climate action with the economic markers politicians are often judged on when elections loom: “To be soft on climate action is to be soft on inflation and the cost of living, soft on sovereignty and security, and soft on economic growth and jobs.”
“Climate cuts across the core concerns of voters, whatever their politics: family health, community safety and economic stability. Affordable food and available water. Jobs, business costs, and household bills.”
So what is Stiell suggesting EU policymakers should do?
To achieve affordability, economic stability, energy security, and policy-making autonomy, Stiell asserts: “Clean energy is the surest path to deliver, cheaply and safely.“
While China leads the way on energy generated from clean sources, Stiell asserted that EU countries are doing well. “Thanks to growing investment, renewables now provide around half of Europe’s power. In the first six months of this Middle East conflict, solar alone saved Europe more than €30 billion in avoided gas imports.”
Stiell drove home the many economic opportunities in clean energy, saying Europe is already leading the way on clean tech.
What does the UN want Europe to focus on at COP31?
Stiell used his speech to emphasise the importance of “throw[ing] itself behind helping COP31 in Türkiye deliver further progress.”
This year’s UN-led climate talks – COP31 – will be held in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026.
The talks bring together governments and industry from all over the world, making them the catalyst for climate-related policy – the Paris Agreement was born at COP21 in 2015. Based around days of negotiation to reach the final deal, lawmakers’ commitment to attend and push for strong climate action during COPs is vital.
Stiell explained how each set of recent talks has built on the last: “No single COP can solve the climate crisis overnight, but each moves global efforts forward – building on the last, and looking to the next: From a global agreement in Dubai to transition away from all fossil fuels. To a new climate finance goal in Baku. And steps forward on a just transition in Belem, which ushered in the era of implementation.”
Stiell asked politicians to arrive at the talks prepared with what they want the final deal to include, and prepared to make compromises.
One of the COP Presidency’s priorities is for 35 per cent of final global energy demand to be met by electricity by 2035. Stiell emphasised the EU’s strength here: “Around one in four new cars sold in Europe is now electric. And battery deployment is accelerating.”
He also pointed to methane, food waste and security, and making cities more resilient to climate extremes as “areas where the impact and urgency are greatest”.

Want to Get Off Your Phone? Mina Kimes Suggests Having a Baby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

As an NFL analyst and podcast host, Mina Kimes consumes a lot of news online, but ask her to spend more than 15 minutes on “any social media platform” and you might have a problem. “It's like simultaneously pouring molasses into your brain and lighting it on fire,” she says.
These days, a declaration of social media hatred isn’t exactly a hot tech take. But Kimes is full of those too. For one, she thinks FaceTiming anyone outside of your family is “insane behavior.” She also prefers to keep her phone perpetually unlocked and practices inbox zero like it’s a religion. And she loves finding corners of the internet where she can see men encouraging other men.
For our latest User Behavior, Kimes tells WIRED all about her favorite heartwarming subreddits, her “hijacked” Spotify Wrapped, and her folder of memes.
I just got it replaced because I cracked the screen with my car. I was resting it on the roof and it slid down as I was opening the trunk, and it was a real crime scene. When you bring a cracked phone to an Apple store, you know that they've seen everything, but you still feel deeply ashamed. Usually I'm pretty good about not cracking it, which is amazing because I have a toddler who likes to drop it and throw it and stuff. I got it replaced, and I didn't get the new one because I like this model.
It’s dying on me a little bit. The fan, at inappropriate times, starts making noises like an air-conditioning unit circa 1985. It's like a radiator whistle. And it's one of those things where you start developing weird habits and superstitions. I'm like, “Maybe if I tilt it this way and don't plug it in and don't run too many things, it'll be fine. It won't make noises.” But the truth is, I probably should just get it serviced or replaced.
I actually don't have it set up to show me, which sounds a little bit like the meme “I pretend I do not see it,” but I would estimate it's probably around four hours a day. This is going to sound insane, but I have my phone set to where it doesn't lock because I don't like seeing a clock at night. So my way of hiding that information was to just have my phone not lock. When I did that, I realized it would register as a very high screen time, but I'm not actually on my phone. I realized the screen-time feature was kind of functionally useless for me.
To be honest, I don't feel bad about screen time generally, because I use my phone for reading the news, studying, looking at tape, preparing for work, answering emails. None of that stuff bothers me. However, I would feel terrible if I saw how much time I spend on social media. I think those things kind of get conflated a little bit when we think about screen time and phones. At least for me, I think there's a pretty big distinction.
I feel bad when I spend more than 15 minutes on any social media platform, because it's like simultaneously pouring molasses into your brain and lighting it on fire. And I have very much noticed a very pronounced and obvious correlation between my happiness and how much time in any given day I spend on social media in particular.
On my phone, I have Instagram, Reddit, and Bluesky. But I've taken stuff off. It's a little bit tricky because when I post clips or promote my podcast or YouTube or the various things I do at ESPN, I often do that on my phone, which makes it hard to eliminate them. But something I'll do is when I'm done, I'll just log out immediately: post, log out, walk away.
The best way to digital detox is to have a kid, because when I spend time with him I'm just not on my phone by necessity. I think that's been the most helpful thing. So there you go, Zoomers. There's a reason to have children. And honestly, I do notice when I spend a day with him, whether it's hiking or at the beach, and I'm not on my phone, I'm infinitely happier at the end of the day than any other day in my life.
I primarily use Spotify. The data is completely cooked because of the aforementioned 3-year-old. So when they do Spotify Wrapped, I swear to God, it used to be cool, but now it's been hijacked by Raffi, Elmo, Ms. Rachel, Mickey Mouse. My son is really into Mickey’s Countdown lately. I feel like 99 percent of my Spotify listening now is just atrocious kids' music. Raffi's the GOAT though. I don't want to lump him in with some of the people that I mentioned. Raffi stands alone.
This is probably the thing where you're going to learn the most about me. Zero unread emails and inbox 10 and under is how I live my life. It's such an important part of how I work and get stuff done.
The number one thing I should lead with is, for a litany of reasons, I just do not let communication build up, which can be difficult, because I subscribe to a couple newsletters, and I won't archive them until I've either read them or scanned them. But I can't get to work until I feel like my mind is clear, and my mind isn't clear if my inbox isn't clear. I think it's probably something I inherited from my dad, who was an Air Force major, and from a very young age he taught me the importance of to-do lists, which I also abide by. Sometimes, on a to-do list, I’ll set aside half an hour or whatever to get my inbox back down to sub-10.
Sometimes that means that when I reply to emails, my response is a fraction of the email that was sent to me. And I think people feel social pressure to match an email with a commensurate email. To live the Inbox 10 lifestyle, you cannot abide by that pressure.
Same thinking, same principle, same possible OCD.
I FaceTimed with my brother, who's on vacation with his family in Delaware at the moment. I'm not a big FaceTimer. And candidly, I feel like FaceTiming someone who is outside of your family is insane behavior. But that's another way in which having a child changed how I use technology, I suppose, because it really is a wonderful way for young children to see distant relatives and communicate with them.
I recently, and I'm very late to this, started strength training at a gym for the first time in my life. For my entire life, I've only gone to the gym to run. And now I'm just learning what all these machines do and how to use them. But I'm like a child. I'm a total neophyte in this world. I have a trainer, but I've also found it’s a really encouraging and fun section of the internet.
It's a picture of my son standing next to a tower he built in his room. I feel like at this point, 95 percent of the photos on my phone are of my son. It's kind of sad; you can see the exact point where we had him because it used to be all pictures of my dog, and then it just completely switches to pictures of my son.
I can’t even remember what I was using it as a meme for, but I clearly needed that screenshot to use as a meme.
I don't really use LLMs. If I do, it's for either menial household questions or basic search. And I only use it for search because search is now useless due to AI.
I've read and listened to a lot of people talk about how it's revolutionized their workflow, and they're training agents to make appointments and they're building these elaborate meal plans. And to me, that doesn't sound interesting. That just sounds exhausting. We have this phrase in football called “looking for work,” when a player on the field is looking for work—looking for someone to block, for example. And I just think about that whenever I hear those stories. It just sounds like you're looking for work.
Also, just fucking do it yourself. It’s not that hard to make a fucking restaurant reservation.
Whether you use vertical cry or laugh cry is a strong divide between different types of people.
I post everywhere to try and get my work out there and get it seen and read. But I would say the one that I use the most is Bluesky. While it has its flaws, there's definitely the occasional sports ball person in my mentions. I’ve found the interactions on there are the most like interactions I have with people in the real world, which is a rarity on the social internet these days.
Everyone says Twitter, right? Which is a bummer because it used to be really fun and essential for news. When breaking news was happening, it was a place you'd go to get on-the-ground impressions. You could meet friends, you could find new writers and comedians, and all of that feels lost just because Elon completely killed the vibe. And I say that because obviously he's done things far more serious in terms of poisoning the discourse, and the place is a cesspool for racism and misogyny and misinformation, but it's also just, like, a terrible fucking hang. Everyone either seems miserable or is determined to make other people miserable.
I am a dedicated Times reader. I know it has its pluses and minuses. I read the Times daily newsletter every day. I find it's generally a pretty good way to stay informed, and there's still really good journalism. There's another newsletter I love for people in Los Angeles called L.A. Material that I've really enjoyed, just getting more local news, which seems to be where things are headed newswise.
Whenever I'm watching a TV show, I do like to read the subreddits, whether it's Love Island or Silo. I find that the conversations about the TV shows are best there. I also like some of the popular ones that are general interest, like r/mildlyinteresting or r/food.
Sometimes the algorithm on the main feed surfaces subreddits for me that I'm intrigued by. One thing, this is going to sound so weird, is the reddit for bald people, r/bald. It's guys, and women, posting pictures of themselves, asking the community if it's time to “come home,” as they call it: shave their heads. Or people who have done it and are asking what people think. And then it's thousands of people being like, "You look amazing. Congrats, king." And I just love that. I love that sort of encouraging corner of the internet.
I got this Bose Bluetooth speaker as a giveaway at some event I did. It has completely made car rides with my kids so much easier, because he holds it and he feels like he has control over the music. I play music out of there instead of my car now, and he loves it. And he’s now so much more willing to take long car rides because of it.
I have a folder. It's a lot of Simpsons stuff just because I'm a Simpsons fanatic. J.R. Smith. I haven't thought about that one in a while. That's a good one. Oh, I love the one of Marge Simpson dancing. I don't even know how to describe that. There’s also the José Mourinho “I prefer not to speak. If I speak, I am in big trouble.” It's a sports thing.
Anything I want to say, I'll just say it.
Especially when I was a writer and business journalist, but even afterwards, I loved Google Reader as a way to organize news articles and feel like I got through them. It was just a great interface. I use Feedly now, which is pretty good to read news, but doesn't quite hit like Google Reader used to hit.
I have recently gotten into trivia after competing on Celebrity Jeopardy and getting introduced to that world a bit. I started to get more into trivia and studying it and tactics. And something I do now at night is just try to learn as much as I can about random topics and then make flashcards.
So last night I made a bunch of flashcards about the Chinese dynasties: Han dynasty, Tang dynasty, Song dynasty.

Natural History Museum opens 64th mushroom exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Natural History Museum opens 64th mushroom exhibition
Researchers recommend heading out to forage, but warn against picking poisonous mushrooms, 15 species of which found in Estonia can be fatal.
The first mushrooms to arrive at the Natural History Museum's exhibition came from Mustamäe: common puffballs, which are edible.
"Our botanists still recommend not eating mushrooms that grow in the city. It is better to choose mushrooms found in forests, farther away from urban areas," said Liisa Johanna Lukk, communications manager at the Estonian Museum of Natural History.
Mushrooms growing in cities and alongside roads may contain heavy metals, including lead, cadmium, mercury and arsenic.
The Natural History Museum's mushroom foragers have a busy night ahead of them, as their haul from Lahemaa must be arranged before Thursday. The most intriguing specimens are, of course, the poisonous mushrooms. Estonia has around 200 poisonous species, 15 of which can be fatal. Visitors to the exhibition can learn which poisonous mushrooms can be easily mistaken for edible species.
"One of the deadly poisonous mushrooms found in Estonia's forests is the death cap. It can, for example, be confused with the green brittlegill. Viewed from the cap, the green brittlegill is also green. The important differences are on the stem, which is why we emphasize that you should not cut a mushroom off in the forest, but instead remove the entire mushroom from the moss," said mushroom exhibition curator Marja-Liisa Kämärä.
The mushroom exhibition opens at 4 p.m. Thursday. It is the museum's 64th mushroom exhibition and also the last to be held in its old building before the museum begins moving to its new location this fall.
The mushroom exhibition will remain open until September 20.

South Africa processes over 86,000 foreigners for deportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:28:33 UTC

South Africa processes over 86,000 foreigners for deportation
South Africa has processed 86,596 foreign nationals for deportation or repatriation in just over two months, the government announced amid heightened tensions over undocumented migration.
Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi, who chairs the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration, said the cases were handled June 14 to August 20 through coordinated law-enforcement operations.
Kubayi told reporters on Tuesday that Malawian nationals formed the largest group processed during the two-month period, followed by Zimbabweans and Mozambicans. Government data indicated that 90% of those repatriated entered South Africa illegally, with 95% classified as crossing the border outside official entry points.
The minister blamed deteriorating infrastructure along South Africa’s 4,471 km land border for creating vulnerabilities “exploited by illegal crossings, smuggling and transnational crime.”
The mass returns follow anti-immigration protests and attacks that began in March and escalated ahead of a June 30 deadline for undocumented migrants to leave the country, prompting accusations of xenophobia against South Africa.
Mozambique initially said seven citizens died following the unrest, including five in what it described as xenophobic attacks and two in a road accident while fleeing the alleged violence. The South African authorities disputed the account, linking only two deaths to the unrest.
Several African governments, including Ghana, Nigeria, Malawi, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe, have since evacuated nationals fleeing the violence.
In response to mounting tensions, President Cyril Ramaphosa unveiled a five-point plan in June to deport undocumented migrants, tighten border controls, overhaul immigration laws, and expand cooperation with other African countries.
Ramaphosa warned against vigilantism, saying immigration enforcement is the sole responsibility of authorized state officials. He said “xenophobia, Afrophobia, or any other form of intolerance” has “no place” in South Africa.
Pretoria has denied targeting foreigners indiscriminately and pledged to prosecute those responsible for violence. The government also opened a temporary processing center in Musina, near the Zimbabwean border, to handle a surge in returnees. Justice Minister Kubayi said the center processed more than 4,000 people on its busiest day in July, but only 58 in August, prompting its closure.

Kyiv Shortens Curfew, Changes Metro Rules as Russian Drone Attacks Intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:28:03 UTC
18:28:03 KST

Kyiv has shortened its curfew and introduced new rules for public transport and bridges as Russia steps up attacks on the capital with jet-powered drones.
Starting Thursday, Sept. 10, the curfew will run from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m., one hour shorter than before, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The change will allow public transport to operate for an additional hour. Restaurants, shopping and entertainment centers, and other leisure venues will keep their existing hours.
Four special bus routes will run from Kyiv’s Central Railway Station during curfew hours to help passengers whose trains arrive late. Overnight transit of oversized vehicles will also remain permitted.
Metro service will depend on threat level
Kyiv’s metro crosses the Dnipro via the Southern Bridge, meaning parts of the network are exposed during Russian missile and drone attacks. Under the new rules, service will change depending on the threat level.
On the Green Line, trains will continue crossing the Southern Bridge during a yellow threat level. If the level rises to red, the line will split into two sections: Syrets-Vydubychi on the right bank and Slavutych-Chervonyi Khutir on the left bank.
The Red Line will operate only underground during alerts, between Akademmistechko and Arsenalna. Replacement bus Route 1M will connect the two sides of the Dnipro, running between Palats Sportu and Lisova.
Passengers should expect delays or temporary service changes when an alert begins or the threat level changes.
3,200 km Into Russia: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Gas Facilities in Record-Breaking Strike
New rules for Kyiv’s bridges
The Dnipro divides Kyiv into its right and left banks, with several major bridges carrying cars, buses and other ground transport between them. The crossings are particularly exposed during Russian attacks.
The Southern Bridge will remain open, but traffic will be suspended for 30 minutes after an air raid alert is declared and again for 30 minutes after it is lifted. Entrances from Saperno-Slobidska Street and Mykhaila Boichuka Street will be blocked.
The Podilskyi-Voskresenskyi Bridge will also have 30-minute pauses after alerts begin and end and will operate in reversible traffic mode.
The Paton, Metro, Northern, and Darnytskyi bridges will continue operating normally.
What the yellow and red levels mean
A yellow threat level signals a potential danger but does not automatically shut down businesses or public institutions. They can continue operating if they follow safety rules and provide easy access to shelters.
A red threat level indicates a higher and more immediate danger and can trigger tighter restrictions on transport and other services.
The threat level is separate from an air raid alert. The alert tells residents to seek shelter, while the threat level determines how city services and transport operate.
Residents can check the current status through the Kyiv Digital app.
Events banned, businesses can stay open
Kyiv has temporarily banned outdoor entertainment and sporting events, as well as indoor events at venues without shelters.
Shopping centers, cafes, and service businesses can continue operating during a yellow threat level if they follow safety protocols and ensure staff and visitors can reach shelters.
Administrative service centers and social institutions will also operate normally under a yellow threat level. Schools and medical facilities will continue under previously approved rules.
The changes come as Russia has intensified attacks on Kyiv with jet-powered drones, with the capital now facing more than 10 air raid alerts a day.

'The days of safety are over': Russian airports face record closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:27:21 UTC
18:27:21 KST

Ukraine's drone campaign forced an average of 32 airport closures a day across 32 Russian airports including Moscow and St Petersburg, with summer totals already exceeding all of 2025, as Zelenskyy warned airlines and insurers that "the days of safety in Russia's skies are over."
Russian airports temporarily closed 993 times in August — an average of 32 times a day — as Ukrainian drone operations forced repeated airspace shutdowns across the country.
Industry data shows it was the most disruptive month for Russian civil aviation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in early 2022.
Figures from aviation security firm Osprey Flight Solutions state that restrictions were imposed at 32 airports in August, including Moscow and St Petersburg.
Over the summer as a whole, 2,182 closures were recorded — already exceeding the full-year total for 2025.
The Insider, an investigative Russian outlet, calculated that the August closures reached more than six times the 2025 monthly average.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines and insurers on 1 September that Russian airspace "is becoming completely unsafe" for civil aviation.
"We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That's why we are warning our partners: the days of safety in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said.
Andriy Zagorodnyuk, a former Ukrainian defence minister, said the goal was not to attack civilian aircraft but to create lasting uncertainty.
"Ukraine is not seeking to shoot down civilian aircraft, but it is making Russia's skies unsafe for flying," he said in last week's comments to Ukrainska Pravda.
The trigger for airport closures is the activation of what Russia calls the "Kover" — Russian for "carpet" — protocol, an air defence procedure designed for rare emergencies that grounds or redirects all civil aircraft when a drone threat is detected in the area.
Military analyst Mykhailo Samus, of the Centre for Army, Conversion and Disarmament Studies, said airport closures were part of a broader strategy of economic exhaustion, alongside rising insurance premiums, the withdrawal of foreign carriers and reduced domestic mobility.
"Airport closures are the new reality for Russian aviation," he said.
'Impossible to take off or land'
Russia's Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said no significant disruptions to civil aviation would be allowed, yet operational data contradict his statement.
In the first three days of September, an average of 86 flights per day were cancelled in Russia, according to FlightRadar24 — a level comparable to August's worst periods.
On the most severe nights around Moscow, between 77 and more than 100 flights were delayed or cancelled in a single overnight period.
Passengers have documented the disruption in detail on social media and in regional news feeds.
"We've been sitting on the plane for an hour, Vnukovo has been closed, nobody is explaining anything," one traveller wrote on Telegram.
"Pulkovo won't let the flight depart, Moscow won't receive it." another posted. A third passenger said, "The online board is all red, it's impossible to take off or land."
Some foreign carriers that had continued to fly to Russia after the full-scale invasion have since adjusted routes or suspended operations.
Changes have affected Pegasus, Flydubai and Air India, according to industry media.
Passenger numbers on the Moscow-St Petersburg route have fallen by 20-23%, while rail demand has risen by roughly 20% in response.
The investigative outlet Agentstvo has noted that the aviation disruption overlaps with pressure on other parts of the Russian economy, including declining oil refining capacity, higher logistics costs and interruptions to warehouse operations caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on industrial facilities.

Over the summer as a whole, 2,182 closures were recorded — already exceeding the full-year total for 2025.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines and insurers on 1 September that Russian airspace "is becoming completely unsafe" for civil aviation.
"We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That's why we are warning our partners: the days of safety in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said.
Andriy Zagorodnyuk, a former Ukrainian defence minister, said the goal was not to attack civilian aircraft but to create lasting uncertainty.
"Ukraine is not seeking to shoot down civilian aircraft, but it is making Russia's skies unsafe for flying," he said in last week's comments to Ukrainska Pravda.
The trigger for airport closures is the activation of what Russia calls the "Kover" — Russian for "carpet" — protocol, an air defence procedure designed for rare emergencies that grounds or redirects all civil aircraft when a drone threat is detected in the area.
Military analyst Mykhailo Samus, of the Centre for Army, Conversion and Disarmament Studies, said airport closures were part of a broader strategy of economic exhaustion, alongside rising insurance premiums, the withdrawal of foreign carriers and reduced domestic mobility.
"Airport closures are the new reality for Russian aviation," he said.
'Impossible to take off or land'
Russia's Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said no significant disruptions to civil aviation would be allowed, yet operational data contradict his statement.
In the first three days of September, an average of 86 flights per day were cancelled in Russia, according to FlightRadar24 — a level comparable to August's worst periods.
On the most severe nights around Moscow, between 77 and more than 100 flights were delayed or cancelled in a single overnight period.
Passengers have documented the disruption in detail on social media and in regional news feeds.
"We've been sitting on the plane for an hour, Vnukovo has been closed, nobody is explaining anything," one traveller wrote on Telegram.
"Pulkovo won't let the flight depart, Moscow won't receive it." another posted. A third passenger said, "The online board is all red, it's impossible to take off or land."
Some foreign carriers that had continued to fly to Russia after the full-scale invasion have since adjusted routes or suspended operations.
Changes have affected Pegasus, Flydubai and Air India, according to industry media.
Passenger numbers on the Moscow-St Petersburg route have fallen by 20-23%, while rail demand has risen by roughly 20% in response.
The investigative outlet Agentstvo has noted that the aviation disruption overlaps with pressure on other parts of the Russian economy, including declining oil refining capacity, higher logistics costs and interruptions to warehouse operations caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on industrial facilities.

Indian regional airlines to buy 105 Russian planes

Indian regional airlines to buy 105 Russian planes
Three Indian domestic airlines have signed agreements on 105 Russian Il-114-300 passenger aircraft, as Moscow and New Delhi move to expand cooperation in civil aviation and manufacturing.
The proposed purchases include 50 aircraft for regional airlines Pinnacle Air, up to 20 for Air Kerala, and 35 for Sleek Aviation.
The companies are yet to start scheduled commercial flights. Another startup, Flamingo Aerospace, previously agreed to buy six of these planes, whose delivery is expected in 2028.
The agreements, memoranda of understanding, and letters of intent were announced in New Delhi just ahead of the BRICS summit starting Friday. This comes as India and Russia seek to broaden industrial and economic cooperation beyond their traditional areas of partnership.
The first planes will be made in Russia, but local production will start once the program is finalized, UAC CEO Vadim Badekha said. “The key task which we are concentrating on is finalizing our agreements on the production of the aircraft here in India,” he told the media at the INNOPROM. India trade fair.
Badekha added that validation in India of the Il-114-300’s Russian type certificate will also be an important step before supplies begin.
The Il-114-300 is a 68-seat turboprop designed for regional routes. It can operate from smaller airports and short runways, making it suited to operate from smaller cities.
India is the world’s third-largest aviation market and has been expanding air links to its fast-growing tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Under its regional connectivity program (UDAN), New Delhi is also seeking to bring more smaller airports into the country’s commercial aviation network.
In June, Badekha said Indian airlines are considering up to 200 Il-114-300 and SJ-100 aircraft combined.
UAC and India’s state-run aerospace manufacturer, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), are working on licensed production of the SJ-100 regional passenger jet in India.
The two companies signed a cooperation agreement in January as a basis for starting licensed production. More than 80% of the agreement has now been finalized, Badekha said.
The SJ-100 is a short-range jet capable of carrying up to 103 passengers. UAC previously said production in India could begin in around three years, with output eventually reaching 20-40 aircraft annually.
UAC has also said it expects to sign a contract with the first Indian operator of the SJ-100 at Aero India 2027. The company is offering not only aircraft supplies, but also production localization, maintenance, and after-sales support.

On eve of 9/11 anniversary, US grapples with Islamophobia and mass surveillance, as American Muslims step up their civic struggle
Americans are getting ready to mark 25 years since 9/11 as Islamophobia remains rampant and mass surveillance has become ingrained in daily life within the United States.
The attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September, 2021 led to a new era that weakened democratic norms and institutions, demonising Muslims and other marginalised communities.
Less than a week after the attacks, then-US President George W. Bush visited a mosque in Washington and said that the Muslim community played an important part in American society.
“Like the good folks standing with me, the American people were appalled and outraged at last Tuesday’s attacks. And so were Muslims all across the world,” Bush said.
“The face of terror is not the true faith of Islam. That’s not what Islam is all about. Islam is peace,” he continued, emphasising that they should be treated with respect.
At that time of fear and anger, Bush’s statement might have saved lives. However, his administration’s establishment of the Department of Homeland Security, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as its chief attack dog, accelerated a climate of fear and bigotry.
Nihad Awad, executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, was with Bush on the day of his visit.
“I stood shoulder to shoulder with the president of the United States denouncing what happened and calling for unity,” he recalled in a local NBC news segment.
“Today, we are living under an administration that has been thriving on division and pitting Americans against each other,” he said of US President Donald Trump, who has weaponised ICE against Muslims, Hispanics and other communities.
Despite a difficult climate, or possibly motivated by it, Muslims now account for more than 250 elected officials across the country.
Arguably the most popular is New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who, days before the 9/11 anniversary, released more than 10,000 documents detailing the environmental impact of the attacks not previously shared with the public.
A petition is being circulated to prevent Mamdani from speaking at the commemoration event, though there appears to be more pushback on Trump’s unsubstantiated claims that he was by the World Trade Centre on 9/11.
Though a climate of fear and bigotry continues as a daily reality, it is now accompanied by a sense of hope for a long-maligned community.
"Today, I can say that American Muslims are deeply civically engaged. American Muslims refuse to be defined by guilt by association," Awad said.

DeepSeek says new Flash AI model beats Kimi K3 on cyber, coding benchmarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:26:24 UTC
18:26:24 KST

DeepSeek says new Flash AI model beats Kimi K3 on cyber, coding benchmarks
Developer’s V4.1 Flash launch highlights China’s AI battle, where efficiency and speed drive competition amid chip curbs
The Chinese artificial intelligence developer said on Thursday that V4.1 Flash used a new “Causal-Encoder-Decoder” architecture. While built on a massive 552 billion-parameter framework, it relies on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design.
In traditional AI, every query runs through the entire system. An MoE system routes tasks only to the specific subnetworks best suited for the job. By activating just 8 billion parameters to process inputs and 16 billion to generate responses, DeepSeek said it significantly reduced the computing power needed per request.
DeepSeek described V4.1 Flash as the smallest model in its new series, with native multimodal visual understanding. The model outperformed V4 Pro on benchmarks evaluating coding, cybersecurity and autonomous agent tasks, the company said.
With rising hardware costs and foreign chip export curbs tightening compute constraints, Chinese players are racing to offer efficient models that deliver high-end reasoning at fraction-of-a-cent operational costs.
On Terminal-Bench 2.1, which tests AI on real-world compute tasks, V4.1 Flash scored 90.6, surpassing OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 at 88.3, and DeepSeek’s own V4 Pro at 87.9.

Fire on ferry off Philippines leaves dozens missing, kills several
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:24:47 UTC
18:24:47 KST

Fire on ferry off Philippines leaves dozens missing, kills at least 5
Manila, Philippines — A fire that burned overnight on a passenger ferry off the western Philippines left dozens of people missing Thursday and killed at least five.
So far, 43 people have been rescued, Coast Guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said. An intense and widespread search was on for the unaccounted for.
The ferry MV June Aster was afloat but listing after the fire was put out. The blaze started Wednesday evening. Tendrils of smoke still wafted over the charred vessel by midday Thursday.
"We are continuing search-and-rescue operations," she said, with a Coast Guard ship and high-speed response boats joined by a military vessel and other government boats, private volunteers and fishermen.
The Coast Guard made a radio broadcast to nearby ships to be on the lookout for passengers from the ferry, and it coordinated with coastal villages in case any passengers drifted to shore.
Images of nighttime rescue efforts showed Coast Guard personnel tossing life jackets to survivors as the ferry burned in the background. Passengers were helped into smaller boats that took them to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port.
The ferry had sailed from the capital Manila and was near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire started around 6:45 p.m. Wednesday.
Bad weather and big waves challenged rescuers. The ferry was around 4 nautical miles off Coron's village of Turda when it sent a distress signal, but strong sea currents had dragged it to a distance of 7.68 nautical miles off Turda.
Rescuers were using drift-modeling tools to identify areas where people may have been carried by currents, the Reuters news agency reported.
Cayabyab said it was unclear what caused the fire, which one survivor said may have begun in the cargo hold, and the Coast Guard was coordinating with the shipping company and maritime authorities to get more details.
She said 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. There was no information about any foreigners on board.
Ferries are a common transportation method in the Philippine archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.
In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world's deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

Desogestrel contraceptives: 1.6 million French women warned of tumour risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:23:50 UTC
18:23:50 KST

The French medicines agency (ANSM) urges women who take desogestrel contraceptives to seek medical advice if they develop suggestive symptoms, such as persistent headaches, visual disturbances or memory loss.
A low risk, but one that affects millions of women. In France, 1.6 million women who have taken a desogestrel-based contraceptive (Antigone, Cerazette, Elfasette and Optimizette...) will receive a letter informing them of an increased risk of developing a meningioma, France's National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM) announced on Thursday. The health authority stresses, however, that this risk remains "low".
At the same time, around 90,000 doctors who have prescribed these medicines will also be notified.
ANSM recommends that the women concerned consult their doctor if they experience persistent headaches, visual disturbances, muscle weakness, problems with balance or speech, memory loss, or the onset or worsening of epileptic seizures. A brain MRI scan may then be prescribed.
A risk that increases with the length of treatment
Meningioma is a tumour that develops from the meninges, the membranes that surround the brain. Most often benign, it can nonetheless cause significant neurological problems depending on its size and location.
According to a study by the Epi-Phare public interest research group published in 2024, one woman in 67,000 who has taken desogestrel develops a meningioma linked to this contraceptive. After five years of treatment, this proportion rises to one woman in 17,000.
The risk is doubled after seven years of use compared with women who have not taken this contraceptive. However, it disappears one year after stopping treatment. Women over 45, as well as those who have previously taken for more than a year a progestogen regarded as high-risk, are particularly affected.
The risk would nonetheless remain far lower than that associated with other progestogens, such as Androcur, Lutényl, Lutéran, Colprone or Depo Provera, for which monitoring by brain imaging is systematically recommended.
"This risk is low, and bears no comparison with that of Androcur, which was 20 times higher after five years", says Isabelle Yoldjian, ANSM's medical director.
Do not stop contraception without medical advice
ANSM is calling on the women concerned not to stop their contraception without medical advice and is urging them to discuss the issue with their doctor, gynaecologist or midwife at their next consultation.
The health authority also reminds women that any contraception should be reassessed every year with a healthcare professional, depending on each woman's needs and state of health.
Following a request from ANSM, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) this summer approved the addition of the risk of meningioma to the patient information leaflets for these contraceptives.

EU cuts primary student-teacher ratio to 13.3 as decade-long growth falters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:22:38 UTC
18:22:38 KST

The EU had 23.2 million primary students in 2024, down 0.2% from 2023. Since 2014, numbers have risen by 2.9%, though trends vary widely: Luxembourg and Slovenia grew the most, while Poland, Croatia and Portugal saw major declines.
In 2024, there were 23.2 million primary school students in the European Union, a figure virtually unchanged from the previous year, but the underlying trend has shifted over the past decade: today there are fewer students per teacher than in 2014.
The latest Eurostat data, released to coincide with International Literacy Day, confirm this and not only set out enrolment numbers but also detail how many teachers are in Europe's classrooms, who they are, and what types of schools they work in.
France remains by far the country with the most primary school children: 4.1 million in 2024. It is followed by Germany (3.3 million), Spain (2.8 million) and Italy (2.6 million). At the other end of the scale, Malta has barely 27,537 students; Luxembourg has 43,020, and Cyprus 60,596, figures that depend both on the size of each country and on the age at which children start primary school, which varies from one member state to another.
Compared with last year, overall primary enrolment in the EU fell by 0.2% (35,153 fewer pupils), a small but real drop.
The picture looks different over a longer period: since 2014, pupil numbers have grown by 2.9% (659,086 more), although the trend is highly uneven across countries. Fifteen member states gained pupils over those ten years, and eleven lost them. Luxembourg (+21.4%) and Slovenia (+18.2%) lead the increases; Poland (-25.7%), Croatia (-10.3%), and Portugal (-10.0%) record the largest declines.
The student-teacher ratio in primary schools has fallen since 2014
The student-teacher ratio, an indirect measure of teaching resources in an education system, also shows change. In 2024, the EU average was 13.3 pupils per primary teacher, compared with 14.2 a decade earlier. Greece (7.4) and Luxembourg (8.2) are the only countries below 10; at the other end, Germany (15.2), the Netherlands (16.3), Czechia and France (both 17.9) and Romania (18.2) all have more than 15 pupils per teacher.
The downward trend was repeated in 23 of the 27 countries between 2014 and 2024, with Bulgaria (from 17.8 to 10.4) and Slovenia (from 15.9 to 10.8) showing the sharpest drops. Austria is the exception that proves the rule: its ratio did not shift by a single decimal point, stuck at 12.0. The remaining countries saw increases, and Lithuania saw the most marked change, rising from 10.2 to 13.7 pupils per teacher.
Eurostat also sets out, in a broader analysis of the primary phase, how many teachers stand behind those students. In 2024, there were nearly 1.9 million primary teachers in the EU. Germany tops the list with 284,000, followed by Italy (251,000), Spain (248,000) and France (242,000, an incomplete figure as it does not include independent private schools).
Teaching remains an overwhelmingly female profession: 85.6% of primary teachers in the EU are women, compared with 14.4% men. In nine countries, the male share is below 10%; the most extreme case is Lithuania, where only 3.9% of teachers are men. Denmark, at 32.8%, has the highest male presence in primary classrooms, though males remain a minority.
By age, 42.1% of European teachers are between 35 and 49, 38.1% are over 50, and only 19.7% are under 35. Italy (58.2%) and Lithuania (57.3%) have the oldest staff; Malta and Luxembourg, by contrast, have more than double the EU average share of young teachers.

Renewables generate record 92 pct of New Zealand electricity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:22:33 CST
18:22:33 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Renewable sources generated 92 percent of New Zealand's electricity in the June 2026 quarter, supported by strong hydro inflows and continued growth in renewable generation capacity, government data showed on Thursday.
Renewables generated more than 90 percent of electricity for the third consecutive quarter, according to the latest energy quarterly data release from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE).
"Strong renewable generation helped meet increasing electricity demand while significantly reducing the need for coal and gas generation," MBIE Domains Manager Amapola Generosa said in a statement.
Overall electricity generation increased 1.9 percent from the same quarter last year, while renewable generation rose 11.4 percent, Generosa said.
Hydro generation increased 14.7 percent, geothermal generation reached a record quarterly high of 2,621 gigawatt-hours, and solar generation recorded its highest-ever June quarter, according to the ministry.
Gas-fired generation fell to its lowest level for a June quarter since 1981, while coal-fired generation fell to its lowest June-quarter level since 1996, statistics showed.
Strong renewable generation also contributed to a 66-percent decline in wholesale electricity prices from a year earlier, Generosa said, adding that residential electricity costs, however, increased 10 percent, primarily due to higher network charges supporting investment in electricity infrastructure.
Outside electricity, gas production fell 19.5 percent and total gas demand declined 20.4 percent compared with the June 2025 quarter, according to the release, which also highlighted the impact of the Middle East conflict on New Zealand fuel prices. ■

Ugandan kingdom gripped by succession battle after monarch's death

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:22:33 UTC
18:22:33 KST

Ugandan kingdom gripped by succession battle after monarch's death
KAMPALA, Sept 10 - The traditional Ugandan kingdom of Tooro was plunged into a bitter succession battle on Thursday after the family of the late king, Oyo Nyimba, rejected clan members' choice of a television news anchor to succeed him.
While Uganda is a constitutional republic, it has several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence.
King Oyo, who became the world's youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in 1995 as a 3-year-old boy, died on August 27 at the age of 34 in the United States, where he had been receiving treatment for cancer. He is scheduled to be buried on Saturday.
NEWS ANCHOR NAMED NEW KING
The royal clan's succession committee announced on Wednesday that it had chosen Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as the new king. Kijanangoma is a cousin of the late king.
But hours after the committee made its announcement, Oyo's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, told a press conference that her brother's will indicated that his son should succeed him.
The kingdom's spokesperson shared a copy of the relevant portion of the will, which is dated September 14, 2022. It states: "I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a Son lawfully recognized as my biological Son, I appoint him as my heir to the Throne of the Kingdom of Tooro."
In a statement published early on Thursday, Oyo's mother, Queen Kemigisa, denounced a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.
She said that Uganda's military had also removed royal guards from the palace without notice and placed the family under house arrest.
A spokesperson for Uganda's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Members of the succession committee could not be immediately reached for comment.
IDENTITY OF SON UNKNOWN
King Oyo, a U.N. goodwill ambassador who championed the fight against HIV and AIDS, never married and was not known to have any children.
The kingdom's prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the son's existence in a social media post on August 27 announcing Oyo's death. He said the late king left behind "a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time".
Andrew Mwenda, a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo's family had not been able to produce a photo of the purported son and declined to disclose details about the family of the boy's mother.
He added that, in Tooro, a king's son could only succeed him if he were born to a queen officially married to the king.
Prime Minister Armstrong called on Thursday for calm from all sides of the dispute.
"There will be time to examine the Will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined," he wrote on X.
"That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial." REUTERS

California enacts new AI auditing laws
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:21:39 CST
18:21:39 KST

SACRAMENTO, the United States, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Wednesday signed into law two artificial intelligence bills, Senate Bill 813 and Assembly Bill 1405, that his office described as first-in-the-nation safeguards.
The Senate Bill sets criteria for designating independent AI verification organizations, while the Assembly Bill requires the California Government Operations Agency to establish an AI Auditor Registry by Jan. 1, 2029, and bars unregistered persons from conducting covered AI audits from that date. Both laws define a "covered AI audit" as an assessment of internal controls, processes or systems needed for compliance with state law.
The Business Software Alliance, a software industry trade association, opposed the bills, saying they would create a California-specific AI auditing and standards regime while national and international AI standards were still developing, potentially adding to regulatory fragmentation.
Meanwhile, OpenAI said Wednesday in a blog post that it supported both measures and urged the U.S. Congress to adopt "mandatory, capability-based" national AI safety requirements.
Newsom previously vetoed a broader frontier AI bill in 2024. He then said that it would apply stringent standards based on model size without adequately considering whether systems were deployed in high-risk environments.
Newsom's office said Wednesday that the governor called on the federal government to establish robust national AI regulations. ■
