Singapore PM increases his salary by $1.1 million amid first government pay raise in 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:26:48 UTC
17:26:48 KST

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the salary increases in parliament on Tuesday, the first for ministers in 15 years. Wong's own benchmark paycheck is set to rise 64 percent to 3.6 million Singapore dollars (€2.4 million) a year.
Singapore’s ministers, already among the world’s highest-paid, are getting a raise for the first time in 15 years, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, explaining that the government cannot attract top talent into politics if salaries remain unchanged.
Wong told Parliament on Tuesday that under a revised salary framework, the benchmark annual pay for a minister at the lowest grade will rise to 1.8 million Singapore dollars (€1.2 million), from Sg$1.1 million (€747,564). The prime minister’s benchmark salary will jump to Sg$3.6 million (€2.4 million) from Sg$2.2 million (€1.5 million), he said.
Ministers' pay has long been politically sensitive in the city-state, especially amid cost-of-living concerns and a 2025 median gross monthly income of Sg$5,775 (€3924) for fully employed residents, according to government figures.
The increases were recommended by an independent committee.
Wong said, however, the ministers will not immediately get the full salary increases. They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9 percent from October 15, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.
Wong also said he would donate his entire salary increase to charity for the next five years.
Mixed reactions among Singaporeans
Singaporeans expressed mixed reactions on Wednesday over hefty pay raises for political leaders, with some saying the demands of governing justified the bump while others questioned their scale and called for transparency.
May Goh, 69, a retiree from the semiconductor industry, said the ministers deserve the increases. "I think their responsibilities are very high. They are doing a good job so far compared to other countries," she said.
A 32-year-old cybersecurity employee in the business district said she "honestly" thought the increases were fair. "They are basically the CEOs of the political world," she said.
Others were more guarded. The increases are "very steep", said a 26-year-old information technology consultant.
"When you see such a huge salary increase, it puts into perspective, like 'wow that's quite a lot'. We don't even spend that much," he said.
A 69-year-old retiree, while voicing support, said he wanted more transparency with the numbers.
"I wish they were a bit clearer and more transparent about these numbers, including bonuses," he said.

Centre tells SC it is open to tougher labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:25:45 UTC
17:25:45 KST

Supreme Court Justice JB Pardiwala questioned why the FSSAI was taking a two-phased approach.
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Thursday told the Supreme Court that it was willing to consider stronger warning labels on packaged food, opening the door to tighter front-of-pack labelling rules that could have a significant impact on the country's packaged food industry.The issue concerns a proposed system under which food packets would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings to alert consumers when products contain high levels of nutrients linked to health risks, reported news agency Reuters.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had recently proposed introducing the labelling system in two phases. Under the initial plan, a product would get a red warning symbol if it crossed the prescribed limits in at least two of three categories, namely added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Tighter provisions were to follow in the second phase.Health experts and activists have opposed this approach, arguing that requiring a product to be high in two nutrients before triggering a warning could allow several unhealthy products to avoid the label.The Supreme Court questioned the need for such a phased approach during Thursday's hearing."It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?" Justice JB Pardiwala asked the government's lawyer, stressing the word "and".
Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for FSSAI, said the regulator could now consider implementing both phases together following the court's observation.That could mean a product would carry a red warning if it crosses the limit for even one of the specified nutrients, whether added sugar, salt or saturated fat.
NIN flags gaps in proposed system
The matter has been under the Supreme Court's consideration for months following petitions seeking stronger front-of-pack nutrition warnings. The court had recently given FSSAI a two-week deadline to come back with its proposals.As that deadline approached, the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad submitted its suggestions to the food regulator.NIN has argued that the proposed system should not focus only on added sugar and added fat. It has suggested that factors such as total calories, total sugar and total fat should also be taken into account when deciding whether a packaged food needs a warning.The concern is that looking at only selected nutrients could allow some foods with an unhealthy overall nutritional profile to escape the warning system.A scientist from NIN explained this using fried snacks as an example. A packet of salty fried chips may contain little added sugar and could fall below the proposed threshold for added fat, while still being extremely calorie-dense because of its fat content.Under a system focused only on added sugar and added fat, such a product could therefore avoid a red warning despite being unhealthy when consumed frequently.
Why the labels matter
Front-of-pack nutrition labelling is intended to give consumers an easy-to-understand warning without requiring them to study detailed nutritional information printed on the back of a packet.The proposed red hexagon is designed to work much like a stop sign, with words such as "high fat", "high sugar" or "high salt" clearly displayed depending on which limit a product crosses.
NIN has also pointed out that the nutritional quality of a food cannot necessarily be determined simply by whether it is ultra-processed. A samosa or jalebi, for instance, may be high in fat or sugar without being classified as an ultra-processed food. At the same time, some whole-grain breakfast cereals may be ultra-processed but relatively low in fat, salt and sugar.The debate before the court is therefore not merely about the shape or colour of a label. It is about what nutritional criteria should trigger a warning and whether the proposed system is strong enough to help consumers identify foods that could be harmful when eaten regularly.

Xinhua Headlines-Xi Focus: Beyond classrooms: Xi inspires teachers to nurture talent for national rejuvenation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:25:07 CST
17:25:07 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- As millions of teachers across China celebrated Teachers' Day on Thursday, they received a familiar message of greetings from President Xi Jinping.
In a congratulatory message released a day earlier, Xi commended teachers nationwide for dedicating themselves to education, imparting knowledge and nurturing young minds, highlighting their significant contributions to the country's development.
He called on teachers to enhance their professional competence and capabilities, and foster a new generation of young people to shoulder the mission of realizing national rejuvenation.
Xi also called for greater respect for educators, stronger support for education, and concerted efforts to make China a leading country in education.
As an inspiring move, the central authorities on Thursday honored 25 teachers from across the country for their outstanding work.
RESPECT FOR TEACHERS
Grounded in the legacies of Confucius and Mencius, reverence for teachers has deep roots in Chinese culture and remains an important value in Chinese society today.
Xi himself has long held the teaching profession in high regard. He once invoked a well-known Chinese saying to capture the profession's significance: "A stick of chalk and a modest podium shape the fate of a nation."
In Xi's view, good educators are expected to possess ideals and convictions, moral integrity, knowledge and benevolence.
His bond with teachers was forged during his school years and has endured ever since.
On the eve of Teachers' Day in 2016, Xi returned to his alma mater, Beijing Bayi School. Seeing his former teachers again, he slowed his pace and held their hands firmly. When addressed as "leader," he demurred: "Here, there are no leaders. Everyone is a student."
Among the teachers was Chen Qiuying, Xi's Chinese teacher and a guide to the world of poetry during his teenage years. For decades thereafter, they remained in touch.
"He would often bring me books over the years," Chen recalled. "Some were his doctoral dissertation or his own works, while others introduced the places where he had recently taken up a new post. Sometimes, he would even send me a few bulbs of Fujian narcissus in the depths of winter."
Xi's respect for teachers goes beyond ceremonial recognition. He has repeatedly called for greater support for teachers, particularly those working in rural areas, by improving their pay, working conditions and social standing.
With his support, China issued a policy document dedicated to rural teachers and took actions to ensure that the average income of primary and secondary school teachers nationwide was on par with or higher than that of local civil servants.
MAKING TEACHERS AND EDUCATION A PRIORITY
From his grassroots posts to the nation's top leadership, Xi has consistently made teachers and education a governance priority.
He has visited schools and campuses to learn about teachers' work and living conditions, discussed education issues with national legislators and political advisors, and supported paired-assistance programs designed to improve education quality in less-developed regions.
For a vast and populous country facing uneven distribution of educational resources, Xi has stressed the need to further expand access to quality basic education and promote educational fairness, emphasizing education's role in promoting greater social equity.
In June 2024, Xi visited an ethnic middle school in Qinghai, a less-developed province in northwest China, where he encouraged teachers to help children grow and thrive.
Funded and supported by Shanghai, the school opened in 2019 to meet the pressing need for quality secondary education among children from pastoral communities on the plateau.
Zhou Quan, a Shanghai teacher who taught at the school through the paired-assistance program, was delighted to learn that many of his students there gained admission to leading universities upon graduation.
"Helping them build confidence, broaden their horizons and achieve their academic goals has been the most rewarding part of my career," said the chemistry teacher.
As AI reshapes education, Xi has emphasized the importance of advancing digital education to make quality educational resources more accessible to students, regardless of where they live.
Efforts to expand access to education have also benefited students with disabilities. In recent years, about 30,000 students with disabilities have entered higher education each year.
Xi has envisioned vocational education in China shifting gears to help more children fulfill their potential. The country now boasts the world's largest vocational education system, with more than 10 million annual graduates.
A little-known fact is that Xi also served as president of a vocational school in Fuzhou for six years in the 1990s, during his tenure as Party chief of the coastal city. He played an active role in the school's development, now known as Minjiang University, championing causes such as enrolling an armless student -- a pioneering move in Fujian Province at the time.
TOWARD A GLOBAL LEADER IN EDUCATION
China has set sights on becoming a global leader in education by 2035. This endeavor fuels its pursuit of modernization and national rejuvenation.
The country boasts the world's largest education system, with roughly 440,000 schools at all levels and of all types, 280 million students, and 18.7 million teachers.
China has made significant progress toward that goal. According to Education Minister Huai Jinpeng, the country's overall level of education modernization now ranks among the upper-middle tier globally. In basic education, coverage and key indicators had surpassed the average levels of upper-middle-income countries, with preschool and compulsory education reaching the average levels of high-income countries.
On the higher education front, 55 million graduates entered the workforce and broader society over the five years leading up to 2025. Meanwhile, vocational education supplied more than 70 percent of the newly added highly skilled workers for modern industries, helping support the country's comprehensive modern industrial system.
Xi regards strengthening the teaching workforce as the most important fundamental work for building China into a leading country in education.
To this end, China plans to launch a national initiative on teacher development, accompanied by integrated reforms in teacher preparation, professional development, management and support in the coming years.
The emphasis on teachers also reflects Xi's broader vision of education -- cultivating the talent needed to drive scientific and technological progress and strengthen the country's capacity for innovation.
In a reply letter in June 2024, he encouraged Andrew Chi-Chih Yao, a Turing Award laureate and professor at Tsinghua University, to explore new approaches to nurturing innovative talent, fostering interdisciplinary work and advancing frontier research.
"Today's students are the major driving force that will realize our great Chinese dream: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," Xi once remarked. "Teachers are dream builders, undertaking their mission to forge a 'dream team.'" ■

NEW YORK, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan and American Coco Gauff advanced to the US Open women's singles semifinals on Wednesday, while top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany reached the men's last four.

Ukrainian forces strike oil infrastructure at Russia's ice-free port of Makhachkala
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SOF) has struck facilities at the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port on the Caspian Sea coast in Russia.
Source: SOF; Oboronka, a defence industry project created within Ukrainska Pravda's holding company
Details: The special forces explained that one of the key elements of the port's infrastructure is its oil harbour, designed to handle tankers with a capacity of up to 10,000 tonnes and a draught of up to 10 metres. An oil depot is also located directly near the port's territory.
Makhachkala port holds strategic importance for Russian logistics. It is Russia's only ice-free, deep-water port on the Caspian Sea, operating year-round. Various types of cargo pass through it, and the port itself is a key link in the North-South international transport corridor, which provides Russia with an alternative route to Iran, India and other South Asian countries.
Striking the oil component of this transport hub directly affects Russia's ability to use the Caspian Sea to transport and transship energy resources, SOF said.
In addition, according to data from the Ukrainian company Fire Point, Makhachkala has been used as one of the delivery points for Iranian attack drones bound for Russia via the Caspian Sea. From there, they were later moved to areas from which they were deployed against Ukraine.

SINGAPORE, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in the central region returned to the unhealthy range on Wednesday night and was still in that range as of Thursday noon, data from the National Environment Agency (NEA) showed.
The 24-hour PSI is considered moderate at 51 to 100 and unhealthy at 101 to 200. It reached a peak of 106 on Thursday morning.
Singapore's 24-hour PSI had entered the unhealthy range due to haze on Sept. 4, the first such occurrence since Oct. 8, 2023.
The NEA said on Wednesday that moderate to dense smoke plumes continued to be detected from fires in southern and central Sumatra and Kalimantan, with smoke haze observed drifting towards Singapore.
While some showers are forecast over central and northern Sumatra in the coming days, dry conditions are expected to persist over Kalimantan and southern Sumatra, the agency said.
With prevailing winds blowing from the southeast or south, there remains a risk of smoke haze affecting Singapore if the fires persist, it added. ■

Trump touts $5,000 payout if Republicans win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:23:13 UTC
17:23:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump touts $5,000 payout if Republicans win as Vance waits in wings
President Donald Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention by proposing to pay every US adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if his party wins November's congressional elections.
Trump delivered the extraordinary overture during a primetime speech that lasted nearly two hours and firmly placed him at the center of the midterm campaign at a time when his sagging approval ratings could weigh on Republicans' chances.
Vice President JD Vance will give the keynote address on Thursday night, though Trump is scheduled to make closing remarks to bring the made-for-television two-day event in Dallas to an end.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Vance's speech could serve as an early audition for the 2028 presidential election and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.
It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would be legal. The proposal would likely cost more than $1 trillion, with approximately 270 million US adults, and could require the approval of Congress.
The convention's focus on Trump–some Republicans have dubbed it "Trumpapalooza"–amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilize the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite opinion polls showing his popularity is at an all-time low.
But it remains to be seen whether his campaign-style speech will appeal to the critical swing voters who have drifted away from Trump's party amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.
"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.
Republican efforts got a boost from an unlikely source on Wednesday, when Democratic U.S. Senator John Fetterman appeared in a pretaped video segment introducing his "great friend," fellow Pennsylvania Senator Dave McCormick, a Republican.
Fetterman said he would always "reject the extremes in socialism," a comment that is likely to bolster Republican attacks on Democrats as too left-wing. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his fellow Democrats, has nevertheless rejected speculation that he might leave the party.
Some vulnerable Republicans in tough races, perhaps mindful of tying themselves too closely to the unpopular Trump, elected to skip the affair, including Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Senator Susan Collins of Maine.
While Republican officials had described the convention as an opportunity to tout Trump's policies, most speakers focused on attacking Democrats as extreme on topics such as transgender women in sports and border security—political red meat for core Trump supporters.
Alabama state Representative Ernie Yarbrough, a convention attendee, said Trump needs to give voters a clearer sense of how long the war in Iran could last.
"People want to feel like we're not getting stuck in an endless cycle," he said.
Trump defended his decision to attack Iran, saying he acted to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would drop "as soon as we win the war with Iran," which he vowed would happen soon.
But the conflict shows little sign of ending more than six months after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran, and analysts have said Iran's nuclear program has not been eliminated. Iran denies seeking a nuclear weapon.
Before Trump took the stage, a parade of speakers called Democrats "socialists" and "communists," echoing one of Trump's favorite attack lines. Democrats are "dangerous, radical and weird," said Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chairman of the party's Senate campaign arm.
The stakes are high for both parties in the United States. With the elections less than two months away, Republicans face the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, with public polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote and Trump's approval ratings deeply underwater.

Australia sends two F-35 fighters to New Zealand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:22:06 UTC
17:22:06 KST

- Two Royal Australian Air Force F-35A stealth fighters made their first visit to New Zealand, training at Ohakea from September 8 to 10.
- New Zealand has had no fast jet combat aircraft since disbanding its Skyhawk fleet in 2001, making the joint exercises notable for its air force.
Two Royal Australian Air Force F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters landed at Ohakea in New Zealand on September 8, the first time the jets have visited the country, the New Zealand Defence Force said.
The aircraft, from the RAAF’s No. 3 Squadron, flew training missions through September 10 alongside New Zealand forces, including mock bombing runs coordinated by New Zealand soldiers on the ground in the Waiouru military training area and mock interceptions of a Royal New Zealand Air Force P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft. The jets departed for Australia the afternoon of September 10.
The visit is notable partly because New Zealand has had no fast jet combat aircraft of its own since 2001, when the government disbanded the air force’s Skyhawk fighter squadrons without replacement, citing cost. New Zealand’s air force has focused since then on maritime patrol, transport and helicopter operations rather than air combat, which means exercises like this one give New Zealand personnel rare direct experience working alongside a fighter jet.
Australia operates 72 F-35A aircraft, a fifth-generation stealth fighter capable of both air-to-air and air-to-surface missions. Sixteen other countries also fly the F-35 in one variant or another, giving allied air forces a shared platform they can integrate more easily during joint operations.
“So the amount of thrust we have during take off is still quite overwhelming, still quite a treat to put the power up and take off,” said Mark Biele, commanding officer of No. 3 Squadron, Royal Australian Air Force.
“There are 16 other nations that fly these planes as well, when we collaborate and use those together, the roles can support our maritime efforts, our overland efforts like we saw here on the range to the north, and they can operate in an air policing role as well,” Biele said. “It’s our 110th year, and who would we want to spend that with but our best mates across the Tasman.”
“It’s about bringing the two nations together, working side-by-side in these training environments so if, for whatever reason, in the future if we need to do it for real, we know how to do that,” said Air Vice-Marshal Darryn Webb, Chief of the Royal Australian Air Force.
The jets spent their final day in New Zealand flying low-level navigation training over the west and central North Island before heading home. Neither country’s defense ministry has announced a date for a follow-up F-35 visit to New Zealand.

Unknown Publisher

Russian police officers stand guard outside the British embassy in Moscow on May 23, 2017. (AFP File Photo)
Russia said on Sept. 10 that it had detained a Russian security guard working at Britain’s embassy in Moscow, alleging he was hired by Ukraine for a false flag attack on the U.K. ambassador.

They include the 2006 poisoning of ex-Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko in London and the 2018 attempted poisoning of double agent Sergei Skripal in Salisbury, which killed a member of the British public.
On Sept. 9, British prosecutors said they had charged a 31-year-old British man for allegedly making contact with a representative of Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency.
Joshua Cammidge was charged with engaging in conduct to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out activities in violation of the National Security Act.

08:21:59 UTC
17:21:59 KST

The record attempt took place during the London museum’s Star Trek Lates night - part of a series of events marking the 60 year anniversary of the hugely popular sci-fi series. It includes the Star Trek Warp Trail, which closes this weekend.
They've made it so.
A total of 934 fans gathered at London's Science Museum on Star Trek Day to mark the seminal show's 60th anniversary. They were there not only to celebrate the anniversary but to attempt to set a new Guinness World Record for the largest simultaneous Vulcan salute.
For the heathens amongst you, the Vulcan salute is the gesture made famous by Leonard Nimoy's character Spock. It involves raising your hand, palm forward, with the middle and ring fingers parted, forming a “V” shape. It first appeared in the 1967 episode of the TV series titled “Amok Time” and is usually accompanied by the phrase “Live long and prosper”.
Those taking part on Tuesday were required to maintain the iconic hand gesture for one minute to successfully secure the title.
Guinness World Records adjudicator Paulina Sapinska has verified the attempt and handed the official certificate to the Science Museum’s commercial operations director Ben Lheureux.
Science Museum head of collections and principal curator Dr Glyn Morgan said they had been “really excited at the idea of breaking a world record”.
“It’s the 60th anniversary of Star Trek and we wanted something people would really remember and would really mark this event as something special – and what’s more special than breaking a world record?” he said.
Also participating was actor Martin Quinn, who plays chief engineer Montgomery "Scotty" Scott in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds. He said: "I’m going to hang my Guinness World Record certificate in my brother’s room to really rub it in."
Morgan previously said about this year's 60th anniversary celebrations: “After a popular Star Trek Lates earlier this year, we’re delighted to invite fans back for another evening exploring the ideas, imagination and real-world science behind the franchise, and a final opportunity to experience the Star Trek Warp Trail.”
The free Star Trek Warp Trail includes props and uniforms from the shows and films, and explores the lasting connection between the franchise’s visionary storytelling and real-world scientific innovation.
The popular exhibit closes on Sunday 13 September.

Asian Games kick off with Qatar basketball win, nine days before opening ceremony

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:20:57 UTC
17:20:57 KST

The Asian Games began in Japan on Thursday with Qatar beating Iran in men's basketball, the first action in the continental multi-sport showpiece that has more participants than the Olympics.
Over 17,000 athletes and officials are expected to take part in 43 sports at the Nagoya-Aichi Games, which do not officially start until the opening ceremony on September 19 and will run until October 4.
Several events such as basketball, football, cricket, hockey and modern pentathlon will get under way before the opening ceremony.
Qatar held off a comeback from Iran to win their Group B encounter 59-35 at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya in the first match of a men's basketball competition that will hold medal finals on September 20, the day after the opening ceremony.
"We know we need to win at least one game so we can qualify for the next round," said Qatar's Michael Lewis, the United States-born player who scored a game-high 21 points.
"Feels good to get some team camaraderie back, and now we have got to keep going."
Later in Group B, Taiwan beat Jordan 83-80.
Los Angeles 2028 Olympics qualifying spots are up for grabs in several sports at the Asian Games, which are returning to Japan for the first time since 1994.
Organisers hope the athletes will have a "unique experience" staying in accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.
10,000 police officers for security
Officials are confident that the plan will not be affected by Japan's typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October.
Weather has already caused disruptions, with record rainfall on Tuesday forcing hundreds of athletes briefly to evacuate their accommodation.
Rainwater also leaked into some competition venues, with more wet weather forecast for the coming days.
Among those in action at the Games will be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of world-class teenage talents in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
Meanwhile, Japan will deploy around 10,000 police officers for security at the opening ceremony of the Asian Games next week in the city of Nagoya, local media reported.
The ceremony will be attended by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, among others, but Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is not expected to take part.
Of the roughly 10,000 officers, some 3,100 will be specially dispatched squads from police forces nationwide, the National Police Agency said, adding it will also use artificial intelligence for security efforts.
Areas within roughly 1 kilometre of the ceremony site and the imperial couple's accommodation will be designated as no-fly zones for drones under a recently promulgated law that imposed tougher regulations on small, unmanned aircraft flights.
It will be the first application of the revised law for an event attended by the emperor.

Extreme heat, fires and floods mark record hot month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:20:24 UTC
17:20:24 KST

August the hottest month in global history after record European summer
In short:
Climate data has confirmed August 2026 was the hottest month on record globally.
The recorded surface air temperature for August 2026 was 1.65 degrees Celsius above the estimated pre-industrial 1850-1900 average.
What's next?
Scientists predict ocean temperatures will continue to rise as an El Niño pattern reaches its peak.
Climate data has been released confirming August 2026 as the hottest month on record after heatwaves and severe drought dominated Western Europe's warmest summer.
The recorded surface air temperature for August 2026 was 1.65°C above the estimated pre-industrial 1850-1900 average, with the period from June to August 2026 the joint-warmest on record globally, on par with 2024.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service, which authored the report with data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), found the extreme conditions had coincided with exceptionally low river flows from the Rhine to the Danube, and had intensified wildfires across Indonesia.
Samantha Burgess, from the ECMWF, said the observations revealed "how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans".
"The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world," Ms Burgess said.
Earlier this month, a landmark report from the UN warned the world was unlikely to keep global warming below 1.8C, predicting that global temperatures would likely pass 1.5C above pre-industrial levels by 2030.
The Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty signed in 2016, requires countries to take action to avoid dangerous warming by keeping temperature increases well below 2C and as close to 1.5C as possible.
Scientists have repeatedly advised that keeping temperatures at or below the 1.5C target would "significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change".
The Copernicus report authors found that parts of North America, northern Siberia, central Asia, the Maghreb, and much of northern Australia were also drier than average in the same period.
El Niño turbocharges warming
The world's ocean temperatures also hit a record high in August, with scientists predicting the water would continue to get hotter until an El Niño weather pattern reached its peak.
University of Adelaide climate scientist Georgy Falster said the record was not unexpected due to the combination of ongoing global warming and the El Niño event.
"El Niño itself is changing with climate change. So, this El Niño, it's likely to be very large, possibly the biggest one on record," she said.
"And it is possible, although not guaranteed, that the strength of this El Niño is related to climate change."
Dr Falster said it was critical to mark the records as they took place.
"We as a species need to keep reminding ourselves that what is happening is unprecedented," she said.
"So, I think it is actually very important to mark every time another record topples over."
Dr Falster said she was hopeful that the extreme weather spurred governments to act.
"There is absolutely no point at which we should stop trying to reduce the effects of future climate change," she said.
"No matter when we start acting, or increasing our efforts, all of that makes the world a better place in the future."

Tourists in England face nightly levy on hotel and Airbnb-style stays under new plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:20:07 UTC
17:20:07 KST

Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs.
The plan, presented on Thursday by Angela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it.
The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028.
But it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used.
UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected.
The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”.
Eddie Nelder, a co-owner of the Choice Hotels chain, which has hotels in Blackpool and the Lake District, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.”
However, Rayner said the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities. “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester.
“It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.”
In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after every Labour metro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level.
In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.”
But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them.
The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European countries and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies.
Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales.
Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.
Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee.
Ministers at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood.
Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis.
Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils.
Kim McGuinness, the mayor of north-east England, backed the move for a visitor levy, saying it could bring money to the local economy during events such as the Great North Run, which is due to take place this Sunday.
“A visitor levy could help us bring major international events to our region, back local businesses, improve visitor attractions, build on the 90,000 jobs already in this sector and unlock opportunities that come from a thriving visitor economy,” she said.
“Most importantly, the money raised here would stay here, helping us invest in the future of our region rather than waiting for Whitehall to do it for us.”
The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders.
It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gave emergency funding worth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt.
But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills.
Earlier this summer, the former chancellor slashed VAT on British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British summer savings scheme”.
Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he would cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget.
Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”

Study finds high levels of microplastics enter Swiss soil each year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:16:54 UTC
17:16:54 KST

Study finds high levels of microplastics enter Swiss soil each year
Every year, 219 tonnes of microplastics enter the soil and water bodies in Switzerland via the air, according to a new study.
A research team from Swiss federal research institutes Empa (material science), Eawag (aquatic science) and Agroscope (agriculture) has, for the first time, systematically investigated atmospheric microplastic pollution, as Empa announced on Thursday.
For the study, which was supported by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), the researchers collected samples at five locations over the course of a year. The measurements were taken in Zurich, Dübendorf, Magadino, Payerne and on the Chaumont in the Jura. Extrapolated to all areas of Switzerland below 2,000 metres in altitude, this means that around 219 tonnes of microplastics are deposited in Switzerland each year.
According to the researchers, around 78 tonnes of this ends up directly on agricultural land and around 10 tonnes directly in water bodies.
+ Microplastics found in faeces of Swiss wild animals
At the urban site in Zurich, they recorded the highest figure of 881 particles per square metre per day. At the other sites, the figures were lower, ranging from 249 to 331 particles.
Health implications unclear
The plastics most frequently identified by the researchers were polyethylene terephthalate (PET) at 31%, polyethylene (PE) at 26% and polypropylene (PP) at 21%. PET is commonly found in drinks bottles and polyester fibres in textiles. PE and PP are mainly used for packaging, films and containers.
In relation to the total mass of all airborne particles, such as desert dust or soot, microplastics account for only a small proportion, ranging from 0.02% to 0.12%.
However, due to constant deposition over large areas, considerable quantities accumulate, which hardly degrade in the environment. The researchers went on to say that much remains unclear regarding the consequences of microplastics for the environment and health.
“But in accordance with the precautionary principle, we should avoid littering, use plastics only where necessary and close material cycles wherever possible,” said Empa researcher and study leader Christoph Hüglin, as quoted in the Empa press release.

The first three sections of the 6.5-kilometre-long cycle highway, or ‘cyclostrade’, between the Brussels borough of Anderlecht and the Laken district in the City of Brussels have been completed. The route forms part of a wider network of cycle highways across Belgium.
Yesterday, a section of the new C223 cycle highway was officially opened. The 6.5-kilometre long route along the L28 railway line will link the Bockstaelplein in Laken with the former Kuregem station, passing through Laken and the boroughs of Jette, Koekelberg, Sint-Jans-Molenbeek and Anderlecht.
The route forms part of a wider network of cycle highways that links up with other ‘cyclostrades’ across the country.
Over the past year, Beliris, the joint venture between the Belgian and Brussels governments involved in construction and renovation in the Brussels capital Region, has been working on three projects in the boroughs of Koekelberg, Jette and Anderlecht. These have now been fully completed. In total, Beliris and the Brussels Mobility agency have invested 7.8 million euros in this work.
A new ramp and a bridge are also due to be completed by autumn. These will improve access to the L28 Park near the Belgica and Bockstael stations.
Brussels’ Mobility Minister, Elke Van den Brandt (Flemish ecologist), is enthusiastic about the project. “A ‘cyclostrade’ is much more than just a cycle path. It represents a fair redistribution of our scarce public space.”

Rheinmetall gets new deal for U.S. Marine Corps robot vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:15:33 UTC
17:15:33 KST

- American Rheinmetall won a $7.28 million contract to deliver 12 Mission Master SP autonomous ground vehicles and five amphibious kits to the U.S. Marine Corps.
- The vehicles run on Rheinmetall's PATH autonomy system and will support continued testing under the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
American Rheinmetall has won a $7.28 million contract to deliver 12 Mission Master SP autonomous ground vehicles and five amphibious kits to the U.S. Marine Corps, the company announced.
The Defense Logistics Agency is managing the procurement, with ADS Inc. serving as prime contractor supporting the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory. The vehicles will be used for continued testing and evaluation as the Marine Corps builds out its autonomous logistics and expeditionary mobility programs, rather than for a specific operational unit.
The Mission Master SP is a robotic ground vehicle that runs on Rheinmetall’s PATH autonomy system, software developed by Rheinmetall Canada that lets a vehicle navigate and plan missions on its own rather than requiring constant remote operator control. The system can be added to existing vehicles or built into new ones. This latest batch adds amphibious kits that let the vehicles operate reliably in littoral, near-shore environments, a capability aimed at the kind of island and coastal operations the Marine Corps has been training for under its expeditionary advanced base concept.
The Marine Corps first took delivery of Mission Master SP vehicles in early 2023, and has since tested them extensively, including during the Talisman Sabre exercise in Australia and the Apollo Shield exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, both in 2023. Those trials covered tasks such as casualty evacuation, resupply runs, and fully autonomous road marches of up to 50 km (31 miles). An armed variant carrying the Fieldranger remote weapon station has also been demonstrated in live-fire testing, adding options like armed reconnaissance and flank security to the vehicle’s role.
“This award represents a significant milestone in our long-standing partnership with the United States Marine Corps,” said Matt Warnick, CEO of American Rheinmetall. “For more than four years, we have worked side-by-side with Marines to mature, refine, and advance autonomous ground capabilities. The Mission Master SP captures the full breadth of those lessons learned and showcases Rheinmetall’s commitment to delivering cutting-edge, reliable, and mission-ready autonomous systems.”
“This collaboration between Rheinmetall colleagues enables the U.S. Marine Corps to deploy the Mission Master SP in multi-domain environments and continue to push boundaries of Canadian innovation,” said Pietro Mazzei, president and CEO of Rheinmetall Canada.
American Rheinmetall is also developing a facility in Maine that it plans to designate as an Advanced Land Autonomy Center of Excellence, focused on PATH system integration, production and long-term support. The company said this latest contract does not by itself require expanding that facility, but fits into its broader push to build up U.S.-based manufacturing for autonomous ground systems.

WATCH: Prosecutors move to indict Beersheba man in sedative-laced baby food case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:15:12 UTC
17:15:12 KST

Prosecutors were expected to notify a court on Thursday that they intend to indict Yan Shemla, a 41-year-old Beersheba resident suspected of deliberately placing sedative drugs in baby fruit purees sold in Jerusalem, police said.
Police will ask the court to keep Shemla in custody for another five days while the indictment is prepared.
The prosecutor’s statement marks the final stage of the investigation before charges are filed.
Shemla is suspected of contaminating jars of Prinok fruit puree that were linked to the hospitalization of at least four children in Jerusalem earlier this year.
The investigation became public in June after children were taken to Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem suffering from unusual weakness, drowsiness and apathy. Tests found benzodiazepines in their blood, while Health Ministry laboratory tests identified the sedative drugs clonazepam and lorazepam in jars of the puree.
The children were released from the hospital after observation.
The affected products had been bought at two branches of the Zol VeGadol supermarket chain in Jerusalem. The Health Ministry issued closure orders against both stores at the time but did not order a blanket recall of Prinok products, saying the evidence pointed to a localized incident.
Police said investigators reviewed hundreds of hours of security-camera footage from several locations and used technological tools to identify Shemla.
According to police, investigators initially had no clear lead because hundreds of people passed through the locations each day and the suspect had no known prior connection to the children or the products.
Police surveilled Shemla before arrest
After identifying Shemla, detectives placed him under covert surveillance, tracking his movements and routine until police believed they had gathered sufficient evidence to arrest him at his home.
Police also released security-camera footage on Thursday showing Shemla inside a supermarket around the time of the alleged acts. The publicly released footage does not show substances being placed inside the jars.
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) assisted the investigation, police said. Thursday’s announcement did not identify a suspected motive or say that the case was being treated as terrorism.

US Treasury yields surge as $6 billion bond buyback disappoints markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:12:54 UTC
17:12:54 KST

The sell-off threatens to push up borrowing costs for American households and businesses.
Yields on long-term US Treasury bonds surged on Wednesday after the government announced a $6 billion (€5.2bn) bond buyback, disappointing investors who had expected a larger intervention.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note rose above 4.85%, its highest level in nearly three years, before easing slightly.
The yield on the 30-year bond stood at 5.29%, up from 5.26% a day earlier. It reached 5.33% in August, its highest level since 2007.
Treasury yields influence interest rates across the US economy, meaning sustained increases can make mortgages, business loans and other forms of borrowing more expensive. Higher borrowing costs can also slow economic growth and weigh on share prices.
The rise came after the Treasury Department said it would buy back up to $6 billion of bonds maturing in 10 to 20 years on Thursday. This is three times the size of its previous long-dated buyback operation.
The move is part of a plan announced last month by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to support liquidity in the bond market.
Yields were also pushed higher as Brent crude climbed above $100 a barrel for the first time since late July amid an escalation in the US-Iran war.
Some bond market participants had expected the buyback to reach $10 billion (€8.6bn) or more, rather than the usual $2 billion (€1.7bn), based on Bessent’s comments, financial commentator Stephen Innes wrote in a Substack column.
The $6 billion figure was “near the lower end of the whisper range,” Innes said.
“The Treasury market spent the morning waiting for Scott Bessent to reveal how much firepower he was prepared to put behind the expanded buyback program,” he wrote.
“When the number finally arrived, it was larger than the original commitment but still too small to satisfy a market already choking on duration.”
Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare said disappointment over the size of the buyback could help explain the jump in yields. Another possibility was that “the market sees it more or less as a shell game,” he said.
Some leading figures in finance have criticised the plan as a short-term fix for deeper problems with US public finances. They argue that the Treasury market is too large for buybacks of this size to have a significant effect.
Bessent’s plan represents a “forced effort that’s too obvious,” O’Hare said.
Controversial plan
Wednesday’s announcement followed a plan unveiled on 19 August to “at least double” buybacks of long-dated government debt.
The Treasury said the programme was intended to maintain sufficient market liquidity after the yield on the 30-year bond jumped to its highest level in nearly two decades.
On 20 August, Bessent told CNBC that the rise in yields had been exacerbated by thin trading during the quieter summer period and “doesn’t reflect the underlying fundamentals”.
Analysts have linked the increase in yields to several factors, including high oil prices, heavy investment in artificial intelligence and a surge in US government borrowing caused by the budget deficit.
The plan has also drawn criticism from prominent figures in finance, including billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, Bessent’s former mentor.
“Markets aggregate information no committee possesses, and prices are how that information reaches decision makers,” Druckenmiller wrote in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece last month.
“Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination,” he added.
Traders also see tension between the Treasury’s buyback plan and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s efforts to tackle persistent inflation.
Futures markets have increased the implied probability of a Fed interest rate rise as oil prices and bond yields have climbed.
Investors will now turn their attention to US wholesale and consumer inflation figures due on Thursday and Friday.
Friday’s consumer price index report will “either exacerbate or temper” concerns about a possible Fed rate rise, O’Hare said.

Defense scandal dominates as Riigikogu parties debate restoring trust
Representatives of all six Riigikogu parties debated the fallout from the defense procurement scandal which led to a ministerial resignation last week.
"Esimene stuudio" hosted the debate after Hanno Pevkur's resignation as defense minister, with opposition parties demanding wider accountability and Reform defending its decision to tap a former Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) commander Gen. (Retd) Martin Herem as next minister.
Reform Party MP and Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga said the world is going through turbulent times, which has made it necessary to make big decisions in the defense arena, and that sometimes these steps had their glitches.
"Unfortunately, major developments also come with areas where things are not done as well as they should be. At such moments, the process needs to be accelerated and trust restored. To that end, we have proposed that former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces Martin Herem take up the post of defense minister. As an expert in the field, he will restore credibility in an area that is extremely important for the Estonian state, all of Europe and Estonia's independence, and I think he will do a very good job," Vaga said.
Social Democratic Party (SDE) leader Lauri Läänemets said Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) should also take responsibility for the failed arms deal with an Indian supplier, and not just Pevkur, who resigned a week ago.
"If we consider where this mess began, it was not only, but mainly, on the day Kristen Michal went on Vikerraadio and said defense spending would be raised to 5 percent. This was carried out in a situation where no one had first calculated things precisely or put a plan in place, and the money simply rained down on the Ministry of Defense," Läänemets said.
The SDE leader added that Pevkur had started distributing these funds, but no one yet knows according to what logic or what its spending destinations were.
"As I understand it, what the media has written about and what the public has heard is not yet the end of all this. So, in light of the Reform Party board's latest decisions, the circle of people who were carrying all this out at the time appears, in some sense, to be returning. It is fair to ask whether all of this looks right and whether the new defense minister can handle a situation in which he needs to turn to the prosecutor's office and say that there were problems here involving close acquaintances of mine and perhaps other people from the time when I was in office," Läänemets continued.
Isamaa chair Urmas Reinsalu said the reputational harm the scandal has inflicted on national defense is highly serious and that citizens acting in good faith have been saddened by the apparent chaos.
"We need to understand two things. First, we still do not know the actual circumstances surrounding these deals. For more than a year now, nearly two years, we have been lied to, misled and had things covered up. The Riigikogu has also been deliberately misled, and the question is who is actually responsible for this? The second thing that must be very important for the public is that we need to get clarity on this matter," Reinsalu said.
According to the Isamaa chair, clarity will come one way or another, but it is important that the government promptly put right the disorder in the defense sector highlighted by the National Audit Office.
"There is no excuse whatsoever. Unfortunately, it must be internalized that the Reform Party has failed in managing Estonia's national defense, and that is a fair, dispassionate diagnosis. In my view, General Herem himself has previously expressed this in several critical statements. In some ways, it demonstrates the Reform Party's bankruptcy that none of its politicians now dared to take responsibility amid this confusion, and instead they brought in General Herem, who has been clearly distancing himself from the Reform Party in one way or another," Reinsalu went on.
Eesti 200 MP and Riigikogu National Defense Committee member Peeter Tali said his party joined the ranks of Pevkur's critics since Ministry of Defense Secretary General Kaimo Kuusk had promised to resolve the issues, yet had failed to do so.
"On a human level, I even feel a little sorry for him [Kaimo Kuusk – ed.]. Now it turns out later that the matter has not been put right, and then there is this whole nonexistent shell deal. The Indians with their invisible, semi-invisible shells – it is simply so sad and ridiculous. That is essentially what broke the political backbone," Tali said.
Center Party leader Mihhail Kõlvart continued to demand that the prime minister resign in addition to Pevkur. Kõlvart said Pevkur's acceptance of political but not personal responsibility did not resolve the matter.
"To leave with the message that someone else is responsible, but I am statesmanlike and prepared to take responsibility – that is not enough. Political responsibility means that politicians are also capable of creating the appropriate system to implement their strategy. We were told that the country's main priority – which is also appropriate – is defense, to which the whole of society must contribute, and society does contribute every day. Yet it turns out that the respected prime minister who came up with the slogan stopped at the slogan, because the system was not ready to deliver on that," Kõlvart said.
Kõlvart called it "incomprehensible" that the public sector could lack basic accounting procedures.
"We see that no procurement system, document management system or storage system has been developed – all of this has been highlighted by the National Audit Office. The question arises: if the system has not been created and prepared, who is responsible for that? The government and the prime minister. Today they have an extraordinary opportunity to demonstrate that through their actions," Kõlvart said.
EKRE chair Martin Helme said Pevkur's resignation has not been followed by a calmer period, for as long as those who breached trust remain in leadership positions.
"Earlier Kristo Enn Vaga said here that we are going to start restoring trust – he seems to somehow gloss over this, but who destroyed that trust in the first place? Who trampled trust in national defense underfoot? The honest answer is that Pevkur has been one of the longest-serving ministers in the current government, having become defense minister in 2022. He has also served as a minister in other posts, and his friendship with [Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) CEO and former chief of police] Elmar Vaher goes back to when he was interior minister and lost [Internal Security Service operative detained by Russia 2014-2015] Mr. [Eston] Kohver across the border. It was Reform Party leadership that destroyed that trust, and now they want to bring us a person alongside whom that trust was destroyed and the schemes were created – Herem," Helme said.
According to Helme, bringing Herem in as minister represents a panicked attempt to put the people who destroyed trust back in charge.
"It has been very rightly said here that the Estonian people have made sacrifices without complaint for the sake of strengthening national defense, agreeing to tax increases, spending cuts and restrictions on certain civil liberties. And what have they received in return? They have not received capabilities in return; hundreds of millions have simply disappeared into some black hole. Let us speak plainly about this scheme. The state itself created the scheme; it was started under Herem and Pevkur. A scheme was created in which shell companies with no track record, no assets and, in most cases, no previous experience in the field were sought out, and shells began to be purchased through them. Now we are in court with them. We are in court with five different companies and preparing court action against two others to recover the money," Helme said, adding that the money would not be recovered from these shell companies and front men.
"All of this responsibility lies with the government! To think that we can replace one person involved in the scheme with another and everything will be put right – it is not possible, it is not possible!" Helme added.
Vaga experienced health issues from around 10 minutes into the show and shortly had to leave the studio to be taken to hospital.

World Suicide Prevention Day: what do latest EU and Spain data show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:11:07 UTC
17:11:07 KST

Suicide deaths in the EU fell slightly in 2023 and are below levels a decade ago. Three in four victims are men. In Spain, figures show a fall, as the WHO calls to end stigma.
48,370 people died by suicide in the European Union in 2023, but the mortality rate continues to fall and is now below the level recorded a decade ago.
This is the picture painted by the latest Eurostat data (source in Spanish), published to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, marked every 10 September to raise awareness of this public-health issue, tackle stigma and promote prevention. Suicide accounted for 1% of all deaths recorded in the EU that year. The standardised rate was 10.4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, compared with 10.6 in 2022 and 12.2 in 2013.
Differences between countries remain large. Lithuania recorded the highest rate in the EU, with 18.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, followed by Slovenia (16.4) and Hungary (16.1). The lowest rates were in Cyprus (3.5), Greece (4.3) and Malta (5.5).
Men accounted for 76.4% of all suicide deaths in the EU. The crude rate was 16.9 per 100,000 men, compared with 5 among women. Mortality also increases with age, reaching 17.3 per 100,000 among people aged 65 and over.
Suicides fall for the third year in a row in Spain
The most recent national figures point in the same direction. In 2025, 3,808 people died by suicide in Spain, 3.7% fewer than in 2024, when 3,953 deaths were recorded, according to provisional data from the National Statistics Institute (INE). (source in Spanish)
This is the third consecutive year of decline since the 4,227 deaths recorded in 2022. In 2025, suicide was the third external cause of death in Spain. Among men, however, it was the leading one, with 2,784 deaths.
Spain has an Action Plan for Suicide Prevention 2025–2027, which tackles the issue from a public-health perspective. Its priorities include improving the information available, addressing stigma and the myths surrounding suicide, strengthening early detection and healthcare provision and improving coordination between the different sectors involved.
The plan (source in Spanish) also focuses on awareness-raising and responsible communication, making it easier to access support services and preventing suicide among people and groups in situations of particular vulnerability.
Breaking the stigma, talking and seeking help
The World Health Organization (WHO) is dedicating its World Suicide Prevention Day campaign (source in Spanish) to the slogan "Changing the Narrative on Suicide" ('cambiar la narrativa sobre el suicidio'). In 2026 its call to action is "Start the Conversation" ('iniciar la conversación'), which aims to challenge myths and stigma and encourage people to talk about what is happening to them and seek help.
For the WHO, changing the narrative also means driving changes in public policy, improving access to quality care and implementing evidence-based prevention strategies. The organisation estimates that more than 720,000 people die by suicide every year worldwide. Seventy-three per cent of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, and suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 globally.
The WHO stresses that asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase the risk and can help them feel understood.

Dutch military to get a GlobalEye radar plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:10:57 UTC
17:10:57 KST

- The Netherlands and Sweden signed a letter of intent for the Dutch military to buy a Saab GlobalEye surveillance aircraft, expected for delivery in 2031.
- Dutch crews will gain earlier access to Swedish GlobalEye aircraft starting in 2028, ahead of a separate NATO-wide order of up to 10 GlobalEyes agreed in July 2026.
The Netherlands and Sweden signed a letter of intent for the Dutch government to buy a Saab GlobalEye surveillance aircraft, the Dutch Ministry of Defence announced September 10.
The Netherlands does not currently operate an aircraft capable of this kind of long-range surveillance and instead relies partly on NATO’s aging AWACS fleet. The Dutch aircraft is expected to be delivered in 2031. Starting in 2028, Dutch crews will get earlier access to Sweden’s own GlobalEye aircraft, letting them train on the platform and its procedures years before their own jet arrives, and potentially use it operationally in the meantime.
GlobalEye is built on the Bombardier Global 6000/6500 business jet, fitted with Saab’s Erieye extended-range radar along with other sensors and communications equipment. It is designed to track activity in the air, at sea and on land over long distances and large areas, detecting threats such as drones and cruise missiles and identifying radar installations. Data the aircraft collects is processed and shared in real time with other aircraft, ships and ground units, and the plane can also serve as an airborne command post.
The Dutch aircraft will join a shared pool with three Swedish GlobalEyes, giving Dutch and Swedish crews access to whichever aircraft in the pool is available. The Netherlands said close cooperation with Sweden on deploying the aircraft would let it operate more independently in deciding when and where to use the plane, rather than relying solely on NATO-controlled assets.
This purchase sits alongside a larger, separate NATO-wide decision. In July 2026, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced that 11 allies, including the Netherlands, had agreed to jointly procure up to 10 GlobalEye aircraft to replace the alliance’s fleet of Boeing E-3A Sentry AWACS planes, which have flown out of Geilenkirchen, Germany, since 1982. That decision followed NATO’s decision to abandon an earlier plan to buy Boeing E-7A Wedgetail aircraft for the same purpose, after the Pentagon canceled its own E-7 program in 2025. Saab has said it has not yet signed a contract with NATO for that larger order, and formal negotiations with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency are ongoing.
GlobalEye has also been ordered by the United Arab Emirates, France and Canada.

====================================================================================================

Europe's housing crisis has become an 'emergency', Commissioner Jørgensen warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:09:53 UTC
17:09:53 KST

A "completely unacceptable" housing crisis in Europe is leaving many "normal people" unable to put a roof over their heads, the EU's housing commissioner has told Euronews, as he announced steps to crack down on short-term rentals.
Europe's housing crisis has escalated to an "emergency", as young people in many member states find it impossible to buy or even rent a home, European Commissioner for Housing Dan Jørgensen has told Euronews, adding that Brussels is taking the situation "extremely seriously".
Housing rental and purchase costs have become increasingly unaffordable across the bloc. European Commission data shows property prices across the EU have skyrocketed by roughly 60% over the past decade, while in the same period, average rents rose by over 20%.
"Prices in many cities in Europe are way too high," Jørgensen told Euronews' flagship morning programme, Europe Today. "We see normal people with normal jobs unable to find a place to live, being crowded out of the cities where they serve as police officers, nurses and teachers and so on. So this is totally unacceptable, and we need to act."
He added that the EU, despite not holding any direct competence or legislative power over housing, is ready to act.
"It's also important from the European Union's side [...] to acknowledge that this is also a European problem. So we need to provide solutions from Brussels," he explained.
Jørgensen's comments came after the European Commission unveiled new rules designed to give national and local authorities clearer rules and legal backing for restricting short-term holiday rentals, part of the Affordable Housing Act.
Across European cities, from Lisbon and Barcelona to Brussels, residents complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up. While such rentals represent just 1.2% of the EU's total housing stock, they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots.
"In some cities, these short-term rentals have crowded out normal people from their homes because there is more money to be made from short-term rentals," Jørgensen explained.
The Commission pointed out that, in some countries, local authorities have tried to take measures to bring down prices, but have been faced with court challenges from operators about "compatibility with EU law."
The new rules give local governments "clarity and predictability" on how they can rein in operators like Airbnb in "areas under housing stress," or where there is such clear evidence of serious housing pressure.
"Where that is the case, we are now giving member states the legal basis to regulate this. [...] We are giving them the ability to actually do something about this important problem," Jørgensen said.
Social emergency
Jørgensen also warned of the social and economic repercussions of the housing crisis, saying that it is preventing people from "starting a family, getting the job they want and having the education they need."
Jørgensen dismissed claims that the EU executive is overreaching by proposing solutions that can only be executed at national and local level, stressing that the decision on whether to act and what measures to take is ultimately in the hands of the authorities.
"It's about finding the balance," he went on to say. "I've really felt a pressure to act on short-term rentals, [...] but we shouldn't prescribe. We shouldn't force member states to do specific things."
The Commissioner also acknowledged that tightening the screws on short-term rentals is not a silver bullet.
"We also need to do more to build more houses, to renovate more houses, to find new purposes for buildings that already exist so that they can become houses," adding that for this, cutting red tape and mobilising funds are needed.
"All of these things need to be done, so this is an important step, but it's not the only step."

Europe's housing crisis has become an 'emergency', Commissioner Jørgensen warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:09:53 UTC
17:09:53 KST

A "completely unacceptable" housing crisis in Europe is leaving many "normal people" unable to put a roof over their heads, the EU's housing commissioner has told Euronews, as he announced steps to crack down on short-term rentals.
Europe's housing crisis has escalated to an "emergency", as young people in many member states find it impossible to buy or even rent a home, European Commissioner for Housing Dan Jørgensen has told Euronews, adding that Brussels is taking the situation "extremely seriously".
Housing rental and purchase costs have become increasingly unaffordable across the bloc. European Commission data shows property prices across the EU have skyrocketed by roughly 60% over the past decade, while in the same period, average rents rose by over 20%.
"Prices in many cities in Europe are way too high," Jørgensen told Euronews' flagship morning programme, Europe Today. "We see normal people with normal jobs unable to find a place to live, being crowded out of the cities where they serve as police officers, nurses and teachers and so on. So this is totally unacceptable, and we need to act."
He added that the EU, despite not holding any direct competence or legislative power over housing, is ready to act.
"It's also important from the European Union's side [...] to acknowledge that this is also a European problem. So we need to provide solutions from Brussels," he explained.
Jørgensen's comments came after the European Commission unveiled new rules designed to give national and local authorities clearer rules and legal backing for restricting short-term holiday rentals, part of the Affordable Housing Act.
Across European cities, from Lisbon and Barcelona to Brussels, residents complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up. While such rentals represent just 1.2% of the EU's total housing stock, they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots.
"In some cities, these short-term rentals have crowded out normal people from their homes because there is more money to be made from short-term rentals," Jørgensen explained.
The Commission pointed out that, in some countries, local authorities have tried to take measures to bring down prices, but have been faced with court challenges from operators about "compatibility with EU law."
The new rules give local governments "clarity and predictability" on how they can rein in operators like Airbnb in "areas under housing stress," or where there is such clear evidence of serious housing pressure.
"Where that is the case, we are now giving member states the legal basis to regulate this. [...] We are giving them the ability to actually do something about this important problem," Jørgensen said.
Social emergency
Jørgensen also warned of the social and economic repercussions of the housing crisis, saying that it is preventing people from "starting a family, getting the job they want and having the education they need."
Jørgensen dismissed claims that the EU executive is overreaching by proposing solutions that can only be executed at national and local level, stressing that the decision on whether to act and what measures to take is ultimately in the hands of the authorities.
"It's about finding the balance," he went on to say. "I've really felt a pressure to act on short-term rentals, [...] but we shouldn't prescribe. We shouldn't force member states to do specific things."
The Commissioner also acknowledged that tightening the screws on short-term rentals is not a silver bullet.
"We also need to do more to build more houses, to renovate more houses, to find new purposes for buildings that already exist so that they can become houses," adding that for this, cutting red tape and mobilising funds are needed.
"All of these things need to be done, so this is an important step, but it's not the only step."
