North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:08:46 UTC
14:08:46 KST

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence that North Korea has built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal.
The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week.
The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media.
The IAEA, whose inspectors were expelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader, Kim Jong-un.
During his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear material had more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”.
Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads.
In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.”
“The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers.
North Korea has made rapid progress in its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state.
North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it last tested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.

14:08:00 KST

Education Ministry to study how teachers spend their working hours
The Ministry of Education is launching a study to determine teachers' work tasks and the time spent on them, and to develop recommendations on how to fit teachers' workload within the working hours set by law. The planned cost of the study is €70,000.
With the study on teachers' working time and tasks, the Ministry of Education wants to map what teachers' duties are under Estonia's current legal acts, determine how much time these tasks take from the perspective of teachers and school leaders, and develop recommendations for education policymakers, school owners, principals, and teachers.
Liis Lehiste, adviser at the ministry's Department of Education Management and Teacher Policy, responded to question about whether the ministry currently lacks such information, saying that the state's goal is to support teachers and help them remain in the profession by contributing to the development of good and sustainable working conditions.
"This requires a better understanding of the factors that influence teachers' workload and their ability to cope well with their work," she said.
Teachers report overload
Lehiste noted that according to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act, a teacher's working time is divided between direct teaching and educational work, and other tasks arising from the employment contract, job description, work‑organization rules, or assignments given by the employer.
According to a government regulation established in 2013, teachers' working time is 35 hours per week.
"Besides contact lessons, a teacher's work includes many other tasks — planning and preparing lessons, giving feedback on students' work, communicating with parents, collaborating with colleagues, individual work with students, and so on. TALIS (the international study of teaching and learning) results show that teachers often assess their workload as greater than their official working time," Lehiste said.
She added that Estonia's education information system collects data on teachers' contact hours, but a teacher's work includes many other tasks beyond lessons, such as planning and preparing teaching, giving feedback on students' work, communicating with parents, collaborating with colleagues, individual work with students, and so forth.
According to the adviser, study results show that teachers often assess their workload as greater than their official working time. Existing studies and data do not clearly show which school‑level factors — such as leadership practices, work organization, and collaboration culture — influence how teachers' workload develops.
"We need an up‑to‑date and comprehensive overview of how teachers' working time is spent, which practices support the efficient use of teachers' working time, and how teachers' work can be organized so that tasks fit within the legally prescribed 35‑hour workweek," Lehiste explained, justifying the need for the study.
The aim of the study is to obtain concrete recommendations for teachers, principals, school owners, and policymakers on how to better organize teachers' work.
"Based on the study results, we can assess what changes may be needed, for example, in work organization, guidelines, professional development, or legal acts," the ministry adviser added.
Age and tenure factors
The study should also determine how teachers' tasks and workload relate to their age, gender, experience, career stage, qualifications, position, type of contract, and other characteristics, and how the situation is influenced by language of instruction, school level, school type and region, school and class size, availability of support specialists, and similar factors.
The Ministry of Education also wants to find out what teachers and principals themselves have done to optimize and better organize workload and tasks, and what recommendations exist to ensure that teachers' duties fit within the legal working time.
The study will be conducted among teachers and leaders of general‑education and vocational schools. The Ministry of Education estimates the cost at €70,000, funded from the state budget.
The ministry hopes to identify the tender winner in autumn, and the study results should be completed within 14 months.

Is Indonesia’s 100 GW Solar Plan Realistic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:04:00 UTC
14:04:00 KST

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has set an extremely ambitious target of building 100 GW of solar capacity by 2029. Naturally, many people are wondering if this a realistic goal. I’ll spare you the suspense. The answer is no. But it does send a strong signal that the government is serious about putting more resources toward cleaner energy.
People often look at Indonesia’s energy sector, dominated by coal and other fossil fuels, and the extremely slow progress on renewables to date, and conclude that clean energy is a non-starter. I don’t agree. The government has been signaling for some time that it is willing to pivot toward clean energy. The catch is that it wants to do so on its own terms, without simply opening Indonesia up as a market for private developers and investors where the state-owned utility PLN ends up on the hook for expensive purchase agreements. This, in my estimation, was the major flaw with how Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition Partnership was originally designed.
The actually important question is not whether Indonesia can build 100 GW of solar power – obviously, it cannot do so in three years. The question is whether we are getting closer to an approach that can actually be implemented and scaled given the peculiarities of Indonesia’s political economy. I think the answer is a tentative yes. Prabowo recently unveiled the first stage of the 100 GW plan, announcing 5.3 GW of solar power projects under development or which will soon be opened for bidding.
The first thing we need to do is unpack the headline figure. 5.3 GW of new solar capacity would be a very significant step forward in Indonesia’s clean energy ambitions, but only eight of these projects are actually in an advanced stage of development. The bulk of the announced capacity, some 4.5 GW worth of projects, are still in the early stages without financing or confirmed project developers. However the eight projects that are further along tell us a lot about how to build clean energy in Indonesia.
Two of the announced projects are small off-grid solar facilities, designed to replace diesel generators in remoter areas. One of these is being developed by a subsidiary of state-owned oil and gas giant Pertamina, and the other by PLN itself. Together they account for under 2 MW of capacity. The other six projects are larger utility-scale solar and battery storage facilities mainly using floating arrays built on top of reservoirs. They range in size from 46 MW to around 133 MW and, once completed, will add almost 670 MW of solar generating capacity to the grid.
These six projects are in various stages of development, with some quite far along or nearly operational. They feature a range of financial backers including state-owned infrastructure fund PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur, development banks as well as European lenders. Private sector developers include local firm TBS Energi, as well as Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Renewables, China’s GCL, and Singapore-based Vena Energy. The 92 MW Saguling facility in West Java is one of the few projects to be developed under the JETP framework.
The really important observation is that in all of these projects, state-owned electric utility PLN is not just the off-taker. They are an active equity partner, in most cases holding 51 percent ownership of the project. This is the same model, and equity split, we saw in the Cirata floating solar project in West Java, the first really successful large-scale solar power plant in Indonesia that went into operation in 2023. The new wave of solar power projects is clearly using the Cirata model.
The big puzzle has always been: how do you get PLN to buy-in to a national solar project? PLN operates a large fleet of Indonesia’s coal-fired power plants, and has been reluctant to simply act as a market-maker and off-taker for private renewable energy developers. Involving PLN in these projects as an equity partner provides the utility with an incentive to actually support them. Is it the most efficient design, or the one private developers and financers would ideally want? Probably not. But it is a model that can scale in Indonesia. We are seeing proof of that now.
As projects get bigger, and as more solar power is added and more investment is required, can state-owned energy firms like PLN and Pertamina continue to dominate the clean energy landscape in this way? That we don’t know. The state-directed model may very well need to change as the scale and pace of investment changes. But for now, after many years of false starts, it appears clean energy is actually gaining some traction in Indonesia. The key is that policy efforts stop viewing Indonesia simply as a market to be opened up to private investment, and start giving serious though to the interests and incentives of powerful local stakeholder like PLN.

Saudi says no danger after Khamis Mushait alert amid clashes with Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:02:29 UTC
14:02:29 KST

Yemen's Houthis close in on Bab el-Mandeb Strait in new threat to shipping
ADEN/DUBAI, Sept 10 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants have seized control of the historic port city of Mocha, four government military sources said, in a strategic shift that could threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.
Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified in recent days, with the militant group shifting its focus to control over Yemen's long coastline instead of just the north, putting them in a stronger position to disrupt maritime trade.
The group has launched attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish, pushing government forces and their allies south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait across from the island of Perim, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.
The escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia's Yemeni allies in the internationally recognised government and the Houthis has created a second theatre of war in the Iran conflict that threatens global energy and commodity supplies.
Brent crude prices hovered above $100 a barrel on Thursday as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted.
To avoid the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has been loading millions of barrels of oil a day from its Yanbu port, which lies further north on the Red Sea coast.
Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks further disruptions to the flow of the kingdom's oil supplies to Asia. The militant group has already declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter.
A U.N.-brokered truce in Yemen in 2022 largely halted years of war but has not led to a lasting settlement, with the latest fighting threatening a return to full-scale conflict.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, is the southern outlet of the Red Sea, between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, or the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
WARNING TO TEHRAN
A military leader allied with Yemen's government forces said on Thursday that he directed his group on the west coast to establish an alternative command centre in a safe location, the Al-Jumhuriya television channel linked to him reported.
The instructions from Tarek Saleh, nephew of assassinated Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, were another sign that the Houthis were pushing his National Resistance Forces from the west.
A group of Houthi fighters armed with rifles and chewing qat, a green leaf narcotic that dominates life in Yemen, celebrated their advances at a security directorate building in the Hays district south of Hodeidah, chanting: "Death to America, death to Israel" in a video verified by Reuters.
Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks on the kingdom, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said, in the hope of preventing the conflict from spiralling.
A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and its response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis".
However, two Iranian sources said Tehran told the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising additional funding and weapons, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks.
The Houthis disrupted Red Sea shipping in 2023, saying they were acting in support of Palestinians during Israel's war in Gaza .
Those attacks on Red Sea shipping, as well as on Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States' war on the Houthis' close ally Iran.
ATTACKS ON SAUDI CITIES
The Houthis said on Wednesday that Saudi strikes hit the Yemeni provinces of Al Jawf, Marib and Saada, bordering the kingdom, as well as Taiz in the south and Hodeidah city along the Red Sea coast, a Houthi stronghold used as a base for their broader campaign of attacks on shipping in the waterway. Saudi Arabia did not confirm the strikes.
Saudi Arabia said Houthi attacks on the kingdom in recent days have wounded 73 people, including women and children, after targeting civilian and economic sites in the south.
In 2014, the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa, driving the internationally recognised government south towards Aden.
Fearful of growing Iranian influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in 2015.
The resulting civil war triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of bitter fighting and devastating air strikes by Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners.
With Iranian support, the group's leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, turned his faction of mountain fighters into a force of tens of thousands. The Houthis have demonstrated significant missile and drone capabilities, attacking oil installations and vital infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in the conflict. REUTERS

‘Summer has shaken us’: Nepal’s flood disaster hits close to home in the shadow of melting Mont Blanc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:02:25 UTC
14:02:25 KST

A Chamonix local official says his town urgently needs to prepare for the dangers of falling chunks of glacier or rock.
For centuries, French and Italian mountain communities have gazed upon the seemingly eternal glaciers and snow that gave Western Europe's highest peak its name: Mont Blanc, the white mountain.
But climate warming is dismantling the picture at alarming speed.
Europe's record heatwaves this summer savaged permafrost that for millennia has acted like glue on the Alpine landscape. Defrosting cliffs came apart, sending rock falls cascading from the heights. A famously dangerous gully that climbers have long braved on ascents to the summit, 4,805 metres up, became temporarily impassable.
“We weep for our mountain, the way it's changing. It hits us in the gut,” says Stéphane Bozon, a deputy mayor in Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, a French town at the foot of the giant that straddles France's border with Italy.
“From mid-July onward, we saw an increase in rock falls. We saw areas becoming difficult to access because of glacial retreat and snowmelt on the glaciers, with crevasses opening up and rock collapses making some areas difficult to reach or traverse,” he says.
Each degree of warming can have an outsized impact. On the Aiguille du Midi peak, which rises to an altitude of 3,842 metres in the Mont Blanc range, average temperatures for July have soared. From a chilly 1.6°C in 1994, the monthly average for this July was the warmest ever recorded, at 3.3°C, says Meteo France, the national weather service.
“The mountain really dried out, with temperatures unlike any I had ever experienced,” Bozon says.
The Himalayan flood disaster hits close to home in the Alps
In the wake of devastating floods in the Himalayas, news agency The Associated Press talked to researchers, climbers and residents coping with the risks and uncertainties of climate change on Mont Blanc.
The floods that swept through Nepal and China on 26 August were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers. Initial assessments of many scientists are that climate change played a key role in creating conditions for the catastrophe.
As Earth’s global average temperature rises because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase.
In the Alps, glaciers once admired for their icy majesty are being eyed with trepidation as they shrink and lose stability.
Bozon, who is in charge of safety for Chamonix, says his town urgently needs to prepare for “serious scenarios” of chunks of glacier or mountain potentially falling onto inhabited areas.
“We have to move quite quickly because this summer has shaken us and year after year we’re being shaken by the glaciers’ retreat,” he says.
In Italy, researchers are also documenting dramatic damage wrought by heat on glaciers this year. In Lombardy, Alpine glaciers have lost more than 40% of their surface area since 1991, according to the region's glacier service.
“While it used to snow at high altitudes in the past, now it rains,” says Vanda Bonardo, head of the Italian branch of the International Commission for the Protection of the Alps, a nongovernmental organisation.
“So we’ve also seen the effects on the stability of the terrain,” she says.
Rock falls in the Mont Blanc area have surged
Permafrost that has held Alpine peaks in its icy grip for thousands of years acts as a cement, helping to hold their steep rock faces together. It took a beating from the succession of heatwaves.
“That doesn't mean that all the rock faces will collapse in the coming years or decades but quite a number of them are on the verge of becoming unstable and remain stable today only because of the presence of that ice,” says Ludovic Ravanel, a researcher at Savoie Mont Blanc University who specialises in climate change's impact on mountain snows, glaciers and frosts. "As the ice changes, we have seen a huge, huge number of rock falls and rock collapses this year."
A collapse is a major fall involving more than 100 cubic metres of rock – more than enough to fill a large shipping container. Ravanel expects this year's tally of collapses in the Mont Blanc massif “will probably reach around 400”. He says that is about 10 times more than two decades ago.
The last time things got close to this bad was the ’’catastrophic year″ of 2022, he says, with nearly 300 collapses.
“This has really been one of the defining features of the summer of 2026,” he says.
A Mont Blanc climbing guide juggles the risks
Chamonix-based mountain guide Stuart MacDonald says it shocks him to see how rapidly and extensively glaciers that hang from the flanks of the Mont Blanc massif are retreating.
When he guides people up the peaks, he points them to “where the glacier was last year and this is where it was 10 years ago. And that usually has quite an effect”.
Melting and the risk of rock falls made his job “pretty challenging” this summer and forced him to cancel plans to lead a group to Mont Blanc's summit last week.
“You hear it before you see it and then you’ll turn round and you’ll just see an enormous cascade of rocks coming down a slope and it can be quite terrifying,” MacDonald says.
“What’s most scary is that sometimes these rocks are falling on routes that we used to be climbing at this time of year,” he adds. “It can be depressing sometimes when you look at something that you maybe climbed in July or August in the past and you see that it’s absolutely impossible to do it now.”

OPINION - Dehumanization and the fiction Israel cannot survive without
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:02:13 UTC
14:02:13 KST

- A child’s kite ‘must’ be shot out of the sky, not because it endangers Israel, but because it endangers the story Israel needs to tell itself and the world to continue its genocide
- Dr. Mohsen al Attar is a Reader in International Law at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
It is difficult to fathom what it is like to be Palestinian these days. The so-called Board of Peace celebrates the progress it has achieved, just as members of the Israeli parliament (Knesset) reaffirm their ambition to ethnically cleanse Palestinians from Gaza, just as Israelis demolish record numbers of homes in the West Bank, just as the UN laments the venomous infestations further immiserating the lives of displaced civilians, and just as Germany justifies its unconditional support for Israel before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), despite tens of thousands of dead children and counting.
In December 2023, as Israel’s genocidal violence was picking up steam, UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned that “the dehumanization of Palestinians” was “very disturbing and must cease immediately.”[1] In fact, Israel’s policy of dehumanizing Palestinians has a history as old as its occupation.
Israeli dehumanization policy
As early as 1969, then-Israeli Prime Minister Golda Meir declared that “there was no such thing as Palestinians.” This was only the beginning. Another former prime minister, Menachem Begin, called them “beasts walking on two legs,” an image echoed by the current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has branded them as wild beasts. According to the then Minister of Defense, Moshe Dayan, they were dogs, fit only to “continue to live like dogs.” And former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, a supposed progressive, cast the region as a jungle and Israel as the lone “villa” within it — beyond the wall, monsters live.
This is not simply a political phenomenon. Shmuel Agnon, a winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature, described Palestinians as dogs and, like a "good novelist," added colorful adjectives such as cheating, filthy and undignified. In a song that soared in the Israeli charts, the Israeli rapper Subliminal condemned Palestinians as “swarms of rats” who “will die in their rat holes.” Study after study of Israeli children’s books and drawings finds Palestinians portrayed as pigs, monsters, vipers and sundry threatening animals.
In a glimmer of hope, alongside the multiplication of Israeli dehumanization practices, we find a boost in the critiques of them. In 2024, a year into Israel’s genocide, the world’s leading medical journal the Lancet published a piece precisely on this theme, challenging the health professionals supportive of Israeli violence: “The justification of indiscriminate Israeli attacks by some health care professionals is possible only because of the dehumanization of Palestinian people, predicated on racial prejudices.” Most telling was the journal’s recognition of the deliberate character of that dehumanization: “Propagating a belief that some lives have lower value and less right to self-determination, usually based on racist or discriminatory notions of worthiness, is a fundamental step toward building acceptance for massacres.”[2]
It would be a mistake to reduce dehumanization to rhetoric or propaganda. Both are outward-facing activities, easily dispelled. Dehumanization runs deeper: it is a socio-educational campaign designed to permanently shape how a people is perceived, consigning them to a lesser category of being, below the threshold at which they are entitled to any rights whatsoever. Dehumanization is aimed at achieving a durable form of domination, one that first governs how the group in question is to be treated, as in the massacres described by the Lancet, and secondly dictates the very definition of who they are.
A fragile fiction
This dehumanization is equally directed at Israelis, relieving the population of any guilt or qualm about the violence done in its name. Children taught that Palestinians are threatening animals bent on harming them grow up without compassion for their neighbors. It is no surprise, then, that a majority of Israeli society has actively supported the genocide, or that a majority now calls for ethnic cleansing, not simply in Gaza, but in the West Bank and Jerusalem as well.
The relationship runs both ways: dehumanization authorizes the violence, just as the violence is marshalled to sustain the dehumanization. Demolishing schools and hospitals, blowing up fishing boats and shooting down kites are acts of destruction, but also of maintenance, seeking to preserve the fiction of Palestinian "inhumanity."
For the fiction is fragile -- if Palestinian children are seen reading books or flying kites, the manufactured image of the "animal" collapses. If a child is pictured with bandages on her arms and tears in her eyes, the human surges forward, compelling Israelis not to ask about Palestinian "inhumanity" but to confront the inhumanity of what Israel does.
Israel has spent half a century telling us stories: none of them about Palestinians, all of them about why Israel "needs" to continue killing them. This is why a child’s kite "must" be shot out of the sky, not because it endangers Israel, but because it endangers the story Israel needs to tell itself and the world to continue its genocide. Three years into a genocide, perhaps it is time we started listening to Palestinian stories instead.

[2] https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(24)00043-6/fulltext

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for a not-sachertorte | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

This column began two years ago, almost to the day, when I made a birthday cake for a friend. “I don’t mind,” was her reply when I first asked what sort of cake she would like. But then, a few minutes later, she said: “Hang on, I mean chocolate with glossy icing. Like the mini ones they make at Barberini.”
Barberini is a local bar and cake shop, and the mini cakes she was referring to are their sacher (inspired by sachertorte, of course) – chocolate sponge cakes with a heart of apricot jam and a glossy, chocolate glaze. At Barberini, each one is the size of a single draughts piece, but deep, so not quite two bites but slightly too big for one, unless you open your mouth very wide. “You mean sachertorte?” I said. “That would be great,” was her reply, before changing the subject to I can’t remember what. Walking home, I regretted asking.
According to the Sacher hotel website, its sachertorte (perhaps the world’s most famous cake) is still handmade using Franz Sacher’s original recipe. It also provides a recipe – a wonderful, quite complicated, anxiety-inducing recipe. It is also an approximate one, with a note in capital letters and highlighted red explaining that the original recipe must remain a tightly kept secret. I have never felt so relieved at not being given a recipe.
It also meant Barberini must be approximating, so I would, too. I would approximate by using my own faithful chocolate sponge recipe, which is inspired by Nigella Lawson’s faithful and tender sponge cake, filling it with my homemade peach jam and topping it with an enthusiastic attempt at the hotel’s approximate glaze recipe. I would make a not-sachertorte.
“Make sure he doesn’t disgrace me tonight,” is, according to legend, what Prince Metternich said on discovering it was apprentice pastry chef Franz Sacher who was charged with making the impressive cake. I certainly worried that my glaze would be a disgrace as I poured it over the surface of the cake, both two years ago and again twice this week. My anxiety was unfounded: while not nearly as smooth as Barbarini’s (let alone the Sacher hotel’s), the results were smooth enough.
The last bit of advice is from the Sacher hotel’s website, which notes that slices of sachertorte are best enjoyed with a dollop of unsweetened whipped cream. Slices of not-sachertorte are, too.
Chocolate cake with peach jam and chocolate glaze – a not sachertorte recipe
Serves 8-12
  200g plain flour
  200g caster sugar
  1 tsp baking powder
  ½ tsp bicarbonate of soda
  40g cocoa powder
  175g soft unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
  2 large eggs
  2 tsp vanilla extract
  150ml soured or single cream
  150g-200g peach or apricot jam
  200g caster sugar
150g  dark chocolate (at least 70% cocoa), chopped
Unsweetened whipped cream, to serve
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line two 20cm cake tins, ideally with removable bases.
Working in a large bowl, mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, bicarb and cocoa. In another bowl, beat the butter, eggs, vanilla and cream, until combined and creamy, then add to the flour bowl, beating well until smooth. (This can also be done in reverse – that is, wet first, then dry – in a food processor.)
Divide the batter between the lined tins and bake for 25-35 minutes, or until a stand of spaghetti inserted into the centre comes out clean. Once out of the oven, wait 15 minutes, then invert the cakes on to a cooling rack – don’t worry about any cracks; the icing will cover that. Once the cakes are cool, sandwich them together using the jam.
Next, make the glaze. Working in a small pan, heat the sugar and 125ml water, boiling hard and stirring constantly, for four minutes, until the sugar has dissolved. Take off the heat and leave cool for five minutes – this is really important – then gradually adding the chopped chocolate, stirring until it forms a thick, shiny glaze.
Once the glaze is lukewarm and thick but not stiff, pour it over the cake (still on the wire rack so the glaze can drip through) and use a flat knife dipped in warm water to smooth it. Leave the glaze to set completely, then carefully transfer the cake to a plate, cut and serve with whipped cream.

UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Some disabled people could receive “in kind” support rather than just cash payments under a radical overhaul of the personal independence payment (Pip) proposed by official government advisers, the Guardian can reveal.
The proposal, from an expert committee largely made up of disabled people, is one of a number of striking “emerging recommendations” likely to form the basis of the government’s Timms review of Pip, expected to be published in the next two months.
Rather than automatically receive weekly cash payments, currently between £30.30 and £194.60 depending on need, some claimants could instead swap part of the cash award for specialist equipment and aids, services, or skills and training.
Pip would remain non-means-tested, but while cash would remain “the foundation” of the award, the idea that claimants would be offered the choice of practical rather than just financial support marks a potentially radical departure in welfare policy.
The committee does not address the costs of Pip – currently about £23bn a year – and does not discuss potential cuts in spending, although it acknowledges its reforms must stay within current Pip spending projections of £41bn a year by 2029.
Although political and media debate has focused on the affordability of increases in Pip spending, the committee has focused primarily on improving people’s experience of Pip and better supporting ill and disabled people to participate in every day life.
Other recommendations include:
Introducing a fast-track process to allow new claimants with a terminal illness to claim Pip more speedily – and reducing the number of benefit reassessments for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions.
Reviewing strict and “unnecessarily stressful” rules that suspend an individual’s Pip award automatically after they have spent more than 28 consecutive days in hospital.
Improving the way Pip assesses fluctuating issues such as mental illness to adequately capture the impact of conditions that vary over time.
While Pip is vital to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability, it should also support individuals to live independently and help give them choice, dignity and control over their lives, the committee says.
Pip should be tailored more closely to individuals’ needs and requirements, offering a wider range of support to help them achieve “participation and opportunity across every day life” including work, care and volunteering, it adds.
The 12-strong committee of expert advisers, the majority of whom have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions, are at the heart of a review commissioned to redesign the Pip benefit after the disastrous collapse of Labour’s planned cuts to disability benefits last year.
A backbench rebellion forced the government into a U-turn on £5bn of cuts in the summer of 2025, amid public opposition to plans that would have slashed household incomes and pushed hundreds of thousands of people with disabilities into poverty.
The subsequent review of Pip, co-chaired by the welfare minister, Sir Stephen Timms, published an interim report in July this year which concluded that Pip was unfit for purpose and too often left vulnerable claimants feeling dehumanised rather than supported.
Pip, which is claimed by nearly 4 million people in England and Wales, is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not linked to employment status, and about a sixth of claimants are in work.
The committee insists the emerging recommendations are not final but will be tested for fairness and workability in a series of workshops involving thousands of people with disabilities across the UK to be held over the next few weeks.
There may be resistance among campaigners to introducing non-cash elements within Pip awards. However, recent polling of Pip recipients by the Good Growth Foundation thinktank found half supported the principle of swapping part of their cash payment for services such as skills and training, home adaptations or therapy.
The committee’s recommendations are likely to be closely scrutinised by a separate review of the youth jobs crisis by former Labour MP Alan Milburn, who has made it clear that some of the cash spent on benefits for young people should be redirected towards providing them with training and skills.
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “These are not the final recommendations. The review will report to the secretary of state this autumn and he will carefully consider the final proposals within it.
“The Timms review interim report, co-produced with disabled people, made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose.
“Our goal is to deliver a system that supports disabled people and those with long-term conditions to live independent lives, while remaining fair, sustainable and fit for the future.”

‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Andy Burnham must overhaul Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms or risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment, the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, has warned.
Speaking ahead of the TUC’s annual congress in Brighton next week, Nowak welcomed the “sense of optimism” around Burnham’s fledgling government, but he urged the PM to act in a series of areas, including migration and the cost of living.
Burnham reappointed Mahmood as home secretary when he became prime minister in July. Her department is consulting on proposals that would force more than 300,000 low-paid workers to wait 15 years for the legal right to remain in the UK.
These include many carers who came to the UK to fill vacancies after the Covid pandemic, and were told they could apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.
“I think it is fundamentally unfair to change the rules when people came to this country with one set of expectations,” Nowak said. “I hope we can think again on that.”
He added: “There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment. I want us to train up as many Brits as possible to do those jobs. But I suspect in a growing economy with an ageing population, we are still going to need people to come and live and work in the UK and work in sectors like social care.”
As well as criticising the backward-looking changes, Nowak also condemned the idea of applying a 10- or 15-year wait to many new arrivals, as the Home Office has proposed.
“Both my granddads came to this country after the second world war – one came from Hong Kong, one came from Poland. Both raised their families here. The idea that you could be here for the next 10, 15 years and you’d still have no legal right to remain in the country … how the hell do you plan? Can you buy a house? What does that mean for your employment? Do you have kids? Do you send them to school? I mean, it cuts across any effort to integrate at all.”
Labour politicians supportive of the changes see them partly as a way of assuaging public concerns about migration, and neutralising the appeal of populist parties, including Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
But Nowak suggested that by significantly lengthening the time before people can consider themselves settled in the UK, the approach could ultimately fuel far-right sentiment.
“I tell you where you end up: you end up with Reform claiming that a woman who was born in Somalia and has lived here for most of her life and worked hard and contributed to our society, somehow isn’t fit to hold elected office in this country.”
Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, was recently accused of “straightforward racism” by Labour after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali, was not British.
Nowak acknowledged that many TUC members will have backed Reform in recent local elections, but suggested the party’s appeal may be waning.
“Our members are a broad cross section of the British public. Of course, large numbers of them voted Reform, like other people did. But certainly the evidence that we’re getting fed back from unions is that just like the British public, the more they see of Nigel Farage, the less keen they are.”
Nowak claimed there was a “direct line” from the rhetoric of Farage and his allies, to what he called the “proto-fascism” of the balaclava-clad vigilantes who blocked infrastructure in Dover and tried to stop migrants arriving in Portsmouth last weekend.
He suggested Labour should focus on cost-of-living issues to combat Reform’s populist appeal – including offering voters more help with rising energy bills.
“The most important thing that Andy Burnham can do is to deliver the change that people voted for back in July 2024. If people feel that the government is taking the stuff that matters to them seriously and is delivering on it, I think it cuts the legs from underneath that rightwing populism.”
Ahead of the budget on 28 October, Nowak called for a “social tariff” to cut energy bills for lower paid users, funded by a windfall tax on the banks. “As well as delivering a boost to hundreds of thousands of households up and down the country, it will help bear down on the cost of inflation,” he said.
“The public bailed the banks out in 2008. For those families who are worried about turning on the heating this year, asking the banks to pay their fair share isn’t unreasonable.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “last November, we set out reforms to double the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute most to the UK.
“A consultation on elements of those reforms has now closed, and we will set out our response in due course.”

Is Burnham trying to appease Trump? Or Reform? What other reason is there for these North Sea oil plans? | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Pinch yourself, it’s happening again. Here is a Labour government spending a vast amount of political capital to earn tiny material gains while risking huge political losses. It occurred repeatedly under Keir Starmer, and now – with the impending decision to approve further gas and oil drilling in the North Sea – it is happening under Andy Burnham. You rack your brains to explain it, but no rational explanation comes.
Burnham is studiously cryptic about his reasons. His clearest statement to date goes as follows: “There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.” Does he mean that oil and gas workers are struggling? If so, this decision will be of little use to them. The Jackdaw gasfield, likely to be approved this week, will generate a grand total of 27 direct full-time jobs. The Rosebank oilfield, whose approval is likely to follow soon, will support 450 UK-based jobs during its lifetime. Yet the UK’s net zero economy directly employs 300,000 people, and a further 400,000 jobs are planned. The rest of the green economy employs more than 600,000. A just transition for fossil fuel workers, securing jobs in the green economy, is better for everyone.
Or does he mean energy consumers are struggling? The gas in the Jackdaw field will make a tiny contribution to our supply and no significant difference to either our energy bills or our energy security. Switching to renewables makes us far better off in both respects. Any oil produced by the Rosebank field is unlikely to be refined in Britain, as we no longer possess much capacity for handling oil of that kind. And as for the national accounts, a recent estimate suggests that the climate damage caused by the fields’ extra emissions would outweigh any economic benefits several times over.
In fact, the two greatest threats to the global economy might now be climate breakdown, which, as a wide range of economists and eminent organisations forecast, threatens comprehensive economic collapse, and the AI bubble, which the governor of the Bank of England warns could burst with dire consequences. Then people will really be struggling. Yet our government and others cheerfully accelerate both forces – claiming, as ever, that the industries driving them will unleash “growth”. Growth in home repossessions, perhaps.
While the small amount of fossil fuel these two fields will produce allows politicians to argue that their climate impacts can be ignored, the diplomatic implications are considerable. The only chance of preventing climate catastrophe is international agreement based on mutual trust. To its credit, the UK – while falling short of what many of us would like to see – has been a leader in these efforts. But when our government refuses to leave fossil fuels in the ground, its credibility diminishes – leaving its negotiating position weakened.
Burnham might believe this decision will get Reform UK and the Conservatives off his back. Of course it won’t. He might imagine it will appease Donald Trump, but you can’t appease Trump. Whatever you give him, he will always want more.
As for the political implications, here the disparity between gain and pain becomes truly enormous. The approval of these fields is a defining issue for many Labour MPs and the voters they fear they might lose. The policy could scarcely be better designed to give the final push to voters who are minded – after so many disappointments since 2024 – to abandon Labour for a progressive alternative.
If Zack Polanski, the Green party leader for England and Wales, wins the seat Keir Starmer has just vacated, this could be a major reason why. Burnham’s North Sea policy is the kind of battle Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney would have urged him to wage – let’s stick it to the Labour left, mwahaha – which is a major reason why Starmer is no longer prime minister.
Few in power seem to understand the fire they are playing with. Last week, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, appeared to acknowledge that we face the risk of potentially catastrophic environmental breakdown and urged us to store some extra food in our homes. The way she put it suggested that either she hasn’t grasped the magnitude of what we face, or she is trivialising the issue: “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t.”
Right. So let’s imagine one of several possible disasters some of us have long been warning of arrives. As a result of harvest failures caused by climate breakdown, severe transport disruptions or – and this now looks alarmingly plausible – sudden systemic collapse in the food sector, the supermarket shelves empty, more or less overnight. We know that the UK government refuses, without explanation, to maintain strategic food reserves. So there are no government supplies, either. As our beans and crackers run out, the emergency services visit all 29 million of our homes. With what? Tea and sympathy? Sorry, no tea. Another slice of sympathy?
Certainly, those of us who have the money and capacity to store food should do so: after all, no one else has our backs. But the idea that such individuated solutions would be any use in the face of a societal catastrophe is neoliberal nonsense. As always, it is the poor and excluded, with neither the cash nor the space to lay down significant supplies, who will be hit first and worst. Social breakdown would happen in days. The UK government, then, is being serious about neither the measures required to prevent climate catastrophe nor the measures required to survive it.
The sense in almost every nation is of governments failing to take seriously the most serious of issues, while spending immense political resources on topics that scarcely affect our welfare (such as a few thousand people crossing the Channel in small boats). Or even – as is the case with North Sea oil and gas – using their scarce political capital to make things worse for everyone, including themselves.
Our government is not a doomsday cult like the Trump government, creepily fascinated by the “end times”, as the US vice-president seems to be. But in terms of outcome, is there much difference?
- 
  George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

‘Institutional neglect’: 25 years on from 9/11, experts sound alarm over US counter-terror efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:15 UTC
14:00:15 KST

The US faces growing challenges in countering international terrorism as resources are diverted to other threats, experienced security officials leave and “complacency” spreads, experts have warned.
It is 25 years this week since the 9/11 attacks launched by Osama bin Laden’s al-Qaida on New York and Washington, which killed about 3,000 people and led to decades of conflict, radicalisation and instability across the Middle East and beyond.
Though there have been no successful attacks on anything like a similar scale in the US since, and only a small number inspired by extremist Islamist ideologies, many are warning of growing risks.
Some blame Donald Trump for politicising counter-terrorism efforts, making ill-considered and inappropriate appointments to senior intelligence posts and diverting attention from more urgent threats with a campaign against drug cartels.
Bruce Hoffman, a terrorism expert at Georgetown University, said: “I remember [9/11] and this pure chaos and pandemonium in the streets and I remember thinking that we would never lower our guard again and complacency against a threat that is episodic but when it is revealed highly consequential.”
This year, Hoffmann told the US House permanent select committee on intelligence that “the counter-terrorism architecture built after 9/11 is eroding … through budget cuts, personnel losses, and the diminution of terrorism as a national
  security priority”.
This was “recreating the conditions of under-resourcing and institutional neglect that preceded the 2001 attacks. Moreover, the terrorist threat to Americans has both changed and grown.”
Analysts are split over whether the lack of obvious recent efforts by al-Qaida to strike in the US suggests a lack of ambition or disguises a careful, strategic plan to wait for the right opportunity.
Last month, a UN report based on intelligence supplied by member states’ monitoring said the “al-Qaida senior leadership remained marginalized” while “its capability and intent to conduct external operations remained unclear”.
Colin Clarke, the executive director of the Soufan Center, said the US intelligence community was experiencing a “basket of factors” including “funding, personnel [and] complacency”.
“There is a certain amount of fatigue. We did the global war on terror for 20 years and people were keen to pivot to something else,” he said.
Most analysts support a 2018 shift away from terrorism to focus on “long-term, strategic competition by … revisionist powers” such as Russia and China. But choices made by the Trump administration have exacerbated existing problems.
“There is a real lack of morale because of the way the president has treated the intelligence community … the quiet professionals are really demoralised,” Clarke said.
Intelligence veterans criticised the appointments of Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence and Kash Patel as director of the FBI, accusing both of lacking sufficient top-level experience in law enforcement.
For the 2026 financial year, funding requested for the principal agencies of the
 civilian intelligence community totalled $81bn. But the designation of criminal groups such as the Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organisations has stretched resources.
An updated counter-terrorism strategy released in May by the Trump administration has been controversial. Many intelligence experts and analysts have highlighted how the strategy downplays the rising threat from rightwing extremism in the US and stresses instead the battle against leftwing violence, cartels and gangs.
“It is a very partial document [and] raises the question: are you protecting America or people who agree with you?” said Clarke. “We have finite resources now. You don’t have a blank cheque like after 9/11 and at the same time it’s not just Sunni jihadist groups which are considered the threat.”
Devorah Margolin at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy said that the new strategy was a significant shift. “That is not to say that counter-terrorism policies cannot change as the landscape changes, but this year’s strategy appears more focused on a political agenda than the reality of the threat,” Margolin added.
“While the strategy still acknowledged the threat posed by groups like the Islamic State and al-Qaida, it also expanded definitions of counter-terrorism. It sought to use the vast counter-terrorism bureaucracy that has been built over the last two decades for its own political agenda. This has spread dwindling counter-terrorism resources even thinner.”
The loss of experienced personnel is a significant problem, experts say, with many criticising the dismantlement last year of programmes aimed at countering extremist ideologies and preventing radicalisation.
Don Rassler, the director of strategic initiatives at the Combating Terrorism Center at West Point, said that terrorism became less of a priority as strategic focus shifted to real or potential threats from China and Russia, and warned the US needed to be careful the intelligence community did not “revert back to the dynamics that led to an event like 9/11”.
The 2001 attacks were the culmination of a series of attacks launched
 by Bin Laden on US targets. In 1996 and again in 1998, 10 years after founding al-Qaida, Bin Laden “declared war” on America with statements issued from a base in Afghanistan, listing grievances including US backing for “tyrannical, apostate” regimes in the Middle East such as in his native Saudi Arabia amid a broader diatribe against what he called western aggression against Muslims worldwide.
Shortly afterwards, double bombings demolished two US embassies in east Africa and a suicide attack nearly sank a US warship off Yemen in 2000. The failure of senior officials including George W Bush to act on multiple intelligence warnings was highlighted by the congressional investigation into the 9/11 attacks, as well as the failure of the FBI and the CIA to share with each other vital information that might have prevented the atrocity.
An al-Qaida effort to blow up a passenger plane as it prepared to land in Detroit in 2009 was averted only at the last minute when explosives failed to detonate as intended. An attack a decade later by a single “self-radicalised” Saudi Arabian air force officer in Florida which killed three was linked to the organisation’s affiliate in Yemen.
Since then, there have been more than 100 attacks in the US by violent Islamic extremists linked to the broader “jihadi” movement, according to a count by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Rassler said extremist Islamist groups were still a key priority but with fewer resources and fewer people the US had “to accept more terrorist risk”.
“There hasn’t been another attack … but there is a danger of believing that the [terrorist] threat isn’t there. The threat is different in many ways from 10 years ago and we have to be as clear-eyed as possible about it.”

The top 10 most walkable cities have been ranked – and seven are in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:06 UTC
14:00:06 KST

The best city breaks don’t always need taxis, metros or complicated transport plans. A new index has ranked the most walkable up-and-coming destinations around the world, with European cities dominating the list.
Many of us enjoy a city break, and the most seasoned travellers know that a successful trip is often down, in part, at least, to a destination being walkable.
Now Skyscanner has revealed the best up-and-coming cities for a break which aren’t the obvious choices – think Berlin or Dubrovnik.
Experts at the travel booking platform looked at flight data for destinations outside the United States which are walkable and easy to navigate.
A total of 14 factors for each city were evaluated, including the distances between the main attractions, the number of walking trails, average elevation, air quality and safety.
The result is a walkability index, which focuses on the walking distance between a place’s main attractions and the total steps and time taken to do it. The index also examines population density as well as the number of trails to explore in and around each city, and the amount of attractions in each place.
While Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan and Victoria in Canada were in the top 10, the rest of the spots were taken up by European cities.
The top 10 most walkable cities
How they ranked according to the Skyscanner data:
- 1. Córdoba, Spain
- 2. Nagasaki, Japan
- 3. Hiroshima, Japan
- 4. Reggio Calabria, Italy
- 5. Monte Carlo, Monaco
- 6. Tartu, Estonia
- 7. Bursa, Türkiye
- 8. Bolzano, Italy
- 9. Sarajevo, Bosnia & Herzegovina
- 10. Victoria, British Columbia, Canada
Europe’s most walkable cities
Córdoba, Spain
In the heart of Andalusia, Córdoba was once an important Roman city and, historically, a major Islamic centre.
Today, it’s arguably most famous for its striking mosque, La Mezquita, which can, of course, be seen on foot.
Be sure to check out the Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as well as the Palacio de Viana, La Judería, and the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos.
According to Skyscanner, not only does it take just 26 minutes to walk around the main attractions, but there are also an impressive 29 walking trails to enjoy in and around the city.
Reggio Calabria, Italy
Reggio Calabria is often overlooked in favour of busier destinations in Italy, but this city in the south is ideal to explore on foot.
The coastal city, separated from Sicily via the Strait of Messina, offers stunning beaches as well as views across to Mount Etna.
As well as the impressive waterfront, visit the Rabarama statues along Via Marina and the Museo Nazionale Della Magna Grecia.
Best of all, all of the attractions can be seen on foot in just 25 minutes and 2,321 steps.
Monte Carlo, Monaco
Although Monte Carlo goes hand-in-hand with fancy cars and super yachts, it’s actually a great place to explore on two feet.
Meander through the streets packed with designer shops – whether you’re strictly window shopping or otherwise – before taking in incredible views of the ocean from Rue des Remparts.
Head to the glamorous harbour as well as top attractions including the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, Casino Square and the Private Cars Collection of HSH Prince of Monaco.
While Monte Carlo is certainly very walkable, as the city limits are less than one square kilometre, be warned that the hills here are pretty steep.
Tartu, Estonia
Despite being the second largest city in Estonia and a European Capital of Culture in 2024, Tartu is relatively unknown.
That’s despite a pretty old town, ruins and neighbourhoods made up of wooden houses.
The city, which is committed to sustainable practices and has the lowest air pollution of all destinations on the list, also boasts street art, plenty of parks and riverside walks.
Must-see attractions include the Estonian National Museum, the Town Hall Square and the Botanical Garden of the University of Tartu.
Bursa, Türkiye
This modern and industrial city in the northwest of Türkiye is home to the Royal Springs – renowned hot mineral waters, popular since Roman and Byzantine times.
Today, Bursa is a fusion of Ottoman heritage, as it was the first Ottoman capital. You’ll find buzzy bazaars and plenty of natural beauty, as well as the Tomb of Osman Gazi, Bursa Grand Mosque and Kozahan İpekçiler Bazaar.
Skyscanner data found that it will take a visitor about an hour to walk between the main attractions here.
Bolzano, Italy
Known as the “gateway to the Dolomites”, Bolzano is often overlooked, with people simply passing through on their way to hike or ski.
The capital of the South Tyrol province, though, is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of city breaks.
Set in a valley surrounded by hilly vineyards, the city’s major attractions can be ticked off in about an hour on foot, and include Piazza Walther, Via dei Portici and the South Tyrol Archaeological Museum.
Bolzano also has a solid 505 walking trails in and around the city and is the safest city in the ranking.
Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina
The Bosnian capital isn’t only compact and walkable, but it also offers stunning scenery from its location on the Miljacka River and into the surrounding Dinaric Alps.
The city, filled with cobbled streets and eclectic architecture, is a great spot to learn about the country’s rich history on a walking tour. Follow that with a visit to the Museum of Crimes against Humanity and Genocide, and the War Childhood Museum.
Take the weight off in one of Sarajevo’s many cafes to try its famed coffee culture for yourself, before heading to the city hall, as well as the lively Baščaršija bazaar and the Latin Bridge.

Is Vilnius ready to handle the traffic around the national stadium?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

With the national stadium nearing completion in Vilnius, members of the public are raising questions about whether this will mean more pressure on the already strained road network.
Three streets in Vilnius are currently most at risk of major congestion affecting public transport and cars, according to Kristina Čižiūnienė, an associate professor at Vilnius Gediminas Technical University (VILNIUS TECH).
They are Ozo, Ukmergės and Siesikų streets. Local roads in the Šeškinė district could also come under additional pressure.
"Šeškinė's existing transport infrastructure is not capable of handling tens of thousands of stadium visitors, especially if a large proportion of them arrive by car," Čižiūnienė says.
The expert also identified measures Vilnius city authorities could take to reduce the impact on the city's transport system:
"Reconstruction of the main road network around the stadium; efficient public transport operations, such as more frequent services before and after events and priority for bus lanes; temporary traffic management measures during events; a Park and Ride system; and improvements to pedestrian and cycling infrastructure."
However, to avoid congestion, the associate professor recommends travelling to events by public transport or on foot.
"For the transport system to operate smoothly enough, most stadium visitors should choose public transport, walking or cycling rather than cars. Can this goal be achieved? The answer is not straightforward, as it will depend on many factors, as well as on how responsibly event-goers behave," Čižiūnienė says.
Assessing how Vilnius is preparing for increased visitor numbers, the associate professor believes the municipality started getting ready too late.
"The stadium project was discussed and developed for a very long time, while transport solutions around the stadium only began to be implemented more intensively as the end of construction approached.
"The main challenge in this case is not the stadium itself, but the fact that it will be built in an already busy part of the city, where both the transport system and the wider infrastructure will have to adapt to increased periodic flows of people and vehicles," Čižiūnienė says.
City authorities: Akropolis car park will help
Only 300 new parking spaces will be built next to the stadium, Vilnius city authorities say. However, they believe the 13,000 sq m Akropolis car park, which is owned by the municipality, should help ease the problem.
Preliminary estimates suggest that about 50% of people attending events or competitions could arrive by car, the municipality says.
However, some of them are expected to leave their vehicles further away.
The municipality estimates that the average daily traffic load on surrounding streets should increase by about 6%, while potential congestion should be eased by the reconstruction of the Ozo and Ukmergės streets junction that is currently being carried out.
JUDU promises more frequent services
To improve access to the stadium, Vilnius’ public transport also promises changes.
Special public transport services will also operate during events, while existing services will run more frequently.
The main public transport and traffic management solutions are due to be prepared before the stadium opens, according to Indrė Žvirblienė, a representative of the city’s transportation department, JUDU.
JUDU plans to collect traffic data after events and adjust traffic management accordingly, based on the flows observed.
"The stadium is planned to be served by the main public transport routes along Ozo and Ukmergės streets. From there, routes would connect to the most densely populated districts, major interchange hubs, bus and railway stations, and the airport," Žvirblienė says.

Instagram boss warns users will be 'overwhelmed' without algorithm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:59:38 UTC
13:59:38 KST

Instagram chief Adam Mosseri warns against turning off algorithm as Australia debates opt-out laws
In short:
The head of Instagram says the average person who turns off their algorithm will have a much worse "user experience" and he does not think the platform is addictive.
The comments come two days after the Albanese government announced a proposal to force platforms to give Australians a choice to quit their algorithmically-curated feed.
Chronological feeds are already available to Instagram users in Australia but Adam Mosseri said user awareness was low, and there was "room to improve discoverability".
As the Australian parliament considers new rules for opting out of the social media algorithm, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, has warned most users do not enjoy what they find on the other side.
The federal government unveiled a proposal this week to force platforms to give users the choice, via push notifications, to opt out of the algorithm that curates their feed and instead view posts chronologically.
It is part of a long-awaited Digital Duty of Care framework, designed to shift responsibility onto big tech to proactively reduce harms, or face $100 million fines.
Mr Mosseri weighed in to the debate indirectly, during a rare Australian press briefing today, intended to promote the platform's new short-form series Algo Confessions, as well as the Your Algorithm feature, which theoretically allows users to see and even edit their algorithm.
A Meta spokesman told reporters on the call that the Instagram chief would not be commenting on the government's proposal, but Mr Mosseri volunteered his view on chronological feeds.
Citing the company's experience in other countries, he said "the average user experience gets much worse".
"If you go to a chronological feed, it ends up getting overwhelmed with content from companies, brands, and publishers," he said.
"Creators get drowned out, and then your friends get drowned out even more."
The reason, he said, was that the best way to achieve reach in a chronological feed was to post more often, and businesses could afford to post more often than ordinary people.
While he did not provide figures, he said engagement ultimately fell by as much as 50 per cent.
"You miss a lot more content … and you spend a lot less time on the platform," he said.
For the people shaping these laws, causing users to spend less time on the platform is one of the main goals, but Mr Mosseri said crucially, user satisfaction also suffered.
"We ask people every day how satisfied they are with the experience," he said.
"Both at the aggregate [experience], 'are you satisfied?' and at the specific post, 'was this worth your time?', those numbers fall off a cliff.
"So, there's this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community."
Mr Mosseri said he assumed the "passionate few" who really wanted to opt out of the algorithm were happy with the choice, but those users were in the minority.
Australians can opt out of their algorithm now, but few realise it
What few users realise is that a chronological feed is already available on Instagram globally, including in Australia.
On Instagram, users can tap on the logo to access a drop-down menu, which offers a "following" setting.
If selected, the user's feed transforms into a stream of posts from followed accounts in reverse chronological order, minus the algorithmic recommendations.
But unlike in the Netherlands, the feed reverts to using the algorithm when you close and re-open the app.
Mr Mosseri said, although he did not have figures, that uptake in Australia had been low.
"An educated guess would be in the low single-digit percentages," he said.
He said users probably did not know about the option, but "that's not on purpose".
"I'm not trying to hide it…. I think we can make it more prominent,"
"Instagram is too complicated, if you ask me.
"There's a lot of things to squeeze into the page … so we've been trying not to just add more buttons for everything.
"There's definitely room to improve the discoverability of that."
The federal government's My Feed, My Way bill comes less than a year after a court decision brought about similar rules in the Netherlands.
Since 2023, the European Union has had laws in effect for 27 member states requiring large platforms such as Instagram to give users the option of a chronological feed.
Under those rules, the choice must also be made accessible to users, rather than being buried in settings controls, where many users might never find it.
But in October 2025, a Dutch court went a step further, ordering platforms provide chronological feeds as a default.
This morning, Mr Mosseri said in the absence of defaults, uptake would probably remain low.
"Anything that isn't the default just doesn't get used the majority of the time, which is why defaults are so important," he said.
The federal government's push on chronological feeds was not originally slated as a centrepiece of the Digital Duty of Care, but the idea gained prominence after Meta's landmark $23 billion US court settlement last month, in which the company also agreed to allow US teens to choose a chronological feed.
The suit, brought by 29 US states, was premised on the accusation that Instagram's parent company had intentionally designed its platforms to addict young people.
Mr Mosseri said he did not believe Instagram was addictive, although that might be "controversial to say".
"I do think we often, in English anyway, conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted, like, 'I'm addicted to this show and I'm binge-watching it,'… [as opposed to] clinical addiction," he said.
"I just think those things are different."
Mr Mosseri acknowledged that social media users were increasingly frustrated by the "black box" nature of the algorithms that decide what they see.
"What we are trying to figure out now is how do we bring back more agency, bring back more transparency, bring back more control?" He said.
He said ultimately, Instagram wants people to enjoy the app, and that the company needed to take "a long view" when it came to how much time people using it.
"We try to optimise for things like… satisfaction, preference, which I think [it's] hard to imagine benefit from people compulsively using the platform."

Born in Magdeburg in 1949, Ulrich Wüst began attracting attention in the 1980s, particularly for his numerous urban landscapes photographed in East Germany. The images often capture the seemingly unstoppable decay of historic architecture. Wüst is drawn to the absurdities of the urban environment – the result of neglect and ignorance, but also of senseless demolition and uncontrolled development.

Vietnam’s To Lam Concludes State Visit to Russia, Departs For France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:56:00 UTC
13:56:00 KST

Vietnam’s top leader To Lam yesterday wound up a state visit to Russia during which he and Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged to develop their cooperation in the realms of trade, energy, and defense.
Lam arrived in Russia on Monday for a three-day visit, before departing yesterday for France, where he was scheduled to meet with President Emmanuel Macron and attend the International Space Summit in Paris.
During the visit, Lam, who serves both as president and general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held talks with Putin, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Chairman of the State Duma Vyacheslav Volodin, and other high-ranking officials.
Ahead of their meeting, Putin praised Vietnam’s “impressive results” under the CPV’s rule, and said that he was “delighted” to welcome Lam and his delegation to the Kremlin. In turn, the Vietnamese leader described Putin as “a great friend of our country,” and said that Hanoi views its relationship with Moscow as “a priority, a consistent pillar of our foreign policy, and a strategic choice of enduring significance.” Both sides made ample reference to the Cold War-era cooperation between communist North Vietnam and the Soviet Union.
Addressing the media after the meeting, Putin described the talks as “very meaningful and substantive” and said that the two sides had signed an “impressive package” of bilateral agreements. These included MoUs in areas such as justice, finance, investment, transport, ethnic affairs, energy, nuclear safety, science and technology, education, and mineral resources, Vietnamese state media reported.
Putin said that economics and trade was a particular focus of talks. He noted that while trade had increased by more than 5 percent last year, progress that he attributed to the free trade agreement between Vietnam and the Russia-dominated Eurasian Economic Union, “the overall volume of trade in absolute terms does not yet match the potential.” The two sides agreed to target $15 billion in two-way trade by 2030.
Another priority was cooperation in the energy sector, which has been a recent priority for both governments. In a joint statement released yesterday, the two sides described energy as an area of “strategic breakthrough in Vietnam-Russia relations” that would help shore up energy security for both countries. Both sides “agreed to improve the efficiency of ongoing projects and continue to expand cooperation in the oil and gas sector in Vietnam and Russia,” the statement said. It also referenced the March 2026 agreement with Russia that will likely make Vietnam the first Southeast Asian nation to achieve a civilian nuclear energy capacity, stating that it had “opened a new chapter” in the two countries’ partnership.
Specifically, Vietnam’s state energy firm Petrovietnam signed a framework agreement with the Russian state-owned oil and gas company Zarubezhneft on cooperation in a project to set up a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam.
“The Russian side has proposed that its partners consider the idea of jointly establishing strategic fuel reserves in Vietnam,” Putin told the media after his meeting with Lam. “Our companies are also interested in establishing transit energy supplies through Vietnamese territory to neighboring countries.”
Lam said that Vietnam “welcomes more active investment by Russian corporations and enterprises in the development of renewable energy, oil and gas sector and the development of deep-sea resources.” He added that the Russian side would strive to “create favorable conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to expand their investment and business activities in Russia in such areas as agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and seafood.”
Above all, Lam’s visit testifies to the energy that Vietnam has invested in its foreign partnerships since he took over the leadership of the CPV just over two years ago. In that time, Lam has paid official visits to China, Russia, Belarus, India, and Cuba, as well as the U.S., France, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, and regional partners including Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
He has also spearheaded a rapid expansion of Vietnam’s circle of Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships, welcoming France (October 2024), Malaysia (November 2024), New Zealand (February 2025), Indonesia (March 2025), Singapore (March 2025), Thailand (May 2025), the U.K. (October 2025), and the European Union (January 2026) to the top tier of Hanoi’s diplomatic hierarchy.
In recent weeks, Lam supplemented this to state visits to Australia and New Zealand and met with Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Hanoi. According to Reuters, he is also expected to address the U.N. General Assembly in New York later this month, and to make a state visit to Canada. In October, the news agency added, the Vietnamese leader “is expected to return to Europe, where he could meet EU leaders in Brussels as part of a broader trip, according to three people informed about the plans.”
The varied political hue of Vietnam’s key partnership, and its ability to maintain good relationships with them is the essence of its doctrine of “bamboo diplomacy.” Judging by Lam’s crowded travel schedule, Hanoi is doubling down on this approach as the world enters a period of global perturbation and flux.
