John Major’s rise from obscure whip to PM part of new National Theatre season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

A new play about John Major’s rise to power, written by James Graham, will premiere at the National Theatre in London next year, as part of a season that puts political upheaval and global conflict at the heart of its programme.
Major reunites Graham with Jeremy Herrin, the director behind the acclaimed parliamentary drama This House. It will chart Major’s emergence from relatively obscure whip to prime minister, taking over from Margaret Thatcher at a pivotal moment in Britain’s relationship with Europe.
The National Theatre said the play would explore what leadership means at times of political change, with Graham returning to the recent political history that has become a recurring subject of his work.
It is one of eight world premieres announced by the theatre for next year, with a programme that its director, Indhu Rubasingham, said would examine “the perspectives, cultures and conflicts that continue to shape our world”.
Also on the programme is The Great Indaba, written by Moira Buffini and directed by Rubasingham, which dramatises an extraordinary 1997 meeting in South Africa involving Nelson Mandela’s new national unity government and political rivals from Northern Ireland, as the Good Friday agreement negotiations approached a breakthrough.
Another new play, Samira, by Carmen Nasr, is set during the Arab Spring and will be directed by Emily Burns. The Adeyemis – A Family Saga, a new political family drama by the British Nigerian writer Oladipo Agboluaje, will have its world premiere in the Dorfman theatre, directed by Lucian Msamati and starring Uzo Aduba.
Among the season’s other new work is Mr Loverman, Natasha Gordon’s stage adaptation of Bernardine Evaristo’s acclaimed novel about a married Caribbean man confronting his sexuality. Gary Beadle, Jo Martin and Danny Sapani are among the initial cast, with Paulette Randall directing.
There is also a new British musical, Glorious Madness, featuring songs by Joan Armatrading, with a book by Iman Qureshi and directed by Phyllida Lloyd.
The multi-award-winning theatre company Punchdrunk open a new immersive production called Ghostlight, conceived and directed by founder and artistic director Felix Barrett and curated by writer Lucy Kirkwood.
The programme is not without established works, but the balance is notable. Rather than a season dominated by Shakespeare and the traditional theatrical canon, the National has announced a series of modern classics and 20th-century works: West Side Story, co-directed by Marianne Elliott and Miranda Cromwell; Tennessee Williams’ Suddenly Last Summer, directed by Michael Grandage and starring Emma Corrin and Harriet Walter; David Hare’s Plenty, directed by former National Theatre director Richard Eyre and starring Emilia Clarke; and Death of a Salesman, starring Paul Mescal and Tracy Letts.
Tom Murphy’s A Whistle in the Dark and Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead will also return to the stage, with Mescal leading a repertory production alongside Death of a Salesman.
Notably, however, there is no Shakespeare production among the National’s three main stages in the new season. Hamlet will instead be among new titles added to the National Theatre Collection, the organisation’s streaming and education service.
The National says the 2027 programme will include 18 productions, eight of them world premieres, alongside touring productions and work reaching audiences through cinema, streaming and schools.
Rubasingham said the season was united by “themes of resilience and hope” and was intended to reflect “the international spirit at the heart of our National Theatre”.
Kate Varah, the theatre’s executive and co-chief executive, said the programme represented an investment in “original storytelling” and in “bold artistic voices”, at a time when theatre was increasingly reaching audiences beyond its South Bank stages.

====================================================================================================

‘A completely unique opportunity’: the secretive process that will decide the BBC’s future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

In a temperature-controlled room in a suburb of Reading, the basis of the BBC’s existence is kept in a flat, square, faded navy case, the size of a large pizza box. Inside is a stack of vellum – calfskin, pounded until it forms a milky and translucent paper that is supposed to last for thousands of years. The queen’s red wax seal is secured to its base with red and gold cord. The pages are strapped down with two strips of white elastic, more PE kit than Buckingham Palace.
The document is unique. Like hundreds of other British organisations, the BBC was founded via a Royal Charter, granted by the monarch of the day. But unlike Oxford colleges, the British Film Institute, or the Worshipful Company of Makers of Playing Cards, the BBC was given an expiry date. When the British Broadcasting Corporation was founded, in the 1920s, radio was seen as such an uncertain, risky technology that the government only gave it a 10-year guarantee, after which it would have to seek a new charter.
Ever since, the BBC has been forced to repeatedly regenerate, much like the lead character in its beloved series Doctor Who. Most governments have granted decade-long charters, with some variation. (The 2017 charter was set at 11 years to unhook it from the five-year British general election cycle.) Like the Doctor, in each iteration the BBC retains the same name, the same job, and does many of the same things. Yet at midnight on the night of its renewal, it disappears, and is replaced by a new version of itself. If the charter is not renewed, the BBC would cease to exist as a legal entity: it could no longer employ its staff, broadcast or publish, and its assets would automatically pass to the state.
The current charter will expire on 31 December 2027, and its replacement is now the subject of lobbying, scaremongering and dealmaking as its contents are debated, tugged apart and rewritten. The charter is produced via a two- or three-year negotiation between government and the BBC. It is a process that has a claim to being one of the largest acts of public participation in British politics, yet it is also a black box, its inner workings hidden from view. The last charter renewal process involved 16 focus groups, two independent reports, nine industry round tables and 300 meetings with organisations and experts. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) received 190,000 responses to a public consultation and had to hire a new building in order for staff to read them all.
Charter renewal is partly an exercise in predicting the future: in deciding what Britain and the media landscape will look like in a decade, and how the BBC must transform accordingly. This is why it is so difficult, and so fraught. The charter is the only way that the BBC’s purpose, funding model or governance can be drastically changed. It is through charter renewals that the BBC built Britain’s television infrastructure, launched its first website and built a streaming platform, the iPlayer, while Netflix was still sending out DVDs through the post.
The risk of failing to meet the moment bedevils every charter renewal. Debates about the BBC are so familiar that they have become a kind of white noise: whether it is secretly right or leftwing; whether it contributed to Brexit or sought to undermine it; whether its stars are paid too much, and so on. But to look at the history of charter renewal is to see that the real existential threats it faces are never the stuff of fleeting scandals or culture wars. In 2026, what is really threatening the BBC are the much larger tides of changing technology and changing habits. Year on year, fewer and fewer people are using the BBC, and fewer and fewer people are paying for it. Hundreds of millions of pounds in cuts are under way to balance the books. This charter renewal is its only chance to turn back those tides.
And yet in my interviews with 30 experts and BBC and government insiders over the past year, most struggled to tell me exactly what the charter is. One former director general told me simply: “The charter is … the charter.” Part of the difficulty of comprehending the charter lies in the difficulty of grasping the breadth and depth of the BBC itself. On a single day in 2026, the BBC staged a Stravinsky concert, brought its Strictly Come Dancing tour to Liverpool, broke a news story about cameras spying on people having sex in Chinese hotel rooms, broadcast a Gaelic news roundup, reported on speed limits in the Welsh town of Barry, interviewed Venezeula’s opposition leader, unveiled the lineup for the music festival it was putting on in Manchester, knocked on 10,000 doors of licence fee non-payers, and broadcast the opening ceremony of the Milan Winter Olympics. The BBC is so baked into British life that it is hard to unpick exactly what it represents, and what it would mean for it to change, shrink or even disappear.
In Reading, the navy blue box sits on its shelf in the BBC’s archive, rarely consulted, gathering dust. As long as the negotiation is completed in time, it will be replaced on 1 January 2028. The BBC’s survival depends on that new stack of calfskin, and whether its predictions hold true. “I don’t think we’ve had a charter renewal as consequential as this – and as potentially fantastically good – since the second world war,” Jean Seaton, the BBC’s official historian, told me. “It is a completely unique opportunity.”
On 16 December 2025, nearly a year later than promised, the charter renewal process officially began. In a 38,000 word green paper, Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, set out her vision for the BBC and invited feedback from the public. She described the BBC as a “light on the hill”, an institution as vital to Britain as the NHS. She suggested that the BBC could focus more on countering disinformation, and that it could move more of its work out of London. This was all well and good, but for the kind of readers who were impatiently awaiting this document – thinktanks, unions, politicians, media professionals inside and outside the BBC – most will have flicked first to the end: the bit about the funding.
Everyone agrees the funding model isn’t working. “A busted flush” is how the new BBC director general, former Google executive Matt Brittin, described it recently. About 65% of the BBC’s funding comes from the £180 licence fee, which is paid by any household that watches any live TV or uses iPlayer. The problem is that takings have dropped by a quarter – about £1.3bn in real terms – since 2017. Some of that is down to governments imposing below-inflation fee rises or no rises at all; some is down to the growing number of those refusing or unable to pay.
In the green paper, Nandy ruled out funding the BBC via taxation or a household levy, a model used in Germany and elsewhere. That leaves only three options: advertising, subscriptions or a reformed licence fee (or some combination of the above). The green paper also suggested growing BBC Studios, its commercial production company, and setting up partnerships with tech companies, but commercial revenues fund about 8% of the BBC’s public service output – they can’t replace the licence fee.
The green paper ended with 32 questions, to be answered by any member of the public or organisation who wished to give their view. Not everyone was happy with this. The questions were “leading, lacking and limited”, said Paul Fleming, general secretary of the performing arts union Equity, which announced it would be boycotting the survey. The Media Reform Coalition, which campaigns for more accountability, put out an “alternative green paper” as a “direct response to this hollow exercise in public consultation”. At the launch event in March, policy experts read out their own ideas; one performed a poem calling for BBC governance that is both “broad and shallow” and “deep and narrow”. That month, the BBC released its own response to the green paper, rejecting the idea of subscriptions or advertising, and asking the Foreign Office to fund the World Service in its entirety, as it did before 2014, when George Osborne shifted the costs on to the BBC.
By the time it finished in March, the public consultation had brought in about 120,000 responses. These must all be read and summarised for the culture minister, to meet a legal obligation that responses should be “conscientiously taken into account”. In the last charter process, Radio Times magazine threatened DCMS with legal action after it found that a memory stick containing 6,085 of its readers’ consultation responses had never been opened.
A varied cast of politicians and experts sought to influence the debate in the wood-panelled room of the culture, media and sport select committee. (The committee has no direct role in charter renewal, but invites guests to give evidence to inform the debate.) There was no shortage of ideas. Between May and August, plans were floated for “public service algorithms” to counter the narrowing effect of social media. Others proposed a kind of global iPlayer, bringing together public service broadcasters around the world, and called for a “citizens’ panel” to give the public a voice in the way the BBC is run. Jordan Schwarzenberger, the manager of YouTube stars the Sidemen, was brought in to suggest how the BBC could attract younger audiences. It needs to focus on “the slightly harsher, more raw and edgy content that young audiences are craving”, he argued. When asked if the Sidemen might appear on Celebrity Gladiators, he delicately explained that for the money on offer, it wouldn’t be worth their while.
What do all these thousands of words of debate, discussion, reports, responses and meetings actually add up to? It is not entirely clear. Because while experts, industry professionals and the public are asked to weigh in, they can only offer suggestions. When I asked people involved with previous charter renewals who actually decides what goes into the final text, the answer was unanimous: it’s the culture minister, with the prime minister and chancellor looming behind them. Tom Chivers, a media campaigner who wrote his PhD on the last charter renewal, found it to be an “erratic and decidedly undemocratic” process, marked in its later stages by a “withdrawal from its earlier public settings and into private, bureaucratic channels of elite decision-making”. This first flurry of activity and public debate is, he told me, “just gloss for what they already want to do”.
The latter stages of the charter process are under way now: a negotiation behind closed doors, between a small group of people, only a handful of whom hold any real power.
It is very easy to find people to speak to about the BBC. Almost every person in Britain has interacted with it, and has a view on it. And yet it is difficult to find many people with a view of the corporation in its entirety. As with the story of the blind men and the elephant, even BBC experts tend to have a clear perspective on only one limb: impartiality in news coverage, say, or the funding model, or an obscure sports programme axed back in the 80s. (And as with the story of the blind men and the elephant, the interested parties are overridingly men. A recent book of letters to the new director general did not feature a single woman; most of the books written about the BBC are by men, with a few notable exceptions; there has never been a female director general.)
From the huge array of opinions that swirl around the BBC, however, it is possible to discern three broad schools of thought. The first camp, the custodians, frames the corporation as a vital fortress, to be defended in its current form, at all costs. In this view, the BBC’s primacy in British life is assumed and its founding principles of independence from government and universality are sacrosanct.
The second camp, the shrinkers, views the BBC as one media company among many – one granted unfair advantages. In the past, it was this camp that argued successfully against the BBC’s monopoly first on radio, and then on television. These days, they rail against successful programmes such as The Traitors and Strictly Come Dancing, which, they say, could be made by commercial rivals. The shrinkers argue that the BBC should stick to its USP – the public service meat and potatoes of current affairs and children’s programming. This group also objects to the corporation’s vast scale: its 10 TV channels, 56 radio stations, five orchestras and a workforce that, at 21,000, is larger than that of either the Scottish or Welsh governments.
This second group is often framed as anti-BBC. This is fair if you believe, as the first camp does, that a more limited BBC is not really a BBC at all. But it is worth noting that many in this second camp would say they love the BBC and value public service media. Their objection lies in the idea that the BBC should be all things to all people, at the cost of competitors.
At the far edge of this camp, at least on paper, sits the Reform party, whose official policy is not to scrap the BBC, but to scrap the licence fee and force the BBC to act as a commercial entity, probably via a subscription service. Its chair, Lee Anderson, has boasted in parliament that he personally refuses to pay it (despite the fact he appears on GB News, which you need a TV licence to watch live).
The custodians and the shrinkers have been locked in battle since the BBC’s creation. To justify the licence fee to the first camp, the BBC must appeal to all ages, political persuasions and corners of the country. And yet if it succeeds in this feat, it is accused by the second camp of dominating the market and crowding out competitors. When in government, shrinkers then try to cut the BBC down to size, which in turn leads to questions about a reduced corporation’s ability to appeal to everyone. The cycle continues. In his 1986 book, somewhat prematurely titled The Last Days of the Beeb, the journalist Michael Leapman described the BBC’s bind: “It is like one of those computer adventure games where the player escapes from one mortal peril only to find he has landed himself in another tough spot, still more threatening.”
The latest version of this debate concerns online platforms. The BBC recently struck a deal to grow its number of YouTube channels to at least 50, and the government has suggested it may legislate to give the BBC and other public service news providers more prominence on the platform. YouTube creators have claimed that this will, to quote one, “kill YouTube”. Schwarzenberger, manager of the Sidemen, told the select committee: “Public service broadcasting does not really equate with the gen Z or gen Alpha experience … why [should] the BBC have a leg-up on a private platform like YouTube, when the whole premise of YouTube is that it is totally meritocratic?” On newer platforms, the shrinkers hold sway: the BBC is just one content creator among billions.
A third camp – let’s call them the engineers – believes the argument between the shrinkers and the custodians misses the point entirely. The BBC was founded to both produce radio programmes and to run the wireless network for the public good. That logic, the engineers say, should now be applied to digital media. “If the BBC thinks it’s just in the content business, then it’s already over. It’s lost,” Tony Ageh, one of the architects of the iPlayer, told me.
In an era of streamers, AI and social media platforms, the engineers believe the BBC should be building its own platforms or algorithms, so as to be less reliant on US billionaires, setting up safe social media sites for the under-16s, or offering free internet access for public service content. If it doesn’t, then those without broadband will lose access to BBC channels when terrestrial is switched off, which could be as soon as 2034. Pat Younge, a former BBC chief creative officer and now chair of the campaigning organisation British Broadcasting Challenge, told me: “The biggest threat when Donald Trump said he might sue the BBC wasn’t that he would sue – it was that he would get Jeff Bezos to withdraw Amazon Web Services from them, at which point iPlayer collapses.”
Throughout the summer, 15 formal meetings have taken place between DCMS and BBC officials, with more to come through the rest of the year and into 2027. These meetings are private. No public record is released. It’s here that the real work of drafting the charter is done.
BBC officials may be in the room for these conversations, but it is clear where the power lies. One senior DCMS figure in a previous negotiation recalled reminding the BBC that this was a review, not an automatic renewal: “It’s not an absolute certainty when we start that the charter will be renewed at all.”
With no official levers to pull, the BBC must rely on diplomacy. In 2016-17, Tony Hall, the director general, met the then secretary of state for culture, John Whittingdale, or “Whitto”, as he called him when we spoke, for regular dinners one on one. (Whittingdale told me his officials “hated” that they met in private.) Other director generals have approached the dynamic rather differently: in 1947, the negotiator on the government side sent the director general, William Haley, a testy letter in response to changes he’d made to a draft of the charter. Haley passed it on to a colleague with a note scrawled in fountain pen: “This will amuse you. I do not intend to reply. I have stated the corporation’s view and the matter will be left till they raise it again.”
While ministers hold the power, they do not always have much expertise or interest. “Going quite a long way back, I can remember one secretary of state who fell asleep during a meeting with me,” said Stewart Purvis, who worked on broadcast policy for years at Ofcom. “No one dared say anything.” Purvis went on to advise DMCS on the 2017 charter and was asked by civil servants to help draft its text. This experience did not fill him with confidence. “DCMS has never been highly regarded in Whitehall, and you’re always wondering: ‘This is all very well. I’m a cog in this wheel, but at the end of the day, does Downing Street agree with any of this?’” Advisers to ministers would leak stories to further DCMS’s agenda, whether with the public or with Downing Street. “That seemed to be their principal role, to do the leaks,” Purvis said. “There was always pressure within DCMS to find a big story about charter renewal for the Sunday Times. That seemed to be the comms plan, if you like.”
Meanwhile, back at the BBC, since the 1940s a “war room” committee has been convened to feed into the negotiations. Former employees described a frantic scramble across departments, each quizzed on “what they were doing for charter renewal”, and rushing to launch projects to justify their existence. A recent internal call about charter renewal was joined by more than 6,000 staff.
The BBC has one other weapon at its disposal: public opinion. In their 2020 book The War Against the BBC, Patrick Barwise and Peter York blasted the Conservatives’ approach to the BBC in the run up to the last charter, which was widely seen as an attempt to shrink its power. And yet, in their view at least, this was mitigated by the “open, democratic and evidence-based charter renewal process”. A petition to “save the BBC” was signed by 305,000 people, and there were marches and protests against the closure of BBC Three. When the white paper – a kind of draft charter, which lays out the government’s proposals – was released, some of Whittingdale’s more outlandish ideas, such as government input on the scheduling of popular programmes, were absent. A DCMS civil servant involved in that negotiation confirmed that there was a strong sense that “at the point that the government takes on the BBC and the public chooses a side, the government loses, because the public values the BBC so highly”.
Over coffee in Portcullis House in February, Whittingdale looked back with pride on the marches and aerated parliamentary debate of that charter review, despite the fact they were largely directed against him. “There was a lot of parliamentary interest, there was commercial interest, and a lot of public interest. None of which, I have to say, seems to be the case now,” he said.
There is a general assumption that Labour governments are more pro-BBC, which may explain why the debate has been more muted this time round. (Jean Seaton told me this has been at times “both true and completely untrue: Harold Wilson hated the BBC”.) Multiple people familiar with the process told me that as prime minister, Keir Starmer wanted to avoid any great focus or debate on this charter renewal. The new PM, Andy Burnham, as a former culture minister, may be more invested and has increased the number of ministers at DCMS from four to seven, but he has yet to address charter renewal publicly in any depth.
Within the BBC, the hope is that recent crises may have actually endeared it to the public. In November 2025, President Trump announced that he would be suing the BBC for $10bn over an allegedly misleading Panorama documentary. For some liberal critics of the BBC, it was a reminder of where their loyalties lay. The timing of the lawsuit was “quite fortuitous, if it had to happen”, said Steve Barnett, a media academic advising the select committee on this charter process.
More surprisingly, senior figures at DCMS seem to believe that current rounds of job cuts – which will eventually amount to one in 10 of the BBC’s workforce – can be spun in the BBC’s favour. Lisa Nandy would not speak to me for this article, but Ian Murray, the DCMS junior minister working on charter renewal, told me he hoped the news of the cuts would show the public “the consequences of an inadequately funded BBC. It’s a really good way of the public realising that the BBC is something that they quite value.”
We are now waiting for the government’s white paper, due “in the autumn”, which in Westminster-speak could mean any time before the end of the year. After this, the final charter will be drafted, along with a framework agreement, which lays out what the charter might mean in practice. Parliament can debate the white paper and draft charter, but its approval isn’t required. The charter is signed off by the privy council, an unelected body of royal advisers also responsible for handing out honours and declaring war. The author Tom Mills notes in The BBC: Myth of a Public Service that “in this sense, [the BBC] is not even formally accountable to parliament, but to the crown”.
Where will Nandy land? Despite a somewhat lacklustre start to what Chivers called the “tiny, crappy” public consultation process, many of those I’ve spoken to have been increasingly impressed by her approach. Over email, the deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, told me he has found meetings with DCMS over the summer “very constructive … It’s clear to me they understand the importance of this moment for the BBC.” Tony Hall, the former director general, told me: “Nandy has been really interesting and thoughtful on the BBC. All her instincts are in the right direction.”
So far, Nandy has confirmed that she will seek to end political appointments to the BBC, and that she will try to establish a permanent charter. Both moves seem designed to defend the BBC from political opposition – from a future Reform government, say – but a permanent charter would still involve government reviews at set intervals, through a process that, bar the threat of extinction, sounds very similar to the current one. (Chivers, who wrote his PhD on the last charter, described the change to me as “a bit of window dressing”.)
The big unknown is the funding. Of the available options, a serious move towards advertising seems unlikely. Even Margaret Thatcher failed on this front. The committee she set up to explore this option found that advertising would slash the income of other channels, and “reduce consumer choice and welfare”. A 2024 plan to run adverts on BBC podcasts on third-party platforms was scrapped after a backlash from the audio industry. DCMS also seems to have backed away from the subscription-based approaches floated in the green paper, for fear that it would create a “two-tier” BBC.
That leaves a reformed licence fee model. Nandy and the BBC’s leadership have emphasised the gap between the 94% of adults using it every month, and the 80% of households who currently pay the licence fee. Closing that gap would seem an obvious way to improve the financial situation, perhaps by extending the licence fee to activities for which it’s not currently required, such as reading the BBC’s websites or listening to its radio and podcasts.
But there is another problem quietly eating away at the BBC, one that its defenders are less willing to highlight. Amid the rise of streamers and limitless online content, there has been an unprecedented decline in audience figures. In 2020, 91% of adults used the BBC every week; the weekly figure has now fallen to 84%. This suggests that almost all weekly users of the BBC are already paying the licence fee. It also means that the government needs to somehow convince the public that paying for the BBC isn’t an equation of money paid, media consumed. Once the BBC is no longer “universal”, the licence fee becomes harder and harder to defend.
In the past few months, ministers and BBC executives have begun emphasising the importance of the BBC to the UK’s “sovereignty”, and its potential uses in standing up to big tech. Brittin, the new director general, told the select committee: “The BBC is the biggest funder of original British content today; people around the world want that content and want those values, but we are being disrupted by a small number of very big and very powerful tech players.” Seaton, the BBC’s historian, believes that taking on the tech giants should be central to its future role: “The world’s five, six richest men own the only ways we can communicate. But then there is the BBC.”
It’s a savvy way to argue that the BBC benefits everyone, whether they use it or not – and to lay the groundwork for a licence fee paid by more people. The concept of sovereignty will probably appear in the charter in some form. But to work, it will need to be matched with specifics. In the 2017 charter, Whittingdale added the word “distinctive” to the description in the charter of the kinds of output the BBC was legally obliged to produce – to “send the message that it must look different to commercial broadcasters”. But by his own admission, it had little effect. It is possible to change the nuts and bolts of the BBC through the charter; attempts to transform it via buzzwords are doomed to fail.
In 1953, Lord Simon of Wythenshawe, who had been BBC chair for five years, summed up the strange paradox of the charter. He dismissed it as a long, “almost bewilderingly vague” document “containing masses of legalistic material which is of no use to any governor in normal times”. And yet, he continued, it has just about worked: “The intentions of successive governments have been well understood by the BBC”, while the BBC has maintained something close to “full freedom and responsibility for their work”.
At times, against the odds, the charter renewal process has set the BBC on the right path towards the future. In the 1940s, parts of the industry were adamant that TV would never take off as home entertainment, and would instead be shown in cinemas. And yet when it came to the BBC’s next charter in 1947, the government, having convened a committee to look into the question, took a swing on home television, introduced a new TV licence fee, and allowed the BBC to borrow money to set up new transmitters. It was right.
In the 1990s, the charter pulled off another reversal in the BBC’s fortunes. The corporation was facing problems it would recognise today. It had just emerged from a fight with a Tory government, only to face the issue of declining audiences. Technology journalist John Naughton wrote a gloomy piece for the London Review of Books in 1992, predicting that BBC TV audience share would drop to 20% by 2010, making a universal licence fee impossible to defend. The green paper for the 1997 charter had just been released, and looked, he said, “suspiciously like a plan for an organised retreat”.
But when the 1997 charter emerged from its secretive drafting process, it was far from a retreat: it paved the way for BBC Online, the corporation’s first network of websites, by allowing licence fee money to be spent on digital output for the first time. That charter prevented the BBC from being left behind by the digital age. By 2005, the fall in overall audience reach had halted. Even predictions of the decline in TV audiences proved pessimistic: in 2010, BBC’s share still stood at 33%.
This strange, flawed process seems to have survived for a century not because it is perfect, or even particularly good, but because no one has yet come up with something better. So again and again, hundreds of thousands of people try to conjure up the BBC they want; one which won’t make the same mistakes, which will reflect the version of Britain that they want to see. And every time the BBC reappears, as though its existence were never in doubt.
“This will be the most important charter negotiation in the history of the BBC,” John Shield, a former director of communications at the BBC, told me. “But then, they always are.”

Enact Trew’s law to automatically review ‘bent copper’ convictions, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:14 UTC
13:00:14 KST

Convictions that imprisoned police officers were involved in obtaining should be automatically reviewed to correct miscarriages of justice such as those perpetrated by the corrupt and racist officer DS Derek Ridgewell, a report says.
The proposed Trew’s law, named after Winston Trew – who was framed by Ridgewell and spent decades fighting to clear his name – would trigger an immediate, independent review of past cases linked to any jailed officer in England and Wales.
Ridgewell’s story has been described as “the real Line of Duty”, with reference to the BBC show about “bent coppers”. Since 2018, 13 victims of Ridgewell, including the Oval Four and members of the Stockwell Six had their convictions quashed. A 14th case involving the British Transport Police (BTP) officer was referred to the court of appeal in February.
Trew, who is working on the campaign for a new law with the miscarriages of justice charity Appeal, said: “When my convictions were finally quashed in 2019, it came after nearly 50 years of fighting to clear my name. No one should have to spend decades uncovering the truth about police wrongdoing. Justice shouldn’t depend on luck, or on victims fighting for years to expose miscarriages of justice. Trew’s law would place responsibility where it belongs: with the state.”
In 1980, Ridgewell was jailed for seven years for stealing mailbags worth £364,000, but an immediate review of his past cases was not initiated. In 2024, Lucy D’Orsi, chief constable of BTP, called the force’s failure to do so “simply inexcusable”.
Dr Joanna Gilmore, from the University of York, which produced the report with Appeal, said that despite D’Orsi’s apology “when we began researching this issue, we were struck by how little exists in law today to prevent history from repeating itself”.
She added: “In many of the cases we examined, judges noted in sentencing remarks how officers had used their police position to facilitate serious offending – and yet the decision to review their past cases remains discretionary, opaque, and unpredictable.”
CPS guidance recognises that a review may be required where a witness, including a police officer, is later “discredited” – but does not mandate it.
The researchers found that between 2023 and 2026, at least 64 current or former police officers received immediate custodial sentences for offences including serious dishonesty, physical and sexual violence, and abuse of position.
They also discovered that there was no central system to record when police officers received custodial sentences, nor whether their past cases were reviewed and, if so, the outcomes.
Dr Mattia Pinto, from the University of York, said: “Even today it is far too common for the lives of innocent people to be completely ruined by convictions based on unchecked evidence from corrupt officers.”
A triage process would focus on cases where the officer’s integrity was central to the conviction, while excluding purely administrative or peripheral involvement.
As well as triggering an immediate review, Trew’s law would require affected individuals to be notified and given disclosure where a material risk to conviction safety was identified, to enable timely access to legal advice.
Materiality includes providing witness evidence, preparing key investigative documents, or handling exhibits and disclosure.
Matt Foot, co-director of Appeal, said: “The criminal justice system takes far too long to correct miscarriages of justice. In the case of the victims of DS Ridgewell and his squads, it has taken an eternity. I believe there are many more victims out there still. It’s high time for Trew’s law so that officers that are doing harm who are imprisoned have their files investigated immediately to stop delay for those that have suffered enough.”
The campaign launch will be held in south London on Thursday night at Lambeth town hall, where an event was held in 1973 protesting against the imprisonment of the Oval Four. They were beaten up and framed for attempted theft and assaulting the police on the London Underground.
The Ministry of Justice has been approached for comment.

‘They poison the population’: Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:14 UTC
13:00:14 KST

Not far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know about Islam.
For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – or Fråga en Muslim – campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back.
With the help of dozens of volunteers from the Ahmadi Muslim community, the campaign had called in at more than 150 farmers markets, squares and city centres, inviting strangers to strike up a conversation in hopes of dispelling myths and shedding light on Islam.
“We have some radical parties and people are genuinely afraid about Islam,” said Virk. “Sometimes people get very rude. But most people in Sweden are lovely, friendly and interested – they want to learn more.”
Ahead of Sweden’s general election on Sunday, polls show the centre-left opposition has a narrow lead, suggesting that the rightwing minority-run coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats could be ousted.
Such a result would not only be significant for the Scandinavian country; it could also reassure mainstream voters across Europe that far-right forces such as the Sweden Democrats or Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) – triumphant after its best showing in a state election last weekend – are not inevitably on the rise.
But even so, the Swedish polls have narrowed slightly in recent weeks, making many nervous, particularly as the right-leaning ruling coalition has for the first time said it would offer ministerial posts to the far right if it wins. Those who have borne the brunt of the far right’s time propping up the government worry that Sweden, long held up as a leading light when it comes to equality and freedom, may have been irrevocably changed, regardless of what happens on Sunday.
“It’s a kind of Pandora’s box that has been opened,” said Munir Niazi, who has long worked with Virk on the Ask-a-Muslim campaign.
During the government of the centre-right prime minister Ulf Kristersson, the far-right Sweden Democrats have used their leverage to steer policies on migration and crime, seizing on the spotlight to spread rhetoric linking the two and scapegoating migrants, Muslims and other minorities for all that ails the country.
The result had shifted Sweden’s national conversation to the right, said Niazi. “In the past four years, the biggest opposition party, the Social Democrats, have slowly adopted and even voted with the right wing on migration, on crime. In the near future, at least, we don’t see the country going back to the policies of the 80s and 90s.”
Virk nodded in agreement. “We see, unfortunately, that everybody plays the anti-Islam card when they need it.”
The repercussions have been felt widely. Last year, a gunman killed 10 people in the Swedish city of Örebro, most of whom had an immigrant background. Across Sweden, mosques have regularly been vandalised and in 2023 the country grappled with a spate of protests in which copies of the Qur’an were burned or otherwise damaged.
Speaking to commuters in Malmö making their way through Hyllie station, many said the politics had started to feel deeply personal, as though their existence in Sweden was a political battleground.
“When the far right talk about my religion and my hijab, it feels like they’re talking about an animal,” said one nurse, 46, who asked not to be named.
Originally from Lebanon, she had settled in Sweden in 1999. “The older people in the hospital say that myself and other immigrants have helped to build Sweden – why doesn’t the far right see this?”
Sitting in a nearby park, Onyango, 42, said the atmosphere in Sweden had become “horrible” for migrants amid the far right’s steady increase in influence. “I feel like they poison the population,” he said. “They’ve created an environment where if you’re not a Swede, you are scared.”
The hostile rhetoric, coupled with efforts by the government to tighten the rules around migration, had left the Kenyan national devising a backup plan despite nine years spent in the country and a good job working with supply chains. “You start thinking maybe I need to have an apartment in Kenya and set aside some money, just in case,” he said.
Sitting next to him, his friend Waithira, 30, nodded in agreement. “Before you wanted to invest here, buy an apartment here, start a business. But now you start thinking twice,” she said. “We don’t know what the future holds, but it’s a bit less attractive than before.”
In the southern reaches of Stockholm’s Södermalm district, Jonna Mannberg and Isaac Kuehnle-Nelson recalled how in 2015, about 1,700 people from across the country spontaneously turned up at the city’s central station, eager to welcome and help settle Syrian and Afghan asylum seekers as they arrived.
In the 11 years since, the initiative, formalised into Refugees Welcome Stockholm, had unwittingly become a shorthand for the changes sweeping Sweden. “We’ve gone from being an organisation that was at the forefront of public political dialogue in Sweden to being a smaller organisation where our funding and ability to reach out have shrunk significantly,” said Kuehnle-Nelson.
They had watched as policy stances once reserved for the far right became mainstream, from a slashing of refugee quotas from 5,000 to 900 people a year, to allowing residency permits to be revoked over the vaguely defined criteria of “bad behaviour”.
“In 2015, people were met with open arms. We had the prime minister say: ‘My Europe doesn’t build walls,’” said Mannberg. “But the harsh reality is that we still have the same people that we were dealing with in 2015. We’re still with them in 2026 and they have not received legal status yet.”
The psychological toll was laid bare during a recent programming course for young, undocumented asylum seekers. “There were days when many were unable to attend because they couldn’t get out of bed,” she said. “To have physically healthy, 20-year-old guys who have been so pushed down by life that they were unable to leave their beds, unable to see any future for themselves, that’s a really hard thing.”
Among those caught up in the crackdown on asylum seekers was an undocumented 14-year-old who, despite being born in Sweden, was facing deportation to Armenia, along with his single-parent mother and his younger brother. “It’s like hell. I’ve been here my whole life,” he told the Guardian. “I feel Swedish.”
His parents had come to Sweden as political asylum claimants, but their separation resulted in the claim becoming mired in bureaucracy. While there had been a visa category that might have given the family another chance of continuing the lives they had built in Sweden, it was scrapped recently by the rightwing government.
Instead, the order looms over them, clouding the life of a child who had sung in a church choir and dreamed of a future as a civil engineer in Sweden. “It feels horrible,” he said, pointing out that he had never been to Armenia, did not speak the language and was terrified about the possibility of being forced to complete its mandatory military service.
The changes to immigration policy, including recently introduced rules barring most asylum seekers from accessing permanent residency, were an example of how the political conversation in Sweden had been transformed by the far right’s time as power-brokers, said journalist Bilan Osman.
“There’s a lot of proposals in Swedish politics today that we couldn’t even imagine 10 years ago,” she said, citing the tens of thousands of euros being offered to migrants to return home as an example. “People would have said: ‘You’re a lunatic.’ Now it’s like: ‘Let’s discuss it.’”
Osman had long researched rightwing extremism, tracking the movement as they created their own media outlets capable of reaching new audiences. What emerged was a steady normalisation of their discourse, blaming migrants and minorities for Sweden’s social and economic ills, while the fallout of the country’s soaring inequality levels was largely overlooked.
The resulting rhetoric had pushed some to the margins, recasting Sweden as a place where some belonged and others were made to feel as though they did not. It was a marked shift that would probably have long-lasting consequences, she said, citing Swedish Muslims, who make up an estimated 8% of the population, as an example.
“I think we are at a breaking point right now in Sweden, where the main question is: ‘Is there a future for Muslims in this country?’” said Osman. “If we continue to have these kinds of discussions, I think a lot of Muslims will feel that there is not a future here. And that’s sad.”

August 2026 was world’s joint hottest month on record, according to Copernicus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:01 UTC
13:00:01 KST

The global average air temperature in August was 1.65°C above the pre-industrial reference value. With prolonged and early heatwaves, Western Europe broke the summer temperature record set in 2003.
August was the hottest month on record, tied with July 2023, according to data published on Thursday by the European climate observatory Copernicus.
Last month, the global average air temperature reached 16.96°C, which is 1.65°C higher than the pre-industrial reference period of 1850–1900. August was the first month since November 2025 to exceed 1.5°C, the limit set by the Paris Agreement on climate change.
The extra-polar oceans also broke a record for their average temperature last month, due to global warming, Copernicus points out. The average temperature reached 21.07°C, the highest ever recorded for August, surpassing the record set in 2023.
"August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record. It was both the warmest August and the warmest month ever recorded", declared Samantha Burgess, Strategic Lead for Climate at ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).
"These observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world", she added.
Hottest summer ever in Western Europe
For the European continent specifically, these figures mark the end of the hottest summer ever recorded in Western Europe, with prolonged, intense and early heatwaves beginning as early as May. For the region, the summer of 2026 broke the record set during the same period in 2003.
In August this year, the average temperature reached 20.26°C over European land, making last month the fourth-warmest August on record, according to Copernicus.
The continent also suffered from widespread drought, with exceptionally low water levels in rivers such as the Rhine, the Danube, the Vistula, the Rhône and the Po. The drier-than-average conditions also led to numerous wildfires in several regions across Europe.
"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling", declared, Simon Stiell, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary.
"Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records", Stiell added.
For the UN Climate Change Executive Secretary the solution to preventing new temperature records from being set is clear: "a faster shift to clean energy."

Quiet layoffs, loud consequences: The hidden costs of a job redundancy in Denmark

Oslo Architecture City Guide: 12 Buildings Contrasting Historic and Contemporary Design
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Oslo is the capital of Norway as well as its largest city, serving as the country's political, economic, and cultural center. Nestled at the head of the Oslofjord and surrounded by forested hills, it's home to roughly 700,000 people in the city, with over a million living in the greater metropolitan area. Founded around a thousand years ago, Oslo has a long history as a trading post and administrative seat. However, much of its modern character was shaped after a major fire in the seventeenth century led to a full rebuilding under Danish rule, when it was briefly renamed Christiania. Today it consistently ranks among the world's most livable cities, prized for its blend of urban life and easy access to nature.
At the same time, Oslo is something of an open-air showcase for contemporary architectural design layered atop older civic landmarks. The Oslo Opera House, for example, features a sloping white marble roof that visitors can walk right up onto and has become a defining symbol of the city's ambition. Nearby, the Barcode district's row of high-rises contrasts with the nineteenth-century Royal Palace and the Oslo City Hall, itself an example of functionalist architecture. Add to this the pedestrian street around Norway's Royal Palace and the Munch Museum along the waterfront, and the overall atmosphere is a city that feels nature-adjacent, yet it also gives space for architectural statements and contemporary city life.

US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:59:55 UTC
12:59:55 KST

Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as “radical” and defended his unpopular war in Iran.
The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. But it laid bare the extent of the Republicans’ concern about their prospects in the pivotal November elections.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour long speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event.
Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”
The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.
Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good.
“If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said.
The buildup to the midterm convention had somewhat of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before the Republican National Committee announced that he would deliver the keynote on Wednesday, and instead give closing remarks on Thursday after his vice-president JD Vance speaks.
Trump made several references to the war in Iran, warning Tehran “not to get cute” or the US “will have to hit them very hard”. But he also appeared to acknowledge the economic pain caused by the soaring price of oil. Trump re-enacted the way he told his economic advisors that the US needed to start the conflict because Iran was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. “I hate to do this to you,” he said he told them, noting the economy had been doing well.
At the convention center, there were signs of middling enthusiasm among the rank and file.
Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long queues to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech.
Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full.
“Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump declared. This was not observed by Guardian reporters.
The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention underway, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page.
Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night, cracking jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year.
“He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.”
Trump spent several minutes attacking Democrats, including Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, who Trump mocked as a “weird looking dude”; the former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is now running for Senate; and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan.
In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”.
“Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said.
The Republicans’ unusual midterm convention features 12 hours of programming across two nights. On Wednesday, the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda.
Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight.
Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10.
Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump.
“One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.”
Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches.
Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much briefer.
“I gave you a lot of material,” he said, capping his remarks on Wednesday, before pleading one more time with voters to “please pretend that I’m running”.

Trump promises US$5,000 to every adult American if they vote Republican – video
US President Donald Trump has said he will pay every adult American US$5,000 if the Republican Party retains control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate following the midterm elections in November.
Source: Trump during a speech at the Republican Party convention in Dallas, Texas
Quote: "If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the US Senate, both of them, because of our tremendous economic success […] I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen of the United States of America for US$5,000."
Details: Trump explained that this would be "very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders".
The president added that the only condition would be that the money must be spent exclusively within the United States.
"We don't want you going to Canada," he said.
This is likely the first time in US history that a president has resorted to openly buying voters during an election campaign.
In addition, the source of funding, the mechanisms for monitoring how the money would be spent and the overall legality of such payments remain unclear.
In 2025, the US adult population stood at around 267 million, meaning the total cost of the payments would exceed US$1.3 trillion.
It is also notable that Trump is promising to hand out trillions of dollars at a time when, during his presidency, US national debt has reached its highest level in history, exceeding US$40 trillion.
During his speech, Trump said a Republican defeat in November would mean Americans would "lose your border, lose your tax cuts, lose your safety and security".
"You'll be going through hell just like you did just two years ago," the US president added.
Trump claimed that the US had been "the laughing stock all over the world", but that no one was laughing at the country anymore.
This latest populist initiative comes amid discouraging opinion polls for the White House, with Democrats holding a solid lead ahead of the elections.
Trump has made no secret of his concern about a possible election defeat. On 21 August, at a rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, Trump told supporters that he expected to be impeached if Republicans lost their majority in Congress.
"[If we lose the midterms] I'm going to be impeached," Trump said at the time.

Pakistan's Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan reaffirmed Islamabad's commitment to the Belt and Road Initiative on Thursday, saying the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor had turned his country into a major regional connectivity hub linking landlocked Central Asia and western China to warm-water ports.
Speaking at the Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong, Khan said deeper collaboration in energy, infrastructure and industrialisation in the corridor, a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), was reshaping Pakistan's economic landscape.
He described the initiative as a transformative vision of a global community with a shared future.
"The Belt and Road Initiative represents a transformative vision of a global community with a shared future and over the past decade has inspired nations to accelerate development, unlock economic opportunity and deepen cultural ties," Khan said during a special address at the summit.
He said regional cooperation was evolving from transport routes towards integrated value chains and that Pakistan was positioning itself as a link between west, central and east Asia.
He cited the Trans-Afghan Railway Initiative and expanded rail and road linkages with China as steps towards making the country the shortest viable route for trade with Central Asia while also opening up markets among the 1.5 billion people in African states.
Khan said Pakistan's economic strategy rested on export-led growth, industrial modernisation and deeper integration into global supply chains.
He noted the country's vast agricultural potential, mineral wealth – from copper to gold and critical minerals – and a young, growing population as key areas for Belt and Road Initiative partnership.
Khan also extended an invitation to Chief Executive John Lee to visit Pakistan, praising his leadership and Hong Kong's initiative in offering around 150 scholarships to students from Belt and Road partner countries.
"Building on BRI's green agenda, we seek deeper cooperation with partners like Hong Kong on climate adaptation and sustainable growth. Our shared future also rests on people-to-people ties," he said.

DALLAS /Texas/, September 10. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) that was signed with Iran in 2015 to settle the problem of the Iranian nuclear program as "one of the worst deals in the history."
"Barack Hussein Obama (the 44th US President - TASS) made a deal, JCPOA. One of the worst deals in the history. It was a road to a nuclear weapon for Iran," he told the Republican midterm convention in Texas.
Germany and five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, or the United Kingdom, China, Russia, the United States, and France signed the JCPOA, known as the Iran nuclear deal, with Iran in 2015, putting an end to a long-running standoff about Iran’s alleged development of nuclear weapons. However, during his first presidential term, Trump withdrew from the deal in 2018 and re-imposed all the anti-Iranian sanctions after they began to be lifted under the deal.
"If I didn't cancel the JCPOA, and if we didn't hit them with our beautiful B2 bombers (against Iranian nuclear sites in Isfahan, Nataz, and Fordow - TASS), they would have a nuclear weapon right now," Trump said, adding that the conflict with Iran would end shortly after the midterm elections. According to Trump, the Iranians "want a deal desperately."
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC expanded its dominance of the global foundry market in the second quarter, with market share reaching a record 72.5%.
Combined revenue from the top 10 foundries approached NT$1.68 trillion (US$53.49 billion), up 11.5% from the previous quarter and another record high, per TrendForce. Samsung Electronics’ market share fell from 6.5% to 5.9%.
TrendForce said demand for advanced chips used in AI and high-performance computing remained stronger than supply, while demand for AI-related peripheral chips, including power management integrated circuits and power discretes, also grew. Continued early stocking by consumer electronics supply chains, including televisions, PCs, and laptops, also tightened capacity for some mature processes.
The research firm expects foundry revenue to rise further in the third quarter as consumer IC designers maintain steady wafer starts amid concerns that mature-process capacity could remain constrained and wafer prices may increase. Flagship smartphone production is entering its stocking cycle, while production of next-generation AI and high-performance computing platforms is beginning to ramp up.
Trailing TSMC and Samsung were China’s Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. (SMIC) at 5.4% and Taiwan's United Microelectronics Corp. (UMC) at 3.9%, ranking third and fourth, respectively. TSMC’s revenue rose 12.1% quarter over quarter to nearly NT$1.27 trillion, while Samsung’s edged up 1.8% to NT$102.66 billion.
SMIC’s revenue surged 20% quarter over quarter to more than NT$94.47 billion. UMC’s revenue rose 12.7% to nearly NT$68.65 billion.

Zverev storms into semi-finals despite late bedtime
- Published
Alexander Zverev booked his place in the US Open semi-finals with a commanding victory over Botic van de Zandschulp - despite staying up until 3:30am to watch Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz's blockbuster quarter-final.
The top seed swept aside the Dutchman with a 6-2 7-5 6-1 win in the night session on Arthur Ashe Stadium.
Following his victory, Zverev revealed he had stayed up to watch Shelton's win over defending champion Alcaraz in a match that ended at 03:34 local time on Wednesday - the latest finish in the tournament's history.
"I watched Shelton-Alcaraz until 3.30am last night," Zverev said.
"I did not go to bed, I was up late, I was watching TV because I was sleeping in until 1pm anyway."
The 29-year-old has had plenty of his own late-night finishes at this year's tournament, with his opening three matches ending at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.
Bidding to reach a third successive Grand Slam final, Zverev will face Russian Karen Khachanov, who advanced after Alexander Blockx retired trailing 6-2 7-5 3-2.
With his win over Van de Zandschulp, Zverev has reached all four Grand Slam semi-finals in a single season for the first time in his career.
"I think the more often that you get to that stage, the more normal it becomes, which is something that you should never take for granted," said Zverev, who ended his wait for a maiden major at this year's French Open.
"I think it's a very special feeling when it becomes normality."

Blockx's dream run in New York ended in cruel fashion earlier on Wednesday as the Belgian was forced to retire after suffering a series of injuries in his quarter-final against Khachanov.

"I think today my body just gave up," said Blockx, who had come close to retiring from his fourth-round win against Francisco Cerundolo with a rib injury.

A former world number eight, a disappointing run of results over the past few months have resulted in Khachanov's ranking dipping to 50 and he is unseeded at a major for the first time since 2018.
The 30-year-old said he will have to come up with his "best form" to defeat Zverev and reach his first major final.
"He's been in the top five for so many years. This year he did also step forward. He won his first Grand Slam, played the final in Wimbledon, as well. He's coming up really in hot form," Khachanov said.
Zverev, meanwhile, says he will have to be wary of his opponent and his extensive knowledge of the game.
"We call him [Khachanov] 'The Professor', actually, because he knows everything about tennis, and he knows every single string tension, knows what everybody does, so that's quite fun," Zverev said.

Jewish groups launch 'Bill of Rights' to protect students from antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:48:17 UTC
12:48:17 KST

A coalition of major American Jewish organizations has released the Jewish Students’ Bill of Rights, a framework calling on schools and districts nationwide to adopt baseline standards to protect Jewish students from discrimination, bullying, and hate.
The initiative was launched by the Jewish Federations of North America, the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), the American Jewish Committee (AJC), the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, and StandWithUs.
The coalition is urging school administrators to implement the guidelines to ensure safe, inclusive learning environments for every student.
The framework arrives as educational institutions grapple with persistent hostility. According to data from the ADL’s Audit of Antisemitic Incidents, nationwide figures fell by approximately one-third over the course of last year.
However, hostile episodes inside non-Jewish elementary and secondary schools failed to follow that downward trajectory, hovering near flat with 825 reported cases compared to 860 the previous year. Bridging that gap is the core objective behind the newly introduced Jewish Students’ Bill of Rights.
The Jewish Students Bill of Rights
To confront these challenges, the bill of rights calls for six core standards for schools and districts to adopt.
First, schools must ensure that staff and administrators are fully equipped to identify modern forms of antisemitism.
Second, institutions need to maintain clear, transparent reporting processes that treat antisemitic incidents with the same gravity and accountability as any other hate or bias incident.
Third, instructional materials covering Jewish culture, history, the Holocaust, antisemitism, and Israel must be accurate and representative.
Fourth, schools should treat religious observances as excused absences and avoid scheduling major events on widely celebrated Jewish holidays.
Fifth, the guidelines call for protecting Jewish students’ rights to freely express their identity and connection to Israel without facing bullying, religious coercion, or pressure to distance themselves.
Finally, educators and curricula must present contested political issues in a balanced manner rather than using classrooms to promote specific ideological agendas.
The coalition emphasizes that Jewish Federations branches, the AJC’s Center for Education Advocacy, the ADL, and the StandWithUs K-12 Fairness Center are available to assist school leaders, policymakers, and families with implementation, resources, and policy guidance.

Israel’s education system is failing the students who will shape its future - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:47:50 UTC
12:47:50 KST

Anyone who has lived in Israel over the past few years can attest to the constant volatility, uncertainty, and stress that we have been living through.
We are in constant survival mode, especially since October 7, 2023, and that state of being can crack even the best of us. With budgets logically earmarked in a top-heavy fashion toward defense and security, other vital resources and issues are suffering from a lack of attention and proper budgeting.
Yet we must promote, finance, and treat education as if Israel were in the middle of a peaceful oasis. It’s the primary realm, besides security, that ensures our future. Based on results published this week, we’re failing in education security.
Israel suffered a dramatic collapse in the 2025 PISA exam, which assesses 15-year-old students’ performance in mathematics, reading, and science. In all three subjects, Israel recorded its lowest-ever scores, significantly below those in the previous exam, held in 2022.
Israel’s average score across the three subjects fell by 29 points, the second-sharpest decline among the 75 countries and economies tested, after Latvia.
Israel’s divided school system is failing its future
Israel’s mathematics score fell to 433 points, down 25 points from 458 in 2022, the second-sharpest decline worldwide after Malta. Israel’s science score fell to 442 points, down 23 points from 465 in 2022 and the third-sharpest decline worldwide.
The steepest decline was in reading. Israel’s score fell to 436 points, down 38 points from 474 in 2022 and the second-sharpest decline worldwide, after Latvia.
Of course, those results must be seen in the context of the upheaval the country – and the nation’s students – have faced over the last three years. Education Minister Yoav Kisch did just that, attempting to put a positive spin on the results.
“After nearly a year and a half of war, the evacuation of communities, and deep disruptions to the continuity of learning, I believe these results demonstrate the extraordinary resilience of Israel’s education system,” Kisch said. “Israel maintained its ranking in reading and science compared with 2018, and in math it dropped just one place.”
The Education Ministry also attributed the low scores to the chaotic disruptions to regular learning schedules forced on the education system by the war.
But as valid as war excuses may be, there’s an underlying factor to the scores that can’t be ignored. The education system desperately needs reform.
In 2025, 23% of all first-graders were Arabic speakers, and 25% were haredim (ultra-Orthodox). Israel’s Arabic-speaking students scored below many Third World countries – including below six of the seven Arab countries that participated in the PISA exam. Nearly all of the haredi students in Israel do not even study the material and, as a result, are not even tested.
According to Prof. Dan Ben-David, president and founder of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research, the bottom line is that about half of Israel’s children – among them haredim, Arab Israelis, and those living in Israel’s geographic and socioeconomic peripheries – are receiving a third-world level education.
“And as if that were not enough, these children belong to the fastest-growing segments of the population. When they eventually constitute half, and later a majority, of Israel’s adult population, they will not be able to maintain a first-world economy,” Ben-David told The Jerusalem Post.
Ben-David’s solution is to dismantle the four separate education streams that currently function in Israel (state, state religious, haredi, and Arab) and replace them with a new, single education system for all.
“The basic tenets of such an overhaul need to include a significant upgrade of the compulsory, identical, core curriculum (allowing the remaining curriculum to reflect local parental preferences). Funding should be only for fully compliant schools, with complete cessation of funding for all others,” he proposed.
Ben-David’s proposal is worth considering, but even if it’s too ambitious, education must take a prominent spot at the table of any future government.
As we head to next month’s election, every party will try to convince the electorate that it has the answer to the country’s pressing issues. They’ll talk about security and the economy. But just as important is what their plans are for the future.
Just as defense is paramount to securing a thriving future for Israel, education is vital to the well-being and continued success of the Jewish state. Brushing the issue aside because we’re fighting for our survival is not an option.

Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
September 10, 2026
US President Donald Trump made a pitch to voters on Wednesday: a $5,000 (€4,300) "dividend" for every American adult if the Republican Party keeps control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.
"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them ... because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," Trump said at the Republican midterm convention on Wednesday.
"The only caveat we have is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America," he added. "We don't want you going to Canada spending the money, we don't want you going to China or Germany."
The president did not say how he would finance the measure, nor how the government would track where citizens spend the funds. He had previously promised citizens $2,000 checks from tariff revenues that have so far not materialized.
What else did Trump talk about?
Trump made the announcement as the two-day event kicked off in Dallas, Texas.
In a wide-ranging speech, Trump talked up some of the biggest — and most divisive — aspects of his second term in office, including the crackdown on immigration, the war in Iran, tariffs and subsequent economic retaliation, the White House ballroom, and restrictions on transgender people.
The president told voters to "pretend” that he's on the ballot at the elections that will see new representatives and senators elected in November.
His attempts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario after America were met with rapturous applause. Later, he riffed on renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait."
Who else was at the Republican convention?
Other speakers focused less on the Trump administration's track record and instead attacked Democrats as "evil," "communists" and "socialists."
Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race against rising Democratic challenger James Talarico, who represents a younger and more progressive wing of that party.
Another Republican senator, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, was introduced by his Democratic counterpart, John Fetterman, in an unusual move.
Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with Democratic Party positions in recent years, introduced the Republican as his "great friend" and pledged to work with Trump to protect the state's steel industry.
Conservative activists were also in attendance.
The Associated Press spotted Stewart Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers extremist group. Rhodes had been sentenced to 18 years in prison for his role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the US Capitol, but later benefited from Trump's sweeping clemency after he returned to office.
Trump also praised Erika Kirk for being in attendance on the eve of the one-year anniversary of the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk.
Vice President JD Vance received a brief shoutout near the end of the speech.
